## Introduction

Industry 4.0 denotes the fusion of cyber-physical systems, the Internet of Things, Artificial Intelligence and Big Data analytics into production, so that machines self-monitor, communicate and decide in real time. Where Industry 3.0 automated individual machines through electronics and computing, Industry 4.0 networks the entire value chain into a single intelligent ecosystem. For India — where manufacturing is targeted to reach 25% of GDP — this transition is central to the National Manufacturing Mission announced in Union Budget 2025-26 (Economic Survey 2025-26).

Cyber-Physical/AI (2011-)) with a rising arrow labelled "human control > machine autonomy".

## Advantages of Adopting Industry 4.0
- Productivity and predictive maintenance: Sensor-fed analytics shift factories from breakdown repair to failure prediction, cutting unplanned downtime — the single largest cause of capacity loss in Indian heavy industry. The Centre for Industry 4.0 (C4i4) Lab, Pune has compiled over 50 implementable Industry 4.0 use-cases and completed 100+ digital maturity assessments for auto companies (PIB, December 2024).
- Mass customisation and flexibility: Additive manufacturing and digital twins allow small-batch, made-to-order production without retooling costs, which matters for India's export competitiveness in auto components and medical devices.
- Export and scale gains: The PLI Scheme across 14 sectors (outlay 71.97 lakh crore) had drawn 22.0 lakh crore of actual investment by September 2025, yielding incremental production of over 718.70 lakh crore, exports above %8.20 lakh crore and 12.6 lakh jobs (Economic Survey 2025-26) — scale that is only manageable with smartfactory monitoring.
- Sustainability: Smart energy management and real-time process control reduce energy and material intensity, aligning manufacturing with India's net-zero-2070 commitment.
- APinstance: The WEF-Andhra Pradesh Centre for Energy and Cyber Resilience, Amaravati (G.O. issued June 2025; %36 crore for three years) is India's first thematic centre under WEF's Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution network, working on energy transition and AI-led cyber resilience — the third C4IR presence in India after Mumbai and Telangana.

## Challenges in Adoption
- Skill deficit: Industry 4.0 demands data engineers and mechatronics technicians rather than machine operators; PMKVY 4.0 has added AI, robotics and IoT modules, but the retraining pipeline lags factory-floor demand.
- MSME capital constraint: MSMEs form the bulk of manufacturing units and lack the patient capital for sensor retrofitting; the 71 lakh crore RDI Scheme (Cabinet approval July 2025; TDB and BIRAC notified as Second-Level Fund Managers, PIB March 2026) is the first serious answer to this financing gap.
- Cyber vulnerability: Connecting operational technology to the internet exposes

plants to ransomware; CERT-In advisories on industrial control systems underline that a single intrusion can halt an entire networked line.

- Interoperability and infrastructure: Legacy machines, absent common data standards and uneven 5G coverage in industrial clusters fragment the ecosystem — which is why C4i4 developed the Industry 4.0 Maturity Model (I4MM) tailored to Indian firms.

## Conclusion

Industry 4.0 is less a technology purchase than a systemic re-engineering of how Indian factories sense, decide and learn. The enabling architecture is now in place — SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, PLI, the India Semiconductor Mission and the National Manufacturing Mission. What will determine outcomes is whether MSMEs, which supply the bulk of value-chain components, are financed and skilled into the transition rather than displaced by it.

## Value addition

- IndiaAI Mission (MeitY): compute, datasets and application pillars — the AI backbone for smart manufacturing.
- Startup ecosystem: DPIIT-recognised startups rose from about 500 in 2016 to over 2 lakh in 2025 (Economic Survey 2025-26), a key supplier base for industrial IoT solutions.
- Concept to quote: WEF "Lighthouse Factories" — plants demonstrating measurable CO, and water reductions through predictive analytics and IoT.

## Introduction

Technology reaches society through three sequential but distinct processes: development (indigenous creation of new knowledge), transfer (acquisition and absorption of technology from external or public sources), and diffusion (its spread to mass users).

India's strategy has evolved from a state-led model built on CSIR, DRDO, ISRO and DAE, to a mixed model in which digital public infrastructure and private capital drive the last two stages. The Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF Act, 2023) is the current pivot of this architecture.

## Development Transfer Diffusion

CSIR, DRDO, ISRO, BARC FDI, JVs, licensing Digital Public Infrastructure

National Missions DRDO TDF, iDEX Extension & skilling

ANRF + RDI Fund IN-SPACe, NSIL Standards & regulation

## Technology Development
- Public R&D backbone: CSIR (1942), BARC (1954), DRDO (1958) and ISRO (1969) remain the core of strategic self-reliance in atomic energy, defence and space.
- Mission-mode programmes: National Quantum Mission (%6,003.65 crore, 2023-31), National Supercomputing Mission (PARAM series), IndiaAI Mission, and the National Green Hydrogen Mission target frontier areas where India cannot rely on imports.
- Newfinancing architecture: The RDI Scheme — 21 lakh crore over six years with =20,000 crore for FY 2025-26 — provides long-tenure, low- or nil-interest capital for private deep-tech research, with the Technology Development Board and BIRAC notified as the first Second-Level Fund Managers, which issued calls for proposals in February 2026 (PIB, March 2026). This addresses the "patient capital" gap that no earlier scheme did.

2. Technology Transfer

- Defence: DRDO's Technology Development Fund and iDEX support MSMEs and startups to absorb and productise defence technologies, with Transfer of Technology to production agencies.
- Space: IN-SPACe and NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) transfer ISRO-developed technologies — including SSLV — to private industry, converting a state monopoly into an industrial base.
- Commercial channels: FDI liberalisation in telecom, defence and renewables, joint ventures and licensing (the Maruti-Suzuki model) remain the largest single conduit of process know-how.
- Public-health flexibility: Compulsory licensing provisions under the Patents Act, 1970 preserve the option of affordable access to patented drugs.
- APinstance: The Amaravati Quantum Valley Tech Park — anchored by an IBM Quantum System Two with a 156-qubit Heron processor, with TCS developing usecases in life sciences, materials and cryptography — is a state-led technology-transfer vehicle bringing frontier hardware and applied know-how into India under the National Quantum Mission.

3. Technology Diffusion

- Digital Public Infrastructure: Aadhaar, UPI, COoWIN and ONDC show that open, interoperable rails diffuse technology faster than any subsidy; cumulative DBT transfers had crossed 743.95 lakh crore by May 2025 (PIB, November 2025).
- Startups as diffusion agents: DPIIT-recognised startups grew from about 500 in 2016 to over 2 lakh in 2025 (Economic Survey 2025-26), carrying technology into agriculture, logistics and health.
- Agriculture and rural reach: eNAM, Soil Health Cards, Kisan Drones and the Namo Drone Didi initiative push technology to the farm gate.
- Standards and safeguards: BIS standards, the National IPR Policy and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 make diffusion safe and trusted.

The cross-cutting weakness: India's Gross Expenditure on R&D has remained around 0.60.7% of GDP, with private industry contributing roughly a third — against over 70% in China, South Korea and the US (DST R&D Statistics). Every limb above is constrained by this.

## Conclusion

India's strengths lie at the two ends — mission-mode public development and populationscale digital diffusion — while the middle, absorption of technology by private industry and MSMEs, remains thin. ANRF and the RDI Fund are designed precisely to thicken this middle. If GERD is raised toward 2% of GDP with private industry as the majority contributor, India can move from being a fast adopter of technology to a source of it — the core requirement of Viksit Bharat@2047.

## Value addition
- ANRF (Act of 2023): Governing Board chaired by the Prime Minister; Executive Council approves RDI guidelines and recommends fund managers; targets 750,000 crore over five years, with the majority expected from non-government sources.
- RDIScheme mechanics: two-tier structure — a Special Purpose Fund within ANRF as custodian, disbursing to Second-Level Fund Managers, who lend to projects at low or nil interest; equity possible for startups; contribution to Deep-Tech Fund of Funds permitted (PIB, July 2025).
- KeyAPscientific institutions to name: Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SHAR), Sriharikota; National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), Gadanki; IIT Tirupati; ISER Tirupati; NIT Andhra Pradesh, Tadepalligudem; AMTZ, Visakhapatnam; Amaravati Quantum Valley Tech Park.
- AP-ISRO linkage: AP's Real Time Governance Society signed a five-year MoU with ISRO's SHAR (June 2025) to integrate satellite data into the state's AWARE platform for agriculture, weather, disaster management and urban planning — a textbook example of technology transfer from a national agency to state administration.
- IP performance: India ranks 4th in trademarks, 6th in patents and 7th in industrial designs in global filings (2024); patent applications nearly doubled from FY20 to FY25 (Economic Survey 2025-26).
- Policy lineage to cite: Scientific Policy Resolution 1958 > Technology Policy Statement 1983 > Science and Technology Policy 2003 > STIP 2013 > draft STIP 2020.

## Introduction

The Science, Technology and Innovation Policy, 2013, released during the centenary Indian Science Congress, was India's fifth S&T policy and the first to place innovation alongside science and technology in its title. Its central slogan — a shift from "science for people" to "science, technology and innovation by the people" — reframed research as a socially embedded activity. Sectoral programmes such as Post-Harvest Technology and the Oilseeds Production Programme illustrate this applied orientation in agriculture.

(a) Main objectives of STI Policy 2013

- Raise R&D investment: increase GERD to 2% of GDP within the decade, with private-sector investment matching public.
- Global positioning: place India among the top five global scientific powers by 2020 and raise its share of global scientific publications.
- Human capital: expand the base of full-time-equivalent R&D personnel by 66% in five years through fellowships and frontier-area training.
- Innovation ecosystem: promote incubators, technology business parks and start-ups; establish PPP-based technology commercialisation.
- Inclusive growth: direct S&T at agriculture, health, energy, water and environment challenges of the poor.
- Open access: mandate that publicly funded research be placed in open digital repositories.
- Science diplomacy: deepen participation in global mega-science projects such as

CERN, ITER and the Thirty Meter Telescope.

(b)(i) Post-Harvest Technology (PHT)

- What it is: the body of technologies applied after harvest — drying, grading, packaging, storage, cold chain, primary processing and value addition — to preserve quantity, quality and nutritional value.
- Why it matters: the NABCONS study commissioned by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries (2022, reference period 2020-22) estimated harvest and postharvest losses at 3.89-5.92% for cereals, 5.65-6.74% for pulses, 2.87-7.51% for oilseeds, 6.02-15.05% for fruits and 4.87-11.61% for vegetables, with total annual value of losses of the order of 1.53 lakh crore. Saving a tonne through better storage is cheaper and less resource-intensive than growing an additional tonne.
- Institutional and scheme support: ICAR-CIPHET, Ludhiana, is the nodal research institute; delivery is through Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (integrated cold chain, agro-processing clusters, Operation Greens), PMFME for micro food enterprises, and the PLI Scheme for Food Processing.
- APrelevance: Andhra Pradesh's horticulture profile — mango, banana, chilli, tomato — is dominated by highly perishable crops, making cold-chain and irradiation infrastructure directly consequential for farmer incomes.

(b) (ii) Oilseeds Production Programme (OPP)

- Origin: launched in 1986 under the Technology Mission on Oilseeds, established to end India's dependence on imported edible oil through improved seed, extension, processing and price support.
- Outcome: it produced the Yellow Revolution, roughly doubling oilseed output and making India briefly near-self-sufficient in edible oils by the mid-1990s — a textbook case of a technology mission delivering a national outcome.
- Why the gains reversed: trade liberalisation and cheap palm-oil imports eroded domestic incentives; imports today meet about 57% of India's edible-oil demand.
- Current successor framework: NMEO-Oil Palm (2021, outlay 711,040 crore) and NMEO- Oilseeds (approved 2024, =10,103 crore for 2024-25 to 2030-31), together targeting primary oilseed production of 69.7 million tonnes and domestic edible-oil output of 25.45 million tonnes by 2030-31, meeting about 72% of projected demand (PIB, 2024).
- APinstance: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana together account for the overwhelming share of India's oil palm cultivation, and NMEO-OP explicitly identifies Andhra Pradesh as a traditional focus State — making the State central to India's edible-oil self-reliance.

## Conclusion

STI Policy 2013 set the direction — innovation-led, inclusive, globally engaged — while programmes such as PHT and OPP show what that direction looks like on the ground. Their combined lesson is instructive: sustained mission-mode effort produced the Yellow Revolution, and its later reversal shows that technological gains require continuous policy support to hold. The renewed NMEO framework, with Andhra Pradesh at its centre, is an attempt to apply that lesson.

## Value addition
- STIPolicy 2013's defining phrase: the shift from "science for people" to "science, technology and innovation by the people" — quote it verbatim; it is the policy's signature.
- Post-harvest institutions to name: ICAR-CIPHET Ludhiana; National Institute of Food Technology, Entrepreneurship and Management (NIFTEM) at Kundli and Thanjavur; Indian Institute of Food Processing Technology.
- Food irradiation: MoFPI supports multi-product irradiation units under the Cold Chain scheme to extend shelf life — a good "technology solution" example for any agriculture-technology question.
- NMEO-OP incentives: assistance for planting material raised from 712,000 to ~29,000 per hectare; a first-of-its-kind Viability Price to insulate oil-palm farmers from international crude palm oil price swings; 7250 per plant for rejuvenating old gardens.
- India's oilseed standing: first in castor, safflower, sesame and niger production; second in groundnut; third in rapeseed-mustard. Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu,

Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka together supply the bulk of groundnut.

- The four "revolutions" for cross-referencing: Green (foodgrains), White (milk, Operation Flood), Yellow (oilseeds), Blue (fisheries, now Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana).
- SDG linkage: SDG 12.3 targets halving per-capita global food waste and reducing food losses along production and supply chains by 2030 — the international frame for PHT.

## Introduction

Data has become a factor of production, and its governance determines who can innovate. The National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy, 2012, notified by the Department of Science and Technology, established the principle that non-sensitive data generated with public funds belongs in the public domain. Alongside institutions such as ISCA, which built India's scientific culture, and CSIR, which built its industrial research capacity, NDSAP forms part of the infrastructure of a knowledge society.

(a) Salient features of NDSAP 2012

- Single national portal: creation of the Open Government Data platform, data.gov.in, to host datasets from all ministries and departments.
- Dataclassification: datasets categorised as open-access, registered-access or restricted-access, with sensitive data exempted consistent with the RTI Act, 2005.
- Machine-readable formats: datasets to be published in usable formats such as CSV, JSON and XML — asmall provision with large consequences, since PDFs are not reusable data.
- Metadata standards: standardised metadata for discoverability and interoperability across departments.
- Proactive disclosure: ministries to publish data suo motu rather than only on request.
- Institutional accountability: designated Data Controllers and nodal officers in each ministry, with negative-list based exemptions.

Benefits

- Transparency and accountability: citizens and researchers can independently verify government claims, strengthening evidence-based public debate.
- Better policymaking: interoperable datasets allow cross-departmental analysis — for example, linking rainfall, cropping and market data for agricultural advisories.
- Innovation and enterprise: agri-tech and weather-analytics start-ups build advisory products directly on public meteorological and crop datasets; open data lowers the entry cost for small innovators who cannot buy proprietary data.
- Foundation for AI: high-quality public datasets are the raw material for indigenous AI models, which is why open data policy has since evolved into a national AI priority.

The policy has since evolved — a line worth adding: the National Data Governance Framework Policy (2022) and the associated India Datasets Programme aim to build a repository of anonymised non-personal datasets for AI research, while the DPDP Act, 2023 governs the personal-data side. NDSAP was the first link in this chain.

(b)(i) Indian Science Congress Association (ISCA)

- Founded in 1914 at Kolkata with 105 members, on the initiative of British chemists J.L. Simonsen and P.S. MacMahon, to stimulate scientific research in India.
- Its annual Indian Science Congress, traditionally inaugurated by the Prime Minister on 3 January, was for a century India's principal scientific gathering, bringing together researchers, teachers and students.
- Current status: the Department of Science and Technology withdrew financial support in September 2023 citing financial irregularities, and the Congress has not been convened since its 108th session at Nagpur in January 2023. The government's flagship platform is now the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC), inaugurated by the Prime Minister at Bharat Mandapam from 3-5 November 2025 under the theme "Imagine, Innovate, Inspire for Viksit Bharat 2047", spanning 11 thematic areas and 13 ministries (PIB, November 2025). The 71 lakh crore RDI Fund was launched there.

(b) (ii) Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)

- Established in 1942 as an autonomous society; the Prime Minister is its President and the Union Minister of Science and Technology its Vice-President; it functions under the Ministry of Science and Technology.
- Operates a national network of 37 laboratories and 39 outreach centres, covering areas from aerospace and drugs to leather, minerals and food technology.
- Contributions: indigenous drug development and generic pharmaceuticals;

components for the Light Combat Aircraft; the SARAS aircraft programme; the Aroma Mission and Floriculture Mission for rural livelihoods; and CSIR-CCMB's role in genomic surveillance during COVID-19.

- Consistently ranked among the world's leading publicly funded research organisations, and one of India's largest filers of patents.
- APrelevance: CSIR-NIO's regional centre at Visakhapatnam supports coastal and ocean research relevant to Andhra Pradesh's 1,053-km coastline and blue-economy plans.

## Conclusion

NDSAP 2012 established open data as a default rather than an exception, and its logic now underpins India's Al-era data governance. ISCA's trajectory is a cautionary counterpoint — an institution that lost relevance and has been superseded by ESTIC — while CSIR demonstrates the enduring value of a well-managed public research network. Together they show that a knowledge society needs not only data and institutions, but institutions that renew themselves.

## Value addition
- data.gov.in: India's Open Government Data platform, hosting lakhs of resources across ministries; India also participates in global open-data benchmarking exercises.
- The data-governance chain to remember: NDSAP 2012 > National Data Governance Framework Policy 2022 > DPDP Act 2023 > India Datasets Programme / AI datasets platform under IndiaAI.
- The central tension: open data maximises innovation, while privacy requires restriction. Anonymised non-personal data is the compromise category, but reidentification risk means anonymisation is never absolute — a strong analytical point.
- CSIR flagship missions: Aroma Mission (lavender, vetiver, lemongrass on rain-fed and degraded land, boosting rural incomes); Floriculture Mission; Phytopharmaceutical Mission; CSIR-CMERI, CSIR-NAL, CSIR-NCL and CSIR-CCMB are the labs most worth naming.
- ESTIC 2025 — the 11 themes: advanced materials and manufacturing, AI, biomanufacturing, blue economy, digital communications, electronics and semiconductor manufacturing, emerging agriculture technologies, energy, environment and climate, health and medical technologies, quantum science and technology, and space technologies.
- Related science-outreach platforms: India International Science Festival (since 2015); National Science Day (28 February, marking the Raman Effect); Vigyan Sarvatra Pujyate.

## Introduction

India's science and technology policy has passed through four distinguishable phases:

state-led institution building, technology absorption for industry, innovation and competitiveness, and the current mission-mode, private-capital-driven phase. Each shift responded to a different diagnosis of what was constraining Indian science — first capacity, then application, then commercialisation, and now financing.

SPR 1958 (CSIR, DAE, ISRO, DRDO) > TPS 1983 (technology absorption) > S&T Policy 2003 / STI 2013 (innovation, PPP) > STIP draft 202@ / ANRF 2023 / RDI 2025 (mission mode)

Phase 1 — Institution building and self-reliance (1950s-1970s)

The Scientific Policy Resolution, 1958 — piloted by Nehru and shaped by Homi Bhabha — committed the State to "cultivate science and scientific research in all its aspects" and made the government the principal patron of research. The output was institutional: CSIR laboratories, the Department of Atomic Energy, INCOSPAR/ISRO and DRDO, plus the IITs. The premise was that a newly independent economy could not import technological sovereignty; it had to build it.

Phase 2 — Technology absorption and industrial application (1980s-1990s)

The Technology Policy Statement, 1983 shifted emphasis from creating knowledge to absorbing and applying it, targeting technological self-reliance in industry. The decade's Technology Missions — drinking water, immunisation, literacy, oilseeds, telecommunications — showed mission mode delivering socio-economic outcomes. Liberalisation after 1991 then opened channels for foreign collaboration and FDI, bringing multinational R&D centres to India and enabling the rise of the software services industry.

Phase 3 — Innovation and competitiveness (2000s-2010s)

The Science and Technology Policy, 2003 first set the 2% of GDP GERD aspiration and emphasised public-private partnership; the STI Policy, 2013 added innovation to the policy's very title and sought to place India among the top five scientific powers. Instruments became commercialisation-oriented: Technology Business Incubators and Science & Technology Entrepreneur Parks under DST, the National Innovation Foundation (2000) for grassroots innovation, and BIRAC (2012) for biotech start-ups.

Phase 4 — Mission mode, decentralisation and private capital (late 2010s to present)

- The draft STIP 2020 — India's fifth S&T policy, still not formally adopted — proposed a decentralised, bottom-up, evidence-informed model with open science, and explicit attention to gender and regional inclusion. ¢ Mission-mode returns at frontier scale: National Quantum Mission (%6,003.65 crore), National Supercomputing Mission, IndiaAI Mission, National Green Hydrogen Mission, Deep Ocean Mission.
- The decisive institutional shift is in funding: the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF Act, 2023) subsumed SERB and is mandated to seed research in State universities and colleges, not just elite institutes; the RDI Scheme (#1 lakh crore, launched November 2025) is designed to make the private sector the driver of R&D through concessional long-tenure capital. Read together, this is the sharpest break since 1958: the State is moving from being the primary performer of research to being its primary financier and convenor.
- APinstance of the decentralised turn: the Amaravati Quantum Valley Tech Park and the WEF-AP Centre for Energy and Cyber Resilience show States becoming independent actors in national technology missions rather than passive implementers.

## Continuing gaps
- Under-investment: GERD has remained around 0.6-0.7% of GDP against 2%+ in competitor economies, with private industry contributing only about a third.
- Thin researcher base: India produces engineers in large numbers but comparatively few full-time researchers per million population.
- Import dependence in semiconductors, medical devices and defence electronics persists despite recent progress.
- Fragmentation: DST, DBT, CSIR, DRDO, ISRO and ICAR operate with overlapping mandates — the coordination problem ANRF was created to address.

## Conclusion

The trajectory runs from building science to applying science to commercialising science to financing science at risk. Each shift corrected the previous phase's blind spot, and the current phase addresses the oldest one — the absence of patient private capital. Whether it succeeds depends less on further policy documents than on execution: sustained funding, genuine industry-academia linkage, and governance that lets ANRF direct resources beyond the established institutional elite.

## Value addition
- The five policy documents in sequence: Scientific Policy Resolution 1958 > Technology Policy Statement 1983 > Science and Technology Policy 2003 > Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013 > draft STIP 2020 (not yet formally adopted). Getting this sequence right is itself a scoring point.
- DST research-capacity schemes: FIST (infrastructure), SAIF (analytical instruments), SATHI (shared facilities), PURSE (university research excellence), CURIE (women's universities), and ANRF's PAIR programme, which pairs researchmature institutions with emerging ones — the clearest example of the decentralisation shift.
- Inclusion instruments: Vigyan Jyotiand WISE-KIRAN for women in STEM; I-STEM portal for shared access to research facilities.
- Constitutional anchor: Article 51A(h) — the fundamental duty to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
- Quotable framing: Nehru's "It is science alone that can solve the problems of hunger and poverty" (SPR context) pairs well with the current "Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan, Jai Vigyan, Jai Anusandhan" formulation — showing continuity of the science-fordevelopment idea across seven decades.
- APinstitutions across phases: SDSC-SHAR Sriharikota (Phase 1 legacy), NARL Gadanki, AMTZ Visakhapatnam (Phase 3), Amaravati Quantum Valley (Phase 4).

## Introduction

The Science, Technology and Innovation Policy, 2013, was released by the Prime Minister at the centenary session of the Indian Science Congress. It responded to a specific diagnosis: India had built research volume but not research impact, and its scientific establishment remained disconnected from enterprise. The policy's answer was to place innovation — the conversion of knowledge into value — at the centre, declaring 2010-20 the "Decade of Innovation".

Salient features and the reasoning behind each

- The GERD target of 2% of GDP. Rationale: India's research spend was under 1% while competitor economies invested two to three times more; critically, the policy specified that the increase must come from private-sector investment matching public spending, because government funding alone cannot sustain applied research at scale. Outcome: not achieved — GERD remained near 0.65%, with private share around a third (DST R&D Statistics).
- Reframing the relationship between science and society. Rationale: earlier policies treated citizens as beneficiaries; STI 2013 shifted from "science for people" to "science, technology and innovation by the people", recognising that grassroots innovators and users are themselves sources of technology. This idea later matured into the Scientific Social Responsibility framework (DST, 2019).
- Human capital expansion. Rationale: the constraint was not funding alone but researchers; the policy sought to expand the full-time-equivalent R&D personnel base by about two-thirds in five years, through INSPIRE fellowships, Ramanujan and Ramalingaswami re-entry schemes to attract the diaspora, and training in biotechnology, nanotechnology and ICT.
- Public-private partnership for commercialisation. Rationale: laboratory results were not reaching markets. Instruments included risk-sharing PPP models, incubators, and BIRAC, whose Biotechnology Ignition Grant supports entrepreneurs from ideation to proof of concept.
- Innovation for inclusive growth. Rationale: affordability determines diffusion ina low-income economy; hence a focus on frugal technologies — solar lighting, low-cost diagnostics, clean cookstoves, affordable housing — aimed at the bottom of the pyramid.
- Global positioning and science diplomacy. Rationale: frontier science is increasingly collaborative and capital-intensive, so India sought participation in mega-science projects such as CERN, ITER, the Thirty Meter Telescope and LIGO-India, alongside raising its share of world publications and patents.
- Open access and knowledge sharing. Rationale: publicly funded research is a public good; the policy mandated deposition in open digital repositories, complementing NDSAP 2012 on the data side.

(2 ERD | By the People | Hunan Capital | PPP | Inclusive | Global} Fast to draw, and it visibly organises the answer.

A brief verdict

STI 2013 succeeded on visibility and volume — India's publication output and patent filings grew strongly, and its Global Innovation Index rank improved from 66th in 2019 to 38th in 2025 (Economic Survey 2025-26). It failed on its central financial premise: private R&D investment did not materialise at the scale assumed. That single unmet assumption is why the ANRF (2023) and the #1 lakh crore RDI Scheme (2025) exist — both are, in effect, corrective instruments for STI 2013's unfinished business.

## Conclusion

STI Policy 2013 was intellectually ambitious and correctly diagnosed India's translation deficit, but it lacked the financing architecture to deliver its own targets. Its enduring contribution is conceptual — establishing innovation and inclusivity as organising principles of Indian science policy, and reframing citizens as participants rather than recipients. The current generation of instruments is best understood as STI 2013's aspirations finally being given the money and institutions they required.

## Introduction

India's science and technology policy has consistently pursued four objectives — building research capacity, achieving technological self-reliance, linking science to social needs, and more recently, driving innovation-led competitiveness. The National Solar Mission, launched in 2010 under the National Action Plan on Climate Change, shows these

objectives converging in a single programme: indigenous capability, affordable technology

## Introduction

A technology mission is a goal-oriented, time-bound programme that mobilises scientific institutions, industry and administration around a single measurable national objective, cutting across the departmental silos that ordinarily fragment implementation. First institutionalised in India in the 1980s, the model has been deliberately revived since 2020 for frontier technologies, making it one of the most durable instruments in Indian S&T governance.

What distinguishes mission mode

- Asingle quantified goal with a deadline, rather than an open-ended mandate.
- Convergence: multiple ministries and laboratories are directed at one problem under unified coordination.
- End-to-end responsibility: from research through manufacture to last-mile delivery — the reason missions succeed where isolated research does not.

The first generation (1980s-1990s)

- Immunisation: the Universal Immunisation Programme and its successors carried India to WHO certification as polio-free in 2014.
- Drinking water: low-cost purification, handpump technology and rainwater harvesting for rural habitations.
- Literacy: the National Literacy Mission (1988) used Total Literacy Campaigns to raise literacy from 52.2% in 1991 to 64.8% in 2001 (Census).
- Telecommunications: C-DOT's indigenous rural exchanges made village telephony viable, laying the groundwork for India's later telecom expansion. ¢ Oilseeds: the Technology Mission on Oilseeds (1986) — developed below as the detailed example.

The contemporary generation (2020 onwards) — this is what updates the answer:

- National Quantum Mission (2023, 6,003.65 crore over eight years): quantum computers of 50-1,000 physical qubits, quantum communication, magnetometry and atomic clocks, delivered through four Thematic Hubs.
- IndiaAI Mission (2024): compute infrastructure, datasets, foundation models and skilling — though a parliamentary review flagged fund under-utilisation and hardware procurement bottlenecks, a reminder that mission mode is not selfexecuting.
- National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023, =19,744 crore): 5 MMT of annual green hydrogen production capacity by 2030.
- Deep Ocean Mission and National Supercomputing Mission (PARAM series) complete the frontier set.
- APinstance: the Amaravati Quantum Valley Tech Park, anchored by an IBM Quantum System Two with a 156-qubit Heron processor, is a State-level vehicle plugged directly into the National Quantum Mission — showing that contemporary missions increasingly work through State partnerships.

The detailed example: Technology Mission on Oilseeds (1986)

- The problem: India was spending scarce foreign exchange on edible oil imports while domestic productivity stagnated.
- The intervention: improved seed varieties, expanded irrigation, extension services, processing infrastructure and assured procurement prices, coordinated across agriculture, cooperation and commerce departments.
- The outcome — the Yellow Revolution: oilseed production rose from about 11 million tonnes in 1986-87 to nearly 25 million tonnes by 1994-95, bringing India close to selfsufficiency in edible oils.
- The instructive sequel: liberalised palm-oil imports eroded domestic incentives and self-sufficiency was lost; imports now meet roughly 57% of demand. The government has therefore returned to mission mode with NMEO-Oil Palm (2021, 11,040 crore) and NMEO-Oilseeds (2024, 710,103 crore), targeting 72% self-sufficiency by 2030-31 (PIB, 2024). Andhra Pradesh, with Telangana, accounts for the overwhelming share of India's oil palm area, placing the State at the centre of this second attempt.

## Conclusion

Technology missions work because they replace diffuse departmental effort with a single accountable objective — and the oilseeds case shows both the model's power and its fragility, since gains reverse without sustained policy support. The revival of mission mode for quantum computing, AI and green hydrogen suggests India has drawn the right lesson, though these frontier missions will be judged, as the earlier ones were, on delivery rather

than design.

## Value addition
- The five original Technology Missions (1986-87): drinking water, immunisation, literacy, oilseeds (later oilseeds and pulses), and telecommunications — often associated with Sam Pitroda and the Rajiv Gandhi government's Technology Missions initiative.
- Contemporary missions with outlays: National Quantum Mission (26,003.65 crore); National Green Hydrogen Mission (219,744 crore); National Supercomputing Mission; IndiaAI Mission; Deep Ocean Mission; National Mission on Natural Farming; National Manufacturing Mission (announced in Budget 2025-26). ¢ The oilseeds numbers to quote: production from about 11 MT (1986-87) to nearly 25 MT (1994-95); NMEO targets primary oilseed production of 69.7 MT and domestic edible oil output of 25.45 MT by 2030-31.
- NMEO-OP incentives: planting-material assistance raised from =12,000 to 729,000 per hectare; a first-of-its-kind Viability Price insulating oil-palm growers from international crude palm oil price swings.
- Asharp analytical point: the 1980s missions targeted deficits (of water, literacy, oil); today's missions target frontiers (quantum, AI, hydrogen). The first kind required delivery at scale; the second requires tolerance of research failure — a different institutional skill, which is why ANRF and the RDI Scheme matter to their success.
- AP linkage: oil palm cultivation in the Godavari districts; Amaravati Quantum Valley under the National Quantum Mission; AP's green hydrogen and pumped-storage targets under the Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024.

## Introduction

India has used mission-mode programmes in two registers: technological missions targeting capability in space, defence, energy and health, and social missions targeting human development. The National Literacy Mission belongs to the second, but shares the first's defining logic — a quantified goal, a deadline, and convergence across agencies. Together they reflect a consistent belief that focused national campaigns can compress timelines that ordinary administration would stretch across decades.

(a) Important technological missions of India and their objectives

- Space —ISRO's mission programme. Objective: self-reliant access to space and its application to communication, navigation, weather and resource mapping. Chandrayaan-3 achieved the first soft landing near the lunar south pole (2023); Aditya-L1 is India's first solar observatory; Gaganyaan aims at indigenous human spaceflight, with launches from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota.
- Defence — Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme. Objective:

strategic deterrence and reduced import dependence, yielding the Agni, Prithvi, Akash, Trishul and Nag systems, and later BrahMos through joint development.

- Nuclear — the three-stage programme. Objective: energy security using India's limited uranium and abundant thorium reserves, through pressurised heavy water reactors, fast breeder reactors and eventually thorium-based systems.
- Clean energy — National Solar Mission and National Green Hydrogen Mission (%19,744 crore). Objective: energy security and decarbonisation; India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its NDC target (PIB, 2025).
- Health and biotechnology — National Biopharma Mission, Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. Objective: indigenous vaccine and biologics capability and a national digital health infrastructure.
- Frontier technology — National Quantum Mission (26,003.65 crore), IndiaAI Mission, National Supercomputing Mission, Deep Ocean Mission. Objective: firstmover capability in technologies that will determine strategic and economic position over the next quarter century.

(b) Essay: the National Literacy Mission

- Genesis and objectives. Launched on 5 May 1988, the NLM aimed at functional literacy for the 15-35 age group, defined as the ability to read, write and compute sufficiently for daily life, together with awareness of social issues and participation in development. Its revised goal was a sustainable threshold literacy level of 75%.
- Design and method. The mission worked through Total Literacy Campaigns at the district level — volunteer-driven, time-bound and area-specific — followed by PostLiteracy Programmes and Continuing Education Centres to prevent relapse into illiteracy. Volunteerism rather than paid instruction was the organising principle, which kept costs low and generated community ownership.
- Achievements. Literacy rose from 52.21% in 1991 to 64.84% in 2001 and 74.04% in 2011 (Census), with female literacy improving from 39.29% to 65.46% over the same two decades — one of the fastest sustained literacy gains recorded in a country of India's size. Saakshar Bharat (2009), the successor, focused on women and certified about 7.64 crore persons as literate between 2009-10 and 2017-18.
- Persisting challenges. Census 2011 counted 25.76 crore non-literate persons aged 15 and above, of whom 16.68 crore were women; regional disparities, dropout and relapse, weak post-literacy support and declining volunteer participation limited the campaign model's reach.
- Thecurrent successor — ULLAS. ULLAS - Nav Bharat Saaksharta Karyakram, also called the New India Literacy Programme, is a centrally sponsored scheme running 2022-2027 with an outlay of ¥1,037.90 crore, aligned to NEP 2020 and targeting five crore non-literate adults aged 15 and above. It has five components — foundational literacy and numeracy, critical life skills, basic education, vocational skills and continuing education — delivered by volunteer teachers through the ULLAS mobile app, with certification via the Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment Test (FLNAT). A State or UT crossing 95% functional literacy is declared "fully literate"; Ladakh was the first (June 2024), followed by Mizoram, Tripura, Goa, Himachal Pradesh and Sikkim (May 2026).
- APrelevance — an uncomfortable but examinable point. Andhra Pradesh's literacy rate remains among the lowest in India — 67.02% in Census 2011, and still below the national average in recent Periodic Labour Force Survey estimates. This makes ULLAS implementation, adult education in Rayalaseema and tribal districts, and the retention of girls in school, live policy priorities for the State rather than settled achievements.

## Conclusion

India's technological missions built capability, and its literacy missions built the capacity of citizens to use it — the two are complementary rather than parallel. The literacy record is genuinely impressive in its trajectory yet incomplete in its coverage, with the largest remaining deficit among adult women. ULLAS represents a smarter, technology-assisted and volunteer-driven revival of the 1988 model, and its success will be measured not by declarations of full literacy but by whether neo-literates retain and use their skills.

## Value addition
- ULLAS ata glance: centrally sponsored, 2022-2027; outlay =1,037.90 crore; target 5 crore learners aged 15+; five components; volunteer-based with no honorarium; ULLAS mobile app; FLNAT certification; teaching-learning material in multiple Indian languages; 95% functional literacy is the threshold for a "fully literate" declaration.
- Fully literate States and UTs declared under ULLAS: Ladakh (June 2024, first), followed by Mizoram, Tripura, Goa, Himachal Pradesh and Sikkim (May 2026) — a list that changes, so check before the exam.
- Literacy data points to memorise: 18.33% (1951) > 52.21% (1991) > 64.84% (2001) > 74.04% (2011), Census; 25.76 crore non-literates aged 15+ in Census 2011, of whom 16.68 crore women; Kerala consistently highest, and Andhra Pradesh and Bihar among the lowest.
- Programme lineage: National Adult Education Programme (1978) > National Literacy Mission (1988) > Saakshar Bharat (2009) > ULLAS/NILP (2022).
- NEP 2020 linkage: NIPUN Bharat targets foundational literacy and numeracy for all children by Grade 3; ULLAS addresses the adult cohort that earlier systems missed. Together they aim at SDG 4.6 — universal youth and adult literacy and numeracy by 2030.
- Conceptual precision worth showing: literacy (reading, writing, arithmetic) is

distinct from functional literacy (using those skills in daily life) and from foundational literacy and numeracy (the Grade 3 competency standard). Examiners notice when a candidate distinguishes these.

- A framing line: the 1988 mission treated illiteracy as a backlog to be cleared; ULLAS treats literacy as lifelong learning — which is why it includes vocational skills and critical life skills, not just the alphabet.

## Introduction

The National Strategy for Robotics, released by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology for public consultation, aims to position India as a global robotics leader by 2030. It builds on Make in India 2.0, which identifies robotics as one of 27 priority sub-sectors, and sits within the wider IndiaAI vision. India’s context makes the strategy urgent: annual industrial robot installations reached a record 9,100 units in 2024, placing India sixth worldwide, yet its operational stock of 52,570 units ranks only tenth, against 300,000 to two million in the most automated economies (IFR World Robotics 2025).

Enablers: R&D · Skilling · Standards · Procurement , with a roof labelled Robotics Innovation Unit (MeitY) . This mirrors the document’s own architecture.

## The four priority sectors identified by the strategy
- Manufacturing. Robotics raises productivity and consistency in automobile, electronics and precision engineering, and is the technical foundation of Industry 4.0. The automotive sector already drives about 45% of India’s robot installations (IFR, 2025). The strategic point for India is collaborative robots (cobots) — lower-cost, fenceless machines that work alongside human operators, which suit MSMEs that cannot justify a full automated line. Without cobot adoption by MSMEs, automation deepens the productivity gap between large firms and small ones rather than closing it.
- Agriculture. Robotics addresses the sector’s specific bottlenecks: labour shortage at peak operations, drudgery, and precision in input application. Drone-based spraying and crop monitoring are the most scaled application, supported by the Kisan Drone initiative, the Namo Drone Didi scheme placing drones with women’s self-help groups, and the Digital Agriculture Mission (approved 2024) which builds the AgriStack data layer that robotic systems require to be useful.
- Healthcare. Surgical robotics improves precision and reduces recovery times in procedures such as joint replacement; assistive and rehabilitation robotics addresses an ageing population and a shortage of trained care personnel. Indigenous development is anchored in DST’s Technology Innovation Hubs under the National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems — notably the I-Hub Foundation for Cobotics at IIT Delhi, which works on surgical and assistive robots.
- National security. Robotics reduces human exposure in hazardous operations — bomb disposal, surveillance, mine detection, and unmanned aerial and underwater systems. DRDO’s DAKSH remotely operated vehicle for explosive ordnance disposal is the established example; unmanned underwater vehicle work at NSTL, Visakhapatnam is the AP-relevant one.

## The institutional and policy framework
- A Robotics Innovation Unit (RIU) proposed under MeitY, functioning as part of IndiaAI, to coordinate regulation and standards.
- A National Robotics Mission to oversee implementation through a two-tier structure.
- Centres of Excellence, split between foundational research and applied research, with private-sector participation in the latter for prototyping and early commercialisation.
- Public procurement as demand aggregation — the government committing to buy domestically manufactured robotic systems to create an assured market, the same logic that worked for defence and solar manufacturing.
- Skilling and IPR: nurturing a robotics workforce and promoting Indian IPR in robotics, supported by Atal Tinkering Labs at school level and PMKVY 4.0 modules in robotics and mechatronics.

## Constraints to acknowledge
- Component import dependence in actuators, precision sensors, harmonic drives and controllers keeps costs high — self-reliance in robotics is really a self-reliance-in-components problem.
- Capital cost versus cheap labour: in a labour-surplus economy the commercial case for automation is weaker, which is why the strategy emphasises cobots and public procurement rather than assuming market pull.
- Skills mismatch and displacement anxiety, requiring credible reskilling pathways.

## Conclusion

The National Strategy for Robotics correctly identifies that India’s constraint is not ambition but ecosystem depth — components, standards, skilled technicians and an assured market. Its choice of manufacturing, agriculture, healthcare and national security as priority sectors is well judged, since each combines large domestic demand with a strategic case for indigenous capability. India’s jump to sixth place in annual installations shows demand is arriving; whether the supply side is Indian will depend on the Centres of Excellence and the procurement policy actually being operationalised.

## Value addition
- India’s robotics position (IFR World Robotics 2025, data for 2024): record 9,100 industrial robots installed in 2024, up 7%; 6th globally in annual installations; operational stock 52,570 units, 10th globally; automotive accounts for about 45% of installations. Globally, 542,000 industrial robots were installed in 2024, with China alone taking 54%.
- DAKSH (DRDO): an indigenous battery-powered remotely operated vehicle for bomb detection, handling and disposal; equipped with a manipulator arm, X-ray device and water-jet disruptor; capable of climbing stairs; deployed with the Army, police and paramilitary forces.
- Related national programmes: National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (Rs. 3,660 crore, 25 Technology Innovation Hubs across IITs, IISc and other institutes); IndiaAI Mission; SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0; PLI for electronics and capital goods.
- Types of robots to distinguish: industrial robots (fixed, caged, high-payload); cobots (collaborative, human-adjacent, low-cost); AMRs/AGVs (mobile, for warehousing); service and humanoid robots; and exoskeletons for assistive use. Naming these correctly signals technical literacy.
- AP-relevant robotics assets: NSTL Visakhapatnam (unmanned underwater systems); Sri City and the Kia plant at Anantapur as automated manufacturing clusters; the WEF–AP Centre for Energy and Cyber Resilience for AI-led industrial transformation.
- The employment counter-argument to hold ready: IFR data show that the most robot-dense economies (Korea, Singapore, Germany) also have low unemployment, suggesting automation shifts rather than destroys employment — but this holds only where reskilling systems function, which is the policy variable India controls.

## Introduction

Big Data refers to datasets so large, fast-moving and heterogeneous that conventional databases and spreadsheets cannot store, process or analyse them. It is conventionally characterised by five attributes — volume, velocity, variety, veracity and value. Its significance for India is governance: administrative records, satellite imagery, sensor feeds and transaction data together allow policy to be designed and evaluated against evidence rather than assumption.

## Why Big Data requires different treatment

Conventional systems assume data is structured, arrives slowly and fits on one machine. Big Data breaks all three assumptions — hence distributed storage and processing, and analytical methods drawn from machine learning rather than classical statistics. The veracity dimension matters most in Indian governance: duplicate and inconsistent beneficiary records mean scale can amplify error as easily as insight.

## India’s initiatives
- Platforms for access. NITI Aayog’s National Data and Analytics Platform (NDAP) standardises and publishes government datasets with search, merge and visualisation tools; data.gov.in, the Open Government Data platform under NDSAP 2012, remains the primary repository of ministry datasets.
- Policy architecture. The National Data Governance Framework Policy (2022) aims to standardise the collection and sharing of non-personal data and proposed an India Data Management Office (IDMO) to administer it, alongside an India Datasets Programme to pool anonymised datasets for research and AI training.
- AI-era data infrastructure. Under the IndiaAI Mission, the datasets pillar (AIKosh) assembles quality datasets for model development, while the compute pillar has provisioned over 38,000 GPUs, with further expansion announced at the India AI Impact Summit 2026 — recognition that data is useless without the compute to process it.
- Legal framework. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with Rules notified in 2025, establishes consent, purpose limitation, data-fiduciary obligations and the Data Protection Board — the boundary condition within which Big Data analytics must operate.
- Sectoral applications. GST and e-way bill analytics for tax compliance; the Integrated Health Information Platform for disease surveillance; PM Gati Shakti’s geospatial layers for infrastructure planning; Krishi-DSS for agriculture; satellite-based crop and forest monitoring by ISRO and the Forest Survey of India.
- Statistical modernisation. MoSPI’s Data Innovation Lab explores alternative data sources such as satellite imagery and machine learning for official statistics; India’s membership of the UN Committee of Experts on Big Data and Data Science for Official Statistics (UN-CEBD) reflects this shift.
- AP instance: Andhra Pradesh’s Real Time Governance Society consolidates departmental data into a unified data lake and runs the AWARE platform, integrating satellite, drone, IoT sensor and CCTV feeds to issue real-time citizen alerts; RTGS Lens has integrated 506 departmental workflows across 28 departments, and an AI-driven City Flood Alert system built with APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar provides 48-hour rainfall outlooks and six-hour flash-flood warnings (2026). This is among India’s most developed State-level Big Data governance systems.

## Challenges and constraints
- Data quality and interoperability: duplicate, inconsistent and non-standardised records across departments; without common identifiers and metadata standards, datasets cannot be joined and remain analytically inert.
- Privacy and regulatory ambiguity: the boundary between personal and non-personal data blurs on aggregation, since anonymised datasets can often be re-identified when combined.
- Infrastructure and skills: shortage of secure storage, sovereign cloud capacity and trained data scientists in government; capacity-building through MeitY and NIELIT lags demand.
- Algorithmic bias and exclusion: models trained on historical administrative data reproduce historical exclusions; a beneficiary absent from the data is invisible to the algorithm, and this failure is silent rather than visible.
- Security: large consolidated databases are high-value targets, and the cost of a breach scales with the size of the repository.

## Conclusion

India has built the platforms (NDAP, AIKosh), the policy (National Data Governance Framework) and the law (DPDP Act) required for a functioning Big Data ecosystem, and States such as Andhra Pradesh demonstrate what integrated data governance can deliver operationally. The binding constraint has shifted from availability to quality and trust: data that is inconsistent produces confident wrong answers, and data that is not trusted will not be shared. Investment in data standards, auditability and skills now matters more than further platform creation.

## Value addition
- The five Vs: volume (scale), velocity (speed of generation), variety (structured, semi-structured, unstructured), veracity (reliability), value (extractable insight). Some frameworks add variability.
- India’s data governance chain: NDSAP 2012 –> National Data Governance Framework Policy 2022 (with IDMO and the India Datasets Programme) –> DPDP Act 2023 with Rules 2025 –> AIKosh under IndiaAI.
- UN-CEBD: India’s membership of the UN Committee of Experts on Big Data and Data Science for Official Statistics supports work on reducing time lags in statistical production and using alternative data sources for policy.
- Distinction to make explicitly:personal data (DPDP Act, consent-based) versus non-personal/anonymised data (National Data Governance Framework, sharing-oriented). Most policy disputes arise at this boundary.

- Related concepts worth naming: data lake versus data warehouse; edge versus cloud processing; federated learning (training models without centralising raw data — the emerging answer to the privacy-versus-analytics trade-off).
Q13:
## Introduction

The Internet of Things is a network of physical objects embedded with sensors and connectivity that sense their environment, transmit data, and act on the resulting analysis without human instruction at each step. Its claim to be a technological revolution rests not on any single application but on being a general-purpose technology — like electricity, it changes production processes across every sector rather than creating one new sector.

Action , then a fan of five sector arrows from “Action”: Industry, Agriculture, Cities, Health, Energy.

## Why IoT is described as a revolution
- It is horizontal, not sectoral. Earlier technology waves were confined — the personal computer to offices, mobile telephony to communication. IoT alters manufacturing, farming, healthcare, logistics and utilities simultaneously.
- It closes the loop between data and action. Big Data and AI analyse; IoT both generates the data and executes the response through actuators, which is what converts analytics into physical outcomes.
- It is a force multiplier for other technologies. IoT supplies the real-world data that AI needs, uses 5G’s low latency and device density, and can write verified records to blockchain ledgers.

## Likely impact on India
- Industry and manufacturing. Condition monitoring and predictive maintenance reduce unplanned downtime — the largest single source of capacity loss in Indian heavy industry. This is the technical substrate of Industry 4.0, supported by SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 centres under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, including C4i4 Pune’s model factory and CMTI Bengaluru’s smart factory.
- Agriculture. Soil-moisture and weather sensors enable irrigation scheduling that responds to plant need rather than the calendar — significant where groundwater is depleting fastest. Sensor data feeds the Krishi Decision Support System under the Digital Agriculture Mission, and drone-based monitoring under the Kisan Drone and Namo Drone Didi initiatives extends the same logic aerially.
- Energy and utilities. The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), with an outlay of Rs. 3.03 lakh crore, is deploying smart prepaid metering toward roughly 25 crore consumers — India’s single largest IoT rollout. Smart meters convert distribution utilities from estimated billing to measured billing, which is the precondition for reducing aggregate technical and commercial losses.
- Urban governance. Under the Smart Cities Mission, Integrated Command and Control Centres in over 100 cities fuse traffic, surveillance, solid-waste and air-quality sensor feeds; CPCB’s continuous ambient air quality monitoring stations provide the real-time data underlying the National Clean Air Programme.
- Healthcare. Remote patient monitoring and connected diagnostic devices extend specialist reach, complementing eSanjeevani’s teleconsultation model; cold-chain temperature sensors protect vaccine potency in last-mile delivery.
- Logistics and mobility. GPS and sensor tracking under FASTag, e-way bills and PM Gati Shakti cut turnaround times at tolls and checkposts, lowering logistics costs that have long been a drag on Indian manufacturing competitiveness.
- Disaster management — an AP instance. The Real Time Governance Society’s AWARE platform integrates satellite, drone, IoT sensor, mobile and CCTV data to issue real-time alerts through SMS and WhatsApp, strengthened by a five-year MoU with ISRO’s SHAR, Sriharikota (June 2025). RTGS has since built a City Flood Alert system with APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar giving 48-hour rainfall outlooks and six-hour flash-flood warnings, beginning with Vijayawada — for a State with a 1,053-km cyclone-exposed coastline, this is IoT applied to survival rather than convenience.

## Examining the claim critically
- Constraints are real. Connectivity gaps persist despite BharatNet and 5G expansion; device costs limit adoption; competing protocols fragment deployments; and the Telecommunication Engineering Centre’s Code of Practice for Securing Consumer IoT exists precisely because cheap devices ship insecure.
- Security is the systemic risk. Connecting operational technology — power grids, water systems, factory controls — to networks converts a cyber incident into a physical one. CERT-In advisories on industrial control systems reflect this.
- A measured verdict: IoT’s transformative potential is genuine but derivative — it delivers value only in combination with connectivity, analytics and AI. It is better described as the sensory layer of a broader digital transformation than as a standalone revolution.

## Conclusion

IoT’s likely impact on India is greatest precisely where the country’s inefficiencies are largest — electricity distribution losses, irrigation water waste, logistics delays and disaster response times — because measurement is the first step to correcting any of them. India’s advantage is that it is deploying IoT through public programmes such as RDSS smart metering and the Smart Cities Mission rather than leaving it to private purchasing power, which determines whether the benefits reach beyond affluent users. The binding conditions are secure-by-design standards and reliable connectivity, without which scale becomes a vulnerability rather than a strength.

## Value addition
- Largest public IoT deployments in India: RDSS smart prepaid metering (Rs. 3.03 lakh crore, about 25 crore consumers); Smart Cities Mission Integrated Command and Control Centres in 100+ cities; CPCB’s continuous ambient air quality monitoring network; FASTag on national highways.
- Enabling infrastructure: 5G for low latency and high device density; NB-IoT for low-power, long-range sensors; BharatNet for rural backhaul; edge computing to process data at the device and reduce bandwidth and privacy exposure.
- Regulatory and security framework: MeitY’s IoT policy framework; TEC (DoT) Code of Practice for Securing Consumer IoT; TEC’s Mandatory Testing and Certification of Telecom Equipment (MTCTE); CERT-In directions on incident reporting; DPDP Act 2023 with Rules 2025.
- Terms worth using precisely:actuator (converts a decision into physical action); digital twin (a live virtual replica of a physical asset — V.O. Chidambaranar Port was the first Indian port to launch one); IIoT (Industrial IoT, distinct from consumer IoT); M2M communication.
- AP-specific IoT assets: RTGS AWARE platform, Amaravati; RTGS–ISRO SHAR MoU (June 2025); City Flood Alert with IIT Gandhinagar and APSDMA; smart metering under RDSS; Google’s AI hub at Visakhapatnam providing the compute for sensor-data analytics at scale.
- How to keep this distinct from Q5 in the exam: Q5 asks about household automation — answer with lighting, security, eldercare, appliance energy use. Q24 asks about national impact — answer with industry, agriculture, utilities, cities, disaster management. Same technology, different unit of analysis; using the household examples here would read as off-target.
- SDG linkage: SDG 9 (industry, innovation, infrastructure), SDG 11 (sustainable cities) and SDG 6 (water) through leak detection and irrigation efficiency.

Sources used: IFR World Robotics 2025 (published September 2025, data for 2024); MeitY draft National Strategy for Robotics; MeitY IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, notified 10 February 2026 (G.S.R. 120(E)); PIB on the India AI Impact Summit 2026 and the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact (February–March 2026); MeitY National Blockchain Framework and blockchain.gov.in; NITI Aayog “Blockchain: The India Strategy” and NDAP; Ministry of Agriculture on the Digital Agriculture Mission and AgriStack; Ministry of Power (RDSS); Telecommunication Engineering Centre, DoT; Government of Andhra Pradesh RTGS/AWARE and the RTGS–ISRO SHAR MoU (June 2025); Nobel Prize records and IACS for the Raman Effect.

Q14:
## Introduction

The Global Positioning System (GPS) is a satellite-based Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) system operated by the United States, using a constellation of about 24 satellites in Medium Earth Orbit. A receiver computes its position by trilateration — measuring signal travel time from at least four satellites, the fourth resolving the receiver’s clock error. India’s own system, NavIC, exists because dependence on a foreign-controlled signal is a strategic vulnerability: the operator can degrade or deny access in a conflict.

## Why India needed an indigenous system

The Kargil conflict (1999) is the standard reference point: India’s request for high-precision GPS data over the conflict zone was declined, demonstrating that a foreign PNT signal is available only at the provider’s discretion. Since PNT underpins missile guidance, troop movement, aviation, shipping, telecom synchronisation and financial time-stamping, this was not a military problem alone but an infrastructure one.

## NavIC — architecture
- Name and status: the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS), operationally NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), developed by ISRO.
- Coverage: India and a region extending about 1,500 km beyond the Indian landmass — regional, not global, which is a deliberate design choice trading global reach for lower cost and faster deployment.
- Constellation: designed around seven satellites — three in geostationary orbit and four in inclined geosynchronous orbit — supported by a ground segment of control centre, precise timing facility, ranging and integrity monitoring stations.
- Two services: the Standard Positioning Service (SPS), open, providing position accuracy better than 20 m and timing accuracy better than 40 nanoseconds over the service area; and the encrypted Restricted Service (RS) for strategic users.

## Recent efforts — the second-generation NVS series
- NVS-01 (May 2023) was the first second-generation NavIC satellite and carried India’s first indigenously developed rubidium atomic clock — significant because imported atomic clocks in the earlier IRNSS satellites had failed, degrading the constellation. Clock failure is the single most common cause of navigation-satellite degradation, so indigenising it addressed the system’s principal weakness.
- NVS-02 was launched on 29 January 2025 aboard GSLV-F15 from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota — ISRO’s 100th launch from Sriharikota. It carries navigation payloads in the L1, L5 and S bands with a C-band ranging payload. ISRO subsequently reported that orbit-raising to its designated slot could not be carried out because the oxidiser valves of the main engine failed to open — a candid illustration that indigenous capability is built through iteration, not uninterrupted success.
- Addition of the L1 signal in the NVS series is technically the most consequential upgrade: L1 is the frequency civilian GPS receivers and smartphone chipsets already use, so NavIC compatibility no longer requires special hardware. Interoperability, not accuracy, was NavIC’s real barrier to civilian adoption.
- Constellation replacement: NVS-01 and NVS-02 are the first two of five planned second-generation replacement satellites, with expansion of the constellation under consideration to improve availability.
- Chipset and device integration: the government has pushed NavIC support in devices sold in India, and several handset manufacturers have introduced NavIC-capable models — supported by chipset design incentives under the Design Linked Incentive scheme.

## Applications and significance
- Strategic autonomy: an assured encrypted PNT signal for defence platforms, independent of foreign policy decisions elsewhere.
- Transport and logistics: vehicle tracking under the AIS-140 standard for public service vehicles; Indian Railways’ Real Time Train Information System uses satellite-based tracking for live train positions.
- Disaster management and fisheries: NavIC messaging capability allows alerts to fishermen and to areas without terrestrial network coverage — directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s cyclone-exposed 1,053-km coastline.
- Precision agriculture and surveying: the SVAMITVA property-mapping programme and drone-based land surveys depend on precise positioning.
- AP linkage: every NavIC satellite has been launched from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh, making the State the physical base of India’s navigation sovereignty.

## Conclusion

NavIC represents a considered strategic choice: a regional constellation delivering assured, sovereign PNT at a fraction of the cost of a global system. The second-generation NVS satellites address its two real weaknesses — imported atomic clocks and the absence of an L1 civilian signal. Sustaining constellation health through timely replacement launches, and driving chipset-level adoption, will determine whether NavIC becomes genuinely used infrastructure rather than a strategic reserve.

## Value addition
- The four global GNSS constellations: GPS (United States), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (European Union), BeiDou (China). The two regional systems are NavIC (India) and QZSS (Japan) — this distinction is frequently tested.
- NavIC specifications to quote: SPS position accuracy better than 20 m (2sigma) and timing accuracy better than 40 ns (2sigma) over the service area; coverage extending about 1,500 km beyond the Indian landmass; signals in L5 and S bands, with L1 added in the NVS series.
- GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation): a joint ISRO-AAI satellite-based augmentation system improving GPS accuracy for civil aviation over Indian airspace — India was the fourth country to have such a system. Often confused with NavIC; distinguishing them earns credit.
- NVS-02 mission facts: launched 29 January 2025 on GSLV-F15 from the Second Launch Pad, SDSC-SHAR; launch mass about 2,250 kg on the I-2K bus; intended slot 111.75deg E to replace IRNSS-1E; ISRO’s 100th launch from Sriharikota.
- Why atomic clocks matter: a timing error of one nanosecond translates to roughly 30 cm of position error, so clock stability is the binding constraint on navigation accuracy — the reason indigenising the rubidium clock was strategically important.
- AP linkage: SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, is India’s only orbital launch site; NavIC messaging services support cyclone and fishermen alerts along the Andhra coast.

## Introduction

Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of computing resources — servers, storage, databases, networking, analytics and software — over the internet, billed by use rather than owned. Its significance for government is fiscal and operational: departments consume capacity instead of procuring and maintaining hardware. Andhra Pradesh, having lost Hyderabad’s IT infrastructure on bifurcation in 2014, had to build its digital backbone from scratch — which is why the AP Cloud Initiative and the AP Fibre Grid were conceived together as complementary layers.

## (a) Cloud computing and the AP Cloud Initiative

Three service models (worth naming — this is what distinguishes a technical answer): - IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) — raw compute, storage and networking. - PaaS (Platform as a Service) — development and deployment environments. - SaaS (Software as a Service) — ready applications delivered over the browser.

Four deployment models: public, private, hybrid and community cloud. Governments typically use community or private cloud for reasons of data sovereignty and security.

Advantages: elasticity (capacity scales with demand — critical for systems facing exam-result or scheme-application surges), capital-to-operating expenditure shift, disaster recovery through geographic redundancy, and faster deployment of new applications.

## The AP Cloud Initiative
- Launched under the State’s “Digital Andhra Pradesh” agenda, its objectives were cloud-based governance, improved e-service delivery, and a workforce skilled in cloud, AI and data analytics.
- The State partnered with global technology firms including Google and Microsoft to set up cloud learning hubs and digital skilling programmes for youth.
- Departmental applications were consolidated onto secure cloud infrastructure — the AP State Data Centre — improving availability and enabling cross-departmental analytics, which today underpins the Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) data lake at Amaravati.
- National context: State cloud initiatives sit within MeghRaj, the Government of India Cloud Initiative, under which NIC has provided national cloud services since 2014 from National Data Centres at Bhubaneswar, Delhi, Hyderabad and Pune, provisioning over 18,000 virtual servers to more than 1,100 ministries and departments.
- Current AP development: Google announced its first AI hub in India at Visakhapatnam — approximately USD 15 billion over 2026-2030, with gigawatt-scale data-centre capacity and a subsea cable gateway, described as its largest AI hub outside the United States (newsonair, Government of India, October 2025). This converts Andhra Pradesh from a consumer of cloud services into a location where cloud capacity is physically hosted.

## (b) The Andhra Pradesh Fibre Grid Project
- Implementing agency and objective: launched in 2015 and implemented by Andhra Pradesh State FiberNet Limited (APSFL), to deliver affordable high-speed internet, television and telephony to every household, institution and enterprise in the State.
- The key design innovation: rather than trenching new ducts — slow, expensive and disruptive — optical fibre was strung aerially along existing electricity distribution poles, covering roughly 23,000 km and reaching villages, mandals and districts. Using the power utility’s existing right-of-way cut both cost and deployment time dramatically, and is the project’s most examinable feature.
- Technology: All-Dielectric Self-Supporting (ADSS) aerial fibre cables, chosen because they carry no metallic component and can therefore be strung safely on live electricity poles, over a Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) backbone that multiplies capacity by carrying many wavelengths on a single fibre.
- Services: “triple play” — internet, IPTV and telephony — at subsidised tariffs, offering roughly 15-50 Mbps for households and up to 1 Gbps for government institutions and businesses.
- Outcomes: enabled e-governance delivery, tele-education, telemedicine and rural entrepreneurship; APSFL also serves as an implementing agency for BharatNet in Andhra Pradesh.
- National linkage: BharatNet, the world’s largest rural broadband programme, aims to connect all Gram Panchayats with optical fibre; the Amended BharatNet Programme approved in 2023 extends it toward village-level connectivity with a substantially enhanced outlay.
- A balanced note: State-owned telecom ventures face persistent challenges of subscriber acquisition, competition from private operators and network maintenance costs. Acknowledging that infrastructure creation is easier than sustainable operation makes the answer analytical rather than promotional.

## Conclusion

The AP Cloud Initiative and the Fibre Grid together illustrate a coherent strategy: the Fibre Grid built the transmission layer, the Cloud Initiative built the compute and application layer, and RTGS now runs analytics on top of both. Their design lesson has wider value — the decision to use electricity poles rather than new trenches shows that infrastructure gaps in India are often solved faster by reusing existing rights-of-way than by building parallel networks. With the Visakhapatnam AI hub adding hyperscale capacity, Andhra Pradesh is positioned to host digital infrastructure rather than only consume it.

## Value addition
- MeghRaj (GI Cloud): the Government of India Cloud Initiative; NIC National Cloud services from National Data Centres at Bhubaneswar, Delhi, Hyderabad and Pune; over 18,000 virtual servers provisioned to more than 1,100 ministries and departments.
- Cloud models to name precisely: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS; public / private / hybrid / community deployment; and the associated concerns of data sovereignty, vendor lock-in and latency.
- BharatNet: implemented through BBNL and BSNL with State agencies such as APSFL; the Amended BharatNet Programme (2023) expands from Gram Panchayat to village-level connectivity and adds a ring-topology design for reliability.
- AP digital infrastructure to name: APSFL (Fibre Grid, ADSS aerial fibre, DWDM backbone, ~23,000 km); AP State Data Centre; APEITA (AP Electronics and IT Agency); RTGS, Amaravati, with its unified data lake, AWARE platform and Mana Mitra WhatsApp governance (1,126 services, 58.2 lakh citizens); Google AI hub, Visakhapatnam.
- Why Visakhapatnam for data centres: coastal location gives direct access to submarine cable landing stations (lower latency to international networks), plus availability of power and land — the same factors that drive global data-centre siting.
- Related national frameworks: National Broadband Mission; National Digital Communications Policy 2018; Digital India; PM-WANI for public Wi-Fi hotspots; Common Service Centres as assisted-access points for citizens who cannot use digital services unaided.
- SDG linkage: SDG 9.c — significantly increase access to ICT and strive to provide universal and affordable internet access.
