## Introduction

Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) is integrated software that unifies an organisation’s core functions — finance, human resources, procurement, supply chain and operations — around a single shared database, so that a transaction entered once updates every dependent record. Its defining benefit is the elimination of reconciliation between departmental systems; its defining difficulty is that it forces the organisation to standardise processes it has historically run its own way.

## (a) Critical issues in the execution of ERP projects
- Process re-engineering versus customisation — the central dilemma. ERP embeds standardised best-practice workflows. An organisation must either change its processes to fit the software, or customise the software to fit its processes. Excessive customisation raises cost, delays go-live and, critically, makes future version upgrades difficult because every customisation must be rebuilt. CAG reports on government IT rollouts have repeatedly noted that over-customisation created long-term maintenance liabilities.
- Change management and user resistance. ERP makes work visible and auditable, removing informal discretion — which is precisely why staff resist it. Where training is inadequate, users maintain parallel manual registers, and the organisation bears the cost of the system without the benefit. In government, transferable postings compound this: trained users move on before proficiency is institutionalised.
- Data migration and master-data quality. Legacy records are typically incomplete, duplicated and inconsistently coded. Migrating them without cleansing means the ERP produces authoritative-looking outputs from unreliable inputs — the most damaging failure mode, because errors become harder to detect once they carry the system’s credibility.
- Vendor and contract governance. Weak tendering, vague Service Level Agreements and unclear ownership of source code create dependence on a single vendor and disputes over scope. Public procurement through GeM and standardised MeitY contract templates address part of this.
- Absence of executive sponsorship. ERP crosses departmental boundaries, so decisions on standardising a process cannot be taken by any one department head. Without sustained ownership at the highest level, projects drift into scope creep and indefinite pilots.
- Integration and interoperability. An ERP must exchange data with payment gateways, statutory systems (GST, TDS) and identity systems (Aadhaar-based authentication); poorly specified interfaces are a common cause of go-live failure.

## Indian public-sector ERP-type systems worth naming
- PFMS (Public Financial Management System): tracks fund flow from the Union Budget to the final beneficiary, integrating with the Aadhaar Payment Bridge — the backbone of DBT.
- IFMIS: Integrated Financial Management Information Systems operated by State treasuries for budgeting, expenditure and accounting.
- GeM (Government e-Marketplace): end-to-end public procurement, from catalogue to payment.
- e-Office (NIC): digital file movement and approvals across ministries, with SPARROW for performance appraisals.
- AP instance: Andhra Pradesh’s Comprehensive Financial Management System (CFMS) consolidated the State’s budgeting, treasury, payroll and pension functions onto an integrated enterprise platform — a State-level ERP implementation, and a useful AP illustration of both the promise and the change-management difficulty of such projects.

## (b) Note on Local Area Network (LAN)
- Definition: a network connecting devices within a limited geographic area — an office, building or campus — under a single administrative control, offering high speed and low latency.
- Components: end devices, network interface cards, switches, routers, wireless access points, and structured cabling.
- Topologies: star (the dominant modern form, all devices connected to a central switch), bus, ring and mesh.
- Standards:IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) for wired LANs, supporting speeds from 100 Mbps to 10 Gbps and beyond; IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) for wireless LANs.
- Distinction to state: LAN (building/campus) versus MAN (city-scale) versus WAN (geographically dispersed). India’s government network hierarchy illustrates this: departmental LANs connect to State Wide Area Networks (SWANs) and NICNET, with the National Knowledge Network (NKN) linking universities and research institutions at multi-gigabit speeds.
- Role in e-governance: LANs carry e-Office file movement, ERP transactions, video conferencing and departmental databases — the physical substrate without which any e-governance application is unusable in the office where work actually happens.
- Security: VLAN segmentation to isolate sensitive traffic, firewalls at the gateway, network access control and monitoring — mandated in government ICT security guidelines and audited under CERT-In’s empanelled auditor framework.

## Conclusion

ERP and LAN operate at opposite ends of the same system: the LAN provides the connectivity, the ERP the integrated logic that connectivity carries. Indian experience with PFMS, GeM and State systems such as AP’s CFMS shows that the technology is rarely the binding constraint — process standardisation, data quality and sustained leadership are. Where these are addressed, integrated systems deliver exactly what governance reform demands: a single, auditable version of the truth.

## Value addition
- ERP modules typically implemented: financial accounting and controlling, human capital management and payroll, materials management and procurement, sales and distribution, plant maintenance, and project systems.
- Indian government platforms with ERP characteristics: PFMS; State IFMIS/CFMS; GeM; e-Office and SPARROW; GSTN; IRCTC and Indian Railways’ freight and asset systems; and the Integrated Government Online Training (iGOT) Karmayogi platform for capacity building — the training complement without which any ERP rollout underperforms.
- The classic ERP failure pattern to cite: “customise to fit legacy processes –> cost and time overrun –> upgrade becomes impossible –> system freezes at go-live version.” The corrective is business process re-engineering before implementation, not after.
- Network terminology for precision: LAN / MAN / WAN; bandwidth versus latency; switch (operates within a network) versus router (connects networks); VLAN (logical segmentation of a physical LAN).
- Government network infrastructure: NICNET; State Wide Area Networks (SWAN); National Knowledge Network (NKN) connecting institutions of higher learning and research; the Secure Government Cloud under MeghRaj.
- A framing line worth using: an ERP does not automate an organisation — it standardises it. That is why ERP projects fail as change-management exercises far more often than as technology projects.

## Introduction

India’s computer and IT industry is the clearest example of a sector that grew despite, rather than because of, its initial policy environment — it expanded after 1991 in an area that pre-liberalisation licensing had barely regulated. From roughly 1% of GDP in the late 1990s, the IT-BPM sector now contributes about 7.5% of GDP, with revenue of approximately USD 283 billion in FY 2024-25 (NASSCOM industry estimates), making it India’s most successful export-oriented services industry.

## Contribution to output and exports
- The sector’s share of GDP rose from a little over 1% in the late 1990s to about 7.5% today. Its export orientation is unusually high: software and IT-enabled services account for roughly half of India’s total services exports, and services exports have been the principal stabiliser of India’s current account, offsetting a persistent merchandise trade deficit. This is the sector’s most important macroeconomic function — it finances India’s oil and electronics imports.

## Employment and human capital
- The industry employs roughly 5.8 million professionals directly (NASSCOM), with an indirect multiplier estimated at three to four times that in transport, real estate, retail and food services around IT clusters.
- Women constitute a substantially higher share of the IT workforce than of India’s organised sector generally — one of the few large industries where formal female participation is comparatively strong.
- It created a demand signal for engineering education that reshaped Indian higher education, for better (mass technical enrolment) and worse (proliferation of low-quality private colleges and persistent employability gaps).

## The structural shift — Global Capability Centres
- The most significant recent change is the move from outsourced services to captive Global Capability Centres (GCCs) — offshore units of multinationals doing R&D, analytics, product engineering and finance in-house. India hosts the large majority of the world’s GCCs. This shifts India up the value chain: from executing specifications to designing products, which raises wages and retains intellectual property-adjacent work in India.

## Spillovers into the wider economy
- Digital public infrastructure: the domestic technical talent pool made Aadhaar, UPI and CoWIN buildable at population scale — arguably the industry’s largest social return, distinct from its export earnings.
- Start-up ecosystem: DPIIT-recognised start-ups grew from about 500 in 2016 to over 2 lakh in 2025 (Economic Survey 2025-26), concentrated in fintech, edtech, healthtech and SaaS.
- The digital economy overall contributed about 11.74% of GVA (Rs. 31.64 lakh crore) and employed 14.67 million workers, growing at nearly twice the rate of the overall economy and projected to reach around 20% of GVA by 2029-30 (MeitY-commissioned assessment).

## Limitations — the basis for a critical comment
- Export dependence: revenues are concentrated in North American and European clients, transmitting their recessions directly into Indian hiring.
- Regional concentration: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, NCR and Chennai capture most activity, so IT growth has widened rather than narrowed inter-regional disparity. Tier-2 expansion — including Visakhapatnam and Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh — is the corrective, and the Google AI hub at Visakhapatnam (about USD 15 billion over 2026-2030, its largest outside the United States) is the most significant such investment announced to date.
- Services-heavy, hardware-light: India built a world-class software industry atop imported hardware. The India Semiconductor Mission and electronics PLI are belated attempts to correct this asymmetry.
- Automation and AI risk: the linear headcount-to-revenue model that built the industry is directly exposed to generative AI, which compresses precisely the routine coding and support work that employed the largest numbers.

## Conclusion

The computer industry transformed India’s economy on three fronts — it financed the external account, created the country’s largest organised white-collar workforce, and supplied the technical capability behind India’s digital public infrastructure. But the growth model that produced these gains is now under pressure from AI-driven automation and client concentration. Sustaining the contribution requires moving from labour arbitrage to product and IP creation, deepening domestic hardware capability, and dispersing activity to tier-2 centres — the direction in which GCCs and investments such as the Visakhapatnam AI hub already point.

## Value addition
- Sector data (NASSCOM industry estimates, FY 2024-25): revenue approximately USD 283 billion; direct employment about 5.8 million; roughly 7.5% of GDP; software and ITeS constitute around half of total services exports.
- Digital economy data: about 11.74% of GVA (Rs. 31.64 lakh crore), 14.67 million workers, projected to reach roughly 20% of GVA by 2029-30 — growing at nearly twice the pace of the overall economy.
- Historical markers to cite: SEEPZ Mumbai (1973) as India’s first software export base; the Software Technology Parks of India scheme (1991) with duty-free imports and single-window clearance; Y2K remediation (1998-2000) as the moment Indian firms won global credibility at scale; the National Task Force on IT and Software Development (1998).
- Global Capability Centres: captive offshore centres performing R&D, engineering and analytics; India hosts the world’s largest concentration; they represent the shift from services delivery to product ownership.
- AP-specific IT assets: Google AI hub, Visakhapatnam; IT corridors at Visakhapatnam and Tirupati; APEITA; Sri City as an electronics manufacturing cluster; the Amaravati Quantum Valley Tech Park.
- The counterpoint worth stating: IT’s contribution to employment is far smaller than its contribution to output — around 5.8 million jobs in a workforce of over 500 million. It is a productivity and foreign-exchange story, not a mass-employment one, and answers that conflate the two miss the point.

## Introduction

Environmental degradation is difficult to govern because it is diffuse, slow and hard to measure — a polluting unit, an encroached wetland or a felled patch of forest is individually small and collectively decisive. Information technology addresses precisely this measurement problem: it makes environmental change visible, continuous and attributable. India has built a substantial set of digital environmental platforms, from CPCB’s monitoring network to MoEFCC’s PARIVESH single-window system.

## Monitoring — making the invisible measurable
- Air: CPCB operates a national network of Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) feeding real-time data into the National Air Quality Index, published to citizens through the SAMEER app. This data is the operational basis of the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), which sets city-wise particulate reduction targets — targets that would be unenforceable without continuous measurement.
- Industrial emissions and effluent:Online Continuous Emission and Effluent Monitoring Systems (OCEMS) transmit stack and outfall readings directly from major polluting industries to pollution control board servers, shifting regulation from periodic inspection to continuous telemetry. This is the single most important structural change in Indian pollution enforcement.
- Water: CPCB’s national water quality monitoring programme and the National Water Informatics Centre consolidate hydrological and quality data.

## Remote sensing and analysis — seeing at scale
- Bhuvan, the NRSC/ISRO geoportal, hosts forest, water, land-use and disaster applications, including the Active Fire Mapper and change-monitoring tools used by State forest departments.
- The Forest Survey of India produces the biennial India State of Forest Report using satellite interpretation; ISFR 2023 assessed India’s forest and tree cover at about 25.17% of geographical area. FSI also runs a near-real-time forest fire alert system that pushes SMS alerts to field staff within hours of a satellite detecting a fire — converting satellite data into an actionable field instruction, which is the real test of any monitoring system.
- GIS and AI analytics map wetlands, wastelands, habitat corridors and vulnerable zones for land-use planning and climate-vulnerability assessment.

## Regulation and compliance — digitising governance
- PARIVESH (Pro-Active Responsive facilitation by Interactive and Virtuous Environmental Single Window Hub), MoEFCC’s web-based workflow platform, handles online submission and tracking of environment, forest, wildlife and CRZ clearance proposals at central, State and district levels. Its contribution is auditability: every stage of a clearance carries a timestamp and an identified decision-maker.
- EPR portals administered by CPCB track producer obligations under the E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022, Plastic Waste Management Rules and battery waste rules, issuing tradable certificates against verified recycling.
- ENVIS hubs disseminate environmental information across thematic areas.

## Conservation and wildlife protection
- M-STrIPES (Monitoring System for Tigers — Intensive Protection and Ecological Status), developed by the Wildlife Institute of India for the NTCA, digitises patrol routes, sightings and threat records from field staff and underpins the quadrennial All India Tiger Estimation — the world’s largest camera-trap-based wildlife survey.
- Camera traps, GPS collars, drones and acoustic sensors track animal movement, detect poaching intrusion and reduce human-wildlife conflict.
- e-Green Watch monitors compensatory afforestation plantations and CAMPA fund utilisation, addressing the long-standing problem that afforestation was recorded on paper but unverifiable on the ground.

## Resource efficiency and citizen mobilisation
- Smart grids and smart metering under RDSS reduce distribution losses; Intelligent Transport Systems cut idling emissions; PM Surya Ghar enables household solar with digital net metering.
- Mission LIFE (Lifestyle for Environment) uses digital campaigns and the Meri LiFE platform to translate climate policy into individual behaviour, and India champions Mission LIFE internationally as a demand-side complement to supply-side decarbonisation.
- AP instance: the Real Time Governance Society’s AWARE platform integrates satellite, drone, IoT sensor and CCTV feeds for real-time environmental and disaster alerts, strengthened by a five-year MoU with ISRO’s SHAR, Sriharikota (June 2025). RTGS has since built an AI-based City Flood Alert system with APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar providing 48-hour rainfall outlooks and six-hour flash-flood warnings — significant for a State with a 1,053-km cyclone-exposed coast and the ecologically sensitive Coringa mangroves and Kolleru Lake.

## Limitations worth noting
- IT has its own environmental footprint: data centres consume large volumes of electricity and water, and e-waste is among India’s fastest-growing waste streams.
- Data without enforcement capacity changes nothing — monitoring stations detect violations that under-staffed pollution control boards cannot act on.
- Coverage gaps: monitoring stations are concentrated in large cities, leaving industrial small towns and rural areas comparatively unmeasured.

## Conclusion

Information technology has shifted Indian environmental governance from periodic, inspection-based and contestable to continuous, sensor-based and auditable — and platforms such as PARIVESH, SAMEER, M-STrIPES and the FSI fire alert system show this is an operating reality rather than an aspiration. Its limits are equally clear: measurement is not enforcement, and the digital infrastructure itself carries an energy and e-waste cost. The task ahead is to extend monitoring beyond metropolitan India and to match detection capacity with the institutional capacity to act on what is detected.

## Value addition
- Indian environmental IT platforms to name: PARIVESH (MoEFCC single-window clearance); SAMEER and the National Air Quality Index (CPCB); OCEMS for industrial emissions; Bhuvan (NRSC/ISRO); FSI forest fire alert system and the India State of Forest Report; M-STrIPES (NTCA/WII); e-Green Watch (CAMPA monitoring); EPR portals for e-waste, plastic and battery waste; ENVIS; National Water Informatics Centre.
- Forest data (ISFR 2023, Forest Survey of India): India’s forest and tree cover stands at about 25.17% of geographical area; the National Forest Policy 1988 target is 33%.
- Global context (FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025): world forest area about 4.14 billion hectares, roughly 32% of land area; India accounts for approximately 72,739 thousand hectares, around 2% of the world total; over half the world’s forests lie in just five countries — Russia, Brazil, Canada, the USA and China.
- Policy anchors: National Clean Air Programme; E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 with EPR; Mission LIFE (launched at COP27, with Meri LiFE); National Action Plan on Climate Change and its eight missions; Green Credit Programme.
- The double-edged argument to include: ICT reduces environmental impact through dematerialisation and efficiency, but data centres are energy- and water-intensive and e-waste is growing rapidly — so “green IT” and “IT for green” are distinct questions, and a strong answer separates them.

Q19:
## Introduction

Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs) are the technologies used to create, store, process, transmit and access information — encompassing hardware (devices, networks) and software (applications, platforms, services). The question of whether they dismantle social hierarchy is genuinely contested: ICTs lower the cost of access to information and services, which historically favours those excluded by gatekeepers, but access to ICTs is itself distributed along the very lines of caste, class, gender and geography they are supposed to erase.

## How ICTs break structural barriers
- Disintermediation removes the gatekeeper. The most direct effect is on the intermediary who historically mediated a poor citizen’s access to the state. Aadhaar-enabled DBT transfers entitlements to a bank account without a village-level broker; cumulative DBT transfers had crossed Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 (PIB, November 2025). Where the middleman’s discretion was the mechanism of exclusion, removing him is a structural change, not merely a convenience.
- Education access decoupled from location and institution.DIKSHA and PM e-VIDYA deliver curriculum content in multiple Indian languages, and SWAYAM offers university-level courses free — allowing a student in a district with no good college to access the same lecture as one in a metropolitan university.
- Health access decoupled from specialist availability.eSanjeevani, developed by C-DAC Mohali, crossed 43 crore consultations across 28 States and 8 UTs as on 23 November 2025 (MoHFW, Rajya Sabha reply). Its hub-and-spoke model lets a paramedic at a village Ayushman Arogya Mandir connect a patient to a district specialist — the specialist’s scarcity no longer determines who receives specialist advice.
- Language as a barrier being dismantled.Bhashini, the National Language Translation Mission, builds AI translation and speech models across Indian languages. This matters structurally: English proficiency has functioned as a class filter on access to formal services, and voice-first, vernacular interfaces bypass both that filter and print literacy itself.
- Gender and livelihood. Common Service Centres run by village-level entrepreneurs, many of them women, deliver services locally; SHG federations use digital tools for microfinance and enterprise; Namo Drone Didi places drone technology and its income with women’s self-help groups, placing women in a technically skilled role in an agrarian setting where that is atypical.
- Voice and civic participation. Grievance portals (CPGRAMS), RTI filing online, and platforms such as MyGov reduce the cost of being heard — historically the resource most unequally distributed.
- AP instance: Andhra Pradesh’s Mana Mitra WhatsApp governance platform delivers 1,126 services across 35 departments to 58.2 lakh citizens (2026). Its significance is interface choice: it uses an application citizens already have and know, rather than requiring them to learn a new government app — meeting people where they are is itself an inclusion strategy.

## Where ICTs reproduce rather than break barriers
- The access gap follows existing fault lines. NFHS-5 (2019-21) found that only about a third of rural women had ever used the internet, against a much higher share of rural men. A technology accessed unequally distributes its benefits unequally.
- Digital exclusion can be harsher than analogue exclusion. Where an entitlement is available only digitally, biometric authentication failure among manual labourers and the elderly, or connectivity failure at a ration shop, converts a technical fault into denial of food or pension. The Supreme Court has emphasised that no one should be denied benefits for want of Aadhaar — an acknowledgement that this risk is real.
- Skill and affordability barriers mean device ownership does not equal capability; households often share a single phone, typically controlled by a male member.
- Algorithmic and platform bias can encode historical exclusion into automated decisions — and unlike a human gatekeeper, an algorithm’s refusal is not visibly contestable.
- Quality of service remains uneven in tribal belts and remote areas even where coverage is nominally present.

## Conclusion

ICTs are best understood as barrier-lowering rather than barrier-breaking: they remove the intermediary, the distance and increasingly the language, but they cannot by themselves supply the device, the literacy or the bandwidth that using them requires. Whether they equalise or entrench therefore depends on design choices — assisted access through Common Service Centres, vernacular and voice-first interfaces such as Bhashini, mandatory offline fallbacks for entitlement delivery, and targeted digital literacy for women. Where those choices are made, as AP’s WhatsApp-based service delivery suggests, ICTs genuinely widen who can reach the state.

## Value addition

(The original had no Value Addition for this question — this section is entirely new.)

- Definition to cite: ICTs cover both hardware (devices, networks, infrastructure) and software (applications, platforms, services) enabling connectivity, information sharing and knowledge dissemination; the UN treats access to ICT as an enabler across the SDGs.
- Digital literacy and access schemes:PMGDISHA (Pradhan Mantri Gramin Digital Saksharta Abhiyan) for rural digital literacy; Common Service Centres as assisted-access points; PM-WANI for public Wi-Fi; BharatNet for Gram Panchayat connectivity; ULLAS for adult literacy through a mobile app.
- Inclusion-specific platforms:Bhashini (National Language Translation Mission) and its Anuvaad and voice models; DIKSHA, PM e-VIDYA, SWAYAM and NPTEL in education; Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan and the Sugamya Bharat app for accessibility for persons with disabilities; e-Sanjeevani in health.
- The key data points: eSanjeevani over 43 crore consultations (MoHFW, November 2025); cumulative DBT transfers Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 (PIB); NFHS-5 (2019-21) internet-use gender gap; UPI as the world’s largest real-time payment system by transaction volume.
- Conceptual distinctions that impress: the first-level digital divide (access to devices and connectivity), the second-level divide (skills and usage capability) and the third-level divide (ability to convert usage into tangible outcomes). Most Indian policy addresses the first; the second and third are where the deficit now lies.
- The exclusion counter-argument to hold ready: technology-mediated entitlement delivery creates a new failure mode — silent exclusion, where a person who cannot authenticate simply does not appear in the system rather than being visibly refused. Robust systems therefore require exception-handling and offline fallback by design.

Q20:
## Introduction

The digital divide is the gap between individuals, groups and regions in their ability to access and benefit from information and communication technologies. It is conventionally understood in three levels: the first-level divide (access to devices and connectivity), the second-level divide (skills and capability to use them), and the third-level divide (ability to convert usage into tangible economic or social outcomes). India’s position has shifted decisively across these levels in the last decade.

## Where India now stands — the first-level divide has narrowed sharply

The NSO’s Comprehensive Modular Survey: Telecom, conducted January-March 2025 as part of the 80th round of the National Sample Survey, found that: - about 86.3% of Indian households have internet access within household premises, and 85.5% possess at least one smartphone; - in the 15-29 age group, 92.7% of rural persons and 95.7% of urban persons had used the internet in the preceding three months — a rural-urban gap of only about three percentage points; - among those in that age group able to bank online, 99.5% could transact through UPI.

This is a transformation, and an answer still quoting sub-30% access figures would be describing a different country.

## Where the divide persists
- Gender. Device ownership and control remain unequal even where household access exists: a shared family phone is typically controlled by a male member, so a woman’s access is mediated and intermittent. NFHS-5 (2019-21) recorded a wide gap in whether women had ever used the internet — the single most persistent dimension of the Indian divide.
- Age. The survey figures above are for 15-29 year-olds; older adults, who disproportionately depend on pensions and health entitlements delivered digitally, have far lower usage.
- Skills, not access (the second level). Possessing a smartphone is not the same as being able to fill an online form, verify a source, or complete an e-KYC — and self-reported ICT skills are consistently lower than device ownership.
- Meaningful use (the third level). A phone used only for calls and video does not generate the livelihood or educational returns that policy assumes; the outcome divide is the least measured and most consequential.
- Quality and reliability, particularly in tribal belts, hilly districts and among the urban poor, where nominal coverage does not mean usable bandwidth.

## Problems this creates
- Economic exclusion: small producers unable to use e-commerce, e-NAM or digital credit remain dependent on local intermediaries.
- Governance exclusion: where entitlements are available only digitally, the least capable users bear the highest cost of failure — and exclusion is silent rather than visibly refused.
- Cyber-fraud vulnerability: first-time users onboarded rapidly into digital payments without corresponding literacy are the primary targets of “digital arrest” and UPI fraud, which the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) tracks. Rapid access expansion without skills expansion actively creates this risk.

## Strategies to overcome the divide
- Infrastructure — largely delivered, now consolidating.BharatNet connects Gram Panchayats with optical fibre, extended by the Amended BharatNet Programme (2023) toward village-level connectivity with a ring topology for reliability; the National Broadband Mission and 5G rollout complete the backbone.
- Affordability.PM-WANI (Department of Telecommunications, December 2020) allows local shops and establishments to operate public Wi-Fi hotspots as Public Data Offices without licence or registration fee — designed to give the urban poor and rural households low-cost access and small entrepreneurs an income stream.
- Digital literacy — where effort must now concentrate.PMGDISHA targeted rural households for basic digital literacy; ULLAS delivers adult literacy through a mobile app; iGOT Karmayogi builds capability within government itself. The policy priority must shift from connecting people to enabling them.
- Assisted access as the bridge.Common Service Centres, staffed by Village Level Entrepreneurs, allow a citizen who cannot transact independently to still receive the service — the pragmatic recognition that not everyone will become a digital user, and that entitlement should not depend on it.
- Language and interface design.Bhashini, the National Language Translation Mission, builds AI translation and speech models across Indian languages. Voice-first vernacular interfaces bypass both the English filter and print literacy — structurally the most promising intervention for the second-level divide.
- Gender-targeted measures. Women-led CSCs, SHG-based digital training, Namo Drone Didi, and DST’s Vigyan Jyoti for girls in STEM.
- Education.DIKSHA, PM e-VIDYA and SWAYAM, with NEP 2020’s emphasis on digital infrastructure in schools.
- AP instance: Andhra Pradesh delivers 1,126 services across 35 departments to 58.2 lakh citizens through Mana Mitra on WhatsApp (2026) — an interface-choice strategy that meets citizens on an application they already use rather than requiring them to learn a government app, complemented by Village and Ward Secretariats as the physical assisted-access layer.

## Conclusion

India’s digital divide has changed shape rather than disappeared: with household internet access at 86.3% and near-parity in youth internet use between rural and urban areas (CMS: Telecom, 2025), the connectivity problem is substantially solved. What remains is harder and less visible — the gender gap in device control, the skills gap among older and less literate users, and the outcome gap between having a smartphone and earning from one. Policy must therefore pivot from laying fibre to building capability, with assisted access through CSCs and vernacular voice interfaces as the guarantee that no entitlement is lost to a skills deficit.

- The three-level divide framework: first level (access), second level (skills and usage), third level (outcomes and benefit). Naming this framework explicitly is the fastest way to signal conceptual command.

Q21:
## Introduction

Information Technology addresses rural India’s defining constraint — distance from services. A farmer’s distance from a market, a patient’s from a specialist, a student’s from a good teacher and a citizen’s from an office are all costs that connectivity reduces. Telemedicine, in particular, has become the clearest demonstration: it substitutes bandwidth for the specialist posting that rural India has never been able to fill.

## (a) Role of IT in rural development — by sector
- Agriculture. IT delivers weather forecasts, market prices, pest advisories and soil information at the point of decision. e-NAM connects mandis into a unified national market, allowing a farmer to see prices beyond the local trader’s quotation — which alters bargaining power, not merely information. The Digital Agriculture Mission (approved 2024) builds AgriStack — the Farmers’ Registry, Geo-referenced Village Maps and Crop Sown Registry — plus the Krishi Decision Support System, so that advisories can finally be farm-specific rather than district-generic. Kisan Call Centres and Kisan Suvidha provide voice-based access for non-literate users.
- Education.DIKSHA and PM e-VIDYA deliver curriculum-linked content in multiple Indian languages; SWAYAM and NPTEL offer higher education free. The structural gain is that a teacher shortage no longer means a content shortage.
- Health. Telemedicine, developed below, plus mobile applications used by ASHA and ANM workers for maternal health, immunisation tracking (U-WIN) and outbreak reporting through the Integrated Health Information Platform.
- Governance and financial inclusion.Common Service Centres deliver certificates, pensions and scheme applications locally; digitised land records reduce disputes; DBT routes entitlements directly to Aadhaar-linked accounts, with cumulative transfers crossing Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 (PIB, November 2025); AePS allows cash withdrawal against a fingerprint at a Business Correspondent’s micro-ATM.

Conditions for effective implementation — the part most answers skip:

- Appropriate technology: low-cost, low-bandwidth, power-tolerant solutions; voice and vernacular interfaces rather than text-and-English apps.
- Connectivity and power: BharatNet backhaul is necessary but insufficient without reliable last-mile bandwidth and electricity at the delivery point.
- Assisted access: CSCs and village-level entrepreneurs, because a significant share of users will always need intermediated help — designing for the independent user alone guarantees exclusion.
- Capacity building and local language: training for both citizens and frontline staff; content in the language of use.
- Community ownership: the classic Indian illustration is the Gyandoot intranet project in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, an early rural e-governance experiment whose lesson was that sustainability depends on local ownership and a viable revenue model, not on the technology.
- Convergence and data quality: platforms must interoperate with Aadhaar, land records and payment rails, and the underlying registries must be accurate.

## (b) Telemedicine — definition and types

Definition: telemedicine is the delivery of healthcare services using information and communication technologies where distance is a critical factor, by healthcare professionals, for diagnosis, treatment, prevention, research and continuing education — the framing used by the WHO and reflected in India’s Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, 2020, which gave teleconsultation formal legal standing.

- **Type** — Mode · Indian example
- **Synchronous** — Live video/audio, real time · eSanjeevani OPD consultation
- **Asynchronous** — Store-and-forward, reviewed later · Teleradiology, teledermatology
- **Remote Patient Monitoring** — Continuous device data · Wearables for BP, glucose, ECG

- Synchronous (real-time) telemedicine: live two-way interaction by video or audio. eSanjeevani, developed by C-DAC Mohali for MoHFW, is the world’s largest such platform, crossing 43 crore consultations across 28 States and 8 UTs as on 23 November 2025 (MoHFW, Rajya Sabha reply).
- Asynchronous (store-and-forward) telemedicine: images, scans or lab reports are transmitted for expert review later. Used extensively in teleradiology, teledermatology and telepathology — efficient because it does not require the specialist and patient to be available simultaneously, which is the binding constraint in scarce-specialist systems.
- Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM): wearable or home devices transmit physiological data continuously for chronic disease management — hypertension, diabetes, cardiac conditions — enabling intervention before an episode rather than after.
- A fourth category worth adding:mHealth — health information, adherence reminders and behaviour-change messaging delivered by mobile, as in the Kilkari and Mobile Academy programmes for maternal health.
- eSanjeevani’s two verticals, an important distinction: eSanjeevani AB-HWC (doctor-to-doctor, assisted, hub-and-spoke, linking Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to specialists) and eSanjeevani OPD (patient-to-doctor, direct). The assisted vertical carries most of the volume, because the patients who need it most cannot use a direct app.

## Conclusion

IT’s contribution to rural development is best understood as the collapsing of distance — to markets, classrooms, specialists and government offices — and telemedicine is its most measurable expression, with eSanjeevani converting a paramedic plus a video link into a specialist consultation. But the technology delivers only where the implementation conditions hold: vernacular interfaces, assisted access, reliable connectivity and accurate underlying data. Where these are absent, rural IT reproduces the exclusion it was meant to remove.

## Value addition
- eSanjeevani: cloud-based national telemedicine platform of MoHFW, designed and maintained by C-DAC Mohali; two modules — eSanjeevani AB-HWC (2019, doctor-to-doctor, hub-and-spoke) and eSanjeevani OPD (2020, doctor-to-patient, launched during the COVID-19 lockdown); over 43 crore consultations as on 23 November 2025.
- Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, 2020: issued by MoHFW with NITI Aayog and the Board of Governors in supersession of the Medical Council of India; they define registered medical practitioner obligations, consent, and which medicines may be prescribed by teleconsultation — the legal foundation without which telemedicine could not scale.

- AP-specific rural service infrastructure:Rythu Bharosa Kendras as village-level agriculture service points integrating input supply, advisory and procurement; Village and Ward Secretariats with Grama Volunteers for doorstep delivery; Mana Mitra for WhatsApp-based service access.
- A precise definitional point:telemedicine (clinical services at a distance) is a subset of telehealth (which also covers non-clinical services such as training, administration and health education). Making this distinction is a quick credibility marker.

## Introduction

Information Technology delivers its largest gains where a system’s constraint is information rather than resources. Medicine and watershed management are both such systems: the doctor’s problem is often incomplete patient information, and the watershed planner’s is that a drainage basin is too large to observe from the ground. IT addresses both by making the invisible measurable.

## (a) Benefits of IT in medicine and medical health
- Access decoupled from location. Telemedicine allows specialist advice to reach where specialists are not posted. eSanjeevani crossed 43 crore consultations across 28 States and 8 UTs as on 23 November 2025 (MoHFW, Rajya Sabha reply) — the world’s largest government telemedicine deployment.
- Portable, longitudinal records. Under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (2021), the ABHA account links a person’s health records with consent-based sharing. The benefit is clinical, not merely administrative: a doctor seeing a patient’s medication history avoids duplicate tests and dangerous drug interactions. Portability matters most for migrant workers, whose records previously ended at the district boundary.
- Diagnostic accuracy and triage. AI-assisted reading of chest X-rays for tuberculosis and retinal images for diabetic retinopathy allows screening at the primary level, reserving scarce radiologists and ophthalmologists for confirmed cases — a rationing gain rather than a replacement of clinicians.
- Disease surveillance in near-real time. The Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) enables outbreak detection from case reporting; NIKSHAY tracks TB patients through treatment and links to Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana payments; U-WIN tracks routine immunisation, preventing dropouts between doses.
- Financial protection and claims integrity.AB-PMJAY processes claims digitally against a beneficiary database, providing Rs. 5 lakh cover to about 12.37 crore families, with fraud analytics on claim patterns.
- Research, training and manufacturing. Genome analysis (as in INSACOG’s SARS-CoV-2 surveillance led by institutions including CSIR-CCMB), virtual simulation in medical training, and digital design in medical devices — the last directly relevant to the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam, India’s first medical devices manufacturing park, which houses the DBT-supported Kalam Institute of Health Technology.
- The constraint to acknowledge: digital health assumes a digitally reachable patient. Where it does not hold, assisted models — teleconsultation at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir rather than a direct-to-patient app — are what actually deliver.

## (b) Watershed and its management through IT

Definition: a watershed (or catchment) is a natural drainage unit — an area of land from which all surface runoff drains to a common outlet, such as a stream, river or reservoir. It is bounded by a ridge line, and is significant because it is the natural unit of hydrological management: water, soil and vegetation behave as one system within it, so treating a watershed as a whole is more effective than treating individual plots.

Why watershed management particularly suits IT: a watershed is defined by terrain, not by revenue boundaries, so its delineation requires elevation data; its condition changes seasonally across large areas; and its treatment structures are dispersed and hard to verify by inspection. Remote sensing, GIS and geotagging solve all three problems.

## Named Indian applications
- WDC-PMKSY 2.0 — the Watershed Development Component of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana, run by the Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, approved in December 2021 for 2021-26 with a physical target of 49.50 lakh hectares and an indicative central outlay of Rs. 8,134 crore. Unit cost was revised from Rs. 12,000 to Rs. 22,000 per hectare for plains and up to Rs. 28,000 for hilly, difficult and LWE areas; springshed rejuvenation was added on NITI Aayog’s recommendation; States are explicitly directed to use GIS and remote sensing for project planning.
- Srishti and Drishti — under a DoLR-NRSC arrangement, Srishti is a customised Bhuvan web platform for satellite-based monitoring, image comparison against Detailed Project Reports, land-cover change analysis and a project dashboard; Drishti is the companion mobile application for geotagged field photography uploaded directly to the web-GIS server. Together they give the landscape view and the ground-truth view — the pairing that makes remote monitoring credible.
- Bhuvan (NRSC/ISRO) provides the underlying geoportal, also used for geotagging assets under Per Drop More Crop; Bhuvan hosts State-specific applications including asset mapping for Andhra Pradesh.
- Digital Elevation Models from CartoSat data enable automated watershed delineation and slope analysis; India-WRIS consolidates national water resources information; Atal Bhujal Yojana uses community-monitored groundwater data for participatory aquifer management.
- Decision support and convergence: GIS overlays of soil, slope, rainfall and land use identify optimal check-dam sites and enable convergence with MGNREGA labour budgets, so that structure siting is evidence-based rather than discretionary.
- AP relevance: Rayalaseema — among India’s most drought-prone regions — depends on watershed treatment and groundwater recharge; satellite-based monitoring of structures and land-cover change is directly consequential for the region’s agricultural viability.

## Conclusion

In both domains, IT’s contribution is the same in kind: it converts something previously unobservable — a patient’s full history, a watershed’s condition across seasons — into data that can be acted upon. eSanjeevani and ABDM have made specialist care and health records portable; Srishti and Drishti have made watershed works verifiable from orbit and from the field simultaneously. In each case the limiting factor is now institutional rather than technical: data changes outcomes only where there is capacity to act on it.

## Value addition
- Watershed terminology:watershed / catchment / drainage basin are used interchangeably in Indian policy; a springshed is the recharge area feeding a spring, added as an activity under WDC-PMKSY 2.0; the ridge-to-valley principle requires treatment to begin at the highest point of the watershed.
- WDC-PMKSY 2.0 details: DoLR, Ministry of Rural Development; 2021-26; 49.50 lakh ha target; Rs. 8,134 crore indicative central outlay; funding 60:40 centre-state (90:10 for hilly and North-Eastern States, 100% central for UTs); project period reduced from 4-7 years to 3-5 years; predecessor was the Integrated Watershed Management Programme (2009-10), merged into PMKSY in 2015-16.
- Geospatial platforms to name: Bhuvan (NRSC/ISRO); Srishti (Bhuvan-based WDC monitoring) and Drishti (geotagged field data app); India-WRIS; Bhuvan-PDMC for Per Drop More Crop; SVAMITVA for drone-based rural property mapping.

## Introduction

India’s software industry is unusually spatially concentrated: a handful of cities account for the bulk of output, employment and exports. This concentration was not planned but path-dependent — it followed the location of engineering institutions, early Software Technology Parks and airport connectivity. Underpinning the whole industry is communication infrastructure: modems, wireless systems and layered networks that make distributed software delivery possible.

## (a) India’s five major IT hubs and their specialisations
- Bengaluru — the “Silicon Valley of India”; headquarters of Infosys and Wipro, the largest concentration of R&D centres and product companies, and India’s densest start-up ecosystem. It accounts for the single largest share of India’s software exports.
- Hyderabad — HITEC City and the Financial District; major R&D and campus presence of global technology firms, with strength in cloud, enterprise software and life-sciences informatics.
- Pune — IT services, software testing, engineering and automotive software, benefiting from proximity to Mumbai and a deep engineering-education base.
- Chennai — strength in hardware, embedded systems, BFSI back-office operations and, increasingly, electronics manufacturing in its wider region.
- Gurugram / NCR (with Noida) — IT-enabled services, business process management, consulting and start-up activity, aided by proximity to corporate headquarters and the national capital.

The current shift — worth adding to any answer on this question: activity is dispersing to tier-2 cities (Coimbatore, Kochi, Indore, Bhubaneswar, Jaipur, Visakhapatnam) driven by lower costs, talent retention and post-pandemic distributed work. Andhra Pradesh’s most significant development is Google’s AI hub at Visakhapatnam — approximately USD 15 billion over 2026-2030, with gigawatt-scale data-centre capacity and a subsea cable gateway, described as its largest AI hub outside the United States (newsonair, Government of India, October 2025).

## Main factors required for the growth of the software industry
- Skilled manpower at scale. India’s engineering education system produces graduates in very large numbers annually — the workforce base without which the labour-arbitrage model could not have worked. The qualification is that employability, not enrolment, is the binding constraint today.
- Policy and infrastructure support.Software Technology Parks of India (1991) offered duty-free imports, single-window clearance and dedicated data links to export-oriented units — the single most consequential policy intervention for the industry’s take-off. Later: SEZs, Digital India, Startup India, and now the RDI Scheme for deep-tech R&D.
- Cost advantage. Wage differentials with developed economies made offshoring commercially compelling; this advantage is narrowing as domestic wages rise and automation reduces headcount requirements.
- English proficiency and time-zone complementarity. English enabled direct client interaction, and the time difference with North America and Europe made overnight delivery cycles possible.
- Connectivity and reliable infrastructure. International bandwidth, submarine cable landing stations, power reliability and urban amenities — which is precisely why coastal cities like Visakhapatnam and Chennai are attractive for data centres.
- A deep domestic market and DPI. UPI, Aadhaar and ONDC created large-scale domestic demand for software engineering, reducing the industry’s earlier total dependence on exports.

(b) Essay: modem, wireless and networking systems

The modem. A modem (modulator-demodulator) converts a computer’s digital signal into a form transmissible over an analogue medium — a telephone line, coaxial cable or optical fibre — and reconverts the incoming signal at the other end. Its evolution tracks the internet’s own: from dial-up modems limited to about 56 kbps, through DSL and cable modems, to today’s Optical Network Terminals in fibre-to-the-home connections, where the conversion is between electrical and optical signals.

Wireless systems. Wireless communication transmits data as electromagnetic waves, removing the physical cable and with it the constraint of location. -Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) for local wireless access, now central to PM-WANI public hotspots. - Bluetooth for short-range personal device pairing. - Cellular generations: 2G (digital voice and SMS), 3G (mobile data), 4G/LTE (broadband mobility), 5G (high bandwidth, very low latency and high device density — the last of which is what makes large-scale IoT deployment feasible). - Satellite communication for locations terrestrial networks cannot economically reach, and NB-IoT for low-power sensor networks.

## Types of networks, classified by geographic scale
- PAN (Personal Area Network): a few metres — a phone paired with earphones or a smartwatch.
- LAN (Local Area Network): a building or campus, under single administrative control; typically Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) over a star topology with switches.
- MAN (Metropolitan Area Network): city-scale, interconnecting multiple LANs — as in a municipal fibre network or a city surveillance backbone.
- WAN (Wide Area Network): spanning regions or countries; the internet is the largest WAN. India’s government hierarchy illustrates the layering: departmental LANs connect to State Wide Area Networks (SWANs) and NICNET, while the National Knowledge Network links universities and research institutions at multi-gigabit speeds.
- Other classifications worth knowing: by topology (star, bus, ring, mesh); by ownership (intranet, extranet, internet); and VPN, which creates an encrypted private channel over a public network.

## Conclusion

India’s IT hubs reflect an accumulation of advantages — institutions, policy and infrastructure — rather than deliberate spatial planning, and their concentration is now both a strength and a limitation. The dispersal to tier-2 centres, of which the Visakhapatnam AI hub is the most significant instance, addresses that limitation directly. Underlying all of it is networking infrastructure whose progression from dial-up modems to 5G and fibre has been the enabling condition of every stage of the industry’s growth.

## Value addition
- Software Technology Parks of India (1991): an autonomous society under MeitY; provided high-speed data communication, duty-free import of capital goods, single-window clearance and tax incentives to export-oriented software units — the policy foundation of the industry.
- Sector data (NASSCOM industry estimates, FY 2024-25): revenue approximately USD 283 billion; about 5.8 million direct employees; roughly 7.5% of GDP; software and ITeS around half of total services exports.
- Global Capability Centres: captive offshore units of multinationals performing R&D, engineering and analytics; India hosts the world’s largest concentration — the shift from executing specifications to owning product work.
- Li-Fi: a wireless technology using visible light from LED sources to transmit data through imperceptible high-speed oscillations in brightness; offers very high bandwidth and inherent security (light does not pass through walls) but requires line of sight.
- Networking standards to name precisely: IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet), IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi), IEEE 802.15 (Bluetooth/PAN); TCP/IP as the internet protocol suite; the OSI seven-layer model as the conceptual reference.
- AP-specific IT infrastructure: Google AI hub Visakhapatnam; APSFL Fibre Grid (ADSS aerial fibre, DWDM backbone, ~23,000 km); APEITA; IT corridors at Visakhapatnam and Tirupati; Amaravati Quantum Valley Tech Park; submarine cable landing stations at Visakhapatnam.
- A sharp framing line: India’s IT industry was built on a “bandwidth-plus-English” arbitrage. Both advantages are eroding — automation compresses the labour component and AI translation erodes the language premium — which is why the shift to GCCs and product work is a necessity rather than an ambition.

## Introduction

Rural disadvantage in India is not a single condition but a set of specific deficits: villagers know less about prices than traders do, live further from services than they can afford to travel, cannot prove their entitlements, cannot reach buyers beyond the local market, and often lack verifiable identity. Information technology is best assessed against these deficits individually, since each is closed by a different application.

## The information deficit — the villager knows less than the intermediary

The trader has historically known prices, weather and grades better than the farmer, and that asymmetry was his margin. e-NAM publishes mandi prices across a unified national market; Kisan Call Centres and Kisan Suvidha deliver advisories by voice, which matters because the users who most need them may not read. The Digital Agriculture Mission (2024) and AgriStack — the Farmers’ Registry, Geo-referenced Village Maps and Crop Sown Registry — are building the data layer that allows advisories to become farm-specific rather than district-generic, which is the difference between information and actionable information.

## The distance deficit — services are where the villager is not
- Health:eSanjeevani crossed 43 crore consultations across 28 States and 8 UTs as on 23 November 2025 (MoHFW, Rajya Sabha reply), with its hub-and-spoke model connecting Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to district specialists.
- Education:DIKSHA, PM e-VIDYA and SWAYAM decouple content quality from teacher availability.
- Banking:AePS turns any Business Correspondent with a micro-ATM into a bank branch, reachable on foot.

## The verification deficit — the villager cannot prove what he is owed

Digitised land records reduce tenure disputes; SVAMITVA uses drone surveys to issue property cards for inhabited village land, converting occupied property into a recognised, mortgageable asset. PM-KISAN and pension databases make entitlement verifiable rather than dependent on an official’s word.

4. The market-access deficit — the villager sells only to whoever comes to the village

ONDC allows small rural sellers to reach buyers beyond their locality without a platform’s gatekeeping; GeM lets local suppliers sell to government; SHG products reach urban markets through e-commerce. Namo Drone Didi places drone services and their income with women’s self-help groups, creating a rural service enterprise rather than only a rural consumer.

## The identity and leakage deficit — the villager cannot be reliably paid

Aadhaar-linked DBT routes entitlements directly, with cumulative transfers crossing Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 and cumulative savings of about Rs. 3.48 lakh crore from plugged leakages (PIB, April and November 2025). e-Shram registers unorganised workers, and eGramSwaraj brings panchayat accounts online.

## The delivery layer that makes all of this work

None of the above reaches a non-digital user without an intermediary. Common Service Centres, run by Village Level Entrepreneurs, provide assisted access for certificates, applications and payments — the recognition that inclusion requires a human at the counter, not only an app on a phone.

AP model worth citing: Andhra Pradesh built a distinctive two-tier last mile — Rythu Bharosa Kendras as village-level agriculture service centres integrating advisory, input supply, testing and procurement, and Village and Ward Secretariats with Grama/Ward Volunteers for doorstep delivery of certificates, pensions and scheme benefits. Layered above these, Mana Mitra delivers 1,126 services across 35 departments to 58.2 lakh citizens via WhatsApp (2026). The design principle is that digital back-ends should be paired with human front-ends.

## Limitations
- Connectivity and electricity gaps in remote and tribal habitations.
- Skills, not access, as the current binding constraint — household internet access reached 86.3% (NSO, CMS: Telecom, 2025), but capability lags far behind.
- Gendered device control, so women’s access remains mediated.
- Silent exclusion where authentication fails and no offline fallback exists.

## Conclusion

Assessed deficit by deficit, IT has demonstrably narrowed rural India’s information, distance and verification gaps — market prices are visible, specialists reachable and entitlements traceable. What it has not done is close the capability gap, which is why assisted-access institutions such as Common Service Centres and Andhra Pradesh’s Rythu Bharosa Kendras and Village Secretariats matter as much as the platforms themselves. The next phase of rural IT will be judged less by how many services are digitised than by how many rural citizens can actually obtain them.

## Value addition
- Rural IT platforms by function:agriculture — e-NAM, Kisan Call Centres, Kisan Suvidha, Soil Health Cards, PM-KISAN, AgriStack and Krishi-DSS, PMFBY (satellite-assisted crop insurance assessment); governance — CSCs, eGramSwaraj, e-Panchayat, SVAMITVA, e-Shram; health — eSanjeevani, U-WIN, NIKSHAY, ABHA; education — DIKSHA, PM e-VIDYA, SWAYAM; markets — ONDC, GeM.
- Digital Agriculture Mission (2024): builds AgriStack — Farmers’ Registry, Geo-referenced Village Maps, Crop Sown Registry — with the Krishi Decision Support System and Soil Profile Mapping.
- SVAMITVA: Survey of Villages and Mapping with Improvised Technology in Village Areas; drone-based survey of inhabited rural land to issue property cards, enabling formal credit against previously unrecorded assets.
- Key figures: DBT cumulative transfers Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 with savings of about Rs. 3.48 lakh crore (PIB); eSanjeevani over 43 crore consultations (MoHFW, November 2025); household internet access 86.3% (NSO CMS: Telecom, 2025).
- AP-specific rural delivery institutions: Rythu Bharosa Kendras (village agriculture service centres); Village and Ward Secretariats with Grama/Ward Volunteers; Mana Mitra WhatsApp governance; APSFL Fibre Grid; RTGS AWARE for weather and disaster alerts to farmers.
- The historical reference examiners appreciate:Gyandoot (Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, 2000) — one of India’s earliest rural intranet e-governance projects; its lesson, that sustainability depends on local ownership and a viable revenue model rather than on technology, remains the standard cautionary case.
- SDG linkage: SDG 1 (poverty), SDG 2 (hunger and agricultural productivity), SDG 8.10 (access to financial services) and SDG 9.c (ICT access).

Q25:
## Introduction

Software development transformed India’s economic profile faster than any other sector: from negligible output in the 1980s to roughly 7.5% of GDP and revenue of about USD 283 billion in FY 2024-25 (NASSCOM industry estimates). But its contribution has been overwhelmingly in services delivered for others rather than products owned by Indian firms — a distinction that defines both its achievement and its ceiling.

## Contribution to output and the digital economy

India’s digital economy contributed about 11.74% of GVA (Rs. 31.64 lakh crore) and employed 14.67 million workers in 2022-23, growing at nearly twice the rate of the overall economy and projected to approach 20% of GVA by 2029-30 (MeitY-commissioned assessment). Software development is its core: the productivity of digital-economy workers is several times the economy-wide average, which is why a sector employing a small share of the workforce contributes disproportionately to output.

## Exports and macroeconomic stability

Software and IT-enabled services constitute roughly half of India’s total services exports. Their strategic function is often understated: services exports offset a persistent merchandise trade deficit, financing India’s oil and electronics imports and stabilising the current account. Software is, in effect, how India pays for what it imports.

## Employment and the skills ecosystem

The sector employs roughly 5.8 million professionals directly, with an indirect multiplier several times larger. It also created the demand signal that reshaped Indian technical education — with the qualification that enrolment grew faster than employability, leaving a persistent skills gap that FutureSkills Prime and similar programmes attempt to close.

## Innovation, IP and the shift to products
- Global Capability Centres (GCCs) — captive offshore units doing R&D, product engineering and analytics for multinationals — represent the most significant structural change: work has moved from executing specifications to designing products. India hosts the world’s largest concentration of GCCs (industry estimates put the share above half, though official figures are not published).
- The National Policy on Software Products, 2019 was the first policy to target products rather than services, aiming to position India as a global software product hub through IP creation and start-up promotion; the Next Generation Incubation Scheme (NGIS) operationalises it, alongside Domain-Specific Centres of Entrepreneurship.
- Digital Public Infrastructure as an export of a different kind: UPI, Aadhaar and CoWIN were built by Indian software talent and are now offered to other countries as a governance model — arguably India’s most valuable software product, though it earns no licence fee.
- Start-ups: DPIIT-recognised start-ups rose from about 500 in 2016 to over 2 lakh in 2025 (Economic Survey 2025-26), concentrated in SaaS, fintech and healthtech — the segment where Indian-owned IP is actually being created.
- AP instance: Google’s AI hub at Visakhapatnam — about USD 15 billion over 2026-2030, gigawatt-scale data-centre capacity and a subsea cable gateway, its largest outside the United States (newsonair, Government of India, October 2025) — brings the compute layer on which software products are built onto Indian soil.

## The pressure on the model

The services model monetised headcount: revenue grew with people. Generative AI compresses exactly the routine coding, testing and support work that employed the most people, which means the linear model cannot be sustained. This is not a distant risk — it is the reason the shift to products, GCC work and IP creation is a necessity rather than an aspiration.

## Conclusion

Software development gave India foreign exchange, a large organised professional workforce and the technical capability behind its digital public infrastructure — an unusually broad set of returns from one sector. Its limitation is equally clear: India has been the world’s software workshop rather than its software owner. Whether the National Policy on Software Products, the GCC transition and the start-up ecosystem convert that workshop into an IP-creating industry will determine the sector’s contribution over the next two decades.

## Value addition
- National Policy on Software Products, 2019: aims to position India as a global software product hub through IP creation, product start-ups and improved access to capital; targets a software product ecosystem contributing significantly to the digital economy.
- Next Generation Incubation Scheme (NGIS): MeitY scheme supporting software product start-ups through incubation, funding and Centres of Entrepreneurship in emerging technology domains.
- Software Technology Parks of India (1991): duty-free imports, single-window clearance and dedicated data links for export-oriented software units — the policy foundation of the industry.
- Key figures: IT-BPM revenue about USD 283 billion and around 5.8 million employees in FY 2024-25 (NASSCOM); digital economy 11.74% of GVA and 14.67 million workers in 2022-23, projected near 20% of GVA by 2029-30 (MeitY assessment); DPIIT-recognised start-ups over 2 lakh in 2025 (Economic Survey 2025-26).
- How to keep this distinct from Q28: Q28 asks about the computer industry’s contribution — answer with GDP, exports, employment and regional concentration. Q37 asks about software development — answer with the services-versus-products distinction, IP creation and the AI disruption. Overlapping facts, different arguments.
- The counterpoint to hold ready: software’s contribution to output far exceeds its contribution to employment — 5.8 million jobs in a workforce above 500 million. It is a productivity and foreign-exchange story, not a mass-employment one.

## Introduction

PSLV and GSLV are not competing vehicles but complementary ones designed for different destinations. PSLV was built to place remote-sensing satellites in polar and Sun-synchronous orbits a few hundred kilometres up; GSLV was built to place heavy communication satellites into geosynchronous transfer orbit at about 36,000 km. That single difference in target orbit explains their differing stages, propulsion and payload capacity — and is the correct starting point for the answer.

- **Feature** — PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle) · GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle)
- **Primary purpose** — Low Earth and Sun-synchronous orbits · Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit; heavy payloads
- **Stages** — Four — 1st and 3rd solid, 2nd and 4th liquid · Three — 1st solid with liquid strap-ons, 2nd liquid, 3rd cryogenic
- **Payload capacity** — About 1,750 kg to SSO · About 2,500 kg to GTO; around 5,000 kg to LEO (Mk II)
- **Key technology** — Solid-liquid combination; restartable fourth stage · Cryogenic upper stage (liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen)
- **Reliability** — ISRO’s proven workhorse, with the longest successful run · Historically lower success rate owing to cryogenic complexity
- **Notable missions** — Chandrayaan-1, Mars Orbiter Mission, IRS and Cartosat series, multi-satellite commercial launches · INSAT and GSAT communication satellites, NVS-02 (2025), NISAR (2025)

## Why the cryogenic stage is the real difference

A cryogenic engine burns liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen at around -253deg C and -183deg C respectively. It delivers far higher specific impulse — thrust per unit of propellant — than solid or storable-liquid stages, which is what makes it possible to push heavy payloads to the very high energy of a geosynchronous transfer orbit. It is also the hardest propulsion technology to master, requiring turbopumps and materials that function at cryogenic temperatures. India was denied this technology in the early 1990s and developed it indigenously; the first successful flight of the indigenous cryogenic upper stage came in January 2014 (GSLV-D5), which is why the vehicle’s history includes more failures than PSLV’s.

## Examining the advantages of GSLV over PSLV
- Access to geostationary orbit. Only GSLV-class vehicles can place INSAT and GSAT communication satellites where they are needed. A geostationary satellite appears fixed above one point on Earth, which is what allows a fixed dish antenna to work — the basis of DTH television, VSAT networks and satellite broadband.
- Higher payload mass, enabling heavier and longer-lived satellites with more transponders and more propellant for station-keeping.
- Strategic autonomy. Before GSLV matured, India had to purchase launches abroad for its heavy communication satellites — expensive, schedule-dependent and subject to political conditions. Indigenous heavy-lift capability removed that vulnerability.
- A foundation for human spaceflight and heavy missions. The LVM3 (GSLV Mk III), the heaviest in the family, launched Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 and its human-rated variant HLVM3 is the launch vehicle for Gaganyaan. This capability line does not exist on the PSLV side.
- Growing versatility. GSLV-F16 placed NISAR into a sun-synchronous polar orbit in July 2025 — the first GSLV mission to that orbit, showing the vehicle is no longer confined to GTO.

## Where PSLV remains superior — the balance the question invites
- Reliability and cost for small and medium payloads, which is why PSLV, not GSLV, became India’s commercial launch workhorse.
- Multi-satellite deployment: its restartable fourth stage allows satellites to be placed in different orbits on one flight; PSLV-C37 famously deployed 104 satellites in a single mission.
- Interplanetary firsts: both Chandrayaan-1 and the Mars Orbiter Mission flew on PSLV, using Earth-orbit-raising manoeuvres to compensate for lower launch energy.
- Flexible configurations — PSLV-G, CA, XL, DL and QL variants matched to payload mass.

AP linkage: every PSLV, GSLV and LVM3 flight lifts off from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota. The 100th launch from Sriharikota was GSLV-F15 carrying NVS-02 on 29 January 2025, and a third launch pad has been approved at Rs. 3,984.86 crore to support next-generation and human-rated vehicles.

## Conclusion

The correct framing is capability, not superiority: GSLV extended India’s reach from a few hundred kilometres to geostationary altitude and, through LVM3 and HLVM3, to lunar missions and human spaceflight, while PSLV remains the more reliable and economical vehicle for the small and medium payloads that constitute most launches. India’s arrival as a full-spectrum launch nation came from mastering the cryogenic stage — and the next step, the Next Generation Launch Vehicle targeting about 30 tonnes to LEO, is designed to make heavy lift routine and eventually reusable.

## Value addition
- India’s launch vehicle family:SLV-3 and ASLV (developmental); PSLV (workhorse, LEO/SSO); GSLV Mk II (GTO, indigenous cryogenic upper stage); LVM3 / GSLV Mk III (heaviest operational, about 4 tonnes to GTO and 8 tonnes to LEO; launched Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3); SSLV (Small Satellite Launch Vehicle, on-demand small-payload launches); HLVM3 (human-rated, for Gaganyaan); NGLV under development, targeting about 30 tonnes to LEO with partial reusability; RLV-TD for reusable launch technology.
- The cryogenic milestone: technology denial in the early 1990s led to indigenous development; the first fully successful flight of the indigenous cryogenic upper stage was GSLV-D5 in January 2014.
- PSLV records worth citing: PSLV-C37 deployed 104 satellites in a single mission (2017); PSLV has launched Chandrayaan-1, the Mars Orbiter Mission and Aditya-L1, and remains India’s principal commercial launcher through NSIL.
- Recent GSLV missions:GSLV-F15/NVS-02 (29 January 2025, 100th launch from Sriharikota); GSLV-F16/NISAR (30 July 2025, first GSLV flight to a sun-synchronous polar orbit).
- Orbit terminology to use precisely: LEO, SSO (Sun-synchronous — passes over a given latitude at the same local solar time, ideal for consistent-illumination imaging), GTO (the elliptical transfer path), GEO (circular equatorial at about 35,786 km, appearing stationary).
- AP linkage: SDSC-SHAR Sriharikota — First and Second Launch Pads operational, third launch pad approved (Rs. 3,984.86 crore); India’s second spaceport is being developed at Kulasekarapattinam, Tamil Nadu, for SSLV launches.

## Introduction

Remote sensing acquires information about the Earth’s surface without physical contact, by measuring reflected or emitted electromagnetic radiation. Its agricultural value rests on a simple physical fact: healthy vegetation reflects strongly in the near-infrared and absorbs in the red, so the ratio between these bands — the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) — measures plant vigour from orbit. India operates one of the world’s largest civilian Earth-observation constellations and applies it to agriculture through several established national programmes.

## Applications of remote sensing in agriculture
- Crop acreage estimation and production forecasting. The FASAL programme (Forecasting Agricultural output using Space, Agro-meteorology and Land-based observations) provides multiple in-season forecasts of crop area and yield for major crops — the basis for procurement, buffer-stock and import decisions taken months before harvest.
- Crop health and precision farming. NDVI and related indices reveal stress from water deficit, nutrient deficiency or pest attack while it is still correctable, allowing variable-rate application of fertiliser to stressed patches rather than uniform application across a field — reducing both cost and runoff.
- Irrigation management. Thermal infrared sensing estimates canopy temperature and soil moisture; a water-stressed crop transpires less and therefore runs hotter. Combined with weather forecasts, this supports irrigation scheduling driven by plant need rather than by the calendar.
- Pest and disease detection.Hyperspectral imagery detects subtle shifts in reflectance that precede visible symptoms, enabling early intervention and lower pesticide use.
- Drought and flood assessment. NDVI time-series and radar-based inundation mapping support drought declaration and relief assessment; NADRES (National Animal Disease Referral Expert System) applies similar geospatial modelling to livestock disease risk.
- Horticulture. The CHAMAN programme (Coordinated Horticulture Assessment and Management using geo-informatics) estimates area and production for horticultural crops — directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s mango, banana, chilli and citrus economy.
- Crop insurance. Under PMFBY, the YES-TECH framework uses remote-sensing-based yield estimation to reduce dependence on crop-cutting experiments, which were slow, sample-limited and dispute-prone. This is remote sensing changing not just information but the administration of an entitlement.
- Decision support and data integration. The Krishi Decision Support System under the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024) integrates satellite, weather, soil and crop-registry data on one platform, alongside AgriStack and Soil Profile Mapping.
- The current frontier — NISAR. Launched on 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16 from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar satellite is the first to carry dual-frequency SAR (NASA’s L-band, ISRO’s S-band). Because radar penetrates cloud, it can monitor soil moisture and crop growth through the monsoon, when optical satellites are blind — precisely when Indian kharif agriculture most needs observation.

(i) Short note: Mobile Satellite Services (MSS)

- What it is: a radiocommunication service providing voice, data and messaging to mobile terminals — handheld satellite phones, ship and aircraft terminals, vehicle-mounted units — through satellites, where terrestrial networks are absent or have failed.
- Architecture: Mobile Earth Stations (the user terminals), GEO or LEO satellites, and gateway stations linking users into public telephone and internet networks.
- Applications: maritime and aviation communication, defence, disaster response when terrestrial towers are down, and agricultural and fisheries advisories in remote areas. India’s INSAT/GSAT系 supports such services, and NavIC’s messaging capability delivers cyclone and fishermen alerts along the coast — directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s 1,053-km coastline.
- Key distinction: MSS serves mobile terminals; FSS (Fixed-Satellite Service) serves terminals at fixed locations.

(ii) Short note: Environmental monitoring

- What it covers: satellite-based observation of forest cover, water bodies, air quality, land degradation, glaciers, coastal zones and climate variables.
- Indian instances: the Forest Survey of India’s biennial India State of Forest Report rests on satellite interpretation, and FSI operates a near-real-time forest fire alert system pushing SMS alerts to field staff; Bhuvan (NRSC/ISRO) hosts forest, water and disaster applications; Srishti and Drishti monitor watershed works under WDC-PMKSY 2.0; CPCB’s continuous ambient air quality stations feed the National Air Quality Index and the SAMEER app.
- Why satellites are indispensable here: environmental change is slow, spatially extensive and politically contested. Only a consistent, repeatable, independently verifiable observation record can settle whether forest cover or a wetland has actually changed — which is the real contribution of remote sensing to environmental governance.

## Conclusion

Remote sensing has moved Indian agriculture from retrospective estimation to in-season management: FASAL forecasts output before harvest, CHAMAN covers horticulture, YES-TECH settles insurance claims from orbit, and NISAR now sees through monsoon cloud. Combined with MSS for last-mile communication and satellite-based environmental monitoring, space technology closes the loop from observation to advisory to action. The remaining constraint is not observational capability but the ability to deliver satellite-derived advice to a specific farmer, in his language, in time to act.
