## Introduction

The Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), or Mangalyaan, launched on 5 November 2013 aboard PSLV-C25 from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, was India’s first interplanetary mission. On 24 September 2014 it entered Martian orbit, making India the first nation to reach Mars orbit on its maiden attempt and the fourth space agency to reach Mars at all, after NASA, the Soviet programme and ESA.

(a) The Mars Orbiter Mission

- Mission profile: the 1,337 kg spacecraft was placed by PSLV-C25 into a 250 x 23,000 km Earth orbit, then raised through a series of orbit-raising manoeuvres before trans-Mars injection. This approach was necessitated by PSLV’s limited launch energy — India substituted orbital mechanics for rocket power, which is the mission’s underlying engineering story. The Earth-Mars minimum-energy transfer window occurs only once in about 26 months.
- Objectives: primarily technological — to demonstrate deep-space communication, autonomous onboard operations, interplanetary navigation and orbit insertion — with scientific study of Martian surface features, morphology, mineralogy and atmosphere as secondary goals.
- Five payloads: Mars Colour Camera (MCC), Thermal Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (TIS), Methane Sensor for Mars (MSM), Mars Exospheric Neutral Composition Analyser (MENCA) and Lyman Alpha Photometer (LAP) — selected on the recommendation of ISRO’s Advisory Committee for Space Sciences.

Distinguishing features

- First-attempt success, unmatched by any other agency — Mars missions historically had a failure rate above 50%.
- Cost. At about Rs. 450 crore, MOM remains among the least expensive interplanetary missions ever flown, achieved through a light spacecraft, an existing launch vehicle, indigenous components and a compressed development cycle.
- Longevity — the fact most often missed. MOM was designed for a six-month mission life. It operated for about eight years, with contact finally lost in 2022 when propellant and battery reserves were exhausted. A mission that outlives its design life sixteen-fold is a statement about engineering margin, not luck.
- Scientific output: the Mars Colour Camera returned over a thousand images including full-disc views of Mars, and a Mars Atlas was published; data was made openly available to global researchers.
- Institutional effect: MOM established India as a credible deep-space actor and materially strengthened the case for subsequent missions — Chandrayaan-2 and -3, Aditya-L1, and the approved Venus Orbiter Mission.

Sept 2014 Mars orbit insertion --> 2022 end of mission , with “designed for 6 months, operated ~8 years” annotated.

(b)(i) Broadband digital communication

High-capacity, always-on transmission using a wide frequency range to carry multiple signals simultaneously over one medium, as against narrowband dial-up. Delivered through terrestrial media (DSL, cable, optical fibre — the basis of BharatNet and the AP Fibre Grid), wireless (4G/5G), and satellite broadband, which is decisive for terrain where laying fibre is uneconomic. India’s high-throughput satellites such as GSAT-11 and GSAT-29 were built specifically to extend broadband to unconnected regions.

(b)(ii) Fixed-Satellite Service (FSS)

- A radiocommunication service linking earth stations at fixed, specified locations through satellites, typically in geostationary orbit for continuous coverage of a defined region — distinct from MSS, which serves mobile terminals.
- Applications: Direct-to-Home television and radio distribution; VSAT networks connecting bank branches, ATMs, stock exchanges and remote offices; international telephony and data trunking; and resilient emergency communication when terrestrial infrastructure fails in a disaster.
- Indian context: the INSAT and GSAT series carry FSS payloads in C, extended-C and Ku bands, supporting broadcasting, VSAT connectivity, tele-education and telemedicine networks.

## Conclusion

The Mars Orbiter Mission demonstrated that interplanetary capability need not require interplanetary budgets — India reached Mars on its first attempt, for about Rs. 450 crore, with a spacecraft that outlived its design life many times over. Together with satellite communication services that carry broadband and broadcasting to areas terrestrial networks cannot reach, it illustrates the two faces of India’s space programme: frontier science that builds national capability, and applied services that reach ordinary citizens.

- MOM mission facts: 1,337 kg spacecraft; PSLV-C25 from SDSC-SHAR on 5 November 2013; injected into a 250 x 23,000 km orbit at 17.864deg inclination; Mars orbit insertion 24 September 2014; cost about Rs. 450 crore; five payloads — MCC, TIS, MSM, MENCA, LAP; Earth-Mars transfer window recurs every 26 months.

## Introduction

The Chandrayaan programme is India’s lunar exploration effort, running from an orbiter that discovered water on the Moon, through a partial landing failure, to the first soft landing ever achieved near the lunar south pole. Its arc is instructive precisely because it includes a setback: Chandrayaan-2’s landing failure in 2019 supplied the engineering lessons that made Chandrayaan-3’s success on 23 August 2023 possible — a date now observed annually as National Space Day.

success, lander failure –> Chandrayaan-3 (2023): Soft landing at the south pole , with an arrow labelled “lessons applied” between the second and third.

## Chandrayaan-1 (2008) — the discovery mission

Launched on 22 October 2008 aboard PSLV-C11, Chandrayaan-1 carried eleven scientific instruments — five Indian and six from international partners including NASA and ESA. Its defining achievement was the discovery of water on the Moon: NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper aboard the orbiter provided spectral evidence of hydroxyl and water molecules, while the Indian Moon Impact Probe detected water vapour in the lunar exosphere before its planned impact near the south pole. This overturned the long-held assumption that the Moon was bone-dry, and it is the reason every subsequent lunar programme worldwide targets the polar regions. The mission also produced a high-resolution three-dimensional atlas of the near and far sides and identified buried lava tubes — candidate shelters for future habitats. It operated for about 312 days before communication was lost in August 2009.

## Chandrayaan-2 (2019) — partial success and its lessons

Launched on 22 July 2019 aboard GSLV Mk III, Chandrayaan-2 comprised an orbiter, the Vikram lander and the Pragyan rover, targeting the unexplored south polar region. - The orbiter succeeded outright and continues to operate, carrying eight instruments including the Orbiter High-Resolution Camera, which produced the highest-resolution images of any lunar mission of its time. Its data was later used to select and validate the Chandrayaan-3 landing site — the failed mission’s orbiter directly enabled the successful one. - The lander did not. During powered descent, deviations in the trajectory led to a hard landing near the intended site. - What ISRO changed as a result is the substance worth writing: Chandrayaan-3 was redesigned on a failure-based rather than success-based design philosophy — a strengthened lander structure and legs, a wider permissible landing area, additional propellant margin, more robust sensors and software, and extensive terrain-simulation testing. The rover was retained but the orbiter was dropped, since Chandrayaan-2’s was still operational and could serve as the communication relay.

## Chandrayaan-3 (2023) — the landing

Launched on 14 July 2023 aboard LVM3-M4, Chandrayaan-3 comprised a propulsion module, the Vikram lander and the Pragyan rover. On 23 August 2023, Vikram executed a successful powered descent and soft landing, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first to do so near the lunar south pole. - Scientific results: Pragyan operated for one lunar day (about 14 Earth days), conducting in-situ chemical analysis and confirming the presence of sulphur — an unambiguous in-situ detection — along with aluminium, calcium, iron, chromium, titanium, manganese, silicon and oxygen. The ChaSTE instrument measured the lunar surface thermal profile, and ILSA recorded seismic activity. - Additional demonstration: the Vikram lander performed a hop experiment, firing its engines to lift and relocate a short distance — a capability directly relevant to future sample-return and ascent missions. - Recognition: the landing site was named Shiv Shakti Point, and 23 August was declared National Space Day.

## Significance and the road ahead
- Scientific: established the presence of water and characterised the composition and thermal behaviour of the previously unexplored south polar region — the area of greatest interest because permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice usable as drinking water, oxygen and rocket propellant.
- Technological: demonstrated soft landing, autonomous hazard avoidance, in-situ analysis and lunar surface operations at a cost far below comparable missions.
- Institutional: the programme’s credibility rests as much on the transparent handling of Chandrayaan-2’s failure as on Chandrayaan-3’s success.
- Forward programme:Chandrayaan-4, approved by the Union Cabinet, is a lunar sample-return mission targeted for around 2027, requiring docking and re-entry technologies India has begun validating through the SpaDeX in-orbit docking demonstration. Chandrayaan-5 / LUPEX, a joint mission with JAXA, will explore the polar region with an ISRO lander and a JAXA rover carrying a drill capable of sampling to about 1.5 m. India’s stated vision includes an Indian crewed lunar landing by 2040.
- AP linkage: every Chandrayaan mission has lifted off from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, making Andhra Pradesh the origin point of India’s entire lunar programme.

## Conclusion

The Chandrayaan programme has taken India from discovering lunar water to standing on the lunar south pole in fifteen years, at costs that redefined what planetary exploration requires. Its most transferable lesson is institutional rather than technical: an agency that publishes its failure analysis and redesigns around it produces Chandrayaan-3. With sample return and a crewed landing on the horizon, the programme has shifted from demonstrating that India can reach the Moon to determining what India will do there.

## Value addition
- Mission-by-mission facts: Chandrayaan-1 — 22 October 2008, PSLV-C11, 11 instruments, ~312 days, discovered lunar water. Chandrayaan-2 — 22 July 2019, GSLV Mk III, orbiter operational, lander hard-landed. Chandrayaan-3 — 14 July 2023, LVM3-M4, soft landing 23 August 2023, landing site Shiv Shakti Point, National Space Day declared.
- Chandrayaan-3 payloads: on the lander — ChaSTE (thermophysical experiment), ILSA (seismic activity), RAMBHA-LP (plasma); on the rover — APXS and LIBS for elemental composition; and SHAPE on the propulsion module for exoplanet studies.
- Why the south pole matters: permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice, which can supply drinking water, breathable oxygen and hydrogen-oxygen propellant — making the pole the logical site for any sustained lunar presence.
- The forward programme:Chandrayaan-4 (sample return, approved by Cabinet, targeted around 2027); Chandrayaan-5 / LUPEX with JAXA (ISRO lander, JAXA rover, drill to ~1.5 m, launch expected 2027-28 on a Japanese H3); Bharatiya Antariksh Station first module by 2028 and operational by 2035; Indian crewed lunar landing by 2040.
- India’s space-science portfolio for cross-reference: Aditya-L1 (solar), AstroSat (multi-wavelength observatory), XPoSat (X-ray polarimetry), the approved Venus Orbiter Mission, and NISAR (Earth observation).
- The “fourth country” claims to keep straight: fourth to soft-land on the Moon (after the USSR, USA and China); first to land near the south pole; first to reach Mars orbit on a maiden attempt.

## Introduction

Gaganyaan, approved in 2018-19, is India’s human spaceflight programme: to carry up to three astronauts to a Low Earth Orbit of about 400 km for up to three days and return them safely to a planned splashdown in Indian waters. Its wider purpose is not the flight itself but the capability set it creates — human-rated launch, life support, crew escape and safe re-entry — on which the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (2035) and an Indian crewed lunar landing (2040) depend.

Objectives

- Demonstrate indigenous human spaceflight capability using the human-rated LVM3 (HLVM3), an orbital module comprising a Crew Module and Service Module, and a Crew Escape System capable of pulling the crew clear at any point from the launch pad through ascent.
- Develop human-rated technologies: environmental control and life support (ECLSS), radiation shielding, thermal protection for re-entry at roughly 7 km/s, parachute-based deceleration, and precise splashdown and recovery, tested with the Indian Navy at the Water Survival Test Facility.
- Enable microgravity research in biological sciences, medicine and materials — the scientific rationale for sustained human presence.
- Build the foundation for the longer roadmap: a Cabinet-approved plan envisages four Gaganyaan missions, the first module of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2028 with four validation missions by December 2028, an operational station by 2035, and a crewed lunar landing by 2040 (PIB, 2024).

Progress achieved — what makes this answer current

- TV-D1 (October 2023): the first Test Vehicle Abort Mission successfully demonstrated the Crew Escape System and crew module separation and recovery in flight — validating the single most critical safety system.
- Astronaut-designates named (February 2024): Group Captains Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Pratap and Shubhanshu Shukla, all Indian Air Force test pilots, trained in Russia and at ISRO’s Astronaut Training Facility in Bengaluru.
- Axiom-4 (2025) — the decisive milestone.Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla flew as Mission Pilot on Axiom Mission 4, launched 25 June 2025, becoming the first Indian astronaut to visit the International Space Station and the second Indian in space after Rakesh Sharma in 1984. He spent 18 days aboard, conducting experiments on muscle regeneration, algal and microbial growth, crop viability, microbial survivability, cognitive performance in space and cyanobacteria behaviour, before splashdown on 15 July 2025. The Union Cabinet passed a formal resolution welcoming his return (PIB, July 2025). Its value to Gaganyaan is direct: India now has an astronaut with genuine orbital experience to inform crew training and procedures.
- SpaDeX: ISRO’s Space Docking Experiment successfully demonstrated autonomous in-orbit docking of two satellites — a prerequisite technology for assembling a space station and for Chandrayaan-4’s sample-return architecture.
- Uncrewed test flights: the G1 mission, carrying the humanoid robot Vyommitra to simulate crew presence and validate life-support and environmental systems, is to precede further uncrewed flights and then the crewed mission. Schedules for human-rated systems are governed by test results rather than calendars, and ISRO has repeatedly stated that safety, not date, drives the sequence.

Benefits

- Technological spin-off. Human-rating forces reliability standards far above those of satellite missions, and the resulting advances in life support, materials, medical monitoring and autonomous systems diffuse into aviation, healthcare and industry. Historically, human spaceflight programmes have been among the most productive sources of civilian technology transfer.
- Industrial and economic. Gaganyaan is being executed with extensive private-sector participation — HAL manufactures the crew module structure — deepening an aerospace supplier base that also serves the wider space economy opened up by IN-SPACe and NSIL.
- Scientific. Sustained microgravity access enables research impossible on Earth, from protein crystallisation to muscle and bone physiology.
- Strategic and diplomatic. Independent human spaceflight would place India in a group of nations comprising Russia, the United States and China. It also strengthens India’s position in cooperative frameworks including the Artemis Accords, which India signed in 2023.
- Inspirational. The visible national effect on STEM interest is real and is part of the programme’s justification.
- AP linkage: Gaganyaan will launch from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, where a third launch pad has been approved at Rs. 3,984.86 crore specifically to support next-generation and human-rated vehicles. Andhra Pradesh will therefore be the point of departure for India’s first crewed flight.

Challenges

- Crew safety above all: re-entry heating at about 7 km/s, radiation exposure, and reliable abort at every flight phase.
- Life support: closed-loop management of oxygen, water, carbon dioxide and waste in a small volume.
- Training and medical infrastructure, historically dependent on foreign facilities, now being built domestically.
- Recovery operations: precise splashdown and rapid retrieval, requiring sustained naval coordination.
- Schedule discipline: in human spaceflight, delay is the correct response to an unresolved test result — a point worth making rather than treating slippage as failure.

## Conclusion

Gaganyaan’s significance lies less in placing three Indians in orbit for three days than in the capability threshold it crosses: once a nation can launch, sustain and safely return humans, a space station and a lunar landing become engineering problems rather than aspirations. The programme has already produced the abort demonstration, an astronaut with ISS experience and autonomous docking. Its remaining test is the one it cannot rush — proving, through uncrewed flights, that the system is safe enough to carry people.

## Value addition
- Mission parameters: up to three crew, about 400 km LEO, up to three days, splashdown recovery; launch vehicle HLVM3 (human-rated LVM3); orbital module comprising Crew Module and Service Module; Crew Escape System functional from pad to orbit.
- Test sequence to name: Integrated Air Drop Test (parachute deceleration), Pad Abort Test, Test Vehicle flights (TV-D1, October 2023), uncrewed missions carrying Vyommitra, and the Water Survival Test Facility exercises with the Indian Navy.
- The astronaut-designates: Group Captains Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Pratap and Shubhanshu Shukla.
- Axiom-4 (2025): launched 25 June 2025 with Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla as Mission Pilot alongside Commander Peggy Whitson and crew from Poland and Hungary; 18 days aboard the ISS; splashdown 15 July 2025; first Indian on the ISS, second Indian in space after Rakesh Sharma (1984, Soyuz T-11); ISRO’s investment in the mission was reported at about Rs. 550 crore.
- Space Vision 2047 milestones: Bharatiya Antariksh Station first module 2028, station operational 2035; Indian crewed lunar landing by 2040; NGLV with about 30 tonnes to LEO; Venus Orbiter Mission targeted for 2028; second spaceport at Kulasekarapattinam; third launch pad at SDSC-SHAR (Rs. 3,984.86 crore).
- Sector reforms enabling all of this:IN-SPACe as single-window authorisation and promotion body; NSIL as ISRO’s commercial arm; the Indian Space Policy 2023; 100% FDI permitted in specified space segments.

## Introduction

A satellite is any object in orbit around a larger body; the Moon is Earth’s natural satellite, while artificial satellites are engineered spacecraft placed in orbit for communication, observation, navigation or research. India operates one of the world’s larger civilian satellite fleets, built around three families — INSAT/GSAT for communication, IRS for Earth observation, and NavIC for navigation.

## Types of satellites in the Indian space programme
- Communication satellites. Placed in geostationary orbit so that a fixed ground antenna can remain locked onto them, they carry telecommunication, broadcasting, VSAT and disaster-warning traffic. Examples: the INSAT and GSAT series; GSAT-11 and GSAT-29 as high-throughput satellites for broadband.
- Earth observation satellites. In low, Sun-synchronous orbits so that each pass occurs at the same local solar time, giving consistent illumination for change detection. Examples: Resourcesat (natural resources), Cartosat (high-resolution cartography), RISAT/EOS (radar, all-weather), Oceansat (ocean colour and winds).
- Navigation satellites.NavIC (IRNSS) — a regional constellation of geostationary and inclined geosynchronous satellites providing position and timing over India and about 1,500 km beyond, with the second-generation NVS series adding indigenous atomic clocks and the L1 civil signal.
- Meteorological satellites.INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR carry imagers and sounders for cyclone tracking, rainfall estimation and weather forecasting — the backbone of IMD’s cyclone warnings for the Andhra and Odisha coasts.
- Scientific and astronomy satellites.AstroSat (multi-wavelength observatory), Aditya-L1 (solar), XPoSat (X-ray polarimetry).
- Experimental satellites.Aryabhata (1975), India’s first satellite, and APPLE (1981), the experimental communication satellite that proved three-axis stabilisation for India.
- Military/strategic communication satellites.GSAT-7 (Rukmini) for the Navy, GSAT-7A for the Air Force.

## A note on GSAT
- What it is: GSAT is ISRO’s series of indigenously built geostationary communication satellites, successor to and complement of the INSAT system. They carry transponders in C, extended-C, Ku and Ka bands and support telecommunication, television broadcasting, DTH, VSAT networks, tele-education, telemedicine, disaster communication and strategic connectivity.
- Why geostationary: at about 35,786 km above the equator a satellite’s orbital period matches Earth’s rotation, so it appears fixed in the sky. Three such satellites can cover almost the entire globe, and a household dish antenna never has to move.
- The current flagship — CMS-03 (GSAT-7R). Launched on 2 November 2025 aboard LVM3-M5 from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, CMS-03 weighs about 4,400 kg and is the heaviest communication satellite ever launched to geosynchronous transfer orbit from Indian soil. A multi-band satellite covering the Indian landmass and a wide surrounding oceanic region, it serves the Indian Navy, replacing GSAT-7 (Rukmini, 2013), and strengthens maritime domain awareness across the Indian Ocean Region.
- A commercial marker worth adding: on 24 December 2025, LVM3-M6 launched BlueBird Block-2 for the US firm AST SpaceMobile under a NewSpace India Limited contract — the heaviest satellite lifted from Indian soil by an Indian launcher, and part of a direct-to-mobile constellation. It shows GSAT-class capability now earning commercial revenue.

## (b) GPS — number of satellites tracked, and uses
- The answer: a receiver must track a minimum of four satellites simultaneously.
- Why four, not three. Three satellites are geometrically sufficient to fix a point in three dimensions by trilateration — each satellite defines a sphere of possible positions, and three spheres intersect at a point. But trilateration depends on measuring signal travel time precisely, and a consumer receiver’s quartz clock is far too imprecise for that. The fourth satellite provides the additional equation needed to solve for the receiver’s clock error, effectively giving every GPS receiver atomic-clock accuracy without an atomic clock. This is the single most elegant idea in satellite navigation and stating it lifts the answer above a one-line reply.
- Constellation: GPS comprises around 24-31 operational satellites in Medium Earth Orbit at about 20,200 km, arranged so that at least four are visible from almost anywhere on Earth at any time.
- Uses: road, air and maritime navigation; surveying and mapping; precision agriculture and machine guidance; fleet and logistics tracking; disaster response and search-and-rescue; scientific applications from tectonic monitoring to atmospheric sounding; and — often overlooked — precise timing for telecom network synchronisation, power-grid management and financial transaction time-stamping, which is arguably GPS’s most economically critical function.
- India’s equivalent:NavIC provides sovereign regional PNT, and GAGAN (a joint ISRO-AAI satellite-based augmentation system) improves GPS accuracy over Indian airspace for civil aviation.

## Conclusion

India’s satellite fleet has evolved from Aryabhata’s experimental beginnings to CMS-03, the heaviest communication satellite ever launched from Indian soil, and to commercial launches for foreign operators. Together with navigation systems whose precision rests on the elegant four-satellite solution to the clock problem, these assets have moved from demonstrating capability to underpinning everyday services — broadcasting, banking timestamps, cyclone warnings and naval communication.

## Value addition
- CMS-03 (GSAT-7R): launched 2 November 2025 on LVM3-M5 from SDSC-SHAR; about 4,400 kg; heaviest communication satellite launched to GTO from Indian soil; C, extended-C and Ku band transponders; serves the Indian Navy, replacing GSAT-7 (Rukmini, launched 2013 from French Guiana).
- BlueBird Block-2 (24 December 2025, LVM3-M6): commercial launch for AST SpaceMobile through NSIL; heaviest satellite lifted from Indian soil by an Indian launcher; part of a direct-to-mobile LEO constellation for 4G/5G connectivity.
- Orbit types and what suits each:GEO (35,786 km, appears fixed — communication and meteorology); SSO (polar, consistent local solar time — imaging and change detection); MEO (~20,200 km — navigation constellations); LEO (160-2,000 km — high-resolution imaging, space stations, mega-constellations).
- Why four satellites for GPS: three for the three spatial coordinates, the fourth to solve the receiver clock bias — a 1-nanosecond timing error corresponds to roughly 30 cm of position error.
- India’s navigation assets:NavIC (regional, SPS accuracy better than 20 m and timing better than 40 ns) and GAGAN (augmentation for civil aviation, India being the fourth country to operate such a system).
- AP linkage: CMS-03, BlueBird Block-2 and every Indian satellite launch originate from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota; a third launch pad has been approved there at Rs. 3,984.86 crore.

## Introduction

Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a communication channel can carry, measured in hertz. Its significance is direct: greater bandwidth carries more information per unit time, which is why a satellite’s usable capacity is expressed in transponder bandwidth. The choice of frequency band is a trade-off between capacity and reliability — higher frequencies carry more data but are more vulnerable to atmospheric attenuation.

## (a) Frequency bands used in the INSAT/GSAT series
- C-band (roughly 4-8 GHz): telecommunication and data trunking; highly resistant to rain fade, which makes it reliable in the Indian monsoon. INSAT-4A and 4B carried 36 MHz transponders in this band.
- Extended C-band: additional spectrum adjacent to C-band, used to meet growing broadcasting and communication demand.
- Ku-band (roughly 12-18 GHz):Direct-to-Home television and VSAT services; higher power permits small dish antennas, at the cost of greater rain attenuation.
- Ka-band (roughly 26-40 GHz): the band of high-throughput satellites such as GSAT-11 and GSAT-29, enabling satellite broadband through spot-beam frequency reuse — the current frontier of satellite capacity.
- S-band (roughly 2-4 GHz): broadcasting and meteorological payloads; also used for mobile satellite services.
- UHF (around 400 MHz):Data Relay Transponders collecting telemetry from unattended weather stations, river gauges and ocean buoys.
- L-band (roughly 1-2 GHz): navigation, including GAGAN and NavIC signals.

## Significance of the thermal band in agriculture

The thermal infrared band measures emitted rather than reflected radiation, i.e. surface temperature. Its agricultural value follows from plant physiology: a well-watered crop transpires and cools its canopy, while a water-stressed crop closes its stomata and runs hotter. Thermal imagery therefore detects water stress before it becomes visible as wilting or yellowing. It supports: - soil moisture and evapotranspiration estimation, the basis of scientific irrigation scheduling; - crop water stress indices for precision irrigation, targeting water to stressed patches; - drought assessment and frost risk mapping; - canal command area performance evaluation — identifying tail-end areas not receiving their entitled water.

## (b) CARTOSAT-2 and the comparison with IKONOS
- Resolution and swath: CARTOSAT-2 carries a panchromatic camera with better than 1 metre spatial resolution (about 0.8 m) and a swath of roughly 9.6 km — a deliberately narrow swath, because very high resolution and wide coverage are competing design goals.
- Uses: large-scale cartographic mapping; urban and rural infrastructure planning; utility and road network mapping; GIS database creation; change detection and encroachment monitoring; disaster damage assessment; and cadastral-scale applications.
- The difference from IKONOS. IKONOS was a commercial US satellite (launched 1999, decommissioned in 2015) offering about 0.82 m panchromatic and 3.2 m multispectral resolution across four spectral bands, selling imagery on the open global market. CARTOSAT-2 is a government-owned mission built primarily for India’s national mapping, planning and strategic requirements, with a panchromatic emphasis suited to cartography. The essential distinction is therefore purpose and ownership — national planning asset versus commercial imagery product — rather than raw resolution, on which the two were comparable.

## Conclusion

Bandwidth and resolution are the two currencies of space-based services: the first determines how much information a communication satellite can carry, the second how much detail an imaging satellite can resolve. India’s fleet spans both — from UHF data-relay transponders gathering river-gauge readings to Ka-band high-throughput satellites delivering broadband, and from Cartosat’s sub-metre mapping to the thermal bands that reveal crop water stress before the eye can. Together they convert orbital capability into services that reach farms, homes and disaster control rooms.

## Introduction

The Chandrayaan programme is India’s lunar exploration effort, and the IRS-P5 (Cartosat-1) satellite is a milestone in its Earth-observation programme. Together they illustrate the two arms of India’s space effort — frontier exploration that builds national capability, and applied observation that serves planning and development on the ground.

## Comment on the Chandrayaan programme
- Chandrayaan-1 (2008, PSLV-C11): an orbiter carrying eleven instruments, five Indian and six international. Its defining outcome was the discovery of water on the Moon — hydroxyl and water molecules detected spectrally, with the Moon Impact Probe confirming water vapour in the exosphere. This finding redirected global lunar exploration toward the polar regions.
- Chandrayaan-2 (2019, GSLV Mk III): the orbiter succeeded and remains operational, carrying the high-resolution camera whose data later helped validate Chandrayaan-3’s landing site; the Vikram lander hard-landed during powered descent.
- Chandrayaan-3 (2023, LVM3-M4): achieved a soft landing near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon and the first at the south pole. The Pragyan rover confirmed sulphur in situ along with several other elements; the site was named Shiv Shakti Point and 23 August declared National Space Day.
- The evaluative comment: the programme’s distinction is not any single mission but its institutional learning curve — Chandrayaan-2’s failure was analysed publicly and its lessons designed into Chandrayaan-3, which adopted a failure-based rather than success-based design philosophy. Chandrayaan-4 (sample return) and Chandrayaan-5/LUPEX with JAXA extend the programme toward returning lunar material and, eventually, a crewed landing targeted for 2040.

## Two salient features of IRS-P5 (Cartosat-1)

Launched in May 2005 aboard PSLV-C6 from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, IRS-P5 was India’s first dedicated cartographic satellite.

Salient feature 1 — Along-track stereoscopic imaging. Cartosat-1 carries two panchromatic cameras mounted at fixed angles, one tilted about +26deg forward and the other about −5deg aft along the direction of travel. As the satellite passes, the two cameras image the same ground from two different angles within seconds of each other. - Why this matters: two views of the same terrain from different angles allow the third dimension to be computed, exactly as human binocular vision produces depth perception. This enables generation of Digital Elevation Models (DEM) and Digital Terrain Models (DTM) directly from satellite data. - Why along-track rather than across-track: imaging both views within seconds means identical illumination and atmospheric conditions, and no seasonal change between them — producing far more reliable elevation models than combining images from different orbits days apart. - Applications: contour mapping, watershed and drainage analysis, slope and terrain modelling for infrastructure alignment, flood inundation modelling, and 3D city modelling.

Salient feature 2 — High spatial resolution optimised for cartography. Cartosat-1 provides about 2.5 metre panchromatic resolution with a swath of roughly 30 km, and its cameras are steerable to permit revisit. - Why this matters: 2.5 m resolution supports mapping at scales suitable for large-scale topographic mapping and land-use planning — the operational scale at which district and municipal planning is actually done. - Applications: the satellite became the backbone of India’s Cartosat DEM, cadastral and land-use mapping, urban sprawl monitoring, rural infrastructure planning under schemes such as PMGSY, and disaster damage assessment.

## Conclusion

Chandrayaan carried India from discovering lunar water to standing at the Moon’s south pole, and Cartosat-1’s stereo cameras gave the country the ability to model its own terrain in three dimensions from orbit. The pairing captures the logic of India’s space programme: exploration that establishes capability, and application that converts capability into roads, watersheds and city plans.

## Value addition
- The IRS naming convention: early Indian Remote Sensing satellites carried both a series designation and a functional name — IRS-P5 = Cartosat-1, IRS-P6 = Resourcesat-1, IRS-P4 = Oceansat-1. Recognising that “IRS-5” in the question means IRS-P5/Cartosat-1 is itself a marker of familiarity with the programme.
- Cartosat-1 specifics: launched May 2005 on PSLV-C6; two panchromatic cameras at approximately +26deg and −5deg along-track; about 2.5 m spatial resolution; swath around 30 km; Sun-synchronous orbit; primary purpose cartography and DEM generation.
- Stereo imaging explained in one line: two images of the same ground taken from different angles allow parallax to be measured, and parallax converts directly into elevation — the same principle as human binocular depth perception.
- The Cartosat lineage: Cartosat-1 (2.5 m, stereo, cartography) –> Cartosat-2 series (sub-metre panchromatic, narrow swath) –> Cartosat-3 (finer still, agile pointing).
- Chandrayaan quick facts for the compact “comment”: Chandrayaan-1 (2008, discovered lunar water, ~312 days); Chandrayaan-2 (2019, orbiter operational, lander failed); Chandrayaan-3 (2023, south polar soft landing, Shiv Shakti Point, National Space Day); Chandrayaan-4 (sample return, approved) and Chandrayaan-5/LUPEX with JAXA.

The Indian space programme has been guided from its inception by the principle of space technology for national development. Satellite-derived soil resource mapping, land capability classification and groundwater prospect mapping identify what a given parcel can sustain. - Pest and disease early warning through hyperspectral detection of reflectance changes before visible symptoms appear.
- Advisories reaching the farmer through Kisan Call Centres, Kisan Suvidha and the Krishi Decision Support System, which integrates satellite, weather, soil and crop-registry data on one platform.

## Harvest forecasting — informing national policy

FASAL (Forecasting Agricultural output using Space, Agro-meteorology and Land-based observations) generates multiple in-season forecasts of crop area and yield for major crops. Its consequence is administrative: procurement, buffer-stock, import and MSP decisions can be taken before harvest rather than after. CHAMAN does the equivalent for horticulture — directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s mango, banana, chilli and citrus economy.

Under PMFBY, the YES-TECH framework uses remote-sensing-based yield estimation to reduce dependence on crop-cutting experiments, which were slow, sample-limited and a frequent source of dispute. NADRES applies geospatial modelling to livestock disease risk. Drought assessment through NDVI time-series informs relief declaration.

- Fisheries:INCOIS Potential Fishing Zone advisories from Oceansat data help fishermen locate shoals, saving fuel and time; ocean-state forecasts and NavIC messaging carry cyclone warnings beyond mobile range.

Satellite-derived information is only as valuable as its last mile. A forecast that reaches a district office but not the farmer changes nothing. ## Introduction

PMFBY (2016) provides comprehensive crop risk coverage on an area-based approach, where compensation is triggered by the average yield of a defined insurance unit — a block or panchayat — falling below a threshold. Everything therefore depends on how accurately that average yield is measured. Space technology entered the scheme precisely because the traditional measurement method could not deliver accuracy at national scale.

assessment (anomaly detection) --> Claim settlement (Krishi-DSS) .

## Why space technology was needed — the limits of Crop Cutting Experiments

Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) require physically harvesting sample plots and weighing the produce. At the scale PMFBY operates, this means millions of experiments per season, and the method is labour-intensive, slow, vulnerable to sampling bias, and open to misreporting. Delays in CCE results translated directly into delays in claim settlement — historically farmers’ principal grievance against crop insurance. India’s fragmented holdings and spatial heterogeneity make the sampling problem worse, not better.

## Role of space and geospatial technology under PMFBY
- Smart sampling and geo-referencing. Satellite-derived crop indices (NDVI and related) are overlaid to identify representative locations for CCEs rather than convenient ones, reducing sampling bias. Geo-tagged plots anchor each yield observation to a verified location, so the measurement can be audited.
- Yield estimation through remote sensing — the core innovation. Multispectral time-series imagery is combined with crop growth models, machine learning and ancillary weather and soil data to estimate yield at the insurance-unit level. The YES-TECH (Yield Estimation System using Technology) framework, introduced for paddy and wheat from Kharif 2023, assigns 30% weightage to technology-derived yield alongside conventional CCE results — a graduated transition rather than a wholesale replacement, which is why it gained acceptance.
- Loss and damage assessment. Anomaly detection in crop health indices reveals the spatial pattern of damage from drought, flood, hail or pest attack. For area-based insurance this is decisive: satellite imagery shows whether loss is localised or widespread, which is exactly what the payout formula turns on.
- Dispute resolution. Where insurer and State disagree on area sown or yield achieved, independent sensor-derived estimates provide a neutral reference. Reported outcome: in Kharif 2023, all States implementing PMFBY used the YES-TECH methodology in claims settlement, with no stakeholder disputes reported.
- Decision support. The Krishi Decision Support System (Krishi-DSS) is a cloud-based geospatial platform hosting weather, soil, water, satellite imagery and field-level data, supporting States, insurers and farmers in planning, monitoring and claim adjudication. FASAL forecasts from ISRO/NRSC feed into PMFBY planning.
- Financial commitment: the Central Government committed Rs. 824.77 crore for integrating advanced technologies into PMFBY and RWBCIS through 2025-26.
- AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s exposure to cyclone-driven crop loss in the Godavari and Krishna deltas and drought in Rayalaseema makes rapid, objective loss assessment particularly consequential; the State’s Rythu Bharosa Kendras provide the village-level interface at which farmers register and verify claims.

## Remaining challenges
- Model calibration across India’s agro-climatic diversity — a yield model trained on one region performs poorly in another.
- Cloud cover during the monsoon, when loss events concentrate; NISAR’s dual-frequency radar (launched July 2025) directly addresses this by imaging through cloud.
- Institutional capacity in States and insurance companies to interpret and act on geospatial outputs.
- Farmer trust in an estimate they cannot physically verify — which is why the graduated 30% weightage matters as much as the technology.

## Conclusion

Space technology has changed PMFBY from a scheme limited by how fast people could harvest sample plots into one that can assess an entire district in a single satellite pass. YES-TECH’s phased introduction, with technology carrying partial rather than total weight, is a model of how to introduce automated assessment into a high-stakes entitlement without forfeiting trust. As radar coverage improves through NISAR, the remaining barrier is institutional rather than technical.

## Introduction

SVAMITVA — Survey of Villages and Mapping with Improvised Technology in Village Areas — was launched in April 2020 by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj to survey rural inhabited (“Abadi”) land and issue Property Cards to owners. It addresses a specific gap: while agricultural land in India has long been surveyed and recorded, the land villagers actually live on was often outside any formal record, leaving homes legally invisible and therefore unusable as collateral.

Photogrammetric processing (2D/3D maps) --> Gram Manchitra GIS + participatory validation --> Property Card .

A precision worth stating: SVAMITVA’s imagery comes from drones, not satellites, because property-level boundaries require centimetre-scale detail that satellite imagery cannot deliver. What is satellite-based is the positioning — the GNSS corrections that anchor every drone image to true ground coordinates. Making this distinction demonstrates technical understanding rather than a general association of “space technology” with anything aerial.

## The technology chain
- CORS network — the positioning foundation.Continuously Operating Reference Stations provide high-precision GNSS corrections through Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) techniques, delivering centimetre-level accuracy. CORS establishes Ground Control Points that anchor aerial imagery to real-world coordinates; without this, stitched drone mosaics drift and boundaries shift. The network, built by the Survey of India, is a permanent national asset usable well beyond SVAMITVA.
- Drone survey and aerial photogrammetry. Survey-grade drones with GNSS and inertial sensors capture overlapping imagery of each village’s Abadi area. Photogrammetric processing converts the overlap into precise 2D and 3D maps and parcel boundaries at roughly 5 cm accuracy — a level at which a boundary wall is individually resolvable.
- GIS integration through Gram Manchitra. Derived maps are ingested into the Gram Manchitra spatial planning platform, layering parcels with village assets — roads, ponds, public buildings — and linking each parcel to attribute data (owner name, area, property card number), enabling spatial queries and updates.
- Participatory validation — the step that makes it legally durable. Villagers examine and verify parcel boundaries on the maps before records are finalised, identifying encroachments and historic boundary shifts. This is what converts a technically accurate map into a socially accepted record; a survey that villagers have not endorsed generates litigation rather than settling it.
- Monitoring and dashboards. Geotagged status updates feed an online dashboard tracking villages surveyed and property cards issued across States in real time.

## Achievements
- As of April 2025, drone surveys had been completed in about 3.20 lakh villages, covering roughly 68,122 sq km of rural Abadi land, with over 2.42 crore property cards issued.
- On 18 January 2025, about 65 lakh property cards were distributed electronically across more than 50,000 villages in multiple States.
- The scheme received recognition as an e-governance innovation under the National Awards for e-Governance (2023).

## Why it matters — the development argument

A property card converts a house from an occupied structure into a recognised, mortgageable asset. This is the economic case: formal title enables institutional credit at bank rather than moneylender rates, supports property taxation that funds panchayat services, reduces boundary litigation, and provides the spatial base for Gram Panchayat Development Plans.

## Challenges
- Uniform accuracy across rugged, forested or densely built terrain, where drone imagery and photogrammetry perform less consistently.
- Reconciliation with legacy cadastral records for non-Abadi land, requiring integration with conventional survey.
- CORS coverage and GNSS reliability, particularly in terrain with signal obstruction.
- Legal follow-through: a property card’s value depends on State law recognising it as evidence of title, which varies.
- Supplementary technologies — high-resolution satellite imagery or LiDAR — may be needed where drone flight is restricted.

AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s Revenue One platform is digitising land and revenue records with over 19,000 revenue officials using it — the administrative layer into which SVAMITVA-type spatial records must integrate if they are to have legal effect.

## Conclusion

SVAMITVA demonstrates a precise division of technological labour: satellites supply the positioning framework, drones supply the imagery, GIS supplies the record, and villagers supply the legitimacy. With over 2.42 crore property cards issued by April 2025, its measurable achievement is the conversion of rural homes into recorded assets. Its lasting contribution may be the CORS network itself — a national high-precision positioning backbone that will outlast the scheme that justified building it.

## Value addition
- SVAMITVA components: establishment of the CORS network; large-scale drone mapping of Abadi areas by the Survey of India; IEC (Information, Education and Communication) activities to build village awareness; and enhancement of the Gram Manchitra spatial planning application to support Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDP).
- Accuracy figures to quote: CORS-enabled RTK positioning gives centimetre-level ground control; drone photogrammetry yields parcel boundaries at roughly 5 cm accuracy — far beyond what satellite imagery can provide at property level.
- Achievement data (April 2025): about 3.20 lakh villages surveyed; roughly 68,122 sq km of Abadi land covered; over 2.42 crore property cards issued; 65 lakh cards e-distributed on 18 January 2025 across 50,000+ villages.
- The economic argument — “dead capital”: unrecorded property cannot be pledged, sold formally or taxed. Formal title converts it into usable capital, the argument associated with Hernando de Soto and directly applicable to SVAMITVA’s rationale.
- Related land-governance initiatives: Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme (DILRMP); Unique Land Parcel Identification Number (ULPIN/Bhu-Aadhaar); National Generic Document Registration System (NGDRS); e-Court integration for land disputes.

## Introduction

Energy security is conventionally defined along four dimensions: availability (physical supply), accessibility (geopolitical reach), affordability (price), and acceptability (environmental sustainability). India, the world’s third-largest energy consumer, faces a distinctive challenge — it must simultaneously expand supply for a growing economy and decarbonise it, a dual task most developed economies did not face.

## Present composition of energy sources
- Electricity capacity. Total installed capacity crossed 500 GW in September 2025. As on 31 March 2026, non-fossil capacity stood at 283.46 GW — renewable energy 274.68 GW (solar 150.26 GW, wind 56.09 GW, large hydro 51.41 GW, bio-power 11.75 GW, small hydro 5.17 GW) and nuclear 8.78 GW (MNRE). - Coal remains the generation backbone. Domestic production reached about 1,047.57 million tonnes in FY 2024-25. Its persistence is a function of dispatchability and domestic availability rather than policy preference.
- Oil and gas dominate non-electricity energy. India imports roughly 85-88% of crude oil and about half its natural gas — the sharpest single vulnerability, because transport and petrochemicals cannot be electrified quickly.

## Growing demand and the challenges it creates

India’s energy demand growth is among the fastest of any major economy, driven by household electrification, industrial expansion, cooling demand and mobility. The consequent challenges are: import exposure in oil and gas; grid stability as variable renewables rise; distribution company finances, which constrain the ability to buy power; and land and mineral constraints on renewable expansion.

## Future energy security scenario — the instruments
- Diversification. The 500 GW non-fossil by 2030 target, the National Green Hydrogen Mission (Rs. 19,744 crore, 5 MMT annual production by 2030) for hard-to-abate sectors, and expansion of nuclear capacity, including the opening of the sector to greater private participation.
- Storage — the decisive variable. Integrating variable renewables requires battery storage and pumped hydro; the National Electricity Plan projects large-scale storage requirements by 2030, and viability gap funding has been extended to battery energy storage systems. Andhra Pradesh targets 22 GW of pumped storage under its Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, and hosts the Pinnapuram Integrated Renewable Energy Storage Project in Kurnool district.
- Reducing oil dependence. The Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme achieved 20% blending (E20) in 2025-26, ahead of schedule (PIB); PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore from 1 October 2024, subsuming FAME-II and EMPS-2024) supports electric mobility, charging infrastructure and testing capacity; Strategic Petroleum Reserves buffer supply shocks.
- Critical minerals — the new dependency. The clean-energy transition substitutes an oil dependency for a mineral one: lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare earths are essential for batteries, wind turbines and solar modules, and their supply is geographically concentrated. The National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) responds, with the Geological Survey of India tasked with 1,200 exploration projects by 2030-31, alongside overseas asset acquisition and recycling. Recognising this substitution of dependencies is the sharpest energy-security point available today.
- Grid and institutional reform. Green Energy Corridors for evacuation, RDSS for distribution loss reduction and smart metering, and the National Electricity Plan for capacity and transmission planning.

## Conclusion

India’s energy composition is shifting faster than most projections anticipated — the 50% non-fossil capacity milestone arrived five years early and E20 blending ahead of schedule. But energy security is not achieved by capacity alone: the binding constraints are now storage, which converts capacity into dependable supply, and critical minerals, which determine whether the transition trades an oil import bill for a mineral one. A secure energy future therefore requires domestic mineral capability and storage at scale as much as further renewable capacity.

## Value addition
- The four dimensions of energy security: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability — a framework worth stating explicitly at the start of any energy-security answer.
- National Critical Mineral Mission (2025): targets self-reliance in critical minerals; 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31; covers exploration, overseas acquisition, recycling and stockpiling; critical minerals include lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, silicon and rare earths.
- Storage instruments: pumped storage projects; viability gap funding for battery energy storage systems; the National Electricity Plan’s storage projections; Andhra Pradesh’s 22 GW pumped storage target under its Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024.
- Transport decarbonisation:E20 achieved in 2025-26; PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore, from 1 October 2024, replacing FAME-II and EMPS-2024, with Rs. 2,000 crore for charging infrastructure and support for 14,000 e-buses); National Green Hydrogen Mission for heavy transport and industry.
- Nuclear expansion: 8.78 GW installed as on March 2026; a 71% rise since 2014; policy moves toward greater private and small modular reactor participation.
- The key analytical distinction:installed capacity (nameplate) versus generation (actual electricity produced) versus primary energy (including transport and industrial fuel). India’s renewable achievement is strongest on the first measure and weakest on the third — a nuance that separates strong answers from generic ones.

## Introduction

A smart grid is an electricity network that uses digital sensing, communication and control to enable two-way flow of both power and information between utility and consumer. The distinction from a conventional grid is precise: a conventional grid pushes electricity one way and discovers faults when someone complains; a smart grid measures continuously, detects faults itself, and allows consumers to feed power back.

## Benefits
- Reduction of aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses. India’s distribution losses have historically been among the world’s highest, and a large share is commercial — theft and unbilled supply — rather than technical. Smart meters make consumption measurable at every point, converting an unquantified loss into an identified one. This is the single largest financial benefit.
- Integration of variable renewables. As solar and wind rise toward half of capacity, the grid must balance supply that changes minute to minute. Smart grids provide the real-time visibility and automated control that make this possible; without them, renewable penetration hits a technical ceiling.
- Reliability and self-healing. Automated fault detection, isolation and service restoration reduce outage duration by rerouting supply around a fault without a crew being dispatched.
- Consumer empowerment and demand management. Smart prepaid meters give households real-time consumption data; time-of-use tariffs allow shifting of load away from peak hours; net metering lets rooftop solar owners export surplus. Under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, net metering is what makes household solar financially viable.
- Utility finances. Prepaid metering shifts billing from estimated post-consumption to measured pre-payment, improving distribution company cash flow — the root cause of the sector’s chronic financial stress.

The flagship deployment: the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), Ministry of Power, with an outlay of about Rs. 3.03 lakh crore, is rolling out smart prepaid metering toward roughly 25 crore consumers alongside loss-reduction and system-strengthening works — India’s largest smart-grid programme by a wide margin, and the answer’s most important single fact.

## Challenges and matching strategies
- **Challenge** — Strategy
- **Ageing infrastructure — legacy transformers, feeders and meters not designed for digital integration** — Phased modernisation under RDSS with feeder and transformer metering; NSGM pilot projects to establish templates
- **Cybersecurity — a digitised grid is an attack surface, and an intrusion becomes a physical outage** — CEA (Cyber Security in Power Sector) Guidelines; CERT-In directions; sectoral CERT for power; mandatory ISO 27001-type controls and testing of imported equipment
- **Interoperability — multi-vendor meters and systems that cannot exchange data** — Standardised communication protocols and BIS/CEA specifications; common data models across utilities
- **Financial constraints — high upfront capital against weak DISCOM balance sheets** — RDSS conditional funding tied to loss-reduction milestones; TOTEX/AMISP models where a service provider funds and operates metering and is paid from realised savings
- **Consumer resistance — distrust of prepaid metering and fear of higher bills** — Consumer awareness campaigns, transparent billing dashboards, and safeguards against disconnection
- **Skills gap — utility staff trained for electromechanical, not digital, systems** — Capacity building under NSGM; training programmes for utility personnel

AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s distribution utilities are implementing smart metering under RDSS, and the State’s AWARE platform under the Real Time Governance Society already demonstrates the integration of sensor networks with real-time decision-making — the governance capability a smart grid presupposes.

## Conclusion

The smart grid is best understood not as an upgrade to the grid but as the precondition for the energy transition: without real-time measurement and control, neither high renewable penetration nor rooftop solar nor demand-side management is technically achievable. India’s approach — mass deployment through RDSS rather than isolated pilots — is the right scale. The determining factors will be cybersecurity, which turns a technical fault into a national one, and consumer trust, without which prepaid metering becomes politically unsustainable.

## Value addition
- RDSS (Ministry of Power, 2021): outlay about Rs. 3.03 lakh crore; smart prepaid metering for roughly 25 crore consumers; feeder and distribution-transformer metering; funding conditional on AT&C loss-reduction and ACS-ARR gap milestones.
- National Smart Grid Mission (NSGM): established under the Ministry of Power to plan and monitor smart grid projects, with a technical committee and a project management unit; supports State-level pilots and capacity building.
- Enabling technologies: Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI); SCADA and Distribution Management Systems; Automatic Meter Reading; Distributed Energy Resource Management Systems; Wide Area Measurement Systems using phasor measurement units for real-time grid stability monitoring.
- Related instruments: Green Energy Corridors for renewable evacuation; PM Surya Ghar with net metering; time-of-use tariffs notified under the Electricity (Amendment) Rules; Electricity Act, 2003 as the governing statute.
- The AT&C loss point: India’s distribution losses have fallen substantially over the past decade but remain high by international standards, and a significant share is commercial rather than technical — which is precisely why metering, not conductor replacement, is the priority intervention.
- AP-specific: RDSS smart metering rollout by AP DISCOMs; RTGS AWARE platform integrating IoT sensor networks; AP’s 22 GW pumped storage target, which will require smart-grid coordination to be usable.

## Introduction

Urbanisation changes the nature of energy demand, not merely its volume: cities concentrate consumption, shift it toward electricity and transport fuels, and create peaks — from air-conditioning and evening lighting — that strain the grid at precisely the hours when solar generation ceases. With India’s urban population projected to approach 600 million by 2036, and cities accounting for the bulk of electricity consumption, an energy policy designed for dispersed rural electrification cannot address the urban problem.

## Why a revamped policy is needed
- The urban demand curve is the problem, not the volume. Cooling demand is the fastest-growing component of urban electricity use, and it peaks in the late afternoon and evening — after solar output falls. This creates a duck-curve problem: high daytime solar generation followed by a steep evening ramp that only dispatchable or stored power can meet. A policy that counts renewable capacity without addressing the evening peak solves the wrong problem. The India Cooling Action Plan (2019) is the dedicated response, targeting reductions in cooling demand, refrigerant transition and improved efficiency.
- Energy poverty persists inside cities. Slums and peri-urban settlements face unreliable supply, unmetered connections and reliance on polluting cooking fuels. PMUY extended LPG access, but affordability of refills, not connection, is the binding constraint. Decentralised rooftop solar and community microgrids need an explicit urban-poor design.
- Transport is the largest urban fossil-fuel consumer. The instruments are PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore from 1 October 2024, subsuming FAME-II and EMPS-2024, supporting e-buses, charging infrastructure and testing agencies), metro rail expansion, the National Green Hydrogen Mission for heavy freight, and the E20 ethanol blending achieved in 2025-26. Public transport electrification matters more than private EV adoption, since a bus displaces far more fuel per subsidy rupee.
- Buildings determine locked-in demand. A building’s energy consumption is fixed at design stage for decades. The Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) for commercial buildings and Eco-Niwas Samhita for residential buildings, administered by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, address this — but adoption depends on State building bye-laws and municipal enforcement capacity, which is where the policy gap lies. The Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 strengthened this framework and introduced a carbon credit trading scheme.
- Efficiency as the cheapest supply.UJALA distributed LED bulbs at scale, and the Street Lighting National Programme replaced conventional streetlights with LEDs — municipal energy bills being one of the largest discretionary costs local bodies bear. Every avoided unit is cheaper than a generated one.
- Waste as an energy resource. Urban solid waste and sewage offer waste-to-energy, biomethanation and compressed biogas opportunities under the GOBARdhan and SATAT initiatives, converting a disposal liability into a fuel supply while addressing landfill pressure.

## Institutional and policy instruments to cite accurately
- Energy Conservation Act, 2001, as amended in 2022, with the Bureau of Energy Efficiency as implementing agency; Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) for industrial efficiency; Standards and Labelling for appliances.
- Smart Cities Mission — integrated command and control centres, smart metering, LED street lighting and rooftop solar within city plans.
- RDSS for distribution modernisation, and PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana for household rooftop solar with net metering.
- National Electricity Policy, 2005 and the National Tariff Policy remain the notified framework instruments; the National Electricity Plan prepared by the Central Electricity Authority provides the operational capacity and transmission roadmap.
- AP instance: Andhra Pradesh’s Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targets 22 GW of pumped storage — directly relevant to the urban evening peak, since pumped storage absorbs surplus daytime solar and releases it after sunset. Visakhapatnam and Amaravati are the State’s principal urban energy demand centres.

## Conclusion

Urban energy policy must address a demand profile rather than a demand quantity: concentrated, electricity-intensive, and peaking exactly when solar generation stops. The instruments exist — ECBC and Eco-Niwas Samhita for buildings, PM E-DRIVE for transport, RDSS for distribution, PM Surya Ghar for rooftop generation — but they sit with different ministries and depend on municipal enforcement capacity that is often weakest where urbanisation is fastest. The revamp required is therefore less about new schemes than about integrating energy planning into urban planning, and building the local capacity to enforce it.

## Value addition
- Correct policy citations:National Electricity Policy, 2005 (notified; a 2021 revision remains a draft); Energy Conservation Act, 2001, amended 2022 (introducing carbon credit trading and extending the code to residential buildings); National Tariff Policy; National Electricity Plan by the CEA.
- Efficiency instruments:ECBC (commercial buildings) and Eco-Niwas Samhita (residential); PAT scheme for energy-intensive industries; Standards and Labelling for appliances; UJALA and the Street Lighting National Programme; India Cooling Action Plan, 2019.
- Transport:PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore, from 1 October 2024, replacing FAME-II and EMPS-2024; Rs. 2,000 crore for charging infrastructure; support for about 14,000 e-buses; Rs. 780 crore for testing agency upgrades); metro expansion; E20 blending achieved 2025-26; National Green Hydrogen Mission.
- Urban waste-to-energy:GOBARdhan, SATAT for compressed biogas, and waste-to-energy plants under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0.
- The duck curve — worth naming: high midday solar generation followed by a steep evening ramp as solar falls and demand peaks. It is the central technical reason storage, not further solar capacity, is now the binding constraint in urban power systems.
- AP-specific: Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 with 22 GW pumped storage; Visakhapatnam and Amaravati as urban demand centres; RTGS AWARE for urban monitoring; Google’s AI hub at Visakhapatnam, itself a very large new urban electricity load.
- SDG linkage: SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy), SDG 11 (sustainable cities) and SDG 13 (climate action).

## Introduction

India’s energy sector has expanded remarkably — installed capacity crossed 500 GW in September 2025, non-fossil capacity reached 283.46 GW by 31 March 2026, and power shortages have fallen to negligible levels. Yet expansion has not resolved the sector’s underlying difficulties, which are less about generating electricity than about paying for it, delivering it reliably, and decarbonising it without disrupting supply.

## Structural challenges
- Import dependence in oil and gas. India imports roughly 85-88% of crude oil and about half its natural gas. This is the sector’s deepest vulnerability, because transport and petrochemicals cannot be electrified at the pace renewables are being added.
- Coal lock-in. Thermal plants have decades of remaining life and outstanding debt; retiring them early creates stranded assets and employment disruption in coal-dependent districts, while running them conflicts with climate commitments.
- The capacity-generation gap. Non-fossil sources exceed 50% of installed capacity but supplied about 29.2% of generation in 2025-26 — so headline capacity figures overstate the transition’s real progress.

## Financial challenges
- Distribution company losses remain the sector’s central weakness: high AT&C losses, tariffs below cost of supply, delayed subsidy reimbursement and accumulated dues to generators. A financially weak DISCOM cannot sign long-term power purchase agreements, which slows renewable procurement regardless of how cheap solar becomes. RDSS (Rs. 3.03 lakh crore) conditions funding on loss-reduction milestones precisely for this reason.
- Cross-subsidy and tariff politics. Agricultural and residential tariffs are held below cost and recovered from industrial and commercial consumers, raising industrial power costs and eroding manufacturing competitiveness.
- Capital intensity of the transition. Renewables, storage, transmission and grid modernisation require sustained investment, and risk perception raises the cost of capital.

## Environmental and social challenges
- Emissions and air quality from coal combustion and transport fuels; thermal plants are also among India’s largest industrial water consumers, competing with agriculture in water-stressed regions.
- Land acquisition for solar parks, wind farms and transmission corridors, with attendant questions of livelihood and common-land access.
- Just transition for workers and districts economically dependent on coal — a challenge of political economy rather than technology.

## Technological challenges
- Storage is the binding constraint. Without it, solar generation cannot serve the evening peak, and the grid depends on thermal capacity for balancing.
- Grid integration of variable renewables requires forecasting, flexible generation, transmission adequacy and real-time control.
- Manufacturing depth. India assembles more solar modules than it once did but remains dependent on imported cells, wafers and polysilicon — the PLI for High Efficiency Solar PV Modules and ALMM address this, but the upstream gap persists.

## Geopolitical and resource challenges
- Critical mineral dependence. Lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare earths are concentrated in a few countries and are essential to batteries, wind turbines and EVs. The transition therefore risks substituting a mineral dependency for an oil dependency — the most important emerging energy-security issue. The National Critical Mineral Mission (2025), with 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31, is the response.
- Supply-chain concentration in solar and battery manufacturing, and exposure to global price and shipping shocks.

## Way forward

Scale storage through pumped hydro and battery systems with viability gap funding; restore DISCOM viability through RDSS-linked reform and cost-reflective tariffs; deepen domestic manufacturing under PLI and ALMM; secure critical minerals through exploration, overseas assets and recycling; and plan a just transition for coal districts. Andhra Pradesh’s Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, with 160 GW of renewable capacity including 22 GW of pumped storage, illustrates a State-level response that treats storage as central rather than incidental.

## Conclusion

India’s energy challenges have shifted in character: a decade ago the problem was shortage, today it is structure — a financially strained distribution segment, a generation mix that cannot yet meet the evening peak without coal, and a transition that trades oil imports for mineral imports. Capacity addition, at which India has been strikingly successful, no longer addresses the binding constraints. Storage, distribution reform and mineral security now determine whether the transition is completed or stalls partway.

- Key data: total installed capacity crossed 500 GW in September 2025; non-fossil capacity 283.46 GW as on 31 March 2026 (renewables 274.68 GW, nuclear 8.78 GW); highest-ever non-fossil addition of 55.29 GW in 2025-26; non-fossil share of generation about 29.2%; coal production about 1,047.57 million tonnes in FY 2024-25; crude oil import dependence roughly 85-88%.
- Achievements worth citing alongside challenges: power shortages down from 4.2% in 2013-14 to about 0.1% in 2024-25; 50% non-fossil capacity reached in June 2025, five years early; E20 ethanol blending achieved in 2025-26; third globally in renewable installed capacity (IRENA, 2026).
- DISCOM reform instruments:RDSS (Rs. 3.03 lakh crore, conditional on AT&C loss and ACS-ARR gap reduction); Late Payment Surcharge Rules; earlier UDAY scheme as a cautionary precedent, since it restructured debt without permanently fixing tariffs.
- Critical minerals:National Critical Mineral Mission (2025); GSI’s 1,200 exploration projects by 2030-31; KABIL for overseas mineral assets; amendments to the MMDR Act enabling auction of critical mineral blocks.
- Just transition: coal-district economies in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal; the need for alternative livelihoods and district-level transition planning — a dimension most answers omit and examiners reward.

## Introduction

An energy crisis arises when supply becomes uncertain, unaffordable or environmentally unsustainable — and contemporary crises combine all three. Renewable energy addresses each simultaneously: it is domestically generated (security), has near-zero marginal cost once built (affordability), and produces no operating emissions (sustainability). For India, importing roughly 85-88% of its crude oil, the security argument alone would justify the transition.

## Scope of renewable energy
- Energy security and self-reliance. Renewables substitute imported fuel with domestic generation. Every unit of solar generated displaces coal or, through electrification, oil — reducing an import bill that is India’s largest single external vulnerability.
- Price stability. Once built, a solar or wind plant has almost no fuel cost, so its tariff is fixed for the life of the power purchase agreement. This insulates consumers from the international price swings that transmit directly into coal- and gas-based tariffs.
- Environmental sustainability. India’s NDC commits to reducing the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030 — a measure of emissions per unit of output, not of absolute emissions, which continue to rise with economic growth. Stating this precisely matters.
- Energy access and rural livelihoods. Decentralised systems — solar microgrids, standalone pumps, biogas — reach where grid extension is uneconomic. Distributed renewable energy contributed 16.3 GW of the 44.61 GW installed in 2025-26, including 7.6 GW under PM-KUSUM.
- Employment and industry. Renewables are more labour-intensive per unit of capacity than thermal generation, with jobs in manufacturing, installation and maintenance; PLI schemes aim to capture the manufacturing segment domestically.
- Technological and industrial opportunity. Battery storage, green hydrogen, electrolysers and smart grids represent new industrial sectors rather than merely a substitution of fuel.
- Demonstrated feasibility: India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years early, and added a record 55.29 GW of non-fossil capacity in 2025-26 — evidence that the scope is realisable, not theoretical.

## Barriers to renewable energy — classified

1. Technical - Intermittency — output depends on sun and wind, with no generation at the evening demand peak. - Storage inadequacy — the binding constraint; without it, renewables cannot displace dispatchable capacity. - Grid integration — forecasting, balancing reserves, reactive power support and frequency management. - Transmission and curtailment — resource-rich regions are distant from load centres, and inadequate evacuation forces generation to be switched off.

2. Financial - High upfront capital, even where lifetime cost is low, raising sensitivity to interest rates. - DISCOM financial weakness — utilities unable to pay generators on time deter investment regardless of tariff competitiveness. - Cost of capital and risk perception, particularly for storage and newer technologies.

3. Land and social - Land acquisition for utility-scale solar parks, wind farms and transmission corridors, with livelihood and common-land questions. -Local resistance and awareness gaps, and competing land uses including agriculture and grazing.

4. Supply chain and resources - Import dependence in solar cells, wafers and polysilicon despite growing module assembly. - Critical minerals — lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare earths are geographically concentrated, so the transition risks substituting a mineral dependency for an oil dependency. The National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) responds, with 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31.

5. Institutional and regulatory - Policy and tariff uncertainty, delays in clearances and in power purchase agreement signing. - Skills and R&D gaps in storage, electrolysers and grid management. - End-of-life management — solar module and battery waste is an emerging problem requiring a recycling regime.

## Conclusion

Renewable energy is no longer a costly hedge against an energy crisis but the least-cost source of new capacity, and India’s record additions confirm it. The barriers have correspondingly shifted: cost and technology maturity are largely resolved, while storage, transmission, DISCOM finances and critical minerals now determine the pace. Addressing these is less a matter of further renewable targets than of building the system that variable generation requires.

## Value addition
- Precision on the NDC target: India’s commitment is a 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels by 2030 — emissions per unit of GDP, not absolute emissions. Also: 50% of cumulative installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030, and net zero by 2070.
- Storage instruments: pumped storage projects; viability gap funding for battery energy storage systems; the National Electricity Plan’s storage projections; Andhra Pradesh’s 22 GW pumped storage target.
- Manufacturing and supply chain: PLI for High Efficiency Solar PV Modules; ALMM (Approved List of Models and Manufacturers) progressively extended from modules to cells; National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) with 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31; KABIL for overseas mineral assets.
- Financial instruments: 100% FDI under the automatic route in renewables; sovereign green bonds; ISTS charge waiver; Renewable Purchase Obligations; RDSS to restore DISCOM viability.
- The emerging waste problem: end-of-life solar modules and lithium batteries; the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 and E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 provide EPR frameworks, but module recycling capacity remains limited — a forward-looking point few answers make.
- AP-specific: Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 (160 GW target, Rs. 10 lakh crore investment, 7.5 lakh jobs); Kurnool and NP Kunta Ultra Mega Solar Parks; Pinnapuram Integrated Renewable Energy Storage Project.
