## Introduction

Energy resources are classified by whether they are replenished at a rate comparable to their consumption. Renewable sources are naturally replenished within human timescales; non-renewable sources — fossil fuels and nuclear fuels — exist in finite stocks formed over geological time. Global primary energy remains dominated by non-renewables, which is why the demand-mitigation question matters as much as the substitution question.

## (a) Renewable versus non-renewable
- **Basis** — Renewable · Non-renewable
- **Replenishment** — Naturally replenished within human timescales · Finite stocks formed over millions of years
- **Environmental impact** — Low operating emissions · High emissions and pollutants
- **Cost structure** — High capital, negligible fuel cost · Lower capital, continuing fuel cost
- **Reliability** — Solar and wind variable; hydro and biomass dispatchable · Dispatchable, provides baseload
- **Distribution** — Widely available · Geographically concentrated
- **Examples** — Solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal, tidal · Coal, petroleum, natural gas, nuclear fuel

A precision worth making: nuclear is non-renewable (uranium is finite) but is classified as non-conventional and low-carbon — which is why “non-conventional” and “renewable” are not interchangeable terms.

## Types of non-conventional energy and their resources in India
- Solar. Installed capacity 150.26 GW as on 31 March 2026 (MNRE), up from about 2.6 GW in 2014. India receives 4-7 kWh per square metre per day over about 300 clear days; Rajasthan, Gujarat and the Deccan plateau have the highest irradiance.
- Wind.56.09 GW installed; the National Institute of Wind Energy assesses very large potential at 120 m hub height. Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh hold most of it. Offshore wind potential is being developed off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.
- Small hydro.5.17 GW, with potential concentrated in Himalayan and Western Ghats streams.
- Biomass and bio-CNG.11.75 GW of bio-power; crop residue, bagasse and municipal waste are the feedstock; SATAT and GOBARdhan promote compressed biogas.
- Geothermal. Identified provinces at Puga and Chumathang (Ladakh), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh) and Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh); commercial generation negligible.
- Tidal and wave. Estimated potential of around 8,000 MW along the Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kutch and the Sundarbans; essentially untapped.
- Green hydrogen. Not a primary resource but an energy carrier produced from renewable electricity; the National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MMT annually by 2030.

## (b) Factors driving worldwide energy demand
- Population growth. The global population crossed 8 billion in 2022, adding residential, transport and food-system energy demand.
- Industrialisation and urbanisation in emerging economies, where manufacturing, construction and infrastructure are energy-intensive and cities concentrate consumption.
- Rising incomes and living standards. Appliance ownership, vehicle ownership and especially space cooling rise sharply with income — cooling is among the fastest-growing components of global electricity demand.
- Digitalisation and AI. Data centres and AI compute have become a materially growing electricity load; India’s own experience illustrates this, with Google’s AI hub at Visakhapatnam planned at gigawatt-scale data-centre capacity.
- Transport growth in both freight and passenger movement, still overwhelmingly oil-based.

## Measures to mitigate demand growth
- Energy efficiency — the cheapest intervention. In India: UJALA for LED lighting, Standards and Labelling for appliances, Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) for industry, and ECBC and Eco-Niwas Samhita for buildings, under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 (amended 2022).
- Electrification with clean generation — electric mobility under PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore) and rail electrification, which reduce energy demand because electric drivetrains are far more efficient than combustion engines.
- Fuel substitution — E20 ethanol blending achieved in 2025-26; green hydrogen for hard-to-abate sectors.
- Demand-side management — time-of-use tariffs and smart metering under RDSS, shifting load away from peak hours.
- Behavioural change — Mission LIFE (Lifestyle for Environment), India’s contribution to framing demand-side action as an individual and community responsibility.
- International cooperation — the Paris Agreement (2015), the International Solar Alliance and the Global Biofuels Alliance.

## Conclusion

The renewable/non-renewable distinction turns on replenishment rate, and the practical consequence is that only renewables can support indefinite growth in consumption. But substitution alone is insufficient: with population, incomes, cooling and digital demand all rising, supply-side transition must be matched by efficiency and demand management. India’s approach — combining record renewable additions with UJALA, PAT, ECBC and Mission LIFE

— reflects that both halves are necessary.

## Value addition
- Current capacity (MNRE, 31 March 2026): solar 150.26 GW; wind 56.09 GW; large hydro 51.41 GW; bio-power 11.75 GW; small hydro 5.17 GW; nuclear 8.78 GW; non-fossil total 283.46 GW.
- Efficiency instruments:UJALA (LED distribution); Standards and Labelling (star ratings); PAT scheme with energy saving certificates; ECBC and Eco-Niwas Samhita; Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, which introduced a carbon credit trading scheme and extended the code to residential buildings; BEE as implementing agency.
- Solar promotion policies: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana; PM-KUSUM; Solar Park Scheme; 100% FDI under the automatic route; ISTS charge waiver; Green Energy Open Access Rules, 2022; PLI for High Efficiency Solar PV Modules.
- Mission LIFE: launched by India at COP26 and elaborated at COP27, framing demand-side, lifestyle-based climate action as complementary to supply-side decarbonisation — the concept India has most successfully exported internationally.
- The cooling point: space cooling is among the fastest-growing electricity loads globally and in India; the India Cooling Action Plan (2019) addresses refrigerant transition, efficiency and demand reduction — a specific and underused example.
- AP-specific: wind and solar resource endowment; Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024; Google AI hub at Visakhapatnam as an example of digitally driven demand growth arriving in India.

## Introduction

The clean-energy transition is being driven by two parallel developments: emerging renewable technologies that extend clean generation into applications solar panels alone cannot serve, and a renewed role for nuclear power, which supplies the low-carbon baseload that variable renewables cannot. India’s Budget 2025-26 announcement of a Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat, targeting 100 GWe by 2047, marks the sharpest policy shift in this field in decades.

## (a) Emerging renewable energy technologies
- Green hydrogen. Water split by electrolysis using renewable electricity, producing a storable, transportable fuel for steel, fertiliser, refining and heavy transport — sectors that cannot be directly electrified. The National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023), with Rs. 19,744 crore, targets 5 MMT annual production by 2030 with about 125 GW of associated renewable capacity, supported by the SIGHT programme for electrolyser manufacturing.
- Floating solar. Panels mounted on reservoirs and water bodies, saving land, reducing evaporation and gaining efficiency from water cooling. NTPC’s Ramagundam (Telangana) plant, at 100 MW, was India’s largest at commissioning; Omkareshwar in Madhya Pradesh has since scaled further.
- Offshore wind. Sea-based turbines achieve higher and steadier wind speeds than onshore sites; zones off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu have been identified, with viability gap funding approved to enable the first projects. Capital costs remain the barrier.
- Battery and long-duration storage. Advanced lithium-ion, sodium-ion and solid-state chemistries, plus pumped storage, which remains India’s most bankable large-scale option — Andhra Pradesh targets 22 GW.
- Bio-CNG and waste-to-energy. Municipal and agricultural waste converted to compressed biogas under SATAT and GOBARdhan, addressing waste disposal and fuel supply simultaneously.
- Agrivoltaics and solar-wind hybrids, raising land productivity by combining generation with cultivation or by co-locating complementary resources on one evacuation line.

(b) Nuclear energy: definition, hazards and mitigation

Definition. Nuclear energy is the energy released from the nucleus of an atom, through fission — the splitting of heavy nuclei such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239, the basis of all current commercial reactors — or fusion, the joining of light nuclei such as isotopes of hydrogen, which powers the Sun and remains experimental (India participates in ITER). Fission releases roughly a million times more energy per unit mass than chemical combustion, and produces no carbon dioxide during operation.

India’s position. India operates around 25 commercial reactors with about 8.78 GW of installed capacity (MNRE, March 2026). It follows a distinctive three-stage programme designed around domestic resource endowment — modest uranium but among the world’s largest thorium reserves: - Stage I: Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors using natural uranium, producing plutonium as a by-product. - Stage II: Fast Breeder Reactors using that plutonium and breeding more fuel than they consume; the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam marks India’s formal entry into this stage. - Stage III: Thorium-based reactors using uranium-233 bred from thorium — the stage that would give India long-term fuel independence.

## Mitigation of nuclear hazards
- Design safety — defence in depth. Multiple independent barriers between fuel and environment: fuel cladding, reactor pressure vessel, and a reinforced containment structure. Passive safety in newer designs relies on gravity and natural convection rather than powered pumps, so cooling continues even in a total power failure — the specific failure that caused Fukushima.
- Operational safety. Independent regulation by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board; periodic safety reviews, probabilistic safety assessment, emergency drills, and off-site emergency plans with district administrations.
- Siting and seismic design, with tsunami and flood assessment for coastal plants — the direct lesson of Fukushima (2011), after which India conducted safety reviews of all operating plants.
- Radiation protection through the ALARA principle (As Low As Reasonably Achievable), dosimetry and shielding.

## Nuclear waste management
- Classification by activity: low, intermediate and high-level waste, each with a distinct route.
- Immediate stage: spent fuel is stored in cooling pools at the reactor site for several years while heat and radioactivity decline.
- Reprocessing. India follows a closed fuel cycle, reprocessing spent fuel to recover plutonium and uranium for reuse. This is not merely waste management but the technical foundation of Stages II and III — recovered plutonium fuels the breeder reactors.
- Long-term: high-level waste is vitrified — immobilised in a stable borosilicate glass matrix — then stored in engineered surface facilities, with deep geological repositories as the eventual solution internationally.
- Institutional: the AERB regulates waste handling; India adheres to IAEA safety standards and safeguards on designated civilian facilities under the India-specific safeguards agreement following the 2008 civil nuclear cooperation arrangements.

## The current policy shift — the essential update
- Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat, announced in Budget 2025-26: Rs. 20,000 crore for research and development of Small Modular Reactors, targeting at least five indigenously designed SMRs operational by 2033, and 100 GWe of nuclear capacity by 2047 to support net zero by 2070.
- Indigenous SMR designs under development by BARC: the BSMR-200 (200 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor, a pressurised water design) and SMR-55 (55 MWe), aimed at brownfield sites — repurposing retiring coal plants, captive generation for energy-intensive industry, and off-grid remote applications. A high-temperature gas-cooled reactor is also under development for hydrogen production.
- The legislative change. Parliament enacted the SHANTI Act, 2025 (Sustainable Harnessing of Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India) in December 2025, repealing the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, and opening the nuclear sector to private and foreign participation for the first time (Department of Atomic Energy, reply in Parliament). This addresses the supplier-liability concerns that had stalled foreign investment since 2010.
- The roadmap to 100 GW: about 54 GW from NPCIL through indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs and imported light water reactors, with the balance of roughly 46 GW from public sector enterprises, State governments, private players and joint ventures.
- AP relevance:Kovvada in Srikakulam district has long been earmarked as a nuclear power project site under international cooperation — making Andhra Pradesh directly relevant to any question on nuclear expansion and on the public-acceptance challenges such projects face.

## Conclusion

Emerging renewables and nuclear power address complementary gaps: green hydrogen and storage extend clean energy into sectors and hours that solar cannot reach, while nuclear supplies dispatchable low-carbon baseload. India’s nuclear policy has shifted decisively — from a closed, state-monopoly sector to one opened by the SHANTI Act, 2025, with an SMR programme designed to repurpose retiring coal plants. The determining constraints are now execution speed and public acceptance rather than technology or law.

## Value addition
- Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat (Budget 2025-26): Rs. 20,000 crore for SMR research and development; at least five indigenous SMRs operational by 2033; 100 GWe by 2047; roadmap of about 54 GW from NPCIL and 46 GW from other public, private and joint-venture participants.
- Indigenous SMR designs:BSMR-200 (200 MWe pressurised water reactor) and SMR-55 (55 MWe) for brownfield sites, coal-plant repurposing, captive industrial power and off-grid use; a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor for hydrogen production — all under BARC.

- India’s three-stage programme: Stage I PHWRs (natural uranium); Stage II Fast Breeder Reactors (plutonium, breeding more fuel than consumed — PFBR at Kalpakkam); Stage III thorium-based reactors using U-233. Designed by Homi Bhabha around India’s large thorium and limited uranium reserves.
- Key institutions: Department of Atomic Energy; NPCIL (operations); BARC (research); AERB (independent regulation); IGCAR Kalpakkam (fast reactor research); Nuclear Fuel Complex, Hyderabad; BHAVINI for breeder reactors.

Q45:
## Introduction

Coal supplies roughly 70% of India’s electricity generation despite non-fossil sources now exceeding half of installed capacity — a gap explained by coal’s dispatchability. Yet new coal projects face sustained local opposition, while renewables, once genuinely underutilised, have expanded to 274.68 GW as on 31 March 2026 (MNRE). The question therefore has a historical and a contemporary dimension, and a good answer addresses both.

## (a) Public resistance to coal-based power plants

policy .

- Health and air quality. Coal combustion emits particulate matter, sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen and mercury. Industrial clusters such as Singrauli (Madhya Pradesh) and Angul (Odisha) have documented respiratory morbidity, and CPCB has repeatedly identified thermal power as a major contributor in critically polluted areas. Resistance here is grounded in measurable local harm, not abstract climate concern.
- Land acquisition and livelihood loss. Plants and associated mining displace agricultural and forest-dependent communities, often Scheduled Tribes with rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and consent requirements under PESA. The Sompeta (Bhavanapadu) and Kakarapalli agitations in Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, in 2010-11 are the closest and most instructive instances: local farmers and fishing communities opposed thermal power projects sited on beela wetlands, arguing the land was neither wasteland nor barren but a productive ecosystem supporting livelihoods and groundwater recharge. The protests turned violent and became a national reference point for how land classification disputes drive energy conflict.
- Water and ash. Thermal plants are among the largest industrial water consumers, competing with irrigation in water-stressed districts, while fly ash disposal has caused repeated pond breaches and contamination of farmland and water bodies. MoEFCC’s fly ash utilisation notifications respond to this, but compliance is uneven.
- Climate awareness and policy signal. India’s Panchamrit commitments and the visibility of climate debate have made coal expansion politically harder to justify, and civil society and youth movements now contest projects on climate grounds in addition to local ones.
- The counter-argument to acknowledge: coal districts also depend on these projects for employment, contractor income and district revenue. Resistance is therefore not uniform, and a just transition framework is required rather than simple closure.

## (b) Reasons for the “sparse” use of renewables — then and now

A necessary reframing: when this question was set in 2011, renewable capacity was around 20 GW. It now stands at 274.68 GW, with India third globally in renewable installed capacity (IRENA, 2026) and the 50% non-fossil capacity milestone crossed in June 2025, five years early. The premise of “sparse use” no longer holds — but the barriers have not disappeared, they have changed character.

- Then: high capital cost. Solar tariffs in 2011 were several times conventional power. Now largely resolved — solar is typically the cheapest source of new generation, following module price declines and competitive reverse auctions.
- Then and now: intermittency and storage. This remains the binding constraint. Solar generates nothing at the evening demand peak, and storage capacity is only beginning to scale — which is why pumped storage (Andhra Pradesh targets 22 GW) has become the priority technology.
- Then and now: transmission and evacuation. Resource-rich regions are distant from load centres; the Green Energy Corridors and the ISTS charge waiver addressed much of this, but curtailment persists where evacuation lags generation.
- Then and now: land acquisition. Utility-scale solar and wind require large contiguous areas, raising the same livelihood and common-land questions that coal projects do — a point often missed in answers that treat renewables as socially frictionless.
- Now more than then: DISCOM finances. Distribution companies unable to pay generators on time deter investment regardless of how cheap solar becomes. RDSS (Rs. 3.03 lakh crore) conditions funding on loss reduction for this reason.
- New barriers that did not exist in 2011: dependence on imported cells, wafers and polysilicon, addressed through PLI and ALMM; and critical mineral dependence for batteries, addressed through the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025).

## Conclusion

Public resistance to coal reflects a genuine and locally grounded conflict over health, land and water — as the Sompeta and Kakarapalli agitations in Srikakulam demonstrated — rather than mere opposition to development. Renewables have meanwhile ceased to be sparsely used, but their remaining barriers are systemic: storage, evacuation, DISCOM viability and supply-chain dependence. India’s task is therefore no longer to choose between coal and renewables but to manage a just transition that retires coal capacity at the pace at which storage can replace it.

## Value addition
- Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS): India’s market-based mechanism, notified under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, under which entities reducing emissions below their target earn Carbon Credit Certificates tradable to those exceeding theirs; administered with BEE as administrator and the Grid Controller of India as registry — the compliance mechanism complementing the earlier PAT scheme.
- The AP instance to name: the Sompeta (Bhavanapadu) and Kakarapalli thermal power protests in Srikakulam district (2010-11), centred on whether beela wetlands classified as wasteland were in fact productive ecosystems — a dispute over land classification, not merely over pollution.
- Coal-related environmental instruments: MoEFCC fly ash utilisation notifications; emission norms for thermal plants (SOx, NOx, particulate matter and mercury) with FGD installation deadlines; CPCB’s Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index for critically polluted areas.
- Just transition: coal-dependent districts in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal and Telangana; the need for alternative livelihoods, district transition plans and repurposing of retiring plants — the BSMR-200 small modular reactor is explicitly designed for brownfield coal sites.
- Current renewable data (MNRE, 31 March 2026): RE 274.68 GW; non-fossil 283.46 GW; record 55.29 GW non-fossil addition in 2025-26; 50% non-fossil capacity reached June 2025; third globally in RE capacity (IRENA, 2026).
- AP-specific: Kurnool and NP Kunta Ultra Mega Solar Parks; Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 (160 GW, 22 GW pumped storage); Simhadri and Vijayawada thermal stations as the conventional counterpart.

## Introduction

Renewable energy resources are those replenished naturally within human timescales. India’s endowment is unusually diverse — high solar irradiance, long coastlines and wind corridors, Himalayan and peninsular river systems, and a very large agricultural residue base. Against an assessed potential exceeding 1,000 GW, installed renewable capacity stands at 274.68 GW as on 31 March 2026 (MNRE) — substantial progress, and substantial headroom.

- **Resource** — Installed (31 Mar 2026) · Assessed potential · Leading States
- **Solar** — 150.26 GW · 748 GW (NISE, on 3% of wasteland) · Rajasthan, Gujarat, Karnataka, AP
- **Wind** — 56.09 GW · 695.5 GW at 120 m; 1,164 GW at 150 m (NIWE) · Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, AP
- **Large hydro** — 51.41 GW · about 1,45,000 MW · Himachal, Uttarakhand, North-East
- **Bio-power** — 11.75 GW · about 28,445 MW from ~228 MT surplus residue · UP, Maharashtra, Punjab, Karnataka
- **Small hydro** — 5.17 GW · about 21,133 MW across 7,000+ sites · Himalayan States, Western Ghats
- **Ocean** — negligible · about 54 GW (incl. 12.4 GW wave) · Gujarat, West Bengal, islands
- **Geothermal** — negligible · about 10 GW (tentative, GSI/MNRE) · Ladakh, Chhattisgarh, Himachal

## How each works, in one line
- Solar: photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly to electricity; solar thermal concentrates heat to raise steam. India receives about 5,000 trillion kWh of solar radiation annually over roughly 300 clear days.
- Wind: turbine blades convert kinetic energy of moving air; output scales with the cube of wind speed.
- Hydro: falling water drives turbines; pumped storage additionally stores energy by pumping water uphill during surplus and releasing it at peak.
- Biomass: combustion, gasification or anaerobic digestion of crop residue, bagasse, animal and municipal waste.
- Small hydro (below 25 MW): run-of-river schemes with minimal reservoir and low ecological disruption.
- Ocean: tidal barrages and turbines, wave devices, current turbines and OTEC using the surface-to-deep temperature gradient.
- Geothermal: Earth’s internal heat raises steam; India’s provinces include Puga and Chumathang (Ladakh), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh) and Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh).

## Reading the potential figures correctly — the point most answers miss

Potential estimates are conditional, not absolute. NISE’s 748 GW solar figure assumes availability of 3% of wasteland; NIWE’s wind figure rises from 695.5 GW to 1,164 GW simply by changing the assumed hub height from 120 m to 150 m. Potential is therefore a function of technology and land assumptions, and improves as technology does. Stating this shows genuine understanding rather than recitation.

## Realisation and constraints

India has crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity (June 2025), five years ahead of its NDC target, and ranks third globally in renewable installed capacity (IRENA, 2026), with a record 55.29 GW of non-fossil addition in 2025-26. Gaps between potential and realisation persist because of land availability, evacuation infrastructure, storage, DISCOM finances and — for ocean and geothermal — technology cost.

AP endowment: Andhra Pradesh has strong solar and wind resources in Anantapur, Kurnool and Kadapa, a 1,053-km coastline for ocean energy and offshore wind, and hosts the Kurnool (1,000 MW) and NP Kunta (about 978 MW) Ultra Mega Solar Parks. Its Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targets over 160 GW.

## Conclusion

India’s renewable endowment exceeds 1,000 GW against installed capacity of 274.68 GW, so the constraint has never been resource availability. What determines realisation is land, evacuation, storage and offtake finance — and the fact that assessed potential itself rises with technology, as NIWE’s revision from 120 m to 150 m hub heights demonstrates. India’s achievement of 50% non-fossil capacity five years early suggests the gap is closing faster than the potential figures once implied.

## Value addition
- Assessing institutions to name:NISE (National Institute of Solar Energy) for solar potential; NIWE (National Institute of Wind Energy) for wind; CEA for hydro; NIOT for ocean; GSI for geothermal. Attributing each estimate to its institution is a quick credibility marker.
- Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO): a mandate under the Electricity Act, 2003 requiring distribution licensees and specified consumers to source a defined share of electricity from renewables; compliance possible through direct purchase or Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs). Ocean energy became RPO-eligible after MNRE’s 2019 classification.
- Solar parks to name:Bhadla (Rajasthan), Pavagada (Karnataka), Rewa (Madhya Pradesh), Kurnool and NP Kunta (Andhra Pradesh) — among the world’s largest.
- The wasteland assumption: NISE’s 748 GW solar estimate assumes just 3% of India’s wasteland is used — which is why land policy, not solar technology, is the real determinant of solar potential.
- Definitions worth being precise about:small hydro is below 25 MW in India (thresholds differ internationally); large hydro was included within renewable energy for RPO purposes from 2019; bio-power covers biomass combustion, bagasse cogeneration and waste-to-energy.
- AP-specific: solar and wind resources in Anantapur, Kurnool and Kadapa; 1,053-km coastline; Kurnool and NP Kunta Ultra Mega Solar Parks; Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targeting 160 GW including 22 GW pumped storage.

## Introduction

India’s installed solar capacity stands at 150.26 GW as on 31 March 2026, against wind at 56.09 GW, large hydro at 51.41 GW and bio-power at 11.75 GW (MNRE) — solar alone exceeds all other renewables combined. Understanding why solar outpaced its alternatives requires comparing it against them rather than against coal.

Predictability | Gestation | Land need .

## Advantages of solar over other renewables
- Modularity — the decisive advantage. Solar works at any scale from a 40-watt lantern to a 2,000 MW park, with essentially the same technology. Wind requires a minimum viable turbine size, hydro requires a river and biomass requires a feedstock catchment. Modularity is why solar, uniquely, can be deployed on a farmer’s pump, a household roof and a desert park simultaneously.
- Siting flexibility. Solar needs irradiance, which is available almost everywhere in India. Wind needs specific corridors, hydro needs specific gradients, and biomass needs an agricultural catchment — all geographically constrained.
- Short gestation. A solar park can be commissioned in months; a large hydro project takes years to over a decade, with clearance, resettlement and geological risk. Speed of deployment matters enormously when capacity must be added at pace.
- No moving parts, minimal maintenance. Photovoltaic panels have no rotating machinery, giving 25-year-plus lifetimes with low operating cost. Wind turbines require gearbox and blade maintenance; biomass plants require continuous fuel logistics.
- No fuel supply chain. Unlike biomass, solar requires no procurement, transport or storage of feedstock.
- Fastest cost decline of any generation technology.

## Disadvantages of solar relative to other renewables
- Zero output at night — worse than the alternatives. Wind often blows at night, hydro is dispatchable, and biomass runs continuously with fuel supply. Solar’s variability is not merely intermittent but perfectly anti-correlated with the evening demand peak, which is a sharper problem than general intermittency.
- Lower capacity utilisation. Solar plant load factor is roughly 20%, against 25-30% for wind and far higher for hydro and biomass — so a MW of solar delivers less energy than a MW of most alternatives.
- Higher land intensity per unit of energy — roughly 4-5 acres per MW, with land occupied continuously, whereas wind farms allow cultivation between turbines.
- No inherent storage. Hydro, particularly pumped storage, is itself a storage technology; solar has none and must be paired with batteries at additional cost.
- Waste stream. Modules have a finite life and their disposal is an emerging problem; hydro and wind have longer-lived and more recyclable components.
- Manufacturing dependence on imported cells, wafers and polysilicon.

## Why solar costs are falling — the mechanisms
- The learning curve. Solar module costs fall by a roughly predictable percentage for every doubling of cumulative production — a self-reinforcing loop in which deployment lowers cost, which drives further deployment. This, rather than any single innovation, is the fundamental explanation.
- Manufacturing scale, overwhelmingly in China, which drove module prices down by over 85% since 2010.
- Technology improvement: rising cell efficiency, thinner wafers using less silicon, bifacial modules capturing reflected light, and larger module formats reducing balance-of-system cost per watt.
- Competitive reverse auctions in India, which forced tariff discovery through bidding rather than administered pricing — the single most effective Indian policy instrument for cost reduction.
- Falling cost of capital as the technology’s track record reduced perceived risk; since solar cost is almost entirely capital, financing terms drive tariffs more than hardware does.
- Policy support: Solar Park Scheme (land and evacuation provided upfront), ISTS charge waiver, must-run status, PLI and ALMM.

## Effect on climate change efforts
- Cheap solar changed the economics of mitigation. When clean energy costs more than fossil energy, decarbonisation requires subsidy and sacrifice; when it costs less, it becomes the commercially rational choice. This is why solar’s cost decline has done more for global climate action than most negotiated commitments.
- India’s targets became achievable rather than aspirational: the 50% non-fossil capacity milestone was reached in June 2025, five years ahead of the NDC target, and a record 55.29 GW of non-fossil capacity was added in 2025-26.
- Enables developing-country mitigation without growth sacrifice, which is the core of India’s negotiating position on common but differentiated responsibilities.
- The limit to acknowledge: cheap solar reduces the cost of generation but not of firming. Emissions fall only when solar displaces coal generation rather than merely adding capacity alongside it — and that displacement requires storage.

## Conclusion

Solar’s advantages over other renewables are structural — modularity, siting flexibility and short gestation — which explain why it now exceeds all other Indian renewables combined. Its disadvantages are equally structural: no night-time output and no inherent storage. The cost decline, driven by the learning curve and competitive auctions, has transformed climate mitigation from a cost to be borne into an economic choice. Converting that into actual emissions reduction, however, depends on storage, since capacity added is not the same as coal displaced.

## Value addition
- Comparative capacity utilisation: solar roughly 20%; wind 25-30%; large hydro and biomass considerably higher; coal 60-70%. This single set of figures explains most of the intra-renewable comparison.
- India’s standing: 150.26 GW solar (MNRE, 31 March 2026); third globally in solar capacity; overtook Japan as the third-largest solar generator; third globally in overall renewable capacity (IRENA, 2026); 50% non-fossil capacity reached June 2025.
- The learning-curve concept: cost falls by a consistent percentage for each doubling of cumulative deployment — worth naming explicitly, as it is the underlying reason solar costs fell rather than any single breakthrough.
- Emerging solar variants:floating solar (Ramagundam, Omkareshwar), agrivoltaics (generation above cultivation), bifacial modules, solar-wind hybrids under the National Wind-Solar Hybrid Policy, and solar-plus-storage bid as firm dispatchable renewable energy.
- Waste and circularity: solar module and battery end-of-life management under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 and Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022; module recycling capacity remains a gap.
- The displacement point: emissions fall only when renewable generation displaces fossil generation, not when it merely adds to total capacity. Since India’s demand is growing rapidly, much new renewable capacity meets incremental demand rather than replacing coal — an honest and sophisticated qualification.
- AP-specific: Kurnool and NP Kunta Ultra Mega Solar Parks; 78.5 GW solar and 22 GW pumped storage targets under the Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024; APSPCL and NREDCAP.

## Introduction

Solar power is now India’s largest renewable source at 150.26 GW as on 31 March 2026, exceeding all other renewables combined, and India ranks third globally in both solar capacity and solar generation (MNRE; IRENA, 2026). Its contribution is genuinely transformative. But the claim examined here is stronger than that: a panacea is a remedy for all ills, and testing solar against that standard reveals what it does and does not solve.

- What solar
- Storage

## Where the claim holds — solar’s genuine achievements
- It has solved the cost problem. Solar is now typically the cheapest source of new generation in India, so decarbonisation of power no longer requires accepting higher costs. This is the single most important change of the last decade.
- It has solved the scale problem. From about 2.6 GW in 2014 to 150.26 GW in 2026 — no other energy source in India has scaled this fast. India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its NDC target.
- It has solved the access problem uniquely well. Solar’s modularity allows it to serve a household roof, a farmer’s pump and a 2,000 MW park with the same technology. PM Surya Ghar targets 1 crore rooftop households; PM-KUSUM solarises agricultural pumps; distributed renewables contributed 16.3 GW of the 44.61 GW added in 2025-26. No other source reaches the last mile this way.
- It reduces import dependence and price volatility, since sunlight is domestic and has no fuel cost.

## Where the claim fails — what solar cannot do
- Solar does not generate at the evening peak. Indian demand peaks after sunset, when solar output is zero. This is not a limitation to be engineered away but a physical property. Until storage scales, every solar MW requires backup capacity — which is why coal remains at roughly 70% of generation despite non-fossil sources exceeding half of capacity.
- Solar addresses electricity, but electricity is a minority of energy use. Transport, cooking, steel, cement and fertiliser consume fuels, not power. India imports 85-88% of its crude oil, and solar does not directly touch that unless demand is first electrified — which is why green hydrogen, E20 ethanol blending (achieved 2025-26) and PM E-DRIVE exist alongside solar.
- Solar has a land problem. At roughly 4-5 acres per MW, utility-scale solar competes with agriculture and commons. NISE’s 748 GW potential estimate is explicitly premised on using 3% of India’s wasteland — a land-policy assumption, not a technical one.
- Solar substitutes one import dependence for another. Cells, wafers and polysilicon remain largely imported, and storage requires critical minerals concentrated in a handful of countries — the reason for the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025).
- Solar creates a waste stream. Modules have finite life and recycling capacity is limited; the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 provide a framework but not yet the infrastructure.
- Solar cannot fix the distribution segment. DISCOM losses, tariff distortions and payment delays are institutional problems. A cheaper generator does not help a utility that cannot pay for power.

## The correct framing — solar as necessary but not sufficient

The panacea framing misdiagnoses the problem. India’s energy challenge is not a shortage of cheap generation; it is a shortage of firm, dispatchable, clean supply and a structurally weak distribution segment. Solar is the essential component of the solution, working alongside storage (Andhra Pradesh alone targets 22 GW of pumped storage), wind, hydro, nuclear under the Nuclear Energy Mission, green hydrogen for industry, and distribution reform through RDSS.

AP illustration: Andhra Pradesh’s Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 is instructive precisely because it does not treat solar as a panacea — it targets 78.5 GW solar and 35 GW wind and22 GW pumped storage, recognising that generation without storage does not deliver reliable supply.

## Conclusion

Solar has solved the problems it can solve — cost, scale and last-mile access — more completely than any other energy technology in Indian history. It has not solved, and cannot alone solve, the evening peak, transport and industrial fuel demand, land competition, mineral dependence or distribution finances. It is therefore the indispensable foundation of India’s energy transition rather than its remedy. The panacea, if there is one, is not solar but solar combined with storage — which is why India’s next decade of energy policy will be measured in gigawatt-hours, not gigawatts.

- The core data: solar 150.26 GW (MNRE, 31 March 2026); RE 274.68 GW; non-fossil 283.46 GW; record 55.29 GW non-fossil addition in 2025-26; 50% non-fossil capacity reached June 2025, five years early; third globally in solar capacity and generation, and in overall renewable capacity (IRENA, 2026).
- The capacity-generation gap — the central fact for this question: non-fossil sources exceed half of installed capacity but supplied about 29.2% of generation in 2025-26, because solar’s plant load factor is roughly 20% against coal’s 60-70%.

## Introduction

The Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM), launched in January 2010, is one of the eight national missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC). Administered by MNRE, its purpose was not merely to install solar capacity but to create the market conditions under which solar would become commercially self-sustaining — that is, to make subsidy unnecessary rather than permanent.

## Genesis and phases
- Phase I (2010-13): grid-connected projects and off-grid applications; about 1,000 MW achieved. Deployment used reverse bidding, which was the mission’s most consequential design choice.
- Phase II (2013-17): scaled to around 9,000 MW, with emphasis on large solar parks where land and evacuation were provided upfront, removing the two biggest project risks.
- Phase III (2017-22): worked toward the revised 100 GW solar target within the wider 175 GW renewable goal.

## Major objectives
- Large-scale deployment. The original target of 20 GW of grid-connected solar by 2022 was raised to 100 GW in 2015, split as 60 GW utility-scale and 40 GW rooftop.
- Achieving grid parity. The central objective: to drive costs down until solar competed with conventional power without subsidy — targeted as grid parity by 2022 and parity with coal-based power by 2030.
- Off-grid and decentralised applications, including a target of 20 million solar lighting systems in rural households by 2022 — recognising that solar’s value in rural India lies in reaching where the grid does not.
- Solar thermal, with a target of 20 million square metres of collector area for water heating and industrial process heat.
- Domestic manufacturing across the value chain, and R&D in cell technology and storage with institutions including the IISc and IITs.
- Emissions reduction, contributing to India’s climate commitments.

## Assessment — which objectives were met
- **Objective** — Outcome
- **100 GW solar by 2022** — Missed on time, exceeded since — 150.26 GW by March 2026
- **Grid parity** — Achieved and surpassed — solar is now cheaper than new coal
- **60 GW utility-scale** — Substantially achieved
- **40 GW rooftop** — Significantly short — rooftop lagged badly, prompting PM Surya Ghar (2024)
- **Solar thermal** — Largely unmet — PV displaced thermal as costs fell
- **Domestic manufacturing** — Partial — modules yes, cells and wafers still import-dependent

The pattern is instructive: JNNSM overshot where competitive bidding could be applied (utility-scale) and undershot where success depended on millions of individual decisions (rooftop) or on industrial policy (manufacturing).

## Achievements and impact
- Installed solar capacity reached 150.26 GW as on 31 March 2026 (MNRE); India ranks third globally in solar capacity and has overtaken Japan as the third-largest solar generator.
- Flagship projects: Bhadla (Rajasthan), Pavagada (Karnataka), Rewa (Madhya Pradesh), and Kurnool (1,000 MW) and NP Kunta (about 978 MW) in Andhra Pradesh.
- Successor instruments now carry the agenda: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana for rooftop, PM-KUSUM for agriculture, PLI and ALMM for manufacturing, and Green Energy Corridors for evacuation.

## Conclusion

JNNSM’s real achievement was not capacity but price discovery: by using reverse auctions and de-risking projects through solar parks, it drove solar tariffs below coal and made every subsequent target achievable. Its shortfalls — rooftop and domestic cell manufacturing — reveal the limits of a mission designed around utility-scale procurement. Those gaps now define the successor programmes.

## Value addition
- The eight NAPCC missions (2008): National Solar Mission; Enhanced Energy Efficiency; Sustainable Habitat; Water; Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem; Green India; Sustainable Agriculture; and Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change. Naming JNNSM’s place among these is a quick structural marker.
- The mechanism that made it work:reverse bidding for tariff discovery, plus solar parks providing land, evacuation and clearances upfront — removing the risks that otherwise raise the cost of capital, which dominates solar economics.
- International Solar Alliance (ISA): conceived by India and France on the sidelines of COP21 (2015); headquartered at Gurugram; opened to all UN member states after a 2020 amendment to its Framework Agreement; over 100 signatories; aims to mobilise USD 1 trillion in solar investment by 2030.
- Successor schemes: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024, 1 crore rooftop households); PM-KUSUM; Solar Park Scheme; PLI for High Efficiency Solar PV Modules; ALMM; ISTS charge waiver.
- Current data (MNRE, 31 March 2026): solar 150.26 GW; RE 274.68 GW; non-fossil 283.46 GW; 50% non-fossil capacity achieved June 2025, five years early; third globally in renewable capacity (IRENA, 2026).
- AP-specific: Kurnool and NP Kunta Ultra Mega Solar Parks developed by APSPCL (a joint venture of SECI, APGENCO and NREDCAP); Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targeting 78.5 GW solar.

## Introduction

The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018, issued by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, provides the framework for biofuel development in India. Its rationale is threefold — reducing an oil import bill running at 85-88% dependence, creating an additional income stream for farmers, and cutting transport emissions. Its central target, 20% ethanol blending, has since been achieved in 2025-26 (PIB), five years ahead of the original 2030 date.

## Vision

To substantially increase biofuel use in India’s energy and transport sectors using domestic feedstock, achieving 20% ethanol blending in petrol and 5% biodiesel blending in diesel by 2030, in support of energy security, farmer welfare and climate goals.

## Goals
- Blending targets: E20 and B5 by 2030 — with the ethanol target advanced to 2025 by the 2022 amendment, and achieved in 2025-26.
- Promotion of advanced biofuels: second and third generation fuels — 2G ethanol from lignocellulosic biomass, bio-CNG, bio-hydrogen and drop-in fuels — to diversify feedstock away from food crops.
- Farmer income and rural employment, by creating a guaranteed market for surplus and damaged produce.

## Strategy
- Categorisation of biofuels — the policy’s key innovation. Biofuels are classified as Basic Biofuels (1G — conventional ethanol from sugar and starch, and biodiesel) and Advanced Biofuels (2G ethanol from lignocellulosic feedstock, bio-CNG, municipal solid waste to fuel; and 3G bio-hydrogen and algae-based fuels). This classification allows differentiated fiscal support, so advanced biofuels receive higher incentives precisely because they are commercially harder.
- Expansion of feedstock. The policy permitted a far wider range: sugarcane juice, sugar beet, sweet sorghum, corn, cassava, and damaged food grains unfit for human consumption — damaged wheat, broken rice and rotten potatoes. This addressed the “food versus fuel” objection while giving farmers an outlet for produce that would otherwise be wasted. Surplus grain from FCI stocks was later permitted during periods of excess.
- Viability Gap Funding: a Rs. 5,000 crore VGF scheme over six years for 2G ethanol bio-refineries, since these are not yet commercially viable without support.
- Protection of supply: allowing use of surplus food grains for ethanol only with National Biofuel Coordination Committee approval, safeguarding food security.

## Conclusion

The National Policy on Biofuels succeeded because it aligned three constituencies at once: refiners gained a domestic blending stock, farmers gained an assured market, and the exchequer gained lower import outgo. Its categorisation architecture allowed support to be targeted where technology was weakest. With E20 achieved, the frontier shifts to 2G ethanol from crop residue — which would simultaneously address stubble burning — and to biodiesel, where feedstock rather than policy remains the constraint.

## Value addition
- The biofuel generations:1G — ethanol from sugarcane, molasses, grain; biodiesel from vegetable oils. 2G — ethanol from lignocellulosic biomass such as crop residue, bagasse and municipal solid waste; bio-CNG. 3G — algae-based fuels and bio-hydrogen. 4G — engineered organisms with carbon capture. Getting these right is the most commonly tested element of this topic.
- Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme milestones: blending under 2% in 2013-14; 10% achieved in June 2022, five months early; E20 fuel available from April 2023; 20% achieved in 2025-26 (PIB).
- Related initiatives:SATAT (Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation) for compressed biogas; GOBARdhan for rural biogas; Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana for 2G ethanol projects; Global Biofuels Alliance launched at the G20 Summit, New Delhi (2023), with 24 countries and 12 international organisations.
- Institutional bodies:National Biofuel Coordination Committee chaired by the Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas; Biofuel Steering Committee under the Secretary.
- The food-versus-fuel debate — hold both sides:for — using damaged grain and surplus stocks creates farmer income without displacing food; against — sugarcane is water-intensive and diverting cane to ethanol in water-stressed regions has ecological cost. A balanced answer states both.
- AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s sugarcane and maize belts supply ethanol feedstock; the State’s rice-fallow and residue base is relevant to 2G ethanol; Rythu Bharosa Kendras provide the procurement interface.

## Introduction

India generates about 1,70,339 tonnes per day of municipal solid waste, of which roughly 92% is collected but only 54% processed, with about 24% landfilled and 22% unaccounted (CPCB, 2021-22). The Swachh Bharat Mission has transformed collection and public attitudes, raising processing from under 20% in 2014. What remains is a problem concentrated not in metros — which attract attention, capital and consultants — but in India’s roughly 4,000 small and medium towns, where capacity is thinnest.

Critical assessment: what has worked

Before listing failures, an honest answer credits the gains — door-to-door collection now covers the overwhelming majority of wards; Swachh Survekshan created genuine competitive pressure between municipalities; Indore demonstrated that segregation compliance above 90% is achievable in an Indian city; and legacy dumpsite remediation has reclaimed over 7,600 acres nationally by September 2025.

## The challenges
- Segregation compliance remains the binding failure. Where wet, dry and hazardous waste are mixed, the wet fraction contaminates recyclables and the dry fraction ruins compost, so mixed waste is worth less than the sum of its parts. Every downstream technology depends on this one household behaviour, which is why it is the root rather than one item on a list.
- The small-town deficit. Metros have technical staff, consultants and capital; a Class II or III town typically has none. It cannot prepare a viable tender, evaluate a technology proposal or supervise a concessionaire. The constraint is capability, not just finance — which is why capital grants alone have not solved it.
- Collection and transport gaps in peri-urban wards, slums and unauthorised colonies, with ageing fleets and unplanned routing raising cost per tonne.
- Landfill dependence and legacy waste. India has around 2,452 dumpsites against roughly 645 operational engineered landfills (CPCB). Sites such as Ghazipur (Delhi) and Deonar (Mumbai) have become garbage mountains prone to fires, leachate discharge and slope failure.
- Weak resource recovery. Recycling rates for plastics, C&D waste and e-waste remain well below potential; C&D waste in particular is voluminous, easily recyclable into aggregate, and largely dumped.
- Municipal finances. Solid waste management is among the largest items in a municipal budget, yet user charges are politically difficult and property tax bases are weak — so revenue does not match the recurring cost of collection and processing.
- Institutional fragmentation. Responsibilities are split between ULBs, state pollution control boards, parastatals and private concessionaires, with weak contract monitoring and thin data for planning.
- The informal sector is excluded rather than integrated. Waste-pickers recover a large share of India’s recyclables at no public cost, yet remain outside formal planning, without identity, safety equipment or a share of EPR revenue — a wasted institutional asset and an equity failure at once.
- Citizen behaviour, including persistent littering and resistance to home composting; in coastal towns such as Visakhapatnam and Chennai, uncollected plastic translates directly into marine litter.

## Roadmap
- Differentiated solutions by city size: decentralised composting and biomethanation for small towns (where land is available and volumes are low), and MRF-plus-RDF systems for large cities.
- Cluster-based facilities allowing several small towns to share one processing plant and one technical team — the only realistic model for towns individually too small to justify either.
- Ring-fenced user charges and performance-linked payments to concessionaires.
- Formal integration of waste-pickers with identity cards, safety equipment and a share of EPR financing.
- Bio-mining of legacy dumps on the Indore and Surat model, releasing land and eliminating fire and leachate risk.
- Capacity building: dedicated solid waste cells with technical staff at municipal and cluster level.

## Conclusion

India’s urban waste problem has shifted from a collection failure to a processing and capability failure, and it is now concentrated in small and medium towns rather than metros. Treating it as a technology problem misdiagnoses it: the technologies are proven, and what is missing is household segregation, municipal technical capacity and a business model that pays for recurring costs. The transition required is from “collect and dump” to “segregate, process, recover” — and it will be decided in Class II towns, not in the metros that dominate the discussion.

## Value addition
- CPCB data (2021-22) with denominators: generation 1,70,339 TPD; collection about 92%; processing 91,511 TPD (54% of generation); landfilled 41,455 TPD (24%); unaccounted about 22%; roughly 645 operational landfills against 2,452 dumpsites.
- SBM-U 2.0: launched 1 October 2021; vision of garbage-free cities by 2026; about 1,437 lakh tonnes of legacy waste remediated by September 2025 of an estimated 2,492 lakh tonnes, reclaiming over 7,600 acres.
- Governance innovations worth naming:Swachh Survekshan annual rankings; the Star Rating Protocol for Garbage Free Cities; the Indore model of ward-level segregation and monitoring; bio-mining at Indore and Surat.
- Circular economy instruments:EPR across plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries and tyres; India’s membership of the Global Alliance on Circular Economy and Resource Efficiency (GACERE); Mission LIFE for demand-side behaviour.
- The waste-picker point: integrating the informal sector is simultaneously an efficiency measure (they already recover material at no public cost), an equity measure, and a requirement under the SWM Rules 2016, which direct ULBs to establish a system for their integration.
- AP-specific: Visakhapatnam’s Swachh Survekshan performance and GPS-enabled collection; coastal plastic leakage along the 1,053-km coastline; Tirupati’s decentralised processing.

## Introduction

India’s energy strategy has explored both unconventional fossil resources and expanded nuclear generation. The Shale Gas Revolution transformed global energy markets and made the United States a net exporter, while India’s nuclear programme, built on indigenous technology and a distinctive thorium-oriented design, provides dispatchable low-carbon power.

## (a) The Shale Gas Revolution
- What it is. Shale gas is natural gas trapped within low-permeability shale rock. It became commercially recoverable through the combination of hydraulic fracturing (“fracking”) — injecting water, sand and chemicals at high pressure to fracture the rock — and horizontal drilling, which exposes far more of the reservoir to a single well. Neither technique was new; their combination at commercial scale was the revolution.
- Global significance. Beginning in the United States in the early 2000s, it reversed the expectation of declining American gas production, lowered global gas prices, turned the US into a leading LNG exporter, revived energy-intensive US manufacturing, and reduced US power-sector emissions as cheap gas displaced coal. It also altered geopolitics by reducing US dependence on West Asian energy.
- India’s position — and why the revolution has not arrived here. India has identified shale prospects in the Cambay, Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Assam-Arakan, Gondwana, Vindhyan and Indo-Gangetic basins, and a policy permitting exploration in existing on-land blocks was framed. Commercial production has nonetheless not materialised, for reasons worth stating: Water intensity. Fracking requires very large volumes of water per well, and India’s shale basins largely lie in water-stressed or agriculturally intensive regions — a direct competition with irrigation. Population density and land access. US shale development occurred over sparsely populated terrain; Indian basins underlie densely farmed land, making well-pad spacing and land acquisition far harder. Geology and data. Indian shales are less well characterised and, in places, geologically more complex. Environmental risk. Groundwater contamination, methane leakage and induced seismicity concerns; hydrogeological uncertainty in aquifer-dependent regions. Economics. With global gas prices lower than in the mid-2010s and renewables falling steeply in cost, the commercial case has weakened.
- India’s alternative unconventional focus has therefore shifted toward coal bed methane, underground coal gasification and compressed biogas under SATAT, alongside the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP) and the Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OALP) for conventional exploration.

## (b) Growth of nuclear power in India — a narration
- Foundations (1948-1960s). The Atomic Energy Commission (1948) and the Department of Atomic Energy (1954) were established under Homi Bhabha, who designed the three-stage programme around India’s limited uranium and vast thorium. Apsara (1956) was Asia’s first research reactor. India’s first power station, Tarapur (1969), used imported boiling water reactors.
- Isolation (1974-2008). Following the 1974 test, technology denial regimes cut India off from international fuel and equipment. The response was indigenisation: India developed its own Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors, scaling from 220 MWe to 540 MWe and then 700 MWe units — capability built precisely because it was denied.
- Re-engagement (2008 onwards). The India-US Civil Nuclear Agreement, IAEA safeguards agreement and NSG waiver restored fuel access, immediately raising PHWR capacity factors that had been suppressed by uranium shortage.
- Current status. About 25 commercial reactors with 8.78 GW installed (MNRE, March 2026) — a rise of roughly 70% over the past decade — generating in the order of 3% of India’s electricity. Reactors under construction target 22,480 MW by 2031-32.
- Stage II achieved. The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam marks India’s formal entry into the second stage of the three-stage programme.
- The current phase. The Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat (Budget 2025-26) targets 100 GWe by 2047 with Rs. 20,000 crore for five indigenous SMRs by 2033; Bharat Small Reactors and BSMR-200/SMR-55 are designed for captive industrial power and coal-plant repurposing. The SHANTI Act, 2025 repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010, opening the sector to private and foreign participation.

## Nuclear fuel reserves in India
- Uranium — modest. Principal deposits at Jaduguda, Bhatin, Narwapahar and Turamdih (Jharkhand); Tummalapalle in Kadapa district, Andhra Pradesh, in the Cuddapah Basin, is among the world’s larger single uranium deposits though of relatively low grade; also Meghalaya (Domiasiat) and Karnataka (Gogi). Mining is undertaken by Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL).
- Thorium — among the world’s largest. Occurs as monazite in the beach and inland placer sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal, processed by Indian Rare Earths Limited. Thorium is not directly fissile: it must be converted to uranium-233 in a reactor, which is why Stage III depends on the Stage II breeder programme succeeding first.
- The strategic logic: India’s entire three-stage design exists because of this asymmetry — scarce uranium and abundant thorium. Stage I generates plutonium, Stage II breeders multiply it and irradiate thorium, and Stage III finally uses the U-233 produced. Explaining this dependency chain, rather than merely listing the three stages, is what demonstrates understanding.

## Conclusion

The shale gas revolution shows how a combination of existing technologies can transform an energy system — and India’s inability to replicate it illustrates that resource endowment alone is insufficient without compatible water availability, land patterns and economics. India’s nuclear growth followed the opposite path: constrained externally, it built indigenous capability, and now, with fuel access restored and the SHANTI Act opening the sector, faces an execution rather than a capability challenge in reaching 100 GW by 2047.

## Value addition
- Shale terminology:hydraulic fracturing; horizontal drilling; proppant (sand holding fractures open); flowback water; induced seismicity; fugitive methane emissions. Indian shale basins: Cambay, Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Assam-Arakan, Gondwana, Vindhyan, Indo-Gangetic.
- Related hydrocarbon policies:HELP (Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy) with a uniform licence for all hydrocarbons including shale and CBM, revenue sharing and marketing freedom; OALP for year-round acreage bidding; NDR (National Data Repository).
- Nuclear milestones to narrate: Atomic Energy Commission (1948); Department of Atomic Energy (1954); Apsara (1956, Asia’s first research reactor); Tarapur (1969, first power station); Pokhran I (1974) and II (1998); indigenous PHWR scaling 220 –> 540 –> 700 MWe; PFBR Kalpakkam (Stage II); Nuclear Energy Mission (2025); SHANTI Act, 2025.
- Fuel reserve specifics: uranium at Jaduguda, Bhatin, Narwapahar and Turamdih (Jharkhand), Tummalapalle (Kadapa, AP), Domiasiat (Meghalaya), Gogi (Karnataka); thorium as monazite in coastal placer sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, AP and West Bengal; UCIL for uranium mining and IREL for rare earths and monazite.
- The thorium caveat worth stating: thorium is fertile, not fissile — it must first absorb a neutron to become U-233. Stage III therefore cannot begin until Stage II breeders operate at scale, which is why the thorium promise has remained decades away.
- AP-specific:Tummalapalle uranium mine, Kadapa district; monazite-bearing coastal sands; Kovvada, Srikakulam district, earmarked for a nuclear project; Krishna-Godavari basin for both conventional and shale hydrocarbons.

## Introduction

Biogeochemical cycles are the pathways through which elements move between the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere. The carbon and nitrogen cycles are the two most consequential for human society: carbon regulates the planet’s climate, and nitrogen determines agricultural productivity. Both have been substantially altered by human activity, and India — a large agricultural economy with significant forest cover and the world’s third-largest emissions — sits at the centre of both.

## The Carbon Cycle
- Photosynthesis — plants and phytoplankton fix atmospheric CO2 into organic matter, the entry point of carbon into the biosphere. India’s forest and tree cover stands at about 25.17% of geographical area (India State of Forest Report 2023, Forest Survey of India), with the Western Ghats and North-Eastern evergreen forests as major sinks.
- Respiration — plants, animals and microbes oxidise organic matter, returning CO2.
- Decomposition — soil microbes break down dead organic matter, releasing CO2 aerobically and methane anaerobically. India’s flooded paddy fields, including in the Godavari and Krishna deltas of Andhra Pradesh and in West Bengal, are significant methane sources; alternate wetting and drying irrigation and the System of Rice Intensification reduce these emissions.
- Combustion — fossil fuel burning transfers carbon from geological reservoirs, sequestered over millions of years, into the atmosphere within decades. This asymmetry of timescales is the essence of the climate problem. Thermal power generation, transport and seasonal stubble burning and forest fires contribute in India.
- Oceanic exchange — the oceans absorb roughly a quarter of anthropogenic CO2, with the consequence of ocean acidification. Coastal mangroves, seagrass and salt marshes store “blue carbon” at far higher density per hectare than terrestrial forest: the Sundarbans and the Coringa mangroves of the Godavari estuary in Andhra Pradesh are India’s principal blue carbon reservoirs.
- Human perturbation and the Indian response. India is the third-largest emitter in absolute terms though far lower per capita. Its NDC includes creating an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through additional forest and tree cover by 2030 — which is why the cycle is directly a policy matter. Instruments: the National Mission for a Green India, CAMPA, the Green Credit Programme, MISHTI for mangrove restoration and the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture.

## The Nitrogen Cycle
- Why it matters: nitrogen is essential to proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll, yet atmospheric N2 — 78% of air — is inert, held by a triple bond that most organisms cannot break. The cycle is therefore about converting abundance into availability.
- Nitrogen fixation — conversion of N2 into ammonia. Biological:Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes (tur, chickpea, groundnut), Azotobacter free-living in soil, and Anabaena and Nostoc cyanobacteria, including the Azolla-Anabaena association traditionally used in Indian paddy. Industrial: the Haber-Bosch process, the basis of India’s urea industry. Atmospheric: lightning, a minor pathway.
- Nitrification — soil bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) oxidise ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate, the form most plants absorb.
- Assimilation — plants take up nitrate and ammonium to build amino acids and proteins; animals obtain nitrogen by consuming plants. Rice, wheat and sugarcane in Punjab, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu are heavily dependent on applied nitrogen.
- Ammonification — decomposers convert organic nitrogen in dead matter and excreta back to ammonia.
- Denitrification — anaerobic bacteria reduce nitrate to N2 and nitrous oxide, completing the cycle. Waterlogged soils — Kuttanad (Kerala) and paddy fields generally — show high denitrification, and N2O is a greenhouse gas roughly 273 times more potent than CO2 over a century.
- Human perturbation — the “nitrogen cascade”. A single atom of reactive nitrogen released into the environment can cause a sequence of effects in turn: groundwater nitrate contamination, eutrophication and algal blooms in surface water, N2O emissions contributing to warming and stratospheric ozone depletion, and soil acidification. India’s fertiliser use is skewed heavily toward urea because of its price structure, producing an imbalanced N:P:K ratio and low nitrogen use efficiency — a large share of applied nitrogen never reaches the crop.
- Indian policy responses:neem-coated urea (mandatory, slowing nitrogen release and curbing diversion), the Soil Health Card Scheme, promotion of biofertilisers and nano urea, PM-PRANAM to incentivise States reducing chemical fertiliser use, and the National Mission on Natural Farming.

## Conclusion

The carbon and nitrogen cycles govern climate stability and food production respectively, and human activity has significantly altered both — transferring geological carbon to the atmosphere and roughly doubling reactive nitrogen in circulation. India’s position is distinctive on each: it holds substantial forest and blue carbon sinks alongside high emissions, and depends on nitrogen fertiliser while suffering its downstream costs. Restoring balance requires expanding sinks under the Green India Mission and MISHTI, and improving nitrogen use efficiency — which is simultaneously an ecological gain and a fiscal one, given the fertiliser subsidy.

## Value addition
- Forest and sink data: forest and tree cover about 25.17% of geographical area (ISFR 2023, FSI), against the National Forest Policy 1988 target of 33%; India’s NDC commits to an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2e by 2030.
- Blue carbon: mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes sequester carbon at far higher density per hectare than terrestrial forests; MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes) and Amrit Dharohar for wetlands were announced in Budget 2023-24; Coringa (AP) and the Sundarbans are key Indian sites.
- Greenhouse gas potency: methane roughly 28 times and nitrous oxide roughly 273 times CO2 over a 100-year horizon — useful figures for explaining why agricultural emissions matter disproportionately.
- Nitrogen-fixing organisms to name:symbiotic — Rhizobium (legumes), Frankia (non-legume actinorhizal plants), Anabaena in Azolla; free-living — Azotobacter, Beijerinckia, Clostridium, Nostoc.
- Fertiliser policy instruments: neem-coated urea; Soil Health Cards; nano urea developed by IFFCO; PM-PRANAM; Nutrient Based Subsidy for P and K; the National Mission on Natural Farming.
- Concepts that lift the answer: the nitrogen cascade; eutrophication and the resulting hypoxic zones; ocean acidification; residence time of carbon in different reservoirs; nitrogen use efficiency.
- AP-specific: methane from Godavari and Krishna delta paddy; Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary mangroves as blue carbon; groundnut and pulse cultivation in Rayalaseema as biological nitrogen fixation; Kolleru Lake eutrophication from aquaculture and fertiliser runoff.

## Introduction

Organisms interact with their environment through symbiosis, ecological service and physiological regulation. Lichens exemplify mutualism and serve as pollution indicators; insects provide ecosystem services on which agriculture depends; and homeostasis and osmoregulation illustrate how animals maintain internal stability against external variation.

## (a)(i) Lichens

What they are: a symbiotic association between a fungus (the mycobiont, usually an ascomycete, forming the body) and a photosynthetic partner (the photobiont — a green alga or cyanobacterium). The alga supplies carbohydrate through photosynthesis; the fungus supplies water, minerals, anchorage and protection from desiccation. This partnership allows colonisation of bare rock, tree bark, and polar and high-altitude environments where neither partner could survive alone.

Forms:crustose (crust-like, tightly attached), foliose (leaf-like, loosely attached) and fruticose (branched, shrub-like) — the last being most sensitive to pollution.

Economic and ecological importance: - Bioindicators of air quality — the most examinable use. Lichens absorb water and nutrients directly from the atmosphere with no protective cuticle or roots, so they accumulate pollutants without any means of excretion. They are exceptionally sensitive to sulphur dioxide, and their absence from urban and industrial areas produces “lichen deserts” — making lichen mapping a low-cost biomonitoring technique used in Indian industrial belts. - Dyes and reagents:Roccella tinctoria and Lecanora yield litmus and orchil dyes; litmus remains the standard classroom pH indicator. - Medicinal:Usnea produces usnic acid, with antibacterial properties; several lichens feature in traditional medicine. - Perfumery: oakmoss (Evernia) is a fixative in perfumery; in India, lichens are traded as charila or stone flower, used as a spice in Indian cooking, particularly in Maharashtrian and Chettinad cuisine — a genuinely Indian economic use. - Soil formation and succession: lichens secrete organic acids that weather bare rock, making them pioneer species in primary ecological succession. - Food and fodder:Cladonia rangiferina (reindeer moss) sustains Arctic reindeer. - Nitrogen fixation: cyanobacterial lichens contribute fixed nitrogen to nutrient-poor ecosystems.

## (a)(ii) Usefulness of insects
- Pollination — the largest economic service. Bees, butterflies, beetles and flies pollinate a large share of flowering plants and many crops. In India this directly affects mustard, sunflower, mango, apple, cotton, pulses and horticultural crops. Insect pollination is an unpriced input on which food security depends, which is why pollinator decline is an agricultural and not merely an ecological concern.
- Products of direct commercial value:honey and beeswax (supported by the National Beekeeping and Honey Mission and the “Sweet Revolution”); silk from Bombyx mori (mulberry) and the tasar, eri and muga silkworms — India is among the world’s largest silk producers, with Andhra Pradesh a leading mulberry silk state; lac from Kerria lacca, used in shellac, dyes and cosmetics.
- Biological pest control: ladybird beetles consume aphids; Trichogramma wasps parasitise crop pest eggs. These underpin Integrated Pest Management, reducing pesticide dependence.
- Decomposition and soil health: dung beetles, termites and detritivorous insects recycle organic matter and return nutrients; earthworm-assisted vermicomposting is widely promoted in Indian agriculture.
- Scientific research:Drosophila melanogaster is the foundational model organism of genetics.
- Food and feed: entomophagy is traditional in parts of North-East India, and insect protein (black soldier fly) is an emerging animal-feed industry.
- Forensic and medical uses: forensic entomology for estimating time of death; maggot debridement therapy for wound care.

## (b)(i) Homeostasis

Definition: the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment despite external fluctuation. Why it matters: enzymes function within narrow ranges of temperature and pH, so physiological stability is the precondition for biochemical function.

Mechanism: homeostasis operates through negative feedback loops — a receptor detects deviation, a control centre processes it, and an effector produces a correction that reduces the deviation. Naming this mechanism is what distinguishes an explanation from a description.

Examples: - Thermoregulation: humans maintain about 37deg C. On heating — sweating and cutaneous vasodilation dissipate heat; on cooling — shivering, vasoconstriction and piloerection conserve it. The hypothalamus is the control centre. - Osmoregulation and blood glucose: kidneys regulate water and solute balance; insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose. - Plants maintain water balance through stomatal regulation, closing stomata under water stress — the trade-off being reduced photosynthesis.

## (b)(ii) Animal response to osmotic conditions

Animals face a constant tendency for water to move across membranes toward higher solute concentration. Two strategies exist:

- Osmoconformers — internal osmotic concentration matches the surrounding medium, so no gradient exists and no energy is spent maintaining one. Almost all are marine invertebrates: jellyfish, sea anemones, most molluscs and echinoderms. The limitation is that they tolerate only narrow salinity variation (stenohaline).
- Osmoregulators — internal concentration is actively maintained regardless of the external medium, at metabolic cost. This allows occupation of freshwater, estuarine and terrestrial habitats (euryhaline species tolerate wide ranges).

How osmoregulators solve opposite problems: - Freshwater fish are hyperosmotic to their surroundings, so water floods in and salts leak out. They do not drink, excrete large volumes of very dilute urine, and actively absorb salts through specialised gill chloride cells. - Marine bony fish face the reverse: they lose water to the sea. They drink seawater, excrete small volumes of concentrated urine, and actively pump salts out through the gills. - Marine cartilaginous fish (sharks, rays) use a third strategy — retaining urea and trimethylamine oxide in the blood to raise internal osmolarity close to seawater, avoiding water loss without the salt load. - Terrestrial animals rely on the kidney; the camel produces highly concentrated urine, tolerates significant body water loss and fluctuating body temperature; desert rodents such as the kangaroo rat survive largely on metabolic water. - Migratory species such as salmon and hilsa switch strategies when moving between salt and fresh water — a physiologically remarkable transition. Hilsa migrating up the Godavari and Hooghly is the Indian example.

## Conclusion

Lichens and insects demonstrate that ecological services often go unpriced until they fail — lichens as free air-quality sensors, insects as the unpaid pollinators of Indian agriculture. Homeostasis and osmoregulation show the same principle within the organism: stability is not passive but actively and continuously maintained at metabolic cost. Recognising both is essential to conservation policy, since the services lost when a pollinator population collapses have no ready substitute.

## Value addition
- Lichen terminology:mycobiont (fungal partner), photobiont (algal or cyanobacterial partner), thallus (the body); growth forms crustose, foliose, fruticose; lichen desert as the term for the pollution-induced absence of lichens around industrial areas.
- Indian insect-based industries:sericulture — India is among the world’s largest silk producers, with mulberry silk concentrated in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal, and muga silk unique to Assam; apiculture under the National Beekeeping and Honey Mission; lac cultivation in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.
- Pollinator decline — driven by pesticide use (notably neonicotinoids), habitat loss, monoculture and disease; a food-security concern given the dependence of horticultural and oilseed crops on insect pollination.
- Homeostasis terms:negative feedback (corrective, the dominant mode) versus positive feedback (amplifying, as in blood clotting or childbirth); set point; receptor-control centre-effector.
- Osmoregulation terms:osmoconformer and osmoregulator; stenohaline and euryhaline; hyperosmotic and hypoosmotic; anadromous (sea to river, as salmon and hilsa) and catadromous (river to sea, as eels).
- AP-specific: mulberry sericulture in Chittoor, Anantapur and Annamayya districts; hilsa migration in the Godavari; lichen-based biomonitoring applicable to the Visakhapatnam industrial belt.
