## Introduction

An ecosystem is a functional unit in which living organisms interact with one another and with their non-living surroundings, linked by one-way energy flow and cyclical nutrient movement. The food chain describes the route energy takes through this system, and understanding it explains why ecosystems are vulnerable to disturbance at any single link — including the disturbance caused by urbanisation.

## (a) Ecosystem and food chain

Components - Biotic: producers (autotrophs), consumers (heterotrophs) and decomposers. - Abiotic: sunlight, temperature, water, soil, minerals and gases. - Examples: natural — forest, grassland, desert, pond, ocean, wetland; artificial — cropland, aquarium, urban ecosystem.

The two defining functions - Energy flow is one-way (unidirectional): solar energy enters through producers and is lost as heat at every step. It cannot be recycled. - Nutrients cycle: carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus are used repeatedly, returned by decomposers to the abiotic pool.

Recognising this asymmetry — energy flows, matter cycles — is the single most important conceptual point in ecosystem ecology.

## Trophic levels in a food chain
- Producers (T1) — green plants, algae and cyanobacteria fixing solar energy through photosynthesis.
- Primary consumers (T2) — herbivores: deer, rabbit, grasshopper, zooplankton.
- Secondary consumers (T3) — carnivores feeding on herbivores: frog, snake, small fish.
- Tertiary consumers (T4) — higher carnivores: eagle, tiger, large predatory fish.
- Decomposers — bacteria and fungi acting at every level, returning nutrients to the soil and closing the cycle.

Types of food chain - Grazing food chain — begins with living plants: Grass --> Grasshopper --> Frog --> Snake --> Eagle . - Detritus food chain — begins with dead organic matter: Litter --> Earthworm/Fungi --> Bird . In many terrestrial ecosystems the detritus chain actually carries more energy than the grazing chain — a point that surprises examiners favourably.

## The 10% law — why food chains are short

Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level transfers to the next; the remaining 90% is lost as metabolic heat, in unassimilated matter and through respiration (Lindeman’s law). This is why food chains rarely exceed four or five links — there is insufficient energy to support a further level — and why top predators are always few in number and vulnerable to disturbance.

Food chain versus food web: a food chain is a linear sequence; in reality organisms feed at multiple levels, forming a food web. Webs are more stable than chains, because the loss of one species can be compensated by alternative pathways.

Ecological pyramids — graphical representations across trophic levels: pyramids of number, biomass and energy. The pyramid of energy is always upright, since energy is lost at each transfer; pyramids of number and biomass can be inverted — as in a single tree supporting many insects (number), or an ocean where a small standing biomass of rapidly reproducing phytoplankton supports a larger zooplankton biomass (biomass).

## (b) Impact of urbanisation on biodiversity
- Habitat loss and fragmentation — the primary driver. Urban expansion converts forests, wetlands and farmland into built-up area. Fragmentation is often more damaging than the loss itself: small isolated patches cannot sustain viable populations, gene flow is interrupted, and edge effects degrade habitat quality well inside the remaining patch.
- Pollution. Air, water, soil, noise and light pollution. Artificial night lighting disrupts nocturnal insects, bats and migratory birds; noise interferes with bird song and therefore with mating.
- Urban heat island effect. Concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, raising city temperatures several degrees above surrounding areas, altering flowering and breeding cycles and stressing species at their thermal limits.
- Hydrological alteration. Impervious surfaces prevent recharge and increase runoff; wetlands and urban lakes are encroached — Kolleru Lake in Andhra Pradesh (a Ramsar site) has faced sustained pressure from aquaculture and encroachment, and Bengaluru’s and Hyderabad’s lake systems illustrate the same process.
- Invasive species. Disturbed urban land favours generalists and exotics — Prosopis juliflora, Lantana camara, Parthenium — which outcompete natives.
- Biotic homogenisation. Cities worldwide converge on the same small set of adaptable species (pigeons, crows, rats, house sparrows in decline), so urban biodiversity becomes similar everywhere — a distinctive and underappreciated form of biodiversity loss.
- Human-wildlife conflict. Settlement and infrastructure expansion into habitat increases encounters — leopards in and around Mumbai and Bengaluru, elephants along expanding corridors in the Eastern Ghats and North Bengal.
- The counter-point: urban areas can also support biodiversity where deliberately managed — urban forests, Miyawaki plantations, wetland restoration, green corridors, and the Nagar Van Yojana, which creates city forests on the urban periphery.

## Conclusion

Ecosystems function through the one-way flow of energy and the cyclical movement of nutrients, with the 10% law setting a hard limit on food chain length and therefore on the abundance of top predators. Urbanisation disrupts this structure at multiple points simultaneously — removing habitat, fragmenting what remains, altering temperature and hydrology, and homogenising species composition. Since India’s urban population continues to grow rapidly, integrating biodiversity into urban planning through green corridors, wetland protection and urban forests is not an amenity but a necessity.

## Value addition
- The 10% law (Lindeman, 1942): approximately 10% of energy transfers between successive trophic levels; the remainder is lost as heat and in unassimilated matter. It explains short food chains, low predator abundance, and why vegetarian diets are more energy-efficient per calorie delivered.
- Ecological pyramids: pyramid of energy — always upright; pyramid of number — can be inverted (a single tree supporting many insects); pyramid of biomass — can be inverted in aquatic systems (small phytoplankton standing crop supporting larger zooplankton biomass).
- Biomagnification — persistent pollutants such as DDT and mercury concentrate at successively higher trophic levels; this is the mechanism by which top predators accumulate the highest toxin burdens, and it is a natural extension of any food chain answer.
- Ecosystem services framework:provisioning (food, water, timber), regulating (climate, flood, disease), supporting (nutrient cycling, soil formation), cultural (recreation, spiritual) — from the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.
- Urban biodiversity instruments:Nagar Van Yojana (urban forests); Miyawaki dense native plantations; Smart Cities Mission green infrastructure; Ramsar designation of urban wetlands; City Biodiversity Index.
- AP-specific:Kolleru Lake (Ramsar site) under pressure from aquaculture and encroachment; Coringa mangroves near expanding Kakinada; Visakhapatnam’s coastal urbanisation and the Kambalakonda sanctuary within the city; human-elephant conflict along the Eastern Ghats.

## Introduction

Essential oils are concentrated, volatile, aromatic compounds extracted from plants, responsible for their characteristic fragrance and many of their therapeutic properties. They are “essential” in the sense of containing the plant’s essence, not in the nutritional sense. Alongside plant nutrition and symbiosis, they illustrate how plant biology translates into human economic use — in India’s case, through a national programme that has made aromatic crops a rural livelihood strategy.

## (a) Essential oils

Nature and chemistry. Essential oils are complex mixtures of terpenes and terpenoids, aldehydes, esters, phenols and alcohols, stored in specialised secretory structures — glandular trichomes, oil ducts and resin canals. They are volatile, lipophilic and typically immiscible with water, which is what makes steam distillation possible.

Extraction methods - Steam distillation — the dominant commercial method; steam volatilises the oil, which is condensed and separated. - Cold pressing (expression) — for citrus peels, where heat would degrade the oil. - Solvent extraction and enfleurage — for delicate flowers such as jasmine and tuberose, yielding concretes and absolutes. - Supercritical CO2 extraction — a modern, solvent-free method giving higher purity.

Major sources - Flowers: rose (Rosa damascena), jasmine, tuberose, lavender. - Leaves and grasses: eucalyptus, mint, lemongrass, palmarosa, citronella. -Bark, wood and roots: sandalwood, cinnamon, vetiver (khus). - Peels: orange, lemon, bergamot. - Seeds and resins: ajwain, fennel, frankincense.

Important uses - Perfumery and cosmetics — the largest market by value: perfumes, soaps, hair oils, skincare. - Medicinal and therapeutic — aromatherapy; eucalyptus and tea tree oils with documented antimicrobial activity; menthol in balms and decongestants; clove oil in dentistry. - Food and beverage — flavouring in confectionery, beverages and processed foods. - Pharmaceutical and industrial — natural preservatives, carminatives, and ingredients in pain-relief formulations. - Agriculture — botanical pesticides and insect repellents, notably neem and citronella, reducing dependence on synthetic chemicals. - Aromatherapy and wellness — a growing segment linked to India’s traditional medicine systems and the AYUSH sector.

The Indian context — the addition that matters. India is a major producer and exporter of essential oils, particularly mint, lemongrass, citronella, vetiver and sandalwood. CSIR’s Aroma Mission promotes cultivation of aromatic crops — lavender, lemongrass, vetiver, palmarosa — on rain-fed and marginal land, providing farmers a high-value alternative where conventional crops are unviable. Its best-known outcome is the “Purple Revolution” in Jammu & Kashmir, where lavender cultivation transformed incomes in Bhaderwah. Aromatic crops suit degraded land, are relatively drought-tolerant and are generally not palatable to wild animals — three properties that make them well suited to marginal Indian farming conditions.

## (b)(i) Autotrophic vs. heterotrophic plants
- **Basis** — Autotrophic · Heterotrophic
- **Nutrition** — Synthesise own food from CO2, water and light · Depend on other organisms
- **Pigment** — Contain chlorophyll · Chlorophyll absent or reduced
- **Ecological role** — Producers — base of the food chain · Consumers or decomposers
- **Examples** — Maize, mango, algae, cyanobacteria · Cuscuta, Monotropa, Rafflesia

Heterotrophic plants — the three modes: - Parasitic — draw nutrients from a living host via haustoria: Cuscuta (dodder, a total stem parasite), mistletoe (partial parasite, retaining some chlorophyll), Rafflesia, and the root parasite Striga, a serious pest of Indian cereals. - Saprophytic — obtain nutrients from decaying organic matter: Monotropa (Indian pipe), Neottia. - Insectivorous (carnivorous) — photosynthesise normally but trap insects to obtain nitrogen, an adaptation to nitrogen-poor acidic soils: Nepenthes (pitcher plant, found in Meghalaya), Drosera (sundew), Utricularia (bladderwort). The key point is that they are not heterotrophic for carbon — they supplement minerals, not energy.

## (b)(ii) Symbiosis

Definition: a close and long-term biological interaction between two different species. Types are distinguished by who benefits:

- Mutualism (+/+) — both benefit: Rhizobium-legume nitrogen fixation; mycorrhiza, in which fungi extend a plant’s effective root surface for phosphorus uptake in exchange for carbohydrate; lichens; pollinator-plant relationships; the fig and fig wasp; gut microbiota in ruminants.
- Commensalism (+/0) — one benefits, the other is unaffected: epiphytic orchids on trees; barnacles on whales; cattle egrets following grazing animals.
- Parasitism (+/−) — one benefits at the other’s expense: Cuscuta on host plants, mistletoe on mango, Plasmodium in humans, ticks on cattle.
- Amensalism (0/−) — one is harmed, the other unaffected: allelopathy, as when Parthenium or eucalyptus suppresses neighbouring plants through chemical exudates.
- Protocooperation — both benefit but the association is not obligatory.

Ecological and economic significance: mutualisms underpin nutrient cycling and pollination. In agriculture, biofertilisers — Rhizobium, Azotobacter, mycorrhizal inoculants, Azolla-Anabaena — commercialise symbiosis directly, reducing chemical fertiliser dependence.

Endosymbiosis — the theory, supported by strong evidence, that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell. It explains why these organelles retain their own circular DNA and double membranes, and it makes symbiosis not merely an ecological interaction but a driver of evolutionary innovation.

## Conclusion

Essential oils illustrate how plant secondary metabolites — evolved for defence and pollinator attraction — become commercial products, and in India, through the Aroma Mission, a livelihood strategy for marginal land. The autotroph-heterotroph distinction defines who produces energy and who consumes it, while symbiosis shows that the boundary between organisms is more porous than it appears: from Rhizobium nodules that feed Indian pulse cultivation to the endosymbiotic origin of the cell’s own organelles.

## Value addition
- CSIR Aroma Mission: promotes cultivation, processing and value addition of aromatic crops — lavender, lemongrass, vetiver, palmarosa, mint — on rain-fed and degraded land; the “Purple Revolution” in Bhaderwah, Jammu & Kashmir, is its flagship outcome. Aromatic crops are drought-tolerant, suited to marginal soil and generally not browsed by wild animals.
- India’s position: a leading global producer of mint oil, lemongrass, citronella and vetiver; CSIR-CIMAP (Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants, Lucknow) is the principal research institute; the National Medicinal Plants Board operates under the Ministry of AYUSH.
- Extraction terminology: steam distillation; hydro-distillation; cold pressing; solvent extraction yielding concrete and absolute; supercritical CO2 extraction; enfleurage for delicate florals.
- Symbiosis terms with signs: mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0), parasitism (+/−), amensalism (0/−), competition (−/−); obligate versus facultative;

allelopathy as a form of amensalism.

- Mycorrhiza types:ectomycorrhiza (sheath around the root, common in trees) and endomycorrhiza/arbuscular (penetrating root cells, the most widespread) — significant for phosphorus uptake and increasingly used as a biofertiliser.
- Biofertilisers to name:Rhizobium (legumes), Azotobacter and Azospirillum (cereals), Azolla-Anabaena (paddy), phosphate-solubilising bacteria, mycorrhizal inoculants — all commercial applications of symbiosis.
- AP-specific: aromatic and medicinal plant cultivation in the Eastern Ghats; Araku Valley coffee and spice agroforestry; lemongrass and citronella potential on Rayalaseema’s rain-fed land; sandalwood in the Seshachalam range.

Sources used: Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023; MoEFCC — Environment Impact Assessment Notification 2006 and subsequent amendments, National Mission for a Green India, MISHTI and E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022; Ministry of Jal Shakti — National Water Policy 2012 and Atal Bhujal Yojana; Central Ground Water Board — Master Plan for Artificial Recharge; Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying — Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana; Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare — Soil Health Card Scheme, neem-coated urea, PM-PRANAM and the National Mission on Natural Farming; MNRE on non-fossil capacity milestones; CSIR and CSIR-CIMAP on the Aroma Mission; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on Nagar Van Yojana; India’s Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement.

## Introduction

Conservation biology is the scientific study of the maintenance and restoration of biological diversity — genes, species and ecosystems. It differs from ecology in being explicitly normative and mission-oriented: it is often described as a “crisis discipline”, drawing on ecology, genetics, economics and law with the declared purpose of preventing extinction. In India, the practical question has increasingly become not whether to conserve, but who conserves — and the answer has shifted decisively toward communities.

- Ecosystems
- habitat loss, over-exploitation, pollution, invasives, climate change .

## Conservation biology — scope and principles
- Three levels of diversity: genetic (variation within species, the raw material of adaptation), species, and ecosystem.
- Core concerns: minimum viable population size, habitat fragmentation and corridor design, island biogeography, ecological restoration, and captive breeding with reintroduction.
- The five principal drivers of biodiversity loss — habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, pollution, invasive alien species, and climate change. Habitat loss remains the largest.
- Two conservation modes:in-situ (within natural habitat — national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, conservation and community reserves) and ex-situ (outside it — zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks, cryopreservation).

## The role of community in conserving nature
- Customary and cultural conservation — the oldest layer.Sacred groves — devarakadu in Karnataka, kavu in Kerala, law kyntang in Meghalaya, oran in Rajasthan — protect biodiversity-rich forest patches through religious prohibition rather than statute. India has thousands of such groves; several harbour species absent from surrounding managed forest, making them living reference ecosystems. The Bishnoi tradition in Rajasthan is the best-known instance of religiously grounded conservation.
- Community-led species and habitat recovery. The Maldhari pastoralists coexisting with lions in Gir; the Apatani of Arunachal Pradesh managing paddy-cum-fish wetland systems; Chilika Lake fisher communities in Odisha participating in lagoon restoration; Khonoma in Nagaland, where a community hunting ban created the Khonoma Nature Conservation and Tragopan Sanctuary.
- The legal architecture — what turns practice into right.

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002, amended in 2023, establishes a three-tier structure: the National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards, and Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at every local body. BMCs prepare People’s Biodiversity Registers (PBRs) documenting local species, uses and traditional knowledge — creating a legal record of what a community holds. Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) provisions require that commercial users of biological resources or associated traditional knowledge share benefits with the communities concerned — implementing the Nagoya Protocol. Community Forest Resource (CFR) rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 empower gram sabhas to protect, regenerate and manage forests they have traditionally used — the strongest legal instrument for community conservation India has. Mendha Lekha and Pachgaon in Gadchiroli, Maharashtra, are the standard demonstrations. Joint Forest Management committees, and Conservation Reserves and Community Reserves created under the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment

Act, 2002 — categories designed specifically for community-managed and privately held land.

- Ecotourism and livelihood linkage.Periyar Tiger Reserve converted former poachers into guides through eco-development committees — the clearest demonstration that conservation succeeds when the community’s income depends on the resource surviving.
- Participation in programmes: Namami Gange, compensatory afforestation, eco-sensitive zone management, MISHTI mangrove restoration.

The honest qualification: community conservation is not automatically successful. It fails where benefits are captured by local elites, where the community is internally divided over resource use, where legal rights are recognised on paper but not implemented, or where external pressure (mining leases, infrastructure) overrides local decisions. Recognising this makes the answer analytical rather than celebratory.

AP instance: Andhra Pradesh has sacred groves in the Eastern Ghats; Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary mangrove protection involves fishing communities; Kolleru Lake (Ramsar site) restoration depends on reconciling fisher livelihoods with aquaculture encroachment; and Vana Samrakshana Samithis function as the State’s Joint Forest Management institutions.

## Conclusion

Conservation biology supplies the science; communities supply the daily presence, local knowledge and enforcement capacity that no forest department can match at scale. India’s distinctive contribution has been to move community conservation from custom to statute — through Biodiversity Management Committees, People’s Biodiversity Registers and Community Forest Resource rights. The remaining task is implementation: recognising CFR rights at scale and ensuring benefit-sharing actually reaches the communities whose knowledge is being used.

## Value addition
- Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023): three-tier structure — NBA (Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards, BMCs; People’s Biodiversity Registers; Access and Benefit Sharing; Biodiversity Heritage Sites notified by State governments.
- Protected area categories in India: National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves and Community Reserves (added by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2002), Biosphere Reserves, Tiger Reserves under Project Tiger, Elephant Reserves, and Ramsar wetland sites — India has among the largest networks of Ramsar sites in Asia.
- Landmark community conservation cases:Mendha Lekha and Pachgaon (Gadchiroli — CFR rights); Khonoma (Nagaland); Periyar (Kerala — eco-development committees); Chilika (Odisha); Apatani (Arunachal Pradesh); Bishnoi (Rajasthan).
- Global frameworks:Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) with its three objectives — conservation, sustainable use, and fair benefit sharing; the Nagoya Protocol on ABS; the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) with the “30 by 30” target of protecting 30% of land and sea by 2030.
- Concepts worth naming:keystone species; umbrella and flagship species; minimum viable population; habitat corridors; rewilding; ecosystem services; biodiversity hotspots — India has four: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
- AP-specific: Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary; Kolleru Lake (Ramsar); Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve, India’s largest tiger reserve; Papikonda and Sri Venkateswara National Parks; Vana Samrakshana Samithis as AP’s JFM institutions; sacred groves in the Eastern Ghats.

## Introduction

Natural selection, proposed by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace and set out in On the Origin of Species (1859), is the process by which heritable traits that improve survival and reproduction become more common in a population over generations. It is the principal mechanism of evolution — not a random process, but the non-random survival of randomly arising variation.

Natural selection — the four necessary conditions

Natural selection operates wherever, and only where, all four hold:

1. Variation — individuals within a population differ in their traits.

2. Heritability — at least some of that variation is passed to offspring.

3. Overproduction — more offspring are produced than the environment can support, so competition is inevitable (the Malthusian insight Darwin drew on). 4. Differential survival and reproduction — individuals with certain traits leave more surviving offspring than others.

The outcome is that the frequency of favourable traits rises over generations. Fitness, in this context, means reproductive success — not strength or longevity.

Types of selection (worth naming): directional (one extreme favoured, shifting the mean); stabilising (intermediate favoured, reducing variance — as with human birth weight); and disruptive (both extremes favoured over the mean, potentially leading to speciation).

Indian and contemporary examples — more useful than the textbook case

- Pesticide resistance in the cotton bollworm. Repeated pesticide application kills susceptible insects but leaves resistant individuals, which then reproduce. Within a few seasons, resistance dominates the population. This is natural selection observable within a farmer’s lifetime, and is why Integrated Pest Management and refuge requirements for Bt cotton exist.
- Antibiotic resistance. The same logic in bacteria — the reason antimicrobial resistance is a national health priority and why India has a National Action Plan on AMR.
- Sickle cell trait and malaria. In malaria-endemic regions, including parts of central and southern India with high tribal prevalence, heterozygous carriers of the sickle cell allele have greater resistance to falciparum malaria. The allele persists despite being harmful in homozygous form — a textbook case of balanced polymorphism and one directly relevant to Indian public health.
- Melanism in moths (the classic British example) illustrates the same principle through camouflage against soot-darkened bark.

Drawing a food chain with a human as top consumer

Terrestrial (grazing) chain:Grass / Fodder crop (Producer) --> Goat (Primary consumer) --> HUMAN (Secondary consumer)

Aquatic chain:Phytoplankton (Producer) --> Zooplankton (Primary consumer) --> Small fish, e.g. sardine (Secondary consumer) --> Large fish, e.g. hilsa or tuna (Tertiary consumer) --> HUMAN (Quaternary consumer)

Why two chains, and what they show

- The human trophic position changes with diet. Eating a plant places a person at the second trophic level; eating goat at the third; eating a large predatory marine fish at the fifth. Humans are omnivores with a variable trophic level — which is precisely why a single fixed chain misrepresents the position.
- Energy implication (the 10% law). Because only about 10% of energy transfers between levels, the aquatic chain above requires roughly 10,000 units of phytoplankton energy to yield 1 unit at the human level, while the terrestrial chain requires around 100. A shorter chain feeds more people from the same primary production — the ecological basis of the argument for plant-based and lower-trophic-level diets.
- Biomagnification implication. Persistent pollutants — mercury, DDT, PCBs — concentrate at each successive level. A human eating a large predatory marine fish therefore ingests a far higher toxin load than one eating a herbivore, which is why advisories on mercury in large fish exist.
- The Indian illustration: the marine chain above describes India’s fisheries directly — hilsa in the Godavari and Hooghly estuaries, and sardine and mackerel along the Andhra and Kerala coasts, where INCOIS Potential Fishing Zone advisories guide the harvest.

## Conclusion

Natural selection explains how populations change: variation arises randomly, but survival does not, and over generations the environment shapes the population’s composition. The food chain places humans within this system rather than above it — and our trophic position is a dietary choice with ecological consequences, determining both how efficiently primary production feeds us and how much accumulated pollutant we ingest. Both concepts point the same way: humans are participants in ecological processes, subject to their constraints.

## Value addition
- The four conditions: variation, heritability, overproduction, differential survival and reproduction. Fitness = reproductive success, not physical strength.
- Types of selection: directional, stabilising, disruptive; also sexual selection (traits favoured for mate attraction, as in the peacock’s tail — an Indian example of a trait that reduces survival but raises reproductive success).
- Related evolutionary concepts:speciation through genetic divergence and reproductive isolation; allopatric (geographic barrier) versus sympatric speciation; adaptive radiation (Darwin’s finches); genetic drift and the founder effect; convergent and divergent evolution; Lamarckism as the superseded alternative.
- The 10% law (Lindeman): approximately 10% energy transfer between trophic levels, limiting chains to four or five links and making shorter chains more efficient in feeding people.
- Biomagnification versus bioaccumulation:bioaccumulation is build-up within one organism over its lifetime; biomagnification is increasing concentration at successive trophic levels. Mercury in large predatory fish and the historic DDT effect on raptor eggshells are the standard cases.
- Contemporary Indian applications of selection: pesticide resistance in the cotton bollworm and the Bt refuge requirement; antimicrobial resistance and the National Action Plan on AMR; sickle cell trait persistence in malaria-endemic tribal populations and the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023), targeting elimination by 2047 — a direct policy link.
- AP-specific: hilsa migration in the Godavari; sardine and mackerel fisheries along the Andhra coast; INCOIS Potential Fishing Zone advisories; sickle cell screening among tribal populations in the Eastern Ghats districts.

## Introduction

An ecosystem is a functional unit in which a community of organisms interacts with its physical environment, linked by one-way energy flow and cyclical nutrient movement. India’s aquatic ecosystems — from Himalayan streams to the Sundarbans mangroves and Lakshadweep reefs — are among the most productive and the most threatened components of this system.

## (a) Meaning of an ecosystem

A self-regulating unit of biotic and abiotic components, its two defining functions being energy flow (unidirectional, entering as sunlight and lost as heat) and nutrient cycling (matter used repeatedly). The essential asymmetry — energy flows, matter cycles — is the concept to state.

## (b) Structure of an ecosystem
- **Biotic components** — Abiotic components
- **Producers (autotrophs) — green plants, algae, cyanobacteria; fix solar energy** — Climatic: sunlight, temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind
- **Consumers (heterotrophs) — primary (herbivores), secondary and tertiary (carnivores), omnivores** — Edaphic: soil type, texture, pH, minerals
- **Decomposers (saprotrophs) — bacteria and fungi returning nutrients to the abiotic pool** — Inorganic: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, water, gases

Functional attributes: productivity (gross and net primary productivity), energy flow, decomposition, nutrient cycling, and ecological succession.

## (c) Types of aquatic ecosystems in India
- Freshwater — lotic (flowing): rivers and streams — the Ganga, Brahmaputra, Godavari and Krishna; Himalayan torrents and peninsular rivers differ markedly in flow regime and species.
- Freshwater — lentic (standing): lakes, ponds, tanks and reservoirs — Wular (Jammu & Kashmir), Loktak (Manipur, with its unique floating phumdis), Chilika (Odisha, Asia’s largest brackish lagoon), and Kolleru (Andhra Pradesh). Peninsular India’s tank systems are a distinctive human-made freshwater ecosystem.
- Marine: the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean; coral reefs at the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands; intertidal zones, continental shelf and deep-sea habitats.
- Brackish/estuarine (transitional): estuaries where the Godavari, Krishna, Hooghly, Mahanadi and Narmada meet the sea; mangroves — the Sundarbans (the world’s largest), Bhitarkanika (Odisha) and Coringa (Andhra Pradesh); salt marshes, lagoons (Chilika, Pulicat — shared between AP and Tamil Nadu) and backwaters (Kerala).
- Wetlands cut across these categories and are recognised internationally through Ramsar designation; India has one of Asia’s largest networks of Ramsar sites.

## (d) Threats and conservation
- **Threat** — Mechanism · Indian conservation instrument
- **Pollution** — Industrial effluent, sewage, agricultural runoff causing eutrophication; plastics and microplastics · Namami Gange; National River Conservation Plan; CPCB effluent standards and OCEMS; single-use plastic ban (July 2022)
- **Habitat loss and encroachment** — Wetland conversion for aquaculture, agriculture and construction; mangrove clearance · Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017; Amrit Dharohar for wetlands; MISHTI for mangroves; Coastal Regulation Zone rules
- **Over-exploitation** — Overfishing, destructive gear, sand mining · Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana; fishing bans in breeding season; mesh-size regulation; Marine Protected Areas
- **Climate change** — Warming, coral bleaching, sea-level rise, ocean acidification · NAPCC missions; National Coastal Mission; mangroves as natural sea defence
- **Invasive species** — Water hyacinth, African catfish, tilapia displacing natives · Invasive species management under State fisheries and forest departments
- **Altered flows** — Dams and barrages fragmenting river continuity and blocking fish migration · Environmental flow requirements; fish ladders; river- basin planning

Additional measures: community participation through fisher cooperatives and Biodiversity Management Committees; restoration of traditional tank systems; scientific aquaculture regulation; and public awareness.

AP instance — a live case.Kolleru Lake, a Ramsar site between the Krishna and Godavari deltas, has faced sustained pressure from fish-pond conversion, encroachment and nutrient runoff, prompting court-directed demolition of illegal aquaculture structures and continuing restoration efforts. It illustrates the entire threat matrix in one location — encroachment, eutrophication, livelihood conflict and enforcement difficulty. Nearby, Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary protects India’s second-largest mangrove formation, functioning as a cyclone buffer for the Godavari delta.

## Conclusion

Aquatic ecosystems deliver disproportionate value — fisheries, water purification, flood buffering, carbon storage and biodiversity — relative to the area they occupy, and are correspondingly the most degraded. India’s instruments now exist across the range: Ramsar designation and the Wetlands Rules for protection, Namami Gange for river restoration, MISHTI for mangroves and PMMSY for sustainable fisheries. The binding constraint is enforcement against livelihood pressure, as Kolleru demonstrates — which is why conservation succeeds only where it offers communities an alternative rather than only a prohibition.

- Wetland conservation instruments:Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017; National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA); Amrit Dharohar and MISHTI, both announced in Budget 2023-24; Save Wetlands Campaign.

- Mangrove significance: cyclone and tsunami buffering, nursery habitat for fisheries, and exceptionally high blue carbon density. Indian mangroves: Sundarbans (largest), Bhitarkanika, Coringa (AP), Pichavaram, Gulf of Kachchh.

## Introduction

The environment is the sum of all external conditions — physical, chemical and biological — surrounding and influencing life. It is conventionally divided into four interacting segments: the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water), lithosphere (land) and biosphere (life), with a fifth, the anthroposphere, now recognised for the human-made systems that increasingly shape the others.

## Atmosphere — the gaseous envelope
- Composition: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.93%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%, plus water vapour, ozone and trace gases. The trace constituents matter disproportionately — CO2 at 0.04% drives the greenhouse effect.
- Layers:troposphere (0-12 km, contains most of the mass and all weather; temperature falls with height); stratosphere (12-50 km, contains the ozone layer absorbing ultraviolet radiation; temperature rises with height, giving stability and making it the preferred altitude for aviation); mesosphere (coldest layer, where meteors burn); thermosphere (auroras and the ionosphere, which reflects radio waves); exosphere.
- Functions: temperature regulation through the greenhouse effect; UV shielding; the medium for the water cycle and weather; supply of oxygen for respiration and CO2 for photosynthesis; burning up of meteoroids.
- Human impact: greenhouse gas accumulation and climate change; stratospheric ozone depletion, addressed by the Montreal Protocol and its Kigali Amendment on HFCs; ambient air pollution, addressed by the National Clean Air Programme.

## Hydrosphere — all water
- Distribution: about 97.5% is saline ocean water; of the remaining 2.5% fresh water, roughly 68.7% is locked in glaciers and ice caps and about 30% is groundwater, leaving well under 1% of fresh water in accessible surface form. This distribution explains why fresh water is scarce despite the planet being predominantly water-covered — a figure worth quoting.
- Components: oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers, soil moisture and atmospheric water vapour.
- Functions: climate moderation through the ocean’s high heat capacity; the hydrological cycle; habitat; carbon sink absorbing roughly a quarter of anthropogenic CO2; and support for agriculture, industry and settlement.
- Human impact: groundwater over-extraction (India is the world’s largest groundwater user); pollution of rivers; ocean acidification; glacial retreat in the Himalaya affecting perennial river flow.

## Lithosphere — the solid Earth and soil
- Structure: the rigid outer shell comprising crust and upper mantle, broken into tectonic plates; beneath lies the asthenosphere, mantle and core.
- Soil — the biologically active layer. A soil profile comprises O horizon (organic litter), A horizon (topsoil, humus-rich), B horizon (subsoil, zone of accumulation), C horizon (weathered parent material) and R (bedrock). Soil formation is extremely slow — on the order of centuries per centimetre — which is why erosion is effectively irreversible on human timescales.
- Indian soil types: alluvial (most extensive and fertile, in the Indo-Gangetic and delta plains including the Godavari and Krishna deltas), black/regur (cotton soil, moisture-retentive, in the Deccan trap region), red and laterite (in peninsular India including much of Rayalaseema), desert, forest and mountain, and saline-alkaline soils.
- Functions: substrate for agriculture and settlement; mineral and fossil fuel reservoir; groundwater storage in aquifers; nutrient cycling.
- Human impact: soil erosion, desertification, salinisation from over-irrigation, mining degradation, and land-use conversion.

## Biosphere — the zone of life
- Extent: a thin shell extending from deep ocean trenches to a few kilometres into the atmosphere and some distance into the crust — remarkably thin relative to Earth’s radius.
- Organisation: organism –> population –> community –> ecosystem –> biome –> biosphere. India’s biomes include tropical evergreen and deciduous forest, thorn scrub, desert, montane, mangrove and marine.
- Functions: photosynthetic oxygen production; food webs; nutrient cycling; pollination; climate regulation through carbon sequestration.
- Human impact: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, invasive species and climate-driven range shifts.

## Anthroposphere — the human-made segment

Buildings, roads, dams, industries, vehicles, farms, communication networks and waste streams. Its recognition reflects the scale of human modification — the basis of the proposed Anthropocene epoch. It interacts with all four natural spheres: drawing minerals from the lithosphere, water from the hydrosphere, discharging into the atmosphere, and displacing the biosphere.

## Interactions between the segments — the section that completes the answer

The spheres are defined by their exchanges, not their separation:

- Water cycle: evaporation from hydrosphere –> condensation in atmosphere –> precipitation onto lithosphere –> transpiration through biosphere –> return to hydrosphere. All four spheres in one cycle.
- Soil formation: atmospheric weathering and hydrospheric water break down lithospheric rock; biospheric organisms — lichens first, then plants and soil fauna — add organic matter. Soil is literally an interface product of all four.
- Carbon cycle: atmospheric CO2 –> biosphere via photosynthesis –> lithosphere as fossil deposits –> hydrosphere via oceanic dissolution –> back to atmosphere.
- Monsoon: differential heating of the lithosphere and hydrosphere drives atmospheric circulation, which determines biospheric productivity across the Indian subcontinent — the clearest illustration for an Indian answer of how sphere interaction governs an entire agricultural economy.

## Conclusion

The environment functions as a single integrated system in which the four natural segments continuously exchange matter and energy, with the biosphere permeating all three physical spheres. Human activity, through the anthroposphere, now alters each of them at planetary scale — changing atmospheric composition, redirecting the hydrological cycle, degrading soil and reducing biodiversity. Because the segments are coupled, disturbance in one propagates to the others, which is why environmental management must be integrated rather than sectoral.

## Value addition
- Atmospheric layers in order with markers: troposphere (weather, temperature falls with altitude); tropopause; stratosphere (ozone layer, temperature rises, jet aircraft cruise here); mesosphere (coldest, meteors burn); thermosphere (auroras, ionosphere reflects radio waves); exosphere.
- Water distribution figures: about 97.5% saline; of the 2.5% fresh, roughly 68.7% in glaciers and ice, about 30% groundwater, and well under 1% in accessible surface water — the figures that explain freshwater scarcity.
- Soil horizons: O, A, B, C, R. India’s major soil types: alluvial, black (regur), red, laterite, desert, forest/mountain, saline-alkaline, peaty.
- The Anthropocene: the proposed geological epoch defined by dominant human influence on Earth systems; markers include radionuclides from nuclear testing, plastics, concrete and altered nitrogen and carbon cycles.
- Planetary boundaries framework (Rockström et al.): nine boundaries including climate change, biodiversity loss, biogeochemical flows (nitrogen and phosphorus), land-system change and freshwater use — a strong analytical frame for any “environment as a system” question.
- Governing international instruments by sphere: atmosphere — UNFCCC/Paris Agreement, Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment; hydrosphere — UNCLOS, Ramsar; lithosphere — UNCCD on desertification; biosphere — CBD, CITES, CMS.
- AP-specific: alluvial soils of the Godavari and Krishna deltas; red and laterite soils of Rayalaseema; the 1,053-km coastline as a lithosphere-hydrosphere interface; Eastern Ghats forests; monsoon dependence and cyclone exposure.

## Introduction

PM2.5 refers to particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less — roughly one-thirtieth the width of a human hair. That single physical property explains its disproportionate danger: particles this small are not filtered by the nose or upper airway, penetrate to the alveoli, and cross into the bloodstream, making PM2.5 a systemic rather than merely a respiratory pollutant.

reaches alveoli ; PM0.1 (ultrafine) --> crosses into bloodstream . This single diagram carries the answer’s central point.

## Why PM2.5 is uniquely harmful
- Deep penetration. Larger particles are intercepted by nasal hairs and mucociliary clearance; PM2.5 bypasses these defences and deposits in the gas-exchange region of the lung.
- Systemic translocation. From the alveoli, fine and ultrafine particles enter the circulation, reaching the heart, brain, liver and placenta — which is why the effects extend far beyond the lungs.
- Chemical composition. PM2.5 is not inert dust: it carries sulphates, nitrates, black carbon, heavy metals and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, several of them carcinogenic. Toxicity depends on composition as well as mass.
- Persistence and transport. Fine particles remain suspended for days and travel hundreds of kilometres, so pollution is regional rather than local — one reason city-level action alone cannot solve it.
- Secondary formation. A large share of PM2.5 forms in the atmosphere from precursor gases (SO2, NOx, NH₃) rather than being emitted directly — which is why controlling only visible emissions is insufficient, and why agricultural ammonia matters to urban air quality.

## Health effects by system
- Respiratory: aggravated asthma, chronic bronchitis, COPD, reduced lung function and impaired lung development in children, increased respiratory infection, and lung cancer — outdoor air pollution is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.
- Cardiovascular — the largest share of mortality. PM2.5 causes systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction and increased blood coagulability, raising the risk of ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, hypertension and stroke. Cardiovascular deaths exceed respiratory deaths in the air-pollution burden — a fact that surprises most readers and is worth stating.
- Neurological: emerging evidence links long-term exposure to cognitive decline, dementia risk, and impaired neurodevelopment in children.
- Metabolic and endocrine: associations with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
- Pregnancy and neonatal: low birth weight, pre-term delivery, and stillbirth risk; particles have been detected on the foetal side of the placenta.
- Mortality: ambient and household air pollution together constitute one of the leading risk factors for premature death globally, with a substantial share of that burden in India.

## Differential vulnerability — who bears the cost
- Children — higher breathing rate per unit body weight, developing lungs and brains, and more time outdoors.
- The elderly and those with pre-existing cardiac or respiratory disease.
- Pregnant women, with effects transmitted to the foetus.
- Outdoor workers — street vendors, traffic police, construction and sanitation workers — with high and unavoidable exposure.
- The urban poor — living near roads, industry and waste-burning sites, in poorly ventilated housing, often using solid cooking fuel, and least able to afford filtration or healthcare. Air pollution exposure is therefore strongly regressive, and this equity dimension is the strongest analytical point available on the topic.

## India versus the global picture
- India’s distinctive features: the Indo-Gangetic Plain experiences an unusual combination of high emissions and adverse meteorology — winter temperature inversion traps pollutants near the surface, and the Himalaya block dispersal. Seasonal crop-residue burning, festival emissions, construction dust and a substantially higher household air pollution burden from solid fuels compound the ambient load. Indian NAAQS limits (PM2.5 annual 40 µg/m³) are considerably above WHO guideline values, so “compliant” air is not necessarily safe air.
- Globally: developed economies substantially reduced PM2.5 through fuel standards, industrial controls and coal phase-out; the residual burden is concentrated in South Asia, parts of East Asia, Africa and West Asia, where growth and combustion have outpaced controls.
- Economic cost: air pollution imposes measurable costs through premature mortality, healthcare expenditure and lost labour productivity — significant fractions of GDP in the worst-affected economies.

## Measures

Source control: BS-VI fuel and vehicle norms; PM E-DRIVE for electric mobility; FGD at thermal plants; construction dust regulation; crop-residue management machinery and bio-decomposer; PMUY for clean household cooking. Institutional: NCAP across 131 cities; CAQM and GRAP for Delhi-NCR; CPCB monitoring with SAMEER for public information. Individual and clinical: air quality advisories, activity modification on high-AQI days, and N95-class masks for high-exposure groups.

## Conclusion

PM2.5’s danger follows directly from its size: it defeats the body’s filtration, reaches the alveoli and enters the bloodstream, making it a cardiovascular and neurological risk as much as a respiratory one — with cardiovascular deaths forming the largest share of the burden. Its impact is also profoundly unequal, falling hardest on children, outdoor workers and the urban poor who contribute least to it. India’s response must therefore shift from PM10 and road dust toward PM2.5 and its precursor gases, and treat household air pollution as an equal component — because for a large share of Indians, the most polluted air they breathe is inside their own kitchen.

## Value addition
- Size comparison to quote: PM2.5 is about 2.5 micrometres or less — roughly 1/30th the width of a human hair (about 70 µm). PM10 is about 1/7th. Ultrafine particles (PM0.1) cross into the bloodstream most readily.
- Composition: sulphates, nitrates, ammonium, black carbon, organic carbon, heavy metals and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; toxicity varies with composition, not mass alone.
- The secondary formation point: much PM2.5 forms in the atmosphere from SO2, NOx and NH₃, so agricultural ammonia and power-sector SO2 contribute to urban PM2.5 — which is why control must be regional and multi-sector.
- Standards comparison: Indian NAAQS PM2.5 annual limit 40 µg/m³ against a far lower WHO guideline; PM10 annual 60 µg/m³. Meeting Indian standards therefore does not mean meeting health-based standards.
- Institutional and regulatory instruments: NCAP (131 cities, 24 States/UTs, 40% PM10 reduction or NAAQS by 2025-26); CAQM (statutory, 2021) and GRAP for Delhi-NCR; SAFAR forecasting; PRANA portal; SAMEER app; NAMP and CAAQMS networks.
- The equity argument: exposure is regressive — those least responsible for emissions face the highest exposure and have the least capacity to avoid or treat its effects. This frames air pollution as an environmental justice issue, not only a public health one.
- AP-specific: Visakhapatnam’s industrial and port emissions; the Vijayawada urban agglomeration; coastal meteorology giving better dispersal than the Indo-Gangetic Plain — a useful contrast showing that geography, not only emissions, determines air quality.

Sources used: MoEFCC and PIB on the National Clean Air Programme (January 2019, revised targets for 2025-26, 131 cities across 24 States/UTs) and the National Ambient Air Quality Standards 2009; Central Pollution Control Board on the Air Quality Index, its eight pollutants and six categories, the NAMP and CAAQMS networks, and the SAMEER app; MoEFCC on the Biological Diversity Act 2002 (amended 2023), Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017, MISHTI and Amrit Dharohar; Ministry of Tribal Affairs on Community Forest Resource rights under the Forest Rights Act 2006; Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying on PMMSY; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas on PMUY; Ministry of Heavy Industries on PM E-DRIVE; Ramsar Convention Secretariat; Convention on Biological Diversity and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework; International Agency for Research on Cancer classification of outdoor air pollution; Government of Andhra Pradesh (Kolleru, Coringa, Vana Samrakshana Samithis).

Q62:
## Introduction

Individual behaviour is the point at which environmental policy either succeeds or fails: segregation rules work only if households segregate, and emission standards matter less if vehicles are poorly maintained. India has formalised this insight through Mission LIFE — Lifestyle for Environment, launched by the Prime Minister at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) and elaborated at COP27, which frames climate and pollution action as “pro-planet people” behaviour rather than as government responsibility alone.

## Mission LIFE — the framework to cite

Mission LIFE identifies seven thematic areas for individual action: save water; save energy; reduce single-use plastic; adopt sustainable food systems; reduce waste; adopt healthy lifestyles; and reduce e-waste. It works through a three-stage strategy — Change in Demand (nudging individual behaviour), Change in Supply (markets responding to altered demand), and Change in Policy. Naming this structure immediately distinguishes the answer from a generic list.

## Waste — where individual action matters most
- Segregation at source into wet, dry and domestic hazardous streams. This is the single highest-leverage individual act, because mixed waste is worth less than the sum of its parts: the wet fraction contaminates recyclables and the dry fraction ruins compost. No downstream technology can recover what the household has already mixed.
- Home composting of kitchen waste, which diverts the largest fraction of municipal waste from landfill.
- Refusing single-use plastic — cloth bags, refillable bottles, avoiding sachets; India banned identified single-use plastic items in July 2022.
- Routing e-waste and batteries through authorised collection channels under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 rather than to informal scrap dealers who burn and acid-leach them.

## Water

Fixing leaks, low-flow fixtures, rooftop rainwater harvesting, reusing greywater for gardens, and — critically — not pouring paint, solvents, medicines or cooking oil into drains, since household chemical discharge bypasses treatment entirely.

## Energy

LED lighting, star-rated appliances under the BEE Standards and Labelling programme, setting air conditioners to 24deg C (the BEE default-setting recommendation), switching off standby loads, and rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, which turns a household from consumer into generator.

## Mobility

Public transport, cycling, walking, carpooling; timely Pollution Under Control certification and vehicle maintenance; avoiding idling; and shifting to electric two-wheelers and vehicles supported under PM E-DRIVE.

## Consumption

Buying durable rather than disposable goods, repairing before replacing, avoiding food waste, and preferring local and seasonal food — which reduces both transport emissions and cold-chain energy.

## Noise and other pollution

Avoiding unnecessary honking, respecting silence zones around hospitals and schools, and observing time restrictions under the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000.

## Awareness, participation and civic action

Educating family and neighbours; joining clean-up drives, plantation programmes and Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam; participating in Biodiversity Management Committees and resident welfare initiatives; and — the most underrated — reporting violations, through the SAMEER app for air pollution complaints or the Swachhata app for waste. Citizens function as the enforcement system’s sensory network.

## The honest limitation — worth stating

Individual action has real but bounded reach. A household cannot choose the fuel mix of its electricity supply, the emission standards of industry, or the availability of public transport. Roughly speaking, the largest emission and pollution sources are systemic — power generation, industry, freight and construction — and individual virtue cannot substitute for regulation of these. Mission LIFE’s own design acknowledges this: it seeks to change demand in order to shift supply and eventually policy. The correct framing is therefore that individual action is necessary but not sufficient — and stating this makes the answer analytically credible rather than merely exhortatory.

## Conclusion

Individual responsibility matters most where households are themselves the source — waste segregation, water use, household energy and personal mobility — and Mission LIFE gives this a national framework organised around seven themes and a demand-to-supply-to-policy logic. But its true significance is aggregative and political: a citizenry that segregates waste, reports violations and demands cleaner options creates the market and electoral conditions for systemic change. Individual action is the foundation on which regulation becomes enforceable, not a substitute for it.

## Value addition

(The original’s Value Addition was on the Air Quality Index, which belongs to Q101; this section is new.)

Seven themes — save water, save energy, reduce single-use plastic, sustainable food systems, reduce waste, healthy lifestyles, reduce e-waste. Three-stage strategy: Change in Demand –> Change in Supply –> Change in Policy. Concept: “Pro-Planet People (P3)”.
- Citizen-facing platforms:Meri LiFE portal and app; SAMEER app for air pollution complaints; Swachhata app for waste grievances; e-waste collection through registered recyclers on the CPCB portal.
- Household-level schemes to name: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (rooftop solar); Ujjwala for clean cooking fuel; BEE Standards and Labelling star ratings; UJALA for LED distribution; PM E-DRIVE for electric mobility.
- Legal duties:Article 51A(g) of the Constitution makes it a Fundamental Duty of every citizen “to protect and improve the natural environment”; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Noise Pollution Rules, 2000 create individually applicable obligations.
- The 3Rs and beyond: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle — extended in circular economy usage to Refuse, Rethink, Repair, Refurbish, Recover.

Q63:
## Introduction

The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs most incoming ultraviolet-B radiation. Its severe seasonal depletion over Antarctica, first reported in 1985, was traced to chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting substances. The Montreal Protocol (1987) — the only UN treaty with universal ratification — mandated their phase-out. Four decades on, the evidence of recovery is real but requires careful qualification.

## Why the hole forms over Antarctica — the chemistry that explains the pattern

In the extreme cold of the Antarctic winter, polar stratospheric clouds form. Chlorine reservoir compounds react on the surfaces of these cloud particles, converting into forms that are readily split by sunlight. When spring sunlight returns in September-October, these release chlorine atoms, each of which catalytically destroys thousands of ozone molecules before being deactivated. The polar vortex isolates the air mass, preventing replenishment. This explains three features at once: why the hole is Antarctic rather than global, why it is seasonal, and why its size varies with meteorology as well as with chemistry — the last being essential to any critical examination.

## Evidence indicating healing
- Phase-out achieved. Nearly 99% of banned ozone-depleting substances have been phased out under the Montreal Protocol (WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment, 2022).
- Declining stratospheric chlorine. Levels of ozone-depleting substances in the Antarctic stratosphere have fallen by roughly a third from their peak around 2000 (NOAA).
- Projected recovery timeline. If current policies hold, total column ozone is expected to return to 1980 values by around 2066 over the Antarctic, around 2045 over the Arctic, and around 2040 for the rest of the world (WMO/UNEP, 2022).
- Recent observations. The 2024 ozone hole was below the 1990-2020 average, with a persistent later onset that WMO describes as a robust indicator of initial recovery. The 2025 hole was the fifth smallest since 1992 and the smallest in five years, and it closed on 1 December 2025 — the earliest closure since 2019 (WMO, with NOAA/NASA and Copernicus).
- Attribution to policy. Peer-reviewed analysis established that September ozone depletion had measurably lessened in a manner attributable to declining chlorine rather than to weather alone — the finding that first justified the word “healing”.

## Critical qualifications — why “healing” must be stated carefully
- Interannual variability is meteorological, not chemical. The size of the hole in any given year depends heavily on stratospheric temperature and vortex dynamics. The unusually large holes of 2020-2023 did not indicate reversal, just as small holes do not by themselves prove recovery. The robust signal is the trend and the timing of onset, not any single year’s area — the most important critical point available.
- Recovery is slow because CFCs are long-lived. Atmospheric lifetimes of decades to a century mean that even complete cessation of emissions leaves a legacy burden. Hence recovery dates in the 2040s-2060s rather than immediately.
- Illegal emissions. Unexpected CFC-11 emissions detected from 2018, traced substantially to East Asia, temporarily slowed the decline in atmospheric concentrations before enforcement action reduced them — demonstrating that compliance, not the treaty text, is the operative variable.
- Climate change interactions cut both ways. Rising CO2 cools the stratosphere, which can promote polar stratospheric cloud formation and delay Antarctic recovery, even while accelerating ozone recovery at mid-latitudes. Ozone and climate are coupled systems, not separate problems.
- Natural perturbations. Volcanic eruptions inject aerosols that provide surfaces for ozone-destroying chemistry — the Hunga Tonga eruption (2022) injected exceptional quantities of water vapour into the stratosphere, with measurable effects; wildfire smoke has similar potential.
- Emerging concerns. Proposals for stratospheric aerosol injection as solar geoengineering carry ozone-depletion risk — significant enough that the forthcoming 2026 WMO/UNEP Assessment includes it as a dedicated topic. Increasing rocket launches and satellite re-entry are also under study.

## Broader implications
- The Montreal Protocol is the most successful multilateral environmental agreement — universally ratified, with a Multilateral Fund financing developing-country compliance and differentiated timetables, features the climate regime has struggled to replicate.
- Its climate co-benefit is substantial: ozone-depleting substances are also potent greenhouse gases, and the Kigali Amendment (2016) on HFC phase-down is estimated to avoid 0.3-0.5deg C of warming by 2100. India ratified Kigali in 2021 with a phase-down schedule beginning in 2032.
- The lesson usually drawn — that the ozone case proves climate action is achievable — requires caution: CFCs had a limited number of producers and available substitutes, whereas fossil fuels are embedded in the entire economy. The institutional lessons (science-policy interface, differentiated timetables, financing compliance) transfer better than the substantive analogy.

## Conclusion

The evidence for Antarctic ozone recovery is genuine and strengthening: chlorine loading has fallen by about a third from its peak, onset is consistently later, and the 2025 hole was among the smallest since 1992 and closed earliest since 2019. But recovery is slow, non-linear and vulnerable to illegal emissions, volcanic events and stratospheric cooling from climate change — so full restoration is not expected before the 2060s. The Montreal Protocol demonstrates that international environmental cooperation can work; sustaining it through monitoring and enforcement is what makes the demonstration meaningful.

## Value addition
- Current data: nearly 99% of banned ODS phased out; stratospheric chlorine down about a third from its 2000 peak; recovery to 1980 values projected by around 2066 (Antarctic), 2045 (Arctic) and 2040 (rest of the world) — WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment 2022, with the next assessment due in 2026. The 2025 ozone hole was the fifth smallest since 1992, ending 1 December, the earliest closure since 2019.
- The chemistry to state precisely: polar stratospheric clouds enable chlorine activation; a single chlorine atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules catalytically; the polar vortex isolates the air mass; spring sunlight triggers the destruction — which is why the hole is Antarctic, seasonal and meteorologically variable.
- Montreal Protocol architecture: adopted 1987, in force 1989; universal ratification — the only UN treaty to achieve it; Multilateral Fund to finance developing-country compliance; Article 5 grace periods; amendments — London, Copenhagen, Montreal, Beijing and Kigali (2016) on HFCs. World Ozone Day: 16 September.
- Kigali Amendment: phases down HFCs (potent greenhouse gases that do not deplete ozone); estimated to avoid 0.3-0.5deg C of warming by 2100; India ratified in 2021, with phase-down starting 2032 in four steps and complementary work through the India Cooling Action Plan (2019).
- Health co-benefit: the Protocol is credited with preventing millions of cases of skin cancer and cataract, and with protecting agricultural productivity and marine phytoplankton from UV-B damage.
- Concepts to name:Dobson Unit (the standard measure of column ozone); ozone hole defined as column ozone below 220 DU; good ozone (stratospheric, protective) versus bad ozone (tropospheric, a pollutant and greenhouse gas) — a distinction examiners test.
- India’s role: a party to the Montreal Protocol since 1992; the Ozone Cell under MoEFCC is the national nodal unit; India completed its CFC and HCFC phase-out obligations on schedule.

## Introduction

Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperature, precipitation and weather patterns, driven in the current period principally by anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions. Global surface temperature has risen roughly 1.1-1.3deg C above the 1850-1900 baseline, with the last decade the warmest on record (IPCC AR6). Agriculture is the sector most directly exposed, because it depends on precisely the variables that are changing — temperature, rainfall timing and water availability.

## Effects of climate change on agriculture
- Crop productivity. Rising temperature shortens the grain-filling period and reduces yields of major cereals. ICAR studies indicate wheat yield declines of the order of 4-5% for every 1deg C rise in India. Heat stress during flowering reduces rice productivity, with observed impacts in coastal Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; higher night temperatures are particularly damaging to paddy because they raise respiration losses without any compensating gain in photosynthesis — a mechanism worth stating, since it explains why warming nights matter more than warming days for rice.
- The CO2 fertilisation caveat. Elevated CO2 modestly increases photosynthesis in C3 crops such as wheat and rice, but research shows it reduces protein, zinc and iron concentrations in the grain. The nutritional quality of the harvest therefore declines even where quantity is maintained — a subtle point that distinguishes a strong answer.
- Water availability and irrigation. Altered monsoon onset, withdrawal and intensity disrupt sowing calendars; higher evaporation raises crop water requirement while reducing supply. Groundwater stress affects a large share of India’s districts (NITI Aayog Composite Water Management Index), and drought recurrence in Rayalaseema and Telangana’s semi-arid zones raises crop failure and farmer distress.
- Pests and diseases. Warming expands the geographic and altitudinal range of pests and shortens their life cycles, permitting more generations per season — fall armyworm, whitefly and stem borer being the significant Indian cases. This raises pesticide use, input cost and resistance pressure.
- Livestock. Heat stress reduces feed intake, milk yield and fertility; dairy productivity declines materially in peak summer, and heat also reduces fodder availability and quality.
- Fisheries. Ocean warming and acidification shift fish distribution and breeding cycles; changes in upwelling affect catch off the Andhra and Odisha coasts, and cyclone frequency reduces safe fishing days.
- Soil. Erratic intense rainfall accelerates erosion; higher temperature reduces soil organic carbon; sea-level rise causes salinity ingress in delta soils — a direct threat to the Godavari and Krishna deltas.
- Socio-economic consequences. Yield volatility and input cost inflation raise indebtedness; distress migration increases from drought-prone regions; and because smallholders have the least buffer, the burden is regressive.

## The response — what makes the answer complete
- Research and resilient varieties:NICRA (ICAR) demonstrating climate-resilient technologies in vulnerable districts; drought- and flood-tolerant varieties; Shree Anna promotion of millets, which are drought-tolerant and nutrient-dense.
- Water: micro-irrigation under Per Drop More Crop; watershed treatment under WDC-PMKSY 2.0; Atal Bhujal Yojana.
- Risk transfer:PMFBY with satellite-based YES-TECH yield estimation.
- Emissions reduction in agriculture: alternate wetting and drying in paddy; neem-coated and nano urea; residue management instead of burning.
- AP instance:Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming (APCNF), run by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha, covers over 1.77 million farmers across 8,168 gram panchayats, with reported income gains of 38-66%, water savings up to 50% and emission reductions up to 46% per acre. It won the 2026 Food Planet Prize and demonstrates that resilience-building is achievable at the scale of millions rather than in pilots.

## Conclusion

Climate change affects agriculture through every channel at once — heat on the crop, uncertainty in the monsoon, scarcity in the aquifer, expansion of the pest range, stress on livestock and salinity in the delta — and its burden falls hardest on smallholders with the least capacity to absorb it. India’s response has moved from research to deployment through NICRA, PMFBY and micro-irrigation, and Andhra Pradesh’s APCNF shows that agroecological transition can operate at scale. The task now is convergence, so that a single farmer receives resilient seed, assured water, timely advisory and insurance as one package rather than as separate schemes.

- Global framework: the Koronivia Joint Work on Agriculture and the Sharm el-Sheikh joint work under the UNFCCC; FAO’s three-pillar climate-smart agriculture framework.

## Introduction

Climate changes through both natural forcings, which have operated throughout Earth’s history, and anthropogenic forcings, which dominate the present episode. Its effects extend across both living systems (biodiversity, health, agriculture) and non-living systems (glaciers, sea level, soils, oceans). Scientists track these changes through a range of indicators, of which the frozen archives of the cryosphere are among the most informative.

## (a) Causes of climate change

Natural causes - Volcanic eruptions — sulphate aerosols reflect sunlight, producing short-term cooling (Pinatubo, 1991); CO2 release is minor by comparison. - Solar variability — the roughly 11-year sunspot cycle and longer-term output changes; measured irradiance has been flat or declining while temperatures rose. - Milankovitch cycles — eccentricity, obliquity and precession, driving glacial-interglacial cycles over tens of thousands of years. -Ocean-atmosphere oscillations — ENSO, and the Pacific and Atlantic decadal oscillations, which redistribute heat and produce year-to-year variability around the trend. - Plate tectonics and continental drift — altering ocean circulation and albedo over geological time.

Anthropogenic causes - Greenhouse gas emissions — CO2 from fossil fuel combustion; methane from livestock, paddy fields and landfills; nitrous oxide from fertiliser; fluorinated gases from industry. - Deforestation and land-use change — removing sinks while releasing stored carbon. - Industrialisation and urbanisation — fossil energy use, cement calcination, and the urban heat island effect. - Agriculture — the second-largest emitting sector after energy in many economies. - Aerosols — a complicating factor: sulphate aerosols from industry actually mask some warming by reflecting sunlight, so air-quality improvements can unmask additional warming. Noting this shows genuine understanding.

## Effects on living systems (biotic)
- Biodiversity. Species ranges shift poleward and to higher altitudes; phenological mismatch occurs when flowering and pollinator emergence decouple. The IPBES Global Assessment (2019) estimated that around one million species are threatened with extinction, with climate change one of five direct drivers alongside land-use change, over-exploitation, pollution and invasive species.
- Human health. Heat mortality; expanded range of vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, chikungunya moving to higher altitudes and latitudes); water-borne disease after floods; malnutrition following crop failure; and mental health effects of displacement.
- Agriculture and food security. Yield reductions, altered sowing calendars, and reduced nutritional quality of grain under elevated CO2.
- Marine life. Coral bleaching from thermal stress; ocean acidification impairing shell and skeleton formation in molluscs, corals and plankton at the base of the marine food web.

## Effects on non-living systems (abiotic)
- Cryosphere. Glacial retreat in the Himalaya, ice sheet mass loss in Greenland and Antarctica, permafrost thaw releasing methane and destabilising ground.
- Sea level. Rising through thermal expansion of warming water and addition of meltwater; causing coastal inundation, erosion and saline ingress into delta aquifers and soils.
- Hydrological systems. Altered river regimes, glacial lake formation and GLOF risk, changed groundwater recharge.
- Land and soil. Desertification, accelerated erosion, salinisation, and loss of soil organic carbon.
- Ocean chemistry and circulation. Acidification; deoxygenation; and potential weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.

## (b) Indicators of climatic change
- **Type** — Examples · What they reveal
- **Atmospheric** — CO2 and methane concentration, global mean temperature, precipitation records · Direct measurement of forcing and response
- **Hydrological/oceanic** — Sea level, ocean heat content, ocean pH, salinity · Where most excess heat actually goes — the oceans absorb over 90%
- **Cryogenic** — Ice cores, glacier mass balance, sea-ice extent, permafrost temperature · Both current change and deep-time records
- **Biological (bioindicators)** — Phenology (flowering, migration timing), species range shifts, tree rings, coral growth bands, pollen records · Ecosystem response, and proxy records where instruments are absent

## Note on cryogenic indicators
- What they are: evidence drawn from the frozen components of the Earth system — ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, snow cover and permafrost.
- Ice cores — the most valuable climate archive. Cores from Antarctica and Greenland contain air bubbles trapped at the time the snow compacted, preserving actual samples of ancient atmosphere. Antarctic cores extend the record back roughly 800,000 years, allowing direct measurement of past CO2 and methane concentrations. The isotopic ratio of oxygen (¹⁸O/¹⁶O) in the ice itself serves as a thermometer, recording the temperature at which the snow originally fell. This dual record — gas composition and temperature from the same layer — is what established the tight historical coupling between CO2 and temperature, and why present CO2 levels are unprecedented in that entire span.
- Glacier mass balance — the net difference between accumulation and ablation; a sustained negative balance is among the clearest visible indicators of warming, and Himalayan glacier retreat has direct consequences for river flow.
- Sea-ice extent — Arctic summer minimum extent has declined markedly; it also drives the ice-albedo feedback, in which melting exposes darker ocean that absorbs more heat, accelerating further melting.
- Permafrost temperature and active-layer depth — record past and present warming, and thaw releases stored methane and CO2, constituting a positive feedback and a potential tipping element.
- Why cryogenic indicators are uniquely valuable: they are sensitive (ice responds sharply to small temperature changes near the melting point), integrative (recording conditions over long periods), and, in the case of ice cores, they are the only indicator providing direct physical samples of past atmospheres rather than inference.

## Conclusion

Climate change arises from natural forcings that have always operated and anthropogenic forcings that now dominate, affecting living systems through biodiversity loss, disease and food insecurity, and non-living systems through melting ice, rising seas and degraded soils. Indicators across the atmospheric, hydrological, cryogenic and biological domains allow these changes to be measured, and cryogenic evidence — particularly the 800,000-year ice core record — provides the long baseline against which present change is judged unprecedented.

## Value addition
- Attribution precision: the IPCC (established 1988 by WMO and UNEP) assesses climate science; IPBES (established 2012) assesses biodiversity and ecosystem services — the “one million species threatened” finding is from the IPBES Global Assessment (2019). UNEP publishes the Emissions Gap and Adaptation Gap reports; WMO publishes the State of the Global Climate.
- Proxy indicators for palaeoclimate: ice cores; dendrochronology (tree rings); coral growth bands; speleothems (cave deposits); ocean and lake sediment cores; pollen analysis; borehole temperature profiles.
- Feedbacks to name:ice-albedo (positive); water vapour (positive); permafrost methane (positive); cloud (uncertain sign); carbon sink saturation.
- Key numbers: CO2 concentration risen from about 280 ppm pre-industrial to over 420 ppm; global warming of roughly 1.1-1.3deg C above 1850-1900; the oceans have absorbed over 90% of the excess heat, which is why ocean heat content is a better warming indicator than surface air temperature alone.
- Indian monitoring institutions:IMD; Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune (which produced India’s first national climate change assessment report, 2020); NCPOR, Goa, for polar and cryospheric research and India’s Antarctic stations Maitri and Bharati; Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology for glacier monitoring; ISRO for satellite-based observation.
- AP relevance: sea-level rise and salinity ingress along the 1,053-km coast; delta vulnerability in the Godavari and Krishna; drought indicators in Rayalaseema; INCOIS ocean monitoring.
