## Introduction

Climate change alters the physical environment and the biological systems within it simultaneously — raising sea level, shifting the geographic ranges of species, and changing the behaviour of insect populations. The Brundtland Report (1987) was the document that first placed such changes within a coherent development framework, introducing the concept of sustainable development to global policy.

## (a)(i) Effects on nature generally

Ecosystem productivity, species composition and ecological interactions all shift. Ocean acidification — as absorbed CO2 forms carbonic acid — impairs calcification in corals, molluscs and plankton, weakening the base of the marine food web. Thermal stress causes coral bleaching, in which corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae and lose both colour and their principal energy source. Terrestrial ecosystems face altered fire regimes, forest dieback and loss of alpine habitat as warming pushes vegetation zones upslope with nowhere further to go.

## (a)(ii) Sea level fluctuations
- Two mechanisms.Thermal expansion — water expands as it warms, and this alone accounts for a large share of observed rise — and addition of meltwater from glaciers and ice sheets. Sea ice melting does not raise sea level, since floating ice already displaces its own mass; only land-based ice does. This distinction is frequently tested.
- Rate. Global mean sea level has risen by roughly 20 cm since 1900, and the rate has accelerated in recent decades.
- Consequences. Coastal inundation and erosion; saline ingress into aquifers and delta soils, damaging agriculture well inland of the shoreline; higher storm surge reaching further; and loss of mangroves and wetlands where they cannot migrate landward against embankments — “coastal squeeze”.
- Local variation. Sea-level rise is not uniform: land subsidence (from groundwater extraction and sediment compaction in deltas), ocean currents and gravitational effects mean regional rates differ substantially. India’s Godavari-Krishna delta and the Sundarbans face compounded risk from subsidence in addition to eustatic rise.

## (a)(iii) Plant and animal migration
- Range shifts. Species track their climatic niche poleward and upslope. The consequences differ by habitat: mountain species can move upslope only until they run out of mountain, producing “summit trapping” and elevated extinction risk for alpine and Himalayan endemics.
- Phenological shifts and mismatch. Timing of flowering, leaf-out, breeding and migration is advancing. The ecological damage arises from mismatch — when a migratory bird’s arrival no longer coincides with the insect peak its chicks depend on, because the two species cue on different signals (day length versus temperature). The species have not failed to adapt; they have adapted at different rates, which is the more precise and more interesting problem.
- Marine migration. Fish stocks shift toward cooler waters, redistributing catch between regions and creating fisheries governance disputes.
- Barriers to movement. Habitat fragmentation, agriculture and infrastructure block migration routes; species that could otherwise track their niche cannot reach it. This is why habitat corridors are a climate adaptation measure, not only a conservation one.
- Winners and losers. Generalists and invasives expand; specialists and endemics contract — producing biotic homogenisation, where ecosystems everywhere converge on the same adaptable species.

## (a)(iv) Changes in insect pests
- Range expansion. Warmer winters allow pests to survive at higher latitudes and altitudes, extending their permanent range — coffee berry borer moving upslope in coffee-growing highlands is the classic case, relevant to the Araku Valley coffee region of Andhra Pradesh.
- Increased voltinism. Warmer conditions shorten development time, allowing more generations per season — the single most consequential effect, since pest population growth is exponential in the number of generations.
- Altered overwintering survival, removing the winter mortality that previously reset populations each year.
- Indian instances:fall armyworm, first reported in India in 2018, spread across maize-growing States within months; whitefly, pink bollworm and brown planthopper outbreaks have been linked to warming and changed cropping patterns.
- Consequences: higher pesticide use, accelerating resistance through natural selection, raising input costs, harming pollinators and beneficial insects, and increasing residue in produce. Pollinators themselves face decline, which is an agricultural risk of a different kind.

## (b) The Brundtland Report — enumerated
- Formally titled Our Common Future, published in 1987 by the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), established by the UN General Assembly in 1983 and chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, then Prime Minister of Norway.
- Its central definition: sustainable development is “development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.”
- Two key concepts identified within that definition: the concept of “needs”, in particular the essential needs of the world’s poor, to which overriding priority should be given; and the idea of limitations imposed by the state of technology and social organisation on the environment’s ability to meet present and future needs.
- Main contents, enumerated:

linked environment and development as a single agenda rather than competing objectives;

identified poverty as both a cause and a consequence of environmental degradation;

addressed population and human resources, food security, species and ecosystems, energy, industry and the urban challenge;

examined the management of the global commons — oceans, Antarctica and outer space;

analysed peace, security and environment linkages;

proposed institutional and legal change, including reorientation of national institutions and strengthening of international cooperation.

- Its consequences: it directly prepared the ground for the Rio Earth Summit (1992), which produced Agenda 21, the Rio Declaration, the UNFCCC, the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Forest Principles — and, through that lineage, for the Millennium Development Goals and the 2030 Agenda with its 17 SDGs.
- Its enduring critique: the definition is deliberately open-ended, specifying no rule for resolving conflicts between present needs and future capacity — which is both why it achieved universal acceptance and why it has been criticised as too accommodating.

## Conclusion

Climate change operates on nature through the physical system — a rising and locally uneven sea level — and through the biological one, as species shift range, break their phenological synchrony with one another, and as insect pests gain both territory and generations. The Brundtland Report supplied the framework within which these changes are addressed as a development question rather than only an ecological one, and its formulation of intergenerational responsibility remains the foundation of the SDGs nearly four decades later.

## Value addition
- Ecological terminology that lifts this answer:range shift (poleward and upslope); phenological mismatch; summit trapping; voltinism (generations per year); biotic homogenisation; coastal squeeze; thermal expansion versus eustatic rise; zooxanthellae and coral bleaching.
- The sea-ice point examiners test: melting sea ice does not raise sea level (it already displaces its own mass); only land ice — glaciers and ice sheets — does. Thermal expansion accounts for a large share of observed rise.
- Brundtland Report facts:Our Common Future, 1987; World Commission on Environment and Development, constituted 1983; chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland; the “needs” and “limitations” concepts; led directly to the Rio Earth Summit (1992).
- Pest management responses:Integrated Pest Management; pest surveillance under the National Pest Surveillance System; biocontrol agents (Trichogramma, ladybird beetles); Bt technology with mandatory refuge requirements to slow resistance; pheromone traps; ICAR-NBAIR for agricultural insect resources.
- Adaptation for species movement:habitat corridors and connectivity; the wildlife corridors identified under Project Tiger and Project Elephant; assisted migration as a contested last-resort intervention; protected area network expansion under the “30 by 30” target of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
- AP-specific: sea-level rise and salinity ingress in the Godavari-Krishna delta; Coringa mangroves as a natural buffer facing coastal squeeze; coffee berry borer in Araku Valley; fall armyworm in AP’s maize belt; species range shifts in the Eastern Ghats.

Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024).*

Q67:
## Introduction

The National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), released in June 2008 by the Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change, is India’s foundational climate policy framework. Its organising principle is the pursuit of “co-benefits” — measures that advance development objectives while also yielding climate gains. This framing was deliberate: for a country with a large development deficit, climate action had to be justified on developmental grounds, not as a cost accepted for global benefit.

## Guiding principles
- Protecting the poor and vulnerable through an inclusive, sustainable development strategy.
- Achieving national growth objectives through a qualitative change in direction that also yields co-benefits.
- Deploying appropriate technologies for both adaptation and mitigation, extensively and at speed.
- Mobilising new and additional funding, and using market mechanisms alongside regulation.
- International cooperation on the basis of CBDR-RC and equity.

## Objectives
- Integrate climate concerns into national development planning across energy, water, agriculture, forestry, habitat and health.
- Strengthen adaptive capacity in climate-sensitive sectors and among vulnerable populations.
- Enhance energy security through efficiency and renewables.
- Build the scientific and institutional base for climate response.

## The eight National Missions — with their own targets
- National Solar Mission (2010). Originally 20 GW of grid-connected solar by 2022, revised in 2015 to 100 GW (60 GW utility-scale, 40 GW rooftop). Its central objective was grid parity — driving costs down until solar competed without subsidy.
- National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE). Operates the PAT (Perform, Achieve and Trade) scheme with tradable Energy Saving Certificates for designated energy-intensive consumers; also Standards and Labelling, and financing mechanisms for efficiency projects.
- National Mission on Sustainable Habitat. Energy efficiency in buildings through ECBC, urban waste management, public transport and urban resilience planning.
- National Water Mission. Five goals, including a 20% improvement in water use efficiency, comprehensive water databases, basin-level integrated management, and focus on over-exploited areas. Operational campaigns include Catch the Rain.
- National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem. Glacier monitoring, biodiversity conservation, and traditional knowledge and livelihoods in the Himalayan states.
- National Mission for a Green India (GIM). Targets improving forest quality on 5 million hectares and afforestation of another 5 million hectares, with enhanced ecosystem services and community-based forest management.
- National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA). Climate-resilient varieties, water-use efficiency, soil health, integrated farming and agro-forestry; implemented through components including Rainfed Area Development and the Soil Health Management scheme.
- National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change. Climate modelling, research networks, a Climate Change Knowledge Network, and support to institutions including IMD, IITM Pune and the IITs.

## The missions added later — the point most answers miss

In 2014-15 the framework was expanded beyond the original eight, with additional missions on health, coastal areas, waste-to-energy and wind energy. The National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health (NPCCHH), launched under the NHM in 2019, operationalises the health dimension.

## Recommendations and the implementation architecture
- State Action Plans on Climate Change (SAPCCs) — every State and UT has prepared one, aligning national missions with local vulnerability. Andhra Pradesh’s SAPCC prioritises cyclone and coastal resilience, drought management in Rayalaseema, and delta protection.
- Financing: the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC), the National Clean Energy Fund, sovereign green bonds, and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022.
- Integration with the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-30) and the SDGs.
- Reporting: Biennial Update Reports and National Communications to the UNFCCC, supported by a national greenhouse gas inventory.

## Assessment — what NAPCC has delivered

The record is uneven but substantial at the energy end. Solar capacity reached 150.26 GW as on 31 March 2026 and non-fossil capacity 283.46 GW, with India crossing 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its NDC target (MNRE). The PAT scheme has delivered measurable industrial energy savings. Progress has been slower on the adaptation missions — water, Himalayan ecosystem and sustainable habitat — where outcomes depend on State capacity and are harder to measure. The structural criticism is that NAPCC operates through existing ministries without independent budget or authority, so mission performance tracks the parent ministry’s priorities rather than climate objectives.

## Conclusion

NAPCC’s enduring contribution is conceptual: by framing climate action as co-beneficial with development, it made climate policy politically sustainable in a developing economy — and the subsequent success of solar demonstrates the framing was correct, since renewables are now chosen on cost. Its weakness is institutional, since the missions lack independent authority and the adaptation side has lagged the mitigation side. Strengthening SAPCC implementation and adaptation financing is the outstanding task.

## Value addition
- NAPCC essentials: released June 2008 by the Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change; organised around co-benefits; eight missions, later expanded with missions on health, coastal areas, waste-to-energy and wind.
- Get the targets right: JNNSM — 20 GW solar by 2022, revised to 100 GW in 2015; National Water Mission — 20% improvement in water use efficiency; Green India Mission — 5 million ha improved plus 5 million ha afforested. The 500 GW non-fossil by 2030 figure belongs to Panchamrit/NDC (COP26, 2021), not to NAPCC.
- Panchamrit (COP26, Glasgow, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% of energy requirements from renewables; one billion tonnes of avoided emissions by 2030; 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels; net zero by 2070.
- Financing and market instruments: NAFCC; National Clean Energy Fund; sovereign green bonds; Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (Energy Conservation Amendment Act, 2022) with BEE as administrator and Grid Controller of India as registry; the earlier PAT scheme as its precursor.
- International reporting obligations: National Communications, Biennial Update Reports and Biennial Transparency Reports to the UNFCCC; NDCs on a five-year ratchet; the Global Stocktake.
- AP-specific: the Andhra Pradesh SAPCC; APCNF contributing to the sustainable agriculture mission; the State’s Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 (160 GW) advancing the solar and wind missions; RTGS AWARE and the City Flood Alert system serving the strategic knowledge and disaster preparedness dimensions.

## Introduction

India is among the world’s most climate-vulnerable large economies for four structural reasons: a long coastline with dense delta populations, dependence on a single monsoon for most annual rainfall, a large agricultural workforce with limited buffers, and reliance on Himalayan glaciers for perennial river flow. Global temperature has risen roughly 1.1-1.3deg C above the 1850-1900 baseline (IPCC AR6), and the consequences for India are already measurable.

heat, wheat yield loss ; Rainfed Deccan --- drought ; East coast --- cyclones, surge ; Deltas --- salinity ingress ; Cities --- heat island, flooding .

## Sectoral impacts
- Agriculture and food security. Heat stress shortens grain-filling; ICAR estimates wheat yield declines of about 4-5% per 1deg C rise (the figure to use consistently). Erratic monsoon onset and withdrawal disrupt sowing; higher night temperatures reduce paddy yields by raising respiration losses. Pest ranges expand — fall armyworm spread across India’s maize belt within months of its 2018 arrival.
- Water resources. Himalayan glacial retreat alters flow in the Ganga and Brahmaputra; erratic rainfall and groundwater depletion produce simultaneous drought and flood exposure in the same year. Bundelkhand, Marathwada and Rayalaseema are the recurrent drought regions. NITI Aayog’s Composite Water Management Index has documented severe stress across a large share of districts.
- Coastal vulnerability. Sea level along India’s coast is rising at roughly 3 mm per year on average, with regional variation and additional land subsidence in deltas. Impacts include inundation, erosion, higher storm surge, and saline ingress into aquifers and farmland. Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata and the Godavari-Krishna delta are principal exposure zones.
- Cyclones. The Bay of Bengal generates the majority of India’s severe cyclones; warmer sea surface temperatures raise intensity and rapid-intensification frequency. Andhra Pradesh’s 1,053-km coastline and Odisha are the most exposed stretches — though improved forecasting and evacuation have cut cyclone mortality dramatically, which is itself an important adaptation success.
- Health. Heatwave mortality rising, particularly among outdoor workers; expanded range of dengue, malaria and chikungunya to higher altitudes and latitudes; water-borne disease after floods; and worsened air quality. Over 250 Heat Action Plans are now in place across cities and States, following the Ahmedabad model of 2013.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems. Coral bleaching in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep and the Gulf of Mannar; mangrove stress in the Sundarbans; increasing forest fire incidence — the Forest Survey of India’s alert system recorded high fire counts in several States including Andhra Pradesh; species range shifts in the Western and Eastern Ghats.
- Economy and livelihoods. Yield volatility, infrastructure damage, lost labour productivity from heat exposure, and climate-induced migration from drought-prone districts. The burden is regressive, falling on those with the least capacity to absorb it.

## The response architecture
- Policy: NAPCC with eight missions and State Action Plans on Climate Change; India’s NDC under the Paris Agreement and the Panchamrit commitments.
- Energy: non-fossil capacity 283.46 GW as on 31 March 2026; 50% non-fossil installed capacity reached June 2025, five years early (MNRE).
- Disaster preparedness: NDMA; over 250 Heat Action Plans; the National Heatwave Framework; the Common Alerting Protocol for multi-hazard early warning; Mission Mausam for improved forecasting.
- Water: Jal Jeevan Mission; Atal Bhujal Yojana; Catch the Rain; WDC-PMKSY 2.0.
- Agriculture:NICRA; PMFBY with YES-TECH; National Mission on Natural Farming — with APCNF in Andhra Pradesh covering over 1.77 million farmers as the largest State-level demonstration.
- Transport and industry:PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore, from October 2024, replacing FAME-II); PAT scheme; Carbon Credit Trading Scheme.
- Ecosystems: Green India Mission; MISHTI for mangroves; Amrit Dharohar for wetlands; CAMPA.

## Conclusion

Climate change affects India across every sector that matters to livelihoods — the monsoon, the aquifer, the coast, the harvest and public health — and its burden falls disproportionately on smallholders, coastal fishers and outdoor workers. India’s mitigation record is strong and ahead of schedule on non-fossil capacity, but adaptation remains the binding need, since the impacts already committed cannot be mitigated away. Heat action plans, cyclone early warning and climate-resilient agriculture are therefore not secondary measures but the primary line of defence.

## Value addition
- Use figures consistently: ICAR estimates wheat yield decline of about 4-5% per 1deg C; sea-level rise along India’s coast averaging about 3 mm per year; global warming of roughly 1.1-1.3deg C above 1850-1900 (IPCC AR6).
- Adaptation instruments to name: over 250 Heat Action Plans; National Heatwave Framework; Common Alerting Protocol; Mission Mausam (2024) for weather and climate forecasting; NDMA guidelines on heat, cyclone and flood; the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, co-founded by India.
- The cyclone success story worth citing: cyclone mortality in India has fallen sharply — from tens of thousands in the 1999 Odisha super cyclone to double or single digits in recent severe cyclones — through IMD forecasting, the Common Alerting Protocol and mass evacuation. It is India’s clearest demonstration that adaptation works.
- Assessment reports: IITM Pune produced India’s first national Climate Change Assessment Report (2020); IMD’s annual Statement on Climate of India; the Economic Survey’s climate chapter.
- Financing: NAFCC; sovereign green bonds; Loss and Damage Fund operationalised at COP28; the New Collective Quantified Goal agreed at COP29.
- AP-specific exposure: 1,053-km coastline with high cyclone frequency; salinity ingress in the Godavari-Krishna delta; Rayalaseema drought; heat stress in coastal paddy; RTGS AWARE and the City Flood Alert system with IIT Gandhinagar and APSDMA; APCNF as the State’s flagship adaptation programme.

## Introduction

Climate change and acid rain are both consequences of fossil fuel combustion, but they operate through different mechanisms and at different scales. Climate change is a global, long-term alteration of the Earth’s energy balance by greenhouse gases. Acid rain is a regional phenomenon caused by sulphur and nitrogen oxides, which is why it proved far more tractable to policy.

## (i) Climate change
- Definition: long-term shifts in temperature, precipitation and weather patterns, driven in the present period principally by anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions.
- Mechanism: greenhouse gases — CO2, methane, nitrous oxide, fluorinated gases — absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it, warming the lower atmosphere. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable (about +15deg C rather than −18deg C); the problem is its enhancement.
- Causes: fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, agriculture and livestock, industrial processes and waste.
- Evidence and scale: CO2 concentration has risen from about 280 ppm pre-industrially to over 420 ppm; global warming of roughly 1.1-1.3deg C above 1850-1900; the IPCC AR6 (2021) concluded it is “unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land”.
- Impacts: extreme weather, sea-level rise, glacial retreat, biodiversity loss, agricultural stress, health effects and displacement.
- Response:UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto Protocol (1997), Paris Agreement (2015); India’s NAPCC, Panchamrit commitments and net-zero-by-2070 pledge.

## (ii) Acid rain
- What it is. Precipitation — rain, snow, fog or dry deposition — with a pH below about 5.6, the natural pH of rainwater made slightly acidic by dissolved atmospheric CO2. Anything below this is termed acid deposition.
- The chemistry, stated properly:

Sulphur dioxide (SO2) from coal combustion, smelting and refining oxidises in the atmosphere to sulphur trioxide, which dissolves in water vapour to form sulphuric acid (H2SO₄). Nitrogen oxides (NOx) from high-temperature combustion in vehicles and power plants form nitric acid (HNO₃). Ammonia from agriculture contributes to secondary particulate formation and to nitrogen deposition. Deposition occurs as wet deposition (dissolved in precipitation) or dry deposition (particles and gases settling directly), the latter being significant in arid regions.

- Effects:

Aquatic ecosystems — lake and stream acidification kills fish eggs and aquatic invertebrates; below about pH 5 most fish species cannot reproduce. Aluminium leached from acidified soils enters water and is directly toxic to fish gills. Soils and forests — leaching of calcium, magnesium and potassium removes essential nutrients while mobilising toxic aluminium; combined with direct foliar damage, this causes forest dieback, historically severe in Central Europe and Scandinavia. Buildings and monuments — acid attacks calcium carbonate in marble and limestone, converting it to soluble gypsum, which flakes away. This is stone leprosy. Human health — the precursor gases and the fine sulphate and nitrate particles they form cause respiratory and cardiovascular harm; SO2 and NOx are among the eight pollutants monitored under India’s AQI. Materials — corrosion of metal structures, paint and infrastructure.

- The transboundary problem — why it required a treaty. Precursor gases travel hundreds of kilometres before depositing, so emissions in one country acidify lakes in another. Scandinavian lake acidification from British and continental European emissions was the case that produced the Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (1979) and its Helsinki (sulphur) and Sofia (NOx) protocols. Acid rain is the classic demonstration that some pollution problems cannot be solved nationally.
- The Indian dimension — the Taj Mahal. Emissions from refineries, foundries and vehicular traffic around Agra caused yellowing and pitting of the Taj Mahal’s marble. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (the Taj Trapezium case, 1996), the Supreme Court directed 292 industries in the Taj Trapezium Zone — an area of about 10,400 sq km around the monument — either to switch to natural gas or relocate, and prohibited coal and coke use. It remains India’s most cited environmental judgment on acid deposition and applies the precautionary principle explicitly.
- India’s broader control measures:FGD (flue gas desulphurisation) installation mandated at thermal power plants; BS-VI fuel with drastically reduced sulphur content from April 2020; SO2 and NOx limits under the National Ambient Air Quality Standards, 2009; NCAP; and CPCB’s continuous emission monitoring.
- Why acid rain was more tractable than climate change — the analytical point. Sulphur emissions come from a limited number of large point sources with available technological fixes (scrubbers, low-sulphur fuel), and the benefits accrue regionally to the same countries that bear the cost. Greenhouse gases come from every sector of the economy, the benefits are global and diffuse, and no equivalent end-of-pipe technology exists. Acid rain is therefore the encouraging precedent that also explains why climate change is harder.

## Conclusion

Climate change and acid rain share a source in fossil fuel combustion but differ fundamentally in scale and tractability. Acid rain was substantially controlled within decades through regional treaties and end-of-pipe technology, and India’s Taj Trapezium Zone directions show the same logic applied judicially. Climate change admits no such solution, because its sources are economy-wide and its benefits global — which is precisely why the acid rain precedent is instructive about institutions rather than about technology.

## Value addition
- The chemistry to state precisely: natural rainwater pH is about 5.6 owing to dissolved CO2; acid rain falls below this. SO2 –> SO₃ –> H2SO₄; NOx –> HNO₃. Wet versus dry deposition.
- The Taj Trapezium Zone: about 10,400 sq km across Agra, Firozabad, Mathura, Hathras and Etah districts in UP and Bharatpur in Rajasthan; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) directed 292 industries to switch to natural gas or relocate and banned coal and coke use; the case applied the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
- International regime:Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (CLRTAP, Geneva, 1979) with the Helsinki Protocol on sulphur (1985) and Sofia Protocol on NOx (1988); the US Acid Rain Program under the Clean Air Act Amendments (1990) pioneered cap-and-trade for SO2 — a mechanism later borrowed by carbon markets.
- Indian control measures: FGD mandates for thermal power stations; BS-VI fuel with sulphur reduced to 10 ppm; NAAQS limits for SO2 and NOx; NCAP; CPCB continuous emission monitoring; the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme, which includes rainwater pH monitoring at selected stations.
- Related phenomena to distinguish:acid rain (SO2/NOx, regional); ozone depletion (CFCs, stratospheric, global); photochemical smog (NOx + VOCs + sunlight –> ground-level ozone, urban); global warming (greenhouse gases, global). Examiners frequently test whether candidates keep these separate.
- AP relevance: industrial emissions around Visakhapatnam’s refinery and steel complex; coastal humidity accelerating material corrosion; monument exposure at Amaravati’s Buddhist heritage sites and Lepakshi.

## Introduction

State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) are statutory bodies constituted under Section 4 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and additionally empowered under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. They are the operative arm of environmental regulation, since almost all enforcement occurs at State level. The Environmental Clearance process under the EIA Notification, 2006 complements this by assessing projects before they are built.

## (a) Functions of the State Pollution Control Board
- Consent management — the principal instrument. SPCBs issue Consent to Establish (CTE) before construction and Consent to Operate (CTO) before commencement, renewable periodically. This is the operative control: no industry may lawfully function without a valid CTO, and its refusal or withdrawal is the SPCB’s most effective sanction.
- Enforcement of pollution laws. Regulating effluent discharge and stack emissions; laying down standards not less stringent than CPCB’s; inspecting premises; and taking action for violations.
- Planning comprehensive programmes for prevention, control and abatement of water and air pollution in the State, and securing their execution — including action plans for polluted river stretches identified by CPCB, and for non-attainment cities under NCAP.
- Monitoring and data management. Operating ambient air and water quality monitoring stations, including CAAQMS; receiving data from Online Continuous Emission and Effluent Monitoring Systems installed at major polluting industries — the shift from periodic inspection to continuous telemetry.
- Advisory functions. Advising the State Government on the siting of industries, on any matter concerning pollution prevention, and on the location of new industrial estates.
- Research, training and awareness. Investigating pollution problems, evaluating treatment technologies, training personnel, and conducting public awareness programmes.
- Statutory enforcement powers: issuing directions under Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act, including for closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, and for stoppage or regulation of electricity, water or other services — the powers that give SPCB orders practical force. SPCBs also prosecute offences and levy environmental compensation.
- Waste rule administration: authorisation and monitoring under the Hazardous Waste, Bio-Medical Waste, Solid Waste, Plastic Waste, E-Waste and Battery Waste Rules.
- Air quality declarations: identifying and notifying air pollution control areas under the Air Act.

Andhra Pradesh: the AP Pollution Control Board (APPCB), headquartered at Vijayawada, discharges these functions, with particular attention to the Visakhapatnam industrial belt, coastal aquaculture effluent, and pharmaceutical clusters.

## (b) Procedure for Environmental Clearance under the EIA Notification, 2006

issues ToR) --> PUBLIC CONSULTATION (SPCB conducts hearing) --> APPRAISAL (EAC/SEAC recommends) --> DECISION (MoEFCC or SEIAA) .

Categorisation, which precedes everything - Category A — larger projects and those in specified locations; appraised by the Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) and cleared by MoEFCC at the Centre. - Category B — appraised by the State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) and cleared by the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA).

Stage 1 — Screening. Applies only to Category B projects. The SEAC determines whether an EIA report is required, classifying the project as B1 (EIA required) or B2 (EIA not required). Category A projects require EIA automatically and skip this stage.

Stage 2 — Scoping. The EAC or SEAC determines the Terms of Reference (ToR) — the specific environmental concerns the EIA study must address, based on the application, site visit where necessary, and any other information. The ToR is normally conveyed within sixty days.

Stage 3 — Public Consultation. Two components: a public hearing at or near the site, conducted district-wise by the State Pollution Control Board or UT Pollution Control Committee, and written responses from other concerned persons having a plausible stake. The applicant then addresses the concerns raised and revises the draft EIA report accordingly. Certain categories are exempt — modernisation of irrigation projects, projects within approved industrial estates, expansion of roads and highways not requiring further land acquisition, specified building and township projects, all Category B2 projects, and projects concerning national defence and security or other strategic considerations.

Stage 4 — Appraisal. The EAC or SEAC scrutinises the final EIA/EMP report, the outcome of public consultation and all supporting documents, and makes a categorical recommendation to the regulatory authority for grant or rejection, with terms and conditions. The applicant may be heard.

Decision and after. MoEFCC or SEIAA grants or rejects clearance, normally within forty-five days of receiving the recommendation. Clearance carries conditions, and the project proponent must submit half-yearly compliance reports. The PARIVESH portal now handles submission, tracking and monitoring end-to-end, giving each stage a timestamp and an identified decision-maker.

Appeals lie to the National Green Tribunal under the NGT Act, 2010.

## Conclusion

SPCBs and the EIA process operate at two different points in time: EIA assesses whether a project should proceed and on what conditions, while the SPCB’s consent regime governs whether it may continue operating. Together they form India’s principal preventive and continuing controls on industrial pollution. Their effectiveness depends less on the adequacy of the law — which is substantial — than on institutional capacity, since SPCBs are frequently under-staffed relative to the number of units they must inspect.

## Value addition
- Statutory basis: SPCBs constituted under Section 4 of the Water Act, 1974; further empowered by the Air Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; CPCB constituted in September 1974 under the Water Act. Directions issued under Section 33A (Water Act) and Section 31A (Air Act).
- The consent mechanism:Consent to Establish (CTE) before construction and Consent to Operate (CTO) before commencement; industries classified Red, Orange, Green and White by pollution potential, with White category exempt from consent requirements — a categorisation examiners like.
- EIA institutional map: EAC and MoEFCC for Category A; SEAC and SEIAA for Category B; SPCB conducts the public hearing; PARIVESH portal for submission and tracking; appeals to the National Green Tribunal.
- EIA history: environmental clearance made mandatory by the EIA Notification, 1994, replaced by the EIA Notification, 2006 which introduced the A/B categorisation and decentralised Category B to States; the draft EIA Notification 2020 proposed post-facto clearance and expanded exemptions, drew substantial public objection and was not notified.
- Principles applied by the NGT and courts:polluter pays, precautionary principle, public trust doctrine, sustainable development — read into Indian environmental law through Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) and the M.C. Mehta line of cases.
- AP-specific:APPCB, Vijayawada; environmental clearance disputes over thermal power siting in Srikakulam (Sompeta, Kakarapalli); Visakhapatnam industrial cluster monitoring; aquaculture effluent regulation around Kolleru.

## Introduction

Urban flooding is the inundation of built-up areas by rainfall that exceeds the drainage system’s capacity. It differs fundamentally from riverine flooding: it develops within hours rather than days, is caused by local rainfall rather than upstream catchment conditions, and is largely self-inflicted — the product of how a city has been built rather than of the rain alone. Urbanisation can increase peak runoff by several multiples for the same rainfall, simply by replacing absorbent surfaces with impermeable ones.

Why urban floods recur — the causes

Hydrological and climatic - Short-duration, high-intensity rainfall is increasing with warming, since a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture. Drainage systems designed for historical rainfall intensities are overwhelmed by cloudbursts that deliver a month’s rain in hours. - Coastal cities face compound flooding — high tide or storm surge preventing drainage discharge while rainfall continues, as in Chennai and Mumbai.

Planning and land-use - Encroachment of natural drains, lakes and floodplains — the primary cause. Cities were historically built around drainage networks; construction over them removes the pathway water must take, and water then follows that pathway anyway, through streets and houses. Bengaluru’s rajakaluves, Chennai’s Pallikaranai marsh, Hyderabad’s lake system and Vijayawada’s Budameru are all instances. - Concretisation and loss of permeable surface, eliminating infiltration and groundwater recharge simultaneously — the same cities flood in monsoon and face water scarcity in summer. - Development in low-lying areas without adequate plinth levels or flood-risk zoning.

Infrastructural - Under-designed and outdated drainage, often built for a much smaller population and lower rainfall design standard. - Silting and solid waste blockage — plastic and construction debris clogging drains is a leading proximate cause of localised flooding; desilting is frequently incomplete or poorly timed. - Obstructive infrastructure — roads, metros and flyovers built across natural flow paths without adequate cross-drainage.

Governance - Fragmented institutional responsibility — municipal corporation, development authority, irrigation department, water board and railways each control parts of the drainage system with no single accountable agency. - Absence of updated drainage master plans and of enforcement against encroachment. - Weak early warning at ward level and limited real-time water-level monitoring.

Government measures

National - NDMA Guidelines on Management of Urban Flooding (2010) — India was among the first countries to issue a dedicated urban flooding guideline, covering drainage design standards, watershed-based planning, early warning and the Urban Flooding Cell concept. - AMRUT 2.0 — storm-water drainage, water body rejuvenation and rainwater harvesting. - Smart Cities Mission — Integrated Command and Control Centres with real-time rainfall and water-level sensors. - Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain and Central Ground Water Board recharge plans. - Central Water Commission flood forecasting, and IMD nowcasting with Doppler radar; Mission Mausam (2024) to improve short-range prediction. - National Disaster Mitigation Fund and the XV Finance Commission’s dedicated urban flood mitigation allocation for selected metropolitan cities.

City-specific - BRIMSTOWAD (Mumbai) — drain widening, pumping stations and desilting following the 2005 deluge. - C-FLOWS (Chennai) — an integrated flood warning system developed with NCCR, modelling rainfall, river flow and coastal interaction. - KEIP (Kolkata) — drainage and canal rejuvenation. - Bengaluru — rajakaluve encroachment removal and lake restoration. - AP instance — Vijayawada, September 2024. Exceptionally heavy rainfall caused the Budameru rivulet to breach and inundate large parts of Vijayawada, affecting several lakh residents and requiring one of the State’s largest urban rescue operations. The event was widely attributed to encroachment of the Budameru’s course and floodplain combined with inadequate diversion capacity — the textbook mechanism of urban flooding. The response has included Budameru widening and diversion works, and the State’s City Flood Alert system, developed by RTGS with APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar, now provides 48-hour rainfall outlooks and six-hour flash-flood warnings, beginning with Vijayawada.

Way forward

Watershed-based rather than administrative-boundary-based drainage planning; blue-green infrastructure — restoring wetlands, permeable paving, bioswales and urban forests, since a restored wetland is cheaper than an equivalent drain; mandatory rainwater harvesting; a single accountable agency for urban drainage; real-time ward-level early warning; and enforcement against floodplain encroachment, which is ultimately the only permanent solution.

## Conclusion

Urban floods recur because Indian cities have systematically removed the surfaces that absorb water and the channels that carry it away, while rainfall has grown more intense. The Vijayawada floods of 2024 illustrate the pattern precisely — a natural drain encroached, then overwhelmed. Engineering responses such as BRIMSTOWAD and C-FLOWS are necessary but treat the symptom; the durable solution is to restore the city’s natural hydrology and to make one agency accountable for it.

## Value addition
- The mechanism to state: urbanisation replaces permeable surface with impermeable, raising the runoff coefficient sharply; the resulting hydrograph peaks higher and earlier, so drains designed for a natural catchment fail even without any increase in rainfall.
- NDMA Guidelines on Urban Flooding (2010): recommended Urban Flooding Cells, watershed as the planning unit, a National Hydro-meteorological Network, use of Doppler radar, and design standards for urban drainage.
- City systems to name:BRIMSTOWAD (Mumbai); C-FLOWS (Chennai, with NCCR); KEIP (Kolkata); Bengaluru lake and rajakaluve restoration;

Vijayawada City Flood Alert (RTGS, APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar).

- Landmark Indian urban floods: Mumbai (2005), Chennai (2015), Kerala (2018), Hyderabad (2020), Bengaluru (2022), Vijayawada (2024), Delhi (2023).
- Blue-green infrastructure concepts:sponge city; Sustainable Urban Drainage Systems (SUDS); permeable paving; bioswales and rain gardens; wetland restoration as flood buffer; Amrit Dharohar for wetlands; Nagar Van Yojana for urban forests.
- Institutional point worth making: urban drainage in most Indian cities has no single owner — responsibility is split across the municipal corporation, development authority, irrigation department, water board and railways. Fragmentation, more than funding, explains why master plans go unimplemented.
- AP-specific: Vijayawada-Budameru (2024) and subsequent diversion works; Visakhapatnam’s coastal drainage and cyclone exposure; Kolleru Lake’s role as a natural flood buffer between the Krishna and Godavari deltas, compromised by aquaculture encroachment.

## Introduction

A hazard is a potentially damaging physical event; a disaster occurs only when that hazard strikes a vulnerable and exposed population, causing losses beyond the community’s coping capacity. The distinction is not semantic: an earthquake in an uninhabited desert is a hazard that produces no disaster, while an identical earthquake beneath a city with poor construction produces catastrophe. India’s coastline of about 7,500 km, with dense settlement and economic activity, is exposed to the full range of coastal hazards.

## (a) Hazard versus disaster
- **Hazard** — Disaster
- **A potentially damaging physical event, phenomenon or human activity** — The actual occurrence causing widespread human, material, economic or environmental loss
- **Exists as a possibility** — Is an event that has occurred
- **Natural (earthquake, cyclone) or human-made (chemical spill, industrial accident)** — Results when a hazard meets vulnerability and exposure
- **Cannot usually be eliminated** — Can be prevented or mitigated by reducing vulnerability
- **Example: a cyclone forming over the Bay of Bengal** — Example: the 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone, with about 10,000 deaths

## The risk equation — the conceptual key

## Risk = Hazard x Exposure x Vulnerability ÷ Capacity

Since the hazard itself is largely fixed, disaster risk reduction works on the other three variables — moving people and assets out of harm’s way (exposure), improving construction and livelihoods (vulnerability), and strengthening institutions and preparedness (capacity). This is why the same cyclone that killed 10,000 in 1999 kills a handful today.

Definition under law: the Disaster Management Act, 2005 defines a disaster as a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence arising from natural or man-made causes, resulting in substantial loss of life, human suffering, or damage to property or environment, of such nature or magnitude as to be beyond the coping capacity of the affected community.

## Natural disasters to which coastal areas are prone

Meteorological and hydrological - Tropical cyclones — India’s east coast, especially the Bay of Bengal, generates the majority of severe cyclones. Associated hazards: violent wind, torrential rain and, most lethally, storm surge, which historically causes the largest share of cyclone deaths. - Storm surge and coastal inundation, amplified where surge coincides with high tide and in funnel-shaped bays. - Coastal and urban flooding, including compound flooding where drainage is blocked by high sea level. - Heavy rainfall and lightning during monsoon and cyclone events.

Geological and oceanographic - Tsunamis — generated by undersea earthquakes, landslides or volcanic activity. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, from the M 9.1 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake, killed over 2,00,000 people across the region and more than 10,000 in India, with heavy loss in Tamil Nadu,

Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. - Coastal erosion — a slow-onset hazard removing land and displacing settlements; a significant share of India’s coastline is under erosion, per National Centre for Coastal Research shoreline change assessments. - Earthquakes and liquefaction in saturated coastal soils.

Slow-onset and anthropogenic - Sea-level rise and saline ingress into aquifers and farmland. - Land subsidence in deltas from groundwater extraction and sediment compaction, compounding relative sea-level rise. - Harmful algal blooms, oil spills and industrial accidents at ports.

## (b) India’s Tsunami Warning System
- Genesis. Before 2004, India had no tsunami warning capability. The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) was established at INCOIS, Hyderabad, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, and became operational in October 2007.
- Detection network:

A network of seismic stations (national and global) to detect undersea earthquakes and determine location, depth and magnitude within minutes. Bottom Pressure Recorders (BPRs) on the ocean floor, which detect the passage of a tsunami wave through minute pressure changes in the water column above — the confirming instrument, since not every undersea earthquake generates a tsunami. Tide gauges along the coast and on islands, measuring actual sea-level change. Satellite communication links (INSAT) transmitting data in real time.

- Modelling and decision support. Pre-computed tsunami propagation scenarios for a database of possible source earthquakes allow ITEWC to issue coastal-segment-wise warnings — rather than a blanket coastal alert — within about 10 minutes of a qualifying earthquake.
- Warning levels:Watch, Alert and Warning, graded by expected wave height and arrival time, disseminated to MHA, NDMA, State authorities, the Coast Guard, ports, and directly to communities via SMS, email, fax, sirens and coastal radio; NavIC messaging extends reach to fishermen at sea beyond mobile coverage.
- International role — worth emphasising. ITEWC is recognised by UNESCO’s Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission as a Tsunami Service Provider for the Indian Ocean region, providing warnings not only to India but to more than two dozen Indian Ocean countries. India therefore moved within a decade from having no capability to providing the service regionally.
- Community preparedness: the IOC-UNESCO Tsunami Ready recognition programme has certified coastal villages in India — including in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh — for meeting community preparedness indicators, the first such recognitions in the Indian Ocean region.

Supporting institutional framework:Disaster Management Act, 2005 creating NDMA, SDMAs and DDMAs; NDRF for response; NIDM for training; Coastal Regulation Zone notifications restricting construction in vulnerable zones; and mangrove restoration under MISHTI, since mangroves measurably attenuate surge and wave energy.

## Conclusion

The hazard-disaster distinction is the foundation of modern disaster management: since hazards cannot be prevented, risk reduction must operate on exposure, vulnerability and capacity. India’s coastal record demonstrates that this works — the same Bay of Bengal that produced 10,000 deaths in 1999 now produces cyclones with minimal mortality, and a country with no tsunami warning capability in 2004 became a regional Tsunami Service Provider within three years. The remaining vulnerabilities are slow-onset — erosion, sea-level rise and subsidence — which early warning cannot address.

## Value addition
- Correct statutory citation: the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (not 2004), enacted following the December 2004 tsunami; created NDMA (chaired by the Prime Minister), SDMAs (chaired by Chief Ministers), DDMAs, NDRF, NIDM and the National Disaster Response Fund.
- The risk equation: Risk = Hazard x Exposure x Vulnerability ÷ Capacity. Disaster risk reduction targets the last three because the first is fixed.
- ITEWC facts: established at INCOIS, Hyderabad; operational October 2007; warnings within about 10 minutes; network of seismic stations, Bottom Pressure Recorders, tide gauges and satellite links; recognised by IOC-UNESCO as a Tsunami Service Provider for the Indian Ocean; Tsunami Ready community certification in Indian coastal villages.
- Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-30): four priorities — understanding disaster risk; strengthening governance; investing in resilience; enhancing preparedness for “Build Back Better”. India also co-founded the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) in 2019.
- India’s cyclone record — the citable success: 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone, about 10,000 deaths; recent severe cyclones (Phailin 2013, Fani 2019, Amphan 2020, Biparjoy June 2023) with mortality in single or double digits, through IMD forecasting, the Common Alerting Protocol, cyclone shelters and mass evacuation.
- Coastal protection instruments:Coastal Regulation Zone notifications; the National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project; multipurpose cyclone shelters; mangrove restoration under MISHTI; the National Centre for Coastal Research for shoreline change assessment.
- AP-specific: 1,053-km coastline; 2004 tsunami deaths in Krishna, Guntur, Prakasam and Nellore districts; frequent severe cyclones on the Andhra coast; Coringa mangroves as natural surge buffer; APSDMA; RTGS AWARE and City Flood Alert; Tsunami Ready certified villages.

## Introduction

The Chipko Movement, which began in 1973 in the Garhwal Himalaya, was a non-violent forest conservation movement in which villagers — especially women — embraced trees to prevent commercial felling. Chipko means “to embrace”. It became a defining example of grassroots environmentalism and of what has been called the “environmentalism of the poor” — conservation driven by livelihood dependence rather than by wilderness aesthetics.

## (a) The Chipko Movement

Origin and context. The movement arose in Chamoli district (then Uttar Pradesh, now Uttarakhand) in April 1973, when the Forest Department allotted ash trees to a sporting goods company while denying the same trees to the local Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh (DGSS) cooperative for making agricultural implements. The immediate grievance was therefore about access and equity, not preservation for its own sake. Underlying it was the devastating Alaknanda flood of 1970, which villagers linked to deforestation of the catchment.

Leadership and the slogan - Chandi Prasad Bhatt, founder of the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh, organised the first actions and represented the movement’s livelihood-and-local-industry strand — arguing that forests should serve local needs, not that they should be untouched. - Gaura Devi led the movement’s most celebrated action: on 26 March 1974, with 27 women of Reni village, she confronted loggers who had arrived while the village men were away, and prevented the felling by physically guarding the trees. This is the moment the movement is remembered by. - Sunderlal Bahuguna carried the movement to national and international attention through long foot-marches across the Himalaya, and represented its ecological-preservation strand. He coined the slogan “Ecology is permanent economy”, arguing that environmental protection is not a cost to the economy but its precondition. The movement’s other well-known formulation asks what forests bear — soil, water and pure air — rather than resin and timber.

Impact - Policy: the Government of India imposed a fifteen-year ban on green felling above 1,000 metres in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh in 1980, and the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 was enacted the same year, requiring central approval for diversion of forest land. - Institutional: it strengthened the case for community forest management, feeding into Joint Forest Management from 1990 and eventually into the Forest Rights Act, 2006. - Women’s agency: the movement demonstrated that women, as the primary collectors of fuel, fodder and water, had the most direct stake in forest survival — becoming a founding reference for ecofeminism in India. - Replication: it directly inspired the Appiko Movement (1983) in Karnataka, led by Pandurang Hegde — “appiko” being the Kannada equivalent of “chipko”. - Global recognition: Chipko is internationally cited as a model of non-violent ecological resistance; Bhatt received the Ramon Magsaysay Award (1982) and the Gandhi Peace Prize (2013), and Bahuguna the Padma Vibhushan (2009).

## (b) Medicinal herbs and plants
- The resource base. India has an exceptional endowment — of the order of 7,000-8,000 plant species used medicinally, drawn from the Himalaya, Western and Eastern Ghats, and forest tracts. This underpins Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy and Sowa-Rigpa, and India is among the world’s largest exporters of medicinal plant material.
- Important species and uses:

Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) — adaptogenic and antimicrobial;

Neem (Azadirachta indica) — antiseptic and biopesticide;

Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) — adaptogen, stress and immunity;

Aloe vera — dermatological and digestive;

Turmeric (Curcuma longa) — anti-inflammatory and antioxidant, with curcumin as the active principle; India secured revocation of a US turmeric wound-healing patent, a landmark traditional knowledge case; Sarpagandha (Rauwolfia serpentina) — source of reserpine for hypertension; Isabgol (psyllium), Brahmi, Guggul, Shatavari, Amla, Giloy.

- Government framework:

National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB), under the Ministry of AYUSH, promotes cultivation, conservation, quality standards and market linkage. CSIR-CIMAP (Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants, Lucknow) leads research; the CSIR Aroma Mission promotes aromatic crop cultivation on rain-fed and degraded land — its best-known outcome being the “Purple Revolution” through lavender in Bhaderwah, Jammu & Kashmir.

Medicinal Plants Conservation Areas and herbal gardens; support for cultivation to reduce pressure on wild collection.

Access and Benefit Sharing under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023), implementing the Nagoya Protocol — so that commercial users of biological resources and associated traditional knowledge share benefits with source communities. The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), a CSIR-AYUSH initiative documenting traditional formulations to prevent their wrongful patenting abroad — the instrument that resolved the turmeric and neem patent disputes.

- Challenges: over-harvesting from the wild and consequent species depletion; adulteration and quality standardisation; benefit-sharing with tribal collectors, who capture a small share of the final value; and habitat loss.
- AP relevance: the Eastern Ghats and Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve are rich in medicinal flora, including red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus), endemic to Andhra Pradesh and heavily poached; Araku Valley agroforestry combines coffee with medicinal and aromatic species; tribal communities of the Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam districts hold substantial ethnobotanical knowledge, making ABS implementation directly consequential in the State.

## Conclusion

Chipko established a principle that has shaped Indian environmental policy since: that forest conservation succeeds when the people who depend on the forest are its protectors rather than its adversaries — a principle now embedded in Joint Forest Management and the Forest Rights Act. Medicinal plants illustrate the same logic from the other direction: their conservation depends on cultivation and fair benefit-sharing rather than on prohibition, since the communities holding the knowledge must have a stake in the resource surviving.

## Value addition
- Chipko chronology: 1970 Alaknanda flood; April 1973 first protest at Mandal, Chamoli; 26 March 1974 Reni village action led by Gaura Devi; 1980 fifteen-year ban on green felling above 1,000 m in UP Himalaya and enactment of the Forest Conservation Act, 1980.
- The two strands:Chandi Prasad Bhatt — forests for local livelihood and village industry; Sunderlal Bahuguna — forests for ecological function, slogan “Ecology is permanent economy”. Noting this internal difference is a mark of depth.
- Other Indian environmental movements:Bishnoi (1730s, Amrita Devi, Khejarli — 363 lives lost protecting khejri trees); Silent Valley (1970s-80s, KSSP and Sugathakumari — project cancelled, National Park declared 1985); Jungle Bachao Andolan (1980s, Singhbhum — against replacement of sal with teak); Appiko (1983, Pandurang Hegde, Karnataka); Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar).
- Medicinal plant institutions:National Medicinal Plants Board (Ministry of AYUSH); CSIR-CIMAP Lucknow; CSIR Aroma Mission and the Purple Revolution; Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL); Medicinal Plants Conservation Areas.
- Landmark traditional knowledge cases: revocation of the turmeric wound-healing patent (US) and the neem fungicide patent (European Patent Office) — both cited as vindicating the TKDL approach; the basmati case as the third in the standard set.
- Legal framework:Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023) with Access and Benefit Sharing, National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and Biodiversity Management Committees; the Nagoya Protocol.
- AP-specific:red sanders, endemic to the Seshachalam hills and subject to severe poaching pressure and CITES listing; Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve; Araku Valley agroforestry; ethnobotanical knowledge in the Eastern Ghats tribal districts.

## Introduction

Social forestry is the practice of raising trees on non-forest land — village commons, farmlands, roadsides, canal banks and wastelands — to meet local needs for fuelwood, fodder, small timber and minor forest produce, thereby relieving pressure on natural forests. Dams and reservoirs, by contrast, deliver water and power at the cost of substantial ecological and social disruption. Both illustrate the central theme of development versus environment.

(a) Types of social forestry

The concept was introduced in India on the recommendation of the National Commission on Agriculture (1976), which classified it into:

- Farm forestry. Trees raised by farmers on their own agricultural land, on bunds and field boundaries, either for their own use (non-commercial farm forestry) or for sale (commercial farm forestry). Advantage: supplementary income, windbreak effect, soil stabilisation and, where nitrogen-fixing species are used, improved soil fertility. Poplar in Punjab-Haryana and eucalyptus and casuarina in peninsular India, including coastal Andhra Pradesh, are the standard examples.
- Community forestry. Trees raised on community land — village commons and panchayat land — with the produce shared by the community. Advantage: meets the fuelwood and fodder needs of the landless, who have no farm on which to plant. Its documented weakness: benefit-sharing disputes and unclear tenure over commons frequently undermine it.
- Extension forestry. Planting along linear features — roadsides, canal banks, railway lines, and on degraded and barren land. Advantage: uses land with no competing use; provides shade, dust and noise attenuation, and canal-bank stabilisation.
- Agroforestry. Deliberate integration of trees with crops and/or livestock on the same land unit — including alley cropping, silvopasture and home gardens. Advantage: the most productive form, since it yields wood, fodder, fruit and crops simultaneously while improving soil organic matter and providing climate resilience. India adopted a National Agroforestry Policy in 2014 — the first country to do so.

Advantages of social forestry overall

- Relieves extraction pressure on natural forests, which is its founding purpose.
- Supplies fuelwood, fodder, small timber and NTFP locally, reducing collection drudgery — which falls mainly on women.
- Supplementary rural income and employment; raw material for small industry.
- Environmental services: soil conservation and erosion control, groundwater recharge, windbreak and shelterbelt effects, carbon sequestration, and microclimate moderation.
- Contributes to national commitments — the National Mission for a Green India, India’s NDC target of an additional 2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent carbon sink by 2030, and the National Forest Policy target of 33% forest and tree cover.

The honest critique — worth including

India’s social forestry programmes of the 1980s achieved large planting numbers but attracted a well-documented criticism: commercial farm forestry with fast-growing exotics (eucalyptus) displaced food crops on good land and produced pulpwood for industry rather than fuelwood and fodder for the poor — the opposite of the intended distributional effect. Meanwhile community and extension forestry on marginal land, which would have served the landless, was under-resourced. The lesson is that species choice and land category determine who benefits, and a scheme judged only by seedlings planted can miss its own objective entirely.

(b) Parameters for constructing a dam and reservoir

Hydrological parameters - Catchment area, long-term inflow and runoff records, and rainfall pattern. - Design flood — the peak flood the spillway must safely pass, derived from probable maximum precipitation; under-designed spillways are the leading cause of dam failure. - Reservoir storage capacity and yield relative to demand; evaporation losses. - Sedimentation rate, which determines the reservoir’s useful life — a critical Indian issue, since many reservoirs have lost substantial capacity to silt faster than designed.

Geological and geotechnical parameters - Foundation rock strength, permeability and bearing capacity. - Seismicity of the site and zoning under IS 1893; the risk of reservoir-triggered seismicity, as at Koyna. - Watertightness of the reservoir basin (avoiding leakage through permeable strata) and slope stability of the reservoir rim, since large landslides into a reservoir can generate overtopping waves. - Availability of suitable construction material nearby.

Engineering and topographic parameters - A narrow gorge with a wide upstream valley — the ideal configuration, minimising dam length while maximising storage. - Dam type selected to suit site conditions: gravity, arch, buttress or embankment. - Spillway design and energy dissipation; outlet works, penstocks and powerhouse layout. - Provision for fish passage, sediment flushing and environmental flow releases.

Socio-environmental and economic parameters - Extent of submergence — land, settlements, forest and agricultural area lost. - Displacement, and the resettlement and rehabilitation plan; requirements under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, and consent requirements under PESA and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 in Scheduled Areas. - Environmental clearance under the EIA Notification, 2006, with public consultation; forest clearance under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980; wildlife clearance where protected areas are affected. - Cost-benefit analysis, including downstream effects, and dam safety obligations under the Dam Safety Act, 2021.

Environmental impacts of dams

Adverse: - Submergence of forest, farmland and habitat; loss of biodiversity, including endemic riverine species. - Displacement of communities, disproportionately tribal, with historically poor rehabilitation records. - Fragmentation of river continuity — blocking fish migration and interrupting sediment transport, causing downstream channel erosion and delta starvation and coastal erosion, since deltas require sediment to keep pace with sea-level rise. - Reduced environmental flows downstream, degrading river ecology and estuarine salinity balance. - Waterlogging and salinisation in command areas from over-irrigation. - Methane emissions from decomposition of submerged vegetation in tropical reservoirs — reservoirs are not emission-free. - Reservoir-triggered seismicity, as at Koyna. - Health effects — expansion of vector habitat for malaria and schistosomiasis.

Beneficial: - Irrigation supporting food security; hydropower as dispatchable low-carbon generation; pumped storage, increasingly vital for firming variable renewables; flood moderation; drinking and industrial water supply; navigation and fisheries.

AP instance: the Polavaram multipurpose project on the Godavari — a national project intended to deliver irrigation, drinking water, hydropower and Godavari-Krishna river linkage — illustrates the full parameter set: substantial submergence including tribal habitations across State boundaries, extensive rehabilitation obligations, forest and environmental clearance requirements, and complex engineering including one of the world’s largest spillway discharge capacities. Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam on the Krishna are the State’s other major impoundments, both relevant to the reservoir-triggered seismicity question.

## Conclusion

Social forestry and large dams represent two opposite approaches to the development-environment question: one distributed, low-cost and community-based, the other centralised, capital-intensive and transformative. The record suggests each succeeds under specific conditions — social forestry when species and land category are chosen to benefit the intended group rather than industry, and dams when submergence, rehabilitation and environmental flows are treated as design parameters rather than as afterthoughts.

## Value addition
- Social forestry classification (National Commission on Agriculture, 1976): farm forestry, community forestry, extension forestry, agroforestry. India adopted the world’s first National Agroforestry Policy in 2014.
- Related programmes:National Mission for a Green India; CAMPA and e-Green Watch; Nagar Van Yojana for urban forests; the Sub-Mission on Agroforestry; MISHTI for mangroves; Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam.
- The eucalyptus critique — name it: commercial farm forestry with fast-growing exotics served pulp industry demand rather than local fuelwood and fodder needs, and in places displaced food crops; the distributional lesson is that species choice determines beneficiary.
- Dam classifications: by purpose (single or multipurpose); by structure (gravity, arch, buttress, embankment/earthfill); by height (large dams defined by ICOLD criteria). India has among the largest numbers of large dams in the world.
- Dam Safety Act, 2021: created the National Dam Safety Authority and National Committee on Dam Safety, with State Dam Safety Organisations; mandates regular inspection, emergency action plans and safety reviews — enacted because a large share of India’s dams are over fifty years old.
- Concepts to name:environmental flow; sedimentation and reservoir life; delta starvation and consequent coastal erosion; reservoir-triggered seismicity; rehabilitation and resettlement; cumulative impact assessment for cascades of dams on a single river.
- AP-specific:Polavaram on the Godavari (submergence, inter-State rehabilitation, spillway scale); Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam on the Krishna; casuarina and eucalyptus farm forestry along the Andhra coast; Vana Samrakshana Samithis as the State’s JFM institutions.

Sources used: ISRO and PIB on NISAR (GSLV-F16, 30 July 2025), INSAT-3D/3DR/3DS, MOSDAC, Bhuvan and the Disaster Management Support Programme; IMD and Ministry of Earth Sciences on cyclone forecasting, Mission Mausam (2024) and the National Center for Seismology; INCOIS and the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre, with IOC-UNESCO Tsunami Service Provider and Tsunami Ready recognition; NDMA — Disaster Management Act 2005, Guidelines on Management of Urban Flooding (2010) and earthquake guidelines; Bureau of Indian Standards IS 1893 and IS 13920; Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs on AMRUT 2.0 and the Smart Cities Mission; Ministry of Jal Shakti — Dam Safety Act 2021 and the National Dam Safety Authority; MoEFCC on the Forest Conservation Act 1980 / Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam and the National Mission for a Green India; Ministry of Agriculture on the National Agroforestry Policy 2014; Ministry of AYUSH and the National Medicinal Plants Board; CSIR-CIMAP and the CSIR Aroma Mission; CSIR-AYUSH Traditional Knowledge Digital Library; Government of Andhra Pradesh (APSDMA, RTGS City Flood Alert, Polavaram Project Authority).
