Q75:
## Introduction

River sand is not inert material awaiting extraction: it is a functional component of the river system, forming the bed that stabilises the channel, the aquifer medium that stores and filters groundwater, and the substrate on which benthic life and fish breeding depend. Sand is, after water, the most extracted natural resource on Earth, and India’s construction demand substantially exceeds legally permitted supply — a gap that is the direct economic driver of illegal extraction.

## Why sand matters — the mechanism
- The sand bed acts as a natural aquifer, storing water during the monsoon and releasing it slowly to sustain dry-season flow and recharge adjacent wells.
- It filters water percolating through it, which is why riverbank filtration is used as a drinking water source.
- It provides channel stability — the bed resists erosion and holds the river in its course.
- It is the habitat and breeding substrate for benthic organisms, fish and turtles.
- Sand in transit maintains downstream sediment supply, sustaining deltas and beaches against erosion.

## Impacts on river ecology
- Bed incision and channel instability. Extraction beyond the natural replenishment rate lowers the bed level. Once incised, the river’s energy increases and it erodes further, undermining bridge piers, barrages, embankments and pipelines. Incision of several metres has been recorded in over-mined stretches, including parts of the Yamuna.
- Groundwater depletion. As the bed lowers, the adjacent water table falls with it, drying wells and reducing dry-season base flow. This is the impact that most directly reaches households, and it is often the first sign villagers notice.
- Bank erosion and collapse. Removal of bed and bank material destabilises the banks, which then collapse, taking farmland, roads and houses.
- Biodiversity loss. Destruction of breeding grounds for fish and freshwater turtles; the gharial and the Gangetic dolphin are among the affected species, since both depend on specific channel morphology.
- Downstream and coastal effects. Sediment retained or removed upstream starves deltas and beaches, accelerating coastal erosion — an impact felt hundreds of kilometres from the mining site, which is why sand mining is a coastal issue as well as a riverine one.
- Increased flood risk. Destabilised banks and weakened embankments raise flood exposure, and altered channel geometry changes where floodwater goes.
- Water quality. Turbidity from disturbance, and contamination from machinery, fuel and effluent at extraction sites.

## Impacts on people
- Water security. Falling water tables affect drinking water wells and irrigation — the most widespread human impact.
- Agriculture. Loss of riverbank farmland to erosion; reduced soil moisture in adjoining fields.
- Fisheries. Declining fish stocks from habitat destruction, affecting traditional fishing communities.
- Housing and infrastructure. Bank collapse damaging homes, roads and bridges; villagers along several Indian rivers have been displaced by progressive bank erosion.
- Crime, coercion and governance capture. Illegal sand extraction is organised, high-value and locally enforced by intimidation. Attacks on journalists, activists and officials attempting enforcement are documented, and the Durga Shakti Nagpal case (Uttar Pradesh, 2013) brought national attention to the political economy involved.
- Occupational conditions. Manual sand workers, often informal and including migrant labour, work in hazardous conditions with drowning risk and no protection.

## Critical assessment — why regulation has under-performed
- The demand-supply gap is the root cause. Where legal supply is capped well below construction demand, the price differential makes illegal extraction extremely profitable and creates a market that enforcement alone cannot suppress. Any durable solution must address substitutes — manufactured sand (M-sand) from crushed rock, and recycled construction and demolition waste — not only enforcement.
- Jurisdictional fragmentation. Sand is a minor mineral under the MMDR Act, with regulation devolved to States, producing wide variation in rules, royalty and enforcement quality; rivers crossing State boundaries can be mined under different regimes on either bank.
- Weak replenishment science. Extraction should be capped at the annual replenishment rate, established by a District Survey Report — but survey quality is uneven, and where the replenishment estimate is inflated, “legal” mining becomes physically unsustainable.
- Monitoring capacity. Riverbeds are extensive and mining is often nocturnal; conventional inspection cannot cover them.
- Political economy. Local revenue significance and political patronage weaken the will to enforce, which is the constraint most difficult to legislate away.

## Regulatory and technological responses
- Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines, 2016 and Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining, 2020 (MoEFCC) — requiring District Survey Reports, replenishment-based extraction limits, environmental clearance for all sand mining including minor minerals, and river-stretch-wise planning.
- Judicial intervention — the Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have repeatedly held that no sand mining may proceed without environmental clearance, including for minor minerals.
- Technology: GPS-enabled vehicle tracking, weighbridges, e-transit permits with QR codes, drone and satellite monitoring of pit depth and stockpiles, CCTV at reaches, and online sale platforms that remove discretionary allocation.
- Alternatives: promotion of manufactured sand (M-sand), use of recycled construction and demolition waste under the C&D Waste Rules, 2016, and dredged reservoir silt — which simultaneously restores reservoir capacity.
- Community mechanisms: local vigilance committees, grievance helplines and gram sabha involvement, particularly effective because villagers observe extraction directly.
- AP instance: the AP Minor Mineral Policy 2025 provides for e-auction-based allocation of quarry leases, GPS-enabled vehicle tracking, real-time monitoring, mandatory sustainable mining plans and community safeguards, succeeding the AP Sand Mining Policy, 2016. The Krishna and Godavari river stretches are the State’s principal sand reaches, and their proximity to the deltas makes downstream sediment effects directly consequential for coastal stability.

## Conclusion

Illegal sand mining damages rivers through a single physical mechanism with wide consequences: removing the bed lowers the water table, destabilises banks and starves the delta. Its human costs — dry wells, lost farmland, collapsed homes and coerced communities — follow directly. Enforcement, monitoring technology and river-stretch planning are necessary, but as long as legal supply falls far short of construction demand, the incentive to mine illegally will persist. Sustainable management therefore requires reducing demand for river sand itself through M-sand and recycled aggregate, alongside stricter enforcement.

## Value addition
- Governing framework: sand is a minor mineral under the MMDR Act, 1957, regulated by States; Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines, 2016; Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining, 2020; mandatory District Survey Reports and replenishment-based extraction limits; environmental clearance required even for minor minerals following judicial direction.
- The replenishment principle: extraction should not exceed the river’s annual sediment replenishment rate for the reach; exceeding it converts a renewable harvest into permanent depletion. This is the technical test that distinguishes sustainable from unsustainable mining, and it is worth stating explicitly.
- Alternatives to river sand:M-sand (manufactured sand from crushed rock); recycled aggregate from construction and demolition waste under the C&D Waste Rules, 2016; dredged reservoir silt, which restores storage capacity while supplying sand; and copper slag and fly-ash-based substitutes for specific applications.
- Species affected:gharial, Gangetic dolphin (National Aquatic Animal), freshwater turtles, and riverine bird nesting on sandbars — the ecological argument is not abstract.
- Monitoring technology: GPS vehicle tracking; e-transit permits with QR codes; drone and satellite pit-depth monitoring; weighbridge integration; Mining Surveillance System developed by the Ministry of Mines using satellite imagery to flag unauthorised extraction.
- AP-specific:AP Minor Mineral Policy 2025 (e-auction, GPS tracking, real-time monitoring, sustainable mining plans); the earlier AP Sand Mining Policy, 2016; Krishna and Godavari sand reaches; downstream delta and coastal erosion implications; APMDC.

## Introduction

Dams are classified on several bases — by structure and design, by material, by function and by hydraulic behaviour. The structural classification is the most fundamental, because it describes how the dam transmits the water load to the ground, and that in turn determines which site conditions each type requires.

## (a) Classification of dams by structure and design

1. Gravity dams - Principle: resist water pressure by their own weight, with a broadly triangular cross-section transmitting the load vertically into the foundation. - Site requirement: a strong rock foundation capable of bearing very large loads; suits narrow to moderately wide valleys. - Material: concrete or masonry. - Indian examples:Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna, Andhra Pradesh — among the world’s largest masonry dams; Srisailam on the Krishna, AP — a masonry gravity dam; Bhakra on the Sutlej — a concrete gravity dam; Koyna, Maharashtra.

2. Arch dams - Principle: curved in plan with the convex side upstream, transferring water pressure horizontally into the abutments by arch action rather than resisting it by weight. This allows a far thinner, more economical section. - Site requirement: a narrow gorge with sound, strong rock abutments capable of taking the thrust — the most demanding site requirement of any dam type, which is why arch dams are uncommon in India. - Indian example: Idukki (Kerala) — India’s first and most prominent arch dam, a double-curvature arch across the Periyar.

3. Buttress dams - Principle: a relatively thin upstream face (a flat slab or series of arches) supported on the downstream side by a line of buttresses that carry the load to the foundation. - Advantage: uses substantially less concrete than a gravity dam of comparable height, so it suits sites where material is expensive; the open structure also reduces uplift pressure. - Site requirement: a reliable foundation, since load is concentrated at the buttress footings. -Note for accuracy: true buttress dams are relatively rare in India; the internationally cited example is the Daniel-Johnson dam in Canada.

4. Embankment dams (earthfill and rockfill) - Principle: resist water by the mass and internal friction of compacted earth or rock, with an impervious core (clay or a membrane) to control seepage. - Site requirement: the most tolerant of weak foundations, and suitable for wide valleys where a concrete dam would be prohibitively expensive; locally available material keeps cost low. - Vulnerability: cannot tolerate overtopping, which rapidly erodes the embankment — so spillway capacity is critical. - Indian examples:Tehri on the Bhagirathi — India’s tallest dam, an earth-and-rockfill embankment; Pulichintala on the Krishna, AP; Hirakud on the Mahanadi, a composite structure with the world’s longest major earthen dam section.

5. Composite dams - Combine two or more types along the length of a single barrier, using each where site conditions suit it — typically a concrete gravity section across the deep river channel with earthen flanks across the wider valley. Hirakud and Nagarjuna Sagar both have composite elements.

Other classifications worth naming briefly: by function (storage, diversion, detention, coffer); by hydraulic behaviour (overflow versus non-overflow); and by height (large dams as defined by ICOLD criteria).

## (b) Note on the Andhra Pradesh Sand Mining Policy, 2016
- Context and purpose. River sand extraction had become a source of ecological damage, revenue leakage and organised illegality. The 2016 policy sought to make allocation transparent, traceable and scientifically limited, replacing discretionary allotment.
- Key features:

e-auction of sand reaches, removing discretionary allocation and improving price discovery;

online booking and delivery, with consumers ordering sand through a portal;

GPS-enabled tracking of transport vehicles and e-way permits, so each load can be matched to a legal source;

environmental safeguards — limits on extraction depth, prohibition of mining in specified stretches, seasonal restrictions during the monsoon when replenishment occurs, and riverbank restoration obligations; community and local body involvement in reach management in some models, with revenue sharing.

- Outcomes and limitations. The policy improved traceability and revenue capture, and reduced the most visible forms of unauthorised extraction. Sand policy in the State has nonetheless been revised repeatedly across successive governments — a pattern common to several States — reflecting the difficulty of balancing affordable supply for construction, revenue for the exchequer, and ecological limits on extraction. Persistent challenges include the demand-supply gap, cross-border movement of sand, and monitoring at night.
- The successor framework. The AP Minor Mineral Policy 2025 carries the same architecture forward for sand, gravel, road metal and granite — e-auction-based leases, GPS-enabled vehicle tracking, real-time monitoring, mandatory sustainable mining plans, environmental compliance and community safeguards — while adding an emphasis on value-addition industries and cluster-based operations to generate local employment.
- National alignment: both policies operate within MoEFCC’s Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines, 2016 and the Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines, 2020, which require District Survey Reports and replenishment-based extraction limits.

## Conclusion

Dam classification by structure reflects a single underlying question — how the water load is carried to the ground — and each form answers it differently, which is why gravity dams need strong foundations, arch dams need sound abutments, and embankment dams suit wide valleys with weaker ground. Andhra Pradesh’s sand policies address a parallel problem in resource governance: making extraction traceable and limited rather than discretionary. Both illustrate that engineering and regulatory design must be matched to the specific conditions they govern.

## Value addition
- Get the examples right:gravity — Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam (AP), Bhakra, Koyna; arch — Idukki (Kerala), India’s principal arch dam; embankment — Tehri (India’s tallest), Pulichintala (AP); composite — Hirakud (world’s longest major earthen dam section), Nagarjuna Sagar.
- Design principle in one line each: gravity resists by weight; arch transfers thrust to abutments; buttress uses a thin face on supporting ribs; embankment resists by mass and friction with an impervious core.
- Dam Safety Act, 2021: established the National Dam Safety Authority and National Committee on Dam Safety, with State Dam Safety Organisations; mandates inspection, emergency action plans and periodic safety review — significant because a large proportion of India’s dams are more than fifty years old.
- Sand governance instruments: MoEFCC Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines, 2016; Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines, 2020; District Survey Reports; Mining Surveillance System (Ministry of Mines) using satellite imagery to detect unauthorised extraction; M-sand and C&D-recycled aggregate as substitutes.
- AP water infrastructure to name: Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam on the Krishna; Polavaram on the Godavari; Pulichintala; Somasila and Kandaleru on the Pennar; the Godavari-Krishna link.
- The recurring policy problem to note critically: sand policy in several States has been revised with successive governments, because the same policy must simultaneously keep construction sand affordable, generate revenue, and stay within ecological limits — three objectives that pull in different directions.

## Introduction

Crop suitability and mineral occurrence are both determined by natural endowment modified by human choice — climate and soil set the boundaries of what can be grown, geology sets what can be mined, and in each case policy, price and technology determine what actually is. Both are foundational to Andhra Pradesh’s economy, which combines a large agricultural base with substantial mineral wealth.

## (a) Basis and justification for crop suitability and cropping pattern

Cropping pattern means the proportion of area under different crops at a point in time, and the sequence in which they are grown on the same land across seasons.

Physical determinants - Climate — temperature range, rainfall amount and distribution, humidity, day length and frost-free period. Rice requires high water and humidity; wheat requires a cool growing season and warm ripening; millets tolerate low and erratic rainfall. - Soil — texture, depth, pH, drainage, organic matter and nutrient status. Cotton suits the moisture-retentive black regur soils of the Deccan; groundnut suits the light red sandy soils of Rayalaseema; rice suits the clayey alluvium of the Godavari and Krishna deltas. - Water availability — assured irrigation permits water-intensive crops; rainfed conditions require drought-tolerant and short-duration varieties. - Topography — slope determines mechanisation, erosion risk and irrigation feasibility; terracing enables cultivation on hill slopes.

The formal framework — worth naming. India is divided into 15 agro-climatic zones (Planning Commission) and, in a finer classification by ICAR, into agro-ecological regions. These are the analytical basis on which crop planning is formally justified, and citing the framework rather than only the factors demonstrates policy literacy. Andhra Pradesh spans several distinct zones, from the coastal deltaic to the scarce-rainfall Rayalaseema zone — which is precisely why a single State-wide cropping recommendation is inappropriate.

Technological and input determinants - Availability of improved and climate-resilient seed; fertiliser and plant protection; farm machinery; and irrigation technology such as micro-irrigation under Per Drop More Crop. - Soil Health Cards and the Krishi Decision Support System now provide farm-specific rather than district-generic recommendations.

Economic determinants - Price and market access — the expectation of remunerative price is the dominant single determinant of farmer choice; MSP and procurement arrangements strongly shape it. - Cost of cultivation and the farmer’s capital and credit access. - Farm size — small holdings favour intensive, high-value crops; larger holdings permit mechanised field crops. - Storage, processing and transport infrastructure, which determines whether perishables are viable.

Socio-cultural and policy determinants - Food habits and subsistence requirements; traditional practice and risk aversion. - Policy signals — procurement, input subsidies, crop insurance under PMFBY, and mission priorities such as NMEO-Oilseeds and Shree Anna for millets.

Justification — why suitability analysis matters - Sustainability: growing water-intensive crops in water-scarce zones — paddy and sugarcane in low-

rainfall regions — depletes groundwater irreversibly. Matching crop to endowment is a water policy as much as an agricultural one. - Productivity and income: suitability determines yield stability and therefore income. - Risk reduction: diversified cropping patterns spread climate and price risk. - Soil health: rotation with legumes fixes nitrogen and breaks pest cycles; continuous monoculture depletes specific nutrients. - Food and nutritional security at national and household level.

## (b) Mineral resources

Meaning. A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic, homogeneous substance with a definite chemical composition and an ordered internal atomic structure. A mineral resource is a concentration of such material in or on the Earth’s crust in a form and quantity that makes eventual economic extraction reasonable. The related distinction worth making: a reserve is that part of the resource which is economically and technically extractable at present prices and technology — so reserves change with price and technology, while the resource does not.

## How minerals form — the genesis, which the question specifically asks
- Igneous (magmatic) processes. As magma cools, minerals crystallise in sequence; heavier metallic minerals settle to form magmatic segregation deposits (chromite, nickel). Late-stage residual fluids form pegmatites, coarse-grained bodies hosting mica, feldspar, beryllium and lithium minerals.
- Hydrothermal processes. Hot, mineral-rich fluids circulate through fractures and precipitate metals as veins and lodes on cooling — the origin of most gold, copper, lead, zinc and silver deposits.
- Sedimentary processes. Deposition and accumulation in basins: chemical precipitation (rock salt, gypsum, some iron and manganese formations), organic accumulation (coal from plant matter, petroleum from marine organic matter), and evaporation of enclosed water bodies producing evaporites.
- Metamorphic processes. Existing rocks transformed by heat and pressure, producing graphite, marble, slate, asbestos and some forms of iron ore.
- Weathering and residual concentration. Prolonged chemical weathering in warm humid climates leaches soluble material and leaves an insoluble residue — the origin of bauxite (from laterisation) and residual iron and manganese ores.
- Placer deposits. Heavy, chemically resistant minerals eroded from source rock and concentrated by flowing water in river beds or by wave action on beaches — the origin of beach sand heavy minerals (ilmenite, rutile, zircon, garnet, monazite), gold placers and diamonds.

## Types of mineral resources
- **Basis** — Categories · Examples
- **Metallic** — Ferrous (containing iron) · Iron ore, manganese, chromite, nickel, cobalt
- **Non-ferrous** — Copper, bauxite/aluminium, lead, zinc, tin
- **Precious** — Gold, silver, platinum
- **Non-metallic** — Industrial and construction minerals · Limestone, dolomite, mica, gypsum, barytes, ball clay, granite, quartz
- **Energy/fuel** — Fossil and atomic minerals · Coal, petroleum, natural gas, uranium, thorium (monazite)
- **Strategic/critical** — Essential to clean energy and high technology · Lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, rare earth elements

Other classifications: by legal status under the MMDR Act into major and minor minerals (the latter including sand, gravel, building stone and ordinary clay, regulated by States); and by renewability — minerals are exhaustible and non-renewable on human timescales, which is the basis for the principle of inter-generational equity in the National Mineral Policy, 2019.

Andhra Pradesh’s mineral endowment - Barytes at Mangampet, Kadapa district — among the world’s largest single deposits; - Limestone supporting a major cement industry, and dolomite; - Uranium at Tummalapalle, Kadapa district, in the Cuddapah Basin; - Beach sand heavy minerals — ilmenite, garnet, zircon, monazite — along the coast, monazite being India’s thorium source; - Granite and dimension stone, ball clay, quartz, silica sand, laterite, mica; - Diamonds historically at Wajrakarur (Anantapur district) and gold at Ramagiri; - Coal in the Godavari valley basin, largely on the Telangana side following bifurcation.

Governance framework:MMDR Act, 1957 (amended 2015, 2021, 2023) with auction-based allocation of mineral concessions; National Mineral Policy, 2019; District Mineral Foundation and PMKKKY directing a share of royalty to affected communities; National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) with 1,200 GSI exploration projects targeted by 2030-31, offshore mineral auctions and recycling as supply routes; APMDC and the AP Minor Mineral Policy 2025 at State level.

## Conclusion

Crop suitability and mineral occurrence are both determined first by nature and then by economics: climate and soil define what can grow, geology defines what can be extracted, and price, technology and policy determine what actually happens. For Andhra Pradesh both matter directly — a State spanning deltaic and drought-prone agro-climatic zones, and holding barytes, limestone, uranium and beach-sand minerals of national significance. In each case the governing principle is the same: matching use to endowment, and extracting within the limits of renewal or, for minerals, with regard to inter-generational equity.

## Value addition
- The framework to name: India’s 15 agro-climatic zones (Planning Commission) and ICAR’s agro-ecological regions — the formal basis for crop planning. Andhra Pradesh spans coastal deltaic, southern plateau and scarce-rainfall zones.
- Mineral genesis processes: igneous/magmatic segregation and pegmatites; hydrothermal veins and lodes; sedimentary (chemical, organic, evaporite); metamorphic; residual concentration by weathering (bauxite); placer concentration (beach sand minerals, gold, diamonds).
- The resource-versus-reserve distinction: a resource is a concentration that may become economic; a reserve is the part currently extractable at prevailing price and technology. Reserves therefore grow when prices rise or technology improves, without any new discovery.
- Mineral governance:MMDR Act, 1957 (amended 2015 introducing auctions, 2021 and 2023 adding critical and deep-seated minerals); National Mineral Policy, 2019; DMF and PMKKKY; Star Rating of Mines; National Critical Mineral Mission, 2025 with 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31, offshore auctions and recycling.
- Crop-related schemes: MSP and procurement; PMFBY with YES-TECH; Soil Health Card; Per Drop More Crop; NMEO-Oilseeds; Shree Anna for millets; Krishi-DSS and AgriStack for farm-specific advisory.
- AP-specific:Mangampet barytes (Kadapa); Tummalapalle uranium (Kadapa, Cuddapah Basin); beach sand heavy minerals along the coast; limestone for the cement belt; Wajrakarur diamonds; APMDC; cropping patterns from delta paddy to Rayalaseema groundnut and millets; APCNF as the State’s agroecological transition programme.
Q78:
## Introduction

India possesses a diverse mineral endowment — substantial reserves of coal, iron ore, bauxite, limestone, manganese, chromite and mica, with significant deficiencies in petroleum, copper, gold, nickel, cobalt and lithium. Mining contributes to GDP and underpins steel, cement, power and infrastructure, but it is also among the most environmentally disruptive economic activities, because it necessarily involves removing large volumes of earth from a fixed location.

## An account of India’s mineral resources — by belt
- North-Eastern Peninsular Belt (Chhotanagpur plateau — Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh). India’s richest mineral region, sometimes called the “Ruhr of India”: coal, iron ore, manganese, bauxite, chromite (Sukinda, Odisha, holds most of India’s chromite), copper (Singhbhum), uranium (Jaduguda) and mica.
- Central Belt (Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, southern UP). Manganese, bauxite, limestone, coal, and diamonds at Panna (India’s only significant diamond mine).
- Southern Belt (Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu). Iron ore (Bellary-Hospet), gold at Kolar and Hutti (Karnataka), barytes at Mangampet (AP) — among the world’s largest single deposits, uranium at Tummalapalle (AP), limestone, granite and dimension stone, and beach sand heavy minerals along the Andhra and Tamil Nadu coasts.
- South-Western Belt (Karnataka, Goa). Iron ore, ferro-manganese, garnet, clay and limestone.
- North-Western Belt (Rajasthan, Gujarat). Non-ferrous metals — lead and zinc (Zawar, Rampura Agucha), copper (Khetri) — with marble, gypsum, and Gujarat’s petroleum and natural gas.

India’s position: among the world’s larger producers of coal, iron ore, bauxite, chromite, manganese and mica; largely self-sufficient in coal, iron ore and limestone; heavily import-dependent in petroleum (85-88%), copper, gold, nickel, cobalt and lithium and rare earths — the last group being the binding constraint on the clean energy transition.

## Impacts of mining on the environment

Land - Direct land loss to pits, dumps, haul roads and processing plants; overburden dumps that are unstable and erode. - Topsoil loss — irreversible on human timescales, since soil formation takes centuries. - Subsidence over underground workings, damaging surface structures and altering drainage. -Land degradation and abandonment — India carries a legacy of abandoned mines predating closure regulations.

Water - Acid mine drainage — sulphide minerals oxidising to sulphuric acid, mobilising heavy metals; persists for decades after closure. - Water table depletion from dewatering; wells dry in surrounding villages. - Siltation and turbidity in streams; contamination from tailings, and tailings dam failure as a catastrophic risk. - Heavy metal contamination entering the food chain through irrigation and fish.

Air - Fugitive dust from drilling, blasting, haulage and dumps — the most immediate community health impact, causing respiratory disease and reducing crop productivity. - Emissions from machinery and mineral processing; methane release and spontaneous combustion in coal.

Biodiversity and forests - India’s mineral belts substantially overlap forest and tribal areas, so mining and forest conservation compete for the same land — the structural reason mining is India’s most contested land-use question. - Habitat loss and fragmentation; disruption of wildlife corridors; loss of endemic species where mining intersects biodiversity-rich hills, as in the Eastern and Western Ghats.

Social and health - Displacement and inadequate rehabilitation, disproportionately affecting Scheduled Tribes in Fifth Schedule areas. - Loss of forest-based and agricultural livelihoods; in-migration and social stress. - Occupational disease — pneumoconiosis and silicosis among mine workers, often unrecognised and uncompensated. - Illegal mining and its associated coercion of local communities.

Climate - Coal mining and combustion as India’s largest single emissions source; methane from coal seams; loss of forest carbon sinks; and the emissions embedded in mineral processing, particularly for steel and cement.

## Governance and mitigation framework
- MMDR Act, 1957 (amended 2015 introducing auction-based allocation, and in 2021 and 2023 to cover critical and deep-seated minerals) and the National Mineral Policy, 2019, which frames mining as a temporary land use requiring restoration and asserts inter-generational equity.
- District Mineral Foundation (DMF) funded by a levy on royalty, with expenditure through PMKKKY on drinking water, health, education, sanitation and livelihoods in mining-affected areas — the principal benefit-sharing mechanism.
- Environmental and forest clearance under the EIA Notification 2006 and the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam; consent from State Pollution Control Boards; consent requirements under PESA and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 in Scheduled Areas — the Niyamgiri gram sabha consultation being the landmark instance of communities exercising this right.
- Star Rating of Mines (Indian Bureau of Mines) scoring mines on sustainable practice; Mining Surveillance System using satellite imagery to detect unauthorised extraction; Progressive and Final Mine Closure Plans with escrowed financial assurance.
- Sustainable practices: concurrent reclamation; topsoil conservation; dust suppression and green belts; mine water treatment and reuse; backfilling; and repurposing of reclaimed land for afforestation, water bodies or solar parks.
- The critical mineral dimension: the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) targets 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31, with overseas acquisition through KABIL, offshore mineral auctions and recycling — since urban mining of e-waste recovers metals at concentrations often exceeding natural ore, directly linking mineral security to waste policy.

AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s mineral economy rests on Mangampet barytes, limestone for cement, Tummalapalle uranium, granite and dimension stone, ball clay, laterite and coastal heavy mineral sands. Because much of the Eastern Ghats mineral belt lies in Fifth Schedule tribal areas, consent under PESA and the Forest Rights Act is legally and politically central — bauxite proposals in the agency areas have been among the State’s most contested. APMDC is the State corporation and the AP Minor Mineral Policy 2025 governs minor minerals.

## Conclusion

India’s mineral endowment is substantial but unevenly matched to its needs — abundant in coal, iron ore and limestone, deficient in the petroleum, copper and critical minerals on which its industrial and energy transitions depend. Mining’s environmental cost is inseparable from its method, and is intensified in India because mineral belts coincide with forests and tribal habitations. The governance framework — auction-based allocation, DMF benefit-sharing, mine closure with financial assurance, and gram sabha consent in Scheduled Areas — is substantially sound; the deficit is in enforcement, in closure of legacy sites, and in ensuring that affected communities receive a meaningful share of what is extracted from beneath them.

## Value addition
- The five mineral belts: North-Eastern Peninsular (Chhotanagpur); Central; Southern; South-Western; North-Western — the most efficient way to organise a resource account.
- Self-sufficiency profile: largely self-sufficient in coal, iron ore, bauxite and limestone; import-dependent in petroleum (85-88%), copper, gold, nickel, cobalt, lithium and rare earths.
- Governance instruments:MMDR Act, 1957 (amended 2015, 2021, 2023); National Mineral Policy, 2019; DMF and PMKKKY; Star Rating of Mines; Mining Surveillance System; Progressive and Final Mine Closure Plans with financial assurance; National Critical Mineral Mission, 2025.
- The Niyamgiri precedent: gram sabhas in Odisha’s Niyamgiri hills rejected bauxite mining following Supreme Court direction that their views on community, religious and cultural rights be obtained — the landmark instance of Forest Rights Act consent being exercised against a mining project.
- Occupational health:silicosis and pneumoconiosis among mine and quarry workers; the National Human Rights Commission has repeatedly raised under-diagnosis and inadequate compensation — a dimension most answers omit entirely.
- Urban mining: recovery of metals from e-waste at concentrations frequently exceeding natural ore; recognised as a supply route within the National Critical Mineral Mission, linking the E-Waste Rules 2022 to mineral security.
- AP-specific: Mangampet barytes (Kadapa); Tummalapalle uranium; limestone for the cement belt; beach sand heavy minerals; granite and dimension stone; contested bauxite in Eastern Ghats Fifth Schedule areas; APMDC; AP Minor Mineral Policy 2025.

Sources used: Ministry of Mines — MMDR Act 1957 as amended, National Mineral Policy 2019, District Mineral Foundation and PMKKKY, Star Rating of Mines, Mining Surveillance System, and the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) with Geological Survey of India exploration targets; Indian Bureau of Mines on mine closure plans and financial assurance; MoEFCC — EIA Notification 2006, Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines 2016, Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining 2020, and the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam 1980 as amended 2023; Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023; Ministry of Jal Shakti — Dam Safety Act 2021 and the National Dam Safety Authority; Central Water Commission on dam classification; Ministry of Tribal Affairs on Forest Rights Act consent and the Niyamgiri proceedings; Planning Commission agro-climatic zone classification and ICAR agro-ecological regions; Ministry of Agriculture on Soil Health Cards, PMFBY, Per Drop More Crop and Krishi-DSS; Government of Andhra Pradesh — APMDC, AP Sand Mining Policy 2016 and AP Minor Mineral Policy 2025.

Q79:
## Introduction

India’s varied geology — ancient Precambrian shields, Gondwana sedimentary basins, Deccan traps and coastal placers — has produced a diverse mineral endowment. India is a leading global producer of coal, iron ore, bauxite, chromite, manganese and mica, while remaining substantially import-dependent for petroleum, copper, gold, nickel, cobalt, lithium and rare earths. Deposits are concentrated in identifiable mineral belts rather than distributed evenly.

## India’s mineral belts
- North-Eastern Peninsular Belt (Chhotanagpur plateau — Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh). The richest belt, often called the “Ruhr of India”: coal, iron ore, manganese, bauxite, chromite, mica, copper (Singhbhum) and uranium (Jaduguda).
- Central Belt (Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, southern Uttar Pradesh): manganese, bauxite, limestone, coal, and diamonds at Panna.
- Southern Belt (Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu): iron ore (Bellary-Hospet), gold at Kolar and Hutti, barytes at Mangampet (AP), uranium at Tummalapalle (AP), limestone, granite and beach-sand heavy minerals.
- South-Western Belt (Karnataka, Goa, Kerala): iron ore, ferro-manganese, garnet, clay, and monazite sands along the Kerala coast — India’s principal thorium source.
- North-Western Belt (Rajasthan, Gujarat): lead and zinc (Zawar, Rampura Agucha), copper (Khetri), marble, gypsum, and Gujarat’s petroleum and natural gas.

## Classification of India’s mineral resources

## Metallic minerals

Ferrous: - Iron ore — India holds large reserves of high-grade haematite and magnetite; principal producers are Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Karnataka and Goa. Production reached 289 million tonnes in FY 2024-25, a record, up 4.3% from 277 MT the previous year, and iron ore accounts for roughly 70% by value of minerals produced under the MCDR regime (Ministry of Mines). - Manganese — essential for steel alloys; Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka. Output rose to 3.8 MT in FY 2024-25, up 11.8%. - Chromite — concentrated overwhelmingly in the Sukinda valley, Odisha.

Non-ferrous: - Bauxite — Odisha is the largest producer, with Gujarat, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh; output 24.7 MT in FY 2024-25. Primary aluminium production reached 42.0 lakh tonnes. - Copper — reserves modest relative to demand; Khetri (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Malanjkhand (Madhya Pradesh). Refined copper output grew 12.6% to 5.73 lakh tonnes in FY 2024-25. - Lead and zinc — Rajasthan dominates (Zawar, Rampura Agucha).

Precious:gold at Kolar and Hutti (Karnataka) and Ramagiri (AP), with production far below consumption — India is among the world’s largest gold importers.

2. Non-metallic minerals - Limestone — the raw material of the cement industry; widespread in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat,

Chhattisgarh and Karnataka. - Mica — India was historically the world’s largest producer of sheet mica, particularly from Koderma (Jharkhand) and the Nellore belt (AP); the sheet-mica industry has since contracted with synthetic substitution. - Barytes — Mangampet, Kadapa district, Andhra Pradesh, among the world’s largest single deposits, used in oil-well drilling fluid. - Gypsum and dolomite — for cement, fertiliser and steel-making. - Granite and dimension stone — a major export from Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Rajasthan and Karnataka. - Ball clay, quartz, silica sand, kaolin and asbestos.

3. Energy and atomic minerals - Coal — India’s most abundant energy mineral, in the Gondwana fields (Jharia and Raniganj in Jharkhand-West Bengal, Singrauli in Madhya Pradesh, Talcher in Odisha, Korba in Chhattisgarh, and the Godavari valley) and, in smaller quantity, the Tertiary fields of the North-East. Domestic production reached about 1,047.57 million tonnes in FY 2024-25. - Petroleum and natural gas — offshore Mumbai High, the Krishna-Godavari basin off the Andhra coast, Assam (Digboi, Naharkatiya), Gujarat (Ankleshwar), and Rajasthan (Barmer). Import dependence in crude remains 85-88%. - Atomic minerals — uranium at Jaduguda and Turamdih (Jharkhand) and Tummalapalle (Kadapa, AP); thorium as monazite in the beach placer sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, giving India among the world’s largest thorium reserves.

4. Critical and strategic minerals — lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, and rare earth elements, essential to batteries, wind turbines, semiconductors and defence. India is heavily import-dependent, which is why the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) targets 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31, alongside overseas acquisition through KABIL, offshore mineral auctions and recycling.

Governance:MMDR Act, 1957 (amended 2015 for auction-based allocation, and 2021 and 2023 for critical and deep-seated minerals); National Mineral Policy, 2019; District Mineral Foundation and PMKKKY; Star Rating of Mines; the Geological Survey of India and Indian Bureau of Mines as technical agencies.

## Conclusion

India’s mineral endowment is strong in the bulk minerals that underpin steel, cement and power — coal, iron ore, bauxite and limestone, all at record production in FY 2024-25 — and weak precisely where the future economy will need most: petroleum, copper and the critical minerals of the energy transition. The strategic task is therefore twofold: extracting the abundant resources sustainably, and securing the scarce ones through exploration, overseas assets and recycling.

Coal production about 1,047.57 MT.

- Critical mineral framework:National Critical Mineral Mission (2025); 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31; KABIL for overseas assets; Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act amendments enabling offshore auctions; recycling and urban mining of e-waste as a domestic supply route.

Q80:
## Introduction

India’s forests span an exceptional range because the country crosses climatic zones from equatorial to alpine and receives rainfall varying from under 100 mm to over 11,000 mm annually. Forest and tree cover stands at 8,27,357 sq km — 25.17% of the geographical area (ISFR 2023, Forest Survey of India), comprising forest cover of 21.76% and tree cover of 3.41%, an increase of 1,445 sq km over 2021, against the National Forest Policy 1988 target of 33%.

## (a) Types of forests in India

The formal framework to cite: the standard classification is that of Champion and Seth (1968), which recognises 16 forest type groups under five major categories — tropical, montane subtropical, montane temperate, sub-alpine and alpine. Naming this framework immediately signals command of the topic.

1. Tropical forests - Tropical wet evergreen — over 2,500 mm rainfall; dense, multi-storeyed, no leafless period. Western Ghats, North-East, Andaman & Nicobar. Species: mahogany, rosewood, ebony, bamboo. - Tropical semi-evergreen — 2,000-2,500 mm; a transition type with both evergreen and deciduous species; Western Ghats and eastern Himalayan foothills. - Tropical moist deciduous — 1,000-2,000 mm; India’s most commercially valuable forest. Trees shed leaves in the dry season to conserve water. Central India, eastern slopes of the Western Ghats, and parts of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh. Species: teak, sal, sandalwood, shisham, bamboo. - Tropical dry deciduous — 700-1,000 mm; the most widespread type, across the peninsular interior and the Indo-Gangetic plain. Species: teak, axlewood, tendu. - Tropical thorn and scrub — under 700 mm; Rajasthan, Gujarat, and parts of Rayalaseema in Andhra Pradesh. Species: babul, khejri, kikar, cactus, with deep root systems and reduced leaf area. - Littoral and swamp (mangrove) — coastal and deltaic; the Sundarbans (world’s largest mangrove forest), Coringa (AP), Bhitarkanika, Pichavaram. Species: sundari, rhizophora, avicennia, with pneumatophores (breathing roots) and viviparous germination as adaptations to saline waterlogged soil.

2. Montane subtropical forests — 1,000-2,000 m; subtropical broadleaved hill forests (oak, chestnut) in the eastern Himalaya; subtropical pine (chir pine) in the western Himalaya; and subtropical dry evergreen in the north-west.

3. Montane temperate forests — 1,500-3,500 m; wet temperate in the Nilgiris and eastern Himalaya (the Nilgiri shola forests being a distinctive stunted evergreen type in valley folds); moist temperate in Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh with deodar, blue pine, spruce and fir; dry temperate in the inner Himalaya and Ladakh with juniper and chilgoza pine.

4. Sub-alpine forests — around the treeline, 3,000-3,800 m; stunted conifers and broadleaved species — birch, rhododendron, fir.

5. Alpine forests and scrub — above the treeline; moist alpine scrub with dwarf rhododendron and juniper, and dry alpine scrub in the trans-Himalaya; short, hardy, cold-adapted vegetation grading into pasture.

## (b) How forests help human society — the ecosystem services framework

The most analytically useful structure is the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment’s four categories:

- Provisioning services — timber, fuelwood, bamboo, fodder, and non-timber forest produce (NTFP): tendu leaves, mahua, honey, lac, gum, resin, medicinal plants and wild fruit. NTFP is the livelihood base for a very large number of forest-dependent households, including tribal communities in the

Eastern Ghats, and is protected under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, which vests ownership of minor forest produce in gram sabhas.

- Regulating services — carbon sequestration (India’s NDC commits to an additional sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2e by 2030); climate and rainfall regulation; watershed protection and groundwater recharge; flood and landslide moderation; soil conservation; air purification; and coastal protection by mangroves, which measurably attenuate cyclone storm surge — directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s Coringa mangroves.
- Supporting services — nutrient cycling, soil formation, pollination and primary production; forests host a large majority of terrestrial biodiversity, including India’s four biodiversity hotspots.
- Cultural services — spiritual and religious value, expressed in India through thousands of sacred groves; recreation and ecotourism; aesthetic and educational value; and the identity and knowledge systems of forest-dwelling communities.

Economic dimension: forests supply raw material to paper, plywood, furniture, pharmaceutical and handicraft industries, and generate employment through forestry operations, NTFP collection and ecotourism.

## Conclusion

India’s forest types are the direct product of two gradients — rainfall and altitude — which is why the country holds everything from equatorial evergreen to alpine scrub within its borders, formally classified under Champion and Seth’s sixteen type groups. Their value to society is best understood through the ecosystem services framework, in which the provisioning services that are traded in markets are far smaller than the regulating and supporting services that are not. That asymmetry is precisely why forests are under-valued in development decisions, and why instruments such as the Green Credit Programme and compensatory afforestation attempt to price them.

## Value addition
- Champion and Seth (1968):16 forest type groups in five major categories — tropical, montane subtropical, montane temperate, sub-alpine and alpine. Citing this framework is the single most effective way to distinguish this answer.
- Forest data (ISFR 2023): forest and tree cover 8,27,357 sq km = 25.17%; forest cover 7,15,343 sq km (21.76%); tree cover 1,12,014 sq km (3.41%); increase of 1,445 sq km over 2021; National Forest Policy 1988 target 33% (and 66% in hills).
- Mangrove adaptations to name:pneumatophores (breathing roots for waterlogged anaerobic soil); vivipary (seeds germinating on the parent tree); salt-excreting glands; stilt roots for stability in soft sediment.
- Ecosystem services framework (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment): provisioning, regulating, supporting, cultural — the analytical structure for any “how do forests help” question.
- Forest governance: Indian Forest Act 1927; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980; Forest Rights Act, 2006 vesting minor forest produce ownership in gram sabhas; National Forest Policy 1988; CAMPA; Green India Mission; Green Credit Programme; Joint Forest Management.
- AP-specific: tropical dry and moist deciduous forests of the Eastern Ghats and Nallamala; thorn and scrub in Rayalaseema; Coringa mangroves (India’s second-largest mangrove formation); Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve with endemic red sanders; Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (India’s largest); Vana Samrakshana Samithis for community management.

## Introduction

India’s traditional water management evolved over centuries as a response to a defining hydrological fact: most rainfall arrives in a few monsoon months and must sustain the year. The systems that emerged were decentralised, gravity-fed, locally maintained and adapted to specific terrain — precisely the characteristics that centralised modern engineering lacks. Their contemporary relevance rests on that complementarity rather than on nostalgia.

phad, bandhara | Karnataka/AP/TN --- kere, cheruvu, eri | Himalaya --- kuhl, naula, zing | Meghalaya --- bamboo drip | Kerala --- surangam | Bihar --- ahar-pyne .

## The major traditional systems
- Rajasthan and the arid west:johad (earthen check dams creating percolation ponds); khadin (embankments across slopes capturing runoff for post-monsoon cropping in soil moisture); tanka (underground covered cisterns collecting rooftop and courtyard runoff); baori and bawdi (stepwells); kund.
- Maharashtra:phad (a community irrigation system diverting river water through canals to blocks of fields with rotational sharing); bandhara (check dams).
- Peninsular India — the tank tradition:kere (Karnataka), eri (Tamil Nadu) and cheruvu / kunta (Andhra Pradesh and Telangana). These were built in cascades, with the overflow of an upper tank feeding the next below, so a whole catchment functioned as a single storage system. Tank irrigation was historically the dominant mode in peninsular India and remains substantial in Andhra Pradesh, where thousands of minor irrigation tanks constitute a distributed storage network of considerable aggregate capacity.
- Bihar:ahar-pyne — pynes being diversion channels from streams and ahars rectangular catchment basins with embankments on three sides, an integrated system in south Bihar’s undulating terrain.
- Himalaya:kuhl (Himachal — gravity channels from glacial streams, managed by a kohli under community rules); naula and dhara (Uttarakhand spring-fed structures); zing (Ladakh — tanks collecting glacier meltwater); guhl.
- North-East:bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya — a centuries-old system carrying spring water through bamboo channels over long distances to drip at the plant root, achieving precision irrigation without any manufactured component; apatani wet-rice-cum-fish terraces in Arunachal Pradesh.
- Kerala and Karnataka coast:surangam — horizontal tunnels driven into laterite hillsides to tap subsurface flow by gravity.
- Jammu:kul; Gujarat:virdas in the Rann; Nagaland: zabo, combining water harvesting with forestry and animal care.

## Why they remain relevant — examining the proposition
- They recharge rather than merely store. Structures such as johads and percolation tanks allow water to infiltrate, raising the water table across the surrounding area. Since India is the world’s largest user of groundwater, recharge is the binding need, and traditional structures address it directly where large dams do not.
- They are decentralised and therefore resilient. A failure in one tank affects one village; a failure in a canal system affects a whole command area. Distributed systems degrade gracefully.
- Low cost and locally maintainable, using local material and skills, without dependence on external supply chains or energy.
- Community ownership — traditional systems came with institutions: rules for sharing, labour contribution and maintenance. This is often the more valuable inheritance than the physical structure, since the collapse of maintenance institutions, more than of the structures, explains their decline.
- Terrain-specific design — each system is an adaptation to its particular geology and rainfall pattern, representing accumulated empirical knowledge that generic engineering cannot replicate.

## Relevance to disaster management — the question’s second limb
- Drought mitigation. Stored and recharged water provides carryover through failed monsoons; Rajendra Singh’s revival of johads in Alwar, Rajasthan, is the standard cited case, associated with the return of flow in seasonal rivers and improved drought resilience.
- Flood moderation. Tanks, ahars and bandharas intercept and detain runoff, reducing peak flow downstream — a distributed detention capacity that also protects urban areas below. The loss of tanks to urban encroachment is a documented contributor to urban flooding in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai.
- Groundwater buffer against climate variability, since recharge structures store water where evaporation losses are minimal — a significant advantage over surface reservoirs in hot regions.
- Local self-reliance in emergencies, when centralised supply is disrupted.

## The honest examination — what traditional systems cannot do

A statement beginning “traditional methods are key” invites qualification, and a complete answer supplies it: - Scale. Traditional systems cannot supply the volumes required by modern urban populations, industry or intensive irrigation. They complement rather than replace major storage and distribution infrastructure. - Institutional erosion. The community institutions that maintained them have weakened with changes in landholding, migration, individual borewells and the shift of responsibility to the state. Rebuilding the structure without the institution produces a silted tank within a decade. -Encroachment and siltation — many tanks have been built over or filled; catchments have been altered. - Quality, not only quantity — traditional systems address availability but not contamination from fluoride, arsenic, nitrate or industrial effluent. - The borewell displacement. Cheap submersible pumps allowed individuals to access groundwater privately, removing the incentive to maintain a shared tank — the single most important reason traditional systems declined, and one that revival programmes must confront directly.

## Current programmes reviving traditional systems
- Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain — “catch the rain, where it falls, when it falls”, with a focus on renovation of traditional water bodies.
- Atal Bhujal Yojana — participatory groundwater management through village water security plans, restoring the community institution rather than only the structure.
- Mission Amrit Sarovar — development and rejuvenation of village ponds.
- MGNREGA — a large share of works are water conservation, tank desilting and farm ponds, providing the labour finance that traditional maintenance once obtained through community contribution.
- WDC-PMKSY 2.0 watershed treatment with Srishti and Drishti monitoring; Repair, Renovation and Restoration of Water Bodies scheme; National Water Mission.
- State initiatives:Mission Kakatiya (Telangana) for restoration of minor irrigation tanks; Neeru-Chettu (Andhra Pradesh) linking water conservation with tree planting; Jalyukt Shivar (Maharashtra); Mukhyamantri Jal Swavlamban (Rajasthan).

## Conclusion

The proposition is substantially correct but requires qualification: traditional systems are key as complements rather than as substitutes. Their value lies in recharge, decentralisation and low cost — exactly the attributes centralised infrastructure lacks — and in flood and drought moderation. But their decline was caused less by neglect of structures than by the collapse of the institutions that maintained them and the arrival of the private borewell. Revival programmes such as Atal Bhujal Yojana, which rebuild the community management institution alongside the structure, are therefore closer to the real lesson than desilting alone.

## Value addition
- Regional systems — a memorised list is decisive here:Rajasthan — johad, khadin, tanka, baori, kund; Maharashtra — phad, bandhara; Karnataka — kere; Tamil Nadu — eri; Andhra Pradesh and Telangana — cheruvu, kunta; Bihar — ahar-pyne; Himachal — kuhl; Uttarakhand — naula, dhara, guhl; Ladakh — zing; Meghalaya — bamboo drip irrigation; Kerala/Karnataka coast — surangam; Nagaland — zabo; Gujarat — virdas.
- The tank cascade principle: peninsular tanks were built in series so the overflow of one fed the next, making the catchment a single integrated storage system. Breaking one link disables the chain — which is why piecemeal restoration under-performs.
- Current programmes:Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain; Atal Bhujal Yojana; Mission Amrit Sarovar; Repair, Renovation and Restoration of Water Bodies; WDC-PMKSY 2.0; MGNREGA water conservation works; Mission Kakatiya (Telangana); Neeru-Chettu (AP).
- Institutional insight worth stating: the borewell privatised a resource that tanks had made communal, destroying the incentive for collective maintenance. Any revival that does not restore the shared-benefit logic will not last.
- Recognition: several traditional systems have received UN or national recognition; Rajendra Singh (“Waterman of India”) received the Stockholm Water Prize (2015) for johad revival in Alwar.
- AP-specific: the cheruvu tank tradition and minor irrigation tank network; Neeru-Chettu; Kolleru Lake as a natural flood buffer between the Krishna and Godavari deltas; Rayalaseema’s dependence on tanks and percolation structures in a scarce-rainfall zone.
Q82:
## Introduction

A watershed is a natural drainage unit — the area from which all runoff drains to a common outlet. It is the appropriate planning unit for rainfed agriculture because water, soil and vegetation behave as one system within it, so treating the whole unit is more effective than treating individual plots. The Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP), launched in 2009-10 by the Department of Land Resources, applied this principle at national scale.

## The lineage — essential for currency
- Pre-2009: three separate schemes — the Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP), Desert Development Programme (DDP) and Integrated Wastelands Development Programme (IWDP).
- 2009-10: these were consolidated into the Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP) on the recommendation of the Parthasarathy Committee, under the Common Guidelines for Watershed Development Projects (2008, revised 2011).
- 2015-16: IWMP was merged into the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana as its Watershed Development Component (WDC-PMKSY).
- 2021-26: continues as WDC-PMKSY 2.0, approved in December 2021 with a physical target of 49.50 lakh hectares and an indicative central outlay of Rs. 8,134 crore.

slope: bunding, gully plugs --> Mid slope: farm ponds --> Valley: check dams, percolation tanks . The ridge-to-valley principle is the technical core of the programme.

## Salient features

1. The watershed as the planning unit — projects are planned on hydrological rather than administrative boundaries, treating the entire catchment from ridge to valley.

2. The ridge-to-valley treatment sequence — treatment must begin at the highest point. Building a check dam in the valley while the ridge continues to erode simply fills the structure with silt. This sequencing is the programme’s defining technical discipline.

3. Cluster approach — micro-watersheds of about 1,000-5,000 hectares are clustered into projects of larger size to achieve economies of scale in planning and supervision.

4. Participatory institutional structure — a defining feature. Projects are implemented through: - Watershed Committees at village level, constituted by the gram sabha; - Watershed Development Teams providing technical support; - Self-Help Groups and User Groups for the landless and for specific assets; - Project Implementation Agencies at the district level; - State Level Nodal Agencies for coordination.

5. Equity provisions — a mandated share of benefits for the landless, women and vulnerable groups through livelihood and production-system components, recognising that watershed treatment on private land would otherwise benefit only landowners.

6. Livelihood orientation — the programme funds not only soil and water conservation but production systems and micro-enterprise, so that improved water availability translates into income.

7. Dedicated institutional and capacity funding — separate budget provision for administrative costs, capacity building, monitoring and evaluation, and for the entry point activities that build community confidence at the outset.

8. Phased implementation — a preparatory phase (entry point activities, institution building, detailed project report), a works phase (treatment and production systems), and a consolidation and withdrawal phase with handover to the community.

## What WDC-PMKSY 2.0 changed — the current position
- Revised cost norms: from Rs. 12,000 to Rs. 22,000 per hectare for plains and from Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 28,000 per hectare for hilly, difficult and Left Wing Extremism-affected areas.
- Springshed rejuvenation added as an activity, on NITI Aayog’s recommendation — significant for Himalayan and hilly regions where springs, not wells, are the water source.
- Project period reduced from 4-7 years to 3-5 years, addressing the criticism that long implementation diluted impact.
- Funding pattern of 60:40 between Centre and States (90:10 for hilly and North-Eastern States, 100% central for UTs).
- Mandated use of GIS and remote sensing in planning, with the Srishti Bhuvan-based web platform for satellite monitoring and comparison against Detailed Project Reports, and the Drishti mobile application for geotagged field photography — giving both the landscape view and ground truth.

## Outcomes and limitations

Outcomes: increased groundwater recharge and well water levels; extension of the cropped area and cropping intensity in treated watersheds; reduced soil erosion and runoff; increased fodder and biomass availability; and, in several evaluations, measurable income gains for participating households.

Limitations to acknowledge: uneven implementation quality across States; post-project maintenance, which frequently lapses once the implementing agency withdraws; benefit capture by larger landowners despite equity provisions; delays in fund release; and inadequate convergence with MGNREGA, agriculture and horticulture schemes, which would multiply the impact.

AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s Rayalaseema region — among India’s most drought-prone, with low and erratic rainfall on hard-rock terrain of poor groundwater potential — is precisely the setting watershed development was designed for, and has been a major implementation area under DPAP and its successors. The State’s Neeru-Chettu programme linked water conservation with plantation, and APCNF’s soil-moisture emphasis complements watershed treatment.

## Conclusion

The Integrated Watershed Management Programme’s enduring contribution is a principle rather than a set of structures: that rainfed land must be treated as a hydrological unit from ridge to valley, with the community as the managing institution. Its successor, WDC-PMKSY 2.0, has corrected the most cited weaknesses — inadequate cost norms, over-long project periods and weak monitoring, the last through Srishti and Drishti. The unresolved issue remains post-project maintenance, since a watershed treated once and then neglected reverts within a decade.

## Value addition
- The lineage to state: DPAP + DDP + IWDP –> IWMP (2009-10) –> merged into PMKSY as WDC (2015-16) –> WDC-PMKSY 2.0 (2021-26), with 49.50 lakh ha target and Rs. 8,134 crore indicative central outlay.
- Revised norms under 2.0: Rs. 22,000/ha (plains) and Rs. 28,000/ha (hilly, difficult, LWE); project period 3-5 years; 60:40 central-state funding (90:10 for hilly and NE States); springshed rejuvenation added.
- Monitoring platforms:Srishti — a customised Bhuvan web page for satellite-based monitoring, image comparison against DPRs, land-cover change analysis and a project dashboard; Drishti — the companion mobile app for geotagged field photography uploaded to the web-GIS server. Developed by NRSC with the Department of Land Resources.
- The ridge-to-valley principle: treatment must proceed from the highest point downward; a valley structure built before ridge treatment silts up. This single technical point is the most frequently tested element of watershed questions.
- Related programmes for convergence: MGNREGA (water conservation works); Atal Bhujal Yojana; Per Drop More Crop; Mission Amrit Sarovar; Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain; Neeru-Chettu (AP); Mission Kakatiya (Telangana); Jalyukt Shivar (Maharashtra).
- Institutional structure: Watershed Committee (gram sabha constituted), Watershed Development Team, User Groups and SHGs, Project Implementation Agency, State Level Nodal Agency — with mandated provision for the landless, women and vulnerable groups.
- AP-specific: Rayalaseema as a priority watershed region (Anantapur, Kurnool, Kadapa, Chittoor); hard-rock hydrogeology limiting groundwater potential and making recharge structures essential; Neeru-Chettu; APCNF’s complementary soil-moisture practices.

Sources used: Ministry of Mines — record mineral production data for FY 2024-25, MMDR Act 1957 as amended, National Mineral Policy 2019 and the National Critical Mineral Mission 2025; Geological Survey of India and Indian Bureau of Mines; Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023; Champion and Seth, A Revised Survey of the Forest Types of India (1968); MoEFCC — Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam 1980 as amended 2023, Green India Mission, MISHTI and the Green Credit Programme; Ministry of Tribal Affairs on Forest Rights Act minor forest produce provisions; CPCSEA and the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960, with the 2023 amendment to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act enabling non-animal test methods; Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development — WDC-PMKSY 2.0 guidelines, cost norms and targets, with NRSC’s Srishti and Drishti platforms; Ministry of Jal Shakti — Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain, Atal Bhujal Yojana and Mission Amrit Sarovar; MNRE on non-fossil capacity as on 31 March 2026; Government of Andhra Pradesh — Neeru-Chettu, APMDC, Vana Samrakshana Samithis and APCNF.

Q83:
## Introduction

Interlinking of rivers (ILR) proposes transferring water from basins assessed as surplus to those assessed as deficit, through a network of link canals, reservoirs and lift systems. Its rationale is a striking spatial imbalance: the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna system carries a large share of India’s water resources while draining a much smaller share of its area, and peninsular India experiences recurrent drought in the same years that the east floods. The National Perspective Plan (1980) and the National Water Development Agency (NWDA, 1982) identify 30 links — 16 peninsular and 14 Himalayan.

## How it is intended to conserve water
- Balancing surplus and deficit basins. Transfer from the Ganga-Brahmaputra and from the Mahanadi-Godavari system to the water-short Krishna, Pennar and Cauvery basins, and to western India.
- Flood and drought moderation. Storage created by link reservoirs detains monsoon flow, reducing peak discharge in flood-prone eastern basins while providing carryover for lean-season release in drought-prone regions.
- Reducing “wastage to the sea”. The founding argument holds that water reaching the sea unused is lost — a claim examined critically below.
- Groundwater recharge in command areas receiving assured surface water, relieving pressure on aquifers.
- Assured year-round availability for irrigation, drinking water and industry.

## Contribution to social and economic development
- Irrigation and food security. The full ILR programme is projected to add substantial irrigation potential; the Ken-Betwa Link Project alone is designed to provide annual irrigation to about 10.62 lakh hectares and drinking water to some 62 lakh people in the chronically drought-prone Bundelkhand region of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
- Drinking water security for water-stressed districts and towns.
- Hydropower — Ken-Betwa includes about 103 MW of hydropower and 27 MW of solar capacity.
- Employment during construction and in the expanded agricultural economy thereafter.
- Inland navigation on augmented channels, reducing freight cost.
- Fisheries and allied livelihoods in new reservoirs.
- Reducing regional inequality by extending assured irrigation to rainfed regions that have historically lagged.

## The critical assessment — what “discuss” requires

Hydrological objections — the strongest technical case against: - The surplus-deficit assessment is contested. Basins classified as surplus may not be so in dry years, and climate change is altering the very flow patterns on which the classification was based. A link designed to transfer surplus may find none when it is most needed — since droughts are frequently regional and simultaneous. - Water reaching the sea is not wasted. Freshwater outflow maintains estuarine salinity gradients essential for fish breeding, delivers the sediment that sustains deltas against erosion and sea-level rise, and flushes pollutants. Reduced outflow contributes to delta starvation and coastal erosion — a real cost that the “wastage” framing omits, and directly relevant to the Godavari and Krishna deltas. - Evaporation losses from long open canals and reservoirs in hot regions can be substantial, reducing the water actually delivered.

Environmental and social objections: - Submergence of forest and habitat — Ken-Betwa affects part of the Panna Tiger Reserve, requiring wildlife clearance and a landscape management plan. - Displacement and rehabilitation obligations, and the disruption of river ecology and fish migration. -Interference with the natural flood pulse on which floodplain ecosystems and recession agriculture depend.

Institutional and financial objections: - Inter-State water disputes. Water is a State subject under the Constitution (Entry 17, State List), with the Union competent over inter-State rivers (Entry 56, Union List). Consensus between basin States is the binding constraint, and the Krishna and Cauvery disputes illustrate the difficulty. - Very large capital cost and long gestation; opportunity cost against decentralised alternatives. - Command area inefficiency — transferring water into systems that then lose much of it to conveyance losses and flood irrigation reduces the benefit realised.

## The AP dimension

The Godavari-Cauvery link — proposed to carry Godavari water through the Krishna and Pennar to the Cauvery — passes directly through Andhra Pradesh, making the State both a transit and a beneficiary jurisdiction, and giving it a direct interest in the volumes, timing and cost-sharing involved. Inter-basin transfer within the State, notably the Polavaram-Banakacherla proposal to carry Godavari water to Rayalaseema, has been the subject of inter-State discussion with Telangana. Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram form the existing transfer and storage backbone, and the Pattiseema lift scheme already transfers Godavari water to the Krishna delta.

## The complementary approach

ILR is not an alternative to demand-side and decentralised measures: micro-irrigation under Per Drop More Crop, watershed treatment under WDC-PMKSY 2.0, groundwater recharge under Atal Bhujal Yojana, revival of traditional tanks, crop diversification away from water-intensive cultivation in dry regions, and reduction of canal conveyance losses. Transferring water into an inefficient system multiplies the loss.

## Conclusion

Interlinking addresses a real problem — India’s water is distributed unevenly in both space and time — and Ken-Betwa demonstrates that the concept can move from plan to construction. But the surplus-deficit premise is less secure than it appears under a changing climate, and freshwater outflow to the sea performs ecological functions the “wastage” framing overlooks. The defensible position is selective implementation of links with demonstrated hydrological surplus, robust rehabilitation and environmental flow provisions, and simultaneous investment in demand management — since a link canal delivering water into a flood-irrigated command achieves far less than its cost implies.

## Value addition
- Institutional structure:National Perspective Plan (1980); National Water Development Agency (1982) under the Ministry of Jal Shakti; 30 identified links — 16 peninsular and 14 Himalayan; a Special Committee on ILR constituted following Supreme Court direction (2012).
- Ken-Betwa Link Project — the operative case: the first ILR project under implementation; approved by the Union Cabinet in December 2021 with an outlay of about Rs. 44,605 crore; Daudhan dam in Madhya Pradesh as the key structure; designed for about 10.62 lakh ha of annual irrigation, drinking water for about 62 lakh people, and 103 MW hydropower plus 27 MW solar; affects part of Panna Tiger Reserve, requiring a landscape management plan.
- Other priority links: Damanganga-Pinjal; Par-Tapi-Narmada; Kosi-Mechi; Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal (agreed between MP and Rajasthan); Godavari-Cauvery, the largest peninsular link, routed through Andhra Pradesh.
- Constitutional position: water is Entry 17 in the State List; regulation of inter-State rivers is Entry 56 in the Union List; the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (amended 2019) governs adjudication — the reason ILR is as much a federalism question as an engineering one.
- The ecological case for outflow: estuarine salinity balance for fish breeding; sediment delivery sustaining deltas against erosion and sea-level rise; pollutant flushing; mangrove and coastal ecosystem maintenance.
- AP-specific:Godavari-Cauvery link transiting the State; Pattiseema lift scheme transferring Godavari water to the Krishna delta; Polavaram as the anchor project; Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam; Rayalaseema as the intended beneficiary region of intra-State transfer.
