## Introduction

Water is the resource on which every other one depends, and human activity has altered it in three distinct ways: by withdrawing more than is replenished, by contaminating what remains, and by re-engineering the pathways water follows. India holds about 4% of the world’s freshwater for 18% of its population, which makes each of these alterations consequential.

## (a) Human impact on water resources

sewage, runoff) | Diversion (dams, canals) | Land-use change (concretisation, deforestation) .

- Over-extraction — the largest single impact. India is the world’s largest user of groundwater, and extraction exceeds recharge in many blocks, particularly in the north-west and peninsular hard-rock regions. The NITI Aayog Composite Water Management Index (2018) projected severe groundwater stress in major cities and estimated that a large share of the population faces high to extreme water stress. The mechanism is a collective-action failure: cheap submersible pumps and subsidised power made individual extraction rational while collectively depleting a shared aquifer.
- Pollution. Untreated sewage is the largest contributor by volume; a substantial proportion of urban sewage is discharged without treatment. Industrial effluent adds heavy metals and chemicals, and agricultural runoff adds nitrates and phosphates, causing eutrophication. CPCB’s assessment of water quality identified 311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers in its 2022 review, based on biochemical oxygen demand — the standard figure to cite.
- Dams, diversion and channel modification. Storage and diversion alter flow regimes, block fish migration, interrupt sediment transport (starving deltas and accelerating coastal erosion), submerge forest and displace communities, and cause waterlogging and salinisation in command areas through over-irrigation.
- Land-use change. Urban concretisation prevents infiltration, so cities simultaneously flood in the monsoon and face scarcity in summer; deforestation reduces catchment retention and increases runoff and siltation; wetland encroachment removes natural storage and filtration.
- Climate change. Erratic monsoon, more intense rainfall in fewer events, glacial retreat affecting Himalayan river flow, and higher evaporation — all reducing usable availability while raising demand.
- Coastal and groundwater quality. Over-extraction near the coast draws in saline intrusion; geogenic contamination by fluoride and arsenic affects large populations, and is worsened by deeper drilling.

Policy responses:Jal Jeevan Mission (rural tap water); Atal Bhujal Yojana (participatory groundwater management); Namami Gange; National Water Mission targeting a 20% improvement in water use efficiency; Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain; Per Drop More Crop; Composite Water Management Index for State ranking.

## (b)(i) Sustainable agriculture
- Definition: farming that meets present food and fibre needs while maintaining the ecological, soil and water resource base on which future production depends, and remaining economically viable for the farmer.
- The three pillars: environmental soundness, economic viability, social equity.
- Practices: crop rotation and diversification; integrated pest management reducing pesticide dependence; balanced and organic nutrient management; conservation tillage and residue retention; micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler) under Per Drop More Crop; agroforestry; and precision agriculture using soil and satellite data through the Krishi Decision Support System.
- Indian programmes:National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture; National Mission on Natural Farming; Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana; Soil Health Card; Shree Anna for millets; PMFBY for risk transfer.
- Water-specific gains: the System of Rice Intensification (SRI) — wider spacing, younger seedlings and intermittent rather than continuous flooding — reduces water use substantially while maintaining or raising yield, and has been promoted in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Alternate Wetting and Drying in paddy achieves both water saving and methane reduction.
- AP instance:Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming (APCNF), run through Rythu Sadhikara Samstha, covers over 1.77 million farmers across 8,168 gram panchayats, with reported water savings of up to 50%, income gains of 38-66% and emission reductions up to 46% per acre — among the world’s largest agroecology programmes and winner of the 2026 Food Planet Prize.

## (b)(ii) Acid rain
- Definition: precipitation with pH below about 5.6 — the natural acidity of rainwater from dissolved CO2 — caused by atmospheric conversion of sulphur dioxide to sulphuric acid and nitrogen oxides to nitric acid.
- Sources: coal combustion in power plants and smelters (SO2); vehicle and high-temperature combustion (NOx).
- Impacts: acidification of lakes and streams killing fish and invertebrates; leaching of soil nutrients and mobilisation of toxic aluminium; forest dieback; corrosion of buildings and monuments — “stone leprosy” on marble and limestone, as documented on the Taj Mahal; and respiratory harm from the precursor gases and secondary particulates.
- The transboundary character: precursor gases travel hundreds of kilometres before deposition, which is why acid rain required an international treaty — the Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (1979).
- Indian response:M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Taj Trapezium case, 1996), directing 292 industries in the Taj Trapezium Zone to switch to natural gas or relocate; mandatory flue gas desulphurisation at thermal power stations; BS-VI fuel with sharply reduced sulphur from April 2020; SO2 and NOx limits under the NAAQS 2009 and the National Clean Air Programme.

(Treated more fully at Q117.)

## Conclusion

Human impact on water operates through withdrawal, contamination and diversion, and India’s position — a small share of global freshwater supporting a large share of the world’s population — leaves little margin for any of them. Sustainable agriculture is the single most consequential response, because agriculture accounts for the overwhelming majority of India’s water use, and practices such as SRI and natural farming demonstrate that substantial savings are achievable without yield loss. Acid rain, by contrast, shows what focused regulation can achieve when sources are few and technological fixes exist.

## Value addition
- Water data to cite: India holds about 4% of global freshwater for 18% of world population; agriculture accounts for the overwhelming majority of national water withdrawal; 311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers (CPCB, 2022 assessment); NITI Aayog Composite Water Management Index (2018) for State-wise stress ranking.
- Groundwater governance:Central Ground Water Board block categorisation into safe, semi-critical, critical and over-exploited; Atal Bhujal Yojana with village water security plans; Master Plan for Artificial Recharge.
- PMKSY components:AIBP (Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme), Har Khet Ko Pani, Per Drop More Crop, and the Watershed Development Component — mottoes “Har Khet Ko Paani” and “More Crop Per Drop”.
- Sustainable agriculture instruments: NMSA; National Mission on Natural Farming; Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana; SRI and Alternate Wetting and Drying; Soil Health Card; APCNF in Andhra Pradesh.
- Acid rain chemistry: natural rain pH about 5.6; SO2 –> SO₃ –> H2SO₄; NOx –> HNO₃; wet and dry deposition; Taj Trapezium Zone of about 10,400 sq km.
- AP-specific: APCNF; SRI promotion; Krishna and Godavari delta salinity and drainage congestion; Kolleru Lake eutrophication from aquaculture and fertiliser runoff; Rayalaseema groundwater depletion in hard-rock terrain.

## Introduction

Integrated Water Resource Management (IWRM) is defined by the Global Water Partnership as “a process which promotes the coordinated development and management of water, land and related resources in order to maximise economic and social welfare in an equitable manner without compromising the sustainability of vital ecosystems.” Its premise is that water cannot be managed sector by sector — irrigation, drinking water, industry and ecology draw on one resource, and decisions in each affect all the others.

## The Dublin Principles (1992) — the foundation of IWRM
- Principle 1: Freshwater is a finite and vulnerable resource, essential to sustain life, development and the environment — hence the basin, not the administrative boundary, is the management unit.
- Principle 2: Water development and management should be based on a participatory approach, involving users, planners and policymakers at all levels — the basis for Water User Associations.
- Principle 3:Women play a central part in the provision, management and safeguarding of water, since they bear the primary burden of collection.
- Principle 4: Water has an economic value in all its competing uses and should be recognised as an economic good — while also being recognised as a basic right, a tension IWRM has to hold.

## What IWRM integrates — the conceptual core
- Across sectors — irrigation, drinking water, industry, hydropower, navigation, fisheries and environmental flows planned together rather than in competition.
- Across sources — surface water, groundwater, rainwater and recycled water treated as one resource, since they are hydrologically connected; pumping groundwater depletes river base flow.
- Across scales and jurisdictions — from field to basin, and across State boundaries where basins are shared.
- Across upstream and downstream — recognising that upstream abstraction and pollution determine downstream availability and quality.

## Key elements
- River basin as the planning unit, with basin organisations for coordination.
- Participatory management through user associations at the distributary and minor level.
- Demand management through pricing, volumetric supply, micro-irrigation and crop choice, alongside supply augmentation.
- Environmental flows provided for as a legitimate use, not a residual.
- Data and decision support — hydrological monitoring, India-WRIS, and remote sensing.
- Institutional and legal reform — clear entitlements, regulatory authorities and dispute resolution.

India’s IWRM instruments: the National Water Policy, 2012 (which explicitly endorses IWRM and basin-level planning); the National Water Mission under NAPCC with its 20% water-use efficiency goal; river basin organisations; Namami Gange as a basin-scale programme; Atal Bhujal Yojana; India-WRIS; and the draft National Water Framework Bill.

## Importance of Water User Associations (WUAs)

What they are: statutory bodies of farmers within a defined irrigation command — typically a minor or distributary — responsible for operating, maintaining and distributing water within their area, and collecting water charges. They are the institutional expression of Dublin Principle 2.

The Andhra Pradesh precedent — the point a State examination expects. Andhra Pradesh enacted the AP Farmers’ Management of Irrigation Systems Act, 1997, one of India’s earliest and most far-reaching participatory irrigation management laws. It transferred management responsibility to elected farmer bodies across the State’s irrigation systems in a single step, established a three-tier structure — Water User Associations at the minor level, Distributary Committees, and Project Committees — and became a national reference point, studied and partly emulated by other States.

## Why WUAs matter
- Equity in distribution — the tail-end problem. In any canal system, head-reach farmers can take water first and leave tail-enders short. A WUA with authority over rotation and scheduling is the mechanism through which tail-end farmers obtain their share; this is the single strongest justification for the institution.
- Improved efficiency. Farmers who manage the channel have direct incentive to reduce seepage, desilt regularly and prevent unauthorised outlets — maintenance that a distant department cannot supervise.
- Better maintenance and cost recovery. Local collection of water charges, with a share retained for local maintenance, links payment visibly to service and improves recovery rates.
- Conflict resolution at source. Disputes over turns and shares are settled within the community rather than escalating to the department or the courts.
- Local knowledge. Farmers know their channels, soils and cropping calendars in detail no departmental schedule can capture.
- Reduced government burden, allowing the irrigation department to concentrate on headworks and main canals.
- Empowerment and inclusion, with provision for women’s and small farmers’ representation.
- Enabling demand management. Volumetric supply to a WUA, with internal distribution left to the association, is the practical route to charging for water by volume rather than by area — the reform most likely to induce efficient use.

## Challenges to acknowledge

Elite capture by larger landowners; irregular elections and weakened functioning over time; inadequate financial devolution, so associations carry responsibility without resources; limited technical capacity; tension with panchayati raj institutions over jurisdiction; and low participation where water is abundant and the incentive to organise is weak.

## Conclusion

IWRM’s contribution is a change of unit and of frame: managing the basin rather than the project, and treating water as a single resource with competing legitimate claims including the environment’s. Water User Associations are the institutional layer that makes this operational at field level, and Andhra Pradesh’s 1997 Act demonstrated that transfer of management to farmers can be legislated at scale. Their effectiveness depends on genuine devolution of funds and authority — an association responsible for maintenance without the money to perform it will not survive its first silting season.

## Value addition
- The Dublin Principles (1992) — finite and vulnerable resource; participatory approach; central role of women; water as an economic good. These four supply the intellectual content of IWRM and are worth naming.
- National Water Policy, 2012: endorses IWRM and river basin planning; treats water as an economic good while guaranteeing a minimum quantity as a right; emphasises demand management, water-use efficiency, and provision for environmental flows; recommends a Water Regulatory Authority in each State.
- AP Farmers’ Management of Irrigation Systems Act, 1997: three-tier structure — Water User Associations (minor), Distributary Committees, Project Committees; state-wide transfer in a single step; a national reference point for participatory irrigation management.
- Constitutional and legal context: water as Entry 17 of the State List; Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (amended 2019 creating a single permanent tribunal with benches); the Dam Safety Act, 2021.
- Related instruments:India-WRIS for water resources data; Composite Water Management Index (NITI Aayog); Jal Jeevan Mission; Atal Bhujal Yojana, which is explicitly built on participatory village water security plans; Namami Gange as basin-scale management.
- Concepts to name:environmental flows; conjunctive use of surface and groundwater; volumetric supply; tail-end deprivation; basin closure (where all available water is already allocated); virtual water embedded in traded crops.
- AP-specific: the 1997 Act and its WUA structure; Krishna and Godavari delta systems; Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam commands; Neeru-Chettu; APCNF’s water savings.

## Introduction

Wasteland is land that is degraded and currently unproductive, or performing below its potential owing to natural or human-induced constraints. India’s Wastelands Atlas (5th edition, 2019), prepared by the Department of Land Resources with NRSC, mapped wasteland at about 55.76 million hectares — 16.96% of India’s geographical area in 2015-16, reduced from 56.60 million hectares in 2008-09. Separately, the Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (ISRO/SAC) assesses a substantially larger area as degraded, since degradation includes productive land losing quality.

## Types of wasteland — because the strategy depends on the type
- **Type** — Principal cause · Reclamation approach
- **Saline and alkaline (usar) land** — Over-irrigation, poor drainage, high water table · Gypsum application, leaching with drainage, salt- tolerant species
- **Ravines and gullied land** — Water erosion on unconsolidated soils · Gully plugging, check dams, contour bunding, vegetative barriers
- **Waterlogged and marshy land** — Canal seepage, blocked drainage · Surface and subsurface drainage, biodrainage with eucalyptus
- **Degraded forest and shifting-cultivation land** — Over-extraction, fire, jhum cycles · Afforestation, JFM, alternative livelihoods
- **Mining and industrial wasteland** — Overburden dumps, tailings, quarries · Regrading, topsoil respreading, revegetation
- **Sandy and desert land** — Aridity, wind erosion · Shelterbelts, sand dune stabilisation, drought-tolerant species

## Strategies for reclamation

1. Biological and vegetative methods - Afforestation and reforestation — establishing tree cover binds soil, reduces runoff, adds organic matter and recharges groundwater. Species must be matched to the site: casuarina for coastal sands, prosopis and acacia for arid zones, eucalyptus for waterlogged land (biodrainage), and salt-tolerant species such as Salvadora and Atriplex for saline soils. - Agroforestry and silvipasture — integrating trees with crops or pasture, which makes reclamation economically self-sustaining rather than dependent on continued subsidy. Supported by India’s National Agroforestry Policy, 2014. - Phytoremediation — using plants to extract, stabilise or degrade contaminants and salts; particularly relevant for mining and industrially contaminated land. - Green manuring and legume introduction — nitrogen fixation restoring fertility; Sesbania and dhaincha are standard on reclaimed alkaline soils. - Grasses and pioneer species — establishing ground cover first, since bare soil cannot support trees; ecological succession is then allowed to proceed.

2. Soil and water management - Terracing and contour ploughing on slopes, breaking slope length and reducing runoff velocity. - Bunding — contour, graded and field bunds to retain moisture and arrest erosion. - Mulching and residue retention, conserving moisture and building organic matter. - Crop rotation and mixed cropping, restoring nutrient balance and breaking pest cycles. - Leaching and drainage for saline-alkaline soils — the specific technical sequence being gypsum application (calcium replacing sodium on the soil exchange complex), followed by leaching with good-quality water, with subsurface drainage to carry the displaced salts away. Without drainage, leaching merely relocates the salt. - Soil amendments — lime for acidity, gypsum for alkalinity, organic manure and biofertilisers for fertility.

3. Physical and mechanical structures - Check dams, gully plugs and gabion structures to arrest erosion and recharge groundwater. - Sand dune stabilisation using micro-windbreaks and shelterbelts. - Regrading and backfilling of mined land, followed by respreading of preserved topsoil. - Strip cropping and vegetative barriers — vetiver hedges are widely used for their deep binding roots.

4. Institutional, community and technological measures - Community participation — reclamation without local ownership does not survive the project period; Joint Forest Management and Vana Samrakshana Samithis provide the institutional form. - Geospatial technology — the Wastelands Atlas and Bhuvan for mapping and change detection; Srishti and Drishti for watershed monitoring; satellite-based tracking of reclamation progress. - Convergence of schemes — MGNREGA for labour-intensive earthworks; WDC-PMKSY 2.0 for watershed treatment; Green India Mission and CAMPA for afforestation; the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture; the Green Credit Programme for plantation on degraded land. - Secure tenure, since no one invests in restoring land they may not retain — which is why the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and land record digitisation are indirectly reclamation measures.

## Conclusion

Wasteland reclamation succeeds when the treatment is matched to the specific cause of degradation — gypsum and drainage for alkaline soils, gully plugging for ravines, biodrainage for waterlogging — rather than applied as a uniform package of tree planting. Its greater determinant, however, is institutional: reclaimed land reverts within a few seasons unless the community that manages it has both secure tenure and an economic return from the restored land. This is why agroforestry and silvipasture, which make restoration profitable, are more durable than plantation programmes that do not. India’s commitment to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030 under the UNCCD will be met, if it is met, through that combination.

## Value addition
- Wasteland data:Wastelands Atlas of India, 5th edition (2019), Department of Land Resources with NRSC — about 55.76 million ha, 16.96% of geographical area (2015-16), reduced from 56.60 million ha in 2008-09; the Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (ISRO/SAC) provides the wider degradation assessment.
- India’s international commitment: to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030, announced at UNCCD COP14 (New Delhi, 2019), contributing to Land Degradation Neutrality under SDG 15.3; also the Bonn Challenge pledge on forest landscape restoration.
- The saline-alkaline reclamation sequence — the most technically specific point:gypsum (calcium sulphate) application –> calcium replaces sodium on the soil exchange complex –> leaching with good-quality water –> subsurface drainage to remove displaced salts –> salt-tolerant pioneer crops (dhaincha, rice) –> normal cropping. Omitting drainage causes the salts to return.
- Species for specific conditions: casuarina (coastal sand); prosopis, acacia and khejri (arid); eucalyptus (biodrainage in waterlogged land); vetiver (erosion barriers); Salvadora and Atriplex (saline soils); Sesbania/dhaincha (green manure on alkaline land).
- Institutions:Central Soil Salinity Research Institute (CSSRI), Karnal; ICAR-IISWC (Indian Institute of Soil and Water Conservation), Dehradun; CAZRI, Jodhpur for arid zone research; National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning, Nagpur.
- Scheme convergence: MGNREGA; WDC-PMKSY 2.0; Green India Mission; CAMPA; Green Credit Programme; National Agroforestry Policy 2014; Soil Health Card.

Q143 asks why wasteland development is needed, which Q142 does not. This answer therefore leads with the rationale — land hunger, food security, climate commitments and livelihood — and treats reclamation methods compactly, cross-referencing Q142 for the technical detail.

Wasteland development is the restoration of degraded and unproductive land to productive ecological or economic use. India’s need for it is acute and arithmetical: the country supports about 18% of the world’s population on roughly 2.4% of its land area, while about 55.76 million hectares — 16.96% of geographical area — remains classified as wasteland (Wastelands Atlas, 2019). Land is the one resource that cannot be created, so restoring what has been degraded is the only route to expanding the productive base.

## (i) The need for wasteland development

| Livelihoods | International commitments .

- Land scarcity and competing demand. Net sown area has plateaued while demand for land from urbanisation, industry and infrastructure grows. Since agricultural land cannot expand into new territory, restoring degraded land is the only supply-side option — this is the fundamental argument.
- Food and nutritional security. A growing population with rising per-capita consumption requires higher output from a fixed area; bringing wasteland into production adds to the base rather than intensifying pressure on already-cultivated land.
- Fodder and fuelwood security. Degraded common land was historically the grazing and fuelwood resource of the landless and small livestock keepers. Its restoration directly benefits those with no land of their own — making wasteland development an equity intervention, not only a productivity one.
- Employment and rural livelihoods. Reclamation is labour-intensive; through MGNREGA, wasteland works simultaneously provide wages and create a durable asset.
- Ecological restoration. Reversing soil erosion, restoring hydrological function and groundwater recharge, rebuilding habitat and reconnecting fragmented landscapes.
- Climate mitigation. Restored land sequesters carbon in soil and biomass — directly contributing to India’s NDC commitment of an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2030.
- Arresting desertification. Land degradation is self-reinforcing: loss of vegetation exposes soil, erosion removes the fertile layer, and productivity falls further. Intervention becomes exponentially more expensive the longer it is delayed, which is why the need is urgent rather than merely desirable.
- International commitments. India has pledged to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030 (announced at UNCCD COP14, New Delhi, 2019), pursuing Land Degradation Neutrality under SDG 15.3, alongside its Bonn Challenge commitment.
- Reducing distress migration. Land degradation is a documented driver of out-migration from rainfed regions; restoring local productivity addresses the cause rather than the symptom.
- Renewable energy siting. Degraded and barren land is increasingly used for solar parks — NISE’s assessment of 748 GW of solar potential is premised on using just 3% of India’s wasteland — making wasteland an energy-transition asset as well as an agricultural one.

## (ii) Reclamation of wastelands — in brief

(For the full technical treatment, see Q142.)

- Match the method to the cause. Saline-alkaline land requires gypsum, leaching and subsurface drainage; ravines require gully plugging and check dams; waterlogged land requires drainage or biodrainage; mining wasteland requires regrading, topsoil respreading and revegetation; sandy land requires shelterbelts and dune stabilisation.
- Biological methods — afforestation with site-matched species; agroforestry and silvipasture, which make restoration economically self-sustaining; phytoremediation; green manuring with legumes; and grass and pioneer establishment before tree planting.
- Soil and water conservation — contour bunding, terracing, mulching, crop rotation, check dams and percolation structures under WDC-PMKSY 2.0.
- Institutional measures — community management through Joint Forest Management and Vana Samrakshana Samithis; secure tenure, since no one invests in land they may lose; and convergence of MGNREGA, Green India Mission, CAMPA and the Green Credit Programme.

## Conclusion

Wasteland development is needed because India cannot create land but can restore it, and because degraded land is disproportionately the resource of those with nothing else — the landless grazier, the fuelwood collector, the rainfed smallholder. Restoration therefore serves productivity, equity, carbon sequestration and India’s international commitments at once. Its success depends less on technique, which is well established, than on whether the community that manages restored land has secure tenure and an economic stake in keeping it productive.

## Introduction

Solid waste is any discarded solid or semi-solid material arising from human activity that is neither liquid effluent nor gaseous emission. Its classification is operationally decisive: the treatment route is determined by the waste’s composition, so characterisation precedes management. India generates about 1,70,339 tonnes per day of municipal solid waste, of which roughly 92% is collected and about 54% processed (CPCB, 2021-22).

## (a) Types of solid waste

hazardous / hazardous) , showing that the two classifications cut across each other.

- Municipal solid waste (MSW) — household, commercial and institutional refuse: food waste, paper, cardboard, plastics, textiles, glass, metal and garden waste. India’s MSW is 30-55% organic with high moisture content, which shapes every downstream decision.
- Industrial waste — from manufacturing: sludge, chemical by-products, fly ash, process residues and mining tailings; composition varies entirely by industry.
- Hazardous waste — toxic, reactive, flammable, corrosive or infectious: used batteries, solvents, pesticide containers, and specified industrial residues, governed by the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016.
- Bio-medical waste — from hospitals, clinics and laboratories: anatomical waste, sharps, contaminated dressings and expired pharmaceuticals, under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 with its yellow, red, white and blue colour-coded segregation.
- E-waste — discarded electrical and electronic equipment, containing both recoverable metals and toxic substances; the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 cover 106 categories including solar PV modules.
- Construction and demolition waste — concrete, brick, wood, metal and rubble; largely inert but very high in volume, under the C&D Waste Management Rules, 2016.
- Agricultural waste — crop residue, husk, spoiled produce and animal manure.
- Plastic waste and battery waste, each with its own EPR-based rule-set.
- Radioactive waste, regulated separately by the AERB.

## Characteristics of solid waste
- Physical characteristics.Density determines collection vehicle design and transport economics — Indian MSW is denser than Western waste because of higher organic content, so compactor design differs. Moisture content is high in Indian waste, which reduces calorific value and complicates combustion. Particle size and composition determine segregation and sorting technology.
- Chemical characteristics.Proximate analysis — moisture, volatile matter, fixed carbon and ash. Calorific value, which determines whether energy recovery is viable; Indian MSW’s high moisture gives it low calorific value, which is the technical reason mass-burn incineration performs poorly here. Ultimate analysis (C, H, O, N, S) and the C:N ratio, which governs composting efficiency; pH and heavy metal content determine whether compost is safe for agricultural use.
- Biological characteristics. The biodegradable fraction — food and garden waste — decomposes readily, making it suitable for composting and biomethanation, but hazardous in landfills where anaerobic decomposition generates methane, a greenhouse gas roughly 28 times as potent as CO2 over a century. Biodegradability is measured through volatile solids and the lignin content, since lignin resists decomposition.

## (b)(i) Pyrolysis
- Definition: thermal decomposition of organic material at elevated temperature in the absence of oxygen — this is the single defining variable.
- Process: waste is heated in a sealed reactor, typically at 400-800deg C. Because no oxygen is present, the material does not combust; instead complex organic molecules break down into simpler ones.
- Three outputs:syngas (a combustible gas mixture of hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methane); pyrolysis oil or bio-oil (a liquid fuel); and char (a solid carbon-rich residue, usable as a soil amendment or fuel).
- Advantages: produces recoverable fuel products rather than merely destroying material; lower emissions of dioxins and NOx than incineration because combustion does not occur; and the outputs can be stored and transported.
- Applications: best suited to homogeneous, dry, high-carbon streams — waste plastics, used tyres and biomass — rather than mixed municipal waste. Plastic-to-fuel and tyre pyrolysis are the principal Indian applications; biochar production from agricultural residue is an emerging use with carbon-sequestration value.
- Limitations: high capital cost, sensitivity to feedstock consistency, and the need for pre-sorting and drying.

## (b)(ii) Incineration
- Definition: controlled combustion of waste in the presence of sufficient oxygen — the direct contrast with pyrolysis.
- Process: waste is burned at 850-1,100deg C in a specialised furnace. Bio-medical waste incineration requires the higher end of this range with a specified residence time to ensure destruction of pathogens and organic toxins.
- Volume and mass reduction: reduces waste volume by up to about 90% and mass by up to about 75% — its principal advantage where land is scarce.
- Outputs:heat and energy, recovered as steam to drive turbines in waste-to-energy plants; flue gas, which must pass through scrubbers, bag filters and electrostatic precipitators to remove particulates, acid gases, dioxins and heavy metals before release; and ash — bottom ash from the furnace and fly ash from the pollution control system, the latter classified as hazardous waste requiring secure disposal.
- Applications: municipal waste in land-scarce cities; and, critically, bio-medical and specified hazardous waste, where the objective is destruction rather than recovery.
- Why it underperforms on Indian MSW — the point worth making: with 30-55% organic content and high moisture, Indian municipal waste has low calorific value, so incinerators frequently require auxiliary fuel to sustain combustion. This makes them expensive to run and undermines the energy recovery that justifies them. Segregation and pre-processing into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) — which can also be co-fired in cement kilns — is generally the more viable route.

## Conclusion

Classification and characterisation of solid waste are not preliminaries to management but its determinants: density decides collection design, calorific value decides whether energy recovery is viable, and the C:N ratio decides whether composting will work. Pyrolysis and incineration illustrate this directly — they differ by a single variable, the presence of oxygen, and that difference determines whether the output is fuel or heat. For Indian waste, with its high organic and moisture content, the characterisation points clearly toward segregation, composting and biomethanation ahead of thermal treatment.

## Value addition
- The defining distinction:pyrolysis = no oxygen (thermal decomposition, yields syngas, bio-oil and char); incineration = excess oxygen (combustion, yields heat, flue gas and ash); gasification = limited oxygen (partial oxidation, yields syngas) — the third member of the set, worth naming.
- Indian waste data (CPCB, 2021-22): generation 1,70,339 TPD; collection about 92%; processing 54%; landfilled 24%; MSW composition roughly 30-55% organic with high moisture.
- Waste rule-sets to name: Solid Waste Management Rules 2016; Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016; Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016; E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 (106 categories including solar PV modules); Plastic Waste Management Rules; Battery Waste Rules 2022; C&D Waste Rules 2016.
- Bio-medical waste colour coding (BMW Rules 2016):yellow (anatomical, soiled, chemical, expired drugs); red (contaminated recyclable plastics); white/translucent (sharps); blue (glassware and metallic implants).
- Technical terms:proximate and ultimate analysis; calorific value; C:N ratio (optimum around 25-30:1 for composting); volatile solids; bottom ash versus fly ash; refuse-derived fuel; biochar.
- AP-specific (from the original, worth retaining): the CLAP — Clean Andhra Pradesh mission for state-wide solid waste infrastructure; Swachh Andhra Corporation; legacy waste processing of about 85 lakh metric tonnes (roughly 59% of the State’s legacy waste); around 3,100 TPD of dry waste processed through Material Recovery Facilities; a waste-to-energy facility at Visakhapatnam; and about 235 MLD of treated water reused across 14 ULBs for landscaping, industry and road sprinkling.

## Introduction

India’s urban population rose from 31.16% at Census 2011 to an estimated share above a third today, and is projected to approach 40% by 2036 (National Commission on Population). A necessary clarification at the outset: urbanisation is not the problem — it is the principal driver of productivity and income growth. The problem is unplanned urbanisation, where population growth outpaces the provision of housing, water, drainage, transport and waste services. The objective is therefore to manage urban growth, not to arrest it.

## Problems of unplanned urbanisation

Housing and settlements - Slum proliferation. Census 2011 recorded about 6.55 crore slum dwellers, roughly 17% of the urban population. Inadequate affordable housing pushes migrants into informal settlements without tenure, water, sanitation or drainage. - Land and housing affordability, with speculative land pricing pushing the poor to the periphery, lengthening commutes and raising transport cost as a share of income.

Infrastructure - Water supply and sewerage. A large share of urban sewage is discharged untreated; intermittent supply is the norm in most cities. - Solid waste. India generates about 1,70,339 TPD, with roughly 92% collected but only 54% processed (CPCB, 2021-22) — so the deficit is now in processing rather than collection. - Transport. Rapid motorisation without commensurate public transport produces congestion, with measurable losses in productivity and fuel.

Environment - Air pollution. Indian cities feature prominently in global city rankings of particulate pollution compiled by IQAir’s World Air Quality Report — a private index, which should be attributed as such rather than cited as official data. India’s own official position comes from CPCB monitoring and the National Clean Air Programme, covering 131 non-attainment and million-plus cities. - Urban flooding. Encroachment of lakes, wetlands and natural drains removes the pathway water must take. Hyderabad’s 2020 floods and Vijayawada’s Budameru floods of September 2024 are the standard Indian illustrations. - Urban heat island effect, raising city temperatures several degrees above surroundings and increasing cooling demand and heat mortality. -Groundwater depletion and loss of water bodies to construction.

Social - Widening inequality within cities; strain on public health systems; rising non-communicable disease associated with urban lifestyles (NFHS-5); inadequate provision for the urban informal workforce, which forms the majority of urban employment.

Governance — the underlying cause - Weak municipal finance. Urban local bodies have limited own-source revenue, so infrastructure lags growth regardless of planning quality. - Fragmented authority. Water, drainage, roads, transport and land use are controlled by different agencies — corporation, development authority, water board, State departments — with no single accountable body. - Outdated master plans and weak enforcement against encroachment and unauthorised construction.

## Ways and means to manage urbanisation

1. Redistribute growth rather than concentrate it - Balanced regional development through growth centres in small and medium towns; the Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission creating clusters with urban amenities in rural areas; and the Aspirational Districts Programme — addressing the cause of distress migration rather than its symptom. - Strengthening tier-2 and tier-3 cities as employment centres; the dispersal of IT and manufacturing to cities such as Visakhapatnam and Tirupati is an example of this working.

2. Strengthen planning and land use - Enforceable master plans with zoning, transit-oriented development, mandatory green and blue infrastructure, and protection of water bodies and floodplains. - Land pooling rather than acquisition for orderly expansion — the model used for the Amaravati capital region in Andhra Pradesh.

3. Housing - PMAY-Urban and PMAY-U 2.0, prioritising in-situ slum redevelopment, affordable rental housing complexes for migrant workers, and secure tenure — since households without tenure do not invest in their own dwellings.

4. Infrastructure and services - AMRUT 2.0 for water supply, sewerage, septage management, storm-water drainage and green spaces; Swachh Bharat

Mission-Urban 2.0 for garbage-free cities by 2026; Smart Cities Mission with Integrated Command and Control Centres; Jal Jeevan Mission (Urban); metro rail and e-bus expansion under PM E-DRIVE.

5. Municipal finance and governance - Own-source revenue through property tax reform and user charges; municipal bonds; effective devolution of the 18 functions in the Twelfth Schedule under the 74th Constitutional Amendment, including urban planning and solid waste management, which remain incompletely transferred in most States. - A single accountable agency for urban drainage and water.

6. Participation and technology - Ward committees and Area Sabhas under the 74th Amendment; citizen reporting through the Swachhata and SAMEER apps; social audits; and GIS-based property and infrastructure mapping.

AP instances: the CLAP (Clean Andhra Pradesh) mission for urban waste infrastructure; Mana Mitra delivering 1,126 services across 35 departments to 58.2 lakh citizens through WhatsApp; RTGS and the City Flood Alert system for Vijayawada developed with APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar; and Visakhapatnam’s Swachh Survekshan performance.

## Conclusion

The problems attributed to urbanisation are in fact problems of the gap between urban growth and urban capacity — in housing, drainage, transport and waste processing. Arresting urbanisation is neither feasible nor desirable, since cities generate the bulk of national output. The workable response is threefold: redistribute growth to smaller centres so that pressure is shared, strengthen municipal finance so that capacity can keep pace, and enforce planning so that the water bodies and drains cities depend on are not built over.

## Introduction

Solid waste management is unusual among public services in being impossible to deliver without citizen action. A municipality can supply water regardless of household behaviour, but it cannot recover recyclables from waste the household has already mixed. Source segregation happens in the kitchen or it does not happen at all — which is why the proposition in the question is not a platitude but a technical fact.

marking the first link “the only step the state cannot perform” and showing that a break there degrades every subsequent step.

## Why community effort is indispensable — the mechanism

Mixed waste is worth less than the sum of its parts: the wet fraction contaminates paper and plastic, reducing their recycling value, and the dry fraction contaminates compost with glass, metal and plastic fragments, making it unsafe for agricultural use. No downstream technology can undo this. Segregation at source is therefore not one measure among many — it is the precondition for all of them.

## State initiatives

Legal and policy framework - Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 — mandatory three-way source segregation, duties on waste generators and bulk generators, user fees, spot fines for littering, prohibition on landfilling mixed waste, and a requirement that ULBs establish a system for integrating waste-pickers. - Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0 (from 1 October 2021) — targeting garbage-free cities by 2026, covering used water, plastic waste, C&D waste and legacy dumpsite remediation; about 1,437 lakh tonnes of legacy waste remediated by September 2025, reclaiming over 7,600 acres nationally. - EPR regimes under the Plastic Waste, E-Waste, Battery Waste and Tyre Waste Rules, shifting end-of-life cost to producers.

Operational initiatives by State and city governments - Door-to-door collection with segregated compartment vehicles; GPS-tracked fleets and GIS route optimisation. - Decentralised processing — ward-level composting and biomethanation, which avoid long haulage and single points of failure. - Material Recovery Facilities for dry waste sorting. - Bio-mining of legacy dumpsites — Indore and Surat are the standard success cases, releasing land and eliminating fire and leachate risk. - Waste-to-energy and RDF, with the qualification that Indian waste’s low calorific value limits viability without pre-processing. - Swachh Survekshan rankings and the Star Rating Protocol for Garbage Free Cities, which converted municipal cleanliness into a competitive metric — arguably the single most effective governance innovation in the sector.

State-specific illustrations - Indore (Madhya Pradesh) — sustained Swachh Survekshan leadership built on ward-level segregation monitoring, decentralised processing and citizen engagement rather than on capital-intensive technology. - Telangana — municipal waste initiatives alongside urban infrastructure programmes; Hyderabad’s decentralised processing and bio-mining efforts. - Andhra Pradesh — the CLAP (Clean Andhra Pradesh) mission for state-wide waste infrastructure; Swachh Andhra Corporation as the implementing body; the State Solid Waste Management Policy (2018) mandating need-based assessment for common regional sanitary landfills serving groups of municipalities on a cost-sharing model, which is the realistic model for small towns that cannot each afford a landfill; processing of about 85 lakh metric tonnes of legacy waste; around 3,100 TPD of dry waste through MRFs; and about 235 MLD of treated water reused across 14 ULBs.

## The community’s role — and where coordination breaks down

What communities contribute: - Source segregation — the indispensable step. - Home composting, diverting the largest waste fraction before it enters the system. - Payment of user charges, which sustains the recurring cost of collection. - Monitoring and reporting through apps such as Swachhata, effectively providing municipal supervision at no cost. - RWAs, SHGs and NGOs organising ward-level awareness, composting and monitoring; Kudumbashree in Kerala and SHG-run collection in several States are the working models.

The informal sector — the coordination failure worth naming:Waste-pickers recover a substantial share of India’s recyclables at no public cost, yet remain largely outside formal planning — without identity cards, safety equipment, or a share of EPR revenue. The SWM Rules 2016 direct ULBs to integrate them, but implementation is uneven. This is simultaneously an efficiency loss, an equity failure and the clearest instance of the state-community coordination the question asks about not being realised.

Where else the partnership fails: - Segregation compliance falls when collection re-mixes. Where a household segregates and the collection vehicle then tips both streams into one compartment, compliance collapses — and does not readily return. The state’s failure destroys the community’s contribution, not the other way round. - User charges are politically difficult, so the recurring cost falls on a municipal budget that cannot bear it. - Awareness campaigns without enforcement produce short-lived compliance. - Bulk generators — hotels, hospitals, gated communities, markets — are required to process wet waste on site under the SWM Rules, but enforcement is weak.

## Conclusion

The proposition holds, but with a direction that is often reversed: the community’s contribution is indispensable, and the state’s most important task is not to waste it. Segregation at source collapses when segregated collection is not maintained, and recyclable recovery is diminished when waste-pickers are excluded from the formal system. India’s rules already mandate both segregated collection and waste-picker integration; the deficit is in execution. Where both have been sustained, as at Indore, the results demonstrate that the model works.

mining of legacy dumps; Alappuzha (Kerala) for decentralised zero-waste; Kudumbashree SHG-based collection; Ambikapur (Chhattisgarh) for SHG-run material recovery.

## Introduction

Urban governance is the set of institutions, rules and processes through which cities are managed and services delivered — encompassing urban local bodies, parastatals, State departments, the private sector and citizens. Solid waste management is the function that tests it most severely, because it requires daily operational performance across every household in the city, and because it is constitutionally assigned to the tier with the least revenue.

missions and funds . Mark solid waste as a Twelfth Schedule function at ULB level.

## The constitutional framework
- The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 gave urban local bodies constitutional status, mandating three categories — Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council and Municipal Corporation — with regular elections through State Election Commissions, reservation for SCs, STs and women, and State Finance Commissions to recommend devolution.
- The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 functions that States may devolve, including urban planning, water supply, public health, sanitation, solid waste management, slum improvement and urban poverty alleviation.
- It also provides for Ward Committees in larger municipalities, District Planning Committees and Metropolitan Planning Committees — the last two remaining unconstituted or non-functional in most States, which is the single most cited gap in Indian urban governance.

## Why solid waste exposes governance weakness
- It is a daily service with no tolerance for failure. A missed water supply day is inconvenient; missed waste collection is visible, malodorous and politically immediate.
- It requires the weakest tier to perform the hardest task. ULBs have limited own-source revenue — property tax collection efficiency is low in most cities — yet solid waste is among the largest items in a municipal budget.
- Responsibility is fragmented. Collection may rest with the corporation, processing with a State parastatal or private concessionaire, landfill siting with the development authority, and regulation with the State Pollution Control Board — with no single accountable body.
- Incomplete devolution. Many States have not transferred the Twelfth Schedule functions with matching funds, functions and functionaries — the “3 Fs” formulation — leaving ULBs responsible without capacity.

## Institutional structure of MSW governance
- Union level:Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (SBM-U 2.0, AMRUT 2.0, Smart Cities Mission); MoEFCC and CPCB for rules and standards.
- State level: Municipal Administration and Urban Development departments; State Pollution Control Boards for authorisation and monitoring; parastatals such as Swachh Andhra Corporation.
- ULB level: health and sanitation wings; solid waste management cells; ward-level supervisory staff.
- Delivery models: departmental; public-private partnership with performance-linked payment; SHG or cooperative-based collection; and hybrid arrangements.

## The role of community in MSW — as a governance mechanism
- Source segregation — the indispensable input, discussed in full at Q147.
- Ward Committees and Area Sabhas as the constitutional channel for citizen participation in local decisions, including waste collection schedules and facility siting.
- Resident Welfare Associations organising in-situ composting for bulk-generator compliance and monitoring collection performance.
- Self-Help Groups and cooperatives as service providers — Kudumbashree in Kerala and SHG-run collection and MRFs in Chhattisgarh and Andhra Pradesh demonstrate that community organisations can be contractors, not only beneficiaries.
- Waste-picker integration through registration, identity cards, safety equipment and inclusion in EPR revenue — mandated by the SWM Rules 2016 and unevenly implemented.
- Social audit and grievance redress — the Swachhata app, ward-level review, and public disclosure of performance data.
- Behaviour change communication through schools, RWAs and local media, sustained rather than campaign-based.
- Willingness to pay user charges, which is the financial foundation of a sustainable service and requires visible service quality to be politically feasible.

## Reforms needed
- Complete devolution of the Twelfth Schedule functions with funds and functionaries; constitution of Metropolitan and District Planning Committees.
- Municipal finance reform — property tax base and collection improvement, user charges, municipal bonds, and State Finance Commission recommendations acted upon.
- A single accountable agency for the waste chain within each city.
- Technical capacity — dedicated solid waste cells with qualified engineers, since ULBs frequently cannot evaluate a technology proposal or supervise a concessionaire.
- Cluster arrangements for small towns, which individually cannot afford processing or landfill facilities — the model adopted in Andhra Pradesh’s State SWM Policy 2018 through common regional sanitary landfills on a cost-sharing basis.

## Conclusion

Urban governance for solid waste fails not usually for want of rules — the SWM Rules 2016 are comprehensive — but because the tier constitutionally responsible has neither the revenue nor the technical capacity to discharge the duty, and because responsibility is split among agencies none of which is accountable for the outcome. Community participation is not a supplement to this structure but part of it: citizens supply segregation, oversight and the political tolerance for user charges. Strengthening both — devolution with resources, and genuine ward-level participation — is the same reform seen from two ends.

## Introduction

Soil pollution is the presence of chemicals or substances in soil at concentrations above natural levels, sufficient to harm human health or ecosystems. Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound that impairs health or quality of life. Both differ from air and water pollution in an important respect: soil retains contamination because it has no flushing mechanism, while noise leaves no residue at all yet causes measurable physiological harm.

## (a) Soil pollution

Why soil pollution is distinctive. Air disperses and water flows, so both dilute and eventually flush contaminants. Soil does neither. Contaminants bind to soil particles and organic matter and accumulate over decades, which is why soil pollution is cumulative, persistent and expensive to remediate — and why it is often discovered only when it has already entered the food chain through crops or groundwater.

## Causes
- Agricultural practices — the most widespread source.

Excessive fertiliser use, particularly urea, causing nitrate accumulation, soil acidification and imbalance in the N:P:K ratio; India’s fertiliser price structure has produced heavy urea skew. Pesticide and herbicide residues, including persistent organochlorines, which accumulate in soil and biomagnify through the food chain. Irrigation with contaminated water — sewage or industrial effluent used for peri-urban vegetable cultivation transfers heavy metals directly to food crops. Salinisation and alkalinisation from over-irrigation with poor drainage — technically a form of chemical degradation.

- Industrial sources. Effluent discharge onto land; fly ash from thermal plants; tailings and acid mine drainage from mining; leachate from tanneries, electroplating and chemical units contributing chromium, lead, cadmium, mercury and arsenic.
- Waste disposal.Leachate from unlined dumpsites entering soil and groundwater; open burning of waste depositing dioxins and heavy metals; informal e-waste processing through acid leaching and open burning, contaminating soil at recycling clusters.
- Urban and construction sources. Sewage sludge application, construction debris, oil and fuel spills, and road runoff carrying heavy metals.
- Atmospheric deposition.Acid rain leaching soil nutrients and mobilising toxic aluminium; deposition of particulates carrying heavy metals near industrial areas.
- Radioactive contamination from improper handling of radioactive material.
- Plastics and microplastics, an emerging concern from mulch films, sewage sludge and degraded litter.

Effects: reduced soil fertility and crop yield; entry of heavy metals into the food chain; groundwater contamination through leaching; loss of soil microbial diversity, which underpins nutrient cycling; and direct human health effects — lead affecting neurological development in children, cadmium affecting kidneys, arsenic causing skin lesions and cancers.

Control and remediation: balanced fertilisation guided by Soil Health Cards; neem-coated and nano urea; integrated pest management and biopesticides; organic and natural farming — with APCNF in Andhra Pradesh covering over 1.77 million farmers as the largest Indian instance; treatment of effluent before land application; engineered landfills with liners and leachate collection under the SWM Rules 2016; bioremediation and phytoremediation using plants and microbes to extract or degrade contaminants; and reclamation of contaminated sites under the Hazardous Waste Rules.

## (b) Noise pollution

Definition and measurement. Noise is unwanted sound, measured in decibels (dB), usually on the A-weighted scale (dBA), which approximates the sensitivity of human hearing. The scale is logarithmic: an increase of 10 dB represents a tenfold increase in sound intensity and roughly a doubling of perceived loudness — which is why small numerical differences in the standards matter far more than they appear to.

Sources - Transport — road traffic and horns (the largest urban contributor), railways, and aircraft near airports. - Industrial — machinery, generators, compressors and construction equipment. - Construction — piling, drilling, demolition. - Community and social — loudspeakers, public address systems, festivals, firecrackers, marketplaces. - Domestic — generators, air conditioners, appliances.

Effects - Auditory — temporary threshold shift; noise-induced hearing loss with prolonged exposure above about 85 dB; tinnitus. - Physiological — elevated blood pressure, increased cardiovascular risk, elevated stress hormones. - Sleep disturbance, with consequent fatigue and impaired cognition; night-time noise is more harmful than the same level during the day, which is why standards are stricter at night. - Psychological — annoyance, irritability, reduced concentration and impaired learning in children near noisy roads or airports. - Ecological — masking of animal communication; disorientation of birds and, in the marine environment, of cetaceans by shipping and sonar.

## The Indian regulatory framework — the specifics this question expects

Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, prescribe ambient air quality standards in respect of noise by area category:

- **Area code** — Category of area/zone · Day time (6 a.m.-10 p.m.), dB(A) Leq · Night time (10 p.m.-6 a.m.), dB(A) Leq
- **A** — Industrial area · 75 · 70
- **B** — Commercial area · 65 · 55
- **C** — Residential area · 55 · 45
- **D** — Silence zone · 50 · 40

Silence zones are areas of not less than 100 metres around hospitals, educational institutions and courts, as declared by the competent authority.

Other provisions: restriction on the use of loudspeakers and public address systems without written permission, and a general prohibition on their use between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. (with a limited relaxation for cultural or religious occasions permitted by the State, capped at a specified number of days and hours); limits on horns, drums and firecrackers in silence zones; and designation of the District Magistrate or Police Commissioner as the authority for enforcement and complaint redress.

## Control measures
- At source — quieter machinery and vehicle design; noise limits under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules; mandatory silencers; ban on pressure and multi-toned horns; noise limits for generators and firecrackers set by CPCB; electric vehicles, which sharply reduce transport noise.
- In the transmission path — noise barriers along highways and rail corridors; green belts and tree plantation, which attenuate and psychologically buffer noise; distance and building setbacks; acoustic insulation and double glazing.
- At the receiver — personal protective equipment in industrial settings; sound-insulated design for hospitals and schools.
- Planning and zoning — separating residential areas from industry and highways; siting airports and industrial estates away from settlements; silence zone enforcement.
- Regulatory and behavioural — real-time noise monitoring networks operated by CPCB in major cities; enforcement of loudspeaker permissions; “no-honking” campaigns; and judicial intervention, the Supreme Court having laid down directions on loudspeaker use and firecracker noise in In Re: Noise Pollution (2005).

## Conclusion

Soil and noise pollution are the two most under-regulated pollution categories in practice, for opposite reasons: soil contamination is invisible and cumulative, so it is discovered late; noise leaves no residue, so it is treated as a nuisance rather than a health hazard despite documented cardiovascular and cognitive effects. India’s frameworks exist for both — Soil Health Cards and the Hazardous Waste Rules for soil, and the Noise Rules 2000 with zone-wise limits for noise — and in both cases the deficit lies in monitoring and enforcement rather than in the standards themselves.

## Value addition
- Noise standards under the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 — memorise the grid: Industrial 75/70; Commercial 65/55; Residential 55/45; Silence zone 50/40 dB(A) Leq, day/night; silence zone = not less than 100 m around hospitals, educational institutions and courts; day = 6 a.m.-10 p.m., night = 10 p.m.-6 a.m.
- The logarithmic point: the decibel scale is logarithmic — +10 dB is a tenfold increase in intensity and roughly a doubling of perceived loudness. Noise-induced hearing loss risk begins with prolonged exposure above about 85 dB.
- Noise as an “air pollutant”: noise was brought within the definition of air pollutant under the Air Act, 1981, giving Pollution Control Boards jurisdiction — a point examiners test.
- Soil remediation techniques:bioremediation (microbes degrading contaminants); phytoremediation — subdivided into phyto-extraction, phyto-stabilisation and rhizofiltration; soil washing; capping and encapsulation; and electrokinetic remediation.
- Soil health instruments:Soil Health Card Scheme; neem-coated urea and nano urea; PM-PRANAM incentivising reduced chemical fertiliser use; National Mission on Natural Farming; Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana; integrated pest management.

Green Tribunal Act 2010, and the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023; Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs — Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0, AMRUT 2.0, Smart Cities Mission and Swachh Survekshan; Census of India 2011 and National Commission on Population urban projections; Ministry of Agriculture — Soil Health Card Scheme, PM-PRANAM and the National Mission on Natural Farming; Supreme Court of India, In Re: Noise Pollution (2005), M.C. ## Introduction

Air pollution is the presence in the atmosphere of any substance — solid, liquid or gas — in concentrations that are or tend to be injurious to human beings, other living creatures, plants, property or the environment. This is essentially the definition of an “air pollutant” under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, which also brings noise within its scope. India monitors twelve parameters under the National Ambient Air Quality Standards, 2009, of which eight feed the Air Quality Index.

## The distinction that organises everything — primary versus secondary
- Primary pollutants are emitted directly from an identifiable source.
- Secondary pollutants are not emitted at all — they form in the atmosphere through chemical reaction between primary pollutants, often driven by sunlight. Ground-level ozone and a large share of PM2.5 are secondary.
- Why this matters: a city can control every chimney and tailpipe within its boundary and still have high PM2.5, because much of it forms from precursor gases — SO2 from power plants, NOx from vehicles and ammonia from agriculture — that may travel hundreds of kilometres. This is the strongest argument for regional airshed management rather than city-by-city action, and it is the point most answers miss.

## Major air pollutants from human activity

Particulate matter - PM10 and PM2.5. Sources: combustion (vehicles, industry, thermal power, biomass and crop-residue burning), road and construction dust, and secondary formation from precursor gases. PM2.5 is the pollutant that determines the AQI in most Indian cities on most days. - Black carbon, from incomplete combustion of diesel, biomass and coal — both a health hazard and a short-lived climate forcer that also accelerates glacier melt when deposited on snow.

Gaseous pollutants - Sulphur dioxide (SO2) — coal combustion in thermal power plants, refineries, smelters and brick kilns; also a precursor of sulphate particles and acid rain. Controlled by flue gas desulphurisation and low-sulphur fuel. - Oxides of nitrogen (NOx) — high-temperature combustion in vehicles, power plants and industry; a precursor of both ground-level ozone and nitrate particles. - Carbon monoxide (CO) — incomplete combustion, principally from vehicles and biomass burning in poorly ventilated kitchens. - Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) — petrol evaporation, solvents, paints, refineries and chemical industry; includes benzene, a known carcinogen. VOCs plus NOx in sunlight produce ozone. - Ammonia (NH₃) — overwhelmingly from fertiliser application and livestock, not from industry. It reacts with acidic gases to form ammonium sulphate and nitrate particles, making agriculture an unrecognised contributor to urban PM2.5. - Ground-level ozone (O₃) — entirely secondary; damages lung tissue and reduces crop yields. Note the distinction from stratospheric ozone, which is protective: “good up high, bad nearby”. - Lead (Pb) — legacy leaded fuel, battery manufacture and recycling, smelting; a neurotoxin especially damaging to children. - Persistent organic pollutants and dioxins — from open burning of waste, particularly plastics and PVC.

By human activity sector - Transport — NOx, PM, CO, VOCs, black carbon. - Industry and power — SO2, NOx, PM, heavy metals, fly ash. - Agriculture —

ammonia from fertiliser, methane from livestock and paddy, and crop-residue burning producing seasonal PM peaks in north India. - Households — solid fuel combustion for cooking, producing very high indoor PM2.5 and CO; addressed through PMUY. - Construction and roads — dust, a major PM10 contributor in Indian cities. - Waste — open burning and landfill fires; methane from decomposition.

India’s monitoring and regulatory framework:NAAQS 2009 (12 parameters); the Air Quality Index (8 pollutants, 6 categories); CPCB with SPCBs operating CAAQMS and manual stations under NAMP; SAMEER app for public dissemination; National Clean Air Programme covering 131 non-attainment and million-plus cities in 24 States/UTs, targeting up to 40% reduction in PM10 or attainment of NAAQS by 2025-26; CAQM and GRAP for Delhi-NCR.

## Conclusion

Air pollution is best understood not as a list of emitted substances but as a system in which primary pollutants react in the atmosphere to form secondary ones. That distinction has direct policy consequence: because much of India’s PM2.5 forms from precursor gases travelling across administrative boundaries — including ammonia from agriculture — controlling only visible local emissions cannot succeed. Effective abatement requires airshed-level action across sectors, which is why NCAP’s city-by-city design is its most debated feature.

## Value addition
- NAAQS 2009 — 12 parameters: PM10, PM2.5, SO2, NO2, CO, O₃, NH₃, Pb, benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic and nickel. AQI uses 8 of these: PM10, PM2.5, SO2, NO2, CO, O₃, NH₃ and Pb.
- Key NAAQS limits: PM2.5 annual 40 µg/m³ and 24-hour 60 µg/m³; PM10 annual 60 µg/m³ and 24-hour 100 µg/m³ — both well above WHO guideline values, so compliance with Indian standards does not imply safe air.
- The ammonia point: agriculture is a major source of NH₃, which forms secondary particulates — meaning fertiliser policy (neem-coated urea, nano urea, PM-PRANAM) is also air quality policy. Few answers make this link.
- “Good up high, bad nearby”: stratospheric ozone shields from UV; ground-level ozone is a pollutant and a greenhouse gas. Confusing the two is a common and visible error.
- Institutional map: CPCB and SPCBs; NAMP and CAAQMS networks; SAFAR forecasting; NCAP with the PRANA portal; CAQM (statutory, 2021) and GRAP for Delhi-NCR.
- AP-specific: Visakhapatnam’s refinery, steel and port emissions; the Vijayawada urban agglomeration; coastal meteorology providing better dispersal than the Indo-Gangetic Plain — a useful contrast showing geography, not only emissions, determines air quality.

## Introduction

Air pollution control follows a hierarchy of preference: it is always cheaper and more effective to prevent formation than to capture emissions afterwards, and cheaper to capture than to disperse. India’s regulatory framework, built on the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, provides instruments at each level.

## (a) Measures for prevention and control

-> 3. End-of-pipe control --> 4. Dispersion --> 5. Receiver protection .

1. Source reduction and elimination — the most effective - Fuel substitution: LPG and PNG for solid fuels under PMUY; natural gas for coal in industry; electricity from non-fossil sources — India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025 (MNRE). - Cleaner fuel standards:BS-VI fuel and vehicle norms from April 2020, with sulphur cut to 10 ppm, achieved by leapfrogging BS-V. - Electric mobility under PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore from October

2024, replacing FAME-II), and public transport expansion — metro rail and e-buses. - Ethanol blending — E20 achieved in 2025-26 (PIB). - Crop-residue management instead of burning: happy seeders, super straw management systems, bio-decomposer, and residue-to-energy under SATAT and the National Bioenergy Programme.

2. Process modification - Energy efficiency under the PAT scheme, since less fuel burnt means less emitted. - Cleaner production technologies — dry process cement kilns, continuous casting in steel, induction furnaces replacing cupolas. - Leak detection and repair for VOCs in refineries and chemical plants; vapour recovery at petrol stations. - Zigzag firing technology in brick kilns, mandated in several States.

3. End-of-pipe control equipment — the engineering tier - Electrostatic precipitators (ESP) — for fine particulates, discussed technically at Q153; standard on thermal power stations, with efficiency above 99%. - Fabric filters (bag houses) — high efficiency for fine dust, used in cement and metallurgical plants. - Cyclone separators — centrifugal separation of coarse particles; cheap, used as a pre-cleaner. - Wet scrubbers — remove both particulates and soluble gases by contact with a liquid. - Flue Gas Desulphurisation (FGD) — limestone-based absorption of SO2, mandated for Indian thermal power plants. - Catalytic converters and selective catalytic reduction (SCR) for NOx; diesel particulate filters for vehicles under BS-VI. -Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (OCEMS) transmitting stack data directly to pollution control board servers — the shift from periodic inspection to continuous telemetry.

4. Dispersion — the least preferred - Tall stacks disperse rather than remove pollution, converting a local concentration into a regional one. Retained only where treatment is not feasible. - Siting and zoning to keep polluting industry away from settlements; green belts around industrial estates.

5. Receiver protection and ambient management - Air quality forecasting (SAFAR) and advisories through the SAMEER app; GRAP graded restrictions in Delhi-NCR; masks and activity restriction on high-AQI days; indoor air improvement through clean cooking fuel.

6. Urban and dust measures - Mechanised road sweeping, water sprinkling and anti-smog guns; paving of shoulders; covering of construction sites and material transport; C&D waste management under the 2016 Rules.

7. Institutional and economic instruments - NCAP across 131 cities with city-specific action plans and performance-linked funding; XV Finance Commission air quality grants; consent conditions and closure directions by SPCBs; environmental compensation; and market-based instruments — the Surat particulate emissions trading scheme, the world’s first for particulates, is a notable Indian innovation. - Afforestation and urban greening — Nagar Van Yojana, green belts, Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam.

## (b) Rules and legal instruments relating to air pollution control

Primary legislation - Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 — declaration of air pollution control areas; consent for industrial plants; emission standards; Section 31A directions including closure and stoppage of services; noise included within “air pollutant”. - Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 — umbrella statute; source of most subordinate rules and standards. - Commission for Air Quality Management in the NCR and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 — statutory CAQM with overriding powers in the NCR airshed. - Factories Act, 1948 and Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 for workplace and vehicular emissions. - Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 — decriminalised specified offences under the Air Act, EPA and Water Act, substituting monetary penalties determined by adjudicating officers.

Rules, standards and notifications - Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 — the general standards framework, including industry-specific emission standards. - National Ambient Air Quality Standards, 2009 (CPCB notification) — 12 parameters. - Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Rules, 1982 and Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) (Union Territories) Rules, 1983. - Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 — since noise is an air pollutant under the Act. - Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 — vehicular emission norms (BS-VI), Pollution Under Control certification, and noise limits. - Fly Ash Notification — mandatory utilisation of fly ash from thermal power plants. - Construction and Demolition Waste Management Rules, 2016 — dust control at sites. - E-Waste, Plastic Waste, Bio-Medical Waste and Hazardous Waste Rules — insofar as they restrict open burning and incineration. - EIA Notification, 2006 — prior environmental clearance with air quality impact assessment. - Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) — statutory instrument of the CAQM for Delhi-NCR, triggering escalating restrictions by AQI band. - Emission standards for thermal power plants — SO2, NOx, PM and mercury limits with FGD timelines.

## Conclusion

Effective air pollution control depends on working at the highest feasible level of the hierarchy — substituting fuels and modifying processes rather than relying on stacks and scrubbers, since dispersion merely relocates the problem. India’s statutory framework is comprehensive, from the Air Act 1981 through NAAQS to GRAP, and the shift to continuous emission monitoring has strengthened enforcement materially. The remaining gap is that NCAP’s city-based design does not match the airshed scale at which secondary particulates actually form.
