## Introduction

Air pollutants harm through several distinct pathways — direct toxicity, oxidative and inflammatory damage, acid formation and climate forcing — and the pathway determines both the effect and the appropriate control. Where prevention is not feasible, engineering control at the stack becomes essential, and for fine particulates the electrostatic precipitator remains the workhorse technology of Indian thermal power generation.

## (a) Major air pollutants and their effects
- **Pollutant** — Principal sources · Health effects · Other effects
- **PM2.5** — Combustion, secondary formation · Penetrates alveoli and enters the bloodstream; ischaemic heart disease, stroke, COPD, lung cancer, low birth weight · Reduced visibility; deposition on crops
- **PM10** — Dust, construction, industry · Upper respiratory irritation, asthma aggravation · Soiling of materials
- **SO2** — Coal combustion, smelting · Bronchoconstriction, asthma exacerbation · Acid rain; leaf necrosis; corrosion of marble and limestone
- **NOx** — Vehicles, power plants · Airway inflammation; increased respiratory infection in children · Acid rain; ozone precursor; eutrophication through nitrogen deposition
- **CO** — Incomplete combustion · Binds haemoglobin in preference to oxygen — headache, dizziness, impaired cognition, death at high concentration · —
- **Ground-level O₃** — Secondary (NOx + VOCs + sunlight) · Chest pain, coughing, reduced lung function · Crop yield loss — significant for Indian wheat and rice
- **Pb** — Battery manufacture, smelting, legacy fuel · Neurodevelopmental damage in children, anaemia, kidney damage · Soil accumulation
- **VOCs (benzene)** — Solvents, fuel evaporation · Carcinogenic; leukaemia risk · Ozone precursor
- **NH₃** — Fertiliser, livestock · Irritant · Forms secondary particulates; nitrogen deposition
- **Black carbon** — Diesel, biomass burning · Respiratory and cardiovascular effects · Short-lived climate forcer; accelerates glacier melt when deposited on snow

## Effects grouped by category
- Human health. The largest burden is cardiovascular, not respiratory — systemic inflammation from PM2.5 raises the risk of heart disease and stroke above that of lung disease. Outdoor air pollution is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by IARC. Children, the elderly, pregnant women, outdoor workers and the urban poor bear disproportionate exposure.
- Vegetation and agriculture. Ground-level ozone reduces yields of wheat, rice and pulses; SO2 causes chlorosis and necrosis; particulate deposition on leaves reduces photosynthesis. This makes air pollution an agricultural productivity issue, not only a health one.
- Materials and heritage. Acid deposition converts calcium carbonate in marble and limestone to soluble gypsum — “stone leprosy”, documented on the Taj Mahal and addressed through the Taj Trapezium Zone directions in M.C. Mehta (1996).
- Ecosystems. Acidification of soils and water bodies; nitrogen deposition causing eutrophication and shifting species composition.
- Climate. CO2 and methane as greenhouse gases; black carbon as a warming agent that also darkens snow and ice; conversely, sulphate aerosols exert a cooling effect, so air quality improvements can unmask additional warming — a nuance worth noting.
- Visibility and economy. Haze affecting aviation and road transport; economic loss through premature mortality, healthcare cost and reduced labour productivity.

## (b) Electrostatic precipitator (ESP)

Definition. An ESP is an air pollution control device that removes suspended particulate matter from a flowing gas stream by imparting an electrical charge to the particles and then attracting them onto oppositely charged collecting surfaces. Developed by Frederick Cottrell in 1907, it remains the principal particulate control device on thermal power plants worldwide.

## Working principle — the four stages

1. Ionisation (corona discharge). A very high direct-current voltage — typically tens of kilovolts — is applied between thin discharge electrodes (wires) and earthed collecting electrodes (plates). The intense electric field near the thin wire ionises the surrounding gas, producing a visible corona discharge and a supply of free electrons and gas ions. 2. Charging. As the flue gas passes through this region, the gas ions collide with and attach to the suspended dust particles, giving each particle a negative electrical charge. Larger particles charge mainly by field charging (ions driven by the electric field), finer particles by diffusion charging (random thermal motion of ions) — a distinction worth stating. 3. Migration and collection. The charged particles experience an electrostatic force toward the earthed, positively charged collecting plates, and migrate across the gas flow to deposit on them. The velocity at which they migrate depends on particle size, charge and the field strength. 4. Removal. Accumulated dust is dislodged periodically by rapping — mechanical hammers striking the plates — and falls into hoppers below for disposal. Dry ESPs use rapping; wet ESPs use a water film.

Performance and characteristics - Collection efficiency above 99%, and effective down to very fine particle sizes — its principal advantage over cyclones. - Low pressure drop across the unit, so fan power consumption and operating cost are low. - Handles large gas volumes at high temperature, which is why it suits power station flue gas. - The critical variable — resistivity. ESP performance depends on the electrical resistivity of the dust. If resistivity is too low, particles lose their charge on contact and are re-entrained; if too high, an insulating layer builds up on the plate and causes back corona, sharply reducing efficiency. Indian coal has high ash content with high resistivity, which is why Indian ESPs are often larger than equivalents elsewhere and why flue gas conditioning (injecting SO₃ or ammonia to reduce resistivity) is used. - Limitations: high capital cost and large footprint; ineffective against gaseous pollutants (SO2, NOx), which require scrubbers or SCR; performance sensitive to changes in coal quality and load.

Applications: thermal power stations, cement plants, steel and metallurgical industries, paper mills, refineries — and, at small scale, in air purifiers.

Comparison worth adding:bag filters (fabric filters) achieve comparable or higher efficiency on fine particles and are insensitive to resistivity, which is why many newer Indian installations prefer them; but they have a higher pressure drop and the bags require periodic replacement.

## Conclusion

The major air pollutants harm through distinct mechanisms — particulates by penetration into the bloodstream, ozone by oxidative damage to lung and leaf, SO2 and NOx by acid formation — and the largest share of the mortality burden is cardiovascular rather than respiratory. Where emissions cannot be prevented, the electrostatic precipitator provides better than 99% particulate capture at low operating cost, though its dependence on dust resistivity makes it sensitive to Indian coal quality. It removes no gaseous pollutant, which is why FGD and SCR are required alongside it.

## Value addition
- The ESP sequence in four words for recall:ionise –> charge –> migrate –> collect (rap). Efficiency above 99%; developed by Frederick Cottrell (1907).
- Resistivity — the examinable subtlety: dust resistivity must fall within an optimum band; too low causes re-entrainment, too high causes back corona. Indian high-ash coal tends toward high resistivity, addressed by flue gas conditioning.
- Control device matched to pollutant: ESP and bag filter for fine PM; cyclone for coarse PM; FGD for SO2; SCR and low-NOx burners for NOx; activated carbon adsorption for VOCs; catalytic converter and DPF for vehicles.
- Health framing: IARC classifies outdoor air pollution and particulate matter as Group 1 carcinogens; cardiovascular deaths exceed respiratory deaths in the air pollution burden — a fact that surprises most readers.
- The crop dimension: ground-level ozone measurably reduces wheat and rice yields in the Indo-Gangetic plain, making air pollution a food security issue and strengthening the case for controlling NOx and VOCs.
- Acid deposition and heritage: “stone leprosy” on marble; the Taj Trapezium Zone of about 10,400 sq km; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) directing 292 industries to switch to natural gas or relocate.
- AP-specific: ESPs at NTPC Simhadri and Vijayawada Thermal Power Station; APPCB stack monitoring and OCEMS in the Visakhapatnam industrial belt; cement plants in the Kadapa-Kurnool limestone belt using ESPs and bag filters.

## Introduction

Water quality is assessed through indicators of oxygen-demanding organic load, because the fundamental harm caused by organic pollution is the depletion of dissolved oxygen on which aquatic life depends. Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) and Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) measure this load in two different ways, and eutrophication is the ecological consequence when nutrient enrichment accelerates the process.

## (a) BOD and COD differentiated
- **Basis** — BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) · COD (Chemical Oxygen Demand)
- **Definition** — Oxygen consumed by micro-organisms in decomposing organic matter under aerobic conditions · Oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise organic and oxidisable inorganic matter
- **Method** — Biological — incubation of a sealed sample and measurement of dissolved oxygen depletion · Chemical — oxidation with a strong oxidant, conventionally potassium dichromate in acid with a silver catalyst
- **Standard conditions** — 5 days at 20deg C (BOD₅) — India’s standard is 3 days at 27deg C, suited to tropical temperatures · About 3 hours
- **Scope** — Measures only the biodegradable fraction · Measures both biodegradable and non-biodegradable matter
- **Magnitude** — Always lower · Always higher — COD > BOD for the same sample, without exception
- **Interference** — Toxic substances inhibit the micro-organisms, giving falsely low values · Unaffected by toxicity; some inorganics (chlorides) can interfere
- **Reproducibility** — Lower — depends on microbial seed and conditions · Higher — a chemical reaction is more repeatable
- **Best use** — Domestic sewage and biodegradable effluent; regulatory standards · Industrial effluent, and rapid process control

## Importance — beyond “both measure pollution”
- BOD is the regulatory yardstick for organic pollution in India. CPCB classifies river stretches as polluted on the basis of BOD, and the 311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers identified in its 2022 assessment were determined by this parameter. The designated best-use classification sets BOD below 3 mg/L for outdoor bathing (Class B) — the threshold most commonly cited.
- COD gives a rapid answer. BOD takes three to five days, which is useless for controlling a treatment plant in real time; COD takes hours, so plant operators use COD for daily control and BOD for compliance reporting.
- The BOD:COD ratio — the most useful single insight. The ratio indicates the biodegradability of the waste:

BOD/COD above about 0.5 — largely biodegradable; biological treatment (activated sludge, trickling filter, UASB) will work and is the cheapest option. BOD/COD below about 0.3 — largely non-biodegradable or toxic; biological treatment will fail, and physico-chemical or advanced oxidation treatment is required. This ratio is therefore what determines the design of an effluent treatment plant — which is the real answer to “discuss their importance”.

- Diagnostic value. A high COD with low BOD signals industrial or toxic discharge rather than sewage; a high BOD with proportionate COD signals domestic sewage. The pair together identifies the source.
- Regulatory standards: discharge standards under the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 specify BOD and COD limits by industry and by receiving medium (inland surface water, public sewer, land for irrigation, marine coastal areas).

Other water quality parameters worth naming: dissolved oxygen (DO), total dissolved solids, total suspended solids, pH, faecal coliform, nitrate, phosphate, heavy metals — and CPCB’s Water Quality Index.

## (b) Eutrophication
- Definition: the enrichment of a water body with nutrients — principally nitrogen and phosphorus — leading to excessive growth of algae and aquatic plants and consequent degradation of water quality.
- Types:natural eutrophication, a slow process over centuries as lakes age; and cultural (anthropogenic) eutrophication, greatly accelerated by human nutrient inputs — the relevant category.
- Causes: agricultural runoff carrying fertiliser (nitrate and phosphate); untreated or partially treated sewage; detergents containing phosphates; aquaculture feed and waste; industrial effluent; and atmospheric nitrogen deposition.
- The mechanism — worth explaining rather than asserting: excess nutrients trigger rapid algal growth (a bloom), which forms a surface mat blocking sunlight from submerged plants. Those plants die, and bacterial decomposition of the dead biomass consumes dissolved oxygen. Oxygen falls below the level fish and invertebrates require, producing hypoxia and, in severe cases, an anoxic “dead zone”. The paradox worth stating: eutrophication kills through excess nutrients producing oxygen scarcity.
- Effects: fish kills and loss of aquatic biodiversity; harmful algal blooms producing toxins (cyanobacterial blooms can render water unsafe for drinking and bathing); foul odour and taste; reduced light penetration; loss of recreational and aesthetic value; increased water treatment cost; and, at the coast, expansion of marine dead zones.
- Indian instances:Kolleru Lake (Ramsar site, Andhra Pradesh) — nutrient loading from aquaculture and agricultural runoff between the Krishna and Godavari deltas; Bellandur and Varthur lakes, Bengaluru, where nutrient and detergent loading produces the well-documented froth; Dal Lake, Srinagar; Vembanad and Chilika under varying pressure.
- Control measures: sewage treatment before discharge and nutrient removal at STPs; balanced fertiliser use guided by Soil Health Cards, neem-coated and nano urea, and PM-PRANAM; buffer strips and constructed wetlands to intercept runoff; regulation of phosphate in detergents; aquaculture effluent regulation; bioremediation and aeration of affected water bodies; Namami Gange and the National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA); and Amrit Dharohar for wetlands.

## Conclusion

BOD and COD measure the same underlying harm — oxygen demand — through biological and chemical routes respectively, and their ratio, more than either figure alone, determines whether an effluent can be treated biologically. Eutrophication is what happens when that oxygen demand is driven not by direct organic discharge but by nutrient enrichment, and its Indian instances — Kolleru, Bellandur, Dal — show that it arises wherever agricultural runoff and untreated sewage meet a slow-moving water body. Prevention through nutrient management at source is far cheaper than remediating a eutrophied lake.

## Value addition
- Test conditions: BOD is internationally standardised at 5 days at 20deg C (BOD₅); India uses 3 days at 27deg C, reflecting tropical temperatures — a detail examiners appreciate. COD uses potassium dichromate oxidation in about three hours.
- The ratio rule: BOD/COD > 0.5 –> biodegradable, biological treatment suitable; < 0.3 –> non-biodegradable or toxic, physico-chemical or advanced oxidation needed. This is the most practically useful fact about the pair.
- CPCB designated best-use classification: Class A (drinking water without conventional treatment but after disinfection); Class B (outdoor bathing — BOD ≤ 3 mg/L, DO >= 5 mg/L); Class C (drinking after conventional treatment); Class D (propagation of wildlife and fisheries); Class E (irrigation and industrial cooling).
- Water pollution data:311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers (CPCB, 2022 assessment), identified on the basis of BOD.
- Treatment technologies to name: primary (screening, sedimentation); secondary/biological (activated sludge, trickling filter, UASB, sequencing batch reactor); tertiary (filtration, disinfection, nutrient removal, membrane processes); and constructed wetlands as a low-cost natural option.
- Eutrophication terms:oligotrophic (nutrient-poor, clear) –> mesotrophic –> eutrophic (nutrient-rich); algal bloom; hypoxia and anoxia; dead zone; harmful algal bloom; limiting nutrient — usually phosphorus in freshwater and nitrogen in marine systems, which determines which nutrient to control.
- AP-specific:Kolleru Lake (Ramsar) eutrophication from aquaculture and fertiliser runoff; Krishna and Godavari delta drainage; APCNF reducing chemical fertiliser load across 1.77 million farmers; APPCB effluent monitoring.

## Introduction

Marine pollution is the introduction of substances or energy into the marine environment that results in harm to living resources, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities, or impairment of water quality — the definition used in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The critical fact for framing any answer: the overwhelming majority of marine pollution originates from land-based sources, not from ships. India’s exposure is substantial, with a 7,500-km coastline, an Exclusive Economic Zone of about 2.02 million sq km, and Andhra Pradesh contributing 1,053 km of that coast.

## Sources of marine pollution

Land-based — the dominant category - Sewage and municipal wastewater discharged untreated into rivers and coastal waters — the largest single contributor by volume, carrying organic load, nutrients and pathogens. - Agricultural runoff — nitrogen and phosphorus fertiliser causing coastal eutrophication and hypoxic dead zones; pesticide residues. - Industrial effluent — heavy metals (mercury, cadmium, lead), organic chemicals, thermal discharge from power plants and desalination brine. - Plastic and solid waste — carried by rivers and drains; degrading into microplastics which enter the food chain. Rivers are the principal transport pathway from inland cities to the sea. - Atmospheric deposition — mercury, nitrogen compounds and persistent organic pollutants deposited on the ocean surface.

Sea-based - Oil pollution — operational discharges, bilge and ballast water, and accidental oil spills from tankers and offshore platforms. - Ballast water — the principal vector for invasive alien marine species transported between ports, addressed by the IMO Ballast Water Management Convention. -Dumping at sea — dredged material, sewage sludge, industrial waste, governed by the London Convention and Protocol. - Fishing gear — abandoned, lost or discarded nets (“ghost gear”) continuing to trap marine life indefinitely. - Shipping emissions and noise — SOx and NOx from bunker fuel, and underwater noise disorienting cetaceans. - Offshore oil and gas exploration and production, including drilling muds and produced water.

## Impacts
- Marine ecosystems.Coral bleaching and mortality from thermal stress, sedimentation and pollution — affecting the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andamans; mangrove degradation; seagrass loss; destruction of breeding and nursery habitat.
- Hypoxia and dead zones. Nutrient enrichment triggers algal blooms whose decomposition depletes oxygen, producing zones where fish and invertebrates cannot survive — documented seasonally off parts of India’s west coast.
- Bioaccumulation and biomagnification. Mercury, cadmium and persistent organic pollutants concentrate at successive trophic levels, so large predatory fish carry the highest burden — reaching humans through consumption. The Minamata episode in Japan remains the defining case.
- Plastics and microplastics. Entanglement and ingestion killing turtles, seabirds and marine mammals; microplastics now documented throughout the marine food web and in seafood.
- Oil spills. Smothering of intertidal life; damage to mangroves and coral; long-term contamination of sediments; and severe short-term impact on fisheries and tourism.
- Human health and livelihoods. Contaminated seafood; loss of fishery income; damage to coastal tourism; and reduced protective capacity of degraded mangroves and reefs against storm surge — a disaster risk consequence.
- Ocean acidification. Absorbed CO2 forming carbonic acid, impairing calcification in corals, molluscs and plankton at the base of the marine food web — technically a pollution effect of atmospheric CO2.

## Control measures

International framework - MARPOL 73/78 — the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, with six annexes covering oil, noxious liquid substances, harmful packaged substances, sewage, garbage and air pollution from ships; includes designation of Special Areas with stricter discharge standards. - UNCLOS (1982) — obligation on States to prevent, reduce and control marine pollution from all sources; establishes the EEZ regime. - London Convention (1972) and Protocol (1996) — prohibition and regulation of dumping at sea. - Ballast Water Management Convention — treatment standards to prevent transfer of invasive species. - Basel Convention — transboundary movement of hazardous waste, including its 2019 plastic waste amendments. - The ongoing negotiation of a global plastics treaty under UNEP, and the BBNJ Agreement (2023) on marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction, which India has signed.

Indian framework - Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Water Act, 1974, with effluent standards for discharge into marine coastal areas. -Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification, 2019 — regulating construction and activity in coastal zones, with CRZ-I to IV categories, and Coastal Zone Management Authorities at national and State level. - Integrated Coastal Zone Management (ICZM) Project and the National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM), Chennai. - Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 giving effect to MARPOL; the Indian Coast Guard as the central coordinating authority for oil spill response under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (NOS-DCP). - Marine Protected Areas — Gulf of Mannar and Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Parks, Bhitarkanika, and the Andaman & Nicobar network. - Namami Gange and river cleaning programmes, which reduce the land-based load at source — the highest-leverage intervention. - Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar coastal clean-up campaigns; MISHTI for mangrove restoration; Deep Ocean Mission for ocean research and monitoring. - Ban on identified single-use plastics (July 2022) and EPR under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, reducing plastic entering rivers. - INCOIS and NCCR (National Centre for Coastal Research) for monitoring water quality, shoreline change and ocean state.

AP-specific: the 1,053-km coastline with the ports of Visakhapatnam, Krishnapatnam, Kakinada and Gangavaram; industrial effluent from the Visakhapatnam petrochemical and steel complex; the Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary mangroves as both a pollution sink and a vulnerable habitat; aquaculture effluent affecting Kolleru and the coastal belt; and INCOIS, Hyderabad, providing ocean state and Potential Fishing Zone advisories for the Andhra coast.

## Conclusion

Marine pollution is predominantly a land-management problem that manifests at sea: sewage, fertiliser and plastic carried down rivers account for far more than shipping does. This has a direct policy consequence — the most effective marine pollution control measures are inland, in sewage treatment, nutrient management and plastic waste rules, rather than at the coast. International conventions such as MARPOL and UNCLOS govern the sea-based fraction effectively; the land-based fraction depends on domestic waste and agricultural policy, which is where India’s remaining deficit lies.

## Introduction

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was India’s first comprehensive environmental statute and created the institutional machinery — the Central and State Pollution Control Boards — through which almost all subsequent environmental regulation has been administered. Its enactment route is itself notable: since water is a State subject, the Act was passed under Article 252 with the consent of State legislatures.

## (i) The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

Objectives - To prevent and control water pollution. - To maintain or restore the wholesomeness of water. - To establish Boards for these purposes and confer on them the necessary powers.

Institutional framework - Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) — constituted in September 1974; advises the Central Government; coordinates State Board activity and resolves disputes between them; provides technical assistance; sets standards; and organises training and public awareness. It may also perform State Board functions in a Union Territory. - State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) — plan comprehensive programmes for prevention and control; inspect sewage and effluent treatment plants; lay down effluent standards (which may be more stringent than CPCB’s, but not less); and grant or refuse consent. - Joint Boards may be constituted by agreement between two or more States.

## Key provisions
- Sections 25 and 26 — the consent mechanism. No person may establish any industry, operation, process or treatment and disposal system likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent, or begin to make any new discharge, without the previous consent of the State Board. This is Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate, renewable periodically, and it is the Board’s principal day-to-day instrument — since withdrawal of consent halts the operation.
- Section 24 — prohibition on the use of any stream or well for disposal of poisonous, noxious or polluting matter.
- Sections 20-23 — Board powers to obtain information, take samples of effluent (with a prescribed procedure ensuring the occupier is present and receives a portion), and enter and inspect premises.
- Section 32 — emergency measures where pollution of a stream or well is apprehended, allowing the Board to act immediately.
- Section 33 — power to apply to a court for restraining apprehended pollution.
- Section 33A — the decisive enforcement power. The Board may issue directions to any person, officer or authority, including directions for the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process, and for the stoppage or regulation of supply of electricity, water or any other service. This provision, added by amendment, is what gives Board orders practical effect without recourse to prolonged litigation.
- Penalties — Sections 41-45A provided for imprisonment and fine for failure to comply with directions and for contravention of Sections 24 and 25, with enhanced penalties for continuing offences. These provisions were substantially amended by the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 (below).
- Section 49 — cognizance of offences on a complaint by the Board or by any person who has given 60 days’ notice — a citizen enforcement provision.
- Companion legislation: the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977, levying a cess on water consumed by specified industries and local authorities, with rebate for those installing treatment plants; since repealed.

The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 — the current position. This Act decriminalised a range of offences under the Water Act (and the Air Act and EPA), replacing imprisonment with monetary penalties determined by adjudicating officers appointed by the Government, with appeals to the National Green Tribunal and proceeds credited to an Environmental Protection Fund. Serious offences causing substantial harm remain criminal.

## (ii) Issues in the enforcement of environmental legislation

Institutional capacity - Chronic understaffing of Pollution Control Boards. SPCBs are responsible for tens of thousands of units each, with a fraction of the technical staff required. Vacancy levels in scientific and technical posts are high, and the CAG and Parliamentary Standing Committees have repeatedly recorded this. This is the single most important enforcement constraint — the law is adequate; the inspectorate is not. - Inadequate laboratory and monitoring infrastructure, limiting the ability to generate evidence that will survive challenge. - Board composition and autonomy — appointments frequently lack the technical expertise the statute contemplates, and Boards depend financially on consent fees paid by the very units they regulate, creating a structural conflict.

Legal and procedural - Low conviction rates and long delays. Criminal prosecution under environmental statutes has historically produced very few convictions relative to cases filed, with proceedings extending over years — which was the principal justification offered for the 2023 decriminalisation. -Weak penalties relative to profits. Where the fine is smaller than the cost of compliance, penalty becomes a licence fee. This concern applies with particular force to the new monetary penalty regime. - Evidentiary difficulty — establishing causation between a discharge and a harm, especially with multiple contributors to a single water body. - Overlapping jurisdictions among Boards, municipal bodies, and specialised authorities, with unclear primary responsibility.

Technical and informational - Inadequate real-time data, though OCEMS has improved this materially for large units. - Difficulty in regulating the unorganised sector — small units, informal recycling, illegal sand mining — which are numerous, dispersed and often unregistered. - Non-point source pollution — agricultural runoff and urban stormwater — which cannot be regulated through a consent mechanism designed for identifiable point sources. This is a structural gap in the Act’s design, not a failure of enforcement, and is worth identifying as such.

Political economy - Development-versus-environment pressure on regulators, particularly where an industry is a significant local employer or revenue source. - Local political and economic influence over Board decisions. - Public participation limits — public hearings under the EIA process are the main formal channel, and their exemptions and conduct are contested.

Judicial dependence - Much of India’s environmental enforcement has effectively been driven by the judiciary — the National Green Tribunal and the Supreme Court’s M.C. Mehta line of cases — rather than by the executive. Judicial activism has filled the enforcement gap but is episodic, case-driven and cannot substitute for routine regulatory presence.

Reforms suggested - Fill technical vacancies and strengthen Board laboratories; ring-fence Board finances from consent-fee dependence. - Expand continuous emission and effluent monitoring with tamper-proof telemetry and automatic escalation. - Ensure penalties exceed the cost of compliance, and index them, so that violation is never the cheaper option — the essential test of the 2023 regime. - Strengthen citizen enforcement under Section 49 and the EPA’s Section 19, and improve public access to monitoring data. - Address non-point sources through catchment-level instruments — nutrient management, buffer strips and urban stormwater rules — rather than through consent. - Build State-level environmental adjudication capacity to support the new adjudicating officer mechanism.

## Conclusion

The Water Act, 1974 supplied both the substantive prohibition and the institutional machinery for Indian pollution control, and its consent mechanism and Section 33A directions remain the most effective instruments available. India’s enforcement deficit has never been principally a deficit of law: it is a deficit of inspectors, laboratories and financial independence in the Boards, compounded by a design that regulates point sources well and non-point sources not at all. Whether the 2023 shift from prosecution to administrative penalty improves matters will depend on a single variable — whether the penalties are set high enough that compliance remains cheaper than violation.

## Value addition
- Sections worth citing precisely:Section 16 (CPCB functions); Section 17 (SPCB functions); Sections 20-23 (information, sampling, entry and inspection); Section 24 (prohibition on disposal of polluting matter); Sections 25-27 (consent); Section 32 (emergency measures); Section 33 (court restraint); Section 33A (directions including closure and stoppage of services); Section 49 (cognizance on citizen complaint after 60 days’ notice).
- Enactment route: passed under Article 252 with State consent, since water is a State subject — contrast with the Air Act 1981 and EPA 1986, enacted under Article 253 to implement Stockholm Conference decisions.
- The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023: decriminalised specified offences under the Water Act, Air Act and EPA; monetary penalties by adjudicating officers; appeals to the NGT; proceeds to an Environmental Protection Fund; serious offences remain criminal.
- The structural gap to name: the consent mechanism regulates point sources; agricultural runoff and urban stormwater are non-point sources and fall outside it entirely. This is a design limitation, not an enforcement failure — a distinction that lifts the answer.
- Judicial doctrines filling the gap:polluter pays, precautionary principle, public trust doctrine, absolute liability (M.C. Mehta, Oleum gas leak, 1987), and Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum (1996); the NGT Act, 2010 creating specialised adjudication with a six-month disposal norm.
- Water pollution data:311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers (CPCB, 2022 assessment), identified on the basis of BOD; a large share of urban sewage discharged without treatment.
- AP-specific:APPCB, Vijayawada, exercising consent and Section 33A powers; industrial effluent regulation in the Visakhapatnam complex; aquaculture effluent around Kolleru; NGT Southern Zone bench, Chennai, with jurisdiction over Andhra Pradesh.

Sources used: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974, Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and Rules 1986, National Green Tribunal Act 2010, and the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023; Central Pollution Control Board — National Ambient Air Quality Standards 2009, Air Quality Index, designated best-use water quality classification, polluted river stretch assessment (2022), and NAMP/CAAQMS networks; MoEFCC — National Clean Air Programme, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019, Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 and the waste management rule-sets; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways — BS-VI norms and Central Motor Vehicles Rules; Ministry of Heavy Industries — PM E-DRIVE; MNRE on non-fossil capacity as on 31 March 2026; International Maritime Organization — MARPOL 73/78, Ballast Water Management Convention and the London Convention/Protocol; UNCLOS 1982; Indian Coast Guard — National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan; INCOIS, NCCR and NCSCM; Supreme Court of India, M.C. Q99:
## Introduction

Air pollution is India’s most significant environmental health risk, and its effects extend well beyond the respiratory system that most answers focus on — reaching the heart, the brain, the crop, the monument and the climate. Understanding which effect a measure addresses is what makes control policy coherent, since interventions differ sharply in what they actually remedy.

## (i) Effects of air pollution

heritage | Climate | Economy .

Human health — the largest burden - Cardiovascular effects dominate. PM2.5 penetrates the alveoli and enters the bloodstream, causing systemic inflammation, oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction — raising the risk of ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction and stroke. Cardiovascular deaths exceed respiratory deaths in the air pollution burden, a fact most answers omit. - Respiratory — asthma exacerbation, chronic bronchitis, COPD, impaired lung development in children, and increased respiratory infection. Outdoor air pollution is classified a Group 1 carcinogen by IARC. -Neurological and metabolic — emerging evidence links long-term exposure to cognitive decline, dementia risk and impaired neurodevelopment, and to insulin resistance. - Pregnancy and neonatal — low birth weight, pre-term delivery, and stillbirth risk. - Indoor exposure — solid cooking fuel produces very high household PM2.5 and CO, with the burden falling on women and young children.

Vegetation and agriculture - Ground-level ozone reduces yields of wheat, rice and pulses — making air pollution a food security issue, not only a health one. - SO2 causes chlorosis and leaf necrosis; particulate deposition on leaves reduces photosynthesis; acid deposition leaches soil nutrients and mobilises toxic aluminium.

Materials and heritage - Acid deposition converts calcium carbonate in marble and limestone to soluble gypsum — “stone leprosy”, documented on the Taj Mahal; corrosion of metals, paint and infrastructure; soiling of buildings.

Climate - CO2 and methane as greenhouse gases; black carbon as a warming agent that also darkens snow and accelerates glacier melt; conversely sulphate aerosols cool, so air quality improvement can unmask additional warming — a nuance worth noting. - Stratospheric ozone depletion by CFCs, distinct from ground-level ozone pollution.

Ecosystems - Acidification of lakes and soils; nitrogen deposition causing eutrophication and shifting species composition; visibility loss affecting aviation and transport.

Economic - Premature mortality, healthcare expenditure, lost labour productivity from heat and illness, crop yield loss, and damage to heritage tourism.

## (ii) Measures to control air pollution — mapped to the effect they address
- **Effect to be addressed** — Measure · Instrument
- **Household PM2.5 and CO (women, children)** — Clean cooking fuel substitution · PMUY; improved cookstoves; electric cooking
- **Vehicular PM, NOx, CO** — Fuel and engine standards; electrification; public transport · BS-VI (April 2020, sulphur at 10 ppm); PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore); metro and e-bus expansion; E20 blending achieved 2025-26
- **Industrial SO2 and acid deposition** — Desulphurisation; low-sulphur fuel · FGD mandates at thermal plants; natural gas substitution; Taj Trapezium Zone directions (M.C. Mehta, 1996)
- **Industrial particulates** — End-of-pipe capture · Electrostatic precipitators, bag filters, cyclones, wet scrubbers; OCEMS telemetry to Board servers
- **Industrial NOx** — Combustion modification and catalysis · Low-NOx burners; selective catalytic reduction
- **Seasonal crop-residue PM peaks** — Residue management instead of burning · Happy seeder, super straw management system, bio- decomposer; residue-to-energy under SATAT
- **Secondary PM2.5 from ammonia** — Fertiliser efficiency · Neem-coated and nano urea; Soil Health Card; PM- PRANAM — fertiliser policy as air quality policy
- **Construction and road dust** — Dust suppression · Mechanised sweeping, water sprinkling, anti-smog guns, site covering; C&D Waste Rules 2016
- **Ambient exposure during peak episodes** — Forecasting and graded restriction · SAFAR forecasting; SAMEER app; GRAP in Delhi-NCR
- **Overall city-level PM** — Programmatic abatement · NCAP — 131 cities in 24 States/UTs, up to 40% PM10 reduction or NAAQS by 2025-26; PRANA portal; XV Finance Commission grants
- **Emissions from power generation** — Fuel transition · Non-fossil capacity 283.46 GW as on 31 March 2026; 50% non-fossil capacity reached June 2025 (MNRE)
- **Cumulative regional load** — Airshed management · CAQM (statutory, 2021) with jurisdiction over the NCR airshed

Cross-cutting measures - Energy efficiency under the PAT scheme — less fuel burnt means less emitted. - Urban greening — Nagar Van Yojana, green belts around industrial estates, Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam. - Market instruments — the Surat particulate emissions trading scheme, the world’s first cap-and-trade market for particulates. - Behavioural and civic — Mission LIFE; no-honking campaigns; citizen complaint reporting through SAMEER; school-level awareness.

The measure that addresses the least-recognised effect: because a large share of PM2.5 is secondary, formed from SO2, NOx and agricultural ammonia travelling across boundaries, city-level action cannot fully succeed. Airshed-level regulation is the corresponding remedy, and CAQM is India’s only statutory instance of it.

## Conclusion

Air pollution’s effects run from the alveolus to the wheat field to the Taj Mahal, with the largest mortality burden falling on the cardiovascular system rather than the lungs. Control measures are effective only when matched to the effect: FGD addresses acid deposition and sulphate particles, PMUY addresses household exposure, and residue management addresses the seasonal peak — but none of these addresses secondary particulate formation across an airshed, which requires regional coordination India has so far institutionalised only for the NCR.

## Value addition
- Effect hierarchy worth stating: cardiovascular > respiratory in mortality burden; IARC classifies outdoor air pollution and PM as Group 1 carcinogens; ground-level ozone reduces wheat and rice yields, making this a food security issue.
- NAAQS 2009: 12 parameters, of which 8 feed the AQI; PM2.5 annual 40 µg/m³ and PM10 annual 60 µg/m³ — both above WHO guideline values.
- NCAP: January 2019; 131 cities in 24 States/UTs; revised target of up to 40% PM10 reduction or NAAQS attainment by 2025-26; PRANA portal.
- Institutional: CPCB and SPCBs; CAQM (statutory, 2021) and GRAP; SAFAR; NAMP and CAAQMS; SAMEER app.
- The nuance examiners reward: sulphate aerosols exert a cooling effect, so improving air quality can unmask additional warming — climate and air quality policy are not always aligned.
- AP-specific: APPCB monitoring in the Visakhapatnam industrial belt; CAAQMS at Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Guntur, Tirupati and Rajahmundry; ESPs at NTPC Simhadri and Vijayawada Thermal Power Station; coastal dispersal giving AP better ambient conditions than the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
Q100:
## Introduction

Disaster management operates across four phases — mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery — and each fails in a characteristic way. The recurring difficulty is structural: mitigation and preparedness are invisible when they succeed, so they attract less political attention and funding than response, which is highly visible. This asymmetry explains most of what follows.

Phase 1 — Mitigation: the “invisible success” problem

- Political economy of prevention. Money spent on a cyclone shelter that is never needed appears wasted; money spent on relief after a disaster appears responsive. This bias systematically under-funds mitigation despite its far higher returns.
- Enforcement of building codes. India has adequate seismic codes — IS 1893 and IS 13920 — but enforcement in the vast informal construction sector is weak. “Earthquakes do not kill people; buildings do”, and the buildings that kill are those built outside the regulatory system.
- Land-use planning ignored. Construction in floodplains, on unstable slopes and over natural drains continues despite hazard mapping; the Vijayawada-Budameru floods of September 2024 followed encroachment of a natural drain.
- Risk data gaps — hazard, vulnerability and exposure mapping at the granularity required for local decisions, and its integration into development approvals.
- Retrofitting of existing structures, particularly lifeline buildings — hospitals, schools, emergency operation centres — is expensive and politically unrewarding.

Phase 2 — Preparedness: plans that exist on paper

- Plans not tested. District Disaster Management Plans exist under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 but are frequently not exercised through mock drills, so gaps surface during the actual event.
- Last-mile warning dissemination — the recurring weak link. Forecasting has improved dramatically, but the chain fails at the final step: reaching a household without a phone, in a language it understands, with instructions specific enough to act on. The Common Alerting Protocol addresses this by pushing multi-hazard alerts across channels.
- Capacity and training — high turnover of trained officials; limited community-level first responder capacity.
- Resource pre-positioning — stockpiles, equipment and shelter readiness, especially in remote and hill districts.
- Community complacency and warning fatigue, where repeated alerts without event reduce compliance.

Phase 3 — Response: coordination and the first 72 hours

- Multi-agency coordination. NDRF, SDRF, armed forces, police, health, civil supplies, power and telecom, plus NGOs and volunteers — with unified command frequently improvised. The Incident Response System under NDMA is designed to solve this and is unevenly adopted.
- Communication failure exactly when it is most needed, as terrestrial networks fail — the argument for satellite and NavIC messaging backup.
- Access — landslides blocking hill roads, flooding cutting off districts, requiring air-lifted relief.
- Relief distribution equity — reaching the most vulnerable, including women, the elderly, persons with disabilities and marginalised groups, rather than the most accessible.
- Damage assessment speed, now materially improved by satellite and drone assessment through ISRO’s Disaster Management Support Programme and the NDEM database.
- Secondary hazards — aftershocks, dam safety, epidemics, and hazardous material releases.

Phase 4 — Recovery: the phase that is forgotten

- Attention decay. Media and political attention shifts within weeks, while recovery takes years — so rehabilitation is chronically under-resourced relative to relief.
- Building back the same vulnerability. Reconstruction that restores the pre-disaster condition recreates the exposure; the Sendai Framework’s “Build Back Better” principle addresses precisely this.
- Livelihood restoration, which lags physical reconstruction and determines whether displaced populations return.
- Psychosocial support, systematically neglected.
- Insurance penetration — very low in India, so recovery depends on public expenditure rather than risk transfer.

## Cross-cutting challenges
- Financing — the National and State Disaster Response Funds are response-oriented; the National and State Disaster Mitigation Funds created under the DM Act are comparatively under-utilised. Ex-ante risk financing and insurance remain thin.
- Data and interoperability across agencies.
- Climate change increasing the frequency and intensity of events, so historical return periods used in design are no longer reliable — a fundamental challenge to the entire risk assessment basis.
- Urbanisation concentrating exposure in hazard-prone locations.

## What has demonstrably worked — the balancing point

India’s cyclone record is the strongest evidence that these challenges are surmountable: mortality has fallen from about 10,000 in the 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone to single or double digits in comparably severe recent cyclones, achieved through IMD forecasting, the Common Alerting Protocol, multipurpose cyclone shelters and mass evacuation. The lesson is that preparedness and last-mile warning, sustained over decades, produce results — which is precisely the phase most prone to under-investment.

AP instances:APSDMA; RTGS’s AWARE platform integrating satellite, drone, IoT and CCTV data with alerts by SMS and WhatsApp; the City Flood Alert system built with IIT Gandhinagar providing 48-hour rainfall outlooks and six-hour flash-flood warnings, beginning with Vijayawada; the RTGS-ISRO SHAR MoU (June 2025); and Tsunami Ready certified coastal villages.

## Conclusion

The common challenges of disaster management are phase-specific: mitigation is under-funded because its success is invisible, preparedness plans go untested, response suffers from coordination gaps in the first hours, and recovery is abandoned when attention moves on. India’s cyclone experience demonstrates that sustained investment in the least visible phases produces the largest returns — a hundredfold reduction in mortality achieved through forecasting and evacuation rather than through response capacity. Extending that approach from cyclones to floods, heat and earthquakes is the outstanding task.

## Value addition
- The four-phase cycle: mitigation –> preparedness –> response –> recovery; some frameworks add prevention before mitigation and rehabilitation and reconstruction within recovery.
- Institutional framework:Disaster Management Act, 2005 creating NDMA (chaired by the Prime Minister), SDMAs (Chief Ministers), DDMAs, NDRF, NIDM, and the National Executive Committee; National Disaster Response Fund and National Disaster Mitigation Fund; Incident Response System.
- Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-30) — four priorities: understanding disaster risk; strengthening disaster risk governance; investing in resilience; enhancing preparedness for effective response and to “Build Back Better”. Seven global targets. India also co-founded the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) in 2019.
- The cyclone success story — the key evidence: about 10,000 deaths in the 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone against single or double digits in Phailin (2013), Fani (2019), Amphan (2020) and Biparjoy (June 2023) — through IMD forecasting, the Common Alerting Protocol, cyclone shelters and mass evacuation.
- Warning and support systems: IMD and Mission Mausam (2024); INCOIS/ITEWC for tsunami; CWC for floods; ISRO’s Disaster Management Support Programme and NDEM; over 250 Heat Action Plans; NavIC messaging for areas beyond mobile coverage.
- Concepts:Risk = Hazard x Exposure x Vulnerability ÷ Capacity; golden hours; build back better; residual risk; risk transfer through insurance; resilient infrastructure.
- AP-specific:APSDMA; RTGS AWARE and City Flood Alert with IIT Gandhinagar; RTGS-ISRO SHAR MoU (June 2025); 1,053-km cyclone-exposed coastline; Tsunami Ready certified villages; the 2024 Vijayawada-Budameru floods as a mitigation and land-use failure.

Sources used: Central Pollution Control Board — National Ambient Air Quality Standards 2009, Air Quality Index and monitoring networks; MoEFCC — National Clean Air Programme, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019 and MISHTI; National Centre for Coastal Research shoreline change assessment; Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023; Department of Land Resources — WDC-PMKSY 2.0 and the Wastelands Atlas of India (2019); ISRO/SAC Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas; UNCCD COP14 (New Delhi, 2019); UNFCCC — Paris Agreement Article 6, Global Methane Pledge and Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use (COP26, 2021); PIB on the Panchamrit commitments, Mission LIFE and the Green Grids Initiative;

Bureau of Energy Efficiency — Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, PAT and Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022; MNRE on non-fossil capacity as on 31 March 2026; Ministry of Heavy Industries — PM E-DRIVE; NDMA — Disaster Management Act 2005, Incident Response System and hazard guidelines; UNDRR Sendai Framework 2015-30; IMD and INCOIS; Government of Andhra Pradesh — APSDMA, RTGS AWARE and City Flood Alert, APCNF and Neeru-Chettu.

Q101:
## Introduction

The National Green Tribunal (NGT) was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 as a specialised body for effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection and conservation of forests and other natural resources. India was among the first countries — after Australia and New Zealand — to create a dedicated environmental court. Its founding premise was that environmental disputes require technical expertise alongside legal judgement, which ordinary civil courts could not supply.

(West) | Kolkata (East) | Chennai (South) , and beneath, two columns listing Judicial Members and Expert Members .

## Composition and structure
- A Chairperson (a retired Supreme Court judge or Chief Justice of a High Court), Judicial Members (retired High Court judges) and Expert Members — the distinguishing feature. Expert members must hold a postgraduate degree in a relevant science or engineering discipline with substantial practical experience in environmental matters.
- Five benches: the Principal Bench at New Delhi, with zonal benches at Bhopal (Central), Pune (West), Kolkata (East) and Chennai (South) — the Chennai bench exercising jurisdiction over Andhra Pradesh.
- The Tribunal also sits on circuit at other locations, which improves access.

## Jurisdiction — and its limits
- Original jurisdiction over all civil cases raising a substantial question relating to the environment, and appellate jurisdiction over orders under the specified statutes.
- The seven scheduled enactments: the Water Act 1974; Water Cess Act 1977; Forest (Conservation) Act 1980; Air Act 1981; Environment (Protection) Act 1986; Public Liability Insurance Act 1991; and Biological Diversity Act 2002.
- The critical limitation — what falls outside. The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Indian Forest Act, 1927 are not in the Schedule, so matters arising purely under them fall outside the NGT’s jurisdiction. This is a significant gap for wildlife and forest offences, and identifying it is what distinguishes an examining answer from a descriptive one.
- Limitation period: applications must generally be filed within six months of the cause of action, extendable by sixty days for sufficient cause — a strict window that has been criticised for barring meritorious claims where environmental harm manifests slowly.

## Powers and procedure — the sources of speed
- Not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure; guided instead by principles of natural justice, which allows it to dispense with procedural formality that slows civil courts.
- Not bound by the Indian Evidence Act, permitting flexible evidence-taking including site inspection and expert committee reports.
- Statutory disposal norm: applications and appeals are to be disposed of, as far as possible, within six months of filing — the provision that makes

“speedy justice” a statutory expectation rather than an aspiration.

- Powers of a civil court in respect of summoning, discovery, evidence and review.
- Relief and remedies: compensation to victims; restitution of damaged property; and restitution of the environment for such area as the Tribunal thinks fit — the last being unusually broad, since it allows an order directed at ecological restoration rather than only at compensation.
- Principles applied: the Act directs the Tribunal to apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
- Suo motu jurisdiction: the Supreme Court in Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha (2021) upheld the NGT’s power to take cognizance on its own motion — a significant expansion, since environmental harm often has no organised complainant.
- Appeals lie to the Supreme Court, ordinarily within ninety days.

## Achievements — the case for the NGT
- Speed relative to ordinary courts. Disposal within the six-month norm is not universal, but average disposal times are far shorter than in civil courts, and the Tribunal has disposed of a very large proportion of the cases filed before it.
- Technical competence. Expert members allow the Tribunal to evaluate emission data, hydrological models and ecological assessments directly, rather than depending entirely on adversarial expert testimony.
- Access to justice. Low filing fees, relaxed procedure and liberal locus standi allow individuals, community groups and NGOs to approach it — with suo motu cognizance widening this further.
- Substantive contributions: enforcement of environmental compensation on polluting industries; directions on solid waste management and legacy dumpsites across States; river pollution and Ganga and Yamuna directions; regulation of sand mining; air pollution directions including on construction dust and crop-residue burning; and orders on illegal construction in ecologically sensitive areas.
- Development of environmental jurisprudence — the Tribunal has operationalised the polluter pays and precautionary principles into quantified compensation, giving them practical rather than declaratory force.

## Constraints — the case for a qualified verdict
- Vacancies and bench strength — the most serious problem. The NGT has repeatedly functioned below sanctioned strength in both judicial and expert members, with some zonal benches non-functional for periods and matters transferred or heard by video conference. A tribunal designed for speed cannot deliver it while under-staffed, and this is the principal reason the six-month norm is often missed.
- Jurisdictional gaps — the exclusion of the Wildlife Protection Act and the Indian Forest Act, and the strict six-month limitation.
- Enforcement of orders. The NGT can direct, but implementation depends on State machinery and pollution control boards; non-compliance with NGT orders is a documented and recurring problem.
- Appeals and delay. Frequent appeals to the Supreme Court can extend proceedings well beyond the tribunal stage, diluting the speed advantage.
- Criticism of overreach — that the Tribunal has occasionally ventured into policy questions properly for the executive, though this is contested and is arguably a consequence of executive under-enforcement.
- Geographic access — five benches for a country of India’s size means litigants may travel considerable distances, mitigated but not solved by circuit sittings and virtual hearings.

## Conclusion

The NGT has substantially delivered on its founding purpose: environmental disputes are decided faster, by adjudicators competent to read the technical evidence, and at low cost to the applicant — with the power to order restitution of the environment itself. Its effectiveness is nonetheless constrained by factors outside its control: persistent vacancies that leave benches under-strength, a Schedule that excludes the Wildlife Protection Act, and dependence on State agencies to implement its orders. Filling vacancies promptly and extending the Schedule would do more for environmental justice than any further expansion of powers.

## Value addition
- The seven scheduled Acts: Water Act 1974; Water Cess Act 1977; Forest (Conservation) Act 1980; Air Act 1981; Environment (Protection) Act 1986; Public Liability Insurance Act 1991; Biological Diversity Act 2002. Excluded: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and Indian Forest Act 1927 — the gap worth naming.
- Structural facts: established 18 October 2010; five benches — Principal (New Delhi), Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai; Chairperson plus judicial and expert members; six-month disposal norm; six-month limitation period for filing; appeals to the Supreme Court within ninety days.
- Principles the Act directs it to apply: sustainable development, precautionary principle, polluter pays — statutory rather than merely judicial in the NGT’s case.
- Key judicial development:Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha (2021) — Supreme Court upheld the NGT’s suo motu jurisdiction, recognising it as a unique forum with a broad public-interest role.
- India’s environmental courts lineage: National Environment Tribunal Act 1995 and National Environment Appellate Authority Act 1997 — both largely non-functional, and both repealed and replaced by the NGT Act 2010. Citing this lineage shows why the NGT was designed as it was.
- Related institutions: CPCB and SPCBs; CAQM (statutory, 2021); the Supreme Court’s environmental jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 21; and, since the Jan Vishwas Act 2023, appeals from adjudicating officers imposing environmental penalties also lie to the NGT.
- AP relevance: the Chennai (Southern Zone) bench exercises jurisdiction over Andhra Pradesh; matters before it have included coastal aquaculture regulation, Kolleru Lake encroachment, sand mining in the Krishna and Godavari, and industrial pollution in the Visakhapatnam belt.
Q102:
## Introduction

The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 was adopted at the Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction at Sendai, Japan, in March 2015, succeeding the Hyogo Framework for Action (2005-2015). Its defining shift is conceptual: from managing disasters to managing disaster risk — that is, from responding to events to reducing the exposure and vulnerability that turn a hazard into a disaster.

Understand risk | P2 Strengthen governance | P3 Invest in resilience | P4 Enhance preparedness & Build Back Better ; base Seven global targets (A-G) .

## Structure of the Framework
- Expected outcome: substantial reduction of disaster risk and losses in lives, livelihoods and health, and in the economic, physical, social, cultural and environmental assets of persons, businesses, communities and countries.
- Goal: prevent new and reduce existing disaster risk through integrated measures that reduce exposure and vulnerability, and increase preparedness for response and recovery.
- Scope: applies to natural and man-made hazards, and to related environmental, technological and biological hazards — broader than Hyogo, and the reason it covered pandemic risk before COVID-19.

## The four priorities for action

1. Understanding disaster risk — risk assessment, hazard mapping, data collection and dissemination, and incorporation of risk knowledge into education and public awareness. Risk must be understood in all its dimensions: hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity. 2. Strengthening disaster risk governance — clear institutional mandates, national and local strategies, coordination mechanisms, and mainstreaming risk reduction across sectors rather than confining it to a disaster agency. 3. Investing in disaster risk reduction for resilience — structural and non-structural investment, including resilient infrastructure, ecosystem-based measures, and risk transfer through insurance. 4. Enhancing disaster preparedness for effective response, and to “Build Back Better” in recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction — the phrase that has entered general usage, meaning reconstruction that reduces future vulnerability rather than restoring the pre-disaster condition.

The seven global targets (A to G) — substantially reduce, by 2030: (A) disaster mortality; (B) number of affected people; (C) direct economic loss relative to GDP; (D) damage to critical infrastructure and disruption of basic services; and substantially increase (E) the number of countries with national and local DRR strategies; (F) international cooperation with developing countries; and (G) availability of and access to multi-hazard early warning systems and risk information.

Guiding principles include primary State responsibility with shared responsibility across society, protection of persons and their assets while promoting human rights, engagement of the whole of society, and a “build back better” approach.

## Adoption and implementation in India
- India was a signatory at Sendai, and the National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP), 2016 — India’s first national plan of its kind — was explicitly aligned to the four Sendai priorities, with a revised edition issued subsequently. This is the central fact for the second limb.
- Institutional framework under the Disaster Management Act, 2005: NDMA chaired by the Prime Minister; SDMAs chaired by Chief Ministers; DDMAs; NDRF and SDRFs; NIDM for training and capacity building; and the National Executive Committee.
- Priority 1 — understanding risk: hazard and vulnerability mapping; seismic zonation under IS 1893; ISRO’s Disaster Management Support Programme and the National Database for Emergency Management (NDEM); NISAR (launched July 2025) for deformation and flood monitoring; the Bhukamp and Damini apps.
- Priority 2 — governance: State and District Disaster Management Plans; mainstreaming into development schemes; the Incident Response System.
- Priority 3 — investment:National and State Disaster Mitigation Funds created under the DM Act; the National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project; multipurpose cyclone shelters; resilient infrastructure through the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI), which India launched in 2019 and hosts.
- Priority 4 — preparedness and build back better: the Common Alerting Protocol for multi-hazard warning across SMS, radio and television; over 250 Heat Action Plans; Mission Mausam (2024) to strengthen forecasting; the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS, recognised by IOC-UNESCO as a regional Tsunami Service Provider; community programmes including Aapda Mitra; and Tsunami Ready certification of coastal villages, including in Andhra Pradesh.

India’s Ten-Point Agenda on Disaster Risk Reduction — articulated by the Prime Minister at the Asian Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction, New Delhi, 2016, and India’s principal contribution to the Sendai discourse. Its elements include: all development sectors to imbibe DRR principles; risk coverage for all, from poor households to SMEs and nations; greater involvement and leadership of women; investment in risk mapping globally; leveraging technology; developing a network of universities working on disaster issues; utilising social media and mobile technologies; building on local capacity and initiative; ensuring learning from every disaster through studies; and greater cohesion in international disaster response.

Assessment. India’s clearest Sendai-aligned achievement is against Target A (mortality): cyclone deaths have fallen from about 10,000 in the 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone to single or double digits in comparably severe recent cyclones. Progress on Target C (economic loss) is weaker, since asset exposure has grown with development, and on Target G, multi-hazard early warning is strong for cyclones and tsunamis but weaker for floods, landslides and heat at local scale.

## Conclusion

The Sendai Framework’s contribution is the shift from managing disasters to managing risk, expressed through four priorities and seven measurable targets. India adopted it substantively rather than formally — the NDMP 2016 was structured around the Sendai priorities, and the ten-point agenda articulated an Indian addition to it. The record is strongest where preparedness and early warning have been sustained, as with cyclones, and weakest where risk reduction must compete with development pressure, as in floodplain and coastal construction.

## Value addition
- Framework facts: adopted 18 March 2015 at Sendai, Japan; period 2015-2030; successor to the Hyogo Framework for Action (2005-2015); voluntary and non-binding; four priorities; seven global targets (A-G); monitored through the Sendai Framework Monitor.
- The four priorities in short form: understand risk –> strengthen governance –> invest in resilience –> enhance preparedness and Build Back Better.
- India’s alignment:National Disaster Management Plan 2016 (and its revision), the first national plan aligned to Sendai; Disaster Management Act, 2005; NDMA, SDMAs, DDMAs, NDRF, NIDM; National and State Disaster Mitigation Funds.
- India’s Ten-Point Agenda on DRR (New Delhi, 2016) — worth listing; frequently examined and distinctively Indian.
- CDRI: the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, launched by India at the UN Climate Action Summit in 2019 and headquartered in New Delhi; also the Infrastructure for Resilient Island States (IRIS) initiative for small island developing states.
- The three global frameworks of 2015 — Sendai (March), the 2030 Agenda and SDGs (September) and the Paris Agreement (December) — are mutually reinforcing, and noting their coherence is a strong analytical point; SDG target 11.b and 13.1 refer directly to disaster risk reduction.
- AP-specific:APSDMA; RTGS AWARE and the City Flood Alert system with IIT Gandhinagar; Tsunami Ready certified villages; multipurpose cyclone shelters along the 1,053-km coastline; the RTGS-ISRO SHAR MoU (June 2025).

## Introduction

Environmentalism is the social, political and ethical movement concerned with protecting the natural environment and reforming the human activity that degrades it. Indian environmentalism has a distinctive character, often described as the “environmentalism of the poor” — arising from communities whose livelihoods depend directly on forests, rivers and commons, as in Chipko (1973), Silent Valley and the Narmada Bachao Andolan, rather than from a wilderness-preservation impulse. Its principal legislative expression is the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

## Environmentalism in brief

Its core claims are that natural systems have value — instrumental, and for many intrinsic — that human activity must operate within ecological limits, and that those who bear environmental costs are frequently not those who receive the benefits. In India it has expressed itself through movements, judicial activism and legislation, in roughly that order of historical sequence. (For the movement history, see Q94.)

## The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 — context

Enacted in the aftermath of the Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984), which exposed the inadequacy of sectoral pollution laws to deal with a catastrophic industrial release. It was passed under Article 253 — legislation to implement international agreements — giving effect to decisions of the Stockholm Conference (1972), which is why it applies uniformly across India without requiring State consent. It is deliberately an umbrella statute, designed to fill gaps between the Water Act 1974 and the Air Act 1981 rather than to replace them.

## Key features

Noise | Authorities under Section 3 .

- A comprehensive definition of “environment” — water, air and land, and the interrelationship among them and with human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property. This breadth is what makes the Act an umbrella.
- Wide powers to the Central Government (Section 3). Power to take all such measures as it deems necessary for protecting and improving environmental quality and preventing pollution — including setting standards, restricting industrial location, laying down procedures for handling hazardous substances, and constituting authorities. Section 3(3) is the source of bodies such as coastal zone management authorities and the EIA machinery.
- Power to issue directions (Section 5) — including for closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process, and for stoppage or regulation of electricity, water or any other service — the operative enforcement provision.
- Prevention and control (Section 7) — no person carrying on any industry, operation or process shall discharge or emit any environmental pollutant in excess of prescribed standards.
- Handling of hazardous substances (Section 8) — compliance with prescribed procedures and safeguards.
- Duty on accident or apprehended discharge (Section 9) — the person responsible must prevent or mitigate the pollution and immediately intimate the authorities, who may take remedial measures and recover the cost from the person concerned — a statutory expression of polluter pays.
- Powers of entry, inspection, sampling and analysis (Sections 10-13), with government analysts and recognised environmental laboratories.
- Citizen suits (Section 19). Cognizance of offences may be taken on a complaint by any person who has given sixty days’ notice of the alleged offence to the Central Government or the prescribed authority — an important access-to-justice provision, since it does not depend on regulatory initiative.
- Protection for whistleblowing employees and safeguards for officers acting in good faith (Section 17 for corporate liability, Section 18 for good-faith protection).
- Overriding effect (Section 24) — the Act’s provisions have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in other laws, subject to the rule that where an act is punishable under both the EPA and another law, the offender is liable under the other law.
- Rule-making power (Section 25) — the source of India’s entire body of environmental subordinate legislation: the Environment (Protection) Rules 1986, EIA Notification 2006, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019, Noise Pollution Rules 2000, and the waste management rule-sets for hazardous, bio-medical, solid, plastic, e-waste, battery and C&D waste.

## Penalties — the amended position

Section 15 originally provided for imprisonment up to five years or fine up to one lakh rupees, or both, with additional daily fines for continuing contravention and imprisonment up to seven years where failure continued beyond a year. The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 substantially decriminalised contraventions, replacing imprisonment with monetary penalties determined by adjudicating officers, with appeals to the National Green Tribunal and proceeds credited to an Environmental Protection Fund. Offences causing grievous harm or death remain criminal.

## Constitutional and judicial context
- Article 48A — Directive Principle requiring the State to protect and improve the environment (42nd Amendment, 1976); Article 51A(g) — Fundamental Duty of citizens; Article 21 interpreted to include the right to a clean and healthy environment.
- Judicial doctrines read into the framework: polluter pays, precautionary principle, public trust doctrine, sustainable development (Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum, 1996), and absolute liability (M.C. Mehta, Oleum gas leak, 1987) — a rule of no exceptions, developed specifically because the Bhopal context showed strict liability’s exceptions to be inadequate.
- M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024), recognising a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change.

## Critical assessment

The Act’s strength is its breadth and rule-making power; its weakness is that it concentrates authority in the Central Government with limited institutional machinery of its own — it created no dedicated enforcement body, relying on the pollution control boards constituted under the earlier Acts. Enforcement therefore depends on boards that are chronically under-staffed. Whether the 2023 shift from prosecution to administrative penalty improves this will depend on whether penalty levels exceed the cost of compliance.

## Conclusion

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is the constitutional keystone of Indian environmental regulation: it defines the environment broadly, confers wide residuary power on the Centre, provides for citizen enforcement, and supplies the rule-making authority under which the EIA, coastal zone and waste management regimes all operate. Its enduring limitation is institutional rather than textual — it created powers without creating the inspectorate to exercise them, which is why India’s environmental deficit has always been one of enforcement rather than of law.

## Value addition
- Sections worth citing:3 (wide powers and constitution of authorities); 5 (directions including closure); 7 (discharge in excess of standards); 8 (hazardous substances); 9 (duty on accident, and cost recovery); 15 (penalties, as amended 2023); 19 (citizen suits after 60 days’ notice); 24 (overriding effect); 25 (rule-making).
- Enactment route: under Article 253, implementing Stockholm Conference (1972) decisions — contrast with the Water Act 1974, passed under Article 252 with State consent because water is a State subject.
- Subordinate legislation flowing from the Act: Environment (Protection) Rules 1986; EIA Notification 2006; CRZ Notification 2019; Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000; Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016; Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016; Solid Waste Management Rules 2016; Plastic Waste Rules; E-Waste Rules 2022; Battery Waste Rules 2022; C&D Waste Rules 2016.
- The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023: decriminalised specified offences under the EPA, Water Act and Air Act; monetary penalties by adjudicating officers; appeals to the NGT; proceeds to an Environmental Protection Fund.
- Indian environmentalism — the movements to name: Bishnoi (1730s); Chipko (1973); Silent Valley (1970s-80s); Appiko (1983); Jungle Bachao Andolan; Narmada Bachao Andolan. The framing “environmentalism of the poor” is associated with Ramachandra Guha and Madhav Gadgil.
- AP relevance: APPCB exercising powers under the Act and its rules; EIA and CRZ disputes over coastal industry and aquaculture; the Sompeta and Kakarapalli thermal power protests in Srikakulam as instances of livelihood-based environmentalism.
