## Introduction

India’s water law is not a single code but an accumulation of constitutional provisions, colonial-era doctrines, sectoral statutes and judicial doctrine — developed piecemeal over more than a century. The result is a framework that regulates surface water pollution reasonably well, groundwater extraction hardly at all, and treats water simultaneously as State property, private property and a fundamental right, without reconciling the three.

## The existing framework — in brief
- **(Water Act 1974, Water Cess Act 1977, EPA 1986, ISRWD Act 1956, Dam Safety Act 2021)** — –> · Policy (National Water Policy

- Constitutional:Entry 17, State List — water supplies, irrigation, canals, drainage, embankments and water storage; Entry 56, Union List — regulation and development of inter-State rivers to the extent declared by Parliament; Article 262 — Parliament may provide for adjudication of inter-State water disputes and may bar the jurisdiction of courts; Article 21 — the right to water read into the right to life.
- Statutory:Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 (quality); Water Cess Act 1977 (since repealed); EPA 1986 and effluent standards; Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (amended 2019); River Boards Act, 1956 (never effectively used); Dam Safety Act, 2021; the Easements

Act, 1882, whose groundwater doctrine is discussed below.

- Policy:National Water Policy 2012; National Water Mission; model Groundwater Bills circulated to States; a draft National Water Framework Bill.

## Critical examination — the four structural defects

## Fragmentation across the federal divide — the foundational problem

Water is a State subject, but rivers are not. A river basin crosses State boundaries while regulatory authority stops at them, so no single authority manages the hydrological unit. The consequences are visible: prolonged inter-State disputes over the Krishna, Cauvery, Ravi-Beas and Mahadayi; a River Boards Act, 1956 that was never operationalised despite existing for nearly seventy years; and basin organisations without regulatory power. Adjudication under the ISRWD Act, 1956 has itself been slow, with tribunals taking years to decades — which the 2019 amendment sought to address through a single permanent tribunal with benches and a fixed timeframe.

2. Absence of a rights framework — water as property rather than as entitlement

Indian law contains no comprehensive statutory statement of the right to water, its priority of use, or the obligations attaching to it. The right exists judicially, under Article 21, but not legislatively — so entitlements, minimum quantities and priorities between drinking, irrigation and industry rest on policy rather than law. The National Water Policy 2012 recognises water as an economic good while guaranteeing a minimum for life, but a policy is not enforceable.

## The groundwater ownership rule — the most consequential single defect

Under the doctrine inherited from the Indian Easements Act, 1882, groundwater is treated as attached to land: the landowner has the right to extract the water beneath his land, effectively without limit. This has three severe consequences: - It ties access to landholding, so the landless have no groundwater right at all — an equity failure built into the law. - It makes regulation of extraction nearly impossible, since restriction confronts a recognised property interest. - It ignores hydrogeology. Aquifers are shared, connected units; one landowner’s pumping lowers a neighbour’s water table. The law treats as separate what is physically continuous.

India is the world’s largest user of groundwater, and this rule is the legal reason extraction cannot be effectively capped. Model Groundwater Bills proposing that groundwater be held as a public trust have been circulated to States repeatedly since 1970, with limited adoption.

## Point-source design against non-point-source reality

The Water Act’s consent mechanism regulates identifiable discharge points — a factory outfall, a sewage outlet. But a large and growing share of water pollution is non-point: agricultural runoff carrying nitrates and pesticides, urban stormwater, and atmospheric deposition. These have no outfall to license, so they fall entirely outside the regulatory architecture. This is a design limitation, not an enforcement failure, and identifying it as such is the sharpest point available.

## Further weaknesses
- Enforcement capacity — chronically under-staffed pollution control boards, with dependence on consent fees creating a structural conflict.
- Weak penalties, now further diluted for many offences by the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023, which replaced imprisonment with monetary penalties.
- Quality and quantity regulated separately — the Water Act governs pollution, while allocation is governed by State irrigation law and administrative practice, though the two are hydrologically inseparable.
- Environmental flows have no statutory basis; they are provided for in policy and in individual project conditions, not as a legal entitlement of the river.
- Traditional and community rights over tanks and commons are largely unrecognised in modern law.
- Water quality data: CPCB identified 311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers in its 2022 assessment — an indication that the existing framework, whatever its provisions, is not delivering.

## Measures for progressive reform — mapped to the defects

Addressing fragmentation - Enact a National Water Framework Law — which the Mihir Shah Committee (2016) recommended — providing common principles binding on the Union and States without displacing State legislative competence, on the model used for the National Food Security Act. -Establish river basin organisations with regulatory authority across State boundaries, operationalising the River Boards Act or replacing it. - Complete implementation of the ISRWD (Amendment) Act, 2019 — a single permanent tribunal with benches, a Dispute Resolution Committee for prior negotiation, and fixed timelines.

Addressing the rights gap - Statutory recognition of the right to water with a defined minimum quantity, and a legal priority of use — drinking water first, then agriculture and industry. - Statutory basis for environmental flows as a legitimate claim on the river.

Addressing groundwater — the highest-priority reform - Replace the Easements doctrine with a public trust framework in which groundwater is a common pool resource held in trust, with use rights rather than ownership. - Aquifer-level management — the National Aquifer Mapping programme provides the technical basis; Atal Bhujal Yojana provides the participatory model through village water security plans, and is the most promising existing instrument because it changes behaviour without confronting the property question head-on. - Rationalise power subsidies for agricultural pumping, which are the principal economic driver of over-extraction; separate agricultural feeders and use solar under PM-KUSUM with buy-back, so that saving water becomes profitable.

Addressing non-point pollution - Catchment-level instruments — nutrient management, buffer strips, constructed wetlands and urban stormwater rules — since the consent mechanism cannot reach these sources. - Reduce nitrogen load at source: neem-coated and nano urea, Soil Health Cards, PM-

PRANAM, and natural farming — APCNF in Andhra Pradesh covering over 1.77 million farmers with reported water savings up to 50%.

Institutional and demand-side reforms - Independent State Water Regulatory Authorities for tariff setting and entitlement enforcement. - Volumetric supply and metering, at least at the level of Water User Associations, so that water can be charged by quantity — the reform most likely to induce efficiency. Andhra Pradesh’s Farmers’ Management of Irrigation Systems Act, 1997 provides the institutional platform. - Strengthen pollution control boards with technical staff and independent finance; expand OCEMS telemetry. - Mandatory rainwater harvesting and reuse of treated wastewater, with statutory recognition of treated water as a resource.

## Conclusion

India’s water law regulates the visible and the divisible — a factory outfall, a river between two States — and fails at the invisible and the shared: the aquifer beneath a village and the runoff from a field. Its single most consequential defect is the Easements Act doctrine tying groundwater to landownership, which makes the country’s largest water problem legally unregulable and excludes the landless entirely. A National Water Framework Law establishing common principles, a public trust basis for groundwater, and basin-level institutions with actual authority would address the structural problems; without them, further schemes will continue to work against the grain of the law.

## Value addition
- The constitutional provisions to cite precisely:Entry 17, State List; Entry 56, Union List; Article 262 (inter-State water disputes, with power to bar court jurisdiction); Article 21 (right to water, judicially read in).
- The groundwater defect in one line: the Indian Easements Act, 1882 treats groundwater as attached to land, giving the landowner an effectively unlimited extraction right — which ties access to landholding, excludes the landless, and makes extraction limits legally difficult.
- Key committee recommendation: the Mihir Shah Committee (2016) on restructuring the Central Water Commission and Central Ground Water Board recommended a National Water Commission and an integrated approach to surface and groundwater — the most-cited reform proposal in this field.
- ISRWD (Amendment) Act, 2019: a single permanent tribunal with benches replacing multiple ad hoc tribunals; a Dispute Resolution Committee for negotiation before adjudication; fixed timelines for award.
- Instruments that work around the legal gap:Atal Bhujal Yojana (participatory village water security plans); National Aquifer Mapping; Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain; PM-KUSUM with solar buy-back changing the economics of pumping.
- Data:311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers (CPCB, 2022); India as the world’s largest groundwater user; a large share of urban sewage discharged untreated.
- AP-specific:AP Farmers’ Management of Irrigation Systems Act, 1997 — a national reference point for participatory irrigation management through Water User Associations, Distributary Committees and Project Committees; Krishna and Godavari inter-State allocation and the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal; hard-rock aquifers in Rayalaseema where extraction limits matter most; APCNF water savings.

## Introduction

The India State of Forest Report (ISFR) is the biennial national assessment of forest and tree resources published by the Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun, an organisation under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. First published in 1987, it is the authoritative source on India’s forest cover and the basis for national and international forest reporting. The current edition is ISFR 2023, released in December 2024.

## How the assessment is made — the methodology determines the meaning
- Based on satellite remote sensing interpretation, using data from Indian remote sensing satellites at a specified resolution, supplemented by ground verification and the National Forest Inventory field plots.
- The definition that matters:forest cover means all land, more than one hectare in area, with a tree canopy density of more than 10 per cent, irrespective of ownership and legal status, and irrespective of whether the species are of natural or planted origin. The italicised parts are the source of most criticism, discussed below.
- Density classes:Very Dense Forest (canopy density 70% and above); Moderately Dense Forest (40-70%); Open Forest (10-40%); Scrub (below 10%, reported separately and not counted as forest cover).
- Tree cover — patches of trees below one hectare, occurring outside recorded forest areas, assessed separately.
- The report also covers mangroves, growing stock, bamboo resources, carbon stock, and forest fire incidence.

## Key findings of ISFR 2023
- Total forest and tree cover: 8,27,357 sq km — 25.17% of India’s geographical area.
- Forest cover: 7,15,343 sq km (21.76%); tree cover: 1,12,014 sq km (3.41%).
- Net increase of 1,445 sq km in forest and tree cover over the 2021 assessment.
- Mangrove cover: 4,991.68 sq km.
- Total carbon stock in India’s forests estimated at about 7,285.5 million tonnes, an increase over the previous assessment — relevant to India’s NDC commitment of an additional 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2e sink by 2030.
- Largest forest cover by area: Madhya Pradesh, followed by Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Maharashtra.
- Highest forest cover as a percentage of geographical area: Lakshadweep, Mizoram, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands; among the larger States, the North-Eastern States and Chhattisgarh rank highest.
- Andhra Pradesh: forest cover of about 30,084.96 sq km, a decline from 30,223.62 sq km in 2021 — a reduction of 138.66 sq km; the State also recorded a very high number of large forest fire events.
- Methodological change in 2023: forest cover and tree cover are reported separately as well as in combination, improving transparency about what each figure contains.

What ISFR 2015 established — since the question refers to it: that edition reported an increase in forest and tree cover over the 2013 assessment, introduced improved reporting on carbon stock, and continued the biennial series that allows change detection over time. Its principal value now is as a point in the trend line rather than as a current statement.

## The methodological caveat — what makes a “note” complete

The ISFR’s definition of forest cover counts any land above one hectare with over 10% canopy density, regardless of ownership, legal status or species origin. This means: - Plantations, orchards, coffee and rubber estates, and urban tree patches are counted as forest cover, though they are ecologically very different from natural forest. - A dense natural forest degraded into open forest shows no loss of “forest cover” at all, since both exceed the 10% threshold — so degradation is systematically under-captured while area is preserved on paper. - Consequently, a reported increase in forest cover can coexist with a decline in forest quality and biodiversity. Independent assessments using different definitions — including Global Forest Watch (World Resources Institute), which measures tree cover — report different figures for the same period.

Stating this caveat is what converts a recitation of numbers into an informed note, and it is the point examiners most reward on this topic.

## Uses of the ISFR
- Basis for national forest policy and for monitoring the National Forest Policy 1988 target of 33% of geographical area under forest and tree cover (66% in hills).
- Input to India’s NDC carbon sink commitment and to international reporting under the FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment and the UNFCCC.
- Planning basis for CAMPA compensatory afforestation, the Green India Mission, MISHTI for mangroves and the Green Credit Programme.
- Foundation for FSI’s near-real-time forest fire alert system, which pushes SMS alerts to field staff on satellite detection.

## Conclusion

The India State of Forest Report is India’s authoritative forest assessment and shows a slowly rising forest and tree cover — 25.17% of geographical area in ISFR 2023, against the 33% policy target. Its figures must be read with their definition in mind: because plantations count and degradation within the canopy threshold does not register, area can rise while quality falls. The report’s real value lies less in the headline percentage than in the disaggregated data it provides — by density class, by State, on mangroves, carbon stock and fire — which is where the actual condition of India’s forests can be read.

## Value addition
- ISFR 2023 headline figures: forest and tree cover 8,27,357 sq km = 25.17%; forest cover 7,15,343 sq km (21.76%); tree cover 1,12,014 sq km (3.41%); net increase 1,445 sq km over 2021; mangroves 4,991.68 sq km; total forest carbon stock about 7,285.5 million tonnes.
- The definition to quote: forest cover = all land above one hectare with canopy density above 10%, irrespective of ownership, legal status or species origin — the clause that includes plantations and orchards.
- Density classes: Very Dense Forest (>=70%), Moderately Dense Forest (40-70%), Open Forest (10-40%), Scrub (<10%, excluded from forest cover).
- The distinction examiners test:forest cover (satellite-assessed canopy, regardless of legal status) versus recorded forest area (legally notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act or State laws). The two differ substantially, and conflating them is a common error.
- Policy targets and commitments: National Forest Policy 1988 — 33% of geographical area (66% in hills); NDC — additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2e by 2030; Bonn Challenge and UNCCD commitment to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.
- FSI’s other outputs: biennial ISFR; National Forest Inventory; near-real-time forest fire alert system (FAST); forest cover change matrix; and Above Ground Biomass assessment using satellite data.
- AP-specific: forest cover 30,084.96 sq km (2023), down 138.66 sq km from 2021; among the highest counts of large forest fire events nationally; Coringa mangroves; Eastern Ghats and Nallamala forests; Vana Samrakshana Samithis for community management.

## Introduction

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) was constituted in September 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and was subsequently entrusted with functions under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. It is a statutory organisation under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and functions as the apex technical and coordinating body of India’s pollution control system.

## The division of labour — the key distinction

The CPCB is principally a normative and coordinating body; enforcement against individual units rests with State Pollution Control Boards. The CPCB does, however, discharge the functions of a State Board in a Union Territory — a detail worth knowing.

## Functions of the CPCB

1. Advisory - To advise the Central Government on any matter concerning the prevention and control of water and air pollution and the improvement of air quality.

2. Standard-setting — the core normative function - To lay down, modify or annul, in consultation with State Governments, standards for the quality of air and water — including the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (2009) with 12 parameters, and effluent and emission standards for industry. - To lay down standards for the treatment of sewage and trade effluent before discharge. - Note the asymmetry: State Boards may prescribe standards more stringent than the CPCB’s, but not less — establishing the CPCB standard as a national floor.

3. Coordination - To coordinate the activities of State Boards and to resolve disputes among them — a function of increasing importance as pollution problems cross State boundaries. - To provide technical assistance and guidance to State Boards, and to carry out and sponsor investigations and research.

4. Planning and programme functions - To plan and cause to be executed a nationwide programme for the prevention, control and abatement of water and air pollution. - To plan and organise training of persons engaged in pollution control programmes.

5. Monitoring and data - To operate the National Water Quality Monitoring Programme and the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP), with continuous stations (CAAQMS) and manual stations across the country. - To collect, compile and publish technical and statistical data on pollution, and to prepare manuals, codes and guides for treatment and disposal. - To disseminate information — the Air Quality Index through the SAMEER app, and the periodic assessment of polluted river stretches (311 across 279 rivers in the 2022 assessment).

6. Public awareness - To organise mass awareness programmes through media on pollution prevention and control.

7. Laboratory and analytical functions - To establish or recognise laboratories for analysis of water, air and effluent samples, and to certify government analysts.

8. Functions under subordinate legislation - Administration and monitoring under the waste management rules — hazardous, bio-medical, solid, plastic, e-waste, battery and C&D waste — including Extended Producer Responsibility registration and certificate systems operated on the CPCB portal. -Categorisation of industries into Red, Orange, Green and White by pollution potential, with the White category exempt from consent requirements. - The Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index (CEPI) for identifying critically polluted areas, and the associated moratoria on new industry. - Star Rating and compliance frameworks; guidance on Online Continuous Emission and Effluent Monitoring Systems (OCEMS), which transmit stack and outfall readings directly to Board servers.

## Operational programmes through which functions are discharged
- National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) — technical guidance for 131 non-attainment and million-plus cities in 24 States/UTs, with the PRANA portal for tracking.
- Action plans for polluted river stretches, prepared by States under CPCB direction and monitored by the NGT.
- Zero Liquid Discharge norms for specified sectors; guidelines on noise, plastic waste and construction dust.
- Environmental data publication — annual reports, the National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network, and water and air quality series.

## Constraints

The CPCB’s authority is largely normative and advisory; it does not license or inspect individual units outside Union Territories, so the effectiveness of its standards depends entirely on State Boards that are chronically under-staffed. Where a State Board does not act, the CPCB’s remedy is guidance and, ultimately, reference to the Central Government or the NGT rather than direct enforcement.

## Conclusion

The CPCB sets the standards, monitors national air and water quality, coordinates and adjudicates between State Boards, and administers the waste and EPR regimes — but it is not, except in Union Territories, the body that regulates the individual polluter. India’s pollution control architecture therefore depends on a division of labour in which the technically strongest institution has the least direct enforcement power. Strengthening State Boards, rather than expanding the CPCB, is consequently the reform that would improve outcomes most.

## Value addition
- Constitution and legal basis: CPCB constituted September 1974 under the Water Act, 1974; entrusted with air pollution functions under the Air Act, 1981; functions as a State Board in Union Territories; principal functions under Section 16 of the Water Act and Section 16 of the Air Act.
- The standards asymmetry: State Boards may lay down standards more stringent than the CPCB’s, never less — making the CPCB standard a national floor.
- Industry categorisation:Red, Orange, Green and White by pollution potential; White category exempt from consent requirements — a specific detail examiners like.
- CPCB monitoring programmes:NAMP and CAAQMS for air; National Water Quality Monitoring Programme; National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network; CEPI for critically polluted areas; OCEMS telemetry.
- Data outputs to cite:NAAQS 2009 (12 parameters, 8 in the AQI); 311 polluted river stretches across 279 rivers (2022 assessment); municipal solid waste 1,70,339 TPD with 92% collection and 54% processing (2021-22).
- Related bodies:SPCBs and Pollution Control Committees (UTs); CAQM for the NCR airshed (statutory, 2021); NGT for adjudication; and, since the Jan Vishwas Act 2023, adjudicating officers for environmental penalties with appeals to the NGT.
- AP-specific:APPCB, Vijayawada, exercising consent, inspection and Section 33A/31A directions; CAAQMS at Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Guntur, Tirupati and Rajahmundry; CEPI assessments of AP industrial clusters.

Supplementary: Q162(b) — Key points of the COP-21 Paris Agreement

The previous batch covered Q162(a) on disaster management challenges; this completes the question’s second limb.

Adoption and status. The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in Paris in December 2015 and entered into force in November 2016. It is a legally binding international treaty, but with an important qualification examiners test: the content of each country’s Nationally Determined Contribution is nationally determined and not itself legally binding — the binding obligation is to prepare, communicate and maintain successive NDCs and to report on progress.

Key elements

- Temperature goal (Article 2): hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2deg C above pre-industrial levels, and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5deg C.
- Nationally Determined Contributions (Article 4): every Party prepares and communicates an NDC, updated every five years, with each successive NDC representing a progression beyond the previous one — the “ratchet mechanism”.
- Long-term goal: achieve a balance between anthropogenic emissions by sources and removals by sinks in the second half of this century — the formulation underlying “net zero”.
- Adaptation (Article 7): a global goal on adaptation, with national adaptation planning and communication.
- Loss and Damage (Article 8): recognition of loss and damage associated with climate change impacts, through the Warsaw International Mechanism — the basis on which the Loss and Damage Fund was later agreed at COP27 and operationalised at COP28.
- Finance (Article 9): developed countries to provide financial resources to developing countries for mitigation and adaptation, continuing existing obligations; the USD 100 billion per year goal, and its successor, the New Collective Quantified Goal agreed at COP29 (Baku, 2024).
- Technology and capacity building (Articles 10-11).
- Enhanced Transparency Framework (Article 13): common reporting of emissions and progress, with flexibility for developing countries — designed as the accountability mechanism in place of penalties.
- Global Stocktake (Article 14): every five years, assessing collective progress; the first Global Stocktake concluded at COP28 (Dubai, 2023), calling for “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems”.
- Market and non-market approaches (Article 6): cooperative approaches with ITMOs (6.2), a centralised crediting mechanism (6.4) and non-market approaches (6.8).
- Principles:equity and Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities in the light of different national circumstances — the formulation India pressed for.

India’s position and commitments. India ratified the Agreement in 2016. Its updated NDC and the Panchamrit announced at COP26 commit it to 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50% of energy requirements from renewables, a reduction of one billion tonnes in projected emissions by 2030, a 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels, and net zero by 2070. India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of target (MNRE). India has also advanced Mission LIFE as a demand-side contribution and co-founded the International Solar Alliance and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure.

How Paris differs from Kyoto — the comparison worth making: Kyoto imposed top-down, binding targets on developed countries only; Paris uses bottom-up, self-determined contributions from all countries, held together by transparency, peer review and the ratchet rather than by sanctions. This made universal participation possible, at the cost of guaranteed ambition — which is why the Global Stocktake exists.

## Introduction

Environmental protection ultimately depends on millions of individual decisions — whether a household segregates waste, whether a farmer over-applies urea, whether a citizen reports a violation. Environmental awareness is therefore not a supplement to regulation but a precondition for it. In India this has both a constitutional foundation in Article 51A(g) — the Fundamental Duty to protect and improve the natural environment — and a judicial mandate.

institutions | Digital platforms .

## The constitutional and judicial basis — the point that grounds the answer
- Article 51A(g) — Fundamental Duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.
- Article 48A — Directive Principle requiring the State to protect and improve the environment.
- M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991) — the Supreme Court directed that environmental education be made compulsory at all levels, from primary school through university, and that cinema halls and television broadcast environmental awareness material. This is a judicially mandated obligation, not a discretionary programme.
- Following this, the UGC made Environmental Studies a compulsory course for all undergraduate students, and environmental content was integrated into school curricula by NCERT.

## Steps in formal education
- School curriculum integration. Environmental concepts are embedded across science, geography and social science from primary level, following the M.C. Mehta direction. NEP 2020 reinforces this by emphasising environmental awareness, sustainability and experiential learning, and by treating “education about the environment” as part of the value framework.
- Eco-Clubs / National Green Corps. School eco-clubs under the National Green Corps programme of MoEFCC engage students in plantation, waste segregation, water conservation and biodiversity documentation — the largest school environmental network in the country.
- Higher education and research — compulsory undergraduate environmental studies; specialised programmes in environmental science, engineering and law; and research through university departments and national institutes.
- Experiential learning — field visits to sanctuaries, sewage treatment plants, MRFs and biodiversity parks, which change understanding more than classroom instruction.

## Government programmes and institutions
- ENVIS — the Environmental Information System of MoEFCC, a network of hubs and resource partners disseminating environmental information, now reorganised around thematic and State ENVIS Hubs.
- National Environment Awareness Campaign (NEAC) — annual themed campaigns implemented through Regional Resource Agencies and NGOs,

reaching schools, colleges and communities.

- National Green Corps and GLOBE programme for student scientific observation.
- Mission LIFE (Lifestyle for Environment) — announced by India at COP26 (2021) and launched globally in 2022, framing climate and environmental action as “Pro-Planet People” behaviour across seven themes: save water, save energy, reduce single-use plastic, sustainable food systems, reduce waste, healthy lifestyles and reduce e-waste. Its three-stage logic — Change in Demand –> Change in Supply –> Change in Policy — is precisely a theory of how awareness produces systemic change, and is the single most important programme to cite for this question.
- Swachh Bharat Mission — arguably India’s most effective behaviour-change campaign, combining mass communication, celebrity endorsement, competitive ranking through Swachh Survekshan, and infrastructure provision.
- Observances as focal points — World Environment Day (5 June), Earth Day, National Pollution Control Day (2 December), World Wetlands Day (2 February), National Space Day (23 August), Wildlife Week.
- Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam — the plantation campaign linking an environmental act to a personal one, which is why it achieved participation.
- Green Skill Development Programme (MoEFCC) — training youth for employment in the environment and forestry sectors, connecting awareness to livelihood.

## Media and communication
- Mass media — television and radio public service broadcasting, following the M.C. Mehta direction; documentary and science programming on Doordarshan and All India Radio.
- Print and digital journalism — publications such as Down To Earth (Centre for Science and Environment) sustaining sustained rather than episodic coverage.
- Social media and mobile applications — the most effective contemporary channel, particularly for young audiences.
- Citizen-facing data platforms, which are themselves an awareness instrument: the SAMEER app publishing real-time air quality, the Swachhata app for waste grievance reporting, and the Meri LiFE portal. Publishing data converts an abstract problem into a visible one.

## Community and institutional participation
- Panchayats, urban local bodies and Ward Committees under the 73rd and 74th Amendments; Biodiversity Management Committees preparing People’s Biodiversity Registers, which document local species and traditional knowledge and are simultaneously an education exercise.
- Joint Forest Management and Vana Samrakshana Samithis in Andhra Pradesh; Water User Associations; Eco-Development Committees.
- Self-Help Groups, which have proved effective vehicles for waste management, nursery and plantation work.
- NGOs, religious institutions and community leaders, whose credibility often exceeds that of official messaging.
- Corporate participation through CSR obligations under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, and BRSR sustainability reporting for large listed companies.

## Steps to make awareness effective — what the question’s “steps” should build toward
- Localise the message. Generic environmental messaging is ignored; a message about this lake, this landfill or this crop works. Environmental education is most effective when the subject is within walking distance.
- Link awareness to livelihood or saving. Behaviour changes when it pays — rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar, LPG under PMUY, or higher income under natural farming. APCNF in Andhra Pradesh has changed the practices of over 1.77 million farmers because the economics improved, not because of a campaign.
- Combine information with infrastructure. Telling households to segregate fails if collection re-mixes the streams. Awareness and provision must move together.
- Use competition and recognition — Swachh Survekshan converted municipal cleanliness into a ranking that mayors care about.
- Sustain rather than campaign. Episodic drives around observance days produce short-lived compliance; institutionalised programmes such as eco-clubs and school curricula produce durable change.
- Target the decision-maker — advisories reaching a farmer at sowing time, or a builder at design stage, matter more than general publicity.

## Conclusion

Environmental awareness in India rests on a constitutional duty and a Supreme Court mandate, and is delivered through school curricula, ENVIS and NEAC, mass media, community institutions and, most recently, Mission LIFE. Its effectiveness, however, depends less on the volume of messaging than on three conditions: that the message concerns something local and visible, that the recommended behaviour is made economically sensible, and that the infrastructure exists to act on it. Awareness without a functioning collection vehicle, or without a viable alternative to stubble burning, produces informed frustration rather than changed behaviour.

## Value addition
- The judicial mandate:M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991) — the Supreme Court directed compulsory environmental education at all levels of schooling and broadcasting of environmental material by cinema halls and television. The UGC consequently made Environmental Studies a mandatory undergraduate course.
- Constitutional provisions:Article 48A (Directive Principle, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976); Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty); Article 21 as interpreted to include the right to a clean environment.
- Programmes to name:ENVIS; National Environment Awareness Campaign (NEAC); National Green Corps eco-clubs; GLOBE programme; Green Skill Development Programme; Mission LIFE and the Meri LiFE portal; Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam; Swachh Bharat Mission and Swachh Survekshan.
- Mission LIFE’s seven themes: save water; save energy; reduce single-use plastic; adopt sustainable food systems; reduce waste; adopt healthy lifestyles; reduce e-waste. Its three-stage strategy — Demand –> Supply –> Policy — is the most citable framework for this question.
- Data as awareness:SAMEER (real-time AQI), Swachhata (waste grievance), PARIVESH (clearance transparency) — publishing data is itself an awareness instrument, since it makes an invisible problem visible.
- International context: the Stockholm Conference (1972) first recognised environmental education internationally; the Tbilisi Declaration (1977) set its objectives — awareness, knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation; UNESCO’s Education for Sustainable Development and SDG 4.7.
- AP-specific:Vana Samrakshana Samithis; Biodiversity Management Committees and People’s Biodiversity Registers; APCNF as behaviour change achieved through economics; Village and Ward Secretariats as a communication channel; Mana Mitra reaching 58.2 lakh citizens.

## Introduction

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 were designed as a complementary pair: the first created the regulatory machinery, and the second financed it while giving industry an economic incentive to treat effluent. The Cess Act was repealed in 2017 following the introduction of GST, leaving the regulatory structure without its dedicated revenue source.

funding , and a cross through the second labelled repealed 2017 (GST) .

## Salient features of the Water Act, 1974
- Enactment route: passed under Article 252 with the consent of State legislatures, since water is a State subject — a constitutional distinction from the Air Act 1981 and EPA 1986, both enacted under Article 253.
- Objectives: prevention and control of water pollution, and maintaining or restoring the wholesomeness of water.
- Institutions: created the Central Pollution Control Board (September 1974) and State Pollution Control Boards — the machinery on which all subsequent Indian environmental regulation rests.
- The consent mechanism (Sections 25-27) — no person may establish any industry, operation or treatment plant likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent, or make any new discharge, without the previous consent of the State Board. Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate are the Board’s principal instruments.
- Prohibition on polluting discharge (Section 24) into any stream, well, sewer or on land.
- Powers of entry, inspection and sampling (Sections 20-23), with a prescribed sampling procedure protecting the occupier’s rights.
- Emergency powers (Section 32) where pollution is apprehended, and power to seek a court restraint (Section 33).
- Directions (Section 33A) — including closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, and stoppage or regulation of electricity, water or any other service — the provision that gives Board orders practical force.
- Standards: State Boards may prescribe standards more stringent than the CPCB’s, never less.
- Citizen enforcement (Section 49) — cognizance on a complaint by any person giving sixty days’ notice.
- Penalties (Sections 41-45A) — substantially amended by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023, which replaced imprisonment with monetary penalties determined by adjudicating officers for a range of offences, with appeals to the NGT.

## The Water Cess Act, 1977 — features, purpose and repeal

What it was. An Act to provide for the levy and collection of a cess on water consumed by persons carrying on specified industries and by local authorities, with the proceeds intended to augment the resources of the Central and State Pollution Control Boards.

## Salient features
- Levy on water consumption, not on effluent discharged — a deliberate design choice, since consumption is far easier to meter than discharge, and consumption correlates with effluent volume.
- Scope: applied to specified industries listed in a Schedule (including chemicals, petroleum, textiles, paper, metallurgy, mining and processing industries) and to local authorities supplying water.
- Differential rates by purpose of use — with lower rates for domestic use and industrial cooling, and higher rates where water was used in processes producing polluting effluent. The rate structure was therefore itself a pollution signal.
- The rebate — the Act’s key incentive. A rebate of up to 25% of the cess payable was available to a consumer who installed a plant for the treatment of sewage or trade effluent and complied with the consent conditions and effluent standards. This made the Act an early Indian instance of an economic instrument for pollution control: it did not merely command treatment, it made treatment cheaper.
- Measurement: by meters affixed by the consumer; where no meter was installed, the assessing authority could charge on a maximum-consumption basis, creating an incentive to meter.
- Administration: assessment by officers appointed by the State Government; appeals to an appellate authority.
- Proceeds: collected by State Governments and credited to the Consolidated Fund of India, with the Central Government making grants to the CPCB and State Boards — a dedicated revenue stream for pollution regulation.

## The repeal and its consequence

The Act was repealed by the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess (Repeal) Act, 2017, with effect from 2017, because the Goods and Services Tax regime subsumed a range of cesses and the water cess was among them. The consequence is institutionally significant: Pollution Control Boards lost a dedicated, non-discretionary source of finance and became more dependent on consent fees paid by the very units they regulate — which sharpens the structural conflict of interest and weakens their financial autonomy. The polluter pays signal embedded in the differential rate structure was also lost.

## What replaced the incentive function

No direct successor levy exists. The economic-instrument function has partly shifted to other mechanisms: environmental compensation imposed by pollution control boards and the NGT; Extended Producer Responsibility under the waste rules; the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022; and Zero Liquid Discharge norms for specified sectors. None, however, funds the Boards.

## Conclusion

The Water Act 1974 and the Cess Act 1977 were designed as regulation and finance respectively — the Act creating Boards and the cess paying for them while rewarding treatment through a rebate. The Cess Act’s repeal in 2017 under GST removed both the funding stream and the economic incentive, leaving the Boards dependent on consent fees from regulated units. Restoring an independent financing basis for pollution control boards is, on this analysis, a more consequential reform than any further amendment to the substantive law.

## Value addition
- The repeal to state correctly: the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 was repealed by the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess (Repeal) Act, 2017, following GST. Describing it as operative is a factual error.
- The rebate provision — the examinable design feature: up to 25% rebate on cess payable for consumers installing effluent treatment plants and complying with standards — an early Indian economic instrument, rewarding treatment rather than merely mandating it.
- The design logic: levy on consumption rather than discharge, because consumption is meterable and correlates with effluent; differential rates by purpose of use, so that polluting uses paid more.
- Water Act sections to cite: 16 and 17 (CPCB and SPCB functions); 20-23 (information, sampling, entry); 24 (prohibition on polluting discharge); 25-27 (consent); 32 (emergency); 33 (court restraint); 33A (directions including closure and stoppage of services); 49 (citizen complaint after 60 days’ notice).
- Constitutional distinction: Water Act under Article 252 (State consent, water being a State subject); Air Act 1981 and EPA 1986 under Article 253 (implementing international agreements).
- Board finance — the analytical point: with the cess repealed, Boards rely largely on consent and analysis fees from regulated units, creating a structural dependence on those they regulate; this is among the most-cited reasons for weak enforcement.
- AP-specific:APPCB, Vijayawada, exercising consent and Section 33A powers; effluent regulation in the Visakhapatnam industrial complex and coastal aquaculture; NGT Southern Zone bench, Chennai, with jurisdiction over AP.
Q109:
## Introduction

The Disaster Management Act, 2005 defines a disaster as “a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence in any area, arising from natural or man-made causes, or by accident or negligence, which results in substantial loss of life or human suffering, or damage to and destruction of property, or damage to or degradation of environment, and is of such a nature or magnitude as to be beyond the coping capacity of the community of the affected area.” The final clause is the operative test: a hazard becomes a disaster when it exceeds local coping capacity.

## (a) Parameters considered in declaring a disaster

## The constitutional position — the point most answers miss
- Disaster management is primarily a State responsibility. “Public order”, “public health and sanitation” and “land” are State subjects, and relief in the event of calamity is not a Union subject. The State Government declares a disaster in its territory and is the first responder.
- There is no statutory category of “national disaster” or “national calamity” in Indian law. The DM Act does not define one. What exists is a process for enhanced central assistance, not a formal declaration of national status. The Tenth Finance Commission (1995) examined the concept of a “national calamity of rarest severity” and set out indicative criteria, but no legal category was created. States frequently demand that an event be declared a “national disaster”; the correct answer is that no such declaration exists in law.

## The parameters actually applied

Where a State seeks central assistance beyond its State Disaster Response Fund, the following are assessed:

- Magnitude and intensity of the event — physical severity, such as cyclone category, earthquake magnitude, or rainfall departure.
- Loss of human life and injury.
- Extent of area affected — number of districts, blocks and villages.
- Population affected — including those displaced and rendered homeless.
- Damage to property and infrastructure — houses, roads, bridges, power, water and communication.
- Damage to crops and livestock, and loss of livelihoods.
- Environmental damage.
- Coping capacity of the State — whether the State’s own resources and SDRF balance are sufficient. This is the decisive variable, since it converts an absolute measure of severity into a relative one.
- Whether the calamity is of a “severe nature” — the threshold used administratively for assistance from the National Disaster Response Fund.

## The process for central assistance

1. The State Government submits a memorandum with an assessment of damage and requirement.

2. An Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT) visits and independently assesses the damage.

3. A National Executive Committee sub-committee examines the IMCT report.

4. A High-Level Committee, chaired by the Union Home Minister, approves assistance from the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF).

5. Assistance is provided in accordance with norms notified by the Ministry of Home Affairs for each item — house damage, crop loss, cattle loss, and so on — and on the recommendations of the Finance Commission, which determines the SDRF corpus and the Centre-State sharing ratio (currently 75:25 for general category States and 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan States).

The 12 notified disasters eligible for SDRF/NDRF assistance: cyclone, drought, earthquake, fire, flood, tsunami, hailstorm, landslide, avalanche, cloudburst, pest attack, and frost and cold wave. States may spend up to a specified percentage of the SDRF on locally notified disasters outside this list

— a flexibility introduced on Finance Commission recommendation.

## (b) Classification of disasters occurring in India

## Natural disasters
- Geophysical — earthquakes (about 59% of India’s land area is prone to moderate-to-severe seismic hazard; Zones II-V under IS 1893); tsunamis (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami); landslides and avalanches (Himalaya, Western Ghats, North-East); land subsidence (Joshimath, 2023); volcanic activity (Barren Island, Andamans).
- Hydrological — floods (about 12% of India’s land area is flood-prone; Brahmaputra, Ganga, Godavari and Krishna basins); flash floods and cloudbursts (Uttarakhand, Himachal); glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF); urban flooding; coastal erosion; dam failure.
- Meteorological — tropical cyclones (about 8% of land area and the entire 7,500-km coastline exposed; the Bay of Bengal generating the majority of severe cyclones); storm surge; heat waves and cold waves; hailstorms; thunderstorms and lightning; dust storms.
- Climatological — droughts (roughly 68% of cultivated area vulnerable); desertification; forest fires.
- Biological — epidemics and pandemics (COVID-19 managed under the DM Act); pest and locust attacks; animal epidemics; harmful algal blooms.

## Human-induced (man-made) disasters
- Industrial and chemical — gas leaks and chemical accidents (Bhopal, 1984; the Visakhapatnam styrene gas leak, 2020, in Andhra Pradesh); explosions; oil spills.
- Nuclear and radiological — reactor incidents, transport accidents, radiological dispersal.
- Transport and infrastructure — rail, road, air and maritime accidents; building and bridge collapse; stampedes at religious and public gatherings.
- Fire — urban and industrial fires, including hospital and commercial building fires.
- Cyber and technological — attacks on critical infrastructure including power grids, water systems and financial networks.
- Conflict-related — terrorism, CBRN threats, and mass displacement.
- Mining accidents — collapses, inundation, and reservoir-induced seismicity.

India’s overall vulnerability profile: approximately 59% of land area prone to moderate-to-severe seismic hazard; about 12% flood-prone; about 8% cyclone-prone with the entire coastline exposed; roughly 68% of cultivated area drought-vulnerable; and hilly regions susceptible to landslides and avalanches. These four figures are the standard set for any Indian disaster question.

## Conclusion

The parameters for declaring a disaster turn ultimately on a relative rather than absolute test — whether the event exceeds the coping capacity of the affected community and of the State. The constitutional position is that declaration is a State function and there is no legal category of “national disaster”, only a graded process for central assistance approved by a High-Level Committee under the Home Minister. India’s disaster profile is unusually broad, spanning every major natural hazard category and a growing range of technological ones — which is why its management framework had to be built as a general-purpose institutional structure rather than around any single hazard.

## Value addition
- The key legal point: there is no statutory category of “national disaster” or “national calamity” under the Disaster Management Act, 2005. Declaration is a State function; the Centre provides assistance following an Inter-Ministerial Central Team assessment and approval by a High-Level Committee chaired by the Union Home Minister. The Tenth Finance Commission (1995) examined “national calamity of rarest severity” without creating a legal category.
- The 12 notified disasters for SDRF/NDRF: cyclone, drought, earthquake, fire, flood, tsunami, hailstorm, landslide, avalanche, cloudburst, pest attack, frost and cold wave — with States permitted to notify additional local disasters within a specified share of the SDRF.
- Funding architecture:SDRF (Centre-State sharing 75:25 general, 90:10 for NE and Himalayan States) as the first resort; NDRF for calamities of a severe nature; National and State Disaster Mitigation Funds for prevention; corpus determined on Finance Commission recommendation.
- India’s vulnerability figures: about 59% of land area seismically vulnerable; 12% flood-prone; 8% cyclone-prone with a 7,500-km coastline exposed; 68% of cultivated area drought-vulnerable.
- Hazard classification framework: geophysical, hydrological, meteorological, climatological and biological (natural); industrial/chemical, nuclear, transport, fire, cyber and conflict-related (human-induced) — the UNDRR-aligned taxonomy.
- The statutory definition to quote: substantial loss of life or human suffering, or damage to property or environment, “beyond the coping capacity of the community of the affected area” — the final clause being the operative test.
- AP-specific: cyclone exposure along the 1,053-km coast; Godavari and Krishna delta flooding; Rayalaseema drought; the Visakhapatnam styrene gas leak (May 2020) as an industrial disaster; 2004 tsunami deaths in Krishna, Guntur, Prakasam and Nellore; APSDMA and RTGS AWARE.
Q110:
## Introduction

India’s disaster management operates through a statutory institutional framework and a set of hazard-specific programmes, while its climate mitigation operates through a parallel structure of missions and market instruments. The two are linked: mitigation of global warming is itself the largest long-term contribution to disaster risk reduction, since climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of the hazards India must manage.

## (i) Disaster management programmes in India

Institutional framework — established under the Disaster Management Act, 2005: NDMA (Prime Minister), SDMAs (Chief Ministers), DDMAs (District Collectors); National Executive Committee; NIDM for training; NDRF and SDRFs; National Disaster Management Plan 2016, aligned to the Sendai priorities.

## Programmes by hazard

Cyclone - National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) — multipurpose cyclone shelters, saline embankments, evacuation roads and early warning dissemination in coastal States including Andhra Pradesh. - IMD cyclone forecasting and the Common Alerting Protocol for multi-channel warning; NavIC messaging for fishermen beyond mobile coverage.

Flood - Flood Management and Border Areas Programme (FMBAP); Central Water Commission flood forecasting network; embankment and drainage works; NDMA Guidelines on Urban Flooding (2010); AMRUT 2.0 storm-water drainage.

Earthquake - National Earthquake Risk Mitigation Programme; seismic zonation under IS 1893; retrofitting of lifeline buildings; the National Center for Seismology network; Bhukamp app; earthquake early warning operational in Uttarakhand.

Tsunami - Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS (operational 2007), an IOC-UNESCO Tsunami Service Provider; Tsunami Ready community certification, including villages in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

Landslide - National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019); GSI landslide susceptibility mapping; early warning pilots in the Nilgiris and Darjeeling.

Drought - Drought Management Manual; NADAMS satellite-based drought assessment; WDC-PMKSY 2.0 watershed treatment; crop insurance under PMFBY with YES-TECH.

Heat - Over 250 Heat Action Plans following the Ahmedabad model (2013); National Heatwave Framework; IMD heat warnings.

Forest fire - National Action Plan on Forest Fires (2018); FSI near-real-time fire alert system pushing SMS alerts to field staff; Van Agni monitoring on Bhuvan.

Chemical, industrial and nuclear - Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules; Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991; off-site emergency plans; AERB oversight for nuclear installations.

Biological - Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme and IHIP; National One Health Mission; the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 — with COVID-19 managed largely under the DM Act, exposing the absence of a dedicated public health emergency statute.

Cross-cutting - Aapda Mitra — training community volunteers in disaster response. - NDMA guidelines for each hazard; school and hospital safety programmes; mock drills. - Space support — ISRO’s Disaster Management Support Programme, NDEM, Bhuvan, and NISAR (July 2025) for all-weather observation. - Mission Mausam (2024) — about Rs. 2,000 crore to expand radar and radiosonde networks and improve forecast accuracy. - International — CDRI (2019) and IRIS, both launched by India.

## (ii) Mitigation methods to address global warming

1. Avoid — reduce the demand for energy and materials - Mission LIFE, framing demand-side behaviour as pro-planet action across seven themes. -Circular economy and Extended Producer Responsibility across plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres; the single-use plastic ban (July 2022). - Compact urban form, public transport and reduced material intensity in construction.

2. Shift — change the energy source - Renewables: non-fossil capacity of 283.46 GW as on 31 March 2026 (solar 150.26 GW, wind 56.09 GW); India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its NDC target (MNRE). Instruments: National Solar Mission, PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM, Solar Parks, ISTS charge waiver, Green Energy Corridors. - Green hydrogen for hard-to-abate sectors — steel, fertiliser, refining, heavy transport — under the National Green Hydrogen Mission (Rs. 19,744 crore; 5 MMT by 2030). - Nuclear — the Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat (Budget 2025-26): Rs. 20,000 crore for Small Modular Reactors, five indigenous SMRs by 2033, 100 GWe by 2047. - Biofuels — E20 ethanol blending achieved in 2025-26; compressed biogas under SATAT. - Electric mobility — PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore from October 2024).

3. Improve — raise efficiency so less energy delivers the same service - PAT scheme with tradable Energy Saving Certificates; Standards and Labelling; UJALA LED distribution; ECBC and Eco-Niwas Samhita for buildings; the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022. - Smart grids and RDSS smart metering (Rs. 3.03 lakh crore, about 25 crore consumers), reducing distribution losses. - Rail electrification and freight modal shift; industrial waste heat recovery.

4. India’s disaster management programmes are organised hazard by hazard on a common institutional base, and are strongest where early warning and evacuation dominate — cyclones and tsunamis — and weakest where risk reduction must confront development pressure. Q111:
## Introduction

Nanotechnology is the manipulation of matter at the scale of 1 to 100 nanometres — a nanometre being one-billionth of a metre. Its significance lies not in miniaturisation but in a physical fact: materials behave differently at this scale. Two mechanisms explain why: the surface-area-to-volume ratio rises dramatically, making nanoparticles far more chemically reactive; and quantum effects become significant, altering optical, electrical and magnetic properties. Gold, inert in bulk, becomes catalytically active as nanoparticles; carbon, soft as graphite, becomes exceptionally strong as nanotubes.

DNA width ~2.5 nm , with the 1-100 nm band highlighted.

## Applications across sectors

Medicine and healthcare - Targeted drug delivery — nanoparticles engineered to release a drug at a specific site, raising efficacy while reducing systemic toxicity; particularly significant in cancer chemotherapy, where the limiting factor is damage to healthy tissue. - Diagnostics — quantum dots and nanoparticle-based assays enabling detection at very low concentrations; lab-on-a-chip devices; nanoparticle contrast agents for imaging. - Vaccines — lipid nanoparticles were the delivery mechanism that made mRNA COVID-19 vaccines possible, the most consequential recent demonstration of the technology. - Regenerative medicine — nano-structured scaffolds for tissue engineering and bone regeneration; nano-coated implants resisting infection. - Antimicrobials — silver nanoparticles in wound dressings and coatings.

Agriculture — where India has commercialised at scale - Nano urea, developed by IFFCO and approved for commercial use in 2021, and nano DAP, approved subsequently, deliver nitrogen and phosphorus as a nanoparticle suspension applied to the leaf. The claimed advantages are higher nutrient use efficiency, reduced volume and transport cost — a 500 ml bottle substituting for a bag of conventional fertiliser — and reduced nitrate leaching and nitrous oxide emissions. India is among the first countries to commercialise nano fertiliser at this scale, though field efficacy remains a subject of ongoing agronomic assessment, which an honest answer should note. - Nano-pesticides and controlled-release formulations, reducing the quantity applied. -Nano-sensors for soil moisture, nutrient status and pathogen detection.

Water treatment - Nanofiltration and membrane technologies for desalination and purification. - Nano-adsorbents for removing arsenic, fluoride and heavy metals — directly relevant to India’s geogenic groundwater contamination problem. - Photocatalytic degradation of organic pollutants using titanium dioxide nanoparticles. - India’s indigenous contribution: nanosilver-based point-of-use water purifiers developed for low-cost household purification without electricity or running water.

Energy - Solar photovoltaics — nanostructured and perovskite cells raising efficiency; anti-reflective coatings. - Batteries and supercapacitors — nano-structured electrodes improving energy density, charging rate and cycle life, central to the electric mobility and grid storage transitions. - Hydrogen — nano-catalysts reducing the platinum loading in electrolysers and fuel cells, a principal cost driver in the National Green Hydrogen Mission. - Insulation and coatings — aerogels and thermal barrier coatings improving building and industrial efficiency.

Electronics and computing - Semiconductor devices already operate at nanoscale nodes; carbon nanotubes and graphene are candidate successors to silicon. - Quantum dots in displays; spintronics and nano-magnetic storage; flexible and wearable electronics. - Relevance to India’s India Semiconductor Mission and National Quantum Mission.

Materials and manufacturing - Carbon nanotubes and graphene — exceptional strength-to-weight ratio and electrical conductivity, with applications in aerospace, defence composites and structural materials. - Self-cleaning, anti-corrosion, scratch-resistant and hydrophobic coatings; nano-additives in concrete and paints. - Textiles — stain-resistant, antimicrobial and UV-protective fabrics.

Environment - Remediation — nano zero-valent iron for treating contaminated groundwater and soil. - Catalytic converters and air purification using nano-catalysts. - Sensors for detecting pollutants at very low concentrations.

Defence and space - Lightweight armour and composites; nano-sensors for CBRN detection; stealth coatings; radiation-shielding materials.

## India’s institutional framework
- Nano Mission, launched by the Department of Science and Technology in 2007 as an umbrella capacity-building programme, following the Nano Science and Technology Initiative (2001). It supports basic research, human resource development, infrastructure creation and application-oriented projects.
- Centres and facilities — Units on Nanoscience, Centres for Nanotechnology, and shared characterisation facilities at IITs, IISc, JNCASR, universities and CSIR laboratories; Nano Science and Technology Consortium for industry linkage.
- Regulatory and safety guidance — DBT-ICMR Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India (2019); FSSAI consideration of nanomaterials in food; BIS standards development; and CIB&RC approval for nano agri-inputs.
- Linkages — nanotechnology underpins the India Semiconductor Mission, the National Quantum Mission, the National Green Hydrogen Mission (catalysts) and the PLI for Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries.

## Risks and the regulatory gap — required for “discuss”
- Nanotoxicity. The same property that makes nanoparticles useful — very high reactivity and the ability to cross biological barriers — makes them potentially hazardous. Nanoparticles can cross the blood-brain barrier and the placenta, and inhaled nanoparticles reach the deep lung. Toxicity depends on size, shape, surface chemistry and dose, and cannot be inferred from the bulk material’s safety profile — a substance safe in bulk is not necessarily safe at nanoscale.
- Environmental persistence and fate — behaviour of engineered nanomaterials in soil and water is imperfectly understood, including potential bioaccumulation.
- Occupational exposure in manufacturing, where standards and monitoring methods are still developing.
- Regulatory gap. Most regulatory frameworks worldwide, including India’s, define substances by chemical identity rather than by particle size, so a nanomaterial may be treated as identical to its bulk form despite behaving differently. Dedicated nanomaterial regulation remains limited.
- Measurement and standards — detecting and characterising nanoparticles in complex matrices such as food, soil or tissue is technically demanding.
- Ethical and equity questions — cost of access to nano-enabled medicine; dual-use concerns in defence.

## Conclusion

Nanotechnology’s promise rests on a genuine physical basis: at 1-100 nanometres, materials acquire properties their bulk forms do not have, which is why it delivers gains across medicine, energy, water and agriculture simultaneously rather than in one sector. India has built research capacity through the Nano Mission and has commercialised nano fertilisers ahead of most countries. The unresolved issue is regulatory: frameworks that classify substances by chemistry rather than by particle size cannot assess materials whose behaviour depends on size. Closing that gap is the precondition for the technology’s responsible scaling.

## Value addition
- The definition and the reason it matters:1-100 nanometres; properties change because the surface-area-to-volume ratio rises sharply (greater reactivity) and quantum effects become significant (altered optical, electrical and magnetic behaviour).
- Scale comparisons for the diagram: human hair ≈ 80,000 nm; red blood cell ≈ 7,000 nm; virus ≈ 100 nm; DNA double helix ≈ 2.5 nm wide.
- India’s programme:Nano Science and Technology Initiative (2001); Nano Mission (2007, DST) — capacity building, infrastructure, human resources and application projects; Units on Nanoscience and Centres for Nanotechnology at IITs, IISc and CSIR labs.
- Indian commercial applications:IFFCO nano urea (approved 2021) and nano DAP — among the first nano fertilisers commercialised at scale globally; nanosilver point-of-use water purifiers; nano-coatings in textiles and defence composites.
- Landmark nanomaterials to name:fullerenes (C60, “buckyballs”); carbon nanotubes; graphene (single-atom-thick carbon sheet, Nobel Prize 2010); quantum dots (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2023); dendrimers; lipid nanoparticles, the mRNA vaccine delivery system.

DBT-ICMR Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India (2019) are India’s principal response.
