Q112:
## Introduction

Nanomedicine applies materials engineered at 1-100 nanometres to diagnosis, drug delivery, imaging and tissue repair. Its relevance to lifestyle diseases follows from a specific clinical problem: conventional chemotherapy and many chronic-disease drugs are systemically distributed, so the dose that reaches the diseased tissue is limited by the toxicity to healthy tissue. Nanoparticles change this by altering where a drug goes and when it is released.

and retention .

## The mechanisms that make nanomedicine work
- Passive targeting — the EPR effect. Tumours grow rapidly and form blood vessels that are leaky and disordered, with gaps far larger than in normal capillaries; they also have poor lymphatic drainage. Nanoparticles of an appropriate size therefore pass out of tumour vessels and remain there, while being excluded from healthy tissue with intact vessels. This enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect is the foundational principle of nano-oncology, and stating it is what distinguishes an informed answer.
- Active targeting. Nanoparticle surfaces can be functionalised with antibodies, peptides or folate that bind receptors over-expressed on cancer cells, so the particle attaches selectively.
- Controlled and stimulus-responsive release. Carriers can be designed to release their payload in response to a trigger — the acidic pH of the tumour microenvironment, an enzyme, temperature, or an applied magnetic or light field — so the drug is delivered where and when required.
- Solubility and stability. Many effective drug molecules are poorly water-soluble; encapsulating them in nanocarriers makes them administrable and extends circulation time.
- Crossing biological barriers. Suitably engineered nanoparticles can cross the blood-brain barrier, which excludes most conventional drugs — significant for brain tumours and neurodegenerative disease.

## Cancer — prevention, diagnosis and treatment
- Targeted chemotherapy. Liposomal and polymeric nanoparticle formulations of cytotoxic drugs raise tumour concentration while reducing systemic exposure — the clinical benefit being reduced cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity and myelosuppression, which are the limiting side effects of conventional chemotherapy.
- Early detection — the prevention dimension.Quantum dots and nanoparticle-based assays detect tumour markers, circulating tumour cells and circulating tumour DNA at very low concentrations, enabling detection at a stage when treatment is far more effective. Nano-biosensors and lab-on-a-chip platforms make such testing potentially point-of-care rather than laboratory-bound.
- Imaging.Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles as MRI contrast agents; gold nanoparticles for CT contrast; fluorescent nanoparticles for intraoperative tumour margin visualisation, helping the surgeon see what to remove.
- Photothermal and photodynamic therapy.Gold nanorods and nanoshells absorb near-infrared light and convert it to heat, destroying tumour cells locally while sparing surrounding tissue; photodynamic therapy uses nanoparticle-delivered photosensitisers generating reactive oxygen species on illumination.
- Magnetic hyperthermia. Magnetic nanoparticles concentrated in a tumour and exposed to an alternating magnetic field generate localised heat.
- Theranostics — the concept worth naming. A single nanoparticle platform combining therapy and diagnostics: it images the tumour, confirms that the particle has reached it, and delivers treatment — allowing dosing to be personalised to the individual patient’s biology.
- Immunotherapy support — nanoparticle-based cancer vaccines and adjuvants delivering antigens to dendritic cells.

## Diabetes
- Glucose-responsive insulin delivery — “smart” nanocarriers releasing insulin in proportion to blood glucose, moving toward a closed-loop system without an external pump.
- Oral insulin — nanoencapsulation to protect insulin from gastric degradation and enable intestinal absorption, addressing the compliance burden of injection.
- Continuous glucose monitoring using nano-biosensors, including non-invasive and wearable formats.
- Diabetic wound care — nano-silver and nanofibre dressings, and growth-factor-loaded scaffolds, relevant to diabetic foot ulcers, a leading cause of amputation.

## Cardiovascular disease
- Targeted delivery to atherosclerotic plaque — nanoparticles binding inflamed endothelium to deliver anti-inflammatory or plaque-stabilising agents.
- Drug-eluting stents with nano-structured coatings releasing anti-proliferative drugs to prevent restenosis, and nano-coated surfaces reducing thrombosis.
- Nano-diagnostics — high-sensitivity troponin and biomarker assays enabling earlier detection of myocardial injury.
- Regenerative approaches — nanofibre scaffolds for cardiac tissue repair.

## Other lifestyle-related applications
- Neurodegenerative disease — nanoparticles crossing the blood-brain barrier for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s therapeutics.
- Obesity and metabolic disease — targeted delivery to adipose tissue, at research stage.
- Bone and joint disease — nano-hydroxyapatite for bone regeneration; nano-coated orthopaedic implants resisting infection.
- Vaccines — lipid nanoparticles made mRNA COVID-19 vaccines possible, the most consequential recent demonstration of nanomedicine at scale.

## India’s position
- The Nano Mission (DST, 2007) supports nanomedicine research at IITs, IISc, AIIMS, JNCASR, CSIR laboratories and the Institute of Nano Science and Technology, Mohali.
- DBT-ICMR Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India (2019) provide the regulatory framework for approval, addressing the point that a nanoformulation of an approved drug is a new product requiring separate evaluation.
- Indian relevance is particularly strong in affordable diagnostics — nanoparticle-based point-of-care tests suited to primary health centres, where laboratory infrastructure is absent.
- AP linkage: the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam, with the Kalam Institute of Health Technology, provides shared facilities for medical device and diagnostic development, including nano-enabled products; research capacity exists at IIT Tirupati, IISER Tirupati and Andhra University.

## Limitations — required for a complete elaboration
- The EPR effect is variable. It is well demonstrated in animal models but far less consistent in human tumours, which differ in vascularity — a principal reason many nano-oncology candidates have underperformed in clinical trials.
- Nanotoxicity — the reactivity and barrier-crossing ability that make nanoparticles useful also make them potentially harmful; long-term effects of accumulation are not fully characterised.
- Manufacturing complexity and cost, affecting scalability and affordability.
- Regulatory novelty — safety of the bulk material does not establish safety at nanoscale, so each formulation requires independent evaluation.

## Conclusion

Nanomedicine’s contribution to lifestyle disease is best understood as a change in precision rather than in pharmacology: the same drug delivered to the right tissue at the right time achieves more at lower toxicity. In cancer this operates through the EPR effect and active targeting; in diabetes through glucose-responsive release; in cardiovascular disease through plaque-targeted delivery and nano-coated stents. Its translation to routine clinical use remains constrained by the variability of the EPR effect in humans, by toxicity questions, and by cost — which is why India’s most immediately valuable application may be affordable nano-diagnostics for early detection rather than nano-therapeutics.

## Value addition
- The mechanism to name: the EPR effect — enhanced permeability and retention, arising from leaky tumour vasculature and poor lymphatic drainage. Passive targeting exploits it; active targeting adds ligands binding over-expressed receptors.
- Nanocarrier types:liposomes; polymeric nanoparticles; dendrimers; micelles; gold nanoparticles and nanorods (photothermal); superparamagnetic iron oxide (imaging and hyperthermia); quantum dots (imaging and detection); lipid nanoparticles (mRNA delivery); carbon nanotubes.
- Concepts:theranostics (therapy plus diagnostics in one platform); photothermal and photodynamic therapy; magnetic hyperthermia; stimulus-responsive release (pH, enzyme, temperature, magnetic field); personalised medicine.
- Indian framework:Nano Mission (DST, 2007); Institute of Nano Science and Technology, Mohali; DBT-ICMR Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India (2019); CDSCO for drug approval.
- The honest limitation: the EPR effect is far more consistent in rodent models than in human tumours, which is a principal reason nano-oncology’s clinical translation has lagged the laboratory promise. Stating this shows genuine familiarity rather than promotional summary.
- Lifestyle disease context in India: non-communicable diseases account for the majority of deaths in India; the National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs and the Ayushman Bharat health and wellness centres provide the screening platform on which nano-diagnostics would be deployed.
- AP-specific:AMTZ Visakhapatnam and the Kalam Institute of Health Technology; research capacity at IIT Tirupati, IISER Tirupati and Andhra University; SVIMS Tirupati and AIIMS Mangalagiri as tertiary care centres.
Q113:
## Introduction

An invasive alien species (IAS) is a species introduced outside its natural range which establishes, spreads and causes harm to biodiversity, ecosystem services, economies or human health. The definition contains a distinction worth making: most introduced species do not become invasive — many fail to establish, and many establish harmlessly. The problematic minority are those that escape their natural predators, pathogens and competitors and consequently reproduce without check.

damaging) , illustrating why the proportion that becomes harmful is small but the impact disproportionate.

## The scale — evidence for the claim

The IPBES Invasive Alien Species Assessment (2023), the first global assessment devoted to the subject, found that more than 37,000 alien species have been established through human activity, of which over 3,500 are harmful invasive species; that invasive alien species have played a role in around 60% of recorded global extinctions, and were the sole driver in a significant proportion of them; and that the global economic cost exceeds USD 400 billion annually, having quadrupled every decade since 1970. On islands, invasives are frequently the leading cause of extinction — which is the context in which the question’s ranking holds most strongly.

## Causes — the pathways of introduction

The standard classification, which organises the answer:

- 1. Intentional release. Deliberate introduction for a purpose that later proved harmful.

Prosopis juliflora (vilayati kikar), introduced for afforestation of arid land and fuelwood, now dominating vast tracts in Rajasthan, Gujarat and the Deccan, suppressing native vegetation and lowering water tables through deep root systems. African catfish (Clarias gariepinus) and tilapia, introduced for aquaculture, now established in Indian rivers and lakes where they predate on and outcompete native fish. African catfish farming is prohibited in India for this reason.

Australian acacia and eucalyptus in plantation forestry, altering soil and hydrology.

- 2. Escape from confinement. Species that escape from cultivation, aquaculture, gardens or the pet trade.

Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), introduced as an ornamental for its flower — the “Terror of Bengal” — now choking water bodies across India including Kolleru Lake in Andhra Pradesh, blocking sunlight, depleting dissolved oxygen, impeding navigation and fishing, and providing mosquito breeding habitat. Red-eared slider turtle, released from the pet trade into Indian wetlands, competing with native freshwater turtles.

- 3. Contaminant. Species arriving unintentionally with a traded commodity.

Parthenium hysterophorus (Congress grass, gajar ghas) — widely believed to have entered India with imported wheat consignments in the 1950s; it is now among India’s most widespread weeds, causing allergic dermatitis and asthma in humans, reducing crop yields, and suppressing pasture through allelopathy. Papaya mealybug, fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda, first reported in India in 2018 and spread across the maize belt within months), and the cotton mealybug.

- 4. Stowaway. Species transported on or in a vehicle rather than with the cargo.

Ballast water discharged by ships is the principal marine pathway, carrying larvae and plankton between ports — the reason for the IMO Ballast Water Management Convention. Hull fouling; species in shipping containers and aircraft holds.

- 5. Corridor. Species spreading through human-created infrastructure — canals, road and rail corridors linking previously separated water bodies or habitats.
- 6. Unaided spread. Species crossing borders on their own after being introduced elsewhere in the region.

## Factors that allow establishment and spread
- Globalised trade and transport — the volume and speed of movement is the underlying driver of every pathway above.
- Absence of natural enemies in the new range — the “enemy release” mechanism, the central biological explanation for why an ordinary species in its home range becomes dominant elsewhere.
- Habitat disturbance. This is the crucial interaction: degraded, disturbed and fragmented habitat is far more invasible than intact habitat, because native communities are already weakened and niches are open. Invasion is therefore frequently a consequence of habitat destruction as well as an independent threat — which is why the two leading drivers reinforce each other.
- Climate change, shifting climatic envelopes so that previously unsuitable areas become habitable, and stressing native species.
- Biological traits of successful invaders — rapid reproduction, broad diet, wide environmental tolerance, effective dispersal, and often allelopathy (chemical suppression of neighbours, as in Parthenium and Lantana).
- Weak biosecurity and quarantine capacity at ports and borders, and inadequate risk assessment before intentional introduction.

## Impacts — with Indian instances
- Ecological:Lantana camara, introduced as an ornamental, now infests very large areas of Indian forest including tiger reserves, forming impenetrable thickets that suppress native undergrowth and reduce fodder for herbivores, thereby affecting prey density for large carnivores — an invasion whose effects reach the top of the food chain.
- Agricultural: fall armyworm and papaya mealybug causing crop loss and raising pesticide use; Mikania micrantha (“mile-a-minute weed”) smothering plantations in the North-East and Western Ghats.
- Aquatic: water hyacinth and Salvinia molesta in lakes and canals; African catfish and tilapia displacing native fish.
- Human health:Parthenium dermatitis and asthma; invasive mosquito species as disease vectors.
- Economic: control costs, yield loss, reduced water storage capacity, and blocked irrigation and navigation channels.

## Control and management
- Prevention — the only cost-effective stage. Once established, eradication is rarely feasible; the entire economic case rests on interception. Instruments: the Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003; the Livestock Importation Act; Ballast Water Management Convention compliance; and risk assessment before any intentional introduction.
- Early detection and rapid response — surveillance networks and the capacity to act while a population is small and localised.
- Physical and mechanical removal — manual clearing of Lantana and water hyacinth, labour-intensive and requiring repetition.
- Chemical control — effective but with non-target and residue consequences.
- Biological control — introducing a natural enemy from the species’ native range. The Indian success case is the Mexican beetle Zygogramma bicolorata released against Parthenium. Biological control itself requires rigorous host-specificity testing, since the control agent can become invasive.
- Habitat restoration — restoring native vegetation reduces invasibility, addressing the underlying vulnerability rather than the symptom.
- Utilisation — converting the problem into a resource: Lantana furniture and craft enterprises in central India, and water hyacinth used for compost, biogas and handicraft.
- Legal and policy framework: the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023); the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 on introduction into protected areas; CBD Article 8(h) requiring parties to prevent, control or eradicate invasive species; and Target 6 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022), committing to reduce the introduction and establishment rate of invasive alien species by at least 50% by 2030.

## Conclusion

Invasive alien species cause harm through a single biological mechanism — release from the predators, pathogens and competitors that limited them at home — but they arrive through six distinct human pathways, from deliberate introduction for forestry to ballast water and contaminated grain. India’s principal invasions illustrate the range: Prosopis introduced deliberately, water hyacinth escaped from gardens, Parthenium arriving as a contaminant. Because eradication after establishment is rarely feasible, prevention through quarantine and risk assessment is not one option among several — it is effectively the only one that works, supported by habitat restoration to reduce invasibility at source.

## Value addition
- IPBES Invasive Alien Species Assessment (2023): over 37,000 established alien species, of which 3,500+ are harmful invasives; a role in about 60% of recorded global extinctions; global cost exceeding USD 400 billion annually, quadrupling each decade since 1970.
- The six introduction pathways: intentional release; escape from confinement; contaminant; stowaway; corridor; unaided — the CBD-aligned classification that organises any “causes” answer.
- India’s principal invasives to name with their damage:Lantana camara (forest undergrowth, tiger reserves); Parthenium hysterophorus (health and crops, entered with imported wheat); Prosopis juliflora (arid tracts, water table); Eichhornia crassipes water hyacinth, the “Terror of Bengal” (water bodies, Kolleru); Mikania micrantha (North-East and Western Ghats); African catfish and tilapia (freshwater fish); red-eared slider (pet trade); fall armyworm (2018, maize); papaya mealybug.
- The biological explanation to name:enemy release — freedom from co-evolved predators, pathogens and competitors — plus allelopathy in Parthenium and Lantana.
- The interaction worth stating: disturbed and fragmented habitat is far more invasible than intact habitat, so habitat destruction and invasion reinforce each other rather than acting independently.
- Biological control success: the Mexican beetle Zygogramma bicolorata against Parthenium — India’s standard case, with the caveat that biocontrol agents require rigorous host-specificity testing.
- Legal framework:CBD Article 8(h); Target 6, Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) — reduce introduction and establishment rate by at least 50% by 2030; Biological Diversity Act 2002 (amended 2023); Plant Quarantine Order 2003; IMO Ballast Water Management Convention.
- AP-specific: water hyacinth and Salvinia in Kolleru Lake (Ramsar site); Lantana and Prosopis in the Eastern Ghats and Rayalaseema; Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve affected by Lantana invasion; tilapia and African catfish in Krishna and Godavari waters.

## Introduction

Biodiversity — biological diversity — is defined by the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) as “the variability among living organisms from all sources including, inter alia, terrestrial, marine and other aquatic ecosystems and the ecological complexes of which they are part; this includes diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems.” India is one of the world’s 17 megadiverse countries, holding around 8% of recorded global species on about 2.4% of the world’s land area, with four biodiversity hotspots.

3. Climate change | 4. Pollution | 5. Invasive alien species , with a base bar beneath labelled Indirect drivers: population, consumption, trade, technology, governance .

## Defining biodiversity — the three levels
- Genetic diversity — variation within a species, the raw material of adaptation. India’s crop landraces and livestock breeds, such as the Ongole and Punganur cattle of Andhra Pradesh, are instances.
- Species diversity — the variety of species in a region, measured as richness (number) and evenness (relative abundance).
- Ecosystem diversity — the variety of habitats and ecological processes: forest, grassland, wetland, desert, mangrove, coral reef, marine.

(Developed further at Q178.)

## The major threats — in ranked order

The IPBES Global Assessment (2019) — which estimated that around one million species are threatened with extinction, many within decades — ranked the direct drivers in order of relative global impact:

1. Land and sea use change — the largest driver - Conversion of forest, grassland and wetland to agriculture, plantation, settlement, industry and infrastructure. - Habitat fragmentation is often more damaging than outright loss: small isolated patches cannot sustain viable populations, gene flow is interrupted, and edge effects degrade habitat quality well inside the remaining fragment. A forest halved in area may lose far more than half its species. -Indian instances: agricultural expansion into the Eastern and Western Ghats; wetland conversion for aquaculture around Kolleru Lake; linear infrastructure severing wildlife corridors — the reason corridor protection is central to Project Tiger and Project Elephant.

2. Direct exploitation of organisms - Over-harvesting: overfishing and destructive gear; unsustainable extraction of timber and non-timber forest produce. - Poaching and illegal wildlife trade — tiger parts, pangolin scales, rhino horn, star tortoises, and red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus), endemic to the Seshachalam hills of Andhra Pradesh and subject to severe smuggling pressure. - Medicinal plant over-collection from the wild.

3. Climate change — rising rapidly in relative weight - Range shifts poleward and upslope, with summit trapping of montane endemics that have nowhere further to go. - Phenological mismatch — flowering, breeding and migration timings decoupling because species cue on different signals. - Coral bleaching from thermal stress, affecting the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andamans; ocean acidification impairing calcification. - Altered fire and monsoon regimes; sea-level rise on coastal habitats such as the Sundarbans and Coringa.

4. Pollution - Nutrient enrichment causing eutrophication and hypoxic zones; pesticide residues and biomagnification; heavy metals; plastics and microplastics; and light and noise pollution disrupting nocturnal species, bird song and marine mammal communication. - Nitrogen deposition altering species composition in nutrient-poor ecosystems.

5. Invasive alien species - Discussed fully at Q176. Their rank is fifth globally but first or second on islands and in freshwater systems, and they interact strongly with habitat disturbance.

## Additional and interacting threats
- Human-wildlife conflict, intensified as habitat shrinks and corridors are severed — elephants along the Eastern Ghats, leopards in peri-urban areas.
- Disease, including pathogens transmitted between domestic and wild populations.
- Genetic erosion in agriculture — replacement of diverse landraces by a few high-yielding varieties, and of indigenous livestock breeds by exotics, narrowing the genetic base on which future breeding depends.

## The indirect drivers — the layer beneath

IPBES distinguishes direct drivers from the indirect drivers that produce them: population growth and distribution; patterns of consumption and production; global trade; technological change; and, critically, governance and institutional failure, including unpriced ecosystem services and perverse subsidies. Addressing only the direct drivers treats symptoms; the indirect drivers are where the causes lie.

## Consequences of biodiversity loss

Degradation of ecosystem services — provisioning (food, water, timber, medicine), regulating (climate, flood, disease, pollination), supporting (nutrient cycling, soil formation) and cultural. Pollinator decline alone threatens a substantial share of agricultural output. Reduced ecosystem resilience means systems recover less well from shock, and the loss of genetic diversity narrows the options available to future agriculture and medicine.

## Conclusion

Biodiversity is variability at three levels — genetic, species and ecosystem — and its loss is driven by five direct pressures of unequal weight, with land and sea use change foremost and climate change rising fastest. The essential analytical point is that these drivers interact rather than add: fragmented habitat is more invasible, climate-stressed populations are more vulnerable to exploitation, and polluted systems recover less well. Conservation that addresses one driver in isolation therefore under-performs, which is why the Kunming-Montreal Framework sets integrated targets rather than a single one.

## Introduction

Biodiversity operates at three nested levels — genetic, species and ecosystem — and each is threatened by a distinct set of pressures. Genetic diversity is eroded by breed and variety replacement long before any species is lost; species diversity by habitat loss and exploitation; and ecosystem diversity by conversion and fragmentation. Recognising that the levels fail differently is what makes conservation planning coherent.

## (a) The three types of biodiversity

## Genetic diversity — variation within a species
- The pool of genetic variation among individuals and populations of one species. It is the raw material of adaptation: a population without genetic variation cannot evolve in response to a new disease, pest or climate.
- Expressed in India as landraces of rice, wheat and millets; indigenous livestock breeds — the Ongole and Punganur cattle of Andhra Pradesh, Gir, Sahiwal, Murrah buffalo; and wild relatives of crop plants.
- Threat specific to this level: genetic erosion. Replacement of many landraces by a few high-yielding varieties, and of indigenous breeds by exotic ones, narrows the base. This loss occurs invisibly — no species goes extinct, and the field looks more productive — which is why it attracts least attention and is the most under-recognised form of biodiversity loss.
- Why it matters practically: resistance genes to future pests and diseases exist in landraces and crop wild relatives. When they are lost, they are unrecoverable. Historical crop epidemics have been resolved by locating resistance in a wild or traditional variety.
- Conservation at this level:gene banks — the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (NBPGR), New Delhi, which holds one of the world’s largest collections; NBAGR for animal genetic resources; NBFGR for fish; on-farm conservation of landraces; Rashtriya Gokul Mission for indigenous bovines; Plant Varieties Protection and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001, which recognises farmers as conservers and breeders.

## Species diversity — variety between species
- Measured by species richness (number of species) and evenness (their relative abundance); a community dominated by one species is less diverse than one where several are equally common, even at equal richness.
- India holds around 8% of recorded global species on 2.4% of the world’s land area, with high endemism — species found nowhere else — concentrated in the Western Ghats, the North-East and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
- Threats specific to this level: habitat loss and fragmentation; direct exploitation through poaching and over-harvesting; invasive species; disease; and human-wildlife conflict. Species with small ranges, low reproductive rates, large body size or specialised diets are most vulnerable — which is why large carnivores and endemic amphibians are disproportionately at risk.
- Conservation: the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 with schedule-based protection; species recovery programmes — Project Tiger, Project Elephant, Project Dolphin, Project Lion, Project Cheetah; CITES for trade regulation; captive breeding and reintroduction; the IUCN Red List as the assessment standard.

## Ecosystem diversity — variety of habitats and ecological processes
- The range of ecosystems in a region and the processes operating within them. India spans ten biogeographic zones — Trans-Himalaya, Himalaya, Desert, Semi-Arid, Western Ghats, Deccan Peninsula, Gangetic Plain, Coasts, North-East and Islands — an unusual range for a single country.
- Threats specific to this level: land-use conversion; hydrological alteration by dams and diversion; coastal reclamation and wetland drainage; desertification; and climate change shifting entire biome boundaries.
- Conservation: the protected area network — National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves and Community Reserves, Biosphere Reserves, Tiger and Elephant Reserves, Ramsar sites, and Marine Protected Areas; MISHTI for mangroves; Amrit Dharohar for wetlands; landscape and corridor-level planning.

A fourth level sometimes added:functional diversity — the range of ecological roles performed (pollinators, decomposers, predators, nitrogen fixers). Two ecosystems with equal species counts may differ greatly in functional diversity, and it is functional diversity that determines ecosystem resilience. Noting this is a mark of depth.

## Major threats to biodiversity — the ranked overview

Following the IPBES Global Assessment (2019), which estimated around one million species threatened with extinction, the five direct drivers in order are:

1. Land and sea use change — habitat loss, conversion and fragmentation with edge effects.

2. Direct exploitation — overfishing, poaching, illegal wildlife trade, over-harvesting.

3. Climate change — range shifts, phenological mismatch, coral bleaching, ocean acidification.

4. Pollution — eutrophication, pesticides and biomagnification, plastics, light and noise.

5. Invasive alien species — enemy release and displacement of natives.

With indirect drivers beneath them: population and consumption patterns, trade, technology and governance failure — including the fact that ecosystem services are unpriced, so their loss registers in no account.

## Conclusion

Biodiversity’s three levels fail in different ways and require different remedies: genetic diversity is conserved in gene banks and on farms, species diversity through protected areas and trade regulation, and ecosystem diversity through landscape-scale planning and corridors. The level most easily overlooked is the genetic, because its erosion is invisible and often accompanies rising productivity — yet it is the level that determines whether agriculture can respond to the next pest, disease or climatic shift.

- India’s ten biogeographic zones: Trans-Himalaya, Himalaya, Desert, Semi-Arid, Western Ghats, Deccan Peninsula, Gangetic Plain, Coasts, North-East, Islands.
- India’s biodiversity credentials: one of 17 megadiverse countries; about 8% of recorded global species on 2.4% of land area; four hotspots — Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
- Measurement concepts: species richness and evenness; alpha (within-habitat), beta (between-habitat) and gamma (regional) diversity; endemism; functional diversity; the IUCN Red List categories from Least Concern to Extinct.
- Genetic conservation instruments: gene banks and cryopreservation; on-farm conservation of landraces; Plant Varieties Protection and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001, which uniquely recognises farmers’ rights as conservers; Rashtriya Gokul Mission; Plant Genome Saviour Awards.

Q116:
## Introduction

Ecology is the scientific study of the interactions between organisms and their environment, and it rests on a small number of principles that govern all ecosystems regardless of type. Biodiversity is the variability among living organisms at genetic, species and ecosystem levels, and its value to human society is conventionally classified into several categories, of which consumptive use value is the most direct.

## (a) The principles of ecology
- 1. Energy flows, matter cycles — the foundational principle. Solar energy enters through producers and is progressively lost as heat at each transfer; it cannot be recycled. Matter, by contrast, is used repeatedly, cycling between the biotic and abiotic components through biogeochemical cycles. This asymmetry is the single most important idea in ecology.
- 2. The ten per cent law (Lindeman). Approximately 10% of energy transfers from one trophic level to the next, the remainder being lost as metabolic heat and in unassimilated matter. This limits food chains to four or five links and ensures that top predators are always few — it is why a given area supports many herbivores and few tigers.
- 3. Everything is connected. Species interact through predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism and parasitism, forming food webs rather than isolated chains. Removal of one element propagates through the system — most dramatically where a keystone species is involved, whose effect on the community is disproportionate to its abundance.
- 4. Carrying capacity. Every environment can support only a finite population of a given species, determined by the availability of the limiting factor — the resource in shortest supply. Populations exceeding it decline.
- 5. Liebig’s Law of the Minimum and Shelford’s Law of Tolerance. Growth is limited not by the total resources available but by the scarcest one (Liebig); and every species has a range of tolerance for each environmental factor, beyond which it cannot survive (Shelford). Together these explain species distribution.
- 6. Ecological succession. Communities change in a directional, predictable sequence — from pioneer species colonising bare substrate, through intermediate stages, to a relatively stable climax community. Primary succession begins on bare rock (lichens first); secondary succession on land already possessing soil, as after a fire or abandoned cultivation.
- 7. Ecological niche and competitive exclusion. Each species occupies a niche — its functional role and range of conditions. Gause’s competitive exclusion principle holds that two species cannot occupy an identical niche indefinitely in the same habitat; one will displace the other, or they will diverge through resource partitioning.
- 8. Diversity confers stability. Systems with greater diversity generally recover better from disturbance, because redundancy in ecological function means the loss of one species can be compensated by another — the basis of resilience.
- 9. Nature knows best. Ecosystems have evolved over long periods into self-regulating configurations; interventions that disregard this — introducing an alien species, straightening a river — frequently produce unintended consequences.
- 10. Nothing is free. Every resource use has a cost somewhere in the system; there is no such thing as a free lunch, in Barry Commoner’s formulation of the laws of ecology.

(Commoner’s four laws — everything is connected to everything else; everything must go somewhere; nature knows best; there is no such thing as a free lunch — are the standard compact statement and worth citing.)

## (b) Biodiversity and its consumptive use value

Definition. Biodiversity is “the variability among living organisms from all sources… including diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems” (Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992).

## The value framework — consumptive use value defined against the others
- **Value type** — Meaning · Example
- **Consumptive use** — Goods consumed directly without passing through a market · Firewood, wild fruit, bushmeat, fodder, medicinal plants for household use
- **Productive use** — Goods harvested and sold commercially · Timber, fish, silk, lac, honey, ivory (where legal), pharmaceutical ingredients
- **Social** — Cultural, religious and community significance · Sacred groves, revered species (peepal, tulsi), festivals
- **Ethical/existence** — Intrinsic right of species to exist, independent of use · “Live and let live”; the case for conserving a species no one will ever see
- **Aesthetic** — Beauty and recreation · Ecotourism, birdwatching, landscape amenity
- **Option** — Potential future use, presently unknown · Undiscovered medicinal properties; crop wild relatives holding resistance genes

## Consumptive use value — developed
- Definition: the value of biodiversity goods consumed directly by the household or community without entering a market — and therefore not captured in national accounts. This is its defining characteristic and the source of its policy neglect: because it is not traded, it is not measured, and because it is not measured, it is invisible in cost-benefit analyses of projects that destroy it.
- What it comprises in India:

Fuelwood — the primary cooking energy for a very large number of rural households before PMUY expanded LPG access, and still significant.

Fodder for livestock, gathered from forests, commons and field margins.

Wild food — leafy greens, tubers, mushrooms, fruit, honey, fish and small game, which supply micronutrients that cultivated staples do not, and buffer households in lean seasons. Medicinal plants for household treatment, drawing on the Ayurveda, Siddha and folk traditions; India uses several thousand plant species medicinally. Construction and craft material — bamboo, timber, thatch, cane, leaves. Non-timber forest produce (NTFP) — tendu leaves, mahua, sal seed, gum, resin, lac — consumed and also sold, straddling the consumptive-productive boundary.

- Who depends on it: forest-dependent and tribal communities, and the landless, for whom commons and forests are the only resource base. Consumptive use value is therefore disproportionately the value accruing to the poorest — which is why its exclusion from accounting is an equity failure as well as an analytical one.
- Legal recognition: the Forest Rights Act, 2006 vests ownership of minor forest produce in gram sabhas and recognises rights of use — a statutory acknowledgement of consumptive use value; and the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023) provides for access and benefit sharing where such resources or associated traditional knowledge are commercialised.
- AP instance: tribal communities of the Eastern Ghats — in the Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam districts — depend substantially on NTFP including mahua, honey, gum, tamarind and medicinal plants; Araku Valley agroforestry combines coffee with forest use. Fishing communities along the 1,053-km coastline and around Kolleru Lake derive direct consumptive value from aquatic biodiversity.

Why the distinction matters. Development appraisal typically counts the productive value of a forest (timber revenue) and ignores its consumptive value (fuelwood, fodder, wild food for surrounding villages). A project therefore appears economically justified while imposing an uncounted cost on the households least able to bear it. Recognising consumptive use value is the analytical basis for the environmentalism of the poor and for movements such as Chipko.

## Conclusion

The principles of ecology — one-way energy flow, cyclical matter, the ten per cent law, carrying capacity, succession and niche exclusion — describe a system that is self-regulating within limits and consequential when those limits are crossed. Biodiversity’s consumptive use value is the most direct and the least visible of its values, because it is consumed rather than traded and therefore never enters an account. Making it visible is not merely a measurement improvement; it changes which projects appear worthwhile and who is recognised as bearing their cost.

## Value addition
- Commoner’s four laws of ecology: everything is connected to everything else; everything must go somewhere; nature knows best; there is no such thing as a free lunch — the standard compact formulation.
- Named ecological laws:Lindeman’s ten per cent law; Liebig’s Law of the Minimum; Shelford’s Law of Tolerance; Gause’s competitive exclusion principle; Allen’s and Bergmann’s rules on body form and climate.
- The six value categories: consumptive use, productive use, social, ethical, aesthetic, option value — the last being the strongest argument for conserving species of no known use, since future utility cannot be foreseen.
- Ecosystem services framework (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment): provisioning, regulating, supporting, cultural — a complementary classification worth naming alongside the value framework.
- The measurement problem: consumptive use value does not enter markets and so is absent from GDP; natural capital accounting and the UN’s System of Environmental-Economic Accounting are the response; India has initiated environmental accounting through MoSPI’s EnviStats India.
- Legal recognition of consumptive value:Forest Rights Act, 2006 vesting minor forest produce ownership in gram sabhas; PESA, 1996; Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023) with access and benefit sharing.
- AP-specific: NTFP dependence in the Eastern Ghats tribal districts; Araku Valley coffee agroforestry; fisheries along the 1,053-km coast and at Kolleru; Vana Samrakshana Samithis as the institutional form of community forest use.
Q117:
## Introduction

Biodiversity loss arises from a small set of ranked drivers, foremost among them habitat change. India’s institutional response has been organised substantially around flagship species programmes, of which Project Tiger (1973) is the oldest, the largest and the most instructive — because its history includes a documented failure and a recovery from it.

## (a) Reasons for biodiversity loss — briefly

Following the IPBES Global Assessment (2019), which estimated around one million species threatened with extinction, the direct drivers in order of impact are:

- Habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation — the largest driver; conversion for agriculture, settlement, industry and infrastructure, with fragmentation frequently more damaging than outright loss because isolated patches cannot sustain viable populations.
- Over-exploitation — poaching, illegal wildlife trade, overfishing and unsustainable harvesting.
- Climate change — range shifts, phenological mismatch, coral bleaching, altered fire and monsoon regimes.
- Pollution — eutrophication, pesticides and biomagnification, plastics, light and noise.
- Invasive alien species — displacing natives through enemy release; Lantana infestation within tiger reserves being a direct instance.
- Also: human-wildlife conflict; disease; genetic erosion in crops and livestock; and, beneath all of these, the indirect drivers of population, consumption, trade and governance failure — notably the fact that ecosystem services are unpriced.

## (b) Project Tiger — a conservation case study
- 1973 launch (~1,800 est.) --> 2006 crisis low (1,411) --> 2010 (1,706)
- --> 2014 (2,226) --> 2018 (2,967) --> 2022 (3,682)

Origin and rationale - Launched on 1 April 1973 at Jim Corbett National Park, initially in nine reserves, in response to alarming decline from poaching and habitat loss. - The tiger as an umbrella and flagship species — the conceptual basis of the project. A tiger requires a large territory with adequate prey, which in turn requires intact forest, sufficient herbivores and a functioning water regime. Protecting the tiger therefore protects the entire ecosystem beneath it, which is why a single-species programme became India’s principal habitat conservation instrument.

Structure and approach - Core-buffer strategy — an inviolate core (critical tiger habitat) managed for conservation with no human settlement, surrounded by a buffer permitting regulated multiple use and co-existence. - Relocation of villages from core areas on a voluntary basis with a compensation package, remaining the programme’s most contested element. - Habitat management — water holes, grassland maintenance, fire management, weed removal (notably Lantana), and prey base augmentation. - Protection — anti-poaching camps and patrols, Special Tiger Protection Force in several reserves, intelligence networks, and the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (2007). - Corridor conservation connecting reserves, since isolated tiger populations lose genetic viability.

The 2005 crisis and the institutional reform it produced - Sariska Tiger Reserve was found in 2005 to have lost its entire tiger population to poaching, and Panna subsequently suffered the same fate. This was the programme’s defining failure. - It led directly to the Tiger Task Force, and to the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2006, which created: - the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) — a statutory body chaired by the Union Environment Minister, giving Project Tiger legal standing it had previously lacked as an administrative scheme; - statutory notification of critical tiger habitats; - a requirement of Tiger Conservation Plans for each reserve; - and the Tiger and Other Endangered Species Crime Control Bureau (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau). - Sariska and Panna were subsequently repopulated by translocation — the first such reintroductions of tigers in India, and successful.

Achievements — the record - Population recovery. From the 2006 low of 1,411, estimates rose to 1,706 (2010), 2,226 (2014), 2,967 (2018) and 3,682 (2022 All India Tiger Estimation) — India holding around 75% of the global wild tiger population. - Reserve network expansion from 9 reserves in 1973 to 58 tiger reserves covering a substantial area across 20 States — with Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve, spanning Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, the largest in India by area. - Monitoring capability. The All India Tiger Estimation, conducted every four years, is the world’s largest camera-trap-based wildlife survey, supported by M-STrIPES (Monitoring System for Tigers — Intensive Protection and Ecological Status), which digitises patrol routes, sightings and threat records. India’s estimation methodology is internationally cited. - Ecosystem co-benefits — tiger reserves protect watersheds, carbon stocks and a wide range of co-occurring species; economic valuation studies of Indian tiger reserves have placed the annual flow of ecosystem services from them at very substantial figures. - Global leadership — India hosted the launch of the International Big Cat Alliance (2023), and Project Tiger’s 50th anniversary in 2023 coincided with the Amrit Kaal Ka Tiger Vision.

Criticisms and unresolved issues - Relocation and rights. Displacement of forest-dwelling communities from core areas remains contested, particularly its interaction with the Forest Rights Act, 2006, which recognises community forest rights. Voluntariness of relocation and adequacy of the package are disputed. - Corridor loss. Reserves are becoming islands as linear infrastructure — highways, railways, canals, transmission lines — severs corridors, risking genetic isolation. Mitigation structures such as the underpasses and elevated stretches on NH-44 through Pench are the model, but are not standard. - Uneven performance. Some reserves are at carrying capacity while others hold very few tigers; a small number of reserves account for a large share of the population, and the Central Indian and Western Ghats landscapes perform far better than the North-East. - Human-wildlife conflict rising as populations recover and disperse into human-dominated landscapes. - Species-centric criticism — that concentrating resources on a charismatic species diverts attention from less visible but equally threatened taxa, particularly amphibians, reptiles, invertebrates and plants. The counter-argument is the umbrella effect: protecting tiger habitat protects everything within it. - Prey base and habitat quality — invasive Lantana and weed infestation degrading grasslands and reducing herbivore density in several reserves.

Related species programmes:Project Elephant (1992) with the Gaj Yatra and Elephant Reserves; Project Snow Leopard (2009); Project Dolphin (2020) for the Gangetic dolphin, India’s National Aquatic Animal; Project Lion; Project Cheetah (2022), the first intercontinental large carnivore translocation; and the International Big Cat Alliance (2023).

## Conclusion

Biodiversity loss is driven principally by habitat change, exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasion — and India’s response has run substantially through flagship species programmes. Project Tiger’s value lies in what it demonstrates: that a well-resourced, statutorily backed programme with credible monitoring can reverse decline, taking the population from 1,411 in 2006 to 3,682 in 2022. Its unresolved problems — corridor fragmentation and the rights of forest-dwelling communities — are precisely the questions that determine whether the recovery is sustainable, since a network of isolated reserves surrounded by resentful neighbours is not a stable conservation outcome.

## Value addition
- Project Tiger facts: launched 1 April 1973 at Jim Corbett with 9 reserves; now 58 tiger reserves; administered by the statutory NTCA (created by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2006); core-buffer strategy with statutorily notified critical tiger habitats.
- Population trajectory:1,411 (2006) –> 1,706 (2010) –> 2,226 (2014) –> 2,967 (2018) –> 3,682 (2022); India holds roughly 75% of the global wild tiger population.
- The crisis that produced reform:Sariska lost its entire tiger population by 2005, and Panna subsequently — leading to the Tiger Task Force, the 2006 amendment, the NTCA and the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau; both reserves were later repopulated by translocation.
- Monitoring: the quadrennial All India Tiger Estimation, the world’s largest camera-trap survey; M-STrIPES for patrol and threat digitisation; conducted by NTCA with the Wildlife Institute of India.
- The conceptual justification: the tiger as an umbrella species (protecting it protects the whole ecosystem), flagship species (mobilising public support) and indicator species (its presence signals ecosystem health) — naming all three roles is the strongest framing.
