## Introduction

Mycoses are infections caused by fungi. Most fungi are harmless saprophytes; a relatively small number cause human disease, and they are classified clinically by the depth of tissue they invade — superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous and systemic — with a fifth category, opportunistic mycoses, defined not by depth but by the host’s immune status. India’s warm, humid climate, high diabetes prevalence and widespread corticosteroid use make it particularly susceptible to several of these.

hair, nails / Subcutaneous --- dermis and below, via trauma / Systemic --- bloodstream and internal organs , with the causative fungi labelled at each depth.

## Superficial mycoses — outermost layers only
- Confined to the outer dead layers of skin and hair shaft; no tissue invasion and minimal inflammatory response, which is why they are cosmetic rather than dangerous.
- Malassezia furfur — pityriasis versicolor, producing hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the trunk; very common in humid climates. The same genus causes seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff.
- Hortaea werneckii — tinea nigra; Piedraia hortae and Trichosporon — black and white piedra of the hair shaft.

## Cutaneous mycoses (dermatophytoses) — the most common
- Caused by dermatophytes, fungi that digest keratin and therefore colonise skin, hair and nails.
- Three genera:Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton.
- Diseases are named by body site as tinea (“ringworm”, though no worm is involved):

Tinea capitis — scalp; tinea corporis — body; tinea cruris — groin (“jock itch”); tinea pedis — feet (“athlete’s foot”); tinea unguium / onychomycosis — nails; tinea barbae — beard.

- Transmission — direct contact, contaminated clothing, towels, footwear and floors; and from animals (Microsporum canis).
- The Indian concern worth stating: India has seen a marked rise in chronic, recurrent and treatment-resistant dermatophytosis, associated with misuse of topical steroid-antifungal-antibiotic combination creams sold over the counter. Steroids suppress the local inflammatory response, allowing the fungus to spread while symptoms appear to improve — producing extensive, atypical and resistant infection. Trichophyton indotineae has been characterised as an emerging terbinafine-resistant species associated with the Indian epidemic and has since spread internationally. This is the most examinable contemporary Indian point on cutaneous mycoses.

## Subcutaneous mycoses — entry through trauma
- Fungi present in soil and vegetation, introduced through puncture wounds and thorn pricks; consequently an occupational disease of agricultural workers, and typically affecting the limbs.
- Sporothrix schenckii — sporotrichosis, the “rose gardener’s disease”, producing nodules spreading along lymphatic channels.
- Mycetoma (Madura foot) — chronic swelling with sinuses discharging characteristic granules; caused by fungi (eumycetoma, e.g. Madurella) or by filamentous bacteria (actinomycetoma, e.g. Nocardia), the distinction being clinically important since treatment differs entirely. Named for Madurai, where it was first described — a point of Indian origin worth noting. Mycetoma is a WHO-recognised neglected tropical disease.
- Chromoblastomycosis — Fonsecaea, Cladophialophora, producing warty lesions; rhinosporidiosis — Rhinosporidium seeberi, affecting the nasal mucosa, with a notable prevalence in southern India and Sri Lanka.

## Systemic (deep) mycoses — internal organs
- Acquired usually by inhalation of spores, with the lung the primary site and dissemination possible. Several are caused by dimorphic fungi — existing as mould in the environment at ambient temperature and as yeast in tissue at body temperature, a defining characteristic.
- Histoplasma capsulatum — histoplasmosis; associated with soil enriched by bird and bat droppings; endemic in parts of India, particularly the Gangetic plain.
- Blastomyces dermatitidis — blastomycosis; Coccidioides immitis — coccidioidomycosis (arid regions); Paracoccidioides — South American blastomycosis.
- Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei — significant in HIV-associated infection in South-East Asia.

## Opportunistic mycoses — defined by the host, not the fungus

These are caused by organisms of low intrinsic virulence that cause disease when host defences are impaired — by HIV, cancer chemotherapy, transplantation and immunosuppressive therapy, uncontrolled diabetes, prolonged corticosteroid or broad-spectrum antibiotic use, indwelling catheters, or ICU admission. This is the clinically most important category in modern medicine, because the population at risk has grown with medical advances.

- Candida albicans and other Candida species — candidiasis: oral thrush, vulvovaginal candidiasis, oesophagitis, and invasive candidaemia in ICU patients, which carries high mortality. Candida auris — the emerging concern: multidrug-resistant, persists on hospital surfaces, spreads readily between patients, and is difficult to identify by routine laboratory methods. WHO classifies it in the critical priority group of its fungal priority pathogens list. It was first described in 2009 and has been reported widely from Indian hospitals.
- Aspergillus fumigatus and other species — aspergillosis: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma (a fungal ball in a pre-existing lung cavity, frequently post-tuberculous — a large problem in India given the TB burden), and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in the severely immunocompromised.
- Cryptococcus neoformans — cryptococcal meningitis, a leading opportunistic infection in advanced HIV disease; acquired from soil contaminated with pigeon droppings.
- Pneumocystis jirovecii — Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), an AIDS-defining illness; reclassified from protozoa to fungi on genetic evidence.
- Mucormycosis (“black fungus”) — the Indian case to develop. Caused by fungi of the order Mucorales — Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia — which are ubiquitous in soil and decaying matter. It is angioinvasive: the fungus invades blood vessels, causing thrombosis and tissue necrosis, which produces the black eschar giving the popular name. Forms:rhino-orbito-cerebral (the commonest in India, spreading from the nose and sinuses to the orbit and brain), pulmonary, cutaneous, gastrointestinal and disseminated. Risk factors:uncontrolled diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis above all — India’s very high diabetes prevalence is the underlying reason for its disproportionate burden — plus corticosteroid use, immunosuppression, iron overload and trauma. The 2021 epidemic: India recorded a large surge in mucormycosis during and after the second COVID-19 wave, attributed to the convergence of uncontrolled diabetes, liberal and often unindicated corticosteroid use, and COVID-19-related immune dysregulation. Several States declared it a notifiable disease under the Epidemic Diseases Act, and amphotericin B supply became a national logistics problem. It remains India’s most instructive recent example of an opportunistic mycosis becoming a public health emergency.

Management: control of the underlying condition (glycaemic control), surgical debridement of necrotic tissue, and systemic antifungals — liposomal amphotericin B, posaconazole, isavuconazole.

## Diagnosis and treatment — brief
- Diagnosis: direct microscopy with KOH mount (dissolving keratin to reveal hyphae); culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar; histopathology with special stains; galactomannan and beta-D-glucan antigen assays; molecular methods including PCR; and imaging for deep infection.
- Antifungal classes:azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole); polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin); echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin); allylamines (terbinafine); griseofulvin; flucytosine.
- Emerging problem:antifungal resistance, driven by long-term prophylaxis, over-the-counter use, and — significantly — agricultural azole fungicide use, which selects for azole-resistant Aspergillus in the environment before any patient is exposed. This environmental route makes antifungal resistance a One Health problem, and WHO’s first Fungal Priority Pathogens List (2022) was published in response.

## Conclusion

Fungal disease is classified by the depth of invasion — from Malassezia on the skin surface to Mucorales invading blood vessels — but the clinically decisive variable in modern medicine is the host’s immune status, which is why opportunistic mycoses have become the most consequential category. India’s particular vulnerability arises from a specific combination: high diabetes prevalence, widespread over-the-counter steroid and antifungal use, and a large post-tuberculous population with cavitary lung disease. The 2021 mucormycosis epidemic and the steroid-driven resistant dermatophytosis epidemic are both consequences of that combination rather than of any change in the fungi themselves.

## Value addition
- The four-level classification: superficial (Malassezia); cutaneous/dermatophytoses (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton); subcutaneous (Sporothrix, mycetoma agents); systemic (dimorphic fungi — Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides); plus opportunistic, defined by host immunosuppression.
- The dimorphism concept: dimorphic fungi grow as mould in the environment and as yeast in tissue at body temperature — the property that enables systemic infection.
- Mucormycosis facts: caused by Mucorales (Rhizopus commonest); angioinvasive, causing thrombosis and necrosis; rhino-orbito-cerebral form predominant in India; risk factors uncontrolled diabetes and ketoacidosis, corticosteroids, immunosuppression; the 2021 post-COVID surge; treatment by glycaemic control, surgical debridement and liposomal amphotericin B.
- Candida auris — multidrug-resistant, environmentally persistent in hospitals, difficult to identify by routine methods; WHO critical priority group.
- The Indian dermatophytosis epidemic: chronic, recurrent and terbinafine-resistant tinea associated with over-the-counter steroid-antifungal combination creams; Trichophyton indotineae as the emerging species.
- Diagnostic and therapeutic terms:KOH mount; Sabouraud dextrose agar; galactomannan and beta-D-glucan assays; antifungal classes — azoles, polyenes, echinocandins, allylamines.
- The One Health dimension:agricultural azole fungicide use selects for azole-resistant Aspergillus in the environment, so resistance can arise before any clinical exposure — the reason WHO published its first Fungal Priority Pathogens List (2022).
- AP relevance: humid coastal climate favouring superficial and cutaneous mycoses; high diabetes prevalence raising mucormycosis risk; the State’s tertiary centres — SVIMS Tirupati and AIIMS Mangalagiri — managing invasive fungal disease; over-the-counter combination cream use as a State-level regulatory concern.
Q126:
## Introduction

Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotic organisms, several of which are significant human pathogens. Their public health importance in India is concentrated in two transmission routes: vector-borne infections such as malaria and kala-azar, and faecal-oral infections such as amoebiasis and giardiasis. Because prevention differs entirely between the two — vector control against the first, water and sanitation against the second — classification by transmission route is the most useful organising principle.

## Vector-borne protozoan diseases

1. Malaria - Causative agent:Plasmodium — five species infect humans: P. falciparum (most severe, causing cerebral malaria), P. vivax (commonest in India, with dormant liver hypnozoites causing relapse), P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. knowlesi. - Vector: female Anopheles mosquito — in India principally An. culicifacies (rural) and An. stephensi (urban). - Clinical: periodic fever with chills and rigor, anaemia, splenomegaly; cerebral malaria and multi-organ failure in severe falciparum infection. - Prevention:long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs); indoor residual spraying; larval source management — eliminating stagnant water, larvivorous fish (Gambusia), biolarvicides; environmental management of breeding sites; chemoprophylaxis for travellers; early diagnosis and complete treatment to interrupt transmission — India uses rapid diagnostic tests and artemisinin-based combination therapy for falciparum. - India’s programme: the National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030), targeting elimination by 2030, with categorisation of districts by endemicity and a phased approach; India has recorded substantial declines in cases and deaths, and exited the WHO High Burden to High Impact group in recognition of that progress.

2. Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis) — India’s elimination success - Causative agent:Leishmania donovani. - Vector: female sandfly — Phlebotomus argentipes, which breeds in cracks in mud walls and organic-rich damp soil. - Clinical: prolonged fever, marked splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, weight loss, anaemia, darkening of skin (hence kala-azar, “black fever”); fatal if untreated. A proportion of treated patients develop Post Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL), which acts as a reservoir sustaining transmission — which is why PKDL detection is central to elimination. - Distribution: Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh. - Prevention:indoor residual spraying with synthetic pyrethroids; improved housing with plastered walls eliminating breeding cracks; early diagnosis by rK39 rapid test and treatment with single-dose liposomal amphotericin B; active case search and PKDL management. - Status: India achieved the elimination target of fewer than 1 case per 10,000 population at block level across endemic blocks, and has sustained it — a genuine public health success worth citing, with WHO validation being the subsequent step.

3. Other vector-borne protozoan diseases (not endemic to India) - African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) — Trypanosoma brucei, transmitted by the tsetse fly. - Chagas disease — Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine (kissing) bugs, in Latin America.

## Faecal-oral protozoan diseases

4. Amoebiasis - Causative agent:Entamoeba histolytica, transmitted by cysts in contaminated food and water. - Clinical: amoebic dysentery with blood and mucus in stool; amoebic liver abscess as the important extraintestinal complication. - Prevention: safe drinking water, sanitation and handwashing; food hygiene; avoiding raw vegetables washed in contaminated water; safe sewage disposal.

5. Giardiasis - Causative agent:Giardia lamblia (intestinalis) — flagellated protozoan attaching to the small intestinal mucosa. - Clinical: persistent diarrhoea, foul-smelling greasy stool (steatorrhoea), abdominal cramps, malabsorption — significant because chronic infection contributes to childhood undernutrition and stunting. - Prevention: water treatment — cysts are relatively chlorine-resistant, so filtration or boiling is required; sanitation and hygiene.

6. Cryptosporidiosis - Causative agent:Cryptosporidium parvum/hominis; oocysts are highly chlorine-resistant, making it a recognised cause of waterborne outbreaks even in treated supplies. - Clinical: watery diarrhoea; severe and prolonged in immunocompromised patients, particularly advanced HIV. - Prevention: filtration, boiling, protection of water sources.

7. Cyclosporiasis — Cyclospora cayetanensis, associated with contaminated fresh produce.

## Other transmission routes

8. Toxoplasmosis - Causative agent:Toxoplasma gondii; the cat is the definitive host; humans acquire infection from oocysts in cat faeces, contaminated soil, or undercooked meat containing tissue cysts. - Clinical: usually asymptomatic in the immunocompetent; congenital toxoplasmosis causes foetal damage — hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification; reactivation causing encephalitis in advanced HIV. - Prevention: thorough cooking of meat; hand hygiene after soil and cat litter contact; pregnant women avoiding cat litter handling; antenatal screening where indicated.

9. Trichomoniasis — Trichomonas vaginalis, sexually transmitted; vaginitis and urethritis; prevented by safe sexual practice and partner treatment.

10. Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis — Naegleria fowleri, the “brain-eating amoeba”, acquired through water entering the nose in warm freshwater; extremely rare but almost always fatal.

## India’s institutional framework — the differentiating content
- National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) — the renamed National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP), covering malaria, kala-azar, dengue, chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis and lymphatic filariasis.
- National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030); the kala-azar elimination target achieved at block level; and the Accelerated Plan for Elimination of Lymphatic Filariasis.
- Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme and the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) for outbreak detection.
- Water and sanitation as protozoal disease prevention: Jal Jeevan Mission for household tap water and Swachh Bharat Mission for sanitation are, epidemiologically, faecal-oral disease control programmes.
- National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC); ICMR-National Institute of Malaria Research (NIMR); ICMR-Vector Control Research Centre (VCRC), Puducherry; ICMR-Rajendra Memorial Research Institute (RMRI), Patna for kala-azar.
- National One Health Mission, relevant to zoonotic protozoa such as Toxoplasma.

## The general preventive framework
- For vector-borne: vector control (LLINs, IRS, larval source management, biological control), personal protection, environmental management of breeding sites, early diagnosis and complete treatment, and surveillance.
- For faecal-oral:safe drinking water (recognising that Giardia and Cryptosporidium cysts resist chlorination and require filtration or boiling), sanitation, handwashing, food safety and safe sewage disposal.
- Cross-cutting: health education, community participation, and prompt treatment to reduce the reservoir of infection.

## Conclusion

Protozoan diseases in India divide cleanly by transmission route, and so do their remedies: malaria and kala-azar require vector control, and amoebiasis, giardiasis and cryptosporidiosis require water and sanitation. India’s record differs correspondingly — kala-azar has reached its elimination target through indoor residual spraying, rapid diagnosis and single-dose treatment, while faecal-oral protozoal infection will decline only as far as Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission actually deliver safe water and sanitation. The most consequential protozoal disease control measures in India are therefore infrastructure programmes rather than health programmes.

## Value addition
- Causative agent and vector pairs to memorise: malaria — Plasmodium / female Anopheles; kala-azar — Leishmania donovani / sandfly Phlebotomus argentipes; sleeping sickness — Trypanosoma brucei / tsetse fly; Chagas — T. cruzi / triatomine bug; amoebiasis — Entamoeba histolytica / faecal-oral; giardiasis — Giardia lamblia / faecal-oral; toxoplasmosis — Toxoplasma gondii / cat and undercooked meat.
- The P. vivax point: dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) cause relapse months later, so radical cure requires primaquine in addition to the blood-stage drug — the reason vivax elimination is harder than falciparum despite lower mortality.
- The PKDL point:Post Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis patients are a human reservoir sustaining transmission, so detection and treatment of PKDL is essential to elimination — a detail that distinguishes an informed answer.
- The chlorine-resistance point:Giardia and Cryptosporidium cysts and oocysts resist standard chlorination, so filtration or boiling is required — which is why they cause outbreaks even in chlorinated municipal supplies.
- Programmes:NCVBDC (formerly NVBDCP); National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016-2030; kala-azar elimination target of <1 case per 10,000 at block level, achieved; IDSP and IHIP; Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission as faecal-oral disease control.
- Institutions:NCDC; ICMR-NIMR (malaria); ICMR-VCRC Puducherry (vector control); ICMR-RMRI Patna (kala-azar); NIV Pune.
- AP relevance: malaria transmission in the forested and tribal districts of the Eastern Ghats — Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam — where P. falciparum burden is concentrated; LLIN distribution and IRS in those districts; Jal Jeevan Mission coverage as protozoal disease prevention; tribal health outreach through Village Health Nutrition Days.

Sources used: ISRO and NRSC — INSAT-3D/3DR, Oceansat/EOS-06, RISAT/EOS, NISAR (July 2025), Bhuvan, MOSDAC and NDEM; Central Pollution Control Board — NAAQS 2009, CAAQMS and NAMP networks, SAMEER app and the Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index; MoEFCC National Clean Air Programme; Forest Survey of India forest fire alert data; Indian Coast Guard National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare — Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, Integrated Health Information Platform, U-WIN, eSanjeevani (43 crore consultations as on 23 November 2025), National Urban Health Mission and the National One Health Mission; ICMR and NCDC — INSACOG, AMR Surveillance Network and the National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (2017); CSIR-IGIB (FELUDA); Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 with the Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations 2011 (as amended 2017) and the Food Products Standards and Food Additives Regulations 2011; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notification prohibiting colistin in food-producing animals (2019); Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Schedule H1; WHO Fungal Priority Pathogens List (2022); National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control — National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016-2030 and the kala-azar elimination programme; ICMR-NIMR, ICMR-VCRC and ICMR-RMRI; Government of Andhra Pradesh — RTGS AWARE and Mana Mitra, APPCB, and AMTZ Visakhapatnam.

Q127:
## Introduction

An antibody is a protein produced by B lymphocytes that binds a specific antigen. Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are antibodies produced by a single clone of identical B cells, and therefore all identical to one another and directed against a single epitope — one precise site on one antigen. This contrasts with polyclonal antibodies, obtained from immunised animal serum, which are a mixture produced by many different B cell clones recognising different epitopes on the same antigen. The distinction determines everything: monoclonals give uniform, reproducible, indefinitely renewable reagents, which is why they transformed diagnostics.

- Immunise mouse with antigen --> harvest B cells from spleen --> fuse with myeloma
- cells (PEG) --> HAT selection medium kills unfused cells --> screen and clone single hybridomas --> culture indefinitely
- --> monoclonal antibody

## How they are produced — hybridoma technology

Developed by Georges Köhler and César Milstein in 1975, for which they shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1984:

- A mouse is immunised with the target antigen, and its spleen B cells harvested. These cells produce the desired antibody but cannot survive in culture.
- Myeloma cells (a B cell tumour line) survive and divide indefinitely but produce no useful antibody.
- The two are fused using polyethylene glycol, producing hybridomas that combine both properties: antibody production from the B cell and immortality from the myeloma.
- HAT medium selects for the fusion products, killing unfused myeloma cells (which lack a salvage-pathway enzyme) and allowing unfused B cells to die naturally.
- Surviving hybridomas are screened, and a single clone producing the desired antibody is isolated and cultured indefinitely — producing an unlimited, permanently identical supply.

Later refinements:chimeric, humanised and fully human antibodies (produced by phage display or transgenic mice) reduce the immune reaction that mouse-derived antibodies provoke in patients — reflected in drug naming: -ximab (chimeric), -zumab (humanised), -umab (fully human).

## Why monoclonals suit diagnosis of parasitic disease
- Specificity. Parasites share many antigens with one another and with host tissue. A monoclonal directed at a single unique epitope can distinguish Plasmodium falciparum from P. vivax, or Entamoeba histolytica from the harmless E. dispar — distinctions that microscopy cannot reliably make.
- Reproducibility. Every batch is identical, so test performance does not vary between production lots — essential for a national programme purchasing millions of test kits.
- Unlimited supply, unlike polyclonal antisera, which depend on continuing animal immunisation and vary between animals.
- Antigen detection rather than antibody detection. Detecting the parasite’s own antigen indicates current infection; detecting the patient’s antibodies may only indicate past exposure. This distinction is decisive in endemic areas where much of the population is seropositive from previous infection.
- No requirement for skilled microscopy. Microscopic diagnosis of malaria requires a trained technician and a functioning laboratory. A monoclonal-based rapid diagnostic test can be performed by a health worker in a village in under twenty minutes.

## Applications in detecting parasitic diseases — the named tests

1. Malaria rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) — the largest application - Format: a lateral flow immunochromatographic strip carrying monoclonal antibodies against parasite antigens; a drop of blood produces a visible line within 15-20 minutes. - Target antigens: - HRP-2 (histidine-rich protein 2) — specific to P. falciparum, highly sensitive, but persists in blood for weeks after cure, so it cannot confirm treatment success. - pLDH (parasite lactate dehydrogenase) — available in species-specific and pan-species forms; clears rapidly after treatment, so it can indicate cure. - Aldolase — pan-species. - Combination RDTs using both HRP-2 and pLDH distinguish falciparum from non-falciparum infection, which matters because treatment differs — P. vivax requires primaquine for radical cure against liver hypnozoites. - Indian use:bivalent RDTs are the standard diagnostic tool of the malaria programme at the village and sub-centre level, supplied through the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control, and are central to the “test, treat, track” strategy of the National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030). - A limitation worth noting:P. falciparum strains with deletion of the hrp2/hrp3 genes produce false-negative HRP-2 tests — an emerging concern that WHO monitors and a reason pLDH-based tests are gaining importance.

2. Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) — the rK39 test - The rK39 rapid diagnostic test uses a recombinant antigen from Leishmania to detect patient antibodies on a dipstick, giving a result in minutes from a finger-prick sample. - Its significance for India is programmatic: kala-azar diagnosis previously required splenic or bone marrow aspiration — invasive, requiring a hospital and carrying real risk. The rK39 strip made field diagnosis at the primary health centre possible, and it is a principal reason India was able to pursue and achieve the elimination threshold of fewer than one case per 10,000 population at block level, reached in 2023 and sustained in 2024.

3. Lymphatic filariasis - ICT card test and Og4C3 ELISA detecting circulating filarial antigen of Wuchereria bancrofti — usable during the day, whereas microscopy requires night blood smears because of the parasite’s nocturnal periodicity. This single practical advantage transformed filariasis surveillance, and underpins the Mass Drug Administration programme and India’s elimination effort.

4. Amoebiasis - Monoclonal-based antigen detection distinguishing pathogenic Entamoeba histolytica from morphologically identical, non-pathogenic E. dispar — a distinction microscopy cannot make, and which prevents substantial over-treatment.

5. Other applications - Giardia and Cryptosporidium faecal antigen detection. - Toxoplasmosis — IgM and IgG assays, important in pregnancy screening. -Cysticercosis and hydatid disease serology. - Immunohistochemistry for identifying parasites in tissue sections. - Research and epidemiology — antigen mapping, drug target identification, and monitoring of transmission intensity.

## Beyond diagnostics — the therapeutic dimension

Monoclonal antibodies are also a major therapeutic class: rituximab (lymphoma), trastuzumab (HER2-positive breast cancer), bevacizumab, adalimumab and infliximab (autoimmune disease), and the anti-SARS-CoV-2 cocktails used during COVID-19. India is among the world’s largest producers of biosimilar monoclonal antibodies, supported by the National Biopharma Mission and BIRAC, which has made several of these therapies substantially more affordable than in high-income markets — a genuine Indian contribution worth stating.

## Limitations

Cost and cold chain requirements; sensitivity below microscopy at very low parasite densities; inability of antibody-detecting tests to distinguish current from past infection in endemic populations; antigen persistence after cure (HRP-2); and gene-deletion strains producing false negatives.

## Conclusion

Monoclonal antibodies are single-epitope, indefinitely renewable reagents whose uniformity made mass-produced diagnostic tests possible. For parasitic disease their contribution has been decisive in exactly the settings where laboratories do not exist: the malaria RDT replaced the microscope at village level, the rK39 strip replaced splenic aspiration for kala-azar, and filarial antigen tests replaced night blood collection. Each of these substitutions moved diagnosis from the hospital to the health worker — which is why India’s malaria elimination and kala-azar elimination programmes were operationally feasible at all.

## Value addition
- Origin: hybridoma technology developed by Köhler and Milstein (1975); Nobel Prize 1984; the fusion of an antibody-producing B cell with an immortal myeloma cell, selected in HAT medium.
- Malaria RDT antigens:HRP-2 (P. falciparum-specific, persists after cure); pLDH (species-specific or pan-species, clears after cure, so indicates treatment response); aldolase (pan-species). Bivalent RDTs are India’s programme standard.
- The three field-transforming tests to name: malaria bivalent RDT (replaced microscopy at village level); rK39 for kala-azar (replaced splenic aspiration); ICT/Og4C3 for filariasis (replaced night blood smears).
- Antibody nomenclature:-omab (mouse), -ximab (chimeric), -zumab (humanised), -umab (fully human) — the suffix indicates how much of the molecule is human, and therefore the immunogenicity risk.
- The antigen-versus-antibody detection distinction: antigen detection indicates current infection; antibody detection may indicate past exposure — decisive in endemic populations.
- Indian institutional context:National Biopharma Mission and BIRAC; India as a leading producer of biosimilar monoclonal antibodies; NCVBDC for programme diagnostics; ICMR institutes including NIMR and RMRIMS Patna.
- AP relevance: malaria RDT use in the Eastern Ghats tribal districts (Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam) where microscopy access is limited; AMTZ Visakhapatnam and the Kalam Institute of Health Technology for diagnostic device manufacturing.
Q128:
## Introduction

Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products for human benefit. Its history divides at a specific point: traditional biotechnology used organisms as they were found, selecting empirically for useful behaviour without understanding the mechanism; modern biotechnology deliberately alters an organism’s genetic material to make it do something it would not otherwise do. Louis Pasteur stands at the intellectual boundary — he established that fermentation was a biological process, which made the deliberate use of organisms a science rather than a craft.

## (a)(i) Old versus modern biotechnology
- **Basis** — Traditional (old) biotechnology · Modern biotechnology
- **Period** — From antiquity; systematised from the 19th century · From the 1970s — recombinant DNA (1973) onward
- **Basis** — Empirical; organisms used as found · Molecular — deliberate manipulation of genetic material
- **Unit of work** — The whole organism · The gene
- **Techniques** — Fermentation, selective breeding, hybridisation, composting · rDNA technology, gene cloning, PCR, tissue culture, monoclonal antibodies, genomics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing
- **Precision** — Low — desired and undesired traits transferred together · High — a single defined gene transferred
- **Species barrier** — Cannot cross species · Can cross species and kingdoms — a human gene expressed in a bacterium
- **Timescale** — Generations of breeding · Months
- **Examples** — Bread, curd, cheese, beer, wine, vinegar, silage, crop and livestock breeding · Recombinant human insulin, Bt cotton, recombinant hepatitis B vaccine, monoclonal antibodies, gene therapy, tissue-cultured banana
- **Regulation** — Largely unregulated · Regulated — in India through the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under the Environment (Protection) Act, and the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety

The defining difference: traditional biotechnology selects among existing variation; modern biotechnology creates variation that would not arise naturally, and can move genes across species boundaries that sexual reproduction cannot cross.

## (a)(ii) Pasteur’s discovery on fermentation

The problem as it stood. In the mid-nineteenth century the dominant view, associated with the chemist Justus von Liebig, was that fermentation was a purely chemical decomposition — that yeast was a lifeless catalytic substance breaking down sugar, and that the yeast cells observed were a by-product rather than the cause. This mattered commercially, because French wine and beer producers were suffering large losses from spoilage and had no explanation for it.

Pasteur’s investigations (from 1857).

- The fermentation of lactic acid and alcohol. Studying spoiled beetroot alcohol at Lille, Pasteur observed under the microscope that successful alcoholic fermentation was always accompanied by living, budding yeast cells, while spoiled batches contained different, rod-shaped organisms producing lactic acid instead of alcohol. He concluded that each type of fermentation is caused by a specific micro-organism — “no fermentation without life”, and different organisms give different products.
- Fermentation as life without air. He demonstrated that yeast ferments in the absence of oxygen and respires in its presence — describing fermentation as “la vie sans l’air”, life without air. This was the discovery of anaerobic life, and the inhibition of fermentation by oxygen is still called the Pasteur effect.
- The swan-neck flask experiment (1859-61). To settle whether the organisms arose spontaneously in the broth or entered from the air, Pasteur boiled nutrient broth in flasks with long, S-shaped swan necks open to the atmosphere. Air could enter freely, but dust and microbes settled in the curve of the neck. The broth remained sterile indefinitely — but when the neck was broken, or the flask tilted so the broth touched the trapped dust, growth appeared within days. This disproved spontaneous generation and established that micro-organisms come from pre-existing micro-organisms.
- Diseases of wine and beer. He showed that spoilage — souring, ropiness, bitterness — was caused by specific contaminating organisms, and that gentle heating to about 55-60deg C for a short period killed them without ruining the product. This is pasteurisation, patented in 1865 and applied first to wine, later to beer and milk.

Why it mattered.

- It established the germ theory of fermentation, and by direct extension the germ theory of disease — if micro-organisms spoil wine, they may also cause disease. This led to Lister’s antiseptic surgery and to Pasteur’s own anthrax and rabies vaccines.
- It converted fermentation from craft to controlled industrial process — the foundation of the entire fermentation industry described at Q183 and Q186.
- Pasteurisation remains the basis of milk safety, and by extension of dairy cooperatives such as Amul and India’s milk economy.

## (b) Antibiotics

Definition.Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by micro-organisms — or synthetic and semi-synthetic analogues — which in low concentrations inhibit the growth of (bacteriostatic) or kill (bactericidal) other micro-organisms, principally bacteria. The broader term antimicrobial covers antibacterials, antivirals, antifungals and antiparasitics.

Discovery.Alexander Fleming observed in 1928 that a Penicillium mould contaminating a staphylococcal culture plate had cleared the bacteria around it. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain subsequently purified penicillin and demonstrated its therapeutic effect; the three shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

## Classification
- By spectrum:narrow-spectrum (active against a limited range, e.g. penicillin G) and broad-spectrum (tetracyclines, chloramphenicol).
- By action:bactericidal (penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) and bacteriostatic (tetracyclines, macrolides, sulphonamides).
- By mechanism — the classification worth knowing:

Cell wall synthesis inhibitors — penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin. These are the safest class, because human cells have no cell wall, so the target is absent in the host — the clearest example of selective toxicity. Protein synthesis inhibitors — aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides, chloramphenicol; they exploit the difference between the bacterial 70S and human 80S ribosome. Nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors — fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase), rifampicin (RNA polymerase). Folate pathway inhibitors — sulphonamides and trimethoprim; bacteria synthesise folate, humans absorb it from diet. Cell membrane disruptors — polymyxins including colistin.

## Advantages of antibiotic use
- Treatment of bacterial infection — pneumonia, tuberculosis, typhoid, sepsis, meningitis; conditions that were routinely fatal before 1940.
- Enabling modern medicine. This is the underrated point: surgery, caesarean section, organ transplantation, cancer chemotherapy and neonatal intensive care are only possible because infection can be controlled. Losing antibiotics would not merely return us to the 1930s in infection treatment; it would remove entire fields of medicine.
- Reduced mortality and morbidity, and shortened illness and hospital stay.
- Prophylaxis — surgical prophylaxis, rheumatic fever prevention, and prevention of opportunistic infection in the immunocompromised.
- Public health impact on maternal and neonatal mortality; treatment of leprosy and tuberculosis under national programmes.
- Veterinary and agricultural disease control (though growth promotion is now restricted — see below).

## Disadvantages of antibiotic use
- Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — the central problem. Antibiotic use exerts selective pressure: susceptible bacteria die, resistant ones survive and multiply. This is natural selection operating within months, and it means every use of an antibiotic slightly reduces its future effectiveness. Resistance arises through mutation and, critically, through horizontal gene transfer — plasmids carrying resistance genes moving between bacterial species, so resistance acquired in one organism can appear in another. WHO identifies AMR among the leading global public health threats, and India carries a very high burden.
- Disruption of the normal microbiota — causing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, Clostridioides difficile colitis, and fungal superinfection such as oral and vaginal candidiasis. Emerging evidence links early-childhood antibiotic exposure to longer-term metabolic and immune effects.
- Adverse drug reactions — anaphylaxis to penicillins; nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity with aminoglycosides; tendon rupture and neuropathy with fluoroquinolones; bone marrow suppression with chloramphenicol; and tooth discolouration in children with tetracyclines.
- Ineffectiveness against viruses. A large share of antibiotic prescriptions in India are for viral upper respiratory infections and viral diarrhoea, where they confer no benefit and all the risk. Antibiotics do not act on viruses, because viruses have no cell wall, no ribosome of their own and no independent metabolism — the point most in need of public communication.
- Environmental contamination — antibiotic residues from pharmaceutical manufacturing effluent, hospital waste and animal waste create environmental reservoirs of resistance genes; Indian pharmaceutical clusters have been documented as sites of high environmental antibiotic concentration.
- Cost — the shift to second- and third-line agents when first-line drugs fail imposes large costs on patients and health systems.
- Masking of diagnosis — empirical antibiotic use before culture obscures the pathogen and complicates later management.

## India’s response to AMR
- National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, following a One Health approach across human, animal, food and environmental sectors.
- Schedule H1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules — specified antibiotics and anti-TB drugs may be sold only on prescription, with the pharmacist maintaining a register; the Red Line campaign places a red vertical line on such packs to signal prescription-only status to consumers.
- Prohibition of colistin (2019) for food-producing animals, poultry, aqua farming and feed supplements — colistin being a last-resort human antibiotic.
- FSSAI maximum residue limits for antibiotics in food of animal origin.
- Antimicrobial stewardship programmes in hospitals; ICMR’s AMR Surveillance Network publishing annual resistance data; National Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use.
- Infection prevention as the most effective AMR measure — Kayakalp for hospital hygiene, immunisation (a vaccinated child needs no antibiotic), and water and sanitation through Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat, since fewer infections mean fewer prescriptions.

## Conclusion

The move from traditional to modern biotechnology is a move from selecting among natural variation to creating it, and Pasteur’s demonstration that fermentation is a biological process — through the microscope, the anaerobic experiment and the swan-neck flask — was the intellectual step that made the transition possible. Antibiotics represent the same logic applied to disease, and they underwrite modern medicine far beyond infection treatment. Their central disadvantage is unusual among drug classes: each individual use imposes a small collective cost on everyone else through resistance selection, which is why antibiotic policy must be regulatory rather than left to prescriber discretion alone.

## Value addition
- Pasteur’s experiments to name specifically: the microscopic observation that different fermentations carry different organisms; fermentation as “life without air” (the Pasteur effect); the swan-neck flask experiment disproving spontaneous generation; and pasteurisation (patented 1865).
- The rDNA milestone: recombinant DNA technology (Boyer and Cohen, 1973); recombinant human insulin (Humulin, 1982) was the first rDNA drug approved for human use — the practical beginning of modern biotechnology.
- Antibiotic mechanism classification: cell wall synthesis (penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin — safest, since human cells lack a cell wall); protein synthesis (aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides — exploiting 70S versus 80S ribosomes); nucleic acid synthesis (fluoroquinolones, rifampicin); folate pathway (sulphonamides, trimethoprim); membrane (polymyxins, colistin).
- Why antibiotics do not work on viruses: viruses have no cell wall, no ribosomes of their own and no independent metabolism — so every antibacterial target is absent. This is the single most important public health message on the subject.
- India’s AMR framework:National Action Plan on AMR; Schedule H1 and the Red Line campaign; colistin prohibition (2019); FSSAI residue limits; ICMR AMR Surveillance Network; hospital antimicrobial stewardship; Kayakalp.
- The regulatory body for modern biotechnology:GEAC under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety; the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (DBT).
- AP relevance: Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad pharmaceutical clusters and effluent concerns; poultry and shrimp sectors and veterinary antibiotic use; AMTZ and KIHT for diagnostics that enable targeted rather than empirical prescribing.

## Introduction

Penicillin and insulin are both biologically produced pharmaceuticals, but they differ in almost every respect that matters — chemical nature, biological function, and above all the route of production, which places them on opposite sides of the traditional/modern biotechnology divide. Viruses and bacteria present a comparable contrast: both cause disease, but their fundamental biology differs so completely that the drugs effective against one are useless against the other.

## (a)(i) Penicillin versus insulin
- **Basis** — Penicillin · Insulin
- **Chemical nature** — A secondary metabolite — a small β-lactam molecule · A protein (peptide) hormone — 51 amino acids in two chains linked by disulphide bonds
- **Natural source** — Produced by the fungus Penicillium chrysogenum · Produced by the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the human pancreas
- **Biological role** — An antibiotic — the fungus’s chemical defence against competing bacteria · A hormone regulating blood glucose by promoting cellular uptake
- **Function in medicine** — Kills bacteria by inhibiting cell wall synthesis · Replaces a deficient hormone in diabetes mellitus
- **Production route** — Fermentation — the organism naturally makes it; industry optimises yield. Traditional biotechnology. · Recombinant DNA technology — the human insulin gene inserted into E. coli or yeast. Modern biotechnology.
- **Historical production** — Fermentation from the outset (1940s) · Originally extracted from bovine and porcine pancreas, causing immune reactions; replaced by recombinant human insulin (Humulin, 1982) — the first rDNA drug approved for human use
- **Administration** — Oral or injectable · Injectable (destroyed by digestion if taken orally, being a protein)
- **Necessity** — Used only when infection occurs · Required lifelong in type 1 diabetes

The point that matters: penicillin is a molecule the organism already makes, so production is a matter of selecting a high-yielding strain and optimising conditions. Insulin is a human protein no micro-organism makes, so production required inserting the human gene into a microbe — which is why insulin, not penicillin, marks the beginning of modern biotechnology.

## (a)(ii) Industrial production of penicillin
- 1. Strain. Fleming’s original Penicillium notatum was a poor producer. The industrial organism is Penicillium chrysogenum, derived from a strain isolated from a mouldy cantaloupe in Peoria, Illinois, and improved over decades by mutation and selection — raising yields several thousand-fold. This is a classic demonstration of strain improvement as the foundation of industrial microbiology.
- 2. Inoculum development. Spores are germinated and scaled up through shake flasks and seed fermenters to provide an actively growing inoculum of sufficient volume.
- 3. Medium.Corn steep liquor — a by-product of maize starch manufacture — was the discovery that made large-scale production viable, supplying nitrogen and growth factors cheaply. Lactose or continuously fed glucose serves as carbon source, with mineral salts. Phenylacetic acid is added as a precursor, directing synthesis specifically toward penicillin G (benzylpenicillin) rather than a mixture of natural penicillins.
- 4. Sterilisation of medium, vessel and air supply, since contamination destroys the batch.
- 5. Fermentation.Aerobic, submerged, fed-batch culture in a stirred-tank bioreactor at about 25-27deg C, pH near 6.5, with continuous sterile aeration and agitation for oxygen transfer, over 6-8 days. The critical point: penicillin is a secondary metabolite, produced not during rapid growth but in the stationary or idiophase after growth slows. Industrial practice therefore uses fed-batch operation — feeding carbon source slowly to hold the culture in a low-growth, high-production state rather than allowing rapid growth and early exhaustion. Understanding why fed-batch is used, rather than merely naming it, is what distinguishes a good answer here. Antifoam is added, since aeration and agitation generate foam that reduces working volume.
- 6. Downstream processing.

Filtration to remove mycelium.

Solvent extraction — the broth is acidified and penicillin extracted into an organic solvent such as amyl acetate, then back-extracted into aqueous buffer at neutral pH; the cycle exploits penicillin’s differing solubility with pH. Crystallisation as the potassium or sodium salt, followed by drying and sterile packaging.

- 7. Semi-synthetic derivatives. The penicillin nucleus 6-aminopenicillanic acid (6-APA) is obtained by enzymatic removal of the side chain using penicillin acylase, and different side chains are attached chemically to produce ampicillin, amoxicillin, cloxacillin and piperacillin — extending the spectrum and conferring resistance to β-lactamase. Most penicillins in clinical use today are semi-synthetic, made this way.

## (b)(i) Virus versus bacteria
- **Basis** — Virus · Bacteria
- **Cellular status** — Acellular — not a cell · Cellular — prokaryotic organism
- **Size** — 20-300 nm (electron microscope required) · 0.5-5 µm (visible by light microscope)
- **Genetic material** — Either DNA or RNA, never both · Both DNA and RNA
- **Structure** — Nucleic acid core + protein capsid; some have a lipid envelope · Cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, nucleoid, often plasmids
- **Metabolism** — None — no enzymes for energy generation · Complete independent metabolism
- **Reproduction** — Only inside a host cell, by taking over its machinery · Independently, by binary fission
- **Living status** — Obligate intracellular parasite; inert outside a host — arguably at the boundary of life · Independently living
- **Culture** — Requires living cells (cell culture, embryonated eggs, animals) · Grows on artificial media
- **Response to antibiotics** — Not affected · Susceptible
- **Treatment** — Antivirals; vaccines; often supportive care · Antibiotics
- **Examples** — SARS-CoV-2, influenza, HIV, rabies, measles, polio, dengue · M. tuberculosis, V. cholerae, S. typhi, E. coli, Lactobacillus

Why antibiotics do not work on viruses — the practical consequence. Antibiotics act on structures unique to bacteria: the cell wall, the 70S ribosome, bacterial DNA gyrase, the folate pathway. A virus has none of these — it has no wall, no ribosome and no metabolism, using the host cell’s machinery instead. There is therefore no bacterial target present. Prescribing an antibiotic for viral illness confers no benefit, exposes the patient to adverse effects, and drives resistance in the patient’s own commensal bacteria. Since a large share of Indian antibiotic use is for viral respiratory illness and viral diarrhoea, this is among the highest-value public health messages available.

## (b)(ii) Harmful and useful effects

Bacteria — harmful - Human disease: tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), typhoid (Salmonella typhi), pneumonia, tetanus, leprosy, diphtheria, plague, food poisoning. - Animal disease: anthrax, brucellosis, mastitis in dairy cattle, colibacillosis and fowl cholera in poultry. - Plant disease: bacterial blight of rice, citrus canker, bacterial wilt. - Food spoilage and toxin production (botulinum, staphylococcal enterotoxin). - Antimicrobial resistance and hospital-acquired infection.

Bacteria — useful - Gut microbiota — synthesis of vitamins K and B-complex, digestion, and colonisation resistance excluding pathogens; increasingly recognised in immunity and metabolism. - Food production — curd, cheese, idli and dosa batter, pickles, vinegar (Lactobacillus, Acetobacter); probiotics. -Agriculture — nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium in legume nodules and free-living Azotobacter; phosphate solubilisation; biofertilisers; biopesticides (Bacillus thuringiensis, the source of the Bt gene). - Industry — antibiotics (Streptomyces), amino acids (lysine, glutamate), enzymes, organic acids, vitamins. - Environment — decomposition and nutrient cycling; sewage treatment (activated sludge, UASB); bioremediation of oil spills and heavy metals; biogas production by methanogens. - Biotechnology — E. coli as the workhorse host for recombinant protein production, including insulin; restriction enzymes and Taq polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus, enabling PCR).

Viruses — harmful - Human disease: COVID-19, influenza, HIV/AIDS, rabies (almost invariably fatal once symptomatic), measles, polio, hepatitis, dengue, chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis, Nipah. - Animal disease: foot-and-mouth disease, avian influenza, classical swine fever, lumpy skin disease, Newcastle disease — with major economic consequences for livestock and poultry. - Plant disease: tobacco mosaic virus, leaf curl viruses, banana bunchy top. - Pandemic potential, since viruses mutate rapidly and cross species barriers — most emerging infections are zoonotic.

Viruses — useful - Bacteriophage therapy against antibiotic-resistant bacterial infection, and phage-based control of Salmonella in poultry. - Vaccine vectors — adenoviral and other viral vectors deliver antigens; the ChAdOx1/Covishield platform is the familiar example. - Gene therapy — modified viruses used as vectors to deliver corrective genes; the basis of approved therapies for inherited disease. - Oncolytic virotherapy — viruses engineered to selectively infect and lyse tumour cells. - Biological pest control — baculoviruses against crop insect pests, avoiding chemical pesticide. - Research tools — phages and viral vectors are foundational to molecular biology; CRISPR itself derives from a bacterial defence system against phages. - Ecological role — marine viruses regulate bacterial and algal populations and drive nutrient cycling in the oceans.

## Conclusion

Penicillin and insulin illustrate the two eras of biotechnology: one a molecule a fungus already makes, obtained by optimised fermentation; the other a human protein obtained only by inserting the human gene into a microbe. Viruses and bacteria differ still more fundamentally, and the practical consequence is the one that matters most for public health — antibiotics act on bacterial structures that viruses simply do not possess, so their use in viral illness produces harm without benefit. Both groups are also indispensable: bacteria for nitrogen fixation, digestion, food and industry, and viruses as vectors, phage therapy and biological control.

## Value addition

- The secondary metabolite point: penicillin is produced in the idiophase after growth slows, not during rapid growth — which is why fed-batch operation is used, holding the culture in a low-growth high-production state.
- Insulin milestone:Humulin (1982) — recombinant human insulin, the first rDNA drug approved for human use; replaced bovine and porcine pancreatic extraction, which caused immune reactions.

- Useful viruses: bacteriophage therapy; viral vector vaccines; gene therapy vectors; oncolytic virotherapy; baculoviral biopesticides; and CRISPR, which originated as a bacterial anti-phage defence system.
- AP relevance: pharmaceutical and biotech manufacturing in the Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad corridor; AMTZ and KIHT for diagnostics; poultry and aquaculture disease burden relevant to both bacterial and viral pathogens.

## Introduction

Infection is the entry, establishment and multiplication of a pathogenic micro-organism within the body of a host. Two distinctions are essential and frequently blurred:

- Colonisation versus infection — micro-organisms present on skin or mucosa without invading or causing a host response are colonising, not infecting. A quarter of the population carries Staphylococcus aureus in the nose without disease.
- Infection versus disease — infection is the establishment of the organism; disease is the clinically apparent damage that may follow. Many infections are subclinical: most people infected with poliovirus never develop paralysis, yet they transmit the virus — which is why surveillance cannot rely on clinical cases alone.

## (a) Types of infection — with examples

## By duration and course
- Acute infection — rapid onset, short duration, rapid resolution or death. Examples:cholera (Vibrio cholerae), with profuse watery diarrhoea within hours; influenza; acute viral hepatitis A; measles.
- Chronic infection — slow onset, prolonged course over months or years, often with persistent organism and immune-mediated tissue damage. Examples:tuberculosis, leprosy, chronic hepatitis B and C, HIV/AIDS.
- Subacute infection — intermediate in tempo. Example:subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Streptococcus viridans.
- Fulminating (fulminant) infection — sudden, severe and rapidly progressive, often fatal within hours to days, with an overwhelming host response. Examples:fulminant meningococcal septicaemia with the Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome; fulminant hepatic failure in hepatitis E, particularly in pregnancy; cerebral malaria from P. falciparum; and rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, which India experienced at scale during the COVID-19 second wave.
- Latent infection — the organism persists in a dormant state after the initial illness, capable of reactivation. Examples:varicella-zoster virus in dorsal root ganglia, reactivating as shingles; latent tuberculosis, in which the bacillus persists without disease and may reactivate on immunosuppression — the reason latent TB infection is a target of India’s TB elimination effort; herpes simplex.
- Subclinical (inapparent) infection — infection without recognisable symptoms, but with immune response and often transmission. Examples: poliomyelitis (the great majority of infections are asymptomatic); hepatitis A in children; many SARS-CoV-2 infections.

## By extent of spread
- Localised infection — confined to a limited area at the site of entry. Examples: boil or abscess (Staphylococcus aureus); tinea/ringworm; conjunctivitis; localised wound infection.
- Focal infection — the organism remains localised at a focus but its products or intermittent bloodstream release cause distant effects. Examples: dental abscess or chronic tonsillitis leading to distant complications; rheumatic fever following streptococcal throat infection.
- Generalised (systemic or disseminated) infection — the organism spreads through blood or lymph to involve multiple organs. Examples:typhoid fever; miliary tuberculosis; septicaemia; measles (which begins in the respiratory tract but disseminates); disseminated candidiasis.
- Related terms:bacteraemia (bacteria transiently present in blood without multiplication); septicaemia (multiplication in blood with systemic illness); toxaemia (toxins in blood without the organism, as in tetanus and diphtheria, where the organism remains local but the toxin acts distantly); pyaemia (pus-forming organisms in blood producing multiple abscesses); viraemia.

## By origin and sequence
- Primary infection — the initial infection in a previously uninfected host. Example:primary tuberculosis — the Ghon focus in a child on first exposure; primary herpes simplex.
- Secondary infection — a new infection by a different organism in a host whose defences are already weakened by an existing infection or condition. Examples:bacterial pneumonia following influenza; mucormycosis and secondary bacterial infection in COVID-19, especially with corticosteroid use and diabetes; secondary bacterial infection of measles.
- Reinfection — a subsequent infection by the same organism after recovery. Example: repeated malaria episodes in an endemic area; reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 variants.
- Superinfection — a new infection occurring during treatment for an existing one, typically because antibiotics have eliminated the protective normal flora. Examples:oral or vaginal candidiasis after broad-spectrum antibiotics; Clostridioides difficile colitis — a direct and common consequence of antibiotic use.
- Cross-infection — transmission from one patient to another, typically in hospital.
- Nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infection — acquired in a healthcare facility, not present or incubating on admission. Examples: ventilator-associated pneumonia, catheter-associated urinary tract infection, surgical site infection — a principal reservoir of multidrug-resistant organisms, and the target of India’s Kayakalp and hospital infection control programmes.
- Opportunistic infection — caused by organisms of low virulence that cause disease only when host defence is impaired. Examples:Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV; candidaemia and aspergillosis in the neutropenic.
- Iatrogenic infection — resulting from a medical procedure or treatment.
- Zoonotic infection — transmitted from animals to humans. Examples:rabies, brucellosis, leptospirosis, Nipah, avian influenza.

## (b) Pathogenesis — a short note

Definition.Pathogenesis is the mechanism and sequence of events by which a pathogen causes disease in a host — from entry through multiplication to tissue damage and transmission. It is distinct from aetiology, which is the cause of disease; pathogenesis is the process.

## The stages — the structure that makes this a process account
- 1. Entry through a portal. Respiratory (tuberculosis, influenza, measles), gastrointestinal (cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A), skin and wound (tetanus, rabies), genito-urinary (gonorrhoea, HIV), vector-borne (malaria, dengue), and vertical/transplacental (rubella, HIV, toxoplasmosis). The portal determines the disease: the same organism entering by a different route may produce different illness.
- 2. Adherence. Attachment to host cells using adhesins, pili and fimbriae; without adherence the organism is swept away by mucus, urine flow or peristalsis. This is why blocking adherence is an attractive therapeutic target.
- 3. Invasion. Penetration of epithelium and deeper tissue, aided by enzymes — hyaluronidase (spreading factor), collagenase, coagulase, streptokinase. Some pathogens remain superficial (V. cholerae stays in the gut lumen); others invade deeply (Salmonella typhi).
- 4. Multiplication and spread. Local multiplication, then possible spread by lymphatics or bloodstream to target organs — the incubation period corresponds to this phase.
- 5. Evasion of host defences — the virulence factors. Capsules resisting phagocytosis (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella); intracellular survival within macrophages (M. tuberculosis, Salmonella); antigenic variation (influenza, trypanosomes, HIV); IgA proteases; biofilm formation; and immunosuppression (HIV, measles).
- 6. Damage to the host — by three mechanisms:

Exotoxins — proteins secreted by living bacteria, highly potent and specific; heat-labile; convertible to toxoids for vaccines. Examples: tetanus and diphtheria toxins, cholera enterotoxin, botulinum toxin. Endotoxin — lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, released on lysis; heat-stable; not convertible to a toxoid; causes fever, hypotension and septic shock through massive cytokine release. Immune-mediated damage — much of the tissue destruction in tuberculosis, rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is caused by the host’s own response, not directly by the organism. This is why the disease may worsen as immunity develops, and it is the most clinically important insight in pathogenesis.

- 7. Transmission to a new host, completing the cycle — through respiratory droplets, faecal-oral route, vectors, blood, sexual contact or vertical transmission.

Determinants of outcome: pathogen factors (virulence, infective dose, expressed as ID50, and route of entry) and host factors (age, nutrition, immune status, comorbidity such as diabetes, and genetic susceptibility). The same exposure produces disease in one person and not another because of this interaction.

## Conclusion

Infection describes the establishment of an organism in a host; disease describes the damage that may follow, and the two are not the same — most poliovirus infections were never paralytic, and most tuberculosis infections remain latent. The descriptive terms — acute, chronic, fulminating, localised, generalised, primary, secondary — classify infections by tempo, extent and sequence, and each corresponds to a different clinical and public health response. Pathogenesis explains the process linking them, and its most consequential insight is that much of the damage in chronic infection is inflicted not by the pathogen but by the host’s own immune response.

## Value addition
- The two distinctions to state at the outset:colonisation (present without invasion or host response) versus infection; and infection (organism established) versus disease (clinically apparent damage) — with subclinical infection as the category that makes surveillance difficult.
- Exotoxin versus endotoxin: exotoxins are secreted proteins, highly potent, specific, heat-labile and convertible to toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria vaccines); endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane, released on lysis, heat-stable, not toxoid-convertible, causing fever and septic shock. This comparison is very frequently examined.
- Virulence factors to name: adhesins, pili and fimbriae (adherence); capsule (anti-phagocytic); hyaluronidase, coagulase, streptokinase (invasion); antigenic variation; intracellular survival; biofilm.
- Terms often confused:bacteraemia (transient presence), septicaemia (multiplication with systemic illness), toxaemia (toxin without organism — tetanus, diphtheria), pyaemia (multiple abscesses), viraemia.
- Indian examples worth using: fulminant — cerebral malaria, COVID-19-associated mucormycosis; latent — latent TB, a target of the National TB Elimination Programme; secondary — post-influenza bacterial pneumonia; superinfection — C. difficile colitis after antibiotics; nosocomial — the reservoir of multidrug-resistant organisms addressed by Kayakalp.
- The concepts examiners reward:ID50 (infective dose for 50%), LD50, incubation period, portal of entry determining disease expression, and immune-mediated pathology.
- AP relevance: malaria in the Eastern Ghats tribal districts; tuberculosis burden and the elimination programme; nosocomial infection control in tertiary centres including SVIMS Tirupati and AIIMS Mangalagiri.
