## Introduction

Hydrophobia — literally “fear of water” — is the classical name for rabies, an acute, progressive viral encephalitis. The name derives from its most characteristic symptom: painful, involuntary spasm of the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles on attempting to swallow, which becomes so distressing that the patient develops intense fear at the sight, sound or even mention of water. Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms appear, and it is simultaneously almost entirely preventable — the combination that defines its public health significance.

## (a) Hydrophobia (rabies)

Causative agent - Rabies virus — genus Lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae; a bullet-shaped, enveloped, single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus. -Neurotropic — it has a specific affinity for nervous tissue. - Negri bodies — eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in infected neurons, particularly in the hippocampus and cerebellar Purkinje cells; historically the diagnostic finding at post-mortem.

## How it is caused — transmission and pathogenesis
- Transmission: through the saliva of an infected animal, by bite, scratch, or licking of broken skin or mucous membrane. Rarely by organ transplantation or aerosol in laboratory/cave settings.
- Reservoir in India: the dog. Dog bites account for the overwhelming majority of human rabies cases in India — commonly cited at over 95% — with cats, monkeys, mongooses, jackals and bats also implicated. This is why dog vaccination is the decisive control measure.
- Pathogenesis: the virus replicates locally in muscle, then enters peripheral nerve endings and travels centripetally along axons to the spinal cord and brain, where it causes encephalitis. It then spreads centrifugally to the salivary glands, making the animal infectious. Crucially, it does not travel through the bloodstream — which explains both why there is a long incubation period and why prophylaxis given during that window can still work.
- Incubation period: typically 1-3 months, but ranging from days to over a year. It is shorter when the bite is closer to the brain — face, head and neck bites carry the shortest incubation and the greatest urgency — and when the wound is severe or heavily contaminated.

Clinical features - Prodrome — fever, malaise, and characteristically paraesthesia, pain or itching at the site of the healed bite, which is a distinctive early clue. - Furious rabies (the commoner form) — hyperactivity, agitation, hydrophobia, aerophobia (spasm provoked by a draught of air), excessive salivation, hallucinations, alternating with lucid intervals; progressing to paralysis, coma and death. - Paralytic (dumb) rabies — ascending flaccid paralysis without hydrophobia, frequently misdiagnosed as Guillain-Barré syndrome. - Outcome: death within days of symptom onset, usually from respiratory or cardiac failure. Survival after clinical onset is exceptionally rare.

## Remedial and precautionary measures

## Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) — the definitive intervention
- Step 1 — Immediate wound washing. Wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, then apply a virucidal agent such as povidone-iodine or alcohol. This single step is the most effective and most neglected component of PEP: mechanical removal and inactivation of virus at the wound reduces risk substantially, and it costs nothing. Traditional practices such as applying chillies, turmeric, oil, herbs or cauterising the wound are harmful and delay treatment. Wounds should not be sutured immediately unless unavoidable.
- Step 2 — Categorise the exposure (WHO classification):

Category I — touching or feeding animals, licks on intact skin. No PEP required; wash the area.

Category II — nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding. Wound washing + rabies vaccine.

Category III — single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, licks on broken skin, contamination of mucous membrane with saliva, or any bat exposure. Wound washing + rabies vaccine + Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG).

- Step 3 — Rabies vaccine. Modern cell-culture vaccines (purified chick embryo cell, human diploid cell, purified vero cell). Regimens: intramuscular (Essen, on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28) or intradermal (Updated Thai Red Cross, days 0, 3, 7, 28) — the intradermal route uses a fraction of the dose and is substantially cheaper, which is why India has promoted it for programme use. The older nerve tissue (Semple) vaccine is discontinued because of severe neurological adverse effects.
- Step 4 — Rabies Immunoglobulin (Category III only).Infiltrated into and around the wound to neutralise virus locally before the vaccine-induced antibody response develops. Human RIG or equine RIG; monoclonal antibody preparations are now available and are being adopted for their consistency and supply security. The critical point: RIG must be infiltrated at the wound, not merely injected elsewhere.
- PEP is effective at any interval after exposure, provided symptoms have not appeared — because of the long incubation period. There is no time limit on starting PEP, which is worth stating, since delay often follows a mistaken belief that it is “too late”.

2. Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) — a three-dose schedule for those at continuing risk: veterinarians, animal handlers, laboratory workers, wildlife personnel, and children in highly endemic areas. It simplifies subsequent PEP (no RIG required, fewer doses).

## Animal-level control — the measure that actually eliminates the disease
- Mass dog vaccination. Achieving and sustaining coverage of about 70% of the dog population interrupts transmission — the epidemiological threshold. Human PEP saves individuals; dog vaccination eliminates the disease. This is the single most important point in the answer.
- Animal Birth Control (ABC) programmes combining sterilisation with vaccination, under the Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023 (which replaced the 2001 Rules), implemented by local bodies.
- Responsible pet ownership, licensing and leash regulation; humane management of community dogs; waste management, since uncollected food waste sustains stray dog populations — linking solid waste management to rabies control.

## Surveillance, awareness and programmes
- National Rabies Control Programme under the National Health Mission, providing free vaccine and RIG at government facilities and training health workers.
- National Action Plan for Dog Mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) by 2030, aligned with the global “Zero by 30” goal of WHO, FAO, WOAH and GARC. Rabies has been made a notifiable disease in several States, improving surveillance.
- One Health coordination between health, animal husbandry and municipal departments — rabies is the textbook case for One Health, since the human intervention alone can never eliminate it.
- Public awareness — that any dog bite requires washing and medical attention; that home remedies are dangerous; and that free PEP is available at government facilities.
- India’s burden: India accounts for a very large share of global rabies deaths, overwhelmingly dog-mediated and disproportionately among children, who are bitten more often, on the face and head, and may not report the bite.
- The demonstrated model:Goa achieved sustained interruption of dog-mediated human rabies through systematic mass dog vaccination combined with surveillance and education — an Indian proof of concept for the 2030 target.

## (b) The measles virus — morphology and biological characters

Classification and structure - Family Paramyxoviridae, genus Morbillivirus; a single serotype worldwide, which is why measles vaccine remains effective without reformulation — in contrast to influenza. - Morphology:pleomorphic, roughly spherical, 100-250 nm, enveloped with a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane. - Genome:single-stranded, negative-sense, non-segmented RNA. The non-segmented genome matters: unlike influenza, measles cannot reassort, which limits its capacity for abrupt antigenic change. - Nucleocapsid: helical symmetry, RNA associated with nucleoprotein, phosphoprotein and the large polymerase protein. - Two key envelope glycoproteins — the basis of immunity: - H (haemagglutinin) protein — mediates attachment to host cell receptors (CD150/SLAM on immune cells, and nectin-4 on epithelial cells). Antibodies against H are protective. - F (fusion) protein — mediates fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane and fusion between infected cells, producing the characteristic multinucleated giant cells (Warthin-Finkeldey cells). - M (matrix) protein lines the envelope’s inner surface. Notably, measles lacks neuraminidase, unlike mumps and influenza.

Biological characters - Extremely contagious — among the most transmissible human viruses, with a basic reproduction number typically cited at 12-18, meaning one case can infect a dozen or more susceptible people. This is why measles requires very high vaccination coverage (about 95%) for herd immunity, far above most other vaccine-preventable diseases. - Transmission — respiratory droplets and airborne aerosol; the virus remains infectious in air and on surfaces for up to two hours. - Host range — humans are the only natural reservoir, with no animal host. This makes measles eradicable in principle, like smallpox and polio. - Fragility outside the host — sensitive to heat, light, acid and lipid solvents, which is why the vaccine requires a strict cold chain. - Pathogenesis — entry through the respiratory tract, replication in local lymphoid tissue, primary and secondary viraemia, then dissemination to skin, respiratory tract, conjunctiva and gut. - Immunosuppression — the underappreciated feature. Measles infects and depletes memory lymphocytes, producing “immune amnesia”: the loss of previously acquired immunity to other pathogens, leaving the child susceptible to infections they were formerly protected against, for two to three years afterwards. This is why measles mortality is largely due to secondary pneumonia and diarrhoea rather than to measles itself.

Clinical features and complications - Prodrome — fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis (the “three Cs”), followed by Koplik spots — small white lesions on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, appearing 1-2 days before the rash and pathognomonic for measles. - Rash — maculopapular, beginning behind the ears and on the face and spreading downward, later becoming confluent and desquamating. - Complications — pneumonia (the commonest cause of death), diarrhoea, otitis media, acute encephalitis, corneal ulceration and blindness (aggravated by vitamin A deficiency), and the rare but invariably fatal subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) developing years later. - Management — supportive; vitamin A supplementation on two consecutive days is recommended by WHO for all children with measles and measurably reduces mortality and ocular complications.

Prevention and India’s programme - Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine, a live attenuated vaccine, given at 9-12 months and 16-24 months under the Universal Immunisation Programme. - Mission Indradhanush and Intensified Mission Indradhanush to reach unvaccinated and partially vaccinated children; the nationwide Measles-Rubella vaccination campaign; and U-WIN for digital immunisation tracking. - India’s target of measles and rubella elimination — originally set for 2023 and subsequently revised, with a national Measles-Rubella Elimination Campaign. Elimination requires sustained coverage above 95% with two doses and case-based surveillance with laboratory confirmation. - Surveillance — case-based measles-rubella surveillance with a national laboratory network, integrated with IHIP.

## Conclusion

Rabies and measles are both vaccine-preventable, but they illustrate opposite public health strategies. Rabies is almost always fatal and almost always preventable, and its elimination depends not on treating humans but on vaccinating 70% of dogs — a One Health intervention outside the health department’s direct control, which is why India’s 2030 target requires municipal and animal husbandry action as much as medical. Measles, with no animal reservoir and a single serotype, is eradicable in principle, but its extreme transmissibility demands about 95% two-dose coverage — so it is the disease that most unforgivingly exposes any gap in an immunisation programme.

## Value addition
- The PEP essentials: wash with soap and running water for 15 minutes; Category I — no PEP; Category II — vaccine; Category III — vaccine plus RIG infiltrated into the wound. Intradermal regimens are dose-sparing and cheaper. There is no time limit on starting PEP provided symptoms have not appeared.
- The epidemiological threshold: vaccinating about 70% of the dog population interrupts transmission — which is why dog vaccination eliminates rabies while human PEP only saves individuals.
- Programmes and targets:National Rabies Control Programme; National Action Plan for Dog Mediated Rabies Elimination by 2030, aligned with global “Zero by 30”; Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023; Goa as the demonstrated Indian model of interruption.
- Rabies virus facts:Lyssavirus, Rhabdoviridae; bullet-shaped, enveloped, ssRNA negative-sense; Negri bodies in neurons; travels along nerves, not blood; incubation shorter for bites nearer the head.
- Measles virus facts:Paramyxoviridae, Morbillivirus; pleomorphic, enveloped, ssRNA negative-sense, non-segmented (hence no reassortment); H and F glycoproteins, no neuraminidase; receptors CD150/SLAM and nectin-4; Koplik spots pathognomonic; R0 12-18, requiring about 95% two-dose coverage.
- “Immune amnesia”: measles depletes memory lymphocytes, erasing previously acquired immunity to other pathogens for two to three years — which is why most measles deaths are from secondary pneumonia and diarrhoea.
- AP relevance: dog-bite burden and municipal ABC programmes in AP cities; measles-rubella campaign coverage; Mission Indradhanush and U-WIN implementation; district hospitals and SVIMS Tirupati as referral centres for PEP and RIG availability.

## Introduction

India’s infectious disease burden follows a predictable seasonal calendar, driven principally by the monsoon: rainfall creates vector breeding sites, floods contaminate water supplies, and humidity and temperature shifts alter pathogen and vector survival. Predictability is the opportunity — because the calendar is known in advance, interventions can be delivered before the transmission season rather than in response to it. The failure mode in Indian outbreak control is not ignorance of what is coming, but delivering the response after cases have begun.

E | Jun-Sep: monsoon --- malaria, leptospirosis, cholera, water-borne outbreaks | Sep-Nov: post-monsoon --- dengue, chikungunya, JE, scrub typhus, malaria peak | Dec-Feb: winter --- influenza, respiratory infection, measles .

## The seasonal pattern and its drivers
- **Season** — Diseases · Driver
- **Summer (March-June)** — Cholera, acute diarrhoea, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, heat illness, measles · Water scarcity forcing use of unsafe sources; food spoilage; higher pathogen multiplication
- **Monsoon (June-September)** — Malaria, leptospirosis, cholera and diarrhoeal outbreaks, hepatitis, viral fever · Vector breeding; flooding contaminating water sources and drawing sewage into drinking supply
- **Post-monsoon (September-November)** — Dengue, chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis, scrub typhus, malaria peak · Residual stagnant water in containers and construction sites; Aedes breeds in clean stored water
- **Winter (December-February)** — Influenza, acute respiratory infection, pneumonia, measles · Crowding indoors; low temperature and humidity favouring respiratory virus survival

## The two disease families and their distinct logic
- Vector-borne (malaria, dengue, chikungunya, JE, kala-azar) — controlled by breaking the vector’s breeding cycle, which must be done before the vector population peaks. Once the population has built up, control is far harder.
- Water-borne (cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea, hepatitis A and E) — controlled by water quality and sanitation, which is an infrastructure question rather than a health department one. Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission are, in effect, India’s largest infectious disease control programmes, though they are not administered as such.

## Analysing “in-time” intervention — by timing

## Pre-season (the highest-return window)
- Forecasting and risk mapping. IMD rainfall forecasts, satellite-derived surface water and temperature data, and historical case patterns identify high-risk blocks weeks before transmission begins. NCVBDC uses this for pre-monsoon planning.
- Vector source reduction before the season — desilting drains, removing water-holding containers, larvivorous fish (Gambusia, guppy) introduction into ponds and wells, and construction site inspection. This is the intervention with the highest return per rupee and the one most often deferred.
- Indoor residual spraying (IRS) completed before the transmission season, for malaria and kala-azar — spraying after transmission begins has substantially less effect.
- Long-lasting insecticidal net (LLIN) distribution and coverage verification ahead of the season.
- Chlorination and water source protection — pre-monsoon repair of pipelines, cleaning of overhead tanks and wells, and identification of sources vulnerable to flood contamination.
- Pre-positioning supplies — ORS, zinc, RDTs, antimalarials, IV fluids, chlorine tablets and halogen tablets at PHC level, so that no time is lost procuring after an outbreak begins.
- Vaccination — Oral Cholera Vaccine campaigns in known hotspot areas; typhoid conjugate vaccine; JE vaccination in endemic districts under the Universal Immunisation Programme; influenza vaccination of health workers and vulnerable groups.
- Training and microplanning at block and PHC level, with rapid response teams identified in advance.

## Early detection — the surveillance window
- IHIP (Integrated Health Information Platform) — near-real-time, case-based reporting replacing the earlier aggregate weekly system, enabling detection of a cluster within days.
- Syndromic surveillance — reporting of fever, diarrhoea and jaundice syndromes rather than waiting for laboratory confirmation, which is faster.
- Sentinel and laboratory networks — the VRDL network of ICMR for viral diagnosis; state public health laboratories.
- Wastewater-based surveillance — India’s environmental surveillance for poliovirus through sewage sampling is a proven national capability, detectable before clinical cases appear, and extendable to typhoid, hepatitis and cholera.
- Community-level reporting by ASHA workers, who detect fever clusters in villages before any facility does — the human sensor layer that no digital system replaces.
- Event-based surveillance — media scanning, rumour verification, and unusual mortality reports.
- The threshold principle: outbreak thresholds should be defined in advance for each district, so that response is triggered automatically by case counts rather than awaiting an administrative decision.

## In-season response
- Rapid Response Teams deployed within 24 hours of a cluster.
- Case management — ORS and zinc for diarrhoea (the intervention that has done most to reduce child diarrhoeal deaths globally); prompt RDT-based diagnosis and ACT treatment for malaria under “test, treat, track”; fluid management for dengue with platelet monitoring; oral rehydration corners at PHCs.
- Vector control intensification — fogging (which kills adult mosquitoes but has only short-term effect and does not substitute for source reduction), larviciding, and container surveys.
- Emergency water measures — chlorination, tanker supply, distribution of halogen tablets, and repair of leaking pipelines; identification and closure of contaminated sources, since a single contaminated source can drive an entire outbreak.
- Risk communication — timely, specific, locally-worded advisories; the failure of communication produces both panic and complacency.
- Surge capacity — fever clinics, additional beds, blood and platelet supply for dengue, and referral pathways.
- Cross-departmental coordination — health, municipal, water supply, animal husbandry and education departments, since the causes lie outside the health department.

## Post-season and structural measures
- Outbreak investigation and documentation — identifying the source and the failure, so that the same source does not cause the same outbreak the following year. Learning from every outbreak is explicitly one of India’s ten disaster risk reduction principles.
- Water and sanitation infrastructure — Jal Jeevan Mission household tap water; Swachh Bharat Mission sanitation; AMRUT 2.0 urban sewerage and drainage; 24x7 pressurised supply, which removes the negative-pressure contamination mechanism behind recurrent urban water-borne outbreaks.
- Solid waste and drainage under SBM-U, removing Aedes breeding habitat.
- Housing and ventilation, relevant to respiratory disease and tuberculosis.
- Nutrition — POSHAN 2.0, since undernourished children die of infections that well-nourished children survive; and vitamin A supplementation, which reduces measles mortality.
- One Health integration for zoonoses — leptospirosis, JE (pigs and ardeid birds as amplifying hosts), scrub typhus.

## Case illustrations
- Malaria. India has recorded sustained decline and exited the WHO high-burden grouping. The National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030) uses a category-based district classification with LLINs, IRS, RDTs and ACT. The timing insight: IRS and LLIN distribution completed before the monsoon determine the season’s outcome far more than case management during it.
- Kala-azar. Elimination pursued through pre-season IRS, active case search, rK39 rapid diagnosis and single-dose liposomal amphotericin B; the threshold of fewer than one case per 10,000 at block level was achieved in 2023 and sustained in 2024.
- Cholera and diarrhoeal disease. Controlled less by health interventions than by water supply. The Diarrhoea Roko Abhiyan and ORS-zinc campaigns address case management, while Jal Jeevan Mission addresses the cause. Oral Cholera Vaccine is deployed in hotspot areas.
- Dengue. No specific treatment and no widely deployed vaccine, so control is entirely preventive — source reduction in and around homes, since Aedes aegypti breeds in clean stored water in domestic containers, making this the disease most dependent on household behaviour.
- Japanese encephalitis. Vaccination in endemic districts plus vector control; incidence has fallen substantially where campaigns were sustained.
- COVID-19 demonstrated the full architecture — genomic surveillance through INSACOG, CoWIN for vaccination at scale, and ICCCs repurposed as war rooms — and also the cost of delayed action.

## The economic burden — the question’s second element
- Direct costs — treatment, hospitalisation, and out-of-pocket expenditure, which pushes households into poverty; AB-PMJAY provides Rs. 5 lakh cover to about 12.37 crore families precisely against such shocks.
- Indirect costs — lost wages during illness and caregiving, reduced agricultural productivity during the monsoon when both disease and farm labour demand peak, and long-term losses from child stunting caused by repeated diarrhoeal episodes.
- Macroeconomic — losses to tourism and trade during outbreaks; the cost of emergency response; and the burden on health system capacity displacing routine care.
- The economic case for prevention: pre-season source reduction and water chlorination cost a small fraction of outbreak response and treatment — the standard argument for shifting expenditure upstream, and the same asymmetry that under-funds mitigation in disaster management.

## Conclusion

India’s seasonal disease calendar is predictable, and that predictability is precisely why “in-time” intervention is achievable: the vector season, the water contamination season and the respiratory season arrive on schedule every year. The evidence is that the highest-return actions — pre-monsoon source reduction, IRS completed before transmission, water source protection and pre-positioned supplies — all occur before the first case, while the response that attracts most attention and funding occurs after. Structural investment in water supply and sanitation would do more than any health programme, since cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea are ultimately problems of infrastructure rather than of medicine.

## Value addition
- The seasonal calendar to memorise: summer — cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A/E, diarrhoea; monsoon — malaria, leptospirosis, water-borne outbreaks; post-monsoon — dengue, chikungunya, JE, scrub typhus; winter — influenza, ARI, measles.
- The two control logics:vector-borne diseases require breaking the breeding cycle before the population peaks; water-borne diseases require water quality and sanitation — meaning Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission are India’s largest infectious disease control programmes though not administered as such.
- Surveillance platforms:IHIP (case-based, near-real-time, replacing IDSP’s aggregate reporting); ICMR VRDL laboratory network; environmental/wastewater surveillance (proven through polio); INSACOG for genomic surveillance; ASHA-based community reporting.
- Programme names:National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016-2030 (“test, treat, track”); NCVBDC; kala-azar elimination (threshold achieved 2023, sustained 2024); Diarrhoea Roko Abhiyan and ORS-zinc; Oral Cholera Vaccine in hotspots; JE vaccination under UIP; Mission Indradhanush; U-WIN.
- The dengue-specific point:Aedes aegypti breeds in clean stored water in domestic containers, not in drains — so dengue control depends on household-level container management, and paradoxically, intermittent water supply creates the breeding sites by forcing storage.
- The economic argument: pre-season prevention costs a fraction of outbreak response; child stunting from repeated diarrhoea imposes lifetime productivity losses; AB-PMJAY protects against catastrophic health expenditure.
- AP relevance: malaria in the Eastern Ghats tribal districts (Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam); post-cyclone leptospirosis and water-borne outbreak risk in the delta districts; Vijayawada-Budameru floods (2024) as a flood-to-outbreak pathway; RTGS AWARE for early warning; eSanjeevani and Village Health Clinics for remote case management.

## Introduction

Vector-borne diseases (VBDs) are illnesses caused by pathogens transmitted to humans by living intermediaries — usually haematophagous arthropods — rather than by direct person-to-person contact. WHO estimates VBDs account for over 17% of all infectious diseases globally. India runs a dedicated National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) covering six diseases: malaria, dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic filariasis, kala-azar and Japanese encephalitis. Among these, malaria remains the most consequential historically, and India’s progress against it is now a global reference point.

Vector-borne Diseases: Concept and Classification

- A vector is an organism that carries and transmits an infectious agent; biological vectors (in which the pathogen multiplies or develops, e.g. Anopheles for Plasmodium) are distinguished from mechanical vectors (which merely carry the agent externally, e.g. the housefly transmitting Entamoeba histolytica).
- Mosquitoes:Anopheles –> malaria, lymphatic filariasis; Aedes aegypti –> dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever; Culex –> Japanese encephalitis, Bancroftian filariasis.
- Sandflies:Phlebotomus argentipes –> kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) — India targets elimination as a public-health problem.
- Ticks and fleas: Kyasanur Forest Disease (Karnataka), scrub typhus, plague and murine typhus.

## Epidemiology of Malaria — The Agent-Host-Environment Triad
- Agent factors: Five Plasmodium species infect humans. In India, P. falciparum (causing cerebral malaria and most deaths) and P. vivax (widely distributed, relapsing through dormant liver hypnozoites) dominate. The vivax relapse burden is why a 14-day radical primaquine cure, preceded by G6PD screening, is programmatically critical.
- Vector factors:Anopheles culicifacies is the principal rural vector in peninsular India, An. fluviatilis in forested-hilly tracts and An. minimus/dirus in the North-East. The invasive Anopheles stephensi, which breeds in urban construction-site tanks and overhead reservoirs, has been flagged in India’s Malaria Elimination Technical Report (2025) as the emerging threat to the 2030 goal.
- Host factors: Children, pregnant women (placental sequestration of P. falciparum), migrant labour and forest-dependent tribal populations carry disproportionate risk. Sickle-cell trait and Duffy-negativity confer partial protection — relevant to India’s tribal belts.
- Environmental factors: Temperature above ~18 degrees C (needed for sporogony), humidity above 60%, monsoon-linked stagnant water, forest cover and irrigation. Transmission in India peaks July–November.

## Malaria Situation in India
- Global backdrop: WHO’s World Malaria Report 2025 estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths globally in 2024 — a rise of about 9 million cases over 2023, driven by drug and insecticide resistance, climate shifts and conflict. Against this global stagnation, India’s decline stands out.
- India’s trajectory: Cases fell by over 80% between 2015 and 2023, and deaths by nearly 78% (PIB, World Malaria Day 2025). India exited WHO’s High Burden to High Impact (HBHI) group in 2024. By the end of 2025, 160 districts across 23 States/UTs had reported zero indigenous cases for three consecutive years (MoHFW).
- Policy architecture: The National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016–2030) categorises States 0–3 by Annual Parasite Incidence (API), and the National Strategic Plan (2023–2027) operationalises “Test, Treat, Track” with real-time reporting on the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP). The Intensified Malaria Elimination Project (IMEP-3) targets high-burden districts.
- Andhra Pradesh instance: AP’s burden is now concentrated in its tribal agency areas — Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam districts account for the bulk of State cases, reflecting the national pattern in which roughly 27 tribal-dominated districts holding 5% of the population contribute about 44% of malaria cases (ICMR-NIMR). AP has correspondingly focused IRS and LLIN distribution on agency mandals such as Paderu, Chintapalli and Seethampeta.

## Conclusion

Malaria’s epidemiology in India is no longer a story of nationwide endemicity but of residual, geographically concentrated transmission in tribal, forested and border districts, alongside a newly emerging urban front driven by An. stephensi. With NFME and NSP 2023–27 in place, India is credibly positioned for zero indigenous cases by 2027 and WHO certification by 2030. Sustaining this will require surveillance that does not relax as numbers fall, protection of mobile and migrant populations, and vigilance on artemisinin and pyrethroid resistance — because in elimination, the last mile is the hardest and the most expensive.

## Value addition
- API (Annual Parasite Incidence) = confirmed malaria cases per 1,000 population under surveillance per year. It is the metric on which NFME categorises States: Category 0 (zero indigenous cases), 1 (API <1 in all districts), 2 (State API <1 but some districts >1), 3 (API >=1).
- Certification rule: WHO certifies a country malaria-free only after three consecutive years of zero indigenous cases — hence India’s interim 2027 target precedes the 2030 goal by exactly that margin.
- Vaccines: WHO has recommended two — RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) and R21/Matrix-M (Oxford, manufactured by Serum Institute of India, Pune). Both target P. falciparum and are deployed in African settings; they are not part of India’s programme, whose burden mix is different.
- Institutional anchor:ICMR-National Institute of Malaria Research (NIMR), New Delhi, with field units, provides the scientific backbone; the Malaria Elimination Demonstration Project, Mandla (MP) is the model tribal-district template AP’s agency areas can adapt.
- Related targets: Lymphatic filariasis elimination by 2027, kala-azar sustained elimination as a public-health problem

(<1 case per 10,000 at block level), aligning with SDG 3.3 — end the epidemics of AIDS, TB, malaria and neglected tropical diseases by 2030.

## Introduction

Malaria illustrates in one disease the full chain of infection — a parasite, a vector, a susceptible host and a permissive environment — and its control therefore demonstrates every principle of communicable-disease prevention. India, having reduced malaria cases by over 80% between 2015 and 2023 (PIB, 2025), now aims at zero indigenous cases by 2027. The same layered logic that is working against malaria — interrupting transmission at multiple points simultaneously — underlies prevention of common infections generally.

Part (a): The Malarial Parasite

- Aetiology: Malaria is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium. Five species infect humans — P. falciparum (most lethal; causes cerebral malaria), P. vivax (most widespread in India; relapses from dormant liver hypnozoites), P. malariae, P. ovale and the zoonotic P. knowlesi. India’s burden is essentially a falciparum-vivax mix, which is why the national drug policy is species-specific.
- Mode of Spread: Transmission is through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito — female because only she takes a blood meal, required for egg maturation. Non-vectorial routes exist but are rare: transfusion malaria, contaminated needles, organ transplantation, and congenital (transplacental) transmission. Malaria does not spread by casual contact — a point examiners look for.
- Symptoms: The classic paroxysm has three stages — cold stage (chills, rigors), hot stage (high fever, headache) and sweating stage — recurring at 48-hour (tertian) or 72-hour (quartan) intervals as infected RBCs rupture synchronously and release the toxic pigment haemozoin (NCERT Class XII, Human Health and Disease). Anaemia and splenomegaly follow. Severe/complicated malaria — cerebral malaria, acute kidney injury, ARDS, hypoglycaemia, blackwater fever — is almost always falciparum and is a medical emergency in children and pregnant women.
- Treatment: Governed by the National Drug Policy on Malaria (NCVBDC). P. falciparum is treated with Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy — ACT-SP (artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) nationally and ACT-AL (artemether-lumefantrine) in the North-East where SP resistance exists — plus a single dose of primaquine as a gametocytocidal. P. vivax receives chloroquine for 3 days plus primaquine for 14 days for radical cure, after G6PD screening to avoid haemolysis. Severe malaria requires injectable artesunate. Diagnosis must precede treatment — RDT or microscopy — to protect against resistance.
- Preventive Measures:Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs) and Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) in high-API areas; source reduction of stagnant water and use of larvivorous fish; larvicides and biolarvicides; chemoprophylaxis for non-immune travellers and security personnel; and surveillance-led “Test, Treat, Track” under NSP 2023–27.

Part (b): Preventing Common Infections — A Five-Tier Framework

- Tier 1 — Personal hygiene: Handwashing with soap at critical times can reduce diarrhoeal episodes by roughly 30– 48% and respiratory infections appreciably (WHO). Respiratory etiquette and nail/oral hygiene are the low-cost, high-return interventions. Institutional anchor:Swachh Bharat Mission IEC and school WASH programmes.
- Tier 2 — Food and water safety: Boiling, chlorination or filtration of drinking water; washing produce; avoiding cut fruit and uncovered street food. Institutional anchor:Jal Jeevan Mission, which extended functional household tap connections to about 82% of rural households by 2026 and now runs Field Test Kit-based village water-quality testing, plus FSSAI’s Eat Right India for food safety.
- Tier 3 — Vector control: Weekly “dry day” emptying of coolers and containers, mosquito nets, repellents, screening of windows, and community source-reduction drives. Institutional anchor:NCVBDC’s Integrated Vector Management and urban municipal anti-larval operations.
- Tier 4 — Immunisation: The single most cost-effective preventive tool. India’s Universal Immunisation Programme protects against 12 vaccine-preventable diseases and has been intensified through Mission Indradhanush; the Rotavirus vaccine (introduced 2014, now nationwide) prevents severe childhood diarrhoea, and the HPV vaccination campaign extends the logic to cancer prevention. Full immunisation coverage rose to about 76% (NFHS-5) from 62% in NFHS-4.
- Tier 5 — Environmental and institutional measures: Safe excreta disposal, solid-waste management, ventilation in housing, and antimicrobial stewardship — since irrational antibiotic use converts treatable infections into untreatable ones. Institutional anchor:SBM-Grameen Phase II (ODF Plus), the National Action Plan on AMR, IDSP/IHIP surveillance, and the National One Health Mission for zoonoses.

## Conclusion

Malaria’s control demonstrates that no single intervention interrupts transmission — diagnosis, species-specific chemotherapy, vector suppression and surveillance must act together, which is exactly why India’s decline accelerated only after NFME integrated them. The same principle generalises: common infections yield not to exhortations about hygiene but to layered defences running from the individual to the health system. India’s achievement of near-universal tap water, expanded immunisation and digital surveillance has built that architecture; what remains is consistent last-mile delivery, particularly in tribal and urban-slum populations where the infection burden now concentrates.

## Value addition
- Why Anopheles females only: The male mosquito feeds on plant nectar; the female requires a blood meal for egg maturation — transmission is therefore an incidental by-product of reproduction. A one-line explanation like this reliably distinguishes a written answer.
- Drug-resistance watch: Artemisinin partial resistance is documented in the Greater Mekong sub-region and now in parts of East Africa — the strongest argument for combination therapy and for never treating on presumption without a test.
- G6PD deficiency: Primaquine triggers haemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals — a real constraint in India, making pre-treatment screening a programmatic requirement, not a formality.
- Larvivorous fish caution:Gambusia affinis eats 100–300 larvae per day and has been used in India since 1928 (Urban Malaria Scheme), but the IUCN lists it among the world’s 100 worst invasive alien species — a balanced, two-sided point that examiners reward. Indigenous alternatives such as Aplocheilus are now preferred in sensitive water bodies.
- AP relevance: With over 97% rural tap-water coverage under JJM and a strong Ayushman Arogya Mandir network, Andhra Pradesh’s preventive-health infrastructure is comparatively strong; its residual challenge is agency-area delivery in Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam.
Q135:
## Introduction

Malaria is a protozoan disease requiring two hosts to complete its life cycle — humans, in whom asexual multiplication occurs, and the female Anopheles mosquito, in which sexual reproduction takes place. Technically, therefore, the mosquito is the definitive host and the human the intermediate host, though the mosquito is popularly called the vector. This dual-host dependence is not merely a biological curiosity: it means the transmission chain can be broken at either end, which is the foundation of every control strategy from bed-nets to radical cure.

## Causative Agent
- Malaria in humans is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium (phylum Apicomplexa). Five species infect humans: P. falciparum — most virulent; causes cerebral malaria and the overwhelming majority of deaths; no dormant liver stage but high parasitaemia. P. vivax — most widely distributed outside Africa and dominant in much of India; forms dormant liver hypnozoites causing relapses months later. P. malariae — quartan fever (72-hour cycle), can persist chronically for years. P. ovale — rare in India; also forms hypnozoites. P. knowlesi — zoonotic, from macaques, reported in South-East Asia; the shortest (24-hour) erythrocytic cycle.
- The vector is the female Anopheles mosquito — in India principally An. culicifacies (rural plains), An. fluviatilis (forested foothills), An. minimus and An. dirus (North-East), and the invasive urban breeder An. stephensi.

Life Cycle — Phase I: In the Human Host (Asexual Schizogony)

- Sporozoite inoculation: An infected female Anopheles, while feeding, injects sporozoites (the infective form) with its saliva into the human bloodstream. Within about 30 minutes they reach the liver.
- Exo-erythrocytic (hepatic) schizogony: Sporozoites invade hepatocytes, multiply into schizonts, and release thousands of merozoites into the blood. In P. vivax and P. ovale, a fraction remain dormant as hypnozoites — the biological reason a 14-day primaquine course is needed for radical cure.
- Erythrocytic schizogony: Merozoites invade red blood cells, pass through ring –> trophozoite –> schizont stages and rupture the RBC, releasing fresh merozoites and the pigment haemozoin, which triggers the characteristic paroxysm of chills and fever every 48 or 72 hours depending on species (NCERT Class XII).
- Gametogony: A proportion of merozoites differentiate into male microgametocytes and female macrogametocytes, which circulate and are ingested by the next feeding mosquito. Gametocytes cause no symptoms but are the only transmissible stage — hence single-dose primaquine as a gametocytocidal.

Life Cycle — Phase II: In the Mosquito Host (Sexual Sporogony)

- Gamete formation and fertilisation: In the mosquito’s midgut, the microgametocyte undergoes exflagellation producing motile microgametes, which fertilise the macrogamete to form a zygote.
- Ookinete and oocyst: The zygote elongates into a motile ookinete, penetrates the midgut wall and encysts beneath the basal lamina as an oocyst.
- Sporozoite formation: Within the oocyst, thousands of sporozoites develop; the oocyst ruptures and sporozoites migrate to the salivary glands, rendering the mosquito infective. This sporogony takes about 10–14 days and requires ambient temperature above roughly 18 degrees C — which is precisely why malaria is a warm-climate, post-monsoon disease and why climate warming extends its altitudinal range.

## Preventive Measures — Mapped to the Life Cycle
- Blocking sporozoite inoculation (mosquito –> human):LLINs and IRS under NCVBDC’s Integrated Vector Management; repellents, screened housing, full-sleeved clothing.
- Preventing vector breeding (larval stage): Source reduction of stagnant water, larvicides and biolarvicides, and larvivorous fish — with the caveat that Gambusia, though effective, is IUCN-listed among the 100 worst invasive species.
- Clearing the human reservoir (blood and liver stages): Prompt diagnosis by RDT/microscopy, ACT for falciparum, and 14-day primaquine after G6PD screening for vivax — the only way to remove hypnozoites and prevent relapse-driven re-seeding.
- Blocking gametocyte pick-up (human –> mosquito): Single low-dose primaquine with ACT, which sterilises gametocytes without curing the patient — a purely transmission-blocking measure.
- Vaccines: WHO recommends RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M (manufactured by Serum Institute of India) — both are pre-erythrocytic P. falciparum vaccines deployed in high-burden African settings. India’s programme currently relies on vector control and case management rather than vaccination.

## Conclusion

The Plasmodium life cycle is not merely descriptive biology — it is a map of intervention points. Every major control tool corresponds to a specific stage: nets and sprays block sporozoite delivery, larvicides destroy the vector before it flies, ACT clears the blood stage, primaquine eliminates hypnozoites and gametocytes, and vaccines pre-empt hepatic invasion. India’s success — an over-80% reduction in cases between 2015 and 2023 and exit from WHO’s HBHI group in 2024 — came from attacking several of these points at once. Reaching zero indigenous cases by 2027 now depends on completing radical cure for vivax and containing the urban vector An. stephensi.

## Value addition
- Historical anchors:Charles Laveran first observed the parasite in blood (1880, Nobel 1907); Sir Ronald Ross, working at Secunderabad (Deccan), demonstrated the mosquito transmission of malaria in 1897 — World Mosquito Day, 20 August, marks that discovery and is a strong regional reference for APPSC/TGPSC.
- Terminology precision: The mosquito is the definitive host (sexual reproduction) and the human the intermediate host (asexual). Most candidates state the reverse — getting it right is an easy differentiator.
- Incubation periods:P. falciparum ~9–14 days; P. vivax ~12–17 days (but relapse possible up to 3 years); P. malariae ~18–40 days.
- Diagnostics ladder: Peripheral blood smear (thick film for detection, thin film for speciation) remains the gold standard; Rapid Diagnostic Tests detecting HRP-2/pLDH antigens enable point-of-care testing by ASHAs — the single biggest reason surveillance reached remote tribal habitations; PCR is used for low-density and research settings.
- Climate link worth one line: Every 1 degree C rise shortens the sporogonic cycle and extends transmission to higher altitudes — IPCC AR6 flags expanding vector-borne disease range as a health consequence of warming, making this question climate-linkable.
Q136:
## Introduction

Diarrhoea is defined by WHO as the passage of three or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours, resulting from infection of the intestinal tract that impairs fluid absorption or drives active secretion. It remains among the leading causes of under-five mortality in India, despite being both preventable and treatable at a cost of a few rupees. Its burden is intensely seasonal — clustering in the summer and monsoon months — and outbreak-prone in flood- and cyclone-affected areas, making it as much an administrative and engineering challenge as a clinical one.

## Causative Agents
- Bacterial:Vibrio cholerae (profuse, painless “rice-water” stools), enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC — the leading cause of travellers’ diarrhoea), Shigella species (bacillary dysentery with blood and mucus), Salmonella and Campylobacter jejuni.
- Viral:Rotavirus — historically the single largest cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in children under five in India, which is precisely why it was prioritised for vaccination; also Norovirus (a common outbreak agent in institutional settings) and Adenovirus.
- Protozoal:Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery — stools with mucus and blood clots, transmitted mechanically by houseflies, per NCERT Class XII) and Giardia lamblia (chronic malabsorptive diarrhoea).
- Mechanistically, agents act either by secretory toxin (cholera toxin, ETEC) or by invasion of the mucosa (Shigella, E. histolytica) — which is why the former causes watery stool and the latter bloody stool. Naming this distinction demonstrates conceptual grip.

## Symptoms
- Frequent loose or watery stools, abdominal cramps, nausea and vomiting; fever and tenesmus in invasive (dysenteric) infections.
- Dehydration is the decisive clinical finding and the actual cause of death — graded as no/some/severe dehydration on WHO criteria. In infants, warning signs include sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle, dry mouth, absent tears, reduced skin turgor, lethargy and reduced urine output.
- Complications: electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia), metabolic acidosis, hypovolaemic shock, acute kidney injury, and in the chronic setting, malnutrition — diarrhoea and undernutrition reinforce each other in a vicious cycle.

## Modes of Infection
- Transmission is overwhelmingly by the faeco-oral route, summarised by the classic “F-diagram” — Fluids, Fields, Flies, Fingers, Food — all leading from Faeces to a new host.
- Specific pathways: consumption of contaminated drinking water; unsafe household water storage; open defecation contaminating surface and groundwater; fly-borne mechanical transfer; unwashed hands during food preparation; and unsafe complementary feeding of infants.
- Outbreak triggers in Andhra Pradesh: cyclones and floods that breach sewage lines and contaminate open wells, and pipeline leakages that draw in sewage under negative pressure — typical of coastal districts during the north-east monsoon.

## Government Preventive Measures During and Around Outbreaks
- Immediate outbreak response:Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) are activated under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP, 2004), now reporting through the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), with the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) coordinating investigation. Actions include source identification, super-chlorination of water sources, water sample testing, ORS depot creation at the village level, and case-management camps.
- Clinical management: Free distribution of Oral Rehydration Salts and zinc, IV fluids for severe dehydration, and antibiotics restricted to dysentery and cholera. ORT alone, correctly used, can prevent the overwhelming majority of diarrhoeal deaths.
- STOP Diarrhoea Campaign: MoHFW rebranded and expanded the Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight (IDCF) into the STOP Diarrhoea Campaign in 2024, extending it from a two-week to a two-month drive covering the summer-monsoon peak. Under it, ASHAs pre-position 2 ORS packets and a 14-tablet zinc course in every household with an under-five child, set up ORS-Zinc corners at facilities, and demonstrate ORS preparation. Its stated goal is zero child deaths from diarrhoea.
- Immunisation: India was the first country to introduce an indigenously developed Rotavirus vaccine (2014); it is now nationwide under the Universal Immunisation Programme, given in three doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, and has substantially reduced severe rotaviral hospitalisations.
- Structural WASH measures: The Jal Jeevan Mission, whose rural tap-water coverage rose from about 17% in 2019 to roughly 82% of households by 2026, was extended by the Union Cabinet in March 2026 as JJM 2.0 up to December 2028 with an enhanced outlay of about Rs. 8.69 lakh crore, guaranteeing 55 litres per capita per day meeting BIS 10500 standards. Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen Phase II (ODF Plus) addresses excreta and greywater management, while Village Water and Sanitation Committees conduct Field Test Kit-based water-quality testing at source. Andhra Pradesh reports over 97% rural tap-water coverage, placing it among the better-performing States.

## Conclusion

Diarrhoea is the clearest case in public health where mortality is a function of governance rather than of medicine — the cure, oral rehydration, costs almost nothing and has existed for half a century. India’s decline in diarrhoeal deaths has come from the combination of a vaccine (rotavirus), a treatment campaign (STOP Diarrhoea) and infrastructure (JJM and SBM), working together. The unfinished agenda is functionality rather than coverage: ensuring that taps actually deliver safe water year-round, that ODF status is sustained, and that ORS-zinc reaches the last household before the monsoon, not after the first death.

## Value addition
- Why zinc alongside ORS: Zinc restores intestinal mucosal integrity, shortens the episode by about 25% and reduces recurrence over the following 2–3 months — which is why the two are now co-packaged rather than distributed separately.
- The ORS story: Oral rehydration solution was developed and field-proven during the 1971 Bangladesh refugee crisis at camps in West Bengal; The Lancet has called it potentially the most important medical advance of the twentieth century. ORS Day is observed on 29 July.
- Dysentery vs diarrhoea:Dysentery specifically means diarrhoea with visible blood — caused by Shigella (bacillary) or E. histolytica (amoebic). The syllabus lists them separately; conflating them costs marks.
- Surveillance architecture to name: IDSP (2004, World Bank-assisted) –> IHIP (digital, real-time) –> NCDC –> State and District Surveillance Units –> Rapid Response Teams. Zoonotic and water-borne outbreak coordination now also sits under the National One Health Mission.
- Cross-linkage for extra depth: Repeated diarrhoea causes environmental enteric dysfunction, a major driver of child stunting — linking this answer to POSHAN Abhiyaan and NFHS-5 nutrition indicators, and to SDG 6 (water and sanitation) alongside SDG 3.
Q137:
## Introduction

Tuberculosis is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus discovered by Robert Koch in 1882, transmitted by air and preventable and curable in the overwhelming majority of cases. India carries the world’s largest TB burden — roughly a quarter of global cases — yet is also recording one of the fastest declines: per the WHO Global TB Report 2025, India’s TB incidence fell 21% between 2015 and 2024 (from 237 to 187 cases per lakh population), nearly double the global rate of decline, and TB mortality fell 28% over the same period (PIB, March 2026).

## Types of Tuberculosis
- By site of infection:

Pulmonary TB — affects the lung parenchyma; the most common and the only substantially infectious form, since transmission requires expulsion of bacilli in respiratory aerosols. Extra-pulmonary TB (EPTB) — lymph nodes (the commonest EPTB site in India), pleura, bones and joints, kidneys, intestines, and meninges. Spinal TB (Pott’s disease) causes vertebral collapse and paraplegia. EPTB is generally not contagious, spreading within the body from a primary lung focus. Miliary (disseminated) TB — haematogenous spread producing millet-seed-like lesions across organs; severe, and most common in children and the immunosuppressed.

- By drug susceptibility:Drug-sensitive TB; MDR-TB (resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin); pre-XDR and XDR-TB (additional resistance to fluoroquinolones and injectables/bedaquiline). India accounts for a disproportionate share of the global MDR/RR-TB burden, making resistance the single greatest threat to elimination.
- By activity:Latent TB infection (bacilli present, no disease, not infectious — but with lifetime risk of reactivation) versus active TB disease. Latent infection is the reservoir from which future cases emerge, which is why TB Preventive Treatment (TPT) for household contacts and PLHIV is now a programme pillar.

## Modes of Infection
- Airborne droplet-nuclei transmission: when a person with infectious pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, sings or speaks, bacilli-laden particles remain suspended and are inhaled. Risk rises sharply with crowding, poor ventilation and prolonged exposure — hence the concentration in urban slums, prisons, hostels and mines.
- TB does not spread through handshakes, sharing food or utensils, public toilets or ordinary social contact (PIB/MoHFW) — a point worth stating explicitly, since stigma born of this misconception is itself a barrier to diagnosis.
- Patients on effective treatment generally cease to be infectious after about two weeks, which is why prompt treatment initiation is simultaneously a public-health and a clinical act.
- Bovine TB (M. bovis) via unpasteurised milk is a minor secondary route relevant in dairy-dependent rural settings.

## Symptoms
- Constitutional: persistent cough of two weeks or more, evening rise of temperature, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue.
- Pulmonary: chest pain, breathlessness, and haemoptysis (blood-stained sputum) in advanced disease.
- Site-specific in EPTB: painless cervical lymph node swelling, chronic back pain with deformity in spinal TB, headache and altered sensorium in TB meningitis, sterile pyuria in renal TB.
- Critically, a substantial share of cases are asymptomatic or sub-clinical — under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, about 9 lakh of the 28 lakh patients diagnosed since December 2024 were asymptomatic and would have been missed by symptom-based screening alone (PIB, March 2026). This finding has reshaped the programme towards X-ray-led screening.

## Common Diagnostic Tests — The Diagnostic Ladder
- Screening:Chest X-ray, now increasingly AI-enabled — over 500 AI-enabled hand-held X-ray units are deployed with 1,500 more being supplied to States, alongside DeepCXR for automated reading and Cough Against TB (CATB), an acoustic-AI smartphone tool that has screened over 1.6 lakh people with a 12–16% higher case yield than conventional methods.
- Bacteriological confirmation:Sputum smear microscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen / fluorescent) — cheap and decentralised; Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAAT/CBNAAT/TrueNat) — rapid molecular tests that detect M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance simultaneously within about two hours, with more than 9,800 rapid molecular testing facilities now operational.
- Culture and Drug Susceptibility Testing:Liquid culture (MGIT) remains the gold standard for confirmation; India operates 107 Culture and DST laboratories — the world’s largest such network. Universal Drug Susceptibility Testing (UDST) under NTEP means every diagnosed patient is tested for resistance, not only treatment failures.
- Latent infection:Tuberculin Skin Test (Mantoux) and Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRA) — these detect infection, not disease, and cannot distinguish latent from active TB.
- Genomic:Whole-Genome Sequencing for resistance profiling and outbreak tracing.

## Causes for Its Prevalence in India
- Undernutrition — the single largest attributable risk: Studies indicate starvation-related malnutrition can raise TB incidence six- to eight-fold. India’s high burden of undernutrition therefore translates directly into TB incidence, which is why Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana provides Rs. 1,000 per month to every notified patient — Rs. 4,454.68 crore has been disbursed to 1.38 crore beneficiaries since 2018 (PIB, March 2026).
- Overcrowding and poor ventilation: Dense urban slums, migrant labour housing, prisons and mining settlements create ideal aerosol transmission conditions.
- A large, fragmented private sector: A majority of patients first seek care privately, causing diagnostic delay, irregular regimens and under-notification — addressed through the Ni-kshay notification incentive for private providers.
- Treatment interruption and resistance: Long regimens, drug side-effects, stigma and migration drive non-adherence, converting drug-sensitive TB into MDR-TB. Occasional drug stock-outs at State level compound this.
- Co-morbidities:Diabetes (India’s large diabetic population roughly triples TB risk), HIV, silicosis, tobacco use and alcohol dependence.
- Social determinants: Poverty, low health literacy, stigma delaying care-seeking, and weaker diagnostic reach in tribal and remote areas — illustrated by the NTEP campaign in Gurez valley, Kashmir, where screening 1,250 people over three days threw up over 250 presumptive cases previously invisible to the system.

## Conclusion

Tuberculosis in India is simultaneously a bacteriological and a socio-economic disease: the bacillus is ancient and curable, but it thrives on undernutrition, crowding and delayed diagnosis. The recent acceleration — a 21% fall in incidence and 28% fall in mortality between 2015 and 2024, a 90% treatment success rate now exceeding the global average, and 46,118 gram panchayats certified TB-free for 2024 — shows that combining technology (AI screening, UDST, the BPaLM six-month regimen for drug-resistant TB) with social support (Ni-kshay Poshan, Ni-kshay Mitras) works. Sustaining it requires closing the private-sector notification gap and treating nutrition policy as TB policy.

## Value addition
- NTEP at a glance: RNTCP renamed NTEP in 2020; four pillars — Detect, Treat, Prevent, Build; guided by the National Strategic Plan to End TB in India 2020–25, targeting elimination ahead of the global SDG 3.3 deadline of 2030.
- Key sub-schemes to name:Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (2022) — described as the world’s largest crowd-sourced nutritional-support initiative, with 6.77 lakh Ni-kshay Mitras having distributed over 45 lakh food baskets; Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (2018, Rs. 1,000/month); 100-Day TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (launched 7 December 2024 in 347 districts, since scaled nationwide — over 20 crore people screened, 28 lakh patients diagnosed).
- BPaLM regimen: Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid + Moxifloxacin — cuts drug-resistant TB treatment from 18– 24 months to 6 months; over 15,000 MDR/RR-TB patients already initiated.
- Vaccine position:BCG protects children against severe forms (miliary TB and TB meningitis) but gives limited protection against adult pulmonary TB — hence trials of newer candidates and the adult BCG revaccination study conducted across Indian States.
- AP-specific hooks: Andhra Pradesh delivers TB screening and treatment through its Ayushman Arogya Mandir network (India-wide, 1,84,726 centres as on March 2026) and the Family Physician / Jagananna Aarogya Suraksha style village-clinic outreach; the State’s agency mandals in Alluri Sitharama Raju and its migrant-heavy construction and aqua-processing workforce are the priority vulnerable groups for active case finding.
- Global context for a comparative line: WHO’s Global TB Report 2025 records 1.23 million TB deaths worldwide in 2024, keeping TB among the top ten causes of death globally and the leading killer from a single infectious agent.
