205. “Combined consideration of biological and social processes is necessary for cost effective control of viral infections like bird flu, polio, chikungunya.” Discuss. (TGPSC, 2024)

Viral disease control has two levers. The biological lever — vaccines, vector control, culling, diagnostics — acts on the pathogen. The social lever — trust, compensation, sanitation behaviour, occupational practice — determines whether the biological lever is actually pulled. Bird flu, polio and chikungunya illustrate the point sharply: each has a technically adequate biological solution that has repeatedly failed for social reasons. Cost-effectiveness follows from integration because social measures are low-cost and high-leverage, whereas repeated biomedical campaigns after a preventable failure are expensive. India’s institutional recognition of this is the National One Health Mission, which places human, animal and environmental health under a single coordinating architecture.

## Bird Flu (Avian Influenza H5N1) — Biology Meets Livelihood
- Biological control: India follows a strict “detect and cull” policy — culling infected flocks, restricting movement and disinfecting within a 1 km radius of the epicentre (DAHD, PIB, 5 April 2025). DAHD has permitted commercial use of the H9N2 (low-pathogenic) vaccine developed by ICAR-NIHSAD, Bhopal, while HPAI vaccination remains under scientific review because available vaccines reduce viral shedding without giving sterile immunity.
- Why the social lever decides the outcome: Culling destroys a poultry farmer’s entire working capital overnight. Without credible, prompt compensation, farmers conceal sick birds and distress-sell them — which is precisely how a containable outbreak becomes a regional one. Hence compensation for culled birds, destroyed eggs and feed under the Livestock Health and Disease Control Scheme (50:50 Centre-State) is not welfare; it is an epidemiological instrument.
- AP anchor:Andhra Pradesh was among the eight States reporting HPAI outbreaks between 1 January and 4 April 2025 (DAHD, PIB 2025), across 34 epicentres nationally. As one of India’s largest egg-producing States, AP’s exposure is economic as much as epidemiological — which makes farmer trust the binding constraint.
- Integration in practice: DAHD’s three-pronged strategy (April 2025) — stricter biosecurity, strengthened surveillance, and mandatory registration of all poultry farms — is a deliberate fusion of a technical measure (surveillance) with a behavioural-regulatory one (registration).

## Polio — The Textbook Case of Bio-Social Integration
- Biological: The Pulse Polio Immunisation Programme (from 16 March 1995) delivered OPV to every under-five child; injectable IPV was introduced in 2015 and extended nationwide by 2016 after the global switch from trivalent to bivalent OPV. India recorded its last wild polio case on 13 January 2011 (Howrah, West Bengal) and was certified polio-free on 27 March 2014 (PIB, Zero Case: India’s Polio Eradication Saga, Nov 2024).
- Social: The technical vaccine was available for years before eradication succeeded. What closed the gap was social mobilisation — ASHAs, community influencers and religious leaders addressing vaccine refusal in high-risk pockets of western Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, and door-to-door micro-planning for migrant and riverine populations.
- Sustaining it: India continues one National Immunization Day and two Sub-National Immunization Days annually, backed by AFP surveillance plus environmental (sewage) surveillance, which detects silent circulation even without a paralytic case (WHO India). Vigilance is necessary because wild poliovirus remains endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan.

## Chikungunya — Where the Social Lever Dominates
- Biological: Caused by an Alphavirus transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. Control rests on larvicides, biological agents such as Gambusia affinis, and adulticiding through NCVBDC. Vaccines (Ixchiq, live-attenuated, FDA-approved Nov 2023; Vimkunya/PXVX0317, VLP-based, Feb 2025) are not yet in India’s programme.
- Social:Aedes breeds overwhelmingly in domestic and peri-domestic containers — coolers, overhead tanks, discarded tyres, construction sites. No amount of municipal fogging substitutes for weekly household source reduction (“Dry Day”). This is why chikungunya control is essentially a behavioural programme with a chemical supplement.
- Cost logic: Source reduction costs a household five minutes a week; a chikungunya epidemic costs a State weeks of lost labour, since polyarthralgia can disable a working adult for months.
- **Disease** — Biological Lever · Social Lever · What Fails if Social Lever Missing
- **Bird flu** — Test-and-cull, 1 km zone, H9N2 vaccine · Compensation, farm registration, biosecurity habits · Concealment and distress sale of sick birds
- **Polio** — OPV + IPV, AFP & sewage surveillance · ASHA outreach, influencer engagement, micro-planning · Vaccine refusal, missed migrant children
- **Chikungunya** — Larvicide, Gambusia, adulticiding · Household source reduction, Dry Day, waste disposal · Breeding restarts within one week

Alternative diagram: a simple two-overlapping-circles Venn — “Pathogen Control” and “Human Behaviour” — with the intersection labelled “Cost-Effective, Sustained Control (One Health)”.

## Conclusion

The three diseases converge on a single lesson: the biological lever is necessary but never sufficient, and it is the social lever that determines cost per case averted. Polio proves what integration achieves; bird flu shows what its absence costs. India’s National One Health Mission, the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) and the National Joint Outbreak Response Team now institutionalise this convergence across the health, animal husbandry and wildlife departments. Embedding community trust, occupational livelihood protection and sanitation behaviour into the epidemiological design — rather than treating them as afterthoughts — is what converts a technically sound programme into an affordable and durable one.

- National One Health Mission: approved to coordinate human, animal, wildlife and environmental health; anchored institutionally with the National Institute of One Health, Nagpur.
- Gambusia caveat — a high-value nuance: the mosquitofish eats 100-300 larvae a day and has been used in Indian malaria control since 1928 (Urban Malaria Scheme), but the IUCN lists it among the world’s 100 worst invasive alien species for its damage to native fish. Cite it as an example of a biological control with an ecological trade-off.
- Surveillance backbone: IDSP has migrated to the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), enabling near-real-time, case-based digital reporting rather than weekly aggregate returns.
- Compensation as epidemiology: LHDC Scheme, 50:50 Centre-State — the single most under-cited instrument in avian influenza answers.
- India’s global contribution: India has shared H5N1 genomic sequencing data with international networks, supporting global pandemic preparedness (DAHD, 2025).

206. Discuss in detail about HIV; also mention the symptoms associated with the infection, preventive measures and diagnostic test for disease confirmation. (APPSC, 2011)

The Human Immunodeficiency Virus is a lentivirus of the Retroviridae family that selectively destroys CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes, progressively dismantling cell-mediated immunity until opportunistic infections define AIDS. India reported its first case in 1986 in Chennai. Four decades later the epidemic is low-level but not closed: adult prevalence stands at 0.20% in 2024, down from 0.33% in 2010, against a global average of 0.7% (NACO / MoHFW, PIB, 30 November 2025).

## Nature and Structure of the Virus
- HIV carries single-stranded RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which transcribes viral RNA into DNA; integrase then splices this provirus permanently into the host genome. This integration is why HIV is manageable but not curable — antiretrovirals suppress replication, they do not excise the provirus.
- HIV-1 is globally dominant and more virulent; HIV-2 is less transmissible, slower-progressing and concentrated in West Africa, though present in western India.

## Modes of Transmission

Unprotected sexual contact (the dominant route in India); transfusion of infected blood or blood products; sharing of contaminated needles among injecting drug users; and vertical transmission during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding.

## Clinical Staging — draw as a simple timeline
- **Stage** — Duration · Features
- **Acute retroviral syndrome** — 2-6 weeks post-exposure · Fever, sore throat, maculopapular rash, generalised lymphadenopathy; high viraemia and high infectivity
- **Clinical latency** — Years · Largely asymptomatic; continuous viral replication with gradual CD4 decline
- **Symptomatic / AIDS** — CD4 typically below 200/mm3 · Tuberculosis, oral candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis, chronic diarrhoea, wasting, Kaposi’s sarcoma

## Diagnostic Algorithm — the corrected position
- Screening: rapid point-of-care tests or ELISA detecting HIV antibodies at Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres (ICTCs).
- Confirmation: India uses a three-test rapid algorithm — three antibody assays with different antigen preparations or principles — per the National HIV Counselling and Testing Guidelines, 2024. Western Blot has been discontinued in the national programme owing to cost, indeterminate results and turnaround time.
- Infants: antibody tests are unreliable up to 18 months because of transplacental maternal antibody, so DNA-PCR on Dried Blood Spot at 6 weeks is used for Early Infant Diagnosis.
- Blood safety:Nucleic Acid Testing (NAT) shortens the window period in blood banks.
- Monitoring:CD4 count for immune status; routine universal viral load testing to confirm suppression and detect treatment failure.

## Prevention — A Layered Package
- Behavioural: condom promotion, peer-led Targeted Interventions for high-risk groups — 1,587 TI projects operational as of October 2025 (MoHFW).
- Harm reduction: needle-syringe exchange and Opioid Substitution Therapy for injecting drug users.
- Biomedical:“Test and Treat” — ART for every diagnosed person irrespective of CD4 count; Mission Sampark to trace and re-engage those lost to follow-up.
- Vertical transmission: dual HIV-syphilis test kits in antenatal care, maternal ART, and infant prophylaxis. Vertical transmission declined 63.67% between 2020 and 2024 (NACO, HIV Estimation 2025 Technical Report).
- Legal-social: the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 bars discrimination, mandates informed consent and confidentiality; Ombudsmen are appointed in 34 States/UTs to hear complaints.

## Conclusion

India’s HIV response is among the world’s most cost-effective public health programmes. New infections fell 49% from 1.25 lakh (2010) to 64,500 (2024), against a global reduction of 40%; AIDS-related deaths fell 81.4% from 1.73 lakh to 32,200 over the same period; and over 18 lakh people receive free ART, with 94% retention and 97% viral suppression (PIB, 30 November 2025). The unfinished agenda is the first “95” — undiagnosed infection — sustained by stigma, and coverage gaps among injecting drug users. Andhra Pradesh, historically carrying India’s second-highest

PLHIV burden and home to several districts in the 10,000-25,000 PLHIV band (NACO, HIV Estimation 2025), remains central to whether India meets SDG 3.3 — ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

- NACP-V (2021-26): Central Sector Scheme with an outlay of Rs. 15,471.94 crore, aligned to SDG 3.3.
- The generic-drug dimension: India supplies roughly 70% of global antiretroviral medicines, making domestic pharma capacity a global public good — a strong point for Paper-V’s science-society interface.
- UNAIDS 95-95-95: 95% of PLHIV diagnosed; 95% of those diagnosed on ART; 95% of those on ART virally suppressed.
- Programme evolution in one line: NACP-I (1992, awareness and blood safety) –> NACP-II (1999, decentralisation) – > NACP-III (2007, DAPCUs and high-risk group focus) –> NACP-IV (2012, extended 2017-21; Test and Treat, Mission Sampark, HIV Act 2017) –> NACP-V (2021-26, elimination of vertical transmission and stigma).
- Scale comparison: India’s 32,200 AIDS deaths in 2024 were about 5% of the global total of 6.3 lakh — useful for showing proportionality in an evaluative answer.

207. Discuss the transmission dynamics of respiratory tract infections in densely populated urban settings. Propose effective public health strategies for their prevention. (APPSC, 2025)

Respiratory tract infections — tuberculosis, influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 — share a transmission route that makes urban density their natural accelerant. India remains the world’s largest TB contributor at 25% of the global burden, with incidence at 187 per lakh in 2024, down 21% from 237 in 2015 (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025). With over a third of Indians now urban and slum households frequently exceeding four persons per room, the city is simultaneously the site of highest exposure and lowest household ventilation.

## Transmission Dynamics
- The particle continuum: WHO’s 2024 terminology replaced the rigid droplet/aerosol dichotomy with infectious respiratory particles (IRPs) on a size continuum. Large particles settle quickly and drive close-range transmission; fine particles remain suspended for hours and drive far-field, room-scale transmission. This single reframing explains why distancing alone failed indoors while ventilation succeeded.
- Density and contact rate: transmission scales with contact frequency, not merely population. A Mumbai local carriage or a Vijayawada bus stand generates in an hour the contact volume a village generates in a week — which is why urban outbreak curves rise steeply and early, as observed in Mumbai in 2020.
- Ventilation deficit: sealed, air-conditioned offices and windowless single-room tenements both trap IRPs. Indoor CO2 concentration is the practical proxy — readings above roughly 800 ppm indicate insufficient fresh-air exchange and elevated risk.
- Air pollution as a biological co-factor:PM2.5 impairs mucociliary clearance and alveolar macrophage function, converting exposure into infection more efficiently. This is not correlation alone but a documented mechanism, and it links Paper-V’s environment and health sections.
- Mobility and latency: TB’s long latent period means migration disperses infection across cities and back to source districts, so a city’s TB burden is partly imported and partly exported.
- Socio-economic amplifiers: undernutrition, diabetes (a major TB risk multiplier), delayed care-seeking among daily-wage earners, and out-of-pocket costs that push patients to interrupt treatment.

## Public Health Strategies — mapped to mechanism
- **Mechanism** — Targeted Strategy · Instrument / Evidence
- **Late detection** — Active case finding and molecular diagnostics · 100-Day TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (Dec 2024-Mar 2025); upfront NAAT; Ni-kshay portal
- **Treatment interruption** — Nutritional and social support · Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana — Rs. 1,000/month via DBT; Ni-kshay Mitra community adoption
- **Poor ventilation** — Building-code reform · Airborne infection control in health facilities; cross-ventilation norms; CO2-based monitoring
- **Air pollution** — Source-wise abatement · National Clean Air Programme — 130 non-attainment cities, revised target of up to 40% PM10 reduction by 2025-26 against 2017-18 baseline (MoEFCC)
- **Weak surveillance** — Real-time digital reporting · IHIP case-based reporting; sentinel influenza surveillance through ICMR-NIV network
- **Access gaps** — Bring care to the neighbourhood · Urban Ayushman Arogya Mandirs under Ayushman Bharat for screening and free drugs
- **Susceptibility** — Immunisation · Seasonal influenza vaccination for health workers and elderly; BCG; pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in the UIP

AP anchor:Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada are NCAP non-attainment cities, and AP’s coastal industrial corridor combines particulate exposure with dense worker housing — the exact overlap of pollution and crowding that this question is about. Andhra Pradesh’s district-level TB elimination drives under NTEP, delivered through urban Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, are the operative response.

## Conclusion

Respiratory infection in the Indian city is not primarily a shortage of medicine; it is a product of built form, air quality and economic vulnerability. TB mortality has fallen from 28 to 21 per lakh (2015-2024) and treatment coverage has reached 92% — real gains — yet India still records the world’s largest share of drug-resistant TB. The decisive interventions therefore sit outside the health department: municipal building codes that mandate ventilation, NCAP enforcement that cuts PM2.5, and social protection that lets a daily-wage patient finish six months of therapy. Convergent urban governance, not clinical expansion alone, is what will bend the curve.

- Drug resistance: India accounts for about 32% of global MDR/RR-TB cases (WHO, 2025) — the strongest single argument for early molecular diagnosis over empirical treatment.
- Ni-kshay Mitra: citizens, corporates and institutions “adopt” TB patients for nutritional support — a jan bhagidari model worth naming.
- NCAP finance critique: of funds released under NCAP and the XV Finance Commission grants, a large share has gone to road-dust management, while domestic fuel and industry — major PM2.5 sources — received a fraction. Useful for a critical evaluation.
- Why PM2.5 over PM10: NCAP’s targets are framed on PM10, but PM2.5 penetrates to the alveoli and drives respiratory morbidity — a widely made expert recommendation for NCAP 2.0.
- Vaccine pipeline: indigenous TB vaccine candidates VPM1002 and Immuvac (MIP) are in ICMR-supported Phase III trials — India’s most consequential TB science story.

208. (a) Explain different patterns of disease outbreak with examples. Differentiate between epidemic and endemic diseases. (b) What is the cause of Chikungunya? What are its preventive measures and treatment? Give a comparative note on symptomology of Chikungunya and Dengue. (APPSC, 2016)

Epidemiology describes disease along two independent axes: how much disease is present relative to the expected baseline (levels of occurrence), and how it propagates through a population over time (patterns of outbreak). Conflating the two leads to the wrong control response. Chikungunya and dengue — both Aedes-borne, both frequently co-circulating — illustrate why precise classification and precise clinical differentiation both matter operationally.

## (a) i. Levels of Disease Occurrence
- **Level** — Meaning · Example
- **Sporadic** — Irregular, scattered, no discernible pattern · Isolated rabies or tetanus case
- **Endemic** — Constant, predictable presence at baseline in a defined area · Malaria in the tribal districts of the Eastern Ghats; kala-azar in Bihar
- **Hyperendemic** — Persistently high transmission affecting all age groups · Malaria in parts of the North-East
- **Epidemic / Outbreak** — Occurrence clearly in excess of the expected baseline · Chikungunya resurgence, 2016
- **Pandemic** — Epidemic crossing international boundaries over several continents · COVID-19, 2020

## (a) ii. Patterns of Outbreak — read from the epidemic curve
- Common-source outbreak: all cases trace to one exposure source.

Point source — single brief exposure; a sharp, single-peaked curve within one incubation period. Example: a cholera outbreak after one contaminated water tanker. Continuous common source — exposure persists; the curve plateaus. Example: typhoid from a sustained cross-connection between water and sewage lines. Intermittent common source — irregular exposure; a jagged, multi-peaked curve.

- Propagated (progressive source) outbreak: person-to-person spread produces successive waves one incubation period apart, each larger than the last. Example: measles or COVID-19.
- Mixed outbreak: begins as common-source, then propagates. Example: a food-borne hepatitis A outbreak followed by secondary household transmission.

## (a) iii. Epidemic vs Endemic
- **Criterion** — Epidemic · Endemic
- **Definition** — Cases clearly above expected baseline · Cases persisting at a stable expected baseline
- **Onset** — Sudden, time-limited · Continuous, long-term
- **Population immunity** — Typically low or waned · Partial immunity maintained by exposure
- **Example** — COVID-19 (2020); Nipah in Kerala (2018, 2023) · Malaria in Odisha and the North-East; typhoid
- **Response mode** — Emergency — outbreak investigation, containment, mass campaigns (Pulse Polio, CoWIN) · Routine — sustained programme control (NCVBDC, SBM, Jal Jeevan Mission)
- **Financing** — Contingency and emergency funds · Recurrent programme budgets under NHM

## (b) i. Chikungunya — Cause and Transmission

Caused by the Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), an Alphavirus of family Togaviridae, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, which bite during daylight hours — a fact that undermines bed-net-only strategies. India recorded about 1.38 lakh clinically suspected chikungunya cases in 2022, up from 57,813 in 2018 (National Health Profile), with Karnataka, Gujarat and Telangana among the highest-reporting States.

## (b) ii. Prevention and Treatment
- Source reduction — weekly emptying of coolers, tanks, tyres and construction-site containers; community “Dry Day” observance under NCVBDC.
- Personal protection — repellents, full-sleeved clothing, mesh screens; daytime protection is essential given Aedes biting behaviour.
- Vector control — larvicides (temephos), Gambusia in ornamental water bodies, focal adulticiding during outbreaks.
- Treatment — no licensed antiviral; symptomatic management with fluids, rest and paracetamol. NSAIDs and aspirin must be withheld until dengue is excluded, because of bleeding risk in dengue — this single clinical caution is why the comparison below matters.
- Vaccines — Ixchiq (live-attenuated, FDA-approved November 2023) and Vimkunya / PXVX0317 (virus-like particle, approved February 2025); neither is in India’s national programme, and indigenous candidates are under development.

## (b) iii. Chikungunya vs Dengue — the differentiation table
- **Feature** — Chikungunya · Dengue
- **Virus / family** — CHIKV, Alphavirus (Togaviridae) · DENV 1-4, Flavivirus (Flaviviridae)
- **Fever pattern** — Abrupt, high-grade, 2-3 days · Biphasic “saddleback” — spike, remission, second spike
- **Cardinal symptom** — Severe, often incapacitating polyarthralgia of wrists, ankles and small joints; may persist for months · Retro-orbital pain and severe myalgia (“break-bone fever”)
- **Platelet count** — Normal or mildly reduced · Markedly reduced, especially in severe dengue
- **Bleeding tendency** — Rare · Prominent in Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever; plasma leakage in Dengue Shock Syndrome
- **Mortality** — Very low · Significant if severe forms are unrecognised
- **Sequelae** — Chronic arthritis lasting weeks to months · Post-viral fatigue; usually complete recovery

## Conclusion

Classifying an outbreak correctly is the first control measure: a point-source cholera cluster demands water-source investigation, whereas a propagated measles wave demands ring immunisation. India’s dengue programme demonstrates the value of this discipline — national cases fell from 2,89,235 with 485 deaths in 2023 to 2,33,519 with 297 deaths in 2024, and the case fatality rate has fallen from 3.3% in 1996 to 0.17% in 2023 (NCVBDC / MoHFW), driven by 887 Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals and 27 Apex Referral Laboratories offering free diagnosis. Andhra Pradesh reported 2,386 dengue cases in 2025, placing it among the higher-burden States and underlining that surveillance plus household source reduction, not curative capacity, is the decisive lever.

- Reading an epidemic curve: the interval between successive peaks in a propagated outbreak approximates the serial interval, and the distance from exposure to the first peak approximates the incubation period — a diagnostic tool available before any laboratory result.
- Dengue vaccine status:QDENGA (TAK-003) has received DCGI approval; ICMR-Panacea’s indigenous DengiAll is in Phase III — India’s first indigenous dengue vaccine candidate.
- Serotype intelligence: ICMR surveillance indicates DENV-2 predominance across southern States. Serotype matters because secondary infection with a different serotype raises the risk of severe dengue through antibody-dependent enhancement.
- Wolbachia:Wolbachia-infected Aedes releases suppress dengue transmission and have been piloted by ICMR-VCRC, Puducherry — a biological control worth naming.
- Legal instrument: several municipal corporations enforce anti-larval provisions under State Public Health Acts, issuing notices for domestic breeding — prevention backed by law, not merely appeal.

209. Present a note on the promotion of menstrual hygiene and its relevance in social development. (TGPSC, 2016)

Menstrual Hygiene Management is where public health, gender equity and infrastructure intersect. Its trajectory in India has been genuinely positive: the share of women aged 15-24 using a hygienic method of protection rose from 57.6% in NFHS-4 (2015-16) to 77.3% in NFHS-5 (2019-21), and sanitary napkin use from 42% to 64% (MoHFW, PIB). Yet the aggregate conceals extremes — from roughly 95% in Kerala to about 32% in Bihar — so the remaining challenge is one of equity rather than of national direction.

## The Institutional Architecture
- Menstrual Hygiene Scheme (2011), under NHM: subsidised sanitary napkins for rural adolescent girls aged 10-19, distributed by ASHAs who also hold monthly adolescent meetings. Procurement has been decentralised to States, letting them match local product preference and price.
- Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (2014): embeds MHM within adolescent health through peer educators and Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics, covering roughly 243 million adolescents. Its value is that it treats menstruation as one component of adolescent health rather than an isolated commodity problem.
- Pradhan Mantri Bharatiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana — “Suvidha” napkins: oxo-biodegradable pads at Rs. 1 per pad through over 9,000 Janaushadhi Kendras. Cumulative sales reached 96.30 crore pads as on 30 November 2025 (Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Rajya Sabha reply, 18 December 2025) — the single most citable affordability statistic available.
- Swachh Bharat Mission:National Guidelines on Menstrual Hygiene Management (Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation) cover awareness, girl-friendly school toilets and safe disposal.
- Mission Shakti / Beti Bachao Beti Padhao: menstrual hygiene awareness is an explicit objective.
- Higher education: the UGC advisory of 18 March 2025 directs all Higher Educational Institutions to provide sanitary facilities at accessible locations — extending MHM beyond school age.

## Andhra Pradesh — the “Swechha” Model

Launched in October 2021, Swechha supplies 10 branded sanitary napkins per month (120 a year) free to about 10 lakh girls in Classes 7-12 in government schools and junior colleges, at an outlay of roughly Rs. 32 crore. Three design features make it exam-worthy: - a woman teacher as nodal officer in every school, so supply is accompanied by counselling rather than silent distribution; - 6,417 incinerators installed under the Clean Andhra Pradesh (CLAP) programme, closing the disposal loop that most napkin schemes leave open; and - convergence with Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu, which rebuilt school toilets with running water — because a pad without a functioning toilet does not change behaviour.

## Why It Is a Social Development Question — the causal chain

Access to product + WASH facility + awareness –> Reduced infection and absenteeism –> Retention in school – > Delayed marriage, higher workforce participation –> Intergenerational gain

- Health: poor menstrual hygiene raises the risk of reproductive and urinary tract infections; cloth reused without sun-drying in unhygienic conditions is the principal pathway.
- Education: UN estimates indicate roughly 23% of Indian girls miss school during menstruation; each missed cycle compounds into learning loss and dropout risk.
- Economic: SHG-based manufacturing — Maharashtra’s Asmita Yojana — converts a consumption need into rural enterprise and local livelihood.
- Dignity and voice: normalising menstruation reduces the seclusion practices that restrict adolescent girls’ mobility, participation and confidence.
- SDG linkage: SDG 3 (health), 4 (education), 5 (gender equality), 6 (water and sanitation) and 12 (responsible consumption) all converge here.

## The Unfinished Agenda
- Stigma persists — taboos around cooking, worship and mobility survive even where product access has improved.
- WASH infrastructure lags product supply — a napkin without a private, water-supplied toilet and a disposal bin does not translate into safe practice.
- The waste problem is now the binding constraint. Conventional pads are 90% plastic by weight and are classified as solid waste under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, which require wrapping in the manufacturer-supplied pouch. Scaling menstrual cups, reusable cloth pads and biodegradable napkins is the sustainable path.
- Men and boys are largely outside the conversation — yet fathers, brothers, teachers and shopkeepers mediate both access and stigma.

## Conclusion

Menstrual hygiene has moved from an unmentionable subject to a costed line item in national and State budgets within a decade, and the NFHS-5 gains prove that supply-side intervention works. The next phase must shift from product distribution to system design — water in every school toilet, an incinerator or composting route for every napkin distributed, boys included in the curriculum, and reusable alternatives mainstreamed. Andhra Pradesh’s pairing of Swechha with CLAP incinerators and Nadu-Nedu toilets is precisely this integrated model. Treating menstruation as a routine biological event rather than a private burden is finally what converts a health scheme into social development.

- The disposal gap: India generates a very large annual volume of menstrual waste, overwhelmingly non-biodegradable. SWM Rules, 2016 place the onus on manufacturers to supply disposal pouches — an EPR-style provision that remains weakly enforced.
- Menstrual Hygiene Day — 28 May, chosen because menstruation averages 5 days and cycles average 28 days.
- Product hierarchy for a value-added line: menstrual cup (10-year life, near-zero waste) > reusable cloth pad > biodegradable napkin > conventional plastic pad.
- State innovations worth naming: Kerala’s She Pad and free menstrual-cup distribution; Maharashtra’s Asmita Yojana (SHG manufacture); Rajasthan’s Udaan; Odisha’s Khushi.
- The tax milestone: sanitary napkins were exempted from GST in July 2018, ending the “tampon tax” debate in India — a crisp, high-recall fact.
- Data caution: NFHS records product use, not safe practice. A girl may own a napkin and still lack the privacy or water to change it — worth stating to show analytical depth.

210. Trace the evolution of India’s National Biotechnology Development Strategy (NBDS) and discuss its key objectives. Critically evaluate its impact on the growth of the biotechnology sector in India. (APPSC, 2025)

India’s biotechnology policy has evolved from funding research to engineering an economy. The Department of Biotechnology’s National Biotechnology Development Strategy, first issued in 2007 and revised twice since, provided the scaffolding; the BioE3 Policy approved by the Union Cabinet on 24 August 2024 — India’s first dedicated national biotechnology policy — now supplies the industrial ambition. The measurable result is a bioeconomy that has grown from USD 10 billion in 2014 to USD 195.3 billion in 2025, contributing about 4.8% of GDP (India BioEconomy Report 2026, released by BIRAC, 19 March 2026).

## Evolution — draw as a horizontal timeline with four milestones
- **Phase** — Year · Defining Emphasis
- **NBDS-I** — 2007 · Capacity creation. Public investment in laboratories, human resources, university- industry linkage and translational research. The State as principal funder.
- **NBDS-II** — 2015-20 · Translation and globalisation. Public- private partnership, mission-mode programmes, commercialisation of laboratory output, global footprint. BIRAC (2012) became the delivery arm.
- **NBDS-III** — 2021-25 · Bioeconomy. Explicit alignment with Atmanirbhar Bharat; Unnati Biotech Missions; science-society interface; policy enablers and performance metrics.
- **BioE3 Policy** — 2024 · Biomanufacturing. Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment — targeting a USD 300 billion bioeconomy by 2030 and global leadership in high-performance biomanufacturing by 2047.

## Key Objectives
- Capacity building and infrastructure: regional biotech parks, upgraded laboratories, skilled human resources. Under BioE3 this extends to biofoundries, Bio-AI hubs and biomanufacturing hubs, shared facilities that individual startups could never finance alone.
- Translation and commercialisation: move technology from bench to market. Instruments include BIRAC’s BIG (Biotechnology Ignition Grant) and Bio-NEST, which has supported 73 bio-incubators offering over 10 lakh sq. ft. of incubation space — critical because biotech startups, unlike IT startups, need wet-lab access before they need capital.
- Self-reliance in affordable products: indigenous vaccines, diagnostics and bio-agricultural inputs. Covaxin and Gennova’s mRNA vaccine are the proof of concept.
- Strategic partnerships: academia-industry-global collaboration, including the DBT-ISRO memorandum (October 2024) on space biotechnology and space medicine.
- Science to society:Biotech-KISAN takes biotechnology to farmers through farmer-scientist hubs; North-East bioresource centres work on bamboo, silk and medicinal plants.
- Policy and regulatory enablement: BioE3 explicitly identifies regulatory reform requiring inter-ministerial coordination as a core tenet — an admission that regulation, not science, is the bottleneck.

## Critical Evaluation

## Achievements
- Scale: the bioeconomy grew 18% year-on-year in 2025 and has more than doubled since 2020, placing India among the world’s leading biotech destinations (IBER 2026).
- Startup ecosystem:over 11,800 biotech startups as of 2025. BIRAC has channelled more than Rs. 4,200 crore to over 15 lakh startups, entrepreneurs and innovators.
- Public health capability: India manufactures a very large share of the world’s vaccine doses; the COVID-19 response — Covaxin, Covishield production, and Gennova’s mRNA platform — validated the translational investment of NBDS-II.
- Financing depth: the Rs. 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund, with BIRAC entrusted a deep-tech biotech window, addresses the long-standing complaint that Indian biotech had grants but no patient risk capital.

## Limitations
- Regulatory fragmentation: the Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill lapsed, leaving GEAC, RCGM, FSSAI and DBT with overlapping mandates. The GM mustard (DMH-11) approval remained contested for over a decade — deterrent to private investment.
- Regional concentration: the Southern region accounts for about 45.4% (USD 75.2 billion) of the bioeconomy and the Eastern region only 5.8% (USD 9.7 billion) (PIB, September 2025). Growth is real but spatially narrow.
- Translation attrition: only a small fraction of DBT-supported innovations reach commercialisation, because clinical validation costs and timelines exceed grant horizons.
- Skill deficit: shortages in synthetic biology, bioinformatics and computational biology constrain the very frontier areas BioE3 targets.
- Measurement gap: BioE3 has ambitious targets but few published intermediate milestones, making independent progress assessment difficult.

AP anchor:Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam — the world’s first dedicated medical device manufacturing park — is the State’s flagship contribution to this ecosystem, providing shared scientific facilities of exactly the kind BioE3’s biofoundry model envisages. AP’s bulk drug park at Nakkapalli and its position within the high-performing Southern biotech cluster give the State direct standing in the national bioeconomy narrative.

## Conclusion

The NBDS did what a strategy document can do: it built institutions, created BIRAC, seeded incubators and normalised industry-academia collaboration. Twenty-fold growth in a decade is a genuine policy outcome, not an accident of global demand. But the constraints that now bind — a fragmented regulator, capital that thins out after seed stage, and a bioeconomy concentrated in three or four cities — are structural, not financial. Reaching USD 300 billion by 2030 will require a unified regulatory authority, State-level BioE3 cells replicating the DBT-Assam partnership (March 2025) across eastern and central India, and specialised talent pipelines. Strategy has taken India this far; institutional reform must take it the rest of the way.

- BioE3’s six thematic sectors: bio-based chemicals and enzymes; functional foods and smart proteins; precision biotherapeutics; climate-resilient agriculture; carbon capture and utilisation; and marine and space biotechnology.
- Bioeconomy composition (IBER 2026):BioIndustrial is the largest segment at USD 90.2 billion, ahead of biopharma — evidence that the sector’s centre of gravity has shifted from medicines to industrial biomanufacturing.
- Bio-AI hubs: the first DBT-BIRAC joint call (April 2025) drew 284 letters of intent, of which 16 were shortlisted, with roughly 40% of selected proposals industry- or startup-led — a concrete indicator that BioE3 is operational, not aspirational.
- Regulatory map to name precisely:RCGM (DBT) for research-stage approvals; GEAC (MoEFCC) for environmental release; FSSAI for GM food; NBA for access and benefit-sharing under the Biological Diversity Act.
- Long-horizon projection: India’s bioeconomy has been projected to reach USD 1.4-2.7 trillion by 2050 (PIB, 2025) — a striking figure for a concluding line.
- Institutional trivia with high recall value: India is the first country in the world to adopt a dedicated bioeconomy policy of this kind (BioE3, 2024).

## Introduction
The cost-effective control of viral diseases like **bird flu, polio and chikungunya** requires an **integrated approach** — combining **biological interventions** with attention to **social processes** — as India's public-health experience demonstrates.

- **Vaccination**: the **Pulse Polio Immunisation Programme** eradicated wild poliovirus in India (**polio-free, 2014**) — the power of immunisation.
- **Vector management**: for chikungunya/dengue, controlling *Aedes aegypti* through larvicides and biological predators (**Gambusia fish**).
- **Surveillance and diagnostics**: the **Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP)** enables rapid detection and containment; antiviral therapy where available.
- **Animal-health measures** (culling, poultry vaccination) for **bird flu** (avian influenza).

## Social processes in disease prevention
- **Addressing social determinants**: poverty, illiteracy, poor sanitation and misinformation drive spread.
- **Community engagement**: **ASHAs and health volunteers (NHM)** promote vaccination and hygiene.
- **Public awareness (IEC)**: media and school campaigns for behaviour change (source reduction, handwashing).
- **Trust and communication** to overcome vaccine hesitancy.

## Why integration is essential
- **Biological tools work only when socially accepted and delivered** — polio eradication succeeded through vaccination **plus** community mobilisation; a **One-Health, cost-effective** model links human, animal and environmental health.

## Conclusion
Controlling viral diseases cost-effectively demands **combining biological interventions (vaccination, vector control, surveillance) with social mobilisation** (awareness, community engagement, addressing determinants). India's polio success epitomises this integrated **One-Health** approach — the template for tackling emerging viral threats.

## Introduction
**HIV/AIDS** remains a major global and Indian public-health challenge; understanding the virus, its transmission, symptoms, diagnosis and prevention is central to control efforts.

## Structure and nature of HIV
- **HIV** (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) — a **retrovirus** with single-stranded RNA and the enzyme **reverse transcriptase** (converts RNA to DNA, integrating into the host genome); it attacks **CD4 T-cells**, weakening immunity. Two types: **HIV-1** (prevalent, virulent) and **HIV-2**.

## Modes of transmission
- **Unprotected sexual contact**; **contaminated blood/blood products**; **sharing infected needles**; and **mother-to-child** (pregnancy, childbirth, breastfeeding).

## Symptoms (staged)
- **Acute phase**: fever, sore throat, rash, lymph-node swelling (2–6 weeks);
- **Latent phase**: often asymptomatic for years while the virus multiplies;
- **AIDS stage**: severe immunosuppression, **opportunistic infections** (TB, candidiasis), chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and malignancies (Kaposi's sarcoma).

## Diagnostic tests
- **ELISA** (screening), **Western blot/confirmatory tests**, and **rapid antibody tests**; **PCR/viral load** for confirmation and monitoring; **CD4 count** for staging.

## Prevention and control
- **Safe sex/condoms, safe blood, needle safety, prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PPTCT)**, awareness, and **antiretroviral therapy (ART)** (treatment-as-prevention); India's **NACO/National AIDS Control Programme**.

## Conclusion
HIV, a retrovirus that destroys immunity, spreads through blood, sex and mother-to-child routes. Though incurable, it is **preventable and manageable** through **awareness, safe practices, early diagnosis and lifelong ART** — India's NACO-led response has significantly curbed the epidemic toward the goal of ending AIDS by 2030.

## Introduction
Understanding **patterns of disease outbreaks** and specific vector-borne diseases like **chikungunya and dengue** is essential for effective surveillance and public-health response.

## (a) Patterns of disease outbreak; epidemic vs endemic
- **Patterns**:
  - **Sporadic**: irregular, scattered cases (a single rabies case);
  - **Endemic**: constant presence in a region (malaria in the Northeast);
  - **Epidemic**: sudden rise above expected levels (a chikungunya outbreak);
  - **Pandemic**: worldwide spread (COVID-19).
- **Epidemic vs endemic**: **endemic** = baseline, continuous presence; **epidemic** = a sharp, unexpected increase over the baseline.
- **Influencing factors**: host immunity, climate, population density, migration and sanitation; controlled via **surveillance (IDSP), vaccination, vector control and awareness**.

## (b) Chikungunya — cause, prevention, treatment; vs dengue
- **Cause**: the **chikungunya virus (an alphavirus)**, transmitted by **Aedes aegypti/albopictus** mosquitoes.
- **Prevention**: **Aedes vector control** (source reduction, larvicides, avoiding stagnant water), personal protection; no specific vaccine widely used.
- **Treatment**: **symptomatic** (rest, fluids, paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin until dengue excluded).
- **Chikungunya vs dengue** (both Aedes-borne): chikungunya causes **severe, persistent joint pain (arthralgia)** and fever; **dengue** causes high fever, severe body/retro-orbital pain, rash and, critically, **bleeding/plasma leakage (dengue haemorrhagic fever)** with low platelets — dengue is potentially more life-threatening.

## Conclusion
Distinguishing **sporadic, endemic, epidemic and pandemic** patterns guides response, while chikungunya and dengue — both **Aedes-borne** — require **vector control and symptomatic care**. Strong surveillance (IDSP), community source-reduction and awareness are key to preventing and managing these recurrent outbreaks.

Q142:
## Introduction

The Bentham and Hooker system is the most influential natural system of classifying seed plants, set out by George Bentham and Sir Joseph Dalton Hooker in Genera Plantarum (3 volumes, 1862–1883), prepared at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. It classified about 97,205 species under 7,569 genera in 202 families (orders), based on direct examination of actual herbarium specimens rather than published descriptions — a methodological rigour that explains its unusual durability. Crucially, it was framed in the same decade as Darwin’s Origin of Species (1859) but consciously declined to adopt evolutionary descent as its organising principle.

## Structure of the System
- Phanerogams (seed plants) were divided into three classes: Dicotyledons, Gymnospermae and Monocotyledons, in that sequence.
- Dicotyledons — three sub-classes:

Polypetalae (free petals) — 3 series: Thalamiflorae, Disciflorae, Calyciflorae, distinguished by the position and development of the thalamus/disc.

Gamopetalae (fused petals) — 3 series: Inferae, Heteromerae, Bicarpellatae, based on ovary position and carpel number.

Monochlamydeae (single or absent perianth) — 8 series, including Curvembryeae, Multiovulatae, Unisexuales.

- Monocotyledons — 7 series:Microspermae, Epigynae, Coronarieae, Calycinae, Nudiflorae, Apocarpae, Glumaceae — ordered by ovary position, perianth character and seed size. Ranunculaceae was placed first and Gramineae (Poaceae) last.
- Ordines anomali: a residual group for families whose position the authors could not settle — an explicit admission of uncertainty that modern taxonomists respect as intellectual honesty.

## Demerits
- Non-phylogenetic foundation. Written after Darwin but not upon him, the system arranges plants by overall resemblance rather than common ancestry. So what: it can tell you what a plant looks like but not what it descended from — the central question of modern systematics.
- Misplacement of Gymnosperms. Gymnosperms were inserted between Dicots and Monocots, implying they are an intermediate grade. In fact gymnosperms are a distinct lineage that diverged long before the angiosperms, so the placement is not merely inconvenient — it is evolutionarily false.
- The artificiality of Monochlamydeae. This sub-class groups plants merely by reduced or absent perianth. But perianth reduction is a convergent adaptation to wind pollination, arrived at independently by unrelated lineages — so Casuarina, Piperaceae and Amaranthaceae are shelved together despite no close kinship. This is the classic case of homoplasy defeating morphology-only classification.
- Over-reliance on gross morphology. Anatomy, embryology, palynology, cytology and chemistry were not used. Environmental convergence therefore repeatedly misleads the key.
- Fragmentation and inconsistency. Weighting particular floral traits split naturally allied families and, conversely, kept some over-large families intact — producing an uneven treatment across the work.

## Conclusion

Bentham and Hooker produced the most usable classification of its era, and that utility has outlived its theory: Indian herbaria, the Botanical Survey of India’s regional centres and most undergraduate practical courses still arrange specimens on this scheme, because its diagnostic keys work in the field with nothing but a hand lens. But as an account of how plants are related, it has been decisively superseded by the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group (APG IV, 2016) system built on chloroplast and nuclear DNA sequence data. The correct verdict is therefore split — obsolete as science, indispensable as a tool.

## Value addition

Merits worth citing for balance:

- Specimen-based rigour: built from actual plants examined at Kew, not from secondary literature — unusually high reliability for the period.
- Practical keys: clear diagnostic characters make field identification fast; still the working arrangement in most Indian herbaria.
- Intellectual honesty:Ordines anomali deliberately left doubtful families unforced.
- Enduring family circumscriptions: many of its family limits survive largely intact in APG IV.

Institutional and AP anchors:

- Botanical Survey of India (BSI, est. 1890, MoEFCC) maintains ~3 million herbarium specimens across 13 herbaria.
- BSI Deccan Regional Centre, Hyderabad (BSID, est. 2006) holds the mandate for floristic survey of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Odisha, covering the Eastern Ghats and coastal AP, with a dedicated mangrove herbarium section.
- Indian Virtual Herbarium (IVH), launched 1 July 2022 by MoEFCC — India’s largest digital flora database, allowing state-wise extraction of records, so an AP aspirant can retrieve the state’s checklist directly.
- Sequence of classification systems to memorise: Artificial (Linnaeus, 1753 — sexual system) –> Natural (Bentham & Hooker, 1883) –> Phylogenetic (Engler & Prantl, 1887–1915; Hutchinson, 1926) –> Molecular (APG I–IV, 1998–2016).
Q143:
## Introduction

Pharmacogenomics is the study of how an individual’s genetic constitution governs their response to drugs — efficacy, dose requirement and adverse reaction risk. It is the operational core of precision medicine, replacing the “one dose fits all” model with genotype-guided prescription. Its practical importance for India is direct: adverse drug reactions are a substantial and largely preventable cause of hospitalisation, and the Indian population’s genetic variation is poorly represented in global databases — a gap that GenomeIndia (DBT), completed in January 2025 with 10,074 whole genomes, was specifically designed to close.

## The Mechanism of Pharmacogenomics
- Individual variation arises mainly from Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes coding for drug-metabolising enzymes, transporters and receptors — above all the Cytochrome P450 family.
- The causal chain is: SNP –> altered enzyme activity –> “poor” or “ultra-rapid” metaboliser phenotype –> standard dose becomes either toxic or ineffective.
- Indian-relevant examples:CYP2C9/VKORC1 variants require reduced warfarin dosing to avoid bleeding; NUDT15/TPMT variants, notably frequent in South Asians, cause severe myelosuppression with standard thiopurine doses used in childhood leukaemia; G6PD deficiency governs safe primaquine use — directly relevant to India’s malaria elimination programme under NVBDCP/NCVBDC; **HLA-B*15:02** predicts severe skin reactions to carbamazepine.

## Applications of Biotechnology in Human Health
- Molecular diagnostics. Nucleic-acid amplification has moved diagnosis from days to hours. TrueNat, an indigenous chip-based RT-PCR platform, is ICMR- and WHO-endorsed for TB and rifampicin-resistance detection at primary health centre level — decentralising a test that previously required a district laboratory.
- Therapeutics — recombinant and cellular. Recombinant human insulin (E. coli-expressed, 1982) removed dependence on bovine/porcine pancreas and its immunogenicity. Gene therapy now corrects the defect itself: CRISPR-Cas9 based approaches for sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia; NexCAR19 (CDSCO, October 2023) as India’s first indigenous CAR-T therapy; and India’s first gene therapy trial for Haemophilia A at CMC Vellore.
- Vaccines. Recombinant DNA technology gave the world’s first genetically engineered vaccine (Hepatitis B). India then produced ZyCoV-D — the world’s first approved DNA vaccine (2021) — and Covaxin, an indigenous inactivated vaccine developed with ICMR-NIV.
- Data, AI and bioinformatics. The Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC), Faridabad now hosts GenomeIndia data under the BIOTECH-PRIDE guidelines and FeED protocol, enabling variant discovery and adverse-reaction prediction at population scale.

## Conclusion

Pharmacogenomics converts genomics from a research curiosity into bedside decision-making. For India the argument is one of equity as much as efficacy: dosing algorithms derived from European cohorts systematically misfit Indian patients, so a national reference genome is not duplication but a precondition of safe prescribing. With GenomeIndia complete, IBDC operational and cell and gene therapy named a priority sector under the BioE3 Policy (2024), the binding constraint has shifted from science to delivery — integrating genotype-guided prescribing into Ayushman Bharat health facilities and building the clinical genetics workforce to interpret the results.

## Value addition
- Precision medicine tailors prevention and treatment to individual variability in genes, environment and lifestyle — distinct from personalised medicine, which is often used loosely for any individualised care.
- GenomeIndia (DBT, completed January 2025): 10,074 whole genomes; 20,000-sample biobank at CBR-IISc Bengaluru; over 20 institutions including CSIR-CCMB Hyderabad; findings published in Nature Genetics.
- IndiGen (CSIR, 2019): 1,029 whole genomes — the pilot that preceded GenomeIndia.
- National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023): screening target of 7 crore people in tribal-majority districts by 2025-26, elimination by 2047 — India’s largest population-genetics-driven public health programme, and directly relevant to tribal districts of Andhra Pradesh.
- AP anchor: the Kalam Institute of Health Technology at AMTZ Visakhapatnam is a DBT-supported centre for health-technology assessment and medical device innovation — the state’s principal node in this ecosystem.
- Caution to cite for balance: genomic data raise privacy, insurance discrimination and consent concerns; the DPDP Act, 2023 now governs personal data but genomic data is not separately classified as a special category.
Q144:
## Introduction

Genetic engineering is the deliberate, targeted alteration of an organism’s DNA; stem cells are undifferentiated cells capable of self-renewal and of differentiating into specialised cell types. Regenerative medicine sits at their intersection — and the intersection matters because stem cells supply the raw material while genetic engineering supplies the control. Without gene-level direction, a stem cell’s fate is largely a matter of chance; with it, a patient’s own skin cell can be reprogrammed, corrected and redirected into the exact tissue that has failed. The Nobel Prizes for iPSC reprogramming (Yamanaka, 2012) and CRISPR-Cas9 (Doudna and Charpentier, 2020) mark the two enabling breakthroughs.

## Reprogramming — Manufacturing Pluripotency on Demand
- Introducing the four Yamanaka factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) converts an adult somatic cell into an induced Pluripotent Stem Cell (iPSC). Why decisive: it dissolves the ethical objection to destroying embryos and, because the cells are the patient’s own, it removes immune rejection — the two barriers that stalled the field for a decade.

## Editing — Correcting the Defect Before Transplantation
- CRISPR-Cas9 allows the disease-causing mutation to be repaired in the stem cell itself, so the transplanted tissue is healthy from the outset. Illustration: editing the BCL11A enhancer in a patient’s haematopoietic stem cells reactivates foetal haemoglobin, the mechanism underlying approved sickle-cell and beta-thalassaemia therapies; India’s CSIR-IGIB is developing an indigenous equivalent.
- CAR-T therapy applies the same logic to immune cells: NexCAR19 (CDSCO-approved, October 2023) from IIT Bombay–Tata Memorial genetically arms a patient’s own T-cells against CD19-positive blood cancers at roughly a tenth of Western prices.

## Differentiation and Disease Modelling
- Engineered iPSCs can be driven into dopaminergic neurons (Parkinson’s), cardiomyocytes (post-infarction repair) and pancreatic beta cells (Type 1 diabetes). So what: the same lines also serve as human disease models and drug-screening platforms, cutting reliance on animal models that poorly predict human toxicity.

## Tissue Engineering and Organ Regeneration
- Combining engineered stem cells with biomaterial scaffolds and 3D bioprinting moves the field from cell suspension to structured tissue — cartilage, skin, corneal epithelium — with the long-term goal of addressing India’s severe organ shortage.

## The Reality Check — Where India Actually Stands
- Under the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research (NGSCR), ICMR–DBT, 2017, the only approved clinical indication remains Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation for haematological disorders; everything else is investigational.
- The National Apex Committee for Stem Cell Research and Therapy (NAC-SCRT) was dissolved in March 2024, leaving oversight resting on institutional committees (IC-SCR) and CDSCO — a thinning of the two-tier structure at precisely the moment cell therapies are scaling.
- Unproven stem-cell clinics advertising cures for autism, cerebral palsy and spinal injury remain a live consumer-protection and ethics problem.

## Conclusion

Genetic engineering has transformed stem cells from an unpredictable biological resource into a programmable therapeutic platform, and India has already crossed from importer to originator with NexCAR19 and indigenous gene-therapy trials. But the field’s Indian trajectory now depends less on laboratory capability than on three governance choices: restoring a credible national oversight tier after the dissolution of NAC-SCRT; enforcing action against unproven-therapy clinics that trade on desperate patients; and using the precision biotherapeutics theme of the BioE3 Policy (2024) to bring cell and gene therapy costs within reach of public insurance. Regenerative medicine will be judged not by what it can do, but by whom it reaches.

## Value addition

Types of stem cells:

- Embryonic (ESCs): pluripotent, from a 5-day blastocyst; maximum potency but ethically contested and immunologically foreign.
- Adult / somatic: multipotent; bone marrow, adipose tissue, blood; the basis of routine HSCT.
- Induced Pluripotent (iPSCs): reprogrammed somatic cells; patient-matched and ethically uncontroversial — the workhorse of current research.
- Mesenchymal (MSCs): multipotent stromal cells used for bone, cartilage and immunomodulation.

Indian ecosystem:

- DBT-inStem, Bengaluru (Institute for Stem Cell Science and Regenerative Medicine); NCCS Pune; Centre for Stem Cell Research (CSCR), CMC Vellore — site of India’s first gene-therapy trial for Haemophilia A.
- CSIR-CCMB Hyderabad and CSIR-IGIB Delhi for genome editing; BIRAC for translation funding.
- Regulatory chain: NGSCR-2017 (ICMR–DBT) | IC-SCR at institutional level | New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 bringing cell and gene therapy products under CDSCO/DCGI as new drugs.
- AP anchor:AMTZ, Visakhapatnam hosts a Bio Valley Incubation Council funded by DBT, and the state has announced a 500-acre MedTech Zone 2.0 — positioning coastal AP for advanced biotherapeutics manufacturing.
- Ethical touchstone: the 14-day rule on in-vitro culture of human embryos, adopted in NGSCR-2017 in line with international practice.
Q145:
## Introduction

Developing a genetically modified crop requires moving a defined DNA sequence across the cell wall, into the nucleus, and integrating it stably so that it is expressed and inherited. This is gene transfer or plant transformation, and it is the technical bottleneck of crop biotechnology: identifying a useful gene is comparatively easy, delivering it into a regenerable plant cell is not. Methods are classified by whether a biological vector carries the DNA or whether it is introduced directly by physical or chemical means — a distinction that also determines which crops each method suits.

## Category Method Principle Best suited to Example

Vector-mediated (indirect)

Agrobacterium tumefaciens

T-DNA of disarmed Ti plasmid integrates into host genome

Dicots Bt cotton (cry1Ac)

Vector-mediated Plant viral vectors Viral genome carries transgene

Transient expression Molecular farming

Direct — physical Biolistics / gene gun Gold or tungsten microparticles coated with DNA fired at high velocity

Monocots, chloroplasts Golden Rice

Direct — physical Electroporation Electric pulses transiently permeabilise membranes

Protoplasts Rice, maize research

Direct — physical Microinjection DNA injected into nucleus with a fine needle

Single cells, high precision

Research scale

Direct — chemical PEG-mediated uptake Polyethylene glycol destabilises membrane

Protoplast systems Somatic hybrids

Direct — other Silicon carbide whiskers; pollen-tube pathway

Abrasion or natural pollen channel

Recalcitrant species Cotton (China)

1. Agrobacterium-mediated transfer — nature’s own genetic engineer.Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a soil bacterium that causes crown gall disease by transferring a segment of its tumour-inducing (Ti) plasmid, the T-DNA, into the host plant genome, where it directs synthesis of opines the bacterium consumes. Scientists “disarm” the plasmid by deleting the tumour-inducing genes and substituting the gene of interest along with a promoter and selectable marker; the plasmid’s vir (virulence) genes then drive transfer as usual. This is the most widely used method because it produces low-copy, stable, single-site integration with fewer rearrangements. It works best in dicots — cotton, tomato, soybean, brinjal — which is why Bt cotton, carrying cry1Ac from Bacillus thuringiensis, was produced this way. 2. Biolistics (the gene gun) — brute force for the monocots. Cereals were long recalcitrant to Agrobacterium, so DNA-coated gold or tungsten microprojectiles are accelerated by helium pressure directly through the cell wall. It is genotype-independent and is the only practical route into chloroplast (plastid) transformation, which is significant because plastids are maternally inherited in most crops and therefore transgenes do not escape via pollen — an elegant biosafety advantage. Golden Rice, engineered for beta-carotene to address vitamin A deficiency, was developed using this route. 3. Direct physical and chemical methods for protoplasts. Once the cell wall is enzymatically removed to give a protoplast, DNA can be introduced by electroporation (brief high-voltage pulses opening transient membrane pores), PEG-mediated uptake (polyethylene glycol destabilising the membrane), liposome fusion, or microinjection into the nucleus. These offer precision but suffer from low efficiency and, critically, the difficulty of regenerating whole plants from protoplasts — so they remain mainly research tools. Silicon carbide whisker vortexing and the pollen-tube pathway are simpler low-cost alternatives for recalcitrant species.

4. The precision era — delivering editors rather than transgenes. The decisive shift since 2017 is that CRISPR-Cas9 can be delivered as a ribonucleoprotein complex (Cas9 protein pre-loaded with guide RNA) or as a transiently expressed construct that is segregated out in subsequent generations. The edited plant then carries no foreign DNA, only an altered version of its own gene. This is what produced DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1, the world’s first genome-edited rice varieties, released by ICAR in May 2025 — reported to deliver a 19% yield gain, about 20% lower greenhouse gas emissions and a saving of 7,500 million cubic metres of irrigation water. 5. Selection, regeneration and confirmation — the step candidates forget. Transformation efficiency is low, so transformed cells must be identified using a selectable marker (e.g. nptII conferring kanamycin resistance) or a reporter gene (GUS, GFP). Selected cells are regenerated into whole plants through tissue culture on hormone-balanced media, and integration is confirmed by PCR, Southern blotting and sequencing. Multiple independent “events” are then field-evaluated, and only the best-performing event proceeds — commercial Bt cotton in India traces to a small number of such events. Infographic 2 — The pipeline flowchart (draw as a vertical chain):

Gene identification --> Vector construction --> Transfer into plant cell         --> Marker-based selection --> Tissue-culture regeneration         --> Molecular confirmation (PCR/Southern) --> Event selection         --> Biosafety evaluation --> Regulatory approval --> Release

REGULATORY LADDER (India): IBSC (institution) --> RCGM (DBT) --> GEAC (MoEF&CC) --> SBCC/DLC (State/District) [SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants exempted from Rules 7-11: MoEFCC OM, March 2022]

Andhra Pradesh anchor: ANGRAU’s Regional Agricultural Research Station, Maruteru (West Godavari) bred MTU 1010 (Cotton Dora Sannalu) and its Bapatla station bred BPT 5204 (Samba Mahsuri) — the two parent varieties on which India’s genome-edited rice was built (ICAR, May 2025), with both new varieties notified for Zone VII covering Andhra Pradesh. Bt cotton is cultivated extensively in Guntur, Kurnool and Prakasam, making AP a live field laboratory for both the transgenic and the genome-edited pathway.

## Conclusion

Gene transfer methods form a spectrum from the biologically mediated to the physically forced, and the choice is dictated by the target crop’s tissue culture behaviour rather than by any inherent superiority — Agrobacterium for dicots, biolistics for cereals and plastids, protoplast methods for research precision. The larger movement, however, is away from insertion altogether: genome editing delivers a molecular scissor rather than a permanent foreign gene, which is why India could move from laboratory to notified variety in a fraction of the time GM crops required. Technique, regulation and public acceptability are therefore converging — and India’s rice programme is the first global demonstration of that convergence.

## Value addition
- Cisgenesis and intragenesis: transferring genes from a sexually compatible relative using the plant’s own regulatory elements. This avoids “linkage drag” of conventional breeding while producing a plant genetically equivalent to one that could have arisen naturally — a useful middle category between transgenesis and genome editing.
- Chloroplast transformation deserves a separate mention: high transgene expression (thousands of plastid copies per cell) and maternal inheritance preventing pollen-mediated gene flow make it a biosafety-preferred route.
- Marker-free strategies — co-transformation followed by segregation, or site-specific recombinase systems (Cre-lox) — address the objection that antibiotic-resistance markers may transfer to gut microflora.
- Terminator/GURT technology (Genetic Use Restriction Technology) rendering harvested seed sterile is not permitted in India, and the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001 expressly safeguards the farmer’s right to save, use, sow, exchange and sell farm produce including seed.
- Regulatory instruments to name: Rules, 1989 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; MoEFCC Office Memorandum, March 2022 exempting SDN-1/SDN-2 plants; DBT Guidelines for Safety Assessment of Genome Edited Plants, May 2022; Rs. 500 crore for genome editing in agricultural crops, Union Budget 2023-24, with ICAR extending the programme to oilseeds and pulses.
Q146:
## Introduction

Genetic engineering is the deliberate, directed alteration of an organism’s genome using recombinant DNA technology — cutting DNA with restriction endonucleases, joining fragments with DNA ligase, carrying them into a host on a vector (plasmid, bacteriophage or Ti plasmid), and selecting transformed cells. Its application to agriculture produces genetically modified food, which has generated one of the most sustained science-policy controversies in India. The debate is not merely about safety; it is simultaneously about ecology, farmer autonomy and who has the authority to decide.

## Axis The case FOR GM food The case AGAINST GM food

Health/safety No verified case of harm in two decades of cultivation; FSSAI safety assessment applies

Absence of long-term epidemiological data in Indian dietary conditions; allergenicity risk

Ecology Reduced pesticide spraying protects soil, water, applicators

Gene flow to wild relatives; resistant pests; effect on non-target organisms

Socio-economic Higher net income; reduced crop loss; import substitution in edible oils

Seed-market concentration; recurring seed cost; erosion of landraces

Governance GEAC-led scientific appraisal under a statutory framework

Regulatory capture, thin public consultation, conflict of interest

1. The case for GM food — yield, inputs and nutrition.Bt cotton remains the proof of concept in India: approved by GEAC in 2002, it now covers over 90% of India’s cotton area, delivered a substantial reduction in insecticide sprays against bollworm, and made India one of the world’s largest cotton producers. GM mustard DMH-11, developed by the Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants at Delhi University using the barnase-barstar system to enable hybridisation in a self-pollinating crop, is defended on the ground that India imports a majority of its edible oil requirement and that hybrid vigour is otherwise unobtainable in mustard. Golden Rice exemplifies the nutrition argument — biofortification reaches deficiencies that redistribution of ordinary grain cannot. 2. The case against — biosafety and irreversibility. The health objection is not that harm has been demonstrated but that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, particularly for a food crop consumed daily over a lifetime. The ecological objection has partly been vindicated: pink bollworm evolved resistance to Bt cotton in India, confirming that single-toxin monocultures generate selection pressure and that refuge compliance is weak. Herbicide-tolerant crops raise a distinct concern — they may increase, not decrease, chemical use and accelerate herbicide-resistant weeds. Gene flow to wild and weedy relatives is irreversible in a way that chemical pollution is not, which is why the precautionary principle is invoked. 3. The socio-economic and ethical axis. Critics argue that proprietary seed shifts the farmer from a saver of seed to an annual purchaser, concentrating market power. India’s statutory answer is distinctive: the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001 expressly preserves the farmer’s right to save, sow, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, and India has not permitted Genetic Use Restriction Technology. Consumer-choice objections centre on labelling — under an FSSAI order of 21 August 2020, imports of 24 listed food crops require a non-GM origin/GM-free certificate, with a clarified tolerance of 1% for adventitious presence (February 2021), while comprehensive domestic GM food labelling regulations remain at draft stage. 4. The governance axis — where the Indian debate now sits. GM food crops have repeatedly stalled not on science but on process. Bt brinjal received GEAC clearance in 2009 but was placed under an indefinite moratorium in 2010 after public consultations. The Technical Expert Committee appointed by the Supreme Court recommended a moratorium on field trials of GM food crops in 2013. Most decisively, in Gene Campaign v. Union of India (23 July 2024) the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict on DMH-11 — Justice B.V. Nagarathna quashing the approval for procedural failures including the absence of an ICMR representative at the relevant GEAC meeting, Justice Sanjay Karol upholding it — but the Bench unanimously directed the Union to formulate a National Policy on GM crops in consultation with States, farmers and experts, and directed the Environment Ministry to conduct a national consultation.

That direction, and not the science, is now the operative question.

5. The frontier has shifted to genome editing. By an Office Memorandum of March 2022 the MoEFCC exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants free of foreign DNA from Rules 7-11 of the Rules, 1989, followed by DBT’s safety assessment guidelines (May 2022). ICAR’s position is that such edits are indistinguishable from spontaneous or induced mutations and therefore no riskier than mutation breeding practised safely for decades; civil society counters that exemption by executive memorandum bypasses statutory biosafety assessment. This is precisely the debate the released genome-edited rice varieties of May 2025 have made concrete. Infographic 2 — India’s regulatory ladder (draw as a vertical flow):

IBSC (institution-level)  -->  RCGM (DBT: research & confined trials)    -->  GEAC (MoEF&CC: environmental release)  -->  SBCC / DLC (State & District)    -->  FSSAI (food safety of GM food)   -->  Ministerial ratification [Statutory base: Rules, 1989 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986]

Andhra Pradesh anchor: Bt cotton is grown extensively in Guntur, Kurnool and Prakasam, so the resistance and seed-cost debates are lived realities for AP farmers rather than abstractions. On the other side of the ledger, ANGRAU-bred BPT 5204 (Bapatla) and MTU 1010 (Maruteru) supplied the genetic base for India’s genome-edited rice (ICAR, May 2025), and AP is a major non-Basmati rice exporting state — giving the state a direct commercial stake in how India’s GM/GE regulatory reputation is perceived in importing markets.

## Conclusion

Genetic engineering is a technique of extraordinary precision applied to a domain of extraordinary uncertainty, which is why the debate on GM food has proved irreducible to laboratory data alone. India’s twenty-three-year experience is instructive: a transgenic fibre crop was accepted with little resistance, while every transgenic food crop has been stalled — indicating that the decisive variable is public trust rather than biosafety evidence. The Supreme Court’s 2024 direction to frame a National Policy on GM crops through genuine stakeholder consultation offers the correct route out: transparent, participatory, case-by-case appraisal with independent long-term monitoring. Technology can be regulated; legitimacy has to be earned.

## Value addition
- GEAC in one box: functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change; constituted under the Rules, 1989 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; appraises large-scale use of hazardous micro-organisms and recombinants and all proposals for environmental release of genetically engineered organisms including field trials; empowered to take punitive action under the Environment (Protection) Act.
- International instruments: the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000, in force 2003) governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms and enshrines the precautionary approach and Advance Informed Agreement; the Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol addresses liability and redress. India is a party to both.
- Legislative gap: the Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill, 2013 proposed a single independent regulator but lapsed with the dissolution of the 15th Lok Sabha in 2014 — India still has no standalone GM statute, all regulation flowing from subordinate rules under an environmental law.
- Chronology for quick recall: 2002 Bt cotton approved; 2009 Bt brinjal cleared by GEAC; 2010 moratorium imposed; 2013 Supreme Court TEC recommends moratorium on GM food crop trials; Oct 2022 GEAC recommends environmental release of DMH-11; Mar 2022 SDN-1/2 exemption; Jul 2024 Supreme Court split verdict and direction for a National GM Policy; May 2025 world’s first genome-edited rice varieties released.
- Distinction worth one clean line:GM crops introduce DNA from another species; genome-edited (GE) crops alter the plant’s own genes and, in SDN-1 and SDN-2 categories, retain no foreign DNA — which is the legal basis for their differential treatment.

## Introduction

Modern biology advances by proxy and by regeneration. A model organism is a non-human species studied intensively so that findings can be extrapolated to other organisms including humans, exploiting the deep evolutionary conservation of core cellular machinery. Stem cell research and cloning extend the same logic forward — from understanding life to rebuilding it. Together they span the two halves of biotechnology’s promise: the model organism tells us how a gene works; stem cells and cloning let us act on that knowledge in medicine, agriculture and conservation.

## (a) Model Organisms — Meaning and Characteristics

A model organism is a species selected for laboratory study because its biology is representative, its handling is tractable, and knowledge gained from it transfers to species that cannot themselves be experimented upon. Disease pathways for cancer, cystic fibrosis and Alzheimer’s have transgenic mouse models; zebrafish are the standard for cardiac and neural developmental biology; and Arabidopsis underpins nearly all crop gene-function work — the genes edited to produce DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) were understood first through such model systems. In India, CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB), Hyderabad maintains major zebrafish and mouse model facilities, and DBT-supported institutions sustain national model-organism resources.

## (b) Stem Cell Research and the Significance of Cloning

TOTIPOTENT   (zygote, early blastomeres)  -->  entire organism + placenta PLURIPOTENT  (ESCs, iPSCs)                -->  all three germ layers MULTIPOTENT  (haematopoietic, mesenchymal)-->  a related family of cell types UNIPOTENT    (progenitor cells)           -->  a single cell type

Types of stem cells.Embryonic stem cells (ESCs), drawn from the blastocyst, are pluripotent but ethically contested because deriving them destroys an embryo. Adult or somatic stem cells in bone marrow, adipose tissue and cord blood are multipotent and ethically uncontroversial. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) — adult cells reprogrammed to a pluripotent state, an advance recognised by the 2012 Nobel Prize — resolve both the ethical objection and the immune-rejection problem, since they can be made from the patient’s own cells.
