Applications across fields.

- Medicine:haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for leukaemia, lymphoma and thalassaemia is the established therapy. Beyond it, India has produced NexCAR19, a CAR-T cell therapy from IIT Bombay, Tata Memorial Centre and ImmunoACT with DBT-BIRAC support, granted CDSCO market authorisation in 2023, and BIRSA 101, the CRISPR-based sickle cell therapy launched in November 2025 (PIB) which edits the patient’s own blood stem cells before reinfusion — cell therapy and gene therapy converging.
- Agriculture and livestock: cloning propagates elite animals. ICAR-National Dairy Research Institute, Karnal produced “Garima”, a cloned buffalo calf, in 2009 using a hand-guided cloning technique, demonstrating indigenous capability in livestock cloning for genetic conservation of high-yielding germplasm.
- Conservation: cloning of endangered species — the black-footed ferret and the gaur are the standard examples — offers a route to rescue genetic diversity where breeding populations have collapsed.
- Drug development and toxicology: patient-derived iPSCs provide human-relevant screening platforms, reducing dependence on animal testing.

India’s regulatory position — the point that separates a strong answer. Under the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research (ICMR-DBT, 2017), haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for haematological disorders is currently the only approved indication; all other stem cell interventions are investigational and may be conducted only as approved clinical trials. Oversight runs through the Institutional Committee for Stem Cell Research (IC-SCR) at institution level and the National Apex Committee for Stem Cell Research and Therapy (NAC-SCRT) under the Department of Health Research at national level, with clinical trials additionally regulated by CDSCO. Human reproductive cloning is prohibited, as is germline gene therapy under the National Guidelines for Gene Therapy Product Development and Clinical Trials (ICMR-DBT, 2019). This framework exists precisely because unproven stem cell “therapies” were being commercially marketed in the mid-2000s.

Andhra Pradesh anchor:Sri Venkateswara Institute of Medical Sciences (SVIMS), Tirupati — a state-run tertiary institute with haematology and transplant services — represents the approved-indication end of stem cell medicine in AP. Sri Venkateswara Veterinary University, Tirupati works on reproductive biotechnology and embryo transfer in livestock, the applied end of cloning science. Andhra University, Visakhapatnam hosts DBT-supported biotechnology research, and the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ) with the Kalam Institute of Health Technology provides the device and diagnostics infrastructure on which cell therapy depends.

## Conclusion

Model organisms and stem cell science are two ends of a single continuum: the first reveals how genes build and maintain an organism, the second uses that knowledge to repair one. Their trajectory in India has been telling — from importing paradigms to producing them, with an indigenous CAR-T therapy in 2023 and an indigenous CRISPR therapy in 2025 built on the patient’s own stem cells. What sustains this is not only laboratory capacity but the regulatory discipline of the 2017 stem cell guidelines, which distinguish evidence-based therapy from commercially marketed hope. The task ahead is to widen access without loosening that discipline — so that regenerative medicine becomes a public good rather than a private privilege.

Q148:
## Introduction

Sterilization is the complete destruction of all microbial life, including bacterial endospores — which distinguishes it from disinfection, that only reduces the pathogen load. Method selection is governed entirely by material tolerance: what heat destroys, radiation preserves. Transgenic animals, by contrast, are animals carrying a deliberately introduced foreign gene, or “transgene”, which is heritable — making them living platforms for research and biomanufacture.

## Reproducible exam table — the material dictates the method

## Method Operating condition Materials suited to

Moist heat (autoclave) 121 degrees C, 15 psi, 15 min Surgical instruments, culture media, linen

Dry heat (hot-air oven) 160-170 degrees C, 1-2 hr Glassware, powders, oils, greases

Membrane filtration 0.22 micrometre pore Vaccines, antibiotics, sera, heat-labile fluids

Ultraviolet radiation 254 nm Air, work surfaces, laminar flow hoods (non-penetrating)

Gamma radiation Cobalt-60, approx. 25 kGy Single-use plastics, syringes, sutures, implants

Ethylene oxide gas 30-60 degrees C Catheters, endoscopes, heat-labile plastics

Liquid chemicals Glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide Rubber, optical and metal instruments

Why radiation matters commercially: gamma rays penetrate sealed final packaging and leave no chemical residue, which is why they dominate disposable medical device sterilization. Andhra Pradesh hosts a direct instance — the Centre for Gamma Irradiation at the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam, the first such facility in the state and its neighbouring states, operating alongside the DBT-supported Kalam Institute of Health Technology (KIHT) on the same 270-acre campus.

## Transgenic animals and their benefits

A transgenic animal carries a foreign gene stably integrated into its genome, introduced through pronuclear microinjection, somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), or CRISPR-Cas mediated editing. Benefits include:

- Disease models: transgenic mice reproduce the pathology of Alzheimer’s disease, cancer and diabetes, compressing decades of human disease progression into months of observable study.
- Molecular pharming: the transgenic cow Rosie secreted human alpha-lactalbumin in her milk; goats and sheep are engineered as living bioreactors for therapeutic proteins that are difficult to express in microbial systems.
- Vaccine and drug testing: safety and efficacy screening before human trials, reducing clinical risk.
- Improved livestock traits: enhanced growth rate, disease resistance and productivity.
- Indian ecosystem: the DBT-National Institute of Animal Biotechnology (NIAB), Hyderabad inaugurated India’s first Animal Stem Cell BioBank and laboratory in August 2025, supported by the National Biopharma Mission of DBT-BIRAC, covering disease modelling, tissue engineering and reproductive biotechnology (PIB, August 2025).

## Conclusion

Sterilization and transgenesis sit at opposite ends of the same biotechnology chain — one guarantees that the platform is free of contaminating life, the other engineers life to a defined purpose. Neither is self-regulating. Sterilization must be validated against material tolerance and biological indicators, while transgenic work in India operates under the Rules, 1989 framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, with RCGM oversight and CPCSEA animal-ethics clearance. Capacity created under the BioE3 Policy and hosted at AMTZ Visakhapatnam and NIAB Hyderabad shows this chain maturing domestically rather than remaining import-dependent.

## Value addition
- Sterilization control indicators:Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores validate autoclave cycles; Bacillus atrophaeus validates dry heat and ethylene oxide. Bowie-Dick tape confirms steam penetration in vacuum autoclaves.
- Disinfection is not sterilization: pasteurization (63 degrees C for 30 min) and simple boiling do not destroy bacterial spores — a distinction frequently tested.
- Regulatory chain for transgenic animals in India: IBSC (institution level) –> RCGM (Department of Biotechnology) –

> GEAC (MoEFCC) under Rules, 1989; separate animal welfare clearance from CPCSEA.

- Limitations of transgenic animals: unintended insertional mutagenesis, tumours and reduced lifespan; animal welfare and ethical objections; escape risk to wild gene pools; very high cost per founder animal; unpredictable expression across generations.
- AP hook: AMTZ’s gamma irradiation centre, combined with its ICMR-DHR Large Animal House Facility, makes Visakhapatnam one of the few Indian sites integrating sterilization infrastructure with regulated animal research on a single campus.

## Introduction

Genetically Modified crops are plants whose genome has been altered through recombinant DNA technology to insert a defined trait — most commonly insect resistance, herbicide tolerance or enhanced nutrition. In India, the technology’s scientific promise has consistently outrun its regulatory settlement: Bt cotton, approved in 2002, remains the only GM crop cleared for commercial cultivation, and the environmental release of GM crops continues to be adjudicated before the Supreme Court in Gene Campaign vs Union of India and Aruna Rodrigues vs Union of India (PIB, 2025).

## Trait classes
- Insect resistance: Bt cotton expresses Bacillus thuringiensis Cry proteins toxic to bollworm, reducing chemical insecticide dependence.
- Herbicide tolerance: glyphosate or glufosinate-tolerant events permitting broad-spectrum weed control without crop injury.
- Nutritional enhancement: biofortified events such as Golden Rice, engineered to accumulate beta-carotene.

## Reproducible flowchart — India’s GM approval pipeline

IBSC (institutional; laboratory and greenhouse work) –>RCGM under DBT (confined field trials, biosafety data generation) –>GEAC under MoEFCC (large-scale trials and environmental release) –>SBCC / DLC (state and district level field monitoring) –>FSSAI (food safety assessment of GM foods)

Statutory foundation: the Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous Micro-organisms, Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989, framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, administered by MoEFCC. Every application is assessed case-by-case on health, environment, food and feed safety through prescribed guidelines and standard operating procedures (PIB).

## Concerns associated with release
- Environmental: gene flow to wild relatives and landraces; erosion of agro-biodiversity; and above all resistance evolution — pink bollworm has broken Bt cotton resistance in India, requiring mandatory refuge and crop rotation strategies.
- Health and food safety: allergenicity and long-term toxicological uncertainty, requiring toxicity and allergenicity testing before any clearance.
- Socio-economic: dependence on proprietary seed technology and erosion of farmers’ traditional seed sovereignty;

recurring public opposition. Bt brinjal was cleared by GEAC in 2009 but placed under moratorium; indigenous Bt brinjal events (Janak and BSS-793, carrying Cry1Fa1) were permitted biosafety research field trials in eight states during 2020-

23. GM mustard DMH-11 received GEAC approval for environmental release at its 147th meeting on 18 October

2022, but is not in commercial cultivation (PIB).

- Governance: on 23 July 2024, a Supreme Court bench delivered a split verdict on GM mustard and directed the Environment Ministry to undertake stakeholder and expert consultation, preferably within four months, before framing a national policy on GM crops.

## Conclusion

India’s regulatory framework is procedurally elaborate but strategically unsettled — two decades of case-by-case clearance have produced exactly one commercial crop and a litigation backlog reaching the Supreme Court. The Court’s 2024 direction identifies the real gap accurately: it is not the absence of biosafety testing, but the absence of a transparent, participatory policy anchor. Significantly, the exemption of SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants from these Rules has already allowed gene-edited rice to reach release stage in May 2025, showing the regulatory logic evolving toward risk-proportionality rather than blanket caution.

## Value addition
- Status board:Bt cotton — approved 2002, the only commercially cultivated GM crop. Bt brinjal — GEAC clearance 2009, moratorium imposed; indigenous events trialled in eight states, 2020-23. GM mustard DMH-11 — GEAC approval October 2022, sub judice, not commercially cultivated.
- Genome editing carve-out: SDN-1 and SDN-2 edits carry no foreign DNA and are exempted from Rules, 1989 — the

legal basis on which DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1 were announced in May 2025 (PIB).

- BioE3 Policy (2024) — Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment: advanced bio-manufacturing facilities, bio-foundry clusters and bio-AI hubs, targeting a circular bio-economy aligned to net-zero commitments.
- Institutional distinction worth stating: RCGM generates and reviews biosafety data; GEAC is the final approving authority for environmental release. Confusing the two is a common error.
- AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s cotton belt (Guntur, Kurnool) is a frontline Bt-resistance management zone, and ICAR-IIRR’s DRR Dhan 100 was released for Zone VII, which includes Andhra Pradesh — making AP a first-adopter state for India’s gene-edited rice.
Q150:
## Introduction

Genetically modified crops carry a gene transferred across species boundaries by recombinant DNA technology — a capability conventional breeding cannot replicate, since breeding can only recombine genes already present within the sexually compatible gene pool. Globally the first was the Flavr Savr tomato (1994); in India, Bt cotton (2002) remains the sole commercially cultivated GM crop. The Indian debate is unusually well-evidenced, because two decades of Bt cotton supply both the strongest argument for the technology and the sharpest warning about it.

## Reproducible cause-effect chain

Trait insertion –> reduced biotic loss –> higher realised yield –> lower pesticide expenditure –> higher net farm income –>(if refuge discipline fails)–> resistance evolution –> yield reversal

## Role of GM crops in agriculture
- Productivity: cotton productivity rose from 191 kg per hectare in 2002-03 to 477 kg per hectare in 2017-18, with production climbing from 86.21 lakh bales to 348.88 lakh bales, attributed to Bt cotton adoption (PIB). This remains the largest documented yield jump for any Indian crop outside the Green Revolution cereals.
- Input reduction: the in-plant insecticidal protein sharply reduced bollworm sprays, cutting both cash costs and applicator pesticide exposure for smallholders — a health benefit rarely counted.
- Nutritional enhancement: biofortified events such as Golden Rice target hidden hunger directly through the staple, rather than through parallel supplementation programmes that depend on delivery logistics.
- Climate resilience: drought, salinity and submergence tolerance traits reduce yield variance, which matters more than mean yield for a farmer without crop insurance.

## Legitimate concerns about transgenic agriculture
- Resistance is not hypothetical — it has already happened. Pink bollworm overcame Bt cotton, and Indian cotton yields have since plateaued and fallen well below the 2017-18 peak, with farmers reverting to chemical sprays. This is the strongest empirical case for the precautionary position.
- Herbicide-tolerance externality: blanket herbicide spraying drives resistant weed populations and displaces manual weeding labour — a distributional cost borne largely by women agricultural workers.
- Ecological risk: gene flow to wild relatives and landrace erosion. India is a centre of diversity for brinjal and rice, which raises the stakes considerably.
- Seed sovereignty: dependence on proprietary technology and royalty structures, and recurring farmer protest over pricing and access.
- Regulatory trust deficit: delays and limited public consultation under the GEAC process, which the Supreme Court’s split verdict of 23 July 2024 addressed by directing a consultative national GM policy.

## Conclusion

The Bt cotton record demonstrates that GM technology is neither a panacea nor a hazard in the abstract — it is a tool whose returns decay without agronomic stewardship. The yield gains of the 2000s were real; their partial reversal through resistance was equally real and was entirely predicted by entomologists. The credible path is therefore trait-by-trait evaluation with enforced refuge compliance, transparent biosafety data, and public-sector ownership of events — the model already visible in the publicly developed DMH-11 mustard and in ICAR’s gene-edited rice varieties (May 2025), which keep the technology outside proprietary control and align it with India’s Bio-economy ambitions.

## Value addition
- Refuge requirement: a non-Bt border or refuge belt dilutes selection pressure and delays resistance. Poor compliance in India is the accepted proximate cause of pink bollworm resistance — a management failure, not a technology failure.
- Public-sector events matter:DMH-11 was developed by Delhi University’s Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants using the barnase-barstar system to achieve hybrid vigour in mustard, which is otherwise very difficult to hybridise because it is largely self-pollinating.
- Oilseed context: India’s oilseed output reached a record 429.89 lakh tonnes in 2024-25, driven by record groundnut (119.42 lakh tonnes) and soybean (152.68 lakh tonnes) output (PIB, November 2025) — yet edible oil import dependence persists, which is exactly the productivity gap hybrid and GM mustard were intended to close.
- Gene editing as the middle path: SDN-1 and SDN-2 edits introduce no foreign DNA and are exempted from Rules, 1989, sidestepping much of the transgenic controversy while delivering comparable trait gains.
- AP hook: Guntur and Kurnool are among India’s most intensively cropped Bt cotton districts. ANGRAU, Lam (Guntur) carries the state’s IPM and resistance-management extension mandate, making Andhra Pradesh a live laboratory for the refuge-compliance problem.

## Introduction

Plant tissue culture is the aseptic in vitro cultivation of plant cells, tissues or organs on a defined nutrient medium, resting on cellular totipotency — the capacity of a single differentiated plant cell to regenerate an entire organism. This single property is what makes clonal multiplication, virus elimination and genetic transformation possible at all. Golden Rice extends plant biotechnology in a different direction: engineering the nutritional composition of a staple crop itself.

## Reproducible flowchart — the tissue culture sequence

Explant selection –> surface sterilisation –> callus induction on MS medium –> shoot regeneration (high cytokinin) –> root induction (high auxin) –>hardening / acclimatisation–> field transfer

## (a) Applications of tissue culture in agriculture
- Micropropagation: mass clonal multiplication of genetically identical, disease-free planting material in banana, sugarcane, potato, orchids and oil palm. Uniform planting material compresses the harvest window, which is precisely what makes contract farming and processing linkages commercially viable.
- Production of virus-free plants:meristem tip culture exploits the fact that the apical meristem is largely virus-free, allowing recovery of clean stock from infected mother plants — used against sugarcane mosaic and potato leaf roll virus.
- Germplasm conservation:in vitro slow-growth storage and cryopreservation for vegetatively propagated and recalcitrant-seeded species, complementing the National Gene Bank at ICAR-NBPGR.
- Somaclonal variation: culture-induced genetic variability screened for stress tolerance, disease resistance and yield.
- Platform for genetic transformation: every transgenic and gene-edited crop, from Bt cotton to DRR Dhan 100, passes through a tissue-culture regeneration step. Tissue culture is the enabling technology, not a parallel one — a point worth stating explicitly.
- Quality assurance: DBT’s National Certification System for Tissue Culture Raised Plants (NCS-TCP), notified on 10 March 2006 under the Seeds Act, 1966, certifies virus-free and true-to-type plants. It is anchored at NIPGR, New Delhi and operates through five Accredited Test Laboratories, two Referral Centres and 93 recognised Tissue Culture Production Facilities (DBT).

## (b) Golden Rice and its advantages

Golden Rice is a transgenic rice engineered to synthesise beta-carotene (provitamin A) in the endosperm, which normally produces none. It was developed by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer (2000) using the phytoene synthase and carotene desaturase genes; Golden Rice 2 substantially raised provitamin A content.

Advantages:

- Delivers vitamin A through an existing staple, requiring no change in cooking practice or purchasing behaviour — the key adoption advantage over fortified products.
- Targets xerophthalmia, night blindness and child mortality in rice-dependent populations.
- Reduces reliance on supplementation and fortification logistics, which are the weakest link in remote, tribal and hard-to-reach areas.
- Offers economic and social benefit in communities where rice dominates the diet and dietary diversification is not affordable.

## Conclusion

Tissue culture and Golden Rice illustrate the two distinct routes plant biotechnology takes — one multiplies proven genetics at scale, the other rewrites the nutritional content of a crop. Tissue culture has been an unambiguous commercial success in India, backed by a functioning certification system and a mature private industry. Golden Rice, by contrast, remains not commercially cultivated anywhere and has never been submitted to India’s GEAC — a reminder that in agricultural biotechnology, regulatory acceptance and public trust, rather than laboratory proof, are the binding constraints.

## Value addition
- Culture types worth naming: callus culture, suspension culture, meristem or shoot-tip culture, anther culture (haploids yielding instantly homozygous lines, compressing breeding cycles by years), embryo rescue (enabling wide

crosses that would otherwise abort), and protoplast fusion (somatic hybrids across sexually incompatible species).

- Somatic embryogenesis and synthetic seed: encapsulated somatic embryos allow clonally propagated crops to be handled, stored and sown like true seed.
- AP-specific anchor: Andhra Pradesh is India’s leading oil palm state, and ICAR-Indian Institute of Oil Palm Research, Pedavegi (Eluru district) — established in 1995 on a 93-hectare campus and the country’s only dedicated oil palm research institute — works on oil palm clonal propagation and planting material. This matters because oil palm has a four-year gestation, so poor planting material locks in a decade of low yield. India’s oil palm area stands at 5.27 lakh hectares producing 3.80 lakh tonnes of crude palm oil, promoted under NMEO-OP (2021, outlay Rs. 11,040 crore).
- AP horticulture link: tissue-cultured banana and papaya underpin Andhra Pradesh’s horticulture strength. India’s fruit production reached 1,176.49 lakh tonnes in 2024-25, with Andhra Pradesh among the leading fruit-producing states (PIB, March 2026).

## Introduction

Agrarian distress in India is a crisis of income and risk, not of output. India recorded its highest-ever foodgrain production at 357.73 million tonnes in 2024-25 (Final Estimates), with the Third Advance Estimates for 2025-26 projecting a further record 376.56 million tonnes (PIB, May 2026) — even as small and marginal farmers face stagnant net incomes, rising input costs and climate volatility. Crop science research is therefore best judged not by tonnage delivered but by whether its gains actually reach the distressed farmer.

## Reproducible two-column table — achievement against corresponding gap

## Achievement of crop science research Corresponding gap

Foodgrain output 82 MT (1960-61) to 357.73 MT (2024-25) Gains concentrated in the irrigated rice-wheat belt

Bt cotton lifted yields to 477 kg/ha (2017-18) Pink bollworm resistance reversed part of the gain

Genome-edited rice released, May 2025 Rainfed areas, about 60% of net sown area, under-served

Record oilseed output 429.89 lakh tonnes (2024-25) Edible oil import dependence persists

## Achievements
- Varietal breakthroughs: ICAR and the State Agricultural Universities drove the Green Revolution HYVs and continue to deliver. In May 2025 India became the first country in the world to develop genome-edited rice varieties — DRR

Dhan 100 (Kamala) from ICAR-IIRR, Hyderabad (developed from Samba Mahsuri / BPT 5204) and Pusa DST Rice 1 from ICAR-IARI, New Delhi (from MTU 1010). Benefits include a 19% yield increase, a 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, and an estimated saving of 7,500 million cubic metres of irrigation water (PIB, May 2025). Both were released for Zone VII, which includes Andhra Pradesh.

- Stress-tolerant varieties:Sahbhagi Dhan, developed in collaboration with IRRI, is a drought-tolerant, early-maturing rice suited to rainfed and upland conditions and to direct seeding, adopted in Jharkhand, Odisha and Bihar.
- Institutional depth: NICRA, the National Gene Bank at ICAR-NBPGR, and a network of over 700 Krishi Vigyan Kendras form a research-to-field chain few developing countries possess.

## Critical gaps
- Research has, in part, created the distress it is now asked to solve.Pusa 44 — a long-duration rice variety — delivered high yields but is being actively discouraged in Punjab because its late maturity worsens groundwater draw and leaves too narrow a window before wheat sowing, directly driving stubble burning. High-yield breeding without a water and residue objective externalised its own costs onto the commons.
- Regional skew: research dividends concentrated in assured-irrigation regions such as Punjab and Haryana, while rainfed areas constituting roughly 60% of net sown area received disproportionately little.
- Crop skew: pulses, oilseeds and millets were under-researched for decades — precisely the crops carrying nutritional value and dryland income potential.
- Lab-to-land failure: extension is the weak link. Low varietal replacement rates and seed replacement rates mean released varieties do not reach farmers’ fields at scale.
- Research does not price output. No variety protects a farmer from a price crash. Crop science cannot substitute for marketing reform, and treating it as though it can is a category error that has distorted policy expectations.

## Conclusion

Crop science research has decisively won India’s food security battle and is now producing world-first outcomes in genome editing. It has not, however, resolved agrarian distress — because distress is generated at the intersection of yield, water, risk and price, while research has historically optimised only the first of these. The reorientation required is toward rainfed and climate-resilient varieties, water- and emission-efficient breeding objectives, nutrition-dense crops, and a far stronger extension interface, with State Agricultural Universities such as ANGRAU, Lam (Guntur) carrying the location-specific mandate that national institutes structurally cannot.

## Value addition
- DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala): matures about 20 days earlier (approx. 130 days) than Samba Mahsuri, cutting water and

fertiliser use and reducing methane emissions; its stronger stalk resists lodging; grain quality is retained. Pusa DST Rice 1 raises yield by 9.66% to 30.4% in saline and alkaline soils, with potential for up to 20% higher production (PIB, May 2025).

- Why SDN-1 and SDN-2 editing was the legal enabler: these categories introduce no foreign DNA and are exempted under India’s biosafety regulations — which is precisely why gene-edited rice reached release stage while transgenic mustard remains sub judice.
- NICRA — National Innovations on Climate Resilient Agriculture: location-specific climate adaptation research, the correct institutional answer to the rainfed research gap.
- Seed pipeline data: 109,370 quintals of breeder seed and 433,115 quintals of quality seed produced during 2024-25 (PIB) — the pipeline that ultimately determines whether a released variety reaches farmers at all.
- AP anchor:ANGRAU (established 1964 as Andhra Pradesh Agricultural University, headquartered at Lam, Guntur)

serves the state’s districts; ICAR-IIOPR, Pedavegi supports its oil palm economy; and DRR Dhan 100 derives from BPT 5204 (Samba Mahsuri), itself of ANGRAU lineage from Bapatla — making Andhra Pradesh both the genetic source and the target release zone of India’s first gene-edited rice.
Q153:
## Introduction

As the only large-scale converters of solar energy into fixed carbon, plants sit at the base of every food chain, every fossil and biofuel, and most pharmacopoeias. Their applications are not a list of separate uses but a single dependency: food security, public health, industrial raw material supply and climate stabilisation all ultimately resolve into questions of plant productivity and plant diversity.

Reproducible four-quadrant diagram: place PLANTS at the centre, with four quadrants labelled Food and Nutrition, Medicine and Pharmaceuticals, Industry and Energy, and Ecology and Climate — each quadrant carrying two or three named examples.

Food and nutrition: India’s foodgrain output reached a record 357.73 million tonnes in 2024-25, with the 2025-26 Third Advance Estimates at 376.56 million tonnes, including record maize production of 55.09 million tonnes (PIB). Horticulture crossed 3,707.38 lakh tonnes across 301.36 lakh hectares in 2024-25, with fruits at 1,176.49 lakh tonnes and vegetables at 2,177.97 lakh tonnes (PIB, March 2026) — marking a structural shift from calorie security toward nutritional security.

Medicinal and pharmaceutical: Plants underpin the AYUSH systems and a large share of modern pharmacology — Azadirachta indica (neem: antibacterial, antifungal, insecticidal), Ocimum sanctum (tulsi), Papaver somniferum (morphine), Rauvolfia serpentina (reserpine, the first modern antihypertensive), Taxus species (paclitaxel, anticancer), and salicin from willow bark, the chemical parent of aspirin. India hosts roughly 7,000 medicinal plant species, with cultivation and conservation promoted by the National Medicinal Plants Board under the Ministry of AYUSH.

Industrial and energy: Cotton and jute anchor the textile economy; teak, bamboo and pine supply construction, furniture and pulp. Bamboo — reclassified as a grass under the Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 — was thereby freed from felling and transit restrictions when grown outside forest areas, unlocking the rural enterprise potential of the National Bamboo Mission. In energy, India achieved 20% ethanol blending (E20) in ESY 2025-26, five years ahead of the 2030 target set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018, with ethanol procurement rising from about 38 crore litres in 2013-14 to over 1,200 crore litres projected for 2025-26 (PIB, July 2026) — sugarcane, molasses, maize and surplus rice converted directly into transport fuel.

Ecological and climate: Plants regulate the hydrological cycle, anchor soil against erosion, and sequester carbon — the basis of India’s NDC commitment to create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent through forest and tree cover by 2030. Mangroves such as Avicennia and Rhizophora buffer cyclone storm surge along the eastern coast, and urban tree cover moderates heat-island intensity.

Andhra Pradesh instance: AP is among India’s leading fruit-producing states, records the highest coconut productivity in the country, is a major cocoa-growing state, and is India’s largest crude palm oil producer, supported by ICAR-IIOPR, Pedavegi. Guntur chilli drives India’s single largest spice export line — chilli exports stood at USD 1,508.94 million in 2023-24 — and Coringa in the Godavari estuary is among India’s largest mangrove formations.

## Conclusion

Plants are not one resource among many but the substrate on which food, health, industry, energy and climate stability all rest — which is why plant productivity and plant diversity are strategic rather than merely sectoral concerns. The policy implication is that utilisation and conservation cannot be traded off against each other: E20, the National Bamboo Mission and NMEO-OP each expand plant-based value chains, and each depends on the germplasm base that gene banks and in situ conservation protect. Sustainable utilisation, backed by tissue culture and biotechnology, is the only route that keeps both economic and ecological returns intact.

India’s legal answer to biopiracy, the neem and turmeric patent revocations being the canonical cases.

- Bioprospecting infrastructure: the ICAR-NBPGR National Gene Bank, among the world’s largest, conserves crop germplasm as insurance against the genetic narrowing that intensive breeding causes.

Q154:
## Introduction

Crop science research in India is delivered through the National Agricultural Research System — the Indian Council of

Agricultural Research (ICAR) with its network of institutes, over 70 State Agricultural Universities and more than 730 Krishi Vigyan Kendras — working on varietal improvement, agronomy, plant protection and post-harvest technology. Its cumulative outcome is visible in one number: foodgrain output has risen from about 50 million tonnes at Independence to a record 376.56 million tonnes in 2025-26 (Third Advance Estimates, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, May 2026), on a net sown area that has barely expanded. This is a productivity outcome, not an area outcome — which is precisely what crop science research was meant to deliver.

## Phase Core Research Output Measurable Outcome

Green Revolution (1960s-80s) Semi-dwarf HYVs (IR8, Kalyan Sona), fertiliser-responsive agronomy

Diversification (1990s-2010s) Hybrids, Bt cotton, horticulture, quality protein maize

India becomes 2nd largest producer of rice, wheat, cotton, sugarcane

Precision phase (2015-) Marker-assisted selection, biofortification, genome editing

Yield gains with lower water, fertiliser and emissions

1. Varietal outcomes — the primary and most quantifiable deliverable. Varietal replacement is the cheapest yield-raising intervention available to a small farmer because it requires no additional capital. ICAR released 339 crop varieties in 2025-26 matched to different agro-climatic zones (Ministry of Agriculture, May 2026). The impact is concentrated: Basmati exports worth roughly Rs. 50,000 crore rest on just four ICAR-bred varieties, and about 85 per cent of the wheat area is under five climate-resilient ICAR varieties (PIB, ICAR 97th Foundation Day, July 2025). 2. Biotechnological outcomes — from transgenics to genome editing. Bt cotton, approved in 2002, made India the world’s second-largest cotton producer, though pink bollworm resistance has since exposed the limits of a single-gene strategy. The decisive recent outcome is precision breeding: in May 2025 ICAR released the world’s first genome-edited rice varieties — DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala), developed by ICAR-IIRR Hyderabad from Samba Mahsuri, and Pusa DST Rice 1, developed by ICAR-IARI from MTU 1010. Using CRISPR-Cas SDN-1/SDN-2 edits that insert no foreign DNA, they deliver roughly 19 per cent higher yield with about 20 per cent lower greenhouse gas emissions, and mature 15-20 days earlier, saving irrigation water (PIB, 4 May 2025). Both are notified for Zone VII, which includes Andhra Pradesh. 3. Resilience and nutritional outcomes. Abiotic-stress breeding under the National Innovations on Climate Resilient Agriculture (NICRA) has produced submergence-tolerant Swarna-Sub1 and drought-tolerant Sahbhagi Dhan, converting flood and drought years from total loss into partial harvest — a direct income-stabilisation outcome. On nutrition, sustained pulse research lifted output from 16.3 million tonnes in 2015-16 to 24.49 million tonnes in 2023-24, with varietal replacement rates of 99 per cent in lentil and 84 per cent in chickpea (PIB, July 2025). 4. Andhra Pradesh instance — outcomes are locally bred, not merely imported. The MTU series bred at the Regional Agricultural Research Station, Maruteru under ANGRAU is the backbone of coastal Andhra paddy; MTU 1010 is significant enough nationally to have been chosen as the parent for Pusa DST Rice 1. Alongside, ICAR-NIRCA, Rajamahendravaram now leads commercial-crop diversification research, ICAR-IIOPR, Pedavegi anchors the oil palm mission, and Lam farm, Guntur drives chilli and pulse improvement — an institutional chain that converts national research into Godavari-delta yields. 5. The unfinished outcome — distribution. Gains remain skewed towards irrigated systems, while rainfed areas that constitute roughly 60 per cent of net sown area lag. Nominal agriculture GVA growth fell to about 0.8 per cent in FY26 even in a record production year (Business/NSO estimates, January 2026) — showing that a production outcome does not automatically become an income outcome without price and market reform.

## Conclusion

Crop science research has converted India from a food-deficit importer into a structural surplus producer, and has now moved beyond volume to precision — editing genes for yield, water and emissions simultaneously. Its outcomes, however, are strongest where irrigation and markets already exist. Directing the next generation of research at rainfed, saline and coastal systems, and coupling it with assured procurement, is what will convert scientific outcomes into farmer prosperity, in line with the goals of PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana.

## Value addition
- PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana (announced in Budget 2025-26; Cabinet approval July 2025): converges 36 existing schemes across 100 low-productivity districts, with an outlay of about Rs. 24,000 crore a year for six years — the delivery vehicle that is meant to translate research outcomes into district-level productivity.
- Viksit Krishi Sankalp Abhiyan — nationwide scientist-to-farmer outreach campaign taking ICAR varieties and advisories directly to fields, addressing the classic lab-to-land gap. AICRP model: All India Coordinated Research Projects are the multi-location testing mechanism through which any variety, including the genome-edited rice lines, must pass before release — useful for showing procedural rigour.
- Seed chain terminology worth using precisely: Breeder seed –> Foundation seed –> Certified seed; the Seed Replacement Rate (SRR) and Varietal Replacement Rate (VRR) are the standard indicators of whether research reaches farmers.
- Nutritional outcome anchor: the International Year of Millets (2023) and Shree Anna revival mainstreamed millet research, and horticulture output (about 377.8 million tonnes in 2025-26) now exceeds foodgrain output — evidence of diversification.
Q155:
## Introduction

Terrestrial plants are photosynthetic autotrophs that complete their life cycle on land. Their colonisation of land, roughly 470 million years ago, required solving four problems simultaneously: desiccation in dry air, mechanical support without the buoyancy of water, acquisition of water and minerals from a solid substrate, and fertilisation without external water for gamete transfer. Almost every general characteristic of a land plant — cuticle, lignified vascular tissue, roots, pollen and seed — is a structural answer to one of these four problems. Understanding them in this order converts a list into a logic.

## Terrestrial Problem Adaptation Illustration

Water loss to dry air Waxy cuticle; stomata with guard cells for regulated gas exchange

Sunken stomata and thick cuticle in Nerium; CAM night-time stomatal opening in cacti

Gravity and wind Lignified xylem, sclerenchyma, secondary thickening

Teak and sal trees standing decades against cyclonic winds

Water and nutrient uptake Extensive root system with root hairs; symbioses

Rhizobium nodules in pulses; mycorrhizal association extending the absorptive surface

Fertilisation without water Pollen grain (siphonogamy), seed, fruit Angiosperm dominance; seed dormancy surviving a dry season

## Further general characteristics, expanded
- Sporophyte dominance and heteromorphic alternation of generations. In land plants the diploid, vascularised sporophyte is the dominant, long-lived phase, while the gametophyte is progressively reduced and enclosed. This matters because a diploid body masks deleterious recessive mutations and permits large, complex structures that a delicate haploid thallus could not support.
- Division of labour among differentiated organs. Root, stem, leaf, flower and fruit are functionally specialised, with tissue systems — vascular for conduction, sclerenchyma for support, parenchyma for storage — allowing size and longevity impossible in algae.
- Protection of the embryo. The seed coat, endosperm and fruit wall protect and provision the embryo through unfavourable seasons, and enable dispersal in space as well as in time (dormancy) — the single most important reason angiosperms dominate terrestrial vegetation.
- Photosynthetic pathway plasticity. C3, C4 and CAM pathways represent alternative trade-offs between carbon gain and water loss, explaining why sugarcane and maize (C4) thrive in the hot Godavari and Krishna deltas while wheat (C3) does not.

## Uses of plants to mankind — expanded with data
- Food security. Plants supply the overwhelming share of human calories directly or indirectly. India’s foodgrain output reached 376.56 million tonnes in 2025-26 and horticulture about 377.8 million tonnes (Ministry of Agriculture, 2026), the latter exceeding foodgrains for the first time — evidence of a nutritional as well as caloric transition.
- Medicine. Roughly a quarter of modern prescription drugs trace to plant molecules — quinine from Cinchona, artemisinin from Artemisia annua, paclitaxel (Taxol) from Taxus, morphine from Papaver. India’s AYUSH systems rest on a documented base of several thousand medicinal plant species, coordinated by the National Medicinal Plants Board (Ministry of AYUSH).
- Industry and materials. Cotton (about 29.02 million bales in 2025-26), jute, timber, bamboo, resins, gums and dyes underpin textiles, construction, paper and cosmetics. Bamboo’s reclassification out of the definition of “tree” under the Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 was specifically intended to unlock this economic use.
- Energy. Sugarcane molasses and grain-based ethanol underpin India’s Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme, with blending achieving the 20 per cent target ahead of the 2025-26 schedule (Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas) — an outcome directly reducing crude import dependence.
- Ecological services. Forests are India’s principal carbon sink; forest and tree cover stands at 25.17 per cent of geographical area with a total carbon stock of about 7,285.5 million tonnes (India State of Forest Report 2023, Forest Survey of India), central to the Nationally Determined Contribution of an additional 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2-equivalent sink.
- Andhra Pradesh instance.Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus), endemic to the Seshachalam and Veligonda hills, is simultaneously a high-value industrial timber, an IUCN-listed species and a CITES Appendix-II regulated trade item — a single species that illustrates use, over-exploitation and conservation together. Alongside, Guntur chilli and Konaseema coconut anchor AP’s plant-based export economy.

## Conclusion

Terrestrial plants are best understood not as a list of traits but as a set of engineering solutions to life out of water — cuticle against desiccation, lignin against gravity, roots for uptake, seed and pollen for reproduction on dry land. Those same structures are what make plants useful: the lignin becomes timber, the seed becomes grain, the secondary metabolite becomes medicine. Human dependence is therefore total, and the case of Red Sanders shows how quickly utility becomes over-exploitation. Sustainable harvest, in situ conservation in protected areas, and ex situ backup in gene banks and tissue culture repositories are the practical conditions for continued use.

## Value addition
- Ecological classification of terrestrial plants (highly examinable):Mesophytes (moderate water), Xerophytes (arid — reduced leaf area, sunken stomata, succulence, deep tap roots), Halophytes (saline — pneumatophores and vivipary in Coringa mangroves, AP), Epiphytes (velamen roots for atmospheric moisture), Lithophytes (rock surfaces).
- Xerophytic adaptations in one line each: small or spinous leaves reduce transpiring surface; thick cuticle and wax reduce cuticular loss; sunken stomata create a humid boundary layer; deep tap roots (7-10 m) tap sub-soil moisture; succulent parenchyma stores water; CAM shifts stomatal opening to night.
- Conservation instruments to cite:In situ — Biosphere Reserves, National Parks, Sacred Groves; ex situ — National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (NBPGR) gene bank, botanical gardens, cryopreservation and in vitro tissue culture repositories.
- Legal and international anchors: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (as amended in 2023); CITES for regulated species trade; Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing; SDG 15 (Life on Land).
- AP-specific plant wealth: Coringa mangroves (Godavari estuary, second largest mangrove formation on the east coast), Papikonda and Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam forests, and GI-tagged plant products including Guntur Sannam chilli, Banaganapalle mango and Araku coffee.
Q156:
## Introduction

A bio-pesticide is a pest-control agent derived from natural materials — micro-organisms, plants, minerals or beneficial insects — that suppresses pests through biological rather than broad-spectrum chemical toxicity, and is registered in India under the Insecticides Act, 1968 by the CIB&RC. Within this family, entomopathogenic fungi — fungal parasites of insects — occupy a special position: unlike Bacillus thuringiensis and baculoviruses, which must be ingested to act, fungi infect on contact by penetrating the insect cuticle. This single mechanistic difference is what makes them the principal biological option against sap-sucking pests.

## What is a bio-pesticide — four categories with one example each

## Category Basis of Action Example

Microbial Living pathogen infects the pest Bacillus thuringiensis (caterpillars); Beauveria bassiana (sucking pests); NPV (bollworms)

Biochemical Natural compound alters pest behaviour or development

Azadirachtin (neem) — antifeedant and growth regulator; pheromone traps for mating disruption

Plant-incorporated protectant (PIP) Crop itself expresses the protective protein Cry proteins in Bt cotton

Macrobial / natural enemies Predators and parasitoids released Trichogramma egg parasitoid; Chrysoperla; predatory mites

A distinction worth stating explicitly:antagonistic fungi such as Trichoderma viride and Trichoderma harzianum suppress plant-pathogenic fungi in soil and are biofungicides; entomopathogenic fungi such as Beauveria and Metarhizium kill insects. They are both fungal bio-pesticides but act on entirely different targets. B. How fungal parasites of insects are useful in biological control 1. Mechanism — infection cycle (reproduce as a six-step flowchart; it is the highest-value diagram for this question):Conidium adheres to cuticle --> germination and appressorium formation --> enzymatic penetration (chitinase, protease Pr1, lipase) --> proliferation as hyphal bodies in the haemocoel --> toxin release (beauvericin, destruxins) and death --> mycosis and sporulation on the cadaver --> secondary infection of the population 2. Why contact infection matters. Aphids, whiteflies, mealybugs, thrips, jassids and scale insects feed by sucking phloem sap and ingest almost no leaf tissue, so stomach-acting bio-pesticides are ineffective against them. Fungi bypass ingestion entirely. In practice this means entomopathogenic fungi are the biological answer to precisely the pest group that most damages horticulture and drives repeated chemical spraying.

3. Self-perpetuating epizootics. The fungus sporulates on the dead insect and infects neighbours, so a single application can seed a spreading infection within the pest population — a compounding effect no chemical possesses. Under humid conditions this can suppress a pest below the economic threshold for several weeks. 4. Major species and their targets: - Beauveria bassiana (white muscardine) — whiteflies, aphids, thrips, beetles, coffee berry borer. - Metarhizium anisopliae (green muscardine) — termites, white grubs in sugarcane, and the coconut rhinoceros beetle. - Lecanicillium (Verticillium) lecanii — aphids, scale insects and whiteflies in horticulture and polyhouses. -Nomuraea rileyi — lepidopteran larvae including Spodoptera on groundnut and soybean. - Hirsutella thompsonii — phytophagous mites. 5. Practical advantages. Target specificity spares pollinators and natural enemies; multiple modes of attack (enzymatic, mechanical, toxin-mediated) make resistance evolution slow; negligible residue means no MRL barrier for export crops; and compatibility with IPM and organic certification allows stacking with pheromone traps and parasitoid releases. 6. Limitations and how they are managed. Fungal spores need high relative humidity to germinate, are inactivated by UV radiation and take three to seven days to kill — hence evening application, oil-based or encapsulated UV-protected formulations, prophylactic use at low pest density, and decentralised production to overcome short shelf life. 7. Indian and Andhra Pradesh deployment.ICAR-NBAIR, Bengaluru is the national repository and quality reference for biocontrol agents, and State biocontrol laboratories mass-multiply Trichoderma, Beauveria and Metarhizium for distribution. In Andhra Pradesh, Metarhizium is used against rhinoceros beetle in the Konaseema and Godavari coconut belt, and entomopathogenic fungi are among the standard bio-inputs produced at the Bio-Input Resource Centres of the APCNF programme, which covers over 1.77 million farmers (Government of Andhra Pradesh, 2026). The severe invasive thrips outbreak on Guntur chilli underlined both the failure of repeated chemical sprays and the need for a fungal biocontrol component in chilli IPM.

## Conclusion

Bio-pesticides substitute biological specificity for chemical toxicity, and among them entomopathogenic fungi are distinctive because they infect through the cuticle, reach sap-sucking pests that other microbials cannot, and spread through the pest population on their own. Their humidity dependence and slow action are formulation and timing problems, not fundamental defects, and are already being solved through UV-protected and nano-formulations. Mainstreaming them through NMNF’s Bio-Input Resource Centres, NBAIR-certified quality standards and farmer training under Farmer Field Schools is the practical route to residue-free, export-compliant and ecologically stable crop protection.

## Value addition
- Terminology that earns marks:mycosis (fungal disease of the insect); muscardine (the mummified, sporulating cadaver — white for Beauveria, green for Metarhizium); epizootic (an outbreak of disease within an animal population); conidium, appressorium, blastospore, haemocoel.
- Toxins to name: beauvericin and bassianolide (Beauveria), destruxins (Metarhizium) — these are the insecticidal metabolites released after the fungus enters the body cavity. Three-way distinction, frequently confused in answers:bio-fertilizer (supplies nutrients — Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum, phosphate-solubilising bacteria, blue-green algae, Azolla); bio-pesticide (kills or deters pests); bio-control agent (a living organism released to suppress a pest, including predators and parasitoids).
- Institutional and scheme map: ICAR-NBAIR Bengaluru; CIB&RC registration under the Insecticides Act, 1968; Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage; National Mission on Natural Farming (10,000 Bio-Input Resource Centres); PKVY; MOVCDNER; Farmer Field Schools under the IPM programme. Classic biological control successes to cite in one line:Cryptolaemus montrouzieri against mealybugs; Rodolia cardinalis against cottony cushion scale; Cactoblastis cactorum against prickly pear; Trichogramma chilonis against sugarcane and rice stem borers.
- Nano and next-generation formulations: the ICAR nano-formulation derived from Myrothecium verrucaria for powdery mildew in tomato and grape shows how nanotechnology is being used to raise the shelf life and field efficacy of biological agents.
