Q157:
## Introduction

Bio-fertilizers and DNA fingerprinting represent two contrasting but equally transformative applications of biotechnology — one in the field, the other in the courtroom. Bio-fertilizers are formulations of live or latent beneficial microorganisms which, when applied to seed, soil or plant surfaces, mobilise nutrients biologically rather than supplying them chemically. DNA fingerprinting is a molecular identification technique that reads hypervariable non-coding repeat regions of the genome, which differ between any two individuals except monozygotic twins. Their significance has grown sharply: India’s chemical fertilizer dependence and its criminal-justice reliance on scientific evidence both demand these tools. Under the Fertilizer (Control) Order, 1985, 11 bio-fertilizers are notified for regulated manufacture and sale, while the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD), Hyderabad — now under the Biotechnology Research and Innovation Council (BRIC), DBT — anchors India’s forensic DNA capacity.

(a) Bio-fertilizers: Types

- **Functional Class** — Representative Organism · Mode of Action · Crop Use
- **Symbiotic N-fixers** — Rhizobium · Root-nodule fixation of atmospheric N2 to ammonia · Legumes — redgram, groundnut
- **Free-living / associative N- fixers** — Azotobacter, Azospirillum, Clostridium · Non-symbiotic fixation, releases N on cell lysis · Cereals, cotton, sugarcane
- **Cyanobacteria & Azolla** — Anabaena, Nostoc, Azolla- Anabaena complex · Photoautotrophic N-fixation in standing water · Wetland paddy
- **P-solubilisers / mobilisers** — Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, VAM fungi · Secrete organic acids that free bound phosphates; VAM extends root absorptive surface · Horticulture, plantation crops

Why this matters: Indian soils lock up a large fraction of applied phosphorus as insoluble calcium/iron phosphates. A P-solubiliser therefore does not add phosphorus — it unlocks the stock already present, which is why it lowers input cost without lowering nutrition. Similarly, VAM (vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhiza) confers drought and disease resistance as a bonus, making it central to rainfed horticulture in Rayalaseema.

## Advantages of Bio-fertilizers
- Ecologically non-toxic and self-renewing: Being living organisms, they multiply in the rhizosphere and persist across seasons, unlike a single-use chemical dose. They leave no nitrate residue, and so do not contribute to groundwater nitrate contamination or eutrophication of tanks and reservoirs.
- Input-cost reduction and subsidy relief: India is the second-largest fertilizer consumer globally, and the urea subsidy is among the largest single items of agricultural expenditure. Substituting even a fraction with microbial inoculants directly reduces both farm cost and fiscal burden.
- Soil health restoration: They add organic matter, improve aggregate structure and stimulate the native soil microbiome — the very parameters the Soil Health Card Scheme (over 25.17 crore cards issued by July 2025, PIB Factsheet, November 2025) is designed to monitor.
- Policy-embedded, not optional: The National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF), approved by the Cabinet on 25 November 2024 with an outlay of Rs. 2,481 crore, funds 10,000 Bio-input Resource Centres (BRCs) so that Jeevamrit, Beejamrit and microbial inoculants are locally available; over 15 lakh farmers had been enrolled by early 2026 (PIB, 2026).
- AP instance:Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming (APCNF), run by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha

(RySS), has scaled to 8,168 gram panchayats and over 17.7 lakh farmers across ~9.2 lakh hectares, with verified farmer income gains of 38-66%, water savings up to 50% and GHG reductions up to 46% per acre — the world’s largest agroecology transition (APCNF/RySS, Government of Andhra Pradesh, 2026).

(b) DNA Fingerprinting: Principle and Procedure

The technique, developed by Alec Jeffreys (1984), exploits Variable Number Tandem Repeats (VNTRs) and Short Tandem Repeats (STRs) — satellite DNA in which a short sequence is repeated a variable number of times, the copy number varying from person to person. Because these lie in non-coding regions, they are under no selection pressure and accumulate polymorphism freely (NCERT Class XII Biology, Ch. 6). Infographic — draw as a linear flowchart:

Sample collection (blood/hair root/saliva/bone) --> DNA extraction & purification --> Restriction digestion by endonucleases --> PCR amplification of STR loci --> Gel electrophoresis (size separation) --> Southern blotting + labelled VNTR probe hybridisation --> Autoradiography/fluorescence --> Profile comparison & match The decisive modern improvement is PCR: because it amplifies from vanishingly small templates, a single cell now suffices, which is why touch-DNA from a weapon handle or a steering wheel is admissible evidence today but was not three decades ago.

## Forensic Applications
- Crime scene investigation: Matching biological traces to suspects in homicide and sexual-assault cases. Under Section 293 CrPC (now Section 329, BNSS 2023), the Director and notified DNA examiners of CDFD are gazetted Government Scientific Experts empowered to depose in court without personal appearance formalities.
- Paternity, maternity and inheritance disputes: Conclusive resolution of civil claims, immigration parentage checks and maintenance suits.
- Mass-disaster and unidentified-body identification: Victim identification after air crashes, tsunamis and building collapses, where conventional identification is impossible.
- Wildlife forensics: Species and individual identification from seized skins, meat or scat — critical for prosecuting poaching under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, and used in tiger and red-sanders trafficking cases in the Eastern Ghats.
- Population and pedigree genetics: Tracing migration, genetic disease inheritance and germplasm authentication in crop and livestock breeding.

## Conclusion

Bio-fertilizers and DNA fingerprinting demonstrate that biotechnology delivers value at both ends of the development ladder — restoring the ecological base of agriculture, and securing the evidentiary base of justice. Bio-fertilizers convert soil biology into a productive asset, aligning with SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 15 (Life on Land); DNA profiling converts biological uniqueness into legal certainty, advancing SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions). The unfinished agenda differs for each: bio-fertilizers need assured quality control and shelf-life reliability, while DNA technology awaits a dedicated privacy-compliant statute. Scaling the first through NMNF and APCNF, and legislating the second, would let India capture the full public value of both.

## Value addition
- The regulatory gap (highest-value point): The DNA Technology (Use and Application) Regulation Bill, 2019, which proposed a National DNA Data Bank with crime-scene, suspects’, offenders’ and missing-persons indices, was withdrawn from the Lok Sabha on 24 July 2023. The Parliamentary Standing Committee (report tabled February 2021) had flagged the absence of consent safeguards and the risk of caste/community profiling. India therefore uses DNA evidence without a dedicated governing statute.
- FCO, 1985 — the statutory list: 11 bio-fertilizers are notified, including Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum, phosphate-solubilising bacteria, mycorrhizal, potassium-mobilising and zinc-solubilising bio-fertilizers, Acetobacter, carrier-based consortia, liquid consortia and phosphate-solubilising fungal formulations. NCONF, Ghaziabad with its regional centres is the nodal quality-control laboratory.
- Institutional anchors to name: CDFD Hyderabad (est. 1996, now under BRIC-DBT); National Forensic Sciences University, Gandhinagar (Institution of National Importance) — the two signed an MoU in 2025 on forensic genomics and DNA databasing.
- Limitations to concede for balance: probabilistic rather than absolute identity; contamination at scene or bench; degraded samples yielding partial profiles; high capital and skilled-manpower cost; and the privacy risk of indefinite retention.
Q158:
## Introduction

Plant tissue culture is the aseptic in-vitro cultivation of plant cells, tissues or organs on a defined nutrient medium under controlled light, temperature and humidity, so as to regenerate whole plants. It rests on the principle of cellular totipotency — the capacity of any living, nucleated plant cell to reconstitute an entire organism. This single property allows a nursery to convert one elite mother plant into millions of genetically identical, virus-free clones within a season, breaking the seasonal and multiplication-rate limits of conventional propagation. For a country where planting-material quality is a persistent yield constraint — particularly in banana, sugarcane, potato and ornamentals — tissue culture is less a laboratory curiosity than a mainstream agricultural input.

## The Process — draw as a linear flowchart

Explant selection (shoot tip / nodal segment / embryo) --> Surface sterilisation (mercuric chloride / sodium hypochlorite + ethanol) --> Inoculation onto nutrient medium (MS medium: mineral salts + sucrose + vitamins + agar + auxin/cytokinin) --> Callus induction or direct shoot multiplication --> Rooting on auxin-rich medium --> Hardening in greenhouse/shade net --> Field transplanting The auxin:cytokinin ratio is the control lever — a high cytokinin ratio drives shoot proliferation, a high auxin ratio drives rooting. This is worth stating explicitly, as it converts a descriptive answer into a technical one.

## Importance in Agriculture
- Disease-free planting material through meristem culture: The apical meristem is largely free of viral load because vascular connections have not yet differentiated there. Culturing it yields virus-free stock — the operative technique for eliminating Banana Bunchy Top Virus and potato viruses X and Y, which otherwise cause severe yield collapse in ratoon crops.
- Rate of multiplication and uniformity: A single banana sucker yields perhaps 5-10 suckers a year; micropropagation yields thousands of plantlets. Uniform maturity means synchronous flowering and a single harvest window, which is what makes mechanised harvesting and export-grade grading feasible. Yet only 10-30% of Indian banana planting material is currently tissue-cultured, so the headroom is large.
- Season-independent, space-efficient production: Multiplication continues year-round in a laboratory, decoupling nursery supply from monsoon timing — a decisive advantage as rainfall becomes more erratic.
- Conservation of rare and elite germplasm: Cryopreservation and in-vitro gene banks conserve vegetatively propagated and recalcitrant-seeded species; embryo rescue saves wide-cross hybrids whose embryos would abort naturally, widening the breeding base.
- Platform for crop improvement: Somaclonal variation generates novel traits; anther/pollen culture produces haploids and then doubled haploids, compressing varietal development from a decade to a few years; protoplast fusion creates somatic hybrids across sexual barriers. Tissue culture is also the mandatory regeneration step in genetic transformation — no GM or genome-edited crop exists without it.
- Livelihood and enterprise creation: Commercial tissue-culture units and hardening nurseries are a documented rural agri-entrepreneurship route, supported by the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) subsidy for model tissue-culture units.

## Governance and the AP Instance

Quality assurance: The National Certification System for Tissue Culture Raised Plants (NCS-TCP) was established by DBT through a Ministry of Agriculture Gazette notification of 10 March 2006 under Section 8 of the Seeds Act, 1966, making DBT the certification agency for virus-free and true-to-type tissue-cultured propagules. Recognition requires a minimum capacity of 5 lakh plants per annum, with accredited test laboratories checking virus indexing and genetic fidelity. Andhra Pradesh:Dr. Y.S.R. Horticultural University, Venkataramannagudem (West Godavari) — India’s second dedicated horticultural university, established 2007 — lists commercialisation of tissue-cultured banana among its released technologies, working through its Horticultural Research Station, Vijayarai and 20 research stations statewide.

Andhra Pradesh is among India’s largest banana-growing states (~0.08 million ha), making this directly relevant to state cropping systems.

## Limitations (concede for balance)
- Somaclonal variation can produce off-types, defeating the purpose of clonal uniformity — hence the genetic-fidelity testing mandated under NCS-TCP.
- Capital and skill intensity: laminar flow benches, autoclaves, growth rooms and trained tissue-culture technicians place it beyond small nurseries without subsidy.
- Contamination and hardening losses: endophytic bacterial contamination and mortality during acclimatisation remain the principal commercial risks.

## Conclusion

Plant tissue culture has moved from research technique to agricultural infrastructure. By decoupling planting-material supply from season, disease load and multiplication rate, it directly addresses three of the binding constraints on Indian horticulture. Its value compounds with policy: NCS-TCP certification assures the farmer of what he is buying, MIDH finances the units, and the technique itself underpins every genome-edited variety India will release. The frontier now is cost reduction through bioreactor-based liquid culture and automation, and extension of certification to more crops — steps that would let tissue culture serve smallholder food crops, not only high-value export horticulture.

## Value addition

Types of plant tissue culture — a ready classification for any related question:

- Seed culture: sterilised seeds/explants germinated in vitro to study germination and produce clean seedlings.
- Embryo culture (embryo rescue): immature embryos from wide crosses cultured before natural abortion — indispensable in interspecific breeding.
- Callus culture: undifferentiated cell mass on nutrient medium; the platform for somaclonal variation and secondary metabolite production.
- Organ culture: shoots, roots or leaves cultured intact to study organogenesis.
- Meristem/shoot-tip culture: the virus-elimination workhorse.
- Anther and pollen (microspore) culture: produces haploids –> doubled haploids for rapid homozygous line development.
- Protoplast culture and somatic hybridisation: cell-wall-free cells fused to create hybrids across incompatible species.
- Suspension culture in bioreactors: the scale-up route for industrial production of alkaloids, taxol and shikonin.

Key institutions to name: DBT-NCS-TCP (certification agency); ICAR-IIHR Bengaluru; ICAR-NRC for Banana, Tiruchirappalli; Dr. YSR Horticultural University, Venkataramannagudem (AP); ANGRAU, Lam, Guntur.
Q159:
## Introduction

Sustainable agriculture depends on managing two biological processes that industrial farming has disrupted: pest suppression and pollination. Bio-insecticides are pest-control agents derived from living organisms or their natural products — microbes, viruses, nematodes, plant extracts and insect semiochemicals — which suppress insect pests with high host specificity and minimal non-target damage. The flower is the reproductive shoot of angiosperms, a modified condensed axis bearing sterile and fertile whorls, whose entire architecture is an adaptation for transferring male gametes to female gametes. The connection is direct: broad-spectrum chemical insecticides kill the pollinators on which the flower depends, so a shift to specific bio-insecticides protects the reproductive machinery that yields the harvest.

## (a) Types of Bio-insecticides
- **Type** — Example Agent · Target / Mode of Action
- **Microbial (bacterial)** — Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) · Cry crystal proteins solubilise in the alkaline larval midgut, perforate epithelium — lepidopteran larvae in cotton, brinjal, vegetables
- **Microbial (fungal)** — Beauveria bassiana, Metarhizium anisopliae, Verticillium lecanii · Spores adhere, penetrate the cuticle enzymatically, proliferate in haemocoel — whiteflies, thrips, termites, sucking pests
- **Viral** — Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus (NPV) of Helicoverpa and Spodoptera · Ingested occlusion bodies dissolve in midgut, virions replicate and liquefy the larva — extremely host-specific
- **Botanical** — Neem (azadirachtin), pyrethrum, karanj · Antifeedant, repellent and insect growth regulator — disrupts moulting rather than killing outright
- **Nematodes / parasitoids** — Steinernema, Heterorhabditis; Trichogramma egg parasitoid · EPNs release symbiotic bacteria causing septicaemia; parasitoids destroy eggs before hatching
- **Biochemical / semiochemical** — Sex pheromone traps, mating-disruption dispensers · Behavioural manipulation for monitoring, mass trapping and mating disruption

Regulation: All bio-insecticides sold in India must be registered under Section 9(3) of the Insecticides Act, 1968 with the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC), which prescribes efficacy and safety data even for microbial products. This is a frequently-missed governance mark. AP instance: Under APCNF (RySS, Government of Andhra Pradesh), farmers prepare on-farm botanical bio-insecticides — Neemastra, Agniastra, Brahmastra and Dashaparni Kashayam — from neem, chilli, garlic and cow urine, distributed through Bio-input Resource Centres. This lowers cash outlay to near zero, and is the operational reason APCNF records farmer income gains of 38-66% (APCNF/RySS, 2026).

## (b) The Flower and Functions of Its Parts

A flower is a determinate, condensed reproductive shoot in which the internodes are suppressed and appendages are modified into whorls arranged on a swollen thalamus (receptacle). Infographic — draw a labelled longitudinal section, outer to inner:

- Calyx (sepals) — outermost, usually green: protects the developing bud against desiccation, mechanical injury and herbivory; being chlorophyllous, it also contributes photosynthate to the young bud. In Hibiscus, an additional epicalyx lies outside it.
- Corolla (petals) — the advertisement whorl: pigmentation (anthocyanins, carotenoids), scent and ultraviolet nectar guides attract specific pollinators; petals form landing platforms and, in tubular corollas, restrict access to a matched pollinator, promoting outcrossing efficiency.
- Androecium (stamens = filament + anther) — the male whorl: the typical angiosperm anther is bilobed and dithecous, four-sporangiate; microsporangia undergo meiosis to form microspores that mature into pollen grains (male gametophytes) carrying two male gametes. The tapetum nourishes developing pollen and supplies sporopollenin for the resistant exine.
- Gynoecium / pistil (stigma + style + ovary) — the female whorl: the stigma is the receptive landing platform with recognition proteins that accept compatible and reject incompatible pollen; the style is the conduit down which the pollen tube grows; the ovary encloses ovules (megasporangia) containing the embryo sac. Post-fertilisation, ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit. The gynoecium may be monocarpellary or multicarpellary, and the latter either syncarpous (fused, as in Papaver) or apocarpous (free, as in Michelia) — NCERT Class XII Biology, Ch. 2.
- Accessory structures:nectaries secrete the sugar reward that sustains the pollinator mutualism; the pedicel and thalamus provide vascular supply and mechanical support, positioning the flower for pollinator access.

## Conclusion

Bio-insecticides and floral biology are two halves of the same yield equation. Specific, biodegradable bio-insecticides suppress pests without eliminating the bees, syrphids and parasitoids on which pollination and natural biological control depend — whereas broad-spectrum chemicals do both jobs badly by killing indiscriminately. Understanding the flower explains precisely what is at stake: every whorl is an investment in outcrossing, and pollinator decline translates directly into fruit-set failure in crops like mango, cashew and cucurbits that dominate Andhra Pradesh’s horticulture. Integrated Pest Management, which places bio-insecticides at the centre and chemicals at the margin, is therefore not merely an environmental preference but a productivity strategy.

## Value addition

Classification of flowers — ready-made for any floral biology question:

- Complete vs incomplete: a complete flower has all four whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium) — e.g. rose. Absence of any whorl makes it incomplete.
- Perfect (bisexual) vs imperfect (unisexual): a perfect flower has functional stamens and pistil even if petals or sepals are missing. Imperfect flowers are staminate (male) or pistillate (female).
- Monoecious vs dioecious: monoecious plants bear separate male and female flowers on the same individual (maize, coconut, cucurbits — some, like cucumber and squash, bear only male flowers early in the season); dioecious plants bear them on separate individuals (papaya, palmyra), which is why orchard planning must include male plants.
- Symmetry:actinomorphic (radially symmetric — Datura, mustard) vs zygomorphic (bilaterally symmetric — pea, Cassia), the latter usually co-evolved with a specific pollinator.
- Ovary position:hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous, epigynous (inferior ovary) — determines whether the fruit is true or false.

Pollination linkage: outcrossing devices include dichogamy (protandry/protogyny), herkogamy, and self-incompatibility — all floral adaptations to prevent inbreeding depression.
Q160:
## Introduction

Bio-pesticides and genetically modified crops represent two distinct biotechnological responses to the same problem — crop loss — and they attract sharply different levels of public acceptance. Bio-pesticides are pest-control formulations derived from natural materials: micro-organisms, plants, minerals and certain genes engineered into plants themselves.GM crops are plants whose genome has been altered by recombinant DNA technology to introduce a trait not obtainable by conventional breeding. India’s position is telling: bio-pesticides enjoy universal policy support but modest uptake, while GM crops face intense contestation — Bt cotton (approved 2002) remains the only GM crop cleared for commercial cultivation, even as India became the first country in the world to release genome-edited rice varieties in May 2025.

## (a) Types and Uses of Bio-pesticides

BIO-PESTICIDES --> (1) Microbial [bacterial: Bt; fungal: Trichoderma, Beauveria; viral: NPV] | (2) Biochemical [azadirachtin, pheromones, plant oils] | (3) Plant-Incorporated Protectants (PIPs) [Bt cotton] | (4) Mineral-based [kaolin, silica] Uses in practice:

- Seed and soil treatment:Trichoderma viride and Trichoderma harzianum applied to seed or nursery beds suppress soil-borne wilt and damping-off caused by Fusarium, Rhizoctonia and Pythium — the single largest use category in Indian vegetable and pulse cultivation.
- Foliar pest control: Bt and NPV formulations against Helicoverpa armigera and Spodoptera litura in cotton, redgram, chilli and vegetables — crops central to the Guntur-Prakasam belt.
- Monitoring and mass trapping: pheromone traps establish pest thresholds so that any chemical spray is need-based rather than calendar-based — the operational core of IPM.
- Residue-free and export production: bio-pesticides are indispensable for organic certification under PGS-India and for meeting EU/Japan Maximum Residue Limits — directly relevant to AP’s chilli, grape, mango pulp and shrimp exports, where residue rejections carry heavy commercial cost.

Adoption reality (use this figure): Bio-pesticide consumption in India stood at roughly 11,100 tonnes in 2023-24, against far larger chemical pesticide use (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers’ Welfare data placed before Rajya Sabha, 2024). Trichoderma, Pseudomonas fluorescens and neem-based formulations dominate. The gap between policy enthusiasm and field share is explained by slower visible action, shorter shelf-life, sensitivity to heat and UV, and inconsistent product quality — constraints that argue for better formulation science and cold-chain distribution, not abandonment.

(b) GM Crops: Arguments For and Against

## Arguments in favour
- Yield protection and reduced pesticide load: Bt cotton’s insect-resistance trait was adopted by over 90% of Indian cotton farmers within a few years of release, reducing bollworm sprays — an adoption rate that itself evidences farmer-perceived benefit.
- Abiotic stress tolerance and climate resilience: transgenic and edited traits for drought, salinity and heat tolerance address exactly the stresses projected to intensify — critical for Rayalaseema’s drought-prone and coastal AP’s salinity-affected soils.
- Nutritional enhancement (biofortification): Golden Rice (provitamin A) and iron/zinc-enriched lines target hidden hunger, which supplementation programmes reach imperfectly.
- Reduced post-harvest and input cost: herbicide-tolerant and non-browning traits cut labour and wastage; lower spray frequency reduces farmer exposure to organophosphates.
- The genome-editing advance: on 4 May 2025, ICAR released DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) — developed by ICAR-IIRR, Hyderabad from Samba Mahsuri (BPT 5204), maturing ~20 days earlier with roughly 19% higher yield, ~20% lower greenhouse gas emissions and an estimated saving of 7,500 million cubic metres of irrigation water — and Pusa DST Rice 1 (ICAR-IARI) for saline/alkaline soils, with yield gains of 9.66-30.4% (PIB, 4 May 2025). These use CRISPR-Cas SDN-1/SDN-2 editing with no foreign DNA, and are exempted from GMO biosafety rules — a regulatory distinction worth stating precisely. Both are recommended for Andhra Pradesh (Zone VII).

## Arguments against
- Ecological risk: gene flow to wild relatives and landraces, potential harm to non-target organisms, and evolution of resistance — pink bollworm resistance to Bt cotton is the standing Indian example.
- Seed sovereignty and cost: proprietary traits and terminator-type technologies risk locking farmers into recurring seed purchase and eroding the traditional right to save seed.
- Biodiversity erosion: displacement of diverse landraces by a few transgenic hybrids narrows the genetic base precisely when climate variability makes diversity valuable.
- Health and evidentiary concerns: demands for long-term independent feeding studies and for labelling to protect consumer choice.
- Regulatory and process concerns: the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC), constituted under the Rules, 1989 framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, has faced criticism for inadequate post-release monitoring; the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict on GM mustard (DMH-11) in July 2024, leaving the matter unresolved. Critics further argue that SDN-1/SDN-2 exemptions bypass biosafety scrutiny.

## Conclusion

The bio-pesticide and GM debates converge on a single principle: agricultural biotechnology should be judged trait-by-trait on evidence, not accepted or rejected wholesale. Bio-pesticides are uncontroversial and under-adopted — their constraint is formulation and distribution, solvable through the Bio-input Resource Centres now being financed under NMNF. GM and genome-edited crops are contested and potentially transformative — their constraint is trust, solvable only through transparent biosafety data, effective post-release monitoring and labelling that preserves consumer choice. India’s genome-edited rice release shows that precision breeding without foreign DNA may offer a middle path that delivers climate resilience while sidestepping much of the transgenic controversy.

## Value addition
- GEAC: the statutory apex regulator constituted under the Rules for the Manufacture, Use/Import/Export and Storage of Hazardous Micro-Organisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989, framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. GEAC clearance is mandatory for environmental release of any GM crop.
- India’s GM status:Bt cotton is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation (2002). Bt brinjal received environmental-release clearance in 2009 but was placed under an indefinite moratorium in 2010; GM mustard DMH-11 approval is sub judice after the Supreme Court’s split verdict of July 2024.
- Genome editing categories:SDN-1 (double-strand break repaired without template — no foreign DNA), SDN-2 (repair guided by a small template — minor edit, no foreign DNA), SDN-3 (insertion of a full gene — treated as a GMO). MoEFCC exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 plants from Rules 1989 in 2022; DBT issued the guidelines for genome-edited plants, and ICAR conducted the trials under AICRP on Rice.
- Institutional anchors: ICAR-IIRR Hyderabad; ICAR-IARI New Delhi; ICAR-NBPGR (germplasm); NBAIR Bengaluru (bio-control agents); CIB&RC (pesticide registration); NCONF Ghaziabad (bio-input quality).
- AP link: DRR Dhan 100 is derived from Samba Mahsuri (BPT 5204), itself an ANGRAU Bapatla release — an AP-bred variety now the base for India’s first genome-edited rice.
Q161:
## Introduction

Agriculture supports nearly half of India’s workforce and contributes about 18% of GDP, which makes the research-education-extension system a determinant of national food security rather than a specialist concern. That system is coordinated by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), established in 1929 and functioning under the Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE), Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare. ICAR presides over one of the world’s largest agricultural research networks — 113 national research institutes and 74 agricultural universities — and delivers technology to the field through 731 Krishi Vigyan Kendras (PIB Factsheet, Agricultural Education & Training in India, 4 November 2025). Its guiding formulation, “One Nation - One Agriculture -One Team”, expresses precisely the linkage the question asks about.

## Institutional Framework and Linkages

DARE / ICAR (apex, policy + funding) --> 113 ICAR Research Institutes + 4 Deemed Universities (IARI, NDRI, IVRI, CIFE) [basic & strategic research] --> 63 SAUs + 3 CAUs (Pusa, Imphal, Jhansi) [applied research + degree education] --> 11 ATARIs [zonal coordination] --> 731 KVKs [on-farm testing, demonstration, training] --> FARMER

- Vertical linkage — national to regional: ICAR sets research priorities and funds them; SAUs adapt the output to agro-climatic realities. The National Agricultural Research Project (NARP) operationalised this by dividing the country into agro-climatic zones, each served by a regional research station under an SAU, so that a variety bred nationally is validated locally before release.
- Horizontal linkage — across disciplines:All India Coordinated Research Projects (AICRPs) pool scientists from multiple institutes on a single commodity. The AICRP on Rice, for instance, ran the multi-location trials for India’s genome-edited rice lines before their 2025 release.
- Last-mile linkage — lab to land: the 731 KVKs, coordinated through 11 ATARIs, conduct on-farm trials, frontline demonstrations and farmer training. Between 2021-22 and 2023-24 KVKs trained 58.02 lakh farmers, with a further 18.56 lakh in the first ten months of 2024-25.
- Quality-assurance linkage: ICAR sets academic standards through the ICAR Model Act (Revised 2023) and accredits institutions via the National Agricultural Education Accreditation Board (NAEAB).
- Outcome evidence: two ICAR institutions entered the QS World University Rankings by Subject 2026 for the first time — ICAR-IVRI Bareilly in the 51-100 band in Veterinary Science (the only Indian institution in the global top 100 in that field) and ICAR-IARI in the 151-200 band in Agriculture & Forestry (PIB, 26 March 2026).

1. Agriculture: Research and Education

- Research: breeding of high-yielding, pest-resistant and climate-resilient varieties; integrated pest and nutrient management; precision agriculture and remote sensing; conservation agriculture; and now genome editing — ICAR-IIRR Hyderabad and ICAR-IARI released DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1 on 4 May 2025, making India the first country to release genome-edited rice (PIB, May 2025).
- Education: UG, PG and doctoral programmes across 74 agricultural universities; hands-on RAWE (Rural Agricultural Work Experience) and experiential learning modules; extension through ATMA, which trained nearly 1.27 crore farmers between 2021 and 2025.
- AP anchor:Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University (ANGRAU), Lam, Guntur — the state agricultural university — along with ICAR-Indian Institute of Oil Palm Research, Pedavegi and ICAR-Central Tobacco Research Institute, Rajahmundry. Samba Mahsuri (BPT 5204), the base variety for DRR Dhan 100, is itself an ANGRAU-Bapatla release.

2. Animal Husbandry: Research and Education (the limb missing from the booklet answer)

- Research: indigenous breed conservation and genetic upgradation; sex-sorted semen and IVF/embryo transfer for accelerated multiplication; vaccine and diagnostic development; nutrition and fodder research; and disease surveillance. ICAR-IVRI Izatnagar leads veterinary research, ICAR-NDRI Karnal dairy science, ICAR-NBAGR Karnal animal genetic resources, and ICAR-NIHSAD Bhopal high-security animal disease diagnosis. Complementary schemes include the National Livestock Mission and the Animal Husbandry Infrastructure Development Fund.

3. Fisheries: Research and Education

- Research: genetic improvement and broodstock development; open-sea cage culture, RAS and biofloc systems; post-harvest processing and cold-chain technology; stock assessment and satellite-based Potential Fishing Zone advisories. Lead institutes: ICAR-CIFA Bhubaneswar, ICAR-CMFRI Kochi, ICAR-CIFRI Barrackpore, ICAR-CIBA Chennai and ICAR-CIFE Mumbai (Deemed University).
- Education: B.F.Sc. and M.F.Sc. programmes at fisheries universities and colleges; vocational training for fishers in navigation, gear technology and post-harvest handling through CIFNET and the National Fisheries Development Board (NFDB), Hyderabad.

## Conclusion

India’s agricultural research system works because its three pillars are institutionally linked rather than merely co-existing: ICAR institutes generate knowledge, agricultural universities adapt and teach it, and KVKs and ATMA carry it to the field. The results are measurable — genome-edited rice in the same decade as record fish production and the world’s highest bovine productivity gain. The remaining gaps are equally clear: research investment as a share of agricultural GDP remains below the 1% norm, scientist vacancies persist in SAUs, and the KVK-to-farmer ratio leaves most smallholders untouched by formal extension. Strengthening state-level research capacity — ANGRAU, SVVU and Dr. YSR AP Fisheries University in Andhra Pradesh’s case — and deepening digital extension are the logical next steps toward “Viksit Krishi aur Samruddh Kisan.”

## Introduction Bio-fertilizers are preparations containing live or latent cells of efficient strains of nitrogen-fixing, phosphate-solubilising or nutrient-mobilising micro-organisms which, when applied to seed, soil or plant surfaces, colonise the rhizosphere and enhance the availability of nutrients to the host plant. They are not fertilizers in the chemical sense: they supply no nutrient themselves but catalyse biological nutrient cycling. This distinction matters technologically, because the product’s value lies entirely in the number of viable cells delivered to the root zone — which is why mass production is a microbiological problem of maintaining viability, not a chemical manufacturing problem. Under the Fertilizer (Control) Order, 1985, 11 bio-fertilizers are notified with prescribed specifications, and NCONF, Ghaziabad with its regional centres serves as the nodal quality-control laboratory. A. Bacterial Bio-fertilizers — the standard four-stage process Strain selection & screening --> Mother culture --> Starter/seed culture (flask) --> Fermenter multiplication --> Carrier preparation & sterilisation --> Blending & curing --> Packaging --> Storage & dispatch - Stage 1 — Strain selection: high-efficiency strains are isolated from root nodules or rhizosphere soil, screened for nitrogen-fixing or P-solubilising efficiency, competitive saprophytic ability and survival on the carrier, then maintained in a culture collection bank. Loss of authenticated strains is a documented national weakness, which is why NCONF maintains national and regional culture collection banks. - Stage 2 — Inoculum build-up: the mother culture is transferred to broth in shake flasks, then scaled through seed fermenters into production fermenters with controlled pH, temperature, aeration and agitation until the broth reaches 109-1010 cells per ml in late log phase — harvesting at log phase, not stationary phase, is what preserves shelf-life viability. - Stage 3 — Carrier-based formulation: the broth is blended with a finely powdered, neutralised, sterilised carrier — peat, lignite, charcoal, vermiculite or press mud — with particle size below 100 mesh, pH adjusted to near-neutral with calcium carbonate, and moisture held at 40-60%. The blend is cured for a few days to let cells adapt. The carrier’s function is to buffer the cells against desiccation and temperature shock in transit. - Stage 4 — Packaging and storage: packed in low-density polyethylene bags of 50-75 micron thickness (permeable to gas exchange but not to moisture loss), stored away from direct sun at 15-25 degrees Celsius. FCO specifications require a minimum of 10^8 viable cells per gram at manufacture and 10^7 per gram until the date of expiry, typically six months to one year. B. Algal Bio-fertilizers (Cyanobacteria and Azolla) Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria — Anabaena, Nostoc, Aulosira, and the Azolla-Anabaena symbiotic complex — are produced by an open-air multiplication method rather than fermentation: - Cultivation in shallow cemented tanks, metal troughs, polythene-lined pits or field microplots holding 5-15 cm of water. - Soil is spread at the base and amended with single superphosphate as a phosphorus source and lime to hold pH at 7-8; carbofuran may be added against mosquito larvae. - Starter inoculum is broadcast and maintained at 14-40 degrees Celsius under sunlight until a thick algal mat forms. - Water is drained, mats are sun-dried, flaked, powdered and packed. Azolla is maintained as a live culture in nursery ponds and multiplied vegetatively before being incorporated into puddled paddy fields. C. Endophytic and Associative Diazotrophs Diazotrophs such as Azospirillum, Acetobacter diazotrophicus, Herbaspirillum and Burkholderia colonise the interior tissues of non-legumes — rice, wheat, sugarcane, sorghum. Production follows the bacterial fermenter route but requires semi-solid nitrogen-free malate medium for isolation and quality checking, since these organisms are microaerophilic. D. Phosphate-Solubilising Microbes and Mycorrhizal Fungi - PSB/PSF (Bacillus megaterium, Pseudomonas striata, Aspergillus, Penicillium) are fermenter-produced like other bacteria. - VAM fungi are obligate symbionts and cannot be grown on synthetic media. They are therefore mass-produced by a fundamentally different route — pot/trap culture on a host plant (maize, sorghum, Rhodes grass) in sterilised sand-soil or vermiculite for 3-4 months, after which the inoculum consists of colonised root fragments, spores and hyphae. Root-organ culture on transformed carrot roots is the advanced, contamination-free alternative. E. Application Methods - Seed treatment (slurry coating): 200 g inoculant per 10-12 kg seed with a 10% jaggery or gum-arabic adhesive; seed shade-dried and sown within 24 hours — never mixed with fungicide-treated seed. Best for pulses, oilseeds and cereals. - Seedling root dip: roots of paddy, tomato, chilli or onion seedlings immersed in an inoculant suspension for 20-30 minutes before transplanting. - Soil / set treatment: inoculant mixed with well-decomposed farmyard manure or compost and broadcast at planting — standard for sugarcane setts, banana and plantation crops. - Green manuring:Rhizobium-inoculated Sesbania or dhaincha grown and incorporated in situ before the main crop, adding both nitrogen and organic matter. - Paddy field application: dried cyanobacterial flakes broadcast 7-10 days after transplanting into 5-10 cm standing water; Azolla dual-cropped or incorporated as green manure. - Nursery inoculation with VAM: mycorrhizal inoculum mixed into nursery beds of horticultural and forestry species to improve phosphorus uptake, transplant survival and drought tolerance. ## Conclusion The technology of bio-fertilizer production is ultimately a technology of keeping cells alive from fermenter to furrow — which is why strain quality, carrier sterility, moisture control and cold storage matter more than production volume. India’s constraint has never been the availability of microbial technology but the reliability of the product reaching the farmer: short shelf-life, sub-standard cell counts and broken cold chains have repeatedly eroded farmer confidence. The shift to liquid bio-fertilizer formulations — with cell protectants and osmoprotectants giving 12-24 month shelf-life, higher cell counts and heat tolerance up to 45 degrees Celsius — addresses this directly. Combined with FCO enforcement, decentralised Bio-input Resource Centres under NMNF, and NABARD’s capital subsidy for production units, bio-fertilizers can move from a marginal supplement to a mainstream input in India’s transition to natural and organic farming. ## Value addition - Carrier-based vs liquid formulations — the current frontier: carrier-based products carry 10^8 cells/g with a 6-month shelf life and are sensitive to heat and contamination; liquid formulations contain cell-protectant additives, achieve far higher cell counts, tolerate temperatures up to about 45 degrees Celsius, resist contamination, allow lower dosage and are compatible with drip and sprinkler fertigation — decisive for AP’s micro-irrigation-heavy horticulture under Per Drop More Crop. - Financing route: the Capital Investment Subsidy Scheme (CISS), administered through NABARD, provides back-ended subsidy of up to 33% of project cost (within prescribed ceilings) for setting up commercial bio-fertilizer, bio-pesticide and compost production units. MOVCDNER gives Rs. 25,000/ha over three years for organic inputs including bio-fertilizers in the North-East. - Quality-control architecture: FCO, 1985 (issued under Section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955) prescribes specifications; State Governments handle registration, authorisation and inspection; NCONF, Ghaziabad and its regional centres form the national quality-control and culture-collection backbone. - AP delivery instance: under NMNF and APCNF, Bio-input Resource Centres and Rythu Bharosa Kendras function as village-level distribution points for microbial inoculants and on-farm preparations, bypassing the shelf-life problem by producing close to the point of use. APCNF is targeted to reach 19.66 lakh farmers over 9.73 lakh hectares by 2027 with 1,000 additional NMNF clusters. - A caution worth stating: bio-fertilizers are supplements, not substitutes. They typically substitute 15-25% of nitrogen requirement; presenting them as a full replacement for chemical fertilizer is scientifically indefensible and will be marked down. ## Introduction

In biotechnology, a low-volume, high-value (LVHV) product is one manufactured in

milligram-to-kilogram quantities annually yet commanding extremely high value per unit

— because its worth lies in biological specificity, not bulk. Insulin, monoclonal antibodies, clotting factors, vaccines and interferons are the standard examples. Their significance is economic as much as medical: India's bioeconomy grew from USD 10 billion in 2014 to USD 165.7 billion in 2024, contributing 4.25% of GDP, with a target of USD 300 billion by 2030 (DBT, one-year review of BioE3 Policy, PIB, 25 August 2025) — and it is precisely this high-margin therapeutic segment that drives that value.

1. What defines a Low-Volume, High-Value product

The defining feature is a very high value-to-mass ratio, arising from three cost drivers:

## complex living-cell manufacture, stringent purity and regulatory validation, and heavy

upfront R&D. Because the molecule is a protein, not a chemical, it cannot be synthesised in a reactor — it must be grown, then purified to near-absolute homogeneity.

Parameter Low-Volume, High-Value High-Volume, Low-Value

Output scale Grams to kilograms/year Thousands of tonnes/year

Value per unit Very high Low mass

Production Recombinant DNA, mammalian/microbial Open fermentation, bulk platform cell culture processing

Puritydemand Pharmacopoeial, >99% Technical grade

Examples Interferons, insulin, monoclonal Ethanol, citric acid, biofertilizers, antibodies, erythropoietin single-cell protein

Driver of cost R&D + downstream purification Feedstock + energy

Why this matters: the LVHV segment is where a country captures value rather than merely volume. This is the explicit logic of the BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment), approved by the Union Cabinet on 24 August 2024, which prioritises precision biotherapeutics as one of its thematic sectors and funds Biomanufacturing hubs, Bio-AI hubs and Biofoundries to build exactly this capability (PIB, DBT).

2. Interferons: nature and mode of action

Interferons (IFNs) are cytokines — small signalling glycoproteins secreted by host cells within hours of viral infection or other immune stimulus. They do not kill viruses directly. Instead, they bind neighbouring cells' receptors, trigger the JAK-STAT signalling cascade, and switch on hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes that block viral protein synthesis and replication. The infected cell effectively warns its neighbours — hence "interfere".

## Applications
- Antiviral therapy: Pegylated IFN-a remains in use for chronic Hepatitis B, and historically for Hepatitis C — though for HCV it has now been largely displaced by direct-acting antivirals, an important nuance students should state (see Q246).
- Oncology: IFN-a is licensed for hairy-cell leukaemia, chronic myeloid leukaemia, malignant melanoma and Kaposi's sarcoma, acting by inducing tumour-cell apoptosis and enhancing Nk-cell surveillance.
- Immunomodulation: IFN-f reduces relapse frequency in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; IFN-y is used in chronic granulomatous disease.
- Diagnostics: the Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) is a standard test for latent tuberculosis infection — a directly relevant Indian public-health application under the National TB Elimination Programme.

4.General scheme for industrial production

Human IFN gene identified --> cDNA synthesised from mRNA

|

Gene inserted into expression vector (plasmid with strong promoter)

|

Transformation into host: E. coli / Pichia pastoris (yeast) / CHO mammalian cells (where glycosylation is required)

|

UPSTREAM: seed culture --> scale-up --> stirred-tank bioreactor (controlled pH, temperature, dissolved 02, feed)

|

Induction of expression --> biomass harvest

QUALITY CONTROL: potency bioassay, endotoxin, purity (HPLC), sterility --> release under CDSCO / Drugs & Cosmetics Rules

The critical economic point: downstream purification accounts for the majority of production cost in LVHV manufacture — which is why national policy focuses on shared, capital-intensive common facilities rather than expecting each firm to build its own.

5. The Andhra Pradesh dimension

- Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam — India's first dedicated medical-technology park, which received a grant-in-aid of %25 crore from the Department of Pharmaceuticals for acommon facility for superconducting magnetic coil testing and research (PIB). Its shared scientific facilities model is precisely the answer to the downstream-cost problem above.
- Bulk Drug Park, Nakkapalli (Anakapalli district) — approved by the Department of Pharmaceuticals with an internal-infrastructure project cost of ¥1,876.66 crore, planned as an integrated pharma zone within the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (APIIC / Department of Pharmaceuticals project documents).
- APCARL, Pulivendula (YSR Kadapa district) — a Government of Andhra Pradesh entity operating advanced R&D laboratories and BSL-4 biocontainment facilities, which in November 2025 entered a partnership for developing next-generation antiinfective medicines in the State.

## Conclusion

Low-volume, high-value products represent the point at which biology becomes an industry of value rather than volume — a few grams of interferon can carry the economic weight of tonnes of a bulk chemical. Interferons illustrate the full arc: a naturally occurring immune signal, decoded by molecular biology, cloned into a microbial factory, and delivered as a licensed therapeutic. For India, with its bioeconomy targeting USD 300 billion by 2030 under the BioE3 Policy, and for Andhra Pradesh with AMTZ, the Nakkapalli Bulk Drug Park and APCARL's biocontainment capability, the strategic task is to move from being the world's volume supplier of generics to a genuine originator of highvalue biologics.

## Value addition
- Biosimilars — India's real strength: Once a biologic's patent lapses, a highly similar version ("biosimilar") can be made. India is among the largest biosimilar producers globally; the National Biopharma Mission (i3 programme, implemented by BIRAC) was created precisely to build this capacity, with World Bank co-funding.
- Regional concentration: India's bioeconomy is heavily southern — the Southern region contributed 45.4% (USD 75.2 billion) of the 2024 total, ahead of Western (30.3%), Northern (18.5%) and Eastern (5.8%) regions (DBT / PIB, September 2025). This is the statistic that lets an aspirant argue for a dedicated AP biotech cluster.
- National Biofoundry Network — launched 25 August 2025 alongside the BioE3 Challenge for Youth, to provide shared design-build-test-learn infrastructure for biomanufacturing (PIB).
- Terminology to deploy precisely: Cytokine (any cell-signalling protein) > Interferon (antiviral cytokine subclass) > IFN-a (a specific molecule). Using the correct level of the hierarchy signals command of the subject.
- Related LVHV products worth naming: recombinant human insulin, erythropoietin (for renal anaemia), Factor VIII (haemophilia), streptokinase (thrombolysis), and monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab.

## Introduction

Environmental biotechnology is the deployment of living organisms — bacteria, fungi, algae and higher plants — and their enzymes to degrade, detoxify, immobilise or recover pollutants. Its appeal is that it works with natural biogeochemical cycles rather than against them: microbes mineralise contaminants into carbon dioxide, water and biomass, generating no secondary chemical sludge. The scale of the Indian need is substantial — urban India generates 1,59,109 tonnes per day (TPD) of solid waste and currently processes 1,29,207 TPD, while accumulated legacy waste stands at 2,492 lakh tonnes (MoHUA / Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban, PIB, 2025).

1. Bioremediation — the core technique

In-situ (treated where it lies) Ex-situ (excavated and treated elsewhere)

Bioventing — air and nutrients supplied through Landfarming — contaminated soil spread ona wells to stimulate indigenous bacteria prepared bed and periodically tilled for aerobic

degradation

Biosparging — air injected below the water table Biopiles — engineered aerated compost heaps; to raise dissolved oxygen and accelerate used for petroleum-hydrocarbon

## degradation contamination

Bioaugmentation — specialised degrader Bioreactors — contaminated soil, sludge or microorganisms introduced to the site water processed in an engineered containment vessel

Phytoremediation — plants used in place of Composting — organic fraction converted to engineering nutrient-rich manure

Why in-situ is usually preferred: it avoids excavation and transport costs and the risk of spreading contamination, though it is slower and harder to monitor. Progress is tracked indirectly through redox potential, pH, dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide evolution.

2. Phytoremediation — the low-cost option the original omitted

Plants remediate through four distinct mechanisms, and naming them precisely earns marks: phytoextraction (contaminants accumulated in roots and shoots — as with Brassica juncea for heavy metals), phytodegradation (organic contaminants taken up and transformed into less toxic forms), phytostabilisation (leachable constituents bound into plant structure so they cannot re-enter the environment), and rhizodegradation (breakdown by the microbial community in the root zone). Constructed wetlands using Typha and Phragmites apply this to municipal wastewater at negligible operating cost — directly relevant to small Indian towns that cannot afford mechanised sewage treatment

plants.

3. Biomining of legacy waste — biotechnology at national scale

Under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, which mandate "zero waste to landfill", old dumpsites are reclaimed by biomining: the aged waste is aerated and stabilised so the biodegradable fraction decomposes, then screened into soil-like fines, recyclables and refuse-derived fuel (RDF).

- Progress: of 2,492 lakh tonnes of legacy waste, 1,437 lakh tonnes (58%) have been remediated, reclaiming over 7,646 acres of land (MoHUA, PIB, 2025). ¢ Acceleration: the Dumpsite Remediation Accelerator Programme (DRAP) was launched in November 2025 with the objective of "Lakshya: Zero Dumpsites" by

October 2026, built on SBM-U 2.0's 5P framework, with projects worth %6,700 crore approved for 214 targeted sites (PIB).

- Illustration: Rajkot converted a 16-lakh-tonne legacy dumpsite into a 20-acre urban forest using Miyawaki afforestation on the reclaimed land — showing that remediation ends in land value, not merely in waste disposal.

4, Wastewater and industrial effluent treatment

Every sewage treatment plant is a biotechnology installation. The activated sludge process and its variants (sequencing batch reactors, moving-bed biofilm reactors) rely on engineered microbial consortia to oxidise organic load; anaerobic digesters convert the sludge into methane. Under Namami Gange, this is the single largest deployment of environmental biotechnology in India. Biomethanation of the organic fraction of municipal solid waste under GOBARdhan applies the same principle to rural and periurban waste.

5. Biosensors and bio-mining of metals

- Biosensors couple a biological recognition element — an enzyme, antibody or whole microbial cell — to a transducer. In the classic construct, mercury-resistance (mer) genes are fused to bioluminescence genes, so the organism literally lights up in the presence of bio-available mercury. This gives rapid, field-deployable, non-destructive pollution monitoring where laboratory analysis would take days.
- Bio-mining of metals uses acidophilic chemolithotrophs such as Thiobacillus (Acidithiobacillus) ferrooxidans to leach copper, uranium and gold from low-grade ores, replacing smelting and cyanide leaching and thereby cutting both sulphurdioxide emissions and tailings toxicity.
- Engineered degraders: the Pseudomonas putida "superbug" developed by Dr

Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty — the first genetically engineered organism to be patented — degrades multiple hydrocarbon fractions in oil spills; related constructs address polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).

6. Andhra Pradesh instance

In March 2026, the Andhra Pradesh Municipal Administration and Urban Development Department sanctioned approximately %60 crore for five Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) plants in urban local bodies — new plants at Rajamahendravaram, Nellore, Guntur and Ongole, and revival and upgradation of the existing Vijayawada facility. Each hasa capacity of 25 TPD, totalling 125 TPD, and the project is being implemented with technical support from CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Technology. This is anaerobic-digestion biotechnology applied simultaneously to a waste-management problem and an energy problem — the clearest AP example available.

7. Limitations — the balance an examiner looks for

Bioremediation is slower than chemical or thermal treatment; microbial activity collapses at extreme pH, temperature, salinity or toxicant concentration; recalcitrant compounds such as chlorinated dioxins and heavy metals cannot be destroyed biologically, only immobilised or extracted; and the release of genetically engineered microorganisms requires clearance under the Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous Microorganisms/GMOs, 1989 administered by the GEAC under MoEFCC.

## Conclusion

Biotechnology converts environmental clean-up from a disposal problem into a resourcerecovery opportunity: a dumpsite becomes reclaimed land, sewage becomes methane, a low-grade ore becomes copper, and contaminated soil becomes farmland. Its limits are real — slow kinetics, sensitivity to extreme conditions, and inability to destroy elemental toxicants — so it works best as one component of an integrated strategy alongside source segregation, extended producer responsibility and cleaner production. With DRAP targeting zero dumpsites by October 2026 and Andhra Pradesh's CBG network coming up under CSIR-IICT guidance, environmental biotechnology has moved decisively from laboratory demonstration to mainstream public infrastructure.

## Value addition
- The precise definition to open with: environmental biotechnology is the application of biological systems to prevent, monitor and remediate environmental damage — note that it covers all three, not remediation alone; biosensing is the monitoring arm and cleaner bio-based production is the prevention arm.
- Keystatutory framework to cite: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016; Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016; Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016; and the GMO Rules, 1989 for any engineered organism.
- Bioaugmentation vs biostimulation — a distinction that impresses: biostimulation feeds the microbes already present (adding nutrients, oxygen); bioaugmentation adds new organisms. Biostimulation is generally preferred because introduced strains often fail to compete with native flora.
- Mycoremediation and phycoremediation — the use of fungi (white-rot fungi degrading lignin-like pollutants including dyes and PAHs) and algae (nutrient stripping, heavy-metal biosorption) are increasingly cited alongside bacterial bioremediation.

## Introduction

India generates roughly 500 million tonnes of crop residue annually, of which a surplus fraction is burnt in field because the gap between paddy harvest and wheat sowing in the north-west is only two to three weeks — burning is the cheapest way to clear a field within that window. Satellite monitoring under the ISRO/IARI protocol recorded 10,207 fire events in Punjab, 1,832 in Haryana and 259 in NCR districts of Uttar Pradesh during the wheat-harvesting season of 1 April-31 May 2025 (CAQM Statutory Direction, PIB, February 2026). Converting this residue into bio-fuel attacks the problem at its economic root: it gives the straw a price, so it stops being waste.

1. Why burning pollutes — the mechanism to state first

Open-field burning is uncontrolled, oxygen-starved combustion at low temperature. It therefore produces not carbon dioxide and water but a mix of PM2.5, black carbon, carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen, volatile organic compounds and methane — and, being a ground-level source under a shallow winter inversion layer, the plume is trapped rather than dispersed. Beyond air quality, burning destroys soil organic carbon, nitrogen and the microbial biomass in the top few centimetres of soil, so the farmer loses a nutrient asset while creating a public health cost. India is already the world's third-largest methane emitter, with stubble burning among the drivers (UNEP/CCAC Global Methane Status Report 2025).

(a) Second-generation (2G) bioethanol. Lignocellulose is pre-treated to break the lignin seal, enzymatically hydrolysed to fermentable sugars, and fermented to ethanol. Because the feedstock is non-food, this avoids the food-versus-fuel objection that applies to sugarcane- and grain-based 1G ethanol. It is supported under the Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana, with viability gap funding for commercial 2G bio-refineries.

(b) Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG). Anaerobic digestion of straw yields methane-rich biogas, which on upgrading becomes CBG — chemically equivalent to CNG — plus Fermented Organic Manure (FOM) as a co-product that returns nutrients to the soil. This is promoted under the SATAT (Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation) scheme of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, under which oil marketing companies guarantee offtake at a pre-fixed price. Crucially, offtake is no longer voluntary: a phased

CBG Blending Obligation (CBO) in city gas distribution networks begins at 1% in FY 2025-26 and rises to 5% by FY 2028-29.

(c) Pelletisation and torrefaction. Straw is densified into pellets or mildly roasted (torrefied) to raise energy density and reduce moisture, then co-fired with coal. CAQM has directed coal-based thermal power plants within a 300 km radius of Delhi to co-fire biomass pellets, and CAQM Direction 92 of 3 June 2025 mandates the use of paddystraw-based pellets or briquettes in brick kilns in districts of Punjab and Haryana beyond the NCR. The CPCB provides one-time financial support from Environment Protection Charge funds for setting up pelletisation and torrefaction plants (MoEFCC, Rajya Sabha reply, December 2025).

(d) Biochar and in-situ incorporation. Where transport economics fail, pyrolysis to biochar or direct incorporation using Happy Seeder, Super Seeder and Pusa BioDecomposer returns carbon to the soil rather than the atmosphere — the cheapest option for small holdings.

3. How conversion actually reduces air pollution — three distinct effects

- Primary emissions avoided: residue diverted to a bio-refinery or pellet plant is residue that is never set alight, so the PM2.5, black carbon and CO from open burning simply do not occur.
- Cleaner combustion: where the biomass is still burned, it is burned in a controlled boiler with pollution-control equipment, not in an open field — the same carbon released under vastly lower particulate and incomplete-combustion emissions.
- Fossil displacement: every litre of 2G ethanol and every kilogram of CBG displaces petrol or natural gas, cutting lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions. Ethanol blending rose from under 1.5% in 2013-14 to 20% in 2025-26 — five years ahead of the target set under the National Policy on Biofuels (PIB, 2026).

4. Does it work? The 2025 evidence

- The Centre released %4,237.47 crore under the Crop Residue Management scheme for machinery and Custom Hiring Centres, and Punjab and Haryana recorded an estimated over 90% reduction in stubble-burning incidents in the 2025 paddy season compared with 2022 (MoEFCC, PIB).
- Punjab alone recorded a 53% decline in the Kharif 2025 season — from 10,909 incidents in 2024 to 5,114 — following disbursal of ¥395 crore for CRM machinery to 5,358 beneficiaries including 4,181 individual farmers (Government of Punjab, February 2026).
- Haryana reported 206 farm-fire incidents between 15 September and 6 November 2025, against 888 in the corresponding period of the previous year (CAQM review).

5. The constraints that remain

Straw has low bulk density, so collection, baling and transport can cost more than the fuel is worth beyond a 40-50 km radius; the harvest window is short, forcing a whole year's feedstock into a few weeks of logistics. Paddy straw is high in silica and chlorine, which foul and corrode boiler surfaces, limiting the co-firing ratio. And offtake still lags mandates — CAQM found that four thermal power plants in Punjab had co-fired only 3.12 lakh metric tonnes of crop-residue pellets against a 2025-26 target of 11.83 lakh metric tonnes. Enzyme cost Keeps 2G ethanol more expensive than 1G.

6. Andhra Pradesh dimension

Andhra Pradesh, a major paddy state, sanctioned approximately %60 crore in March 2026 for five CBG plants at Rajamahendravaram, Nellore, Guntur and Ongole, plus revival of the Vijayawada unit — 25 TPD each, 125 TPD in total — with technical support from CSIRIndian Institute of Chemical Technology. ## Conclusion

Crop-residue-to-biofuel is the rare intervention that resolves an environmental problem through an economic incentive rather than a prohibition: once straw has a buyer, the farmer's rational choice changes, and the enforcement burden falls away. The 2025 season demonstrates the approach works — over 90% fewer farm fires in Punjab and Haryana than in 2022, alongside E20 achieved five years early. The remaining task is logistical rather than technological: dense networks of aggregation and baling centres, guaranteed offtake through the CBG Blending Obligation, and boiler technology that tolerates high-silica paddy straw. ## Introduction

The "triple vaccine" is the DPT combination against Diphtheria, Pertussis and Tetanus — historically the first multi-antigen preparation of India's Universal Immunization

Programme (UIP), which today reaches about 2.6 crore infants and 2.9 crore pregnant women annually against 12 vaccine-preventable diseases (MOHFW/PIB, 2025). Its success is measurable: full immunisation coverage has risen from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026 (PIB, March 2026). Biotechnology has since carried vaccination far beyond

this whole-organism era into rational, gene-based antigen design.

(a) Triple Vaccination (DPT) — components and mechanism

- Diphtheria toxoid: Corynebacterium diphtheriae kills through an exotoxin causing

myocarditis and pharyngeal obstruction, not through invasion. The vaccine therefore uses the formaldehyde-inactivated toxin, so immunity is anti-toxic rather than antibacterial — which is why boosters are essential as antitoxin titres wane.

- Pertussis antigen: India's UIP uses whole-cell pertussis (wP) — killed Bordetella pertussis. It is cheaper, gives more durable protection and is WHO-recommended for high-burden settings; the acellular (aP) version sold privately is less reactogenic but wanes faster, a trade-off central to India's programmatic choice.
- Tetanus toxoid: neutralises the Clostridium tetani neurotoxin causing spastic paralysis. Maternal Td doses transfer antibody transplacentally — the mechanism behind India's validated elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus in 2015.

Schedule (National Immunization Schedule): the three primary doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks are delivered inside the Pentavalent vaccine (DPT + Hepatitis B + Hib); stand-alone DPT boosters at 16-24 months and 5-6 years; Td at 10 and 16 years.

## (b) Biotechnological transformation — by platform
- Recombinant DNA: the antigen gene alone is expressed in yeast or CHO cells, eliminating pathogen handling. Hepatitis B (yeast-expressed HBsAg) and Cervavac, India's first indigenous HPV vaccine (SII with DBT-BIRAC support), exemplify this. Its policy payoff arrived on 28 February 2026, when India launched a nationwide HPV vaccination programme for ~1.15 crore 14-year-old girls (PIB, February 2026).
- Nucleic-acid platforms: ZyCoV-D, the world's first approved DNA vaccine, and GEMCOVAC-19, India's first mRNA vaccine, compress design-to-vial timelines from years to months because only the sequence, not the pathogen, must change.
- Vector and conjugate technology: Covishield used a chimpanzee adenovirus vector; conjugation chemically links weak polysaccharide antigens to a carrier protein, converting a T-cell-independent response into a T-dependent one — the only reason Hib and PCV work in infants under two.
- Adjuvants and delivery: Covaxin's Algel-IMDG adjuvant, needle-free jet injectors

and thermostable formulations reduce dose requirement and cold-chain loss — decisive in AP's hill districts such as Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam.

- Andhra Pradesh anchor: the AP MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam, with over 100 manufacturing units in medical devices and diagnostics and the Kalam Institute of Health Technology on campus (PIB, 2025), supplies cold-chain and diagnostic hardware; AP's ICMR-VRDL network — SVIMS Tirupati, Andhra Medical College Visakhapatnam, Siddhartha Medical College Vijayawada, Rangaraya Medical College Kakinada — generates the genomic surveillance that guides antigen selection.

## Conclusion

Triple vaccination represents the whole-organism era — effective, cheap and still the backbone of infant immunisation. Biotechnology has replaced that logic with rational antigen design, giving safer, faster and platform-adaptable vaccines. The two are complementary, not sequential: India's task is to sustain DPT-era coverage while using recombinant and nucleic-acid platforms to extend protection to cervical cancer, dengue and tuberculosis, thereby advancing SDG 3.b on vaccine access.

Why they matter — the programmatic case

- Compliance and completion: fewer visits mean fewer drop-outs. India's full immunisation coverage rose from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026, while zerodose children fell from 0.11% (2023) to 0.06% (2024) (PIB, March 2026) — gains impossible without combining antigens.

- Fewer injection events mathematically reduce the opportunity for injection-site reactions and programmatic errors.

The controversies — and what the evidence shows

1. Attribution of Adverse Events (AEFI): clustering of infant deaths reported after Pentavalent introduction in Kerala and Tamil Nadu (2011-13) generated public demands for withdrawal. Causality assessment by the national AEFI Secretariat using the WHO revised classification found the overwhelming majority to be coincidental events falling in the same age window as sudden infant deaths. The

deeper problem is structural: when five antigens are given together, temporal association becomes impossible to disaggregate by component.

2. Immune interference / hyporesponsiveness: reduced anti-Hib response has been documented in certain acellular-pertussis-based hexavalent formulations. Regulators

addressed this by requiring non-inferiority immunogenicity data for every antigen before licensure of a combination — a scientific concern that was met by tightening the licensing standard, not by abandoning combinations.

3. Excipient anxiety: thiomersal preservative in multi-dose vials and aluminium adjuvants attract recurring fears of neurotoxicity. Successive WHO Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety reviews found no causal association, but multi-dose vials remain a perception liability in India.

4. Theretracted MMR-autism claim: Wakefield's 1998 paper, fully retracted by The Lancet in 2010 and its author struck off, continues to circulate. WHO listed vaccine hesitancy among the top ten global health threats (2019) — showing that a discredited claim can outlive its refutation.

## Conclusion

Combination vaccines are not a convenience but a precondition for universal coverage at India's demographic scale. The controversies surrounding them are of two kinds — a genuine scientific one (immune interference), which regulation has answered through non-inferiority licensing, and attribution-driven public anxiety, which only transparent, prompt and published AEFI causality assessment can answer. Strengthening pharmacovigilance is therefore the most effective pro-vaccine intervention available.

## Introduction

A vaccine is a biological preparation that induces protective, specific immunity against a pathogen without causing the disease. It works by presenting an antigen to the immune system, which generates antibodies and, decisively, memory B and T cells that mount a rapid anamnestic response on real exposure. Beyond the individual, high coverage confers herd immunity — the reason India could interrupt wild poliovirus transmission and be certified polio-free in March 2014 (WHO SEA Region certification).

Generation 1 — Whole-organism (conventional) Uses the entire pathogen, liveattenuated or killed. Jenner's cowpox-based smallpox vaccine (1796), BCG (1921), Salk's inactivated polio vaccine (1955) and Sabin's OPV belong here. India's own contribution is early: Waldemar Haffkine developed cholera and plague vaccines in Bombay in the 1890s. These vaccines give strong, broad immunity but carry cold-chain burden and, for live vaccines, rare reversion risk — precisely why India switched to bivalent OPV plus injectable IPV in 2015-16 to counter vaccine-derived poliovirus.

Generation 2 — Subunit, toxoid and conjugate Only the protective component is used, sharply improving safety. Diphtheria and tetanus toxoids are inactivated exotoxins; conjugate vaccines chemically link a weak polysaccharide capsule to a carrier protein, converting a T-independent into a T-dependent response so that infants can respond — the basis of Hib (in Pentavalent) and Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine, expanded nationwide in 2021.

Generation 3 — Recombinant DNA The gene encoding the antigen is cloned into yeast, E. coli or mammalian cells; the pathogen itself is never handled. Hepatitis B (yeast-expressed HBsAg) was the first, and HPV vaccines use virus-like particles (VLPs) — empty protein shells with no genetic material. India's Cervavac, developed by Serum Institute with DBTBIRAC support, is the indigenous exemplar; the nationwide HPV vaccination drive for ~1.15 crore 14-year-old girls launched on 28 February 2026 (PIB, February 2026) marks its

arrival in public policy.

Generation 4 — Nucleic-acid and vector platforms The host's own cells are instructed to make the antigen. India contributed Rotavac (2014, first indigenous rotavirus vaccine, DBTsupported), Covaxin (ICMR-NIV + Bharat Biotech), ZyCoV-D (2021 — the world's first approved DNA vaccine, needle-free) and GEMCOVAC-19 (2022, India's first mRNA

vaccine). Their defining advantage is platform reusability: only the sequence changes

between diseases.

Enabling ecosystem: DBT's Mission COVID Suraksha, the National Biopharma Mission, and the BioE3 Policy, 2024 (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment) which prioritises biomanufacturing and precision biotherapeutics.

Andhra Pradesh anchor: SVIMS, Tirupati — an ICMR-funded Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory in its Centre for Advanced Research — was the first COVID-19 testing centre in the State and served as an ICMR quality-control node for testing laboratories across AP and Telangana. Such VRDLs supply the genomic data on which antigen and variant selection depends.

Salk IPV + 1986 recombinant Hepatitis B > 2014 Rotavac > 2@21 ZyCoV-D (DNA) > 2022.

## Conclusion

The journey of vaccines is a movement from using the whole pathogen to using only its information. Each generation traded biological crudeness for molecular precision, raising safety, scalability and speed. India's transition from importing Generation-1 vaccines to designing Generation-4 platforms — and supplying roughly 60% of global vaccine volume — makes vaccine science a pillar of both public health and technological sovereignty.

- Plug-and-play platform: the mRNA/DNA principle — the manufacturing process stays constant while the encoded sequence is swapped, enabling rapid pandemic response.

## Introduction

A vaccine is a biological preparation containing a whole pathogen, a part of it, or the genetic instructions to make a part of it, which stimulates protective adaptive immunity without causing disease. At population level, coverage above the herd immunity threshold (about 95% for measles, the most transmissible) interrupts chains of transmission and protects those who cannot be vaccinated — infants and the immunocompromised.

## Introduction
The **Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC)** is central to adaptive immunity, enabling the immune system to distinguish self from non-self and mount targeted responses.

## What is MHC?
- The **MHC** is a genetic region on the **short arm of chromosome 6** in humans, encoding cell-surface proteins that **present antigenic peptides to T-cells**. In humans these are the **Human Leukocyte Antigens (HLA)**.
- MHC is **highly polymorphic**, explaining individual variation in immune responses and the challenge of **transplant rejection**.

## Role of MHC classes
- **MHC Class I**:
  - Found on **all nucleated cells**.
  - Presents **endogenous antigens** (viral or tumour proteins made inside the cell) to **cytotoxic T cells (CD8+)**, which destroy infected or abnormal cells.
- **MHC Class II**:
  - Expressed mainly on **antigen-presenting cells** (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells).
  - Presents **exogenous antigens** (engulfed pathogens) to **helper T cells (CD4+)**, which coordinate the immune response and activate B cells.
- **MHC Class III**:
  - Encodes **complement components and cytokines** involved in inflammation.

## Significance
- Vital for **antigen presentation, transplant compatibility (HLA matching), autoimmunity and disease susceptibility**.

## Conclusion
By presenting antigens to the right T cells, MHC molecules orchestrate **targeted immune defence and self/non-self discrimination**, making them fundamental to immunity and transplantation medicine.

## Introduction
**Immunisation** — deliberate stimulation of protective immunity — has a rich history, and modern biotechnology has added novel tools like edible vaccines and precise diagnostics.

## (a) Immunisation and history of vaccines
- **Immunisation**: deliberate exposure to an antigen to provoke an immune response and memory; achieved by **active** (vaccination) or **passive** (antibody transfer) means.
- **History**:
  - **18th-19th century**: Jenner's smallpox vaccine (cowpox, 1796); Pasteur's attenuated **anthrax (1881)** and **rabies (1885)** vaccines.

  - **21st century**: **mRNA** (COVID-19: Pfizer, Moderna) and **vector-based** (Oxford-AstraZeneca) vaccines. WHO estimates vaccines prevent 4-5 million deaths annually.

## (b) Short notes
- **(i) Edible vaccines**: antigens expressed in **transgenic plants** (banana, potato, tomato) so that eating them elicits immunity — needle-free, cheap and easy to store; still largely experimental.
- **(ii) ELISA**: **Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay** — an antigen-antibody test using an enzyme-linked colour reaction to detect and quantify antigens or antibodies; used for **HIV, Hepatitis B, COVID-19** diagnosis.
- **(iii) Autoimmune diseases**: disorders in which the immune system attacks the body's **own tissues** — e.g., **rheumatoid arthritis, type-1 diabetes, lupus (SLE)**.

## Conclusion
From Jenner to mRNA, vaccine science has advanced remarkably, and tools like **edible vaccines and ELISA** highlight biotechnology's expanding role in **prevention and diagnosis**.
